The problem is that Sunni legal and devotional literature preserved practices in which created beings become religious channels: unseen servants are addressed for help, prophetic relics are touched for blessing, and the Prophet is used as a means in supplication after his death. Imam Aḥmad is important because he stands near the beginning of the Sunni legal canon, yet material attached to him already shows the very intermediary logic that the Qurʾān condemns. This article does not need to prove every later grave-practice from Imam Aḥmad. That would be too broad, and it would give defenders an easy way out. The stronger case is narrower. Aḥmad’s own transmitted practice and later Hanbalī reports show three categories that Sunni tradition struggled to contain: calling upon unseen servants, seeking blessing through physical contact with prophetic traces, and making tawassul through the Prophet. Later scholars then expanded the same logic into open defenses of istighātha through the Prophet and righteous figures. The Qurʾānic issue is simple. The Quraysh did not deny God as Creator. Their error was that they placed created beings between themselves and God, claiming that these beings brought them closer to Him or interceded for them. Once that pattern is identified, changing the object from idols to prophets, angels, graves, relics, or saints does not solve the problem. It preserves the structure of the problem while giving it Islamic language. ## The Qurʾānic Baseline: Intermediaries Were the Problem The Qurʾān records that the pagan opponents of Muhammad already acknowledged God as the Creator of the heavens and the earth: Their error was devotional and mediatory. They placed other beings into the religious space between themselves and God, then explained that these beings were only a means of nearness: The same logic appears in the language of intercession: This article uses the Qurʾānic standard rather than the later sectarian vocabulary of the madhhabs. A practice is not purified merely because the person says, “God is the real actor.” The Quraysh also placed their intermediaries beneath God. The Qurʾān rejects the act of invoking and religiously relying upon created intermediaries, even when those intermediaries are framed as channels to God. ## The Evidence at a Glance Practice Sunni / Hanbalī evidence Why it matters Calling unseen servants for help Aḥmad is reported by his son ʿAbd Allāh as saying that, when he lost the road during pilgrimage, he repeatedly called: “O servants of God, guide me to the road.” This is a direct vocative appeal to created beings who are not visible or ordinarily present. Tabarruk through prophetic traces The printed al-ʿIlal wa-Maʿrifat al-Rijāl reports Aḥmad allowing touching the Prophet’s minbar and doing something similar at the grave for nearness to God, while conservative Hanbalī defenses concede at least the minbar/rummāna permission. The debate over the grave wording does not erase the larger principle: blessing is being sought through created physical traces. Tawassul through the Prophet al-Mardāwī records the correct Hanbalī position as permitting tawassul through a righteous man and cites Aḥmad’s instruction to al-Marwadhī to use the Prophet in supplication. This places a created person into the structure of duʿāʾ as a religious means. Later istighātha al-Subkī and Ibn Ḥajar al-Haytamī explicitly defend tawassul, istighātha, and tashaffuʿ through the Prophet. The later material is not an isolated aberration. It develops a logic already present in the earlier Sunni devotional framework. ## 1. Imam Aḥmad Calling Upon the “Servants of God” The clearest report is preserved by al-Bayhaqī in al-Jāmiʿ li-Shuʿab al-Īmān . The chain runs through ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad, who says he heard his father describe what he did when he lost his way during pilgrimage. This report does not describe Aḥmad asking God directly. It describes him addressing “servants of God” in the vocative: يا عباد الله . The request is also direct: دلوني على الطريق , “guide me to the road.” The wording is softer than “save me,” but the religious structure is the same: a person in distress calls upon unseen created beings for practical help. The background to Aḥmad’s action is the well-known report attributed to the Prophet about calling upon the “servants of God” when one is lost or in need of assistance in a deserted place. This report is disputed. Some strengthen it through supporting routes; others, including al-Albānī and Salafi writers, weaken it and argue that it cannot justify calling upon dead saints. That defensive move still concedes the point that matters here. On the restrictive reading, the “servants of God” are not idols and not dead saints, but angels or jinn—created unseen beings. The practice still teaches a person to call upon a created being who is not visibly present. Defenders often say that the report refers to angels or unseen attendants, not the dead. That may protect the report from one kind of grave-cult argument, but it does not protect it from the Qurʾānic critique of invocation. The issue is not whether the invoked being is made of stone, flesh, light, or fire. The issue is that a created being is addressed for rescue in a religious formula. The Qurʾān does not build a devotional category in which believers call upon hidden created agents whenever ordinary help is absent. It directs fear, reliance, worship, and supplication back to God. ## 2. Touching the Minbar, the Grave, and the Problem of Tabarruk The second report comes from al-ʿIlal wa-Maʿrifat al-Rijāl through ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad. In the printed wording, Aḥmad is asked about a man touching the Prophet’s minbar, seeking blessing by touching and kissing it, and doing something similar at the grave while intending nearness to God. Aḥmad replies that there is no harm in it. This report has to be handled carefully because conservative Hanbalī and Salafi writers challenge the grave portion. They argue that the wording is strange, that the Prophet’s grave was not accessible for touching in the way suggested, and that stronger Hanbalī transmissions restrict Aḥmad’s permission to the minbar or the rummāna , the rounded fixture or place connected to where the Prophet sat and placed his hand. That defense weakens one part of the polemical claim but strengthens another. Even when the grave is removed, the concession remains that Aḥmad allowed blessing to be sought through contact with a physical prophetic trace. The disagreement becomes a boundary dispute: minbar yes, grave no; original relic yes, later walls no; surviving prophetic trace yes, ordinary shrine no. A Qurʾān-first critique does not need to accept the shrine version to see the problem. Once blessing can be materially accessed through relic-contact, the logic of devotional mediation has already entered the system. Defense What it concedes Remaining Qurʾānic problem The grave wording is problematic and not the strongest report from Aḥmad. The printed al-ʿIlal wording exists and later scholars had to explain it away. The post does not need the grave wording alone. The admitted minbar/rummāna practice already makes a created object a devotional channel of blessing. Aḥmad only allowed touching the original minbar area because the Prophet physically touched it. Baraka is being attached to matter through historical contact with the Prophet. The Qurʾān does not teach believers to seek nearness to God through relic-contact. Later grave-touching and shrine practices go beyond Aḥmad. Later Sunnism extended earlier categories of tabarruk, tawassul, and sanctified traces. The expansion is not accidental. It grows naturally from the idea that holiness can be accessed through created intermediaries. The Qurʾān repeatedly challenges exactly this kind of religious displacement. Human beings create an object, location, person, or invisible agent that becomes the practical focus of religious dependence. The name of God remains in the theology, but the devotional action is directed elsewhere. ## 3. Aḥmad and Tawassul Through the Prophet The third strand is not about a grave or an emergency formula. It is legal. al-Mardāwī, summarizing the Hanbalī school in al-Inṣāf , states that tawassul through a righteous man is permissible according to the correct view of the madhhab, with another view saying it is recommended. He then cites Aḥmad in connection with al-Marwadhī and tawassul through the Prophet. A defender may reply that this tawassul is not direct worship of the Prophet because the supplication is still addressed to God. That is the standard Sunni defense. It is also why the Quraysh comparison matters. The Qurʾān does not say that the pagan error consisted only in believing idols created the universe. It says they used other beings as channels of nearness and intercession. The Hanbalī passage also contains an internal warning sign. al-Mardāwī notes that Ibn Taymiyya treated this kind of tawassul like the question of swearing by the Prophet. In other words, the practice had to be explained, qualified, or restricted because it sat near the boundary of invoking created status in religious speech. That boundary is not invented by modern polemics. It appears inside the Sunni debate itself. Tawassul usually means asking God by means of someone’s status, righteousness, supplication, or relation to God. Istighātha is more direct: “O so-and-so, help me.” The distinction matters legally, but the Qurʾānic critique reaches the shared structure: a created being is inserted into the act of appeal as a religious channel. ## 4. Later Sunni Scholars Made the Logic Explicit The earlier material around Aḥmad gives the post its historical force. Later Sunni scholars show where that logic leads when expressed openly. Taqī al-Dīn al-Subkī, in Shifāʾ al-Siqām , treats tawassul, istighātha, and seeking intercession through the Prophet as permissible and commendable. Ibn Ḥajar al-Haytamī gives the same logic in a more systematic form. God is the real source of help, he says, while the Prophet is a means or intermediary through whom help is sought in a secondary or causal sense. This is the exact theological move the Qurʾān does not allow. The defender says, “God is the real actor; the Prophet or saint is only a means.” The Qurʾān already quotes the intermediary defense and rejects it. ## 5. The Salafi Escape Route Exposes the Inconsistency Modern Salafi writers often condemn istighātha through the dead as major shirk. On that point, their Qurʾānic instinct is closer to the argument of this article than the later devotional Sunni tradition. Their difficulty is that the Sunni hadith and legal canon they inherit contains material that does not fit their theology. The result is a pattern of selective tightening. The “O servants of God” reports are weakened, or reinterpreted as angels and jinn. The al-ʿIlal grave wording becomes textually problematic, while the minbar permission is retained but fenced off. Aḥmad’s tawassul through the Prophet is explained as a disputed technical issue or analogized to swearing by the Prophet. Later Sunni istighātha is dismissed as deviation, even though its defenders cite earlier legal and devotional categories. Material Conservative handling Problem for the system Aḥmad calling, “O servants of God, guide me.” Explained as angels/jinn or based on a disputed report. The act remains a call to unseen created beings. Aḥmad permitting tabarruk through the minbar and possibly grave. Restrict to the minbar/rummāna and reject later grave-touching. The restricted version still makes physical relic-contact a religious means of blessing. Aḥmad permitting tawassul through the Prophet. Treat as a disputed Hanbalī technical issue or special case. The special case still inserts the Prophet into supplication as a means after his death. al-Subkī and al-Haytamī defending istighātha. Classified as later excess or Sufi deviation. Their argument develops categories already accepted in Sunni law: tawassul, tabarruk, intercession, and causes. A Qurʾān-first critique does not need to defend Salafism against Sufism or Sufism against Salafism. Both remain inside a hadith-based framework that normalizes extra-Qurʾānic devotional categories. The Salafi tries to keep the hadith canon while cutting off its devotional consequences. The Sufi accepts the consequences and supplies theological language to defend them. The Qurʾān rejects the shared premise that created intermediaries belong inside worship and supplication. ## The Qurʾānic Verdict The Qurʾān repeatedly returns the believer to God alone. It does not instruct believers to call upon unseen servants, seek blessing through relics, or place the Prophet’s posthumous status into the mechanics of duʿāʾ. The final verse is especially useful because it frames the issue as a reversal after guidance. The believer has been shown the direct path to God, then is invited back into calling upon what cannot benefit or harm him. That is exactly what intermediary religion does. It keeps the language of God while multiplying channels, patrons, holy objects, and unseen helpers. The material attached to Imam Aḥmad should not be used to make calling upon created beings acceptable. It should be used to expose a contradiction inside Sunni tradition. Aḥmad is remembered as an imam of strict Sunnism, yet reports and Hanbalī legal transmissions connected to him preserve practices that depend on intermediaries: unseen servants, prophetic traces, righteous men, and the Prophet’s status. The Qurʾān cuts through the entire system by directing supplication, reliance, and devotion to God alone. ## Sources Consulted Source Use in this article al-Bayhaqī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Shuʿab al-Īmān , no. 7298 in one common numbering Preserves the report from ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad that Aḥmad called, “O servants of God, guide me to the road,” during pilgrimage. ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad, Masāʾil al-Imām Aḥmad Parallel citation for Aḥmad’s personal use of the “servants of God” formula. al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr , 17:117-118 Source for the report instructing one who is lost or in need in a deserted place to call, “O servants of God, help me.” al-Albānī, Silsilat al-Aḥādīth al-Ḍaʿīfa , no. 656; modern Salafi discussions Used for the restrictive interpretation that the “servants of God” are angels or jinn and that the report cannot justify calling upon dead saints. ʿAbd Allāh b. Aḥmad, al-ʿIlal wa-Maʿrifat al-Rijāl , no. 3243 Printed report in which Aḥmad permits touching the Prophet’s minbar and doing something similar at the grave for nearness to God. Ibn Qudāma, al-Mughnī ; Abū Yaʿlā; Ibn Taymiyya’s later citations of Hanbalī material Used to show the conservative Hanbalī counter-report: Aḥmad is said to allow the minbar/rummāna but not to recognize touching the grave as a Sunnah. al-Mardāwī, al-Inṣāf , Book of Prayer, chapter of istisqāʾ, 2:456 Hanbalī legal statement permitting tawassul through a righteous man and citing Aḥmad’s instruction regarding tawassul through the Prophet. Taqī al-Dīn al-Subkī, Shifāʾ al-Siqām Later Shāfiʿī defense of tawassul, istighātha, and seeking intercession through the Prophet. Ibn Ḥajar al-Haytamī, al-Jawhar al-Munaẓẓam Later Shāfiʿī formulation that God is the real source of help while the Prophet is an intermediary and figurative object of istighātha. Qurʾān 31:25; 39:3; 10:18; 35:14; 46:5-6; 72:20-21; 1:5; 40:65; 19:48; 6:71 The Qurʾānic standard used to evaluate the intermediary logic in the reports and legal claims.

The Qurʾān rejects the shared premise that created intermediaries belong inside worship and supplication. The Qurʾānic Verdict The Qurʾān repeatedly returns the believer to God alone. It does not instruct believers to call upon unseen servants, seek blessing through relics, or place the Prophet’s posthumous status into the mechanics of duʿāʾ. The final verse is especially useful because it frames the issue as a reversal after guidance. The believer has been shown the direct path to God, then is invited back into calling upon what cannot benefit or harm him. That is exactly what intermediary religion does. It keeps the language of God while multiplying channels, patrons, holy objects, and unseen helpers. The material attached to Imam Aḥmad should not be used to make calling upon created beings acceptable. It should be used to expose a contradiction inside Sunni tradition. Aḥmad is remembered as an imam of strict Sunnism, yet reports and Hanbalī legal transmissions connected to him preserve practices that depend on intermediaries: unseen servants, prophetic traces, righteous men, and the Prophet’s status. The Qurʾān cuts through the entire system by directing supplication, reliance, and devotion to God alone. title: ʿIlm al-Rijāl (علم الرجال): A Case Study in Subjective Authentication
description: A strengthened case study of ʿIkrimah, the apostasy report, and the way classical rijāl criticism preserves contradictory testimony that later scholars selectively harmonized into certainty.

Muṣannaf', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'above' } ]; { from: 'ibnAbbas', to: 'ikrimah', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'ikrimah', to: 'ayyub', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'ayyub', to: 'hammad' }, { from: 'ayyub', to: 'sufyan' }, { from: 'ayyub', to: 'mamar' }, { from: 'hammad', to: 'abuNuman' }, { from: 'sufyan', to: 'aliIbnAbdAllah' }, { from: 'abuNuman', to: 'bukhari' }, { from: 'aliIbnAbdAllah', to: 'bukhari' }, { from: 'mamar', to: 'abdRazzaq' } ]; The problem with *ʿilm al-rijāl* is not that every biographical judgment is useless. The problem is that the discipline is often presented as if it produces objective certainty, while its own dictionaries preserve contradictory, politically charged, and theologically motivated testimony. ʿIkrimah, the freedman of Ibn ʿAbbās, is a useful case study because the same tradition that made him a pillar of tafsīr and hadith also preserved accusations that he lied against Ibn ʿAbbās, promoted Kharijite views, and transmitted material that conveniently serves those views. Traditional hadith authentication depends on two major claims. First, the chain must be connected. Second, the transmitters must be upright and precise. The second claim is where the difficulty appears. “Uprightness” and “precision” are not measurable qualities. They are reconstructed from reports, rival memories, sectarian loyalties, student networks, and later scholarly preference. A biographical entry does not usually give the reader a clean verdict. It gives the reader an archive of competing witnesses. The popular apologetic version of the science hides that archive. It gives the final label—*thiqah*, *ṣadūq*, *ḍaʿīf*, *matrūk*—and treats the label as though it were the result of neutral measurement. The classical sources themselves are messier. They record praise and attack, acceptance and suspicion, canonical use and local rejection. A later scholar then decides which testimony matters and which testimony can be explained away. This is not an argument that every narrator in the hadith corpus was a liar. It is also not an argument that every criticism of ʿIkrimah is equally sound. The narrower point is stronger: when a narrator’s file contains serious early accusations, sectarian allegations, and direct legal usefulness for his alleged ideology, the later decision to certify him as reliable is not an empirical result. It is a judgment call. ## The Case Study: ʿIkrimah, Freedman of Ibn ʿAbbās ʿIkrimah was one of the most influential transmitters from Ibn ʿAbbās. The rijāl sources describe him as a major authority in Qurʾānic interpretation, legal reports, maghāzī, and the traditions of Ibn ʿAbbās. This is exactly why his case matters. He is not a marginal weak narrator whose rejection would cost little. He is a narrator whose acceptance became structurally useful for the Sunni canon. The classical record about him is not one-sided. It contains strong praise. The same entry also preserves the familiar statements that made ʿIkrimah valuable to later scholars. Jābir b. Zayd is reported to have called him “the ocean” and “the most knowledgeable of people.” al-Shaʿbī is reported to have said that no one remained more knowledgeable about the Book of God than ʿIkrimah. Qatādah classified him among the leading specialists in tafsīr and sīrah. These statements explain why later tradition fought to keep him. What the praise establishes What it does not establish ʿIkrimah was remembered as a major transmitter of Ibn ʿAbbās material. Major influence is not the same thing as secure attribution. A transmitter can be influential precisely because his reports won later institutional battles. Some Basran and Meccan transmitters treated his knowledge seriously. Local acceptance by some transmitters does not erase criticism from Medina, from the Ibn ʿAbbās household, or from other early critics. Later canonical compilers had inherited reasons to use him. Canonical use is not independent evidence. Once al-Bukhārī and others relied on him, defending ʿIkrimah also became a defense of the canon. ## The Other Side of the File The same biographical tradition preserves severe accusations. The issue is not a single hostile line from an obscure enemy. The criticisms concern three recurring themes: lying against Ibn ʿAbbās, Kharijite affiliation, and instability in transmission. This report matters because it does not come from a later polemicist saying, “I do not like ʿIkrimah.” It places the accusation inside the household whose authority ʿIkrimah claimed to transmit. Even if a defender disputes the chain of this accusation, the fact that such an accusation circulated in the rijāl archive is itself significant. The later science did not discover a clean narrator and then verify him. It inherited a contested narrator and then chose how to manage the contest. The criticisms continue. That last sentence is the whole problem in miniature. Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd says one thing. Ayyūb says the opposite. Later hadith authentication cannot simply quote Ayyūb and pretend the problem disappeared. It has selected one early judgment over another. ## The Sectarian Problem: Kharijite Accusations The Kharijite accusation is not a decorative biographical detail. It becomes historically relevant because the legal report examined below establishes a rule of execution for religious defection and theological deviance. A narrator accused of Kharijite leanings transmitting a maxim that authorizes killing apostates is not a neutral coincidence. It is motive-relevant evidence. The sources also preserve more extreme material: ʿIkrimah allegedly stood at the door of a mosque and declared everyone inside a disbeliever; in another report from Ifrīqiyah, he allegedly wished he were at the pilgrimage season with a spear, striking those present right and left. A defender can challenge the strength of individual reports. The accumulated pattern remains: the tradition itself associated ʿIkrimah with takfīr-oriented sectarian currents. A sectarian accusation is not automatically proof of fabrication. But it becomes probative when the report under review advances precisely the kind of legal-theological logic associated with that sectarian posture. The issue is not simply, “Was ʿIkrimah a Kharijite?” The issue is that the rijāl archive itself preserves accusations of Kharijite affiliation, while the hadith transmitted through him authorizes killing people for religious defection. ## Mālik’s Treatment of ʿIkrimah Mālik b. Anas is especially important because his legal and hadith culture stands closer to the Medinan material than later canonization. The biographical sources report that Mālik did not view ʿIkrimah as reliable and ordered that his reports not be taken. al-Shāfiʿī is quoted as saying that Mālik had a poor opinion of ʿIkrimah and said, “I do not think anyone should accept his hadith.” A later Sunni can answer that Mālik was stricter here than other critics, or that Mālik’s concern was ʿIkrimah’s doctrine rather than his truthfulness. That answer still proves the point. The verdict depends on how the scholar weighs competing considerations: doctrine, memory, canon-use, local acceptance, and inherited legal need. ## The Canonical Counterweight The same rijāl archive also records strong defenses of ʿIkrimah. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal is reported to have said that his hadith may be used as proof. Ibn Maʿīn is quoted declaring him trustworthy alongside Saʿīd b. Jubayr. Some later defenders went further, treating criticism of ʿIkrimah as a suspicious sign. Defense of ʿIkrimah Critical problem left unresolved Aḥmad: “His hadith is used as proof.” Aḥmad is also reported elsewhere as describing ʿIkrimah as “confused in hadith” and “differed over.” The archive does not give one simple Aḥmad-based answer. Ibn Maʿīn: “ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd b. Jubayr are both trustworthy.” Ibn Maʿīn’s confidence does not remove the household accusation, Mālik’s rejection, or the Kharijite reports. al-Bukhārī used him in the Ṣaḥīḥ. Canonical inclusion is not neutral. Once the canon depends on him, later defense of ʿIkrimah also protects al-Bukhārī’s authority. Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said he did not accuse him of lying. The same report places Ayyūb opposite Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, who said the opposite. The choice between the two is interpretive. This is the methodological center of the article. A traditionalist can defend ʿIkrimah. A critic can indict him. Both sides can quote the classical archive. The later label “reliable” does not erase the subjectivity of the path by which that label was chosen. ## The Legal Flashpoint: “Whoever Changes His Religion, Kill Him” The stakes become serious when ʿIkrimah transmits one of the most consequential reports in Islamic legal history. The exact Bukhārī proof-text is not an abstract legal maxim floating independently in the earliest recoverable material. It appears inside a story. ʿAlī burns a group of theological deviants. Ibn ʿAbbās corrects the method but approves the killing. The report therefore does two things at once: it normalizes the execution of religious deviants and places ʿAlī in need of correction by Ibn ʿAbbās. For a narrator accused of Kharijite leanings, this narrative shape is historically suspicious. Kharijite memory had reasons to diminish ʿAlī’s authority. Kharijite legal-theological instincts also had reasons to turn religious deviation into a death-worthy category. The report does not merely say, “Apostasy is punished.” It gives the rule through a scene in which ʿAlī mishandles the punishment and Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the prophetic correction. The strongest argument is not that no later book contains any non-ʿIkrimah wording about apostasy. The stronger argument is that the decisive Bukhārī proof-text, the compact formula, and the early Muṣannaf material are centered on ʿIkrimah → Ibn ʿAbbās, while many claimed parallels either use broader wording such as “leaving the community,” appear as mursal reports, or look like later legal reinforcement of an already circulating formula. ## Earlier and Parallel Evidence Does Not Remove the Problem The broader legal tradition contains other reports about killing people who abandon the community, fight God and His Messenger, or return to unbelief after Islam. These reports are often cited to protect the ʿIkrimah report from criticism. They should be separated rather than blurred together. Report type Example Why it does not erase the ʿIkrimah problem Exact formula man baddala dīnahu fa-qtulūhu — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.” The cleanest and most influential canonical form runs through ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, especially in Bukhārī. Political-community wording “The one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.” This wording is broader and politically framed. It does not independently authenticate the shorter absolute formula. Reports involving fighting or public rebellion Some versions describe one who “fights God and His Messenger” or disrupts the Muslim community. These reports can be read as rebellion/treason material rather than simple change of belief. Mursal and disputed support al-Nasāʾī records a mursal report from al-Ḥasan and says it is more correct than a connected Qatādah → ʿIkrimah version. A mursal support can show circulation of a legal slogan, but it does not give independent Companion-level confirmation of the Bukhārī wording. The early Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq is especially helpful because it shows both the story form and the compact legal formula in close proximity through the same Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah channel. The wording variation is important. The same report oscillates between “changed,” “returned,” and a narrative about people who “disbelieved after their Islam.” That instability does not look like a universally known public pronouncement preserved by multiple independent Companion memories. It looks like a legal maxim stabilized inside a story and then extracted into a shorter slogan. ## Why the Report Serves a Kharijite-Imaginable Agenda A critic does not need to prove that ʿIkrimah personally fabricated the report in a modern courtroom sense. Historical criticism works with probability, motive, transmission shape, and ideological fit. On those terms, this report has a problem. Feature of the report Historical significance ʿAlī is the one whose action requires correction. This is useful in a memory environment hostile to ʿAlī’s authority. Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the prophetic legal maxim. ʿIkrimah’s authority depends on transmitting Ibn ʿAbbās material; the report strengthens his channel. The legal maxim authorizes killing religious defectors. This matches the kind of takfīr-and-punishment logic associated in the sources with Kharijite currents. The report is later used as a broad legal proof-text. A localized story about zanādiqah becomes a general rule for the death of apostates. This is where rijāl reaches its limit. A later scholar may say: “Ayyūb trusted him, Aḥmad used him, Ibn Maʿīn declared him trustworthy, and al-Bukhārī included him.” A historical critic may answer: “Mālik rejected him, the Ibn ʿAbbās household accused him, Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd called him a liar, and the report serves an ideology with which he was associated.” Both sides are working from the same inherited record. The difference is not science versus ignorance. It is canon-preserving judgment versus historical suspicion. ## The Qurʾānic Baseline The Qurʾān repeatedly treats belief as a matter that cannot be compelled by coercive religious authority. A hadith report that creates a death penalty for changing religion therefore carries an unusually heavy burden of proof. It cannot be protected merely by saying that the chain is “sound” after a later scholar has chosen one side of a disputed narrator file. If a report overrides the Qurʾān’s repeated pattern of non-compulsion, reminder, and individual accountability, the evidence for that report must be stronger than a contested transmitter whose own archive preserves accusations of sectarian extremism and lying. The failure is not that rijāl contains criticism. The failure is that later hadith culture can preserve the criticism, acknowledge the controversy, and still treat the resulting hadith as if the controversy has been neutralized. Once a contested narrator receives canonical protection, the hadith becomes “authentic,” the law becomes “Islamic,” and the Qurʾānic baseline is forced to bend around a disputed report. ## The Modern Afterlife The legal afterlife of this hadith is not theoretical. Classical jurists did not agree on every procedural detail—repentance periods, male and female apostates, public rebellion, imprisonment, and state authority were debated—but the Bukhārī formula became one of the most quoted proof-texts for the death penalty. Modern apostasy laws are not produced by this report alone, but the report helped give later legal systems a prophetic slogan for religious coercion. Pew Research Center’s 2019 legal survey, published in 2022, found that 22 of 198 countries and territories had laws or policies against apostasy; 13 of those were in the Middle East and North Africa. That does not mean every modern statute descends directly from ʿIkrimah’s report. It means the legal problem created by these traditions still has public consequences. ## What This Case Study Shows ʿIkrimah’s case exposes the weakness of presenting *ʿilm al-rijāl* as a clean scientific filter. The filter did not remove a narrator accused of lying against his master, associated with Kharijite currents, rejected by Mālik, and attached to a report that supports exactly the kind of punitive sectarian logic with which he was associated. Instead, the filter absorbed the controversy and then allowed later scholars to canonize one side of it. The rijāl dictionaries do not give us certainty. They give us contested memory. When the contested memory concerns a narrator whose report authorizes killing people for changing religion, the burden of proof must be much higher than “al-Bukhārī accepted him.” A Qurʾān-first method has no reason to subordinate explicit non-compulsion to a legally violent report transmitted through such a disputed figure. ## Sources Consulted Source Used for al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl fī asmāʾ al-rijāl , entry on ʿIkrimah mawla Ibn ʿAbbās Biographical notices, praise reports, accusations of lying, Mālik’s rejection, Kharijite/Sufrī/Ibāḍī allegations, and the conflicting Ayyūb/Yaḥyā evaluations. al-Dhahabī, Siyar aʿlām al-nubalāʾ , entry on ʿIkrimah Later Sunni preservation of both the critical allegations and the canonical defenses of ʿIkrimah. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3017 and 6922 The canonical apostasy proof-text and its narrative frame through Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah. ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Muṣannaf , reports 9413 and 18706 in the uploaded corpus Early Muṣannaf witnesses showing the same Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah channel in both narrative and compact formula forms. Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Awsaṭ fī al-sunan wa-l-ijmāʿ wa-l-ikhtilāf , Kitāb al-Murtadd Comparison of the ʿIkrimah formula with broader legal reports about leaving the community, killing, and apostasy. al-Nasāʾī, Sunan , Kitāb Taḥrīm al-Dam, reports around 4059–4065 Parallel and disputed routes, including Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah, Qatādah routes, and the note preferring a mursal al-Ḥasan form over one connected version. Pew Research Center, “Four-in-ten countries and territories worldwide had blasphemy laws in 2019” Modern legal afterlife of apostasy and blasphemy laws, especially the 22-country apostasy-law figure and MENA concentration.

But it becomes probative when the report under review advances precisely the kind of legal-theological logic associated with that sectarian posture. The issue is not simply, “Was ʿIkrimah a Kharijite?” The issue is that the rijāl archive itself preserves accusations of Kharijite affiliation, while the hadith transmitted through him authorizes killing people for religious defection. Mālik’s Treatment of ʿIkrimah Mālik b. Anas is especially important because his legal and hadith culture stands closer to the Medinan material than later canonization. The biographical sources report that Mālik did not view ʿIkrimah as reliable and ordered that his reports not be taken. al-Shāfiʿī is quoted as saying that Mālik had a poor opinion of ʿIkrimah and said, “I do not think anyone should accept his hadith.” A later Sunni can answer that Mālik was stricter here than other critics, or that Mālik’s concern was ʿIkrimah’s doctrine rather than his truthfulness. That answer still proves the point. The verdict depends on how the scholar weighs competing considerations: doctrine, memory, canon-use, local acceptance, and inherited legal need. The Canonical Counterweight The same rijāl archive also records strong defenses of ʿIkrimah. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal is reported to have said that his hadith may be used as proof. Ibn Maʿīn is quoted declaring him trustworthy alongside Saʿīd b. Jubayr. Some later defenders went further, treating criticism of ʿIkrimah as a suspicious sign. Defense of ʿIkrimah Critical problem left unresolved Aḥmad: “His hadith is used as proof.” Aḥmad is also reported elsewhere as describing ʿIkrimah as “confused in hadith” and “differed over.” The archive does not give one simple Aḥmad-based answer. Ibn Maʿīn: “ʿIkrimah and Saʿīd b. Jubayr are both trustworthy.” Ibn Maʿīn’s confidence does not remove the household accusation, Mālik’s rejection, or the Kharijite reports. al-Bukhārī used him in the Ṣaḥīḥ. Canonical inclusion is not neutral. Once the canon depends on him, later defense of ʿIkrimah also protects al-Bukhārī’s authority. Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī said he did not accuse him of lying. The same report places Ayyūb opposite Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Anṣārī, who said the opposite. The choice between the two is interpretive. This is the methodological center of the article. A traditionalist can defend ʿIkrimah. A critic can indict him. Both sides can quote the classical archive. The later label “reliable” does not erase the subjectivity of the path by which that label was chosen. The Legal Flashpoint: “Whoever Changes His Religion, Kill Him” The stakes become serious when ʿIkrimah transmits one of the most consequential reports in Islamic legal history. The exact Bukhārī proof-text is not an abstract legal maxim floating independently in the earliest recoverable material. It appears inside a story. ʿAlī burns a group of theological deviants. Ibn ʿAbbās corrects the method but approves the killing. The report therefore does two things at once: it normalizes the execution of religious deviants and places ʿAlī in need of correction by Ibn ʿAbbās. For a narrator accused of Kharijite leanings, this narrative shape is historically suspicious. Kharijite memory had reasons to diminish ʿAlī’s authority. Kharijite legal-theological instincts also had reasons to turn religious deviation into a death-worthy category. The report does not merely say, “Apostasy is punished.” It gives the rule through a scene in which ʿAlī mishandles the punishment and Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the prophetic correction. The strongest argument is not that no later book contains any non-ʿIkrimah wording about apostasy. The stronger argument is that the decisive Bukhārī proof-text, the compact formula, and the early Muṣannaf material are centered on ʿIkrimah → Ibn ʿAbbās, while many claimed parallels either use broader wording such as “leaving the community,” appear as mursal reports, or look like later legal reinforcement of an already circulating formula. Earlier and Parallel Evidence Does Not Remove the Problem The broader legal tradition contains other reports about killing people who abandon the community, fight God and His Messenger, or return to unbelief after Islam. These reports are often cited to protect the ʿIkrimah report from criticism. They should be separated rather than blurred together. Report type Example Why it does not erase the ʿIkrimah problem Exact formula man baddala dīnahu fa-qtulūhu — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.” The cleanest and most influential canonical form runs through ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, especially in Bukhārī. Political-community wording “The one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.” This wording is broader and politically framed. It does not independently authenticate the shorter absolute formula. Reports involving fighting or public rebellion Some versions describe one who “fights God and His Messenger” or disrupts the Muslim community. These reports can be read as rebellion/treason material rather than simple change of belief. Mursal and disputed support al-Nasāʾī records a mursal report from al-Ḥasan and says it is more correct than a connected Qatādah → ʿIkrimah version. A mursal support can show circulation of a legal slogan, but it does not give independent Companion-level confirmation of the Bukhārī wording. The early Muṣannaf of ʿAbd al-Razzāq is especially helpful because it shows both the story form and the compact legal formula in close proximity through the same Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah channel. The wording variation is important. The same report oscillates between “changed,” “returned,” and a narrative about people who “disbelieved after their Islam.” That instability does not look like a universally known public pronouncement preserved by multiple independent Companion memories. It looks like a legal maxim stabilized inside a story and then extracted into a shorter slogan. Why the Report Serves a Kharijite-Imaginable Agenda A critic does not need to prove that ʿIkrimah personally fabricated the report in a modern courtroom sense. Historical criticism works with probability, motive, transmission shape, and ideological fit. On those terms, this report has a problem. Feature of the report Historical significance ʿAlī is the one whose action requires correction. This is useful in a memory environment hostile to ʿAlī’s authority. Ibn ʿAbbās supplies the prophetic legal maxim. ʿIkrimah’s authority depends on transmitting Ibn ʿAbbās material; the report strengthens his channel. The legal maxim authorizes killing religious defectors. This matches the kind of takfīr-and-punishment logic associated in the sources with Kharijite currents. The report is later used as a broad legal proof-text. A localized story about zanādiqah becomes a general rule for the death of apostates. This is where rijāl reaches its limit. A later scholar may say: “Ayyūb trusted him, Aḥmad used him, Ibn Maʿīn declared him trustworthy, and al-Bukhārī included him.” A historical critic may answer: “Mālik rejected him, the Ibn ʿAbbās household accused him, Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd called him a liar, and the report serves an ideology with which he was associated.” Both sides are working from the same inherited record. The difference is not science versus ignorance. It is canon-preserving judgment versus historical suspicion. The Qurʾānic Baseline The Qurʾān repeatedly treats belief as a matter that cannot be compelled by coercive religious authority. A hadith report that creates a death penalty for changing religion therefore carries an unusually heavy burden of proof. It cannot be protected merely by saying that the chain is “sound” after a later scholar has chosen one side of a disputed narrator file. If a report overrides the Qurʾān’s repeated pattern of non-compulsion, reminder, and individual accountability, the evidence for that report must be stronger than a contested transmitter whose own archive preserves accusations of sectarian extremism and lying. The failure is not that rijāl contains criticism. The failure is that later hadith culture can preserve the criticism, acknowledge the controversy, and still treat the resulting hadith as if the controversy has been neutralized. Once a contested narrator receives canonical protection, the hadith becomes “authentic,” the law becomes “Islamic,” and the Qurʾānic baseline is forced to bend around a disputed report. The Modern Afterlife The legal afterlife of this hadith is not theoretical. Classical jurists did not agree on every procedural detail—repentance periods, male and female apostates, public rebellion, imprisonment, and state authority were debated—but the Bukhārī formula became one of the most quoted proof-texts for the death penalty. Modern apostasy laws are not produced by this report alone, but the report helped give later legal systems a prophetic slogan for religious coercion. Pew Research Center’s 2019 legal survey, published in 2022, found that 22 of 198 countries and territories had laws or policies against apostasy; 13 of those were in the Middle East and North Africa. That does not mean every modern statute descends directly from ʿIkrimah’s report. It means the legal problem created by these traditions still has public consequences. What This Case Study Shows ʿIkrimah’s case exposes the weakness of presenting *ʿilm al-rijāl* as a clean scientific filter. The filter did not remove a narrator accused of lying against his master, associated with Kharijite currents, rejected by Mālik, and attached to a report that supports exactly the kind of punitive sectarian logic with which he was associated. Instead, the filter absorbed the controversy and then allowed later scholars to canonize one side of it. The rijāl dictionaries do not give us certainty. They give us contested memory. When the contested memory concerns a narrator whose report authorizes killing people for changing religion, the burden of proof must be much higher than “al-Bukhārī accepted him.” A Qurʾān-first method has no reason to subordinate explicit non-compulsion to a legally violent report transmitted through such a disputed figure. Sources Consulted Source Used for al-Mizzī, Tahdhīb al-Kamāl fī asmāʾ al-rijāl , entry on ʿIkrimah mawla Ibn ʿAbbās Biographical notices, praise reports, accusations of lying, Mālik’s rejection, Kharijite/Sufrī/Ibāḍī allegations, and the conflicting Ayyūb/Yaḥyā evaluations. al-Dhahabī, Siyar aʿlām al-nubalāʾ , entry on ʿIkrimah Later Sunni preservation of both the critical allegations and the canonical defenses of ʿIkrimah. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3017 and 6922 The canonical apostasy proof-text and its narrative frame through Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah. ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Muṣannaf , reports 9413 and 18706 in the uploaded corpus Early Muṣannaf witnesses showing the same Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah channel in both narrative and compact formula forms. Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Awsaṭ fī al-sunan wa-l-ijmāʿ wa-l-ikhtilāf , Kitāb al-Murtadd Comparison of the ʿIkrimah formula with broader legal reports about leaving the community, killing, and apostasy. al-Nasāʾī, Sunan , Kitāb Taḥrīm al-Dam, reports around 4059–4065 Parallel and disputed routes, including Ayyūb → ʿIkrimah, Qatādah routes, and the note preferring a mursal al-Ḥasan form over one connected version. Pew Research Center, “Four-in-ten countries and territories worldwide had blasphemy laws in 2019” Modern legal afterlife of apostasy and blasphemy laws, especially the 22-country apostasy-law figure and MENA concentration.

The report claims that the Prophet was bewitched until he imagined doing things he had not done. A Qurʾān-first reading immediately has to ask why a story that resembles the Qurʾān’s rejected accusation of a “bewitched man” should override the Qurʾān’s protection of the Prophet’s clarity and mission. Primary route ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām Collateral route Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash Main issue theology + common-link concentration The bewitchment report should not be treated as a secure historical memory merely because it entered the canonical collections. Its main detailed form clusters around Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s family route, while the apparent Kūfan corroboration through al-Aʿmash is shorter, more anonymous, and narratively reshaped. The result is a report that is theologically difficult, textually unstable, and source-critically exposed. ## The Qurʾānic Problem Comes First The Qurʾān does not present the Prophet as a man whose prophetic consciousness could be compromised by magic. It repeatedly rejects the charge that the messenger is mad, deluded, or bewitched. This makes the test broader than chain acceptability on paper. The story asks the reader to accept a category of accusation that the Qurʾān places in the mouths of opponents. Qurʾānic criterion The Qurʾān answers accusations against the Prophet’s mental clarity and mission, making the bewitchment story theologically costly. Hadith claim The report says the Prophet imagined he had done something when he had not, a formulation that creates an immediate clash with the Qurʾānic defense. Method The report has to be tested by both content and transmission. A famous isnād does not erase a Qurʾānic contradiction. Surat al-Furqān records the polemical accusation, “You are following only a bewitched man,” and treats it as the speech of opponents rather than as a valid description of the Prophet. A hadith that effectively validates the same category requires stronger evidence than a single family-dossier route and a thin collateral strand. ## The Isnād Problem: A Famous Report with a Narrow Center The dominant version of the report travels through Hishām b. ʿUrwa from his father ʿUrwa from ʿĀʾisha. Later collections preserve multiple lower routes below Hishām, but that spread should not be mistaken for independent access to the event itself. Once the report rises above the lower transmitters, the main narrative returns to the same household line. Route A ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām The detailed household narrative: Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, Banū Zurayq, a comb, hair-remnants, date-palm material, a well, bedside diagnosis, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the incident. Main narrative stream Route B Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash A shorter Kūfan form: anonymous Jewish man, unnamed well, knots, Gabriel, and ʿAlī as the person sent to extract and untie the material. Collateral, not clean control The diagram makes the transmission problem easier to see. The Hishām side has broader lower diffusion, while the Kūfan side looks like a compressed collateral form. Both may preserve the same story-world, but the al-Aʿmash strand does not automatically become an independent second pillar simply because it ends at a different Companion name. ## The Three Aḥmad Forms Show Narrative Growth The early Aḥmad material is useful because it preserves the report at different levels of narrative expansion. The shortest form contains only the basic claim. The longer forms add the named Jewish figure, the well, the material objects, the diagnostic scene, and the closing explanation. Aḥmad 24237 Concise form حَدَّثَنَا يَحْيَى حَدَّثَنَا هِشَامٌ قَالَ حَدَّثَنِي أَبِي عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سُحِرَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ فَيُخَيَّلُ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ قَدْ صَنَعَ شَيْئًا وَلَمْ يَصْنَعْهُ The Prophet is bewitched and imagines that he has done something when he has not. No Labīd, no well, no comb, no discovery scene. Aḥmad 24348 Expanded form حَدَّثَنَا حَمَّادُ بْنُ أُسَامَةَ قَالَ أَخْبَرَنَا هِشَامٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سُحِرَ رَسُولُ اللهِ ﷺ حَتَّى أَنَّهُ لَيُخَيَّلُ لَهُ أَنَّهُ يَفْعَلُ الشَّيْءَ وَمَا يَفْعَلُهُ... The basic claim is now embedded in an extended story with the two visitors, identification of the sorcery, the well, and the Prophet’s recovery. Aḥmad 24300 Named polemical form حَدَّثَنَا ابْنُ نُمَيْرٍ حَدَّثَنَا هِشَامٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سَحَرَ رَسُولَ اللهِ ﷺ يَهُودِيٌّ مِنْ يَهُودِ بَنِي زُرَيْقٍ يُقَالُ لَهُ لَبِيدُ بْنُ الْأَعْصَمِ... The perpetrator becomes explicit: a Jewish man from Banū Zurayq named Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam. This is the most narratively colored version. The movement from concise claim to detailed scene shows how much of the familiar story is carried by expansion, even before one reaches a final judgment about fabrication. The more vivid the report becomes, the more it depends on Hishām’s transmission world. ## Why Hishām b. ʿUrwa Matters Hishām b. ʿUrwa is not being treated here as a casually weak narrator. The point is more precise. The classical rijāl discussion itself records concern around his later Iraqi transmission and his expanding use of reports from his father. That is exactly the zone this report occupies: a vivid father-from-ʿĀʾisha household story that became widely useful after leaving its Medinan family setting. Mālik b. Anas Reportedly did not approve of Hishām’s narrations for the people of Iraq and objected to the change in his transmission style during his visits to Kūfa. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 Yaʿqūb b. Shayba Regarded him as reliable and firm, but said that criticism attached to his period after moving to Iraq, where he expanded narration from his father. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 Ibn Kharrāsh Preserved the report that Hishām’s Kūfan visits saw a movement from explicit hearing language into looser “my father from ʿĀʾisha” phrasing. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 The criticism should be used precisely. A theologically difficult report that leans heavily on a Hishām-from-his-father route deserves more scrutiny than a normal legal report with broad independent support. Given the absence of a strong independent Medinan control outside Hishām’s orbit, the report cannot simply be defended by saying that later compilers accepted it. Later compilation belongs to the report’s reception history; it cannot substitute for independent access to the event. ## The Kūfan Strand: al-Aʿmash and the Zayd b. Arqam Version The al-Aʿmash version looks at first like a separate Companion witness. It goes through Zayd b. Arqam rather than ʿĀʾisha. But the content is simpler, more anonymous, and regionally re-staged. Gabriel replaces the bedside diagnostic scene, the named Medinan perpetrator disappears, the well is unnamed, and ʿAlī becomes the active rescuer. Feature Hishām / ʿĀʾisha stream al-Aʿmash / Zayd stream What changes Perpetrator Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, tied to Banū Zurayq Anonymous Jewish man The polemical category remains, but the local Medinan identification drops out. Diagnosis Two visitors discuss the Prophet’s condition Gabriel directly explains the magic The extended scene is compressed into angelic notification. Object Comb, hair, male date-palm spathe Knots in an unnamed well The story keeps the removal motif but simplifies the material details. Human actor The Prophet and companions, or unspecified extraction ʿAlī is explicitly sent to retrieve and untie it The Kūfan version becomes more ʿAlī-centered. This evidence does not amount to a confession of fabrication from al-Aʿmash. It leaves the Zayd route too exposed to function as clean independent corroboration. It has the shape of a Kūfan digest of the same story-world: shorter, less domestic, less ʿĀʾisha-centered, and more compatible with an environment where ʿAlī’s role carried special weight. ## Joshua Little and the Hishām Pattern Dr. Joshua Little’s work on the marital-age hadith of ʿĀʾisha is relevant because it gives a comparative pattern for Hishām b. ʿUrwa: a famous report about ʿĀʾisha, concentrated around Hishām, useful in later sectarian memory, and difficult to trace securely behind him. “None of the hadiths can be traced back to Medina in the 7th or 8th centuries CE; they cannot be traced to earlier generations in Iraq either. All versions of the hadith trace back to an ur-version, with Hisham’s version being the most widespread.” The comparison does not collapse the bewitchment report into the marital-age report. It highlights a recurring pattern: Hishām sits at the center of more than one ʿĀʾisha household narration that later communities treated as decisive despite a narrow and ideologically useful recoverable transmission center. ## Dating the Story: Medinan Polemic or Iraqi Reshaping? The bewitchment report makes best sense as a story that developed in a Medinan polemical memory world and then received regional reshaping in Iraq. In the Medinan frame, the Jewish perpetrator, Banū Zurayq, and the well-localization give the story a local anti-Jewish polemical setting. In the Kūfan frame, the same story skeleton is shortened and given a more ʿAlī-centered role. Stage 1 · Medinan story-world Family route and local polemic The report circulates through the ʿUrwa family world with ʿĀʾisha as the household authority. Its details are local: Labīd, Banū Zurayq, the well, the comb, hair-remnants, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the incident. Stage 2 · Kūfan reshaping Compression and ʿAlī-centered action The story appears in a shorter form through al-Aʿmash: the perpetrator is anonymous, the well is unnamed, Gabriel diagnoses the matter, and ʿAlī retrieves and unties the knots. This reconstruction is more modest than saying every transmitter in the chain knowingly lied. It treats the report as a story that moved through transmission environments and changed as it moved. That is precisely why the theological issue cannot be dismissed by simply pointing to the presence of an isnād. ## What Really Happened? The most plausible history is that the bewitchment story began as a Medinan polemical and household-memory narrative, stabilized through Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s father-from-ʿĀʾisha route, and then spread into broader hadith circulation. Once in the Iraqi environment, it could be abbreviated, recast, or supplied with a more regionally meaningful cast of characters. In that process, the Kūfan version through al-Aʿmash reproduced the broad structure while changing the details most tied to Hishām’s family version. Its evidentiary value is limited: it can show that the story circulated, while still failing to prove the event behind the story. The bewitchment report is too theologically costly and too source-critically concentrated to be treated as secure. Its main detailed form depends on Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s family route, and the al-Aʿmash / Zayd version is a thin, reshaped collateral strand rather than a clean independent witness. A Qurʾān-first method has stronger grounds to reject the story than to reinterpret the Qurʾān around it. ## Further Reading Joshua Little: summary of PhD research { .sihr-kicker, .sihr-opening__ledger b, .route-cards span, .variant-card__top span, .critic-grid span, .matn-matrix__head > div, .two-stage span { color: var(--hc-gold); The report claims that the Prophet was bewitched until he imagined doing things he had not done. A Qurʾān-first reading immediately has to ask why a story that resembles the Qurʾān’s rejected accusation of a “bewitched man” should override the Qurʾān’s protection of the Prophet’s clarity and mission. Primary route ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām Collateral route Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash Main issue theology + common-link concentration The bewitchment report should not be treated as a secure historical memory merely because it entered the canonical collections. Its main detailed form clusters around Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s family route, while the apparent Kūfan corroboration through al-Aʿmash is shorter, more anonymous, and narratively reshaped. The result is a report that is theologically difficult, textually unstable, and source-critically exposed. The Qurʾānic Problem Comes First The Qurʾān does not present the Prophet as a man whose prophetic consciousness could be compromised by magic. It repeatedly rejects the charge that the messenger is mad, deluded, or bewitched. This makes the test broader than chain acceptability on paper. The story asks the reader to accept a category of accusation that the Qurʾān places in the mouths of opponents. Qurʾānic criterion The Qurʾān answers accusations against the Prophet’s mental clarity and mission, making the bewitchment story theologically costly. Hadith claim The report says the Prophet imagined he had done something when he had not, a formulation that creates an immediate clash with the Qurʾānic defense. Method The report has to be tested by both content and transmission. A famous isnād does not erase a Qurʾānic contradiction. Surat al-Furqān records the polemical accusation, “You are following only a bewitched man,” and treats it as the speech of opponents rather than as a valid description of the Prophet. A hadith that effectively validates the same category requires stronger evidence than a single family-dossier route and a thin collateral strand. The Isnād Problem: A Famous Report with a Narrow Center The dominant version of the report travels through Hishām b. ʿUrwa from his father ʿUrwa from ʿĀʾisha. Later collections preserve multiple lower routes below Hishām, but that spread should not be mistaken for independent access to the event itself. Once the report rises above the lower transmitters, the main narrative returns to the same household line. Route A ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām The detailed household narrative: Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, Banū Zurayq, a comb, hair-remnants, date-palm material, a well, bedside diagnosis, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the incident. Main narrative stream Route B Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash A shorter Kūfan form: anonymous Jewish man, unnamed well, knots, Gabriel, and ʿAlī as the person sent to extract and untie the material. Collateral, not clean control The diagram makes the transmission problem easier to see. The Hishām side has broader lower diffusion, while the Kūfan side looks like a compressed collateral form. Both may preserve the same story-world, but the al-Aʿmash strand does not automatically become an independent second pillar simply because it ends at a different Companion name. The Three Aḥmad Forms Show Narrative Growth The early Aḥmad material is useful because it preserves the report at different levels of narrative expansion. The shortest form contains only the basic claim. The longer forms add the named Jewish figure, the well, the material objects, the diagnostic scene, and the closing explanation. Aḥmad 24237 Concise form حَدَّثَنَا يَحْيَى حَدَّثَنَا هِشَامٌ قَالَ حَدَّثَنِي أَبِي عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سُحِرَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ فَيُخَيَّلُ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ قَدْ صَنَعَ شَيْئًا وَلَمْ يَصْنَعْهُ The Prophet is bewitched and imagines that he has done something when he has not. No Labīd, no well, no comb, no discovery scene. Aḥmad 24348 Expanded form حَدَّثَنَا حَمَّادُ بْنُ أُسَامَةَ قَالَ أَخْبَرَنَا هِشَامٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سُحِرَ رَسُولُ اللهِ ﷺ حَتَّى أَنَّهُ لَيُخَيَّلُ لَهُ أَنَّهُ يَفْعَلُ الشَّيْءَ وَمَا يَفْعَلُهُ... The basic claim is now embedded in an extended story with the two visitors, identification of the sorcery, the well, and the Prophet’s recovery. Aḥmad 24300 Named polemical form حَدَّثَنَا ابْنُ نُمَيْرٍ حَدَّثَنَا هِشَامٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ قَالَتْ سَحَرَ رَسُولَ اللهِ ﷺ يَهُودِيٌّ مِنْ يَهُودِ بَنِي زُرَيْقٍ يُقَالُ لَهُ لَبِيدُ بْنُ الْأَعْصَمِ... The perpetrator becomes explicit: a Jewish man from Banū Zurayq named Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam. This is the most narratively colored version. The movement from concise claim to detailed scene shows how much of the familiar story is carried by expansion, even before one reaches a final judgment about fabrication. The more vivid the report becomes, the more it depends on Hishām’s transmission world. Why Hishām b. ʿUrwa Matters Hishām b. ʿUrwa is not being treated here as a casually weak narrator. The point is more precise. The classical rijāl discussion itself records concern around his later Iraqi transmission and his expanding use of reports from his father. That is exactly the zone this report occupies: a vivid father-from-ʿĀʾisha household story that became widely useful after leaving its Medinan family setting. Mālik b. Anas Reportedly did not approve of Hishām’s narrations for the people of Iraq and objected to the change in his transmission style during his visits to Kūfa. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 Yaʿqūb b. Shayba Regarded him as reliable and firm, but said that criticism attached to his period after moving to Iraq, where he expanded narration from his father. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 Ibn Kharrāsh Preserved the report that Hishām’s Kūfan visits saw a movement from explicit hearing language into looser “my father from ʿĀʾisha” phrasing. Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb 4/275 The criticism should be used precisely. A theologically difficult report that leans heavily on a Hishām-from-his-father route deserves more scrutiny than a normal legal report with broad independent support. Given the absence of a strong independent Medinan control outside Hishām’s orbit, the report cannot simply be defended by saying that later compilers accepted it. Later compilation belongs to the report’s reception history; it cannot substitute for independent access to the event. The Kūfan Strand: al-Aʿmash and the Zayd b. Arqam Version The al-Aʿmash version looks at first like a separate Companion witness. It goes through Zayd b. Arqam rather than ʿĀʾisha. But the content is simpler, more anonymous, and regionally re-staged. Gabriel replaces the bedside diagnostic scene, the named Medinan perpetrator disappears, the well is unnamed, and ʿAlī becomes the active rescuer. Feature Hishām / ʿĀʾisha stream al-Aʿmash / Zayd stream What changes Perpetrator Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, tied to Banū Zurayq Anonymous Jewish man The polemical category remains, but the local Medinan identification drops out. Diagnosis Two visitors discuss the Prophet’s condition Gabriel directly explains the magic The extended scene is compressed into angelic notification. Object Comb, hair, male date-palm spathe Knots in an unnamed well The story keeps the removal motif but simplifies the material details. Human actor The Prophet and companions, or unspecified extraction ʿAlī is explicitly sent to retrieve and untie it The Kūfan version becomes more ʿAlī-centered. This evidence does not amount to a confession of fabrication from al-Aʿmash. It leaves the Zayd route too exposed to function as clean independent corroboration. It has the shape of a Kūfan digest of the same story-world: shorter, less domestic, less ʿĀʾisha-centered, and more compatible with an environment where ʿAlī’s role carried special weight. Joshua Little and the Hishām Pattern Dr. Joshua Little’s work on the marital-age hadith of ʿĀʾisha is relevant because it gives a comparative pattern for Hishām b. ʿUrwa: a famous report about ʿĀʾisha, concentrated around Hishām, useful in later sectarian memory, and difficult to trace securely behind him. “None of the hadiths can be traced back to Medina in the 7th or 8th centuries CE; they cannot be traced to earlier generations in Iraq either. All versions of the hadith trace back to an ur-version, with Hisham’s version being the most widespread.” The comparison does not collapse the bewitchment report into the marital-age report. It highlights a recurring pattern: Hishām sits at the center of more than one ʿĀʾisha household narration that later communities treated as decisive despite a narrow and ideologically useful recoverable transmission center. Dating the Story: Medinan Polemic or Iraqi Reshaping? The bewitchment report makes best sense as a story that developed in a Medinan polemical memory world and then received regional reshaping in Iraq. In the Medinan frame, the Jewish perpetrator, Banū Zurayq, and the well-localization give the story a local anti-Jewish polemical setting. In the Kūfan frame, the same story skeleton is shortened and given a more ʿAlī-centered role. Stage 1 · Medinan story-world Family route and local polemic The report circulates through the ʿUrwa family world with ʿĀʾisha as the household authority. Its details are local: Labīd, Banū Zurayq, the well, the comb, hair-remnants, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the incident. Stage 2 · Kūfan reshaping Compression and ʿAlī-centered action The story appears in a shorter form through al-Aʿmash: the perpetrator is anonymous, the well is unnamed, Gabriel diagnoses the matter, and ʿAlī retrieves and unties the knots. This reconstruction is more modest than saying every transmitter in the chain knowingly lied. It treats the report as a story that moved through transmission environments and changed as it moved. That is precisely why the theological issue cannot be dismissed by simply pointing to the presence of an isnād. What Really Happened? The most plausible history is that the bewitchment story began as a Medinan polemical and household-memory narrative, stabilized through Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s father-from-ʿĀʾisha route, and then spread into broader hadith circulation. Once in the Iraqi environment, it could be abbreviated, recast, or supplied with a more regionally meaningful cast of characters. In that process, the Kūfan version through al-Aʿmash reproduced the broad structure while changing the details most tied to Hishām’s family version. Its evidentiary value is limited: it can show that the story circulated, while still failing to prove the event behind the story. The bewitchment report is too theologically costly and too source-critically concentrated to be treated as secure. Its main detailed form depends on Hishām b. ʿUrwa’s family route, and the al-Aʿmash / Zayd version is a thin, reshaped collateral strand rather than a clean independent witness. A Qurʾān-first method has stronger grounds to reject the story than to reinterpret the Qurʾān around it. title: Battle of the Isnads: Judaism vs. Christianity vs. Islam
description: A visual comparison of three Abrahamic transmission models: Rabbinic Oral Torah, Christian apostolic succession, and the decentralized hadith isnad system.

collectors", kind: "collector", x: 360, y: 150, labelPos: "right" }, ]; { from: "prophet", to: "companions", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "companions", to: "public", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "companions", to: "regional", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "companions", to: "storytellers", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "public", to: "common", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "regional", to: "common", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "storytellers", to: "common", kind: "trunk" }, { from: "common", to: "collectors", kind: "trunk" }, ]; isnād Question under review Is Islam’s chain of transmission actually unique? The popular apologetic answer is yes. The historical answer is more complicated. Named transmission, master-to-student authority, and guarded memory appear across the Abrahamic world. The real question is not whether Islam had chains, but what kind of social machine those chains belonged to. There is a famous line attributed to the early Muslim scholar ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak: *"The isnād is part of the religion; if not for the isnād, whoever wanted could say whatever they wanted."* In modern apologetics, this line often becomes a civilizational claim. Islam, we are told, invented the serious chain of transmission and therefore produced a uniquely secure historical record of the Prophet's words. The problem is that the basic idea is older and broader than the Islamic hadith sciences. Rabbinic Judaism framed the Oral Torah as a received chain from Moses through judges, prophets, priests, sages, and rabbinic courts. Christianity defended orthodoxy through apostolic succession, tracing bishops and teachers back to the original disciples of Jesus. Islam certainly developed a massive technical apparatus around isnād, but the Abrahamic logic of sacred teaching moving through named authorities was not born in the third Islamic century. 01 Rabbinic Judaism Oral Torah is imagined as a guarded chain from Sinai through Moses, Joshua, elders, prophets, and sages. Model: priestly-rabbinic custody 02 Christianity Apostolic succession anchors orthodoxy in bishops and teachers who claim continuity with Jesus' disciples. Model: institutional succession 03 Islamic hadith Hadith transmission spreads through a much wider marketplace of Companions, Successors, students, jurists, storytellers, and regional transmitters. Model: mass decentralization The isnād is not a uniquely Islamic invention. Islam’s distinctive feature was the scale and later technical refinement of isnād criticism. Structurally, however, the early hadith network was less centralized than the Rabbinic and Christian models, which makes the Islamic system more exposed to regional, political, legal, and sectarian fabrication. ## The Judaic isnād: Oral Torah as guarded succession In Rabbinic Judaism, the Written Torah is not treated as a self-contained legal manual. It is paired with an Oral Torah: the interpretive and practical tradition by which the written commandments were understood, applied, debated, and transmitted. The rabbinic claim is that Moses received not only written instruction, but also an oral explanation that moved from generation to generation through recognized authorities. "The Lord said to Moses, 'Come up to me on the mountain and stay here, and I will give you the tablets of stone, with the law and commandments I have written for their instruction.'" "Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom because Moses had laid his hands on him. So the Israelites listened to him and did what the Lord had commanded Moses." Maimonides gives this tradition a remarkably isnād-like shape in the introduction to the *Mishneh Torah*. The chain begins with Moses and then passes through Joshua, the elders, prophets, courts, and sages until the codification of the Mishnah by Judah ha-Nasi. Whatever one thinks of the historical reliability of the claim, the structure is unmistakable: authority is justified through named continuity. The point is not that every link in the rabbinic chain can be historically verified. The point is that Judaism already had the religious idea of transmitted authority: a teaching is protected because it passes through an authorized line of masters. That is the same conceptual family as isnād, even if the later Islamic sciences developed a different technical vocabulary. ## The Christian isnād: apostolic succession as institutional memory Christianity also developed a chain model. Early Christians did not only argue from scripture. They argued from succession: the true teaching is what the churches received from the apostles, and the reliable churches are the ones whose bishops and teachers can be traced back to those apostolic founders. "And I tell you that you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not overcome it." The most famous lines are the Petrine and Johannine claims. One chain runs through Peter into the Roman memory of episcopal succession. Another runs through John, Polycarp, and Irenaeus. This is not isnād in the Muslim technical sense, but it performs a very similar apologetic function: it tells the audience that doctrine did not appear out of nowhere. It came through a recoverable chain of named witnesses and authorized teachers. Petrine lane Jesus → Peter → Clement of Rome → Roman episcopal memory Johannine lane Jesus → John → Polycarp → Irenaeus of Lyons In both Judaism and Christianity, transmission was guarded by a professional class: rabbis, courts, priests, bishops, and formally recognized teachers. These structures did not make the traditions automatically true, but they did restrict who could plausibly speak in the name of the inherited tradition. The social filter was part of the claim. ## The Islamic comparison: a stronger technique built over a weaker social field Islamic hadith transmission is different. It eventually produced a vast technical literature: narrator evaluation, defect analysis, route comparison, grading terminology, and large biographical dictionaries. On paper, this looks more precise than the Jewish or Christian models. The problem is the field over which this technique was applied. Early hadith transmission was not restricted to a priestly class or a centralized episcopal hierarchy. Reports circulated through Companions, Successors, jurists, family networks, regional schools, clients, freedmen, merchants, soldiers, storytellers, and polemicists. The same openness that traditionalists celebrate as communal preservation also created a massive opening for contamination. Transmission model Social filter Main vulnerability Rabbinic Oral Torah Sinai → Moses → elders / prophets / sages Elite rabbinic and judicial custody Retrospective idealization of an ancient chain Apostolic succession Jesus → apostles → bishops / teachers Institutional churches and episcopal memory Doctrinal control can preserve orthodoxy while filtering rival memories Hadith isnād Prophet → public transmitters → regional routes → compilers Broad and decentralized transmission market Large-scale circulation before later technical filtering A chain does not become secure simply because it contains names. Its strength depends on independence, motive, institutional control, recoverable chronology, and whether the alleged early layer is visible before later transmitters had reasons to create it. ## The vulnerability of democratization Traditional Muslim scholarship often presents the enormous number of transmitters as a sign of strength. The more narrators, the more preservation. The more chains, the more certainty. But volume and reliability are not the same thing. A large network can preserve memory, but it can also amplify rumor, legal argument, sectarian propaganda, political praise, apocalyptic expectation, and pious storytelling. The hadith ecosystem contained material from many social locations: Public circulation Reports moved through mosques, study circles, family memory, legal debate, and regional teaching networks. Weak gatekeeping Early circulation did not depend on one centralized guild capable of deciding who could speak for the tradition. Political pressure Virtue reports, prophecy reports, sectarian claims, and legal proof-texts could serve concrete communal interests. Late filtering The famous compilers worked after generations of circulation, reconstruction, regional stabilization, and dispute. This is why the later hadith sciences should be read as a reaction to a problem, not simply as proof that the problem had been solved. The technical system became necessary because the transmission environment was already crowded, unstable, and full of competing claims. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim were not standing at the beginning of Prophetic memory. They were operating after a long period in which reports had already moved, mutated, and acquired authority in different circles. Judaism and Christianity also have serious historical problems. Their chains are not automatically reliable because they are older or more centralized. The comparison here is narrower: when Muslim apologists claim that Islam uniquely solved transmission through isnād, they ignore that other Abrahamic traditions also used chain-based authority, and that the Islamic hadith field was unusually decentralized before the great filtering projects appeared. ## What the comparison actually shows The real difference is not “chain” versus “no chain.” All three traditions used chain logic. The difference is the relationship between chain, institution, and public circulation. Judaism presents a sacred legal tradition guarded by recognized sages and courts. Christianity presents a church memory guarded through apostolic succession and episcopal continuity. Islamic hadith presents a sprawling report culture in which later critics tried to reconstruct reliability through the names, reputations, routes, and defects of transmitters. Not unique Chain-based authority appears across Abrahamic traditions. Not useless Isnād can still reveal routes, bottlenecks, regional spread, and later editing. Not certainty A chain is evidence to analyze, not a certificate that converts human memory into revelation. The isnād is an ancient Abrahamic tool, not a uniquely Islamic invention. Islam’s achievement was not inventing the idea of transmitted authority, but building an enormous technical discipline around it. Yet the scale and openness of early hadith transmission also made the system vulnerable. The Sunni hadith sciences look less like a pristine preservation machine and more like a later attempt to sort, rank, and rescue a report-culture that had already become decentralized, competitive, and crowded with forged or reshaped material. { .battle-intro, .system-grid, .chain-lanes, .comparison-board, .risk-grid, .takeaway-strip { box-sizing: border-box;
