sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: In modern Islamic discourse, few topics are as actively suppressed as the question of classical racial hierarchy. Today, Muslims universally (and correctly) preach that Islam is a colorblind religion, pointing to the egalitarian message of the Quran. But when we open the theological manuals of the classical Sunni era, we find an entirely different religion. Some of the most revered authorities in Sunni history presented a formalized doctrine of Arab supremacy, framing it not as a cultural preference, but as an essential pillar of orthodox Islamic belief (*ʿAqīdah*). Perhaps the most unabashed defender of this racial hierarchy was **Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyah** (1263–1328 CE). His writings on Arab superiority raise devastating questions about the theological integrity of classical Sunnism when examined alongside the clear teachings of the Quran. ## The Doctrine of Arab Supremacy In his foundational work, *Iqtiḍāʾ al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm mukhālafat aṣḥāb al-jaḥīm* (The Requirement of the Straight Path for Opposing the People of Hellfire), Ibn Taymiyah dedicates an entire chapter to establishing the divinely ordained superiority of the Arab race. What makes his position particularly damning is that he does not present this as his personal opinion. He attributes this racist theology to the absolute consensus of mainstream Sunnism. **Ibn Taymiyah on the Sunni Consensus (Iqtiḍāʾ, Vol. 1, p. 419):** "What the people of Sunnah and the community (Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamāʿah) hold is the belief that the Arab race is superior to the non-Arab races—be they Hebrews, Syriacs, Romans, Persians, or others." Ibn Taymiyah constructs a rigid, divine caste system: Arabs are inherently superior to all non-Arabs; the Quraysh tribe is superior to other Arabs; the Banu Hashim are superior to other Quraysh. Lest modern apologists try to excuse this by claiming he only meant Arabs were superior *because* the Prophet was an Arab, Ibn Taymiyah explicitly shuts that defense down. He argues their superiority is genetic and intrinsic: > *"And the superiority of the Arabs, then of Quraysh, then of Banu Hashim, is not merely because the Prophet was from among them... but rather, they are inherently the best in and of themselves."* (Vol. 1, p. 420) He then goes so far as to excommunicate those who advocate for racial equality (the *Shuʿūbiyyah* movement), labeling them as heretics and innovators: > *"We do not adopt the view of the Shuʿūbiyyah and the base-born mawālī (non-Arab converts) who do not love the Arabs and do not acknowledge their virtue—for their view is an innovation (bidʿah) and contrary to the truth."* (Vol. 1, p. 421) ## The Quranic Annihilation of Racism When we turn to the Quran, we find a text that actively dismantles the very racial hierarchy Ibn Taymiyah spent pages trying to build. The Quran establishes human equality as a biological and spiritual fact. The most direct and famous contradiction to Ibn Taymiyah's orthodox racism is found in Surah Al-Hujurat: This verse destroys the classical Sunni framework of ethnic supremacy on three fronts: 1. **Common Origin:** All humans share the exact same biological start ("a male and a female"). 2. **Horizontal, Not Vertical Diversity:** Tribes and nations exist "that you may recognize one another," not so that one may subjugate or claim inherent superiority over the other. 3. **The Ultimate Criterion:** The *only* measure of superiority in God's sight is righteousness (*Taqwā*), an internal state of piety, not an external bloodline. Furthermore, the Quran presents linguistic and racial diversity not as a hierarchy of divine preference, but as an aesthetic sign of God's creative power: ## Point-by-Point Matrix: Taymiyah vs. The Quran Ibn Taymiyah (Classical Sunnism) The Quran The Basis of Superiority: Arabs are "inherently the best in and of themselves" by divine genetic selection. The Basis of Superiority: "The best among you in the sight of God is the most righteous." (49:13) The Purpose of Diversity: To establish a racial hierarchy with Arabs at the top, narrowing down to the Quraysh elite. The Purpose of Diversity: "That you may recognize one another." (49:13) A horizontal plane of mutual appreciation. Faith and Ethnicity: "Love for the Arabs is faith, and hatred for them is hypocrisy." Faith and Ethnicity: "Anyone who works righteousness, whether male or female, while believing, we will surely grant them a happy life." (16:97) Faith has no ethnic requirement. Divine Selection: God selected the Arab race over Romans, Persians, and Syriacs. Divine Selection: The Quran is guidance "for all the people" (39:41), with no preferential ethnic status. ## A Systemic Theological Infection It is crucial to understand that Ibn Taymiyah was not a lone extremist operating in a vacuum. This doctrine of Arab supremacy infected centuries of Islamic scholarship. It was a cultural bias born out of the Umayyad and Abbasid empires, retroactively justified by fabricating hadiths and writing theological treatises. Respected scholars produced an entire genre of literature dedicated to this racial hierarchy: - **Ibn Qutaybah** wrote *The Virtue of the Arabs and a Note on Their Sciences*. - **Al-ʿIrāqī** wrote *The Path to Nearness in the Virtue of the Arabs*. - **Al-Haythamī** authored treatises on Arab excellence. - **Marʿī al-Karmī** wrote *The Cast Gold on the Virtue of the Arabs and the Nobility of Knowledge over Lineage*. All of these works represent a long, dark tradition where classical scholars treated Arab supremacy as an established religious fact. ## The Irony of Harran There is a profound irony in Ibn Taymiyah's rabid defense of Arab supremacy: **He was not an Arab.** Taqī al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyah was born in 1263 CE in the city of Harran (located in modern-day southeastern Turkey), a region deeply influenced by Turkic, Kurdish, and Syriac populations. His family fled southwest to Damascus to escape the advancing Mongol armies. That a scholar of Turkish/Levantine origins, living under the protection of the Mamluks (a dynasty of freed Turkic and Circassian slaves), would author a theological defense of Arab genetic superiority shows how deeply this imperial propaganda had penetrated the Sunni psyche. It was no longer just Arab tribalism; it had become codified orthodoxy. When a theological tradition elevates the bloodline of the Quraysh above the egalitarian clarity of the Quran, that tradition has lost its moral compass. Ibn Taymiyah's defense of Arab supremacy is not just a relic of medieval cultural bias—it is a direct theological challenge to the justice of God. If the Quran truly is the supreme criterion (*al-Furqān*), then classical Sunni racism must be categorically rejected as an anti-Quranic innovation.

It was no longer just Arab tribalism; it had become codified orthodoxy. When a theological tradition elevates the bloodline of the Quraysh above the egalitarian clarity of the Quran, that tradition has lost its moral compass. Ibn Taymiyah's defense of Arab supremacy is not just a relic of medieval cultural bias—it is a direct theological challenge to the justice of God. If the Quran truly is the supreme criterion (*al-Furqān*), then classical Sunni racism must be categorically rejected as an anti-Quranic innovation.

The argument writes itself: impoverished Bedouins of the desert could never have been expected to build skyscrapers, so the rise of Dubai and Riyadh fulfills a prediction no human could have made. The conclusion is that the Prophet knew the future, and that the corpus carrying his words is therefore trustworthy. The reading inverts the report. The line is not a forecast of a glorious future. It is a complaint about a present, and the present it complains about is the wealth that the Arab conquests dumped into the garrison cities of Iraq. Its natural home is the literature of *zuhd*, the ascetic preaching that warned the new Muslim rich against pouring their conquest spoils into stone and mortar. The Qurʾān itself frames building-rivalry not as a marvel to be predicted but as a vice to be condemned: When the prophet Hūd rebukes the people of ʿĀd, the charge is precisely that they "build on every hill a mansion for vanity's sake" and "set up buildings as if they will last forever." Lavish construction is the scriptural emblem of worldly heedlessness. A saying that lists "competing in tall buildings" among the omens of moral decline is not predicting the Burj Khalifa; it is preaching the same sermon as Sūrat al-Takāthur. Read in that light, four things become clear, and this article takes them in order: the report fails the apologists' own test for a genuine prophecy; its wording will not hold still; its two supposedly independent Companion chains collapse into a single Iraqi source; and what it actually targets is the documented building-and-luxury boom of Umayyad Iraq that the Kūfan ascetics were already lamenting in the mouth of Khabbāb b. al-Aratt. ## The Faulty Logic and Fallacies Before reaching the real origin of the report, it is worth meeting the apologetic on its own ground. The defenders of the prophecy supply four criteria a prediction must satisfy to count as genuine: 1. It must be unintuitive, not something easily expected to happen. 2. It must carry risk, meaning it is falsifiable and could have turned out false. 3. It must be specific, not so vague that any later event can be read into it. 4. A true prophet of God cannot get a prophecy wrong. The "tall buildings" report fails the first three on its own terms. **It is not unintuitive.** Tall and elaborate building was never alien to the Arabs. The Nabataeans, desert Arabs themselves, carved al-Khazneh at Petra and the monumental tombs of al-Ḥijr (Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ) centuries before Islam, the latter named in the Qurʾān. The Quraysh ran caravans into Byzantine Syria, Ghassānid and Lakhmid courts, Ḥimyarite Yemen, and Sasanian Iraq, and the tradition itself has the Prophet travelling these routes as a merchant. A man who had seen the palaces of Hira and the churches of Syria predicting that newly enriched Arabs would build big is not exercising supernatural insight; he is stating the obvious consequence of sudden wealth. **It carries no real risk, because it is not falsifiable.** The report fixes no date, no place, no tribe, and no mechanism. Any group of Arabs that grows wealthy and builds at any point in fourteen centuries can be slotted in after the fact. Had the Gulf stayed poor, the "prophecy" would simply have been attached to some other moment of Arab prosperity. **It is not specific, and its own commentators read it as already fulfilled.** Far from pointing to the twenty-first century, the classical tradition understood the sign to describe something close to the Prophet's own era. Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī says so plainly in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*: قوله: (وحتى يتطاول الناس في البنيان) تقدم في كتاب الإيمان من وجه آخر عن أبي هريرة في سؤال جبريل عن الإيمان قوله في أشراط الساعة: ويتطاول الناس في البنيان، وهي من العلامات التي وقعت عن قُرْبٍ في زمن النبوة، ومعنى التطاول في البنيان أن كلًّا ممن كان يبني بيتًا يريد أن يكون ارتفاعه أعلى من ارتفاع الآخر، ويحتمل أن يكون المراد المباهاة به في الزينة والزخرفة أو أعم من ذلك، وقد وُجد الكثير من ذلك وهو في ازدياد. "His words, 'and that people will compete in building,' were given earlier in the Book of Faith by another route from Abū Hurayra, in the questioning of Gabriel about faith, among the portents of the Hour. This is among the signs that occurred close to the time of prophethood. The meaning of 'competing in building' is that each man who built a house wanted it higher than the next man's, and it may mean vying in ornament and decoration, or something broader. Much of that has already occurred, and it keeps increasing." The tradition's own master commentator does not reach for a future Arabia. He says the sign already happened, near the Prophet's own time, and the only thing it describes is people building competitively higher and more ornately than one another. That is not a window into 2024. It is a description of the building boom of the first Islamic century. Why a first-century Muslim moralist would single that out, and project it onto the lips of the Prophet, is the question the rest of this article answers. ## The wording will not hold still A genuine dictum, transmitted as the fixed speech of a prophet, should arrive in a stable form. This one does not. Even within the single family of chains that runs through one Kūfan transmitter, the central image mutates from telling to telling. Compare the sign clause across the canonical books: Collection (same Abū Zurʿa source) Who competes in building Paired sign Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50 "the herders of the black camels " (ruʿāt al-ibil al-buhm) the slave-girl bears her master Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8e "the herders of the black beasts " (riʿāʾ al-bahm) the naked, barefoot become "heads of the people" Sunan Ibn Mājah 64, 4044 "the herders of the sheep " (riʿāʾ al-ghanam) the barefoot, naked become "heads of the people" Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 10 (no building clause at all here) "the barefoot, naked, deaf and dumb become kings of the earth " Musnad Aḥmad 9128 (a different Companion route) "the hungry vie (yatabārawn) in building" the shepherds of sheep become "heads of the people" The herd cannot decide whether it is camels, black beasts, or sheep. The destitute alternately become "heads of the people," "kings of the earth," or are described as "deaf and dumb." The building clause itself sometimes drops out, replaced by "kings of the earth." Even the verb shifts, from "compete in height" (yataṭāwalūn) to "vie" (yatabārawn). This is the behavior of a circulating homiletic motif that each narrator paraphrased to taste, not the behavior of a fixed prophetic sentence preserved word for word. The two oldest forms read in full show how the line floats inside the larger "questioning of the Prophet" frame: قَالَ: مَتَى السَّاعَةُ؟ قَالَ: «مَا الْمَسْئُولُ عَنْهَا بِأَعْلَمَ مِنَ السَّائِلِ، وَسَأُخْبِرُكَ عَنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا: إِذَا وَلَدَتِ الْأَمَةُ رَبَّهَا، وَإِذَا تَطَاوَلَ رُعَاةُ الْإِبِلِ الْبُهْمُ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ، فِي خَمْسٍ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ إِلَّا اللَّهُ». He asked, "When is the Hour?" He said, "The one asked knows no more than the questioner, but I will tell you of its portents: when the slave-girl gives birth to her master, and when the herders of the black camels compete in tall building, among five things none knows but God." وَلَكِنْ سَأُحَدِّثُكَ عَنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا: إِذَا وَلَدَتِ الْأَمَةُ رَبَّتَهَا فَذَلِكَ مِنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا، وَإِذَا تَطَاوَلَ رِعَاءُ الْغَنَمِ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ فَذَلِكَ مِنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا، فِي خَمْسٍ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ إِلَّا اللَّهُ. "But I will tell you of its portents: when the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, that is one of its portents; and when the herders of the sheep compete in tall building, that is one of its portents, among five things none knows but God." Same transmitter, same teacher (Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī), same book-keeper (Ibn ʿUlayya), and yet the camels of Bukhārī have become the sheep of Ibn Mājah. The text is plastic. ## Two "independent" Companions, one Iraqi source The apologetic leans on the claim that this sign reaches us through two separate Companions, Abū Hurayra and ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, which would make it multiply attested. It does carry two Companion names. But isnād analysis shows that the two are not independent witnesses to anything. Each "family" of chains narrows to a single Iraqi successor, and the two successors were exact contemporaries working the same material. ### Family one: Abū Hurayra, through the Kūfan Abū Zurʿa Every prophetic chain in the Abū Hurayra family passes through one man, **Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī**, a Kūfan successor and grandson of the Companion Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī. Below him the report fans out into Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Mājah, Nasāʾī, Aḥmad, and Ibn Ḥibbān through three of his Kūfan students. Above him there is a single strand to Abū Hurayra. ### Family two: ʿUmar, through the Baṣran Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar The ʿUmar family looks independent on paper, with a chain climbing through Ibn ʿUmar to ʿUmar himself. But it too narrows to one man, **Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar**, a Baṣran who became the judge of Merv. And his version is not a bare report. In every single recension it is welded to a frame that gives the game away: the famous story of Yaḥyā setting out with Ḥumayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān to confront Ibn ʿUmar over the *qadar* heresy of **Maʿbad al-Juhanī**, "the first to speak about qadar in Baṣra." That frame is decisive for dating. Maʿbad al-Juhanī's qadar agitation, and his execution after the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath, belong to the 80s AH. A report whose narrative casing is a Baṣran heresy dispute of the 80s cannot be an untouched dictation from the Prophet's majlis. It is a composition of that generation, in that city, attached to the Gabriel scene. ### The rijāl: contemporaries, not corroborators The two "independent" sources turn out to be a matched pair of middle successors, one in Kūfa and one in Baṣra, ranked in the very same generational layer by Ibn Ḥajar: Common link Region Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī (Family 1) Kūfa "Thiqa, of the third ṭabaqa." His given name is so uncertain that it is reported as Haram, ʿAmr, ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, or Jarīr. Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar (Family 2) Baṣra, then qāḍī of Merv "Thiqa, eloquent, and he used to transmit in mursal form (kāna yursil) , of the third ṭabaqa; died before 100, and it is said after." Both men sit in the third ṭabaqa, the middle successors. They are not a Companion and an unrelated Companion separated by chance; they are two contemporaries of the same generation, in the two neighboring garrison cities, both circulating the identical sign-cluster inside the identical "stranger questions the Prophet about Islam, Īmān, Iḥsān, and the Hour" frame. Yaḥyā in particular is flagged by Ibn Ḥajar as a transmitter who narrated *mursal*, that is, comfortable supplying a chain across a gap. He is also, in his own report, the protagonist who personally manufactures the ascent: it is he who "set out and met Ibn ʿUmar" and drew the saying up to ʿUmar. This is not two independent attestations of a prediction. It is a single Iraqi tradition with two faces. The Kūfan face (Abū Zurʿa, attributed to Abū Hurayra) carries the sign in the bare Gabriel frame. The Baṣran face (Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar, attributed to ʿUmar) carries the same sign in the same frame, but bolted onto an anti-qadarī polemic of the 80s AH and routed to a second, prestigious Companion. The most economical reading is the one the matn forces: the floating Kūfan sign-material reached Baṣra, where Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar gave it a fresh isnād up to ʿUmar through Ibn ʿUmar, producing the appearance of independent corroboration where there was only one source. Two names, one origin, no prophecy. ## What the saying was actually fighting If the sign is not a forecast, what was the moralist who first told it reacting to? The answer is sitting in the canon, in the mouth of a Companion who settled in the same Kūfa that produced Abū Zurʿa: **Khabbāb b. al-Aratt**, an early Muslim, a Badr veteran, and a man who lived to see the conquest wealth arrive. His lament is the prose key to the "tall buildings" sign. دَخَلْنَا عَلَى خَبَّابٍ نَعُودُهُ وَقَدِ اكْتَوَى سَبْعَ كَيَّاتٍ، فَقَالَ: إِنَّ أَصْحَابَنَا الَّذِينَ سَلَفُوا مَضَوْا وَلَمْ تَنْقُصْهُمُ الدُّنْيَا، وَإِنَّا أَصَبْنَا مَا لَا نَجِدُ لَهُ مَوْضِعًا إِلَّا التُّرَابَ، وَلَوْلَا أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ نَهَانَا أَنْ نَدْعُوَ بِالْمَوْتِ لَدَعَوْتُ بِهِ. ثُمَّ أَتَيْنَاهُ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى وَهُوَ يَبْنِي حَائِطًا لَهُ، فَقَالَ: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمَ لَيُؤْجَرُ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ يُنْفِقُهُ إِلَّا فِي شَيْءٍ يَجْعَلُهُ فِي هَذَا التُّرَابِ. "We came to Khabbāb to visit him, and he had been cauterized seven times. He said: 'Our companions who went before us departed, and the world did not diminish their reward; but we have acquired wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust. Were it not that the Prophet forbade us to pray for death, I would pray for it.' Then we came to him another time while he was building a wall of his, and he said: 'The Muslim is rewarded for everything he spends, except for something he puts into this dust.'" This is the whole thesis in one report. The conquests have made the early Muslims wealthy past the point of knowing what to do with it ("we have acquired wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust"), and the one outlet is building, which Khabbāb is shown literally doing ("while he was building a wall of his") even as he condemns it as the one expenditure that earns no reward. The "dust" (turāb) is mortar and foundation. Building is figured as the sink into which surplus conquest wealth is poured, and figured as spiritually worthless. The barefoot shepherds "competing in tall buildings" are the same complaint dramatized as an omen. And the chain is the giveaway. Trace it: **Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid ← Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim ← Khabbāb**. Every link is Kūfan, and two of the three carry the same tribal nisba, al-Bajalī, as Abū Zurʿa, the common link of the building-sign itself. The Khabbāb wealth-lament and the building-sign were circulating in the same Kūfan ascetic milieu, in the same families. Link in the Khabbāb chain Profile (Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb) Khabbāb b. al-Aratt Companion, early Muslim, settled and died in Kūfa. Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim al-Bajalī "Thiqa, of the second ṭabaqa, mukhaḍram" (lived through the Jāhiliyya and Islam); senior Kūfan successor. Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid al-Aḥmasī al-Bajalī "Thiqa thabt, of the fourth ṭabaqa, died 146." Kūfan. There is even a tell that the building-condemnation was an editorial layer added to the Kūfan tradition rather than its original core. In Muslim's recension of the very same chain, only the "do not wish for death" portion survives; the building clause is absent: دَخَلْنَا عَلَى خَبَّابٍ وَقَدِ اكْتَوَى سَبْعَ كَيَّاتٍ فِي بَطْنِهِ، فَقَالَ: لَوْلَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ نَهَانَا أَنْ نَدْعُوَ بِالْمَوْتِ لَدَعَوْتُ بِهِ. "We came to Khabbāb, and he had been cauterized seven times on his belly. He said: 'Were it not that the Messenger of God forbade us to pray for death, I would pray for it.'" So even within the Kūfan transmission, the anti-building moral was a clause that some narrators raised and others did not. The Kūfan tradents took a Companion's deathbed remark and built onto it the lesson that worldly construction is the one valueless expenditure. That is the workshop in which the "tall buildings" sign was made. ### The wider ascetic chorus Khabbāb is not alone. The same anti-building sentiment runs through a cluster of *zuhd* reports, where the Prophet is made to frown on construction itself: مَرَّ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِقُبَّةٍ عَلَى بَابِ رَجُلٍ مِنَ الْأَنْصَارِ، فَقَالَ: «مَا هَذِهِ؟» قَالُوا: قُبَّةٌ بَنَاهَا فُلَانٌ. فَقَالَ: «كُلُّ مَالٍ يَكُونُ هَكَذَا فَهُوَ وَبَالٌ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ». فَبَلَغَ الْأَنْصَارِيَّ ذَلِكَ فَوَضَعَهَا … وَفِي رواية: «أَمَا إِنَّ كُلَّ بِنَاءٍ وَبَالٌ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ إِلَّا مَا لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ». The Messenger of God passed a dome over the door of a man of the Anṣār and asked, "What is this?" They said, "A dome so-and-so built." He said, "Every wealth spent like this is a burden on its owner on the Day of Resurrection." When the Anṣārī heard, he tore it down … In another wording: "Every building is a burden on its owner, except what is indispensable." The pattern is unmistakable. A first-century ascetic current, strongest in Iraq, taught that building beyond bare need was a spiritual liability. It generated the dome story, the "every building is a burden" maxim, the Khabbāb wealth-lament, and, dressed as an omen of the Hour, the "barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings." These are not separate facts about the future; they are one moral campaign against one target. ## The target was real: the building boom of Umayyad Iraq That target is not hypothetical. The conquests really did pour the treasure of two empires into Iraq, and the new Muslim elite really did spend it on monumental building, exactly in the cities where these reports were forged. The ascetics were not predicting a building craze; they were watching one. **The spoils.** When the Muslims took Ctesiphon (al-Madāʾin), they stood before the white palace and arch of Khusraw and saw wealth on a scale they had no category for. The chroniclers record the carpet and crown of Khusraw carried to ʿUmar in Medina, and treasuries counted in the billions of dirhams. This is the windfall Khabbāb meant by "wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust." وَلَمَّا شَاهَدَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ إِيوَانَ كِسْرَى كَبَّرُوا، وَقَالُوا: هَذَا أَبْيَضُ كِسْرَى … وَوُجِدَ فِي بُيُوتِ أَمْوَالِ كِسْرَى مَا لَا يُحْصَى مِنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ وَالتُّحَفِ. "When the Muslims beheld the arch of Khusraw they cried 'God is greatest' and said, 'This is the White Palace of Khusraw' … and in the treasuries of Khusraw was found wealth, jewels, and treasures beyond counting." **The garrison cities turn to stone.** Baṣra and Kūfa began as encampments of reed and clay. Within a generation the conquest money rebuilt them in baked brick. al-Balādhurī records that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī first built the mosque and governor's residence (Dār al-Imāra) of Baṣra in mud-brick, clay, and thatch, and that **Ziyād b. Abīhi** then rebuilt them in gypsum and fired brick, monumental enough that al-Ḥajjāj later wished to strike Ziyād's name off the building. وَبَنَى أَبُو مُوسَى الْأَشْعَرِيُّ الْمَسْجِدَ وَدَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ بِاللَّبِنِ وَالطِّينِ وَسَقَفَهَا بِالْعُشْبِ … [ثُمَّ] بَنَى زِيَادٌ دَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ بِالْبَصْرَةِ … فَلَمَّا قَدِمَ الْحَجَّاجُ بْنُ يُوسُفَ الْعِرَاقَ أُخْبِرَ أَنَّ زِيَادًا ابْتَنَى دَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ، فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يُزِيلَ اسْمَهُ عَنْهَا، فَهَمَّ بِبِنَائِهَا بِجِصٍّ وَآجُرٍّ. "Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī built the mosque and the governor's residence of mud-brick and clay, and roofed them with thatch … Then Ziyād built the governor's residence of Baṣra [anew] … and when al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf came to Iraq and was told that Ziyād had built the residence, he wished to erase his name from it, and resolved to rebuild it in gypsum and fired brick." **The palaces of the governors.** The most spectacular case is al-Ḥajjāj's green-domed palace at the new city of Wāsiṭ, which delighted him "as no building ever had." The episode is preserved with a punchline that no commentary could improve: a captured Khārijite, brought before al-Ḥajjāj and gazing at the construction, throws the Qurʾān's own anti-building verse in his face. أُتِيَ الْحَجَّاجُ بِرَجُلٍ مِنَ الْخَوَارِجِ وَهُوَ فِي خَضْرَاءِ وَاسِطٍ، فَلَمَّا مَثُلَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى بُنْيَانِهِ فَقَالَ: ﴿أَتَبْنُونَ بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ آيَةً تَعْبَثُونَ وَتَتَّخِذُونَ مَصَانِعَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَخْلُدُونَ﴾ … وَكَانَ الْحَجَّاجُ قَدْ بَنَى خَضْرَاءَ وَاسِطٍ فَأَعْجَبَتْهُ مَا لَمْ يُعْجِبْهُ بِنَاءٌ قَطُّ، فَقَالَ لِمَنْ حَوْلَهُ: كَيْفَ تَرَوْنَ قُبَّتِي هَذِهِ؟ A man of the Khārijites was brought before al-Ḥajjāj while he was in the Green Palace of Wāsiṭ. When he stood before him and looked at his building, he recited: "Do you build on every hill a monument for vanity's sake, and take for yourselves strongholds, as if you will last forever?" … al-Ḥajjāj had built the Green Palace of Wāsiṭ, and it pleased him as no building ever had, so he asked those around him: "How do you see this dome of mine?" This single anecdote ties the whole argument into a knot. Here is an Iraqi governor of exactly the era and the cities in question, gazing with pride at the most lavish building of his life, and here is a pious opponent answering him with the very Qurʾānic verse (26:128 to 129) that condemns monumental building as the mark of the doomed. The "barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings" report is the hadith form of that Khārijite's recitation. It is the ascetic and pietist reaction to the Umayyad-Iraqi building boom, turned into an omen and projected back onto the Prophet. **The motif had deep roots in Iraq.** The Arabs of Iraq did not even need to invent the idea that monumental building is vanity doomed to ruin. It was the most famous local legend they had. Beside Kūfa stood the Lakhmid palaces of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr, and the proverbial tale of their builder-king, al-Nuʿmān, who looked out from his tower over all his wealth and dominion and was struck by its transience, then renounced the world. The poet ʿAdī b. Zayd fixed it as a maxim: وَتَذَكَّرَ رَبَّ الْخَوَرْنَقِ إِذْ أَشْـ ـرَفَ يَوْمًا وَلِلْهُدَى تَفْكِيرُ سَرَّهُ مَالُهُ وَكَثْرَةُ مَا يَمْـ ـلِكُ وَالْبَحْرُ مُعْرِضٌ وَالسَّدِيرُ "And remember the lord of al-Khawarnaq, when he looked out one day, and was moved to think on guidance: his wealth had delighted him, and the abundance of his possessions, with the sea stretched before him and al-Sadīr." The lesson that the proud builder's monument is vanity was, quite literally, the view from the edge of Kūfa. When a Kūfan or Baṣran moralist of the first century watched the conquest fortunes rise into brick and dome around him, he had both a live target and a ready cultural script. The "tall buildings" sign is what he produced. ## Verdict The report that "barefoot, naked shepherds will compete in tall buildings" is not a prophecy of Gulf skyscrapers. It is a piece of first-century Iraqi ascetic preaching, condemning the wealth and monumental building that the conquests poured into Kūfa and Baṣra, and projected back onto the Prophet in the Gabriel scene. It fails the apologists' own criteria: building was never beyond the Arabs (Petra, al-Ḥijr), the claim fixes no testable detail, and the tradition's own commentator, Ibn Ḥajar, says the sign already occurred near the Prophet's time. Its matn will not hold still, sliding between camels, black beasts, and sheep, and between "heads of the people" and "kings of the earth," which is the signature of a paraphrased homiletic motif, not a fixed dictum. Its two "independent" Companion attestations collapse into a single source: the Kūfan common link Abū Zurʿa al-Bajalī (in the name of Abū Hurayra), paralleled by the Baṣran common link Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar (in the name of ʿUmar), an exact contemporary who supplied a fresh chain to ʿUmar and wrapped it in the anti-qadarī Maʿbad al-Juhanī frame of the 80s AH, manufacturing the look of corroboration. What the saying actually condemns is documented history: the spoils of Ctesiphon, Ziyād rebuilding Baṣra's residence in fired brick, and al-Ḥajjāj's green dome at Wāsiṭ, against which a Khārijite recited the Qurʾān's own rebuke of vain building (26:128 to 129). The same Kūfan circle that produced the omen also preserved Khabbāb b. al-Aratt's lament, through the Kūfan chain Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, that the believers had acquired wealth they could only sink "into the dust." The hadith is the sermon of the ascetics, not the foresight of a prophet. [^families]: The two families used here. **Abū Hurayra (Kūfan common link Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr al-Bajalī):** Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50 (Musaddad ← Ismāʿīl b. ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī ← Abū Zurʿa), "camels"; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8e (Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba and Zuhayr ← Ibn ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa), "black beasts," "heads of the people"; Muslim 9 (Ibn Numayr ← Muḥammad b. Bishr ← Abū Ḥayyān), with the concubine gloss on the slave-girl sign; Muslim 10 (Zuhayr ← Jarīr ← ʿUmāra b. al-Qaʿqāʿ ← Abū Zurʿa), "deaf and dumb kings of the earth"; Sunan Ibn Mājah 64 and 4044 (Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba ← Ibn ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa), "sheep"; Sunan al-Nasāʾī 4991 (Muḥammad b. Qudāma ← Jarīr ← Abū Farwa ← Abū Zurʿa ← Abū Hurayra and Abū Dharr), with the "clay bench" frame; Musnad Aḥmad 9501 (Ismāʿīl b. ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa); Ibn Ḥibbān 159 (Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm ← Jarīr ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa). A separate Companion route with a paraphrased matn ("the hungry vie in building") is Aḥmad 9128 (Shahr b. Ḥawshab ← Abū Hurayra). [^umar]: **ʿUmar (Baṣran/Mervi common link Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar), all carrying the Maʿbad al-Juhanī / qadar frame:** Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8 and 8a (Zuhayr ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda ← Yaḥyā; and ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muʿādh ← Muʿādh ← Kahmas); Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4695 (ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muʿādh ← Muʿādh ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2610 (Abū ʿAmmār al-Ḥusayn b. Ḥurayth ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Sunan al-Nasāʾī 4990 (Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm ← al-Naḍr b. Shumayl ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Sunan Ibn Mājah 63 (ʿAlī b. Muḥammad ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Musnad Aḥmad 184 (Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd ← ʿUthmān b. Ghiyāth ← Ibn Burayda); Ibn Ḥibbān 168 (Muḥammad b. al-Minhāl ← Yazīd b. Zurayʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda). Maʿbad al-Juhanī's qadar agitation and his death in the aftermath of the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath place the narrative frame in the 80s AH. [^rijal]: Gradings from Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb: Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa, third ṭabaqa," with his given name unstable across the sources (Haram / ʿAmr / ʿAbd Allāh / ʿAbd al-Raḥmān / Jarīr); Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar al-Baṣrī, judge of Merv, "thiqa, eloquent, used to transmit mursal, third ṭabaqa, died before/after 100"; Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa, second ṭabaqa, mukhaḍram"; Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid al-Aḥmasī al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa thabt, fourth ṭabaqa, died 146." [^khabbab]: The Khabbāb wealth-and-building lament, Kūfan chain Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid ← Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim ← Khabbāb: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5672 (Ādam ← Shuʿba), with both the "wealth we find nowhere to put but the dust" and the wall-building clause; Bukhārī 6431 (Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā ← Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays), "building a wall of his"; Bukhārī 6349 to 6350 (the "do not wish for death" portion); Musnad Aḥmad 21059 (Wakīʿ ← Ibn Abī Khālid ← Qays), "the Muslim is rewarded in everything except what he puts in this dust," again while building a wall; al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr 3635 (ʿAlī b. al-Jaʿd ← Shuʿba ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays), the full version. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2681a (ʿAbd Allāh b. Idrīs ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays) preserves only the death-wish portion without the building clause, showing the anti-building moral to be a clause that some Kūfan narrators raised and others did not. al-Bazzār notes that the building-condemnation wording was raised from the Ismāʿīl-Qays-Khabbāb chain only by Abū Muʿāwiya. [^zuhd]: The wider zuhd-against-building cluster: Sunan Ibn Mājah 4161 (ḥasan), the Anṣārī's dome which he demolishes after the Prophet's rebuke, "every wealth like this is a burden on its owner"; Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5237 (← Anas), the raised dome (qubba mushrifa) the Prophet shuns until it is leveled, ending "every building is a burden on its owner except what is indispensable (illā mā lā budda minhu)"; with parallels in Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭaḥāwī's Sharḥ Mushkil al-Āthār, and al-Bayhaqī's Shuʿab al-Īmān. The Qurʾānic frame is Sūrat al-Takāthur 102:1 to 2 and the rebuke of ʿĀd in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:128 to 129. [^iraq]: On the conquest wealth and the Iraqi building boom: the spoils of al-Madāʾin (Ctesiphon), the carpet and crown of Khusraw, and the "White Palace," in al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh, al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, and Ibn Faḍl Allāh al-ʿUmarī, Masālik al-Abṣār; the rebuilding of Baṣra's Dār al-Imāra by Ziyād b. Abīhi in gypsum and fired brick, al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān; al-Ḥajjāj's Green Palace (al-Khaḍrāʾ) at Wāsiṭ and the Khārijite's recitation of Q 26:128 to 129, Ibn ʿAsākir, Tārīkh Dimashq, and al-Tadhkira al-Ḥamdūniyya; the legend of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr and al-Nuʿmān's renunciation, in the verse of ʿAdī b. Zayd preserved by Ibn ʿAsākir and others.

The argument writes itself: impoverished Bedouins of the desert could never have been expected to build skyscrapers, so the rise of Dubai and Riyadh fulfills a prediction no human could have made. The conclusion is that the Prophet knew the future, and that the corpus carrying his words is therefore trustworthy. The reading inverts the report. The line is not a forecast of a glorious future. It is a complaint about a present, and the present it complains about is the wealth that the Arab conquests dumped into the garrison cities of Iraq. Its natural home is the literature of *zuhd*, the ascetic preaching that warned the new Muslim rich against pouring their conquest spoils into stone and mortar. The Qurʾān itself frames building-rivalry not as a marvel to be predicted but as a vice to be condemned: When the prophet Hūd rebukes the people of ʿĀd, the charge is precisely that they "build on every hill a mansion for vanity's sake" and "set up buildings as if they will last forever." Lavish construction is the scriptural emblem of worldly heedlessness. A saying that lists "competing in tall buildings" among the omens of moral decline is not predicting the Burj Khalifa; it is preaching the same sermon as Sūrat al-Takāthur. Read in that light, four things become clear, and this article takes them in order: the report fails the apologists' own test for a genuine prophecy; its wording will not hold still; its two supposedly independent Companion chains collapse into a single Iraqi source; and what it actually targets is the documented building-and-luxury boom of Umayyad Iraq that the Kūfan ascetics were already lamenting in the mouth of Khabbāb b. al-Aratt. The Faulty Logic and Fallacies Before reaching the real origin of the report, it is worth meeting the apologetic on its own ground. The defenders of the prophecy supply four criteria a prediction must satisfy to count as genuine: 1. It must be unintuitive, not something easily expected to happen. 2. It must carry risk, meaning it is falsifiable and could have turned out false. 3. It must be specific, not so vague that any later event can be read into it. 4. A true prophet of God cannot get a prophecy wrong. The "tall buildings" report fails the first three on its own terms. **It is not unintuitive.** Tall and elaborate building was never alien to the Arabs. The Nabataeans, desert Arabs themselves, carved al-Khazneh at Petra and the monumental tombs of al-Ḥijr (Madāʾin Ṣāliḥ) centuries before Islam, the latter named in the Qurʾān. The Quraysh ran caravans into Byzantine Syria, Ghassānid and Lakhmid courts, Ḥimyarite Yemen, and Sasanian Iraq, and the tradition itself has the Prophet travelling these routes as a merchant. A man who had seen the palaces of Hira and the churches of Syria predicting that newly enriched Arabs would build big is not exercising supernatural insight; he is stating the obvious consequence of sudden wealth. **It carries no real risk, because it is not falsifiable.** The report fixes no date, no place, no tribe, and no mechanism. Any group of Arabs that grows wealthy and builds at any point in fourteen centuries can be slotted in after the fact. Had the Gulf stayed poor, the "prophecy" would simply have been attached to some other moment of Arab prosperity. **It is not specific, and its own commentators read it as already fulfilled.** Far from pointing to the twenty-first century, the classical tradition understood the sign to describe something close to the Prophet's own era. Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī says so plainly in *Fatḥ al-Bārī*: قوله: (وحتى يتطاول الناس في البنيان) تقدم في كتاب الإيمان من وجه آخر عن أبي هريرة في سؤال جبريل عن الإيمان قوله في أشراط الساعة: ويتطاول الناس في البنيان، وهي من العلامات التي وقعت عن قُرْبٍ في زمن النبوة، ومعنى التطاول في البنيان أن كلًّا ممن كان يبني بيتًا يريد أن يكون ارتفاعه أعلى من ارتفاع الآخر، ويحتمل أن يكون المراد المباهاة به في الزينة والزخرفة أو أعم من ذلك، وقد وُجد الكثير من ذلك وهو في ازدياد. "His words, 'and that people will compete in building,' were given earlier in the Book of Faith by another route from Abū Hurayra, in the questioning of Gabriel about faith, among the portents of the Hour. This is among the signs that occurred close to the time of prophethood. The meaning of 'competing in building' is that each man who built a house wanted it higher than the next man's, and it may mean vying in ornament and decoration, or something broader. Much of that has already occurred, and it keeps increasing." The tradition's own master commentator does not reach for a future Arabia. He says the sign already happened, near the Prophet's own time, and the only thing it describes is people building competitively higher and more ornately than one another. That is not a window into 2024. It is a description of the building boom of the first Islamic century. Why a first-century Muslim moralist would single that out, and project it onto the lips of the Prophet, is the question the rest of this article answers. The wording will not hold still A genuine dictum, transmitted as the fixed speech of a prophet, should arrive in a stable form. This one does not. Even within the single family of chains that runs through one Kūfan transmitter, the central image mutates from telling to telling. Compare the sign clause across the canonical books: Collection (same Abū Zurʿa source) Who competes in building Paired sign Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50 "the herders of the black camels " (ruʿāt al-ibil al-buhm) the slave-girl bears her master Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8e "the herders of the black beasts " (riʿāʾ al-bahm) the naked, barefoot become "heads of the people" Sunan Ibn Mājah 64, 4044 "the herders of the sheep " (riʿāʾ al-ghanam) the barefoot, naked become "heads of the people" Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 10 (no building clause at all here) "the barefoot, naked, deaf and dumb become kings of the earth " Musnad Aḥmad 9128 (a different Companion route) "the hungry vie (yatabārawn) in building" the shepherds of sheep become "heads of the people" The herd cannot decide whether it is camels, black beasts, or sheep. The destitute alternately become "heads of the people," "kings of the earth," or are described as "deaf and dumb." The building clause itself sometimes drops out, replaced by "kings of the earth." Even the verb shifts, from "compete in height" (yataṭāwalūn) to "vie" (yatabārawn). This is the behavior of a circulating homiletic motif that each narrator paraphrased to taste, not the behavior of a fixed prophetic sentence preserved word for word. The two oldest forms read in full show how the line floats inside the larger "questioning of the Prophet" frame: قَالَ: مَتَى السَّاعَةُ؟ قَالَ: «مَا الْمَسْئُولُ عَنْهَا بِأَعْلَمَ مِنَ السَّائِلِ، وَسَأُخْبِرُكَ عَنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا: إِذَا وَلَدَتِ الْأَمَةُ رَبَّهَا، وَإِذَا تَطَاوَلَ رُعَاةُ الْإِبِلِ الْبُهْمُ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ، فِي خَمْسٍ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ إِلَّا اللَّهُ». He asked, "When is the Hour?" He said, "The one asked knows no more than the questioner, but I will tell you of its portents: when the slave-girl gives birth to her master, and when the herders of the black camels compete in tall building, among five things none knows but God." وَلَكِنْ سَأُحَدِّثُكَ عَنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا: إِذَا وَلَدَتِ الْأَمَةُ رَبَّتَهَا فَذَلِكَ مِنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا، وَإِذَا تَطَاوَلَ رِعَاءُ الْغَنَمِ فِي الْبُنْيَانِ فَذَلِكَ مِنْ أَشْرَاطِهَا، فِي خَمْسٍ لَا يَعْلَمُهُنَّ إِلَّا اللَّهُ. "But I will tell you of its portents: when the slave-girl gives birth to her mistress, that is one of its portents; and when the herders of the sheep compete in tall building, that is one of its portents, among five things none knows but God." Same transmitter, same teacher (Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī), same book-keeper (Ibn ʿUlayya), and yet the camels of Bukhārī have become the sheep of Ibn Mājah. The text is plastic. Two "independent" Companions, one Iraqi source The apologetic leans on the claim that this sign reaches us through two separate Companions, Abū Hurayra and ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb, which would make it multiply attested. It does carry two Companion names. But isnād analysis shows that the two are not independent witnesses to anything. Each "family" of chains narrows to a single Iraqi successor, and the two successors were exact contemporaries working the same material. Family one: Abū Hurayra, through the Kūfan Abū Zurʿa Every prophetic chain in the Abū Hurayra family passes through one man, **Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī**, a Kūfan successor and grandson of the Companion Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Bajalī. Below him the report fans out into Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Mājah, Nasāʾī, Aḥmad, and Ibn Ḥibbān through three of his Kūfan students. Above him there is a single strand to Abū Hurayra. Family two: ʿUmar, through the Baṣran Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar The ʿUmar family looks independent on paper, with a chain climbing through Ibn ʿUmar to ʿUmar himself. But it too narrows to one man, **Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar**, a Baṣran who became the judge of Merv. And his version is not a bare report. In every single recension it is welded to a frame that gives the game away: the famous story of Yaḥyā setting out with Ḥumayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān to confront Ibn ʿUmar over the *qadar* heresy of **Maʿbad al-Juhanī**, "the first to speak about qadar in Baṣra." That frame is decisive for dating. Maʿbad al-Juhanī's qadar agitation, and his execution after the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath, belong to the 80s AH. A report whose narrative casing is a Baṣran heresy dispute of the 80s cannot be an untouched dictation from the Prophet's majlis. It is a composition of that generation, in that city, attached to the Gabriel scene. The rijāl: contemporaries, not corroborators The two "independent" sources turn out to be a matched pair of middle successors, one in Kūfa and one in Baṣra, ranked in the very same generational layer by Ibn Ḥajar: Common link Region Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī (Family 1) Kūfa "Thiqa, of the third ṭabaqa." His given name is so uncertain that it is reported as Haram, ʿAmr, ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, or Jarīr. Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar (Family 2) Baṣra, then qāḍī of Merv "Thiqa, eloquent, and he used to transmit in mursal form (kāna yursil) , of the third ṭabaqa; died before 100, and it is said after." Both men sit in the third ṭabaqa, the middle successors. They are not a Companion and an unrelated Companion separated by chance; they are two contemporaries of the same generation, in the two neighboring garrison cities, both circulating the identical sign-cluster inside the identical "stranger questions the Prophet about Islam, Īmān, Iḥsān, and the Hour" frame. Yaḥyā in particular is flagged by Ibn Ḥajar as a transmitter who narrated *mursal*, that is, comfortable supplying a chain across a gap. He is also, in his own report, the protagonist who personally manufactures the ascent: it is he who "set out and met Ibn ʿUmar" and drew the saying up to ʿUmar. This is not two independent attestations of a prediction. It is a single Iraqi tradition with two faces. The Kūfan face (Abū Zurʿa, attributed to Abū Hurayra) carries the sign in the bare Gabriel frame. The Baṣran face (Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar, attributed to ʿUmar) carries the same sign in the same frame, but bolted onto an anti-qadarī polemic of the 80s AH and routed to a second, prestigious Companion. The most economical reading is the one the matn forces: the floating Kūfan sign-material reached Baṣra, where Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar gave it a fresh isnād up to ʿUmar through Ibn ʿUmar, producing the appearance of independent corroboration where there was only one source. Two names, one origin, no prophecy. What the saying was actually fighting If the sign is not a forecast, what was the moralist who first told it reacting to? The answer is sitting in the canon, in the mouth of a Companion who settled in the same Kūfa that produced Abū Zurʿa: **Khabbāb b. al-Aratt**, an early Muslim, a Badr veteran, and a man who lived to see the conquest wealth arrive. His lament is the prose key to the "tall buildings" sign. دَخَلْنَا عَلَى خَبَّابٍ نَعُودُهُ وَقَدِ اكْتَوَى سَبْعَ كَيَّاتٍ، فَقَالَ: إِنَّ أَصْحَابَنَا الَّذِينَ سَلَفُوا مَضَوْا وَلَمْ تَنْقُصْهُمُ الدُّنْيَا، وَإِنَّا أَصَبْنَا مَا لَا نَجِدُ لَهُ مَوْضِعًا إِلَّا التُّرَابَ، وَلَوْلَا أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ نَهَانَا أَنْ نَدْعُوَ بِالْمَوْتِ لَدَعَوْتُ بِهِ. ثُمَّ أَتَيْنَاهُ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى وَهُوَ يَبْنِي حَائِطًا لَهُ، فَقَالَ: إِنَّ الْمُسْلِمَ لَيُؤْجَرُ فِي كُلِّ شَيْءٍ يُنْفِقُهُ إِلَّا فِي شَيْءٍ يَجْعَلُهُ فِي هَذَا التُّرَابِ. "We came to Khabbāb to visit him, and he had been cauterized seven times. He said: 'Our companions who went before us departed, and the world did not diminish their reward; but we have acquired wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust. Were it not that the Prophet forbade us to pray for death, I would pray for it.' Then we came to him another time while he was building a wall of his, and he said: 'The Muslim is rewarded for everything he spends, except for something he puts into this dust.'" This is the whole thesis in one report. The conquests have made the early Muslims wealthy past the point of knowing what to do with it ("we have acquired wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust"), and the one outlet is building, which Khabbāb is shown literally doing ("while he was building a wall of his") even as he condemns it as the one expenditure that earns no reward. The "dust" (turāb) is mortar and foundation. Building is figured as the sink into which surplus conquest wealth is poured, and figured as spiritually worthless. The barefoot shepherds "competing in tall buildings" are the same complaint dramatized as an omen. And the chain is the giveaway. Trace it: **Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid ← Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim ← Khabbāb**. Every link is Kūfan, and two of the three carry the same tribal nisba, al-Bajalī, as Abū Zurʿa, the common link of the building-sign itself. The Khabbāb wealth-lament and the building-sign were circulating in the same Kūfan ascetic milieu, in the same families. Link in the Khabbāb chain Profile (Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb) Khabbāb b. al-Aratt Companion, early Muslim, settled and died in Kūfa. Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim al-Bajalī "Thiqa, of the second ṭabaqa, mukhaḍram" (lived through the Jāhiliyya and Islam); senior Kūfan successor. Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid al-Aḥmasī al-Bajalī "Thiqa thabt, of the fourth ṭabaqa, died 146." Kūfan. There is even a tell that the building-condemnation was an editorial layer added to the Kūfan tradition rather than its original core. In Muslim's recension of the very same chain, only the "do not wish for death" portion survives; the building clause is absent: دَخَلْنَا عَلَى خَبَّابٍ وَقَدِ اكْتَوَى سَبْعَ كَيَّاتٍ فِي بَطْنِهِ، فَقَالَ: لَوْلَا أَنَّ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ نَهَانَا أَنْ نَدْعُوَ بِالْمَوْتِ لَدَعَوْتُ بِهِ. "We came to Khabbāb, and he had been cauterized seven times on his belly. He said: 'Were it not that the Messenger of God forbade us to pray for death, I would pray for it.'" So even within the Kūfan transmission, the anti-building moral was a clause that some narrators raised and others did not. The Kūfan tradents took a Companion's deathbed remark and built onto it the lesson that worldly construction is the one valueless expenditure. That is the workshop in which the "tall buildings" sign was made. The wider ascetic chorus Khabbāb is not alone. The same anti-building sentiment runs through a cluster of *zuhd* reports, where the Prophet is made to frown on construction itself: مَرَّ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِقُبَّةٍ عَلَى بَابِ رَجُلٍ مِنَ الْأَنْصَارِ، فَقَالَ: «مَا هَذِهِ؟» قَالُوا: قُبَّةٌ بَنَاهَا فُلَانٌ. فَقَالَ: «كُلُّ مَالٍ يَكُونُ هَكَذَا فَهُوَ وَبَالٌ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ». فَبَلَغَ الْأَنْصَارِيَّ ذَلِكَ فَوَضَعَهَا … وَفِي رواية: «أَمَا إِنَّ كُلَّ بِنَاءٍ وَبَالٌ عَلَى صَاحِبِهِ إِلَّا مَا لَا بُدَّ مِنْهُ». The Messenger of God passed a dome over the door of a man of the Anṣār and asked, "What is this?" They said, "A dome so-and-so built." He said, "Every wealth spent like this is a burden on its owner on the Day of Resurrection." When the Anṣārī heard, he tore it down … In another wording: "Every building is a burden on its owner, except what is indispensable." The pattern is unmistakable. A first-century ascetic current, strongest in Iraq, taught that building beyond bare need was a spiritual liability. It generated the dome story, the "every building is a burden" maxim, the Khabbāb wealth-lament, and, dressed as an omen of the Hour, the "barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings." These are not separate facts about the future; they are one moral campaign against one target. The target was real: the building boom of Umayyad Iraq That target is not hypothetical. The conquests really did pour the treasure of two empires into Iraq, and the new Muslim elite really did spend it on monumental building, exactly in the cities where these reports were forged. The ascetics were not predicting a building craze; they were watching one. **The spoils.** When the Muslims took Ctesiphon (al-Madāʾin), they stood before the white palace and arch of Khusraw and saw wealth on a scale they had no category for. The chroniclers record the carpet and crown of Khusraw carried to ʿUmar in Medina, and treasuries counted in the billions of dirhams. This is the windfall Khabbāb meant by "wealth we find nowhere to put except the dust." وَلَمَّا شَاهَدَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ إِيوَانَ كِسْرَى كَبَّرُوا، وَقَالُوا: هَذَا أَبْيَضُ كِسْرَى … وَوُجِدَ فِي بُيُوتِ أَمْوَالِ كِسْرَى مَا لَا يُحْصَى مِنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْجَوَاهِرِ وَالتُّحَفِ. "When the Muslims beheld the arch of Khusraw they cried 'God is greatest' and said, 'This is the White Palace of Khusraw' … and in the treasuries of Khusraw was found wealth, jewels, and treasures beyond counting." **The garrison cities turn to stone.** Baṣra and Kūfa began as encampments of reed and clay. Within a generation the conquest money rebuilt them in baked brick. al-Balādhurī records that Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī first built the mosque and governor's residence (Dār al-Imāra) of Baṣra in mud-brick, clay, and thatch, and that **Ziyād b. Abīhi** then rebuilt them in gypsum and fired brick, monumental enough that al-Ḥajjāj later wished to strike Ziyād's name off the building. وَبَنَى أَبُو مُوسَى الْأَشْعَرِيُّ الْمَسْجِدَ وَدَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ بِاللَّبِنِ وَالطِّينِ وَسَقَفَهَا بِالْعُشْبِ … [ثُمَّ] بَنَى زِيَادٌ دَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ بِالْبَصْرَةِ … فَلَمَّا قَدِمَ الْحَجَّاجُ بْنُ يُوسُفَ الْعِرَاقَ أُخْبِرَ أَنَّ زِيَادًا ابْتَنَى دَارَ الْإِمَارَةِ، فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يُزِيلَ اسْمَهُ عَنْهَا، فَهَمَّ بِبِنَائِهَا بِجِصٍّ وَآجُرٍّ. "Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī built the mosque and the governor's residence of mud-brick and clay, and roofed them with thatch … Then Ziyād built the governor's residence of Baṣra [anew] … and when al-Ḥajjāj b. Yūsuf came to Iraq and was told that Ziyād had built the residence, he wished to erase his name from it, and resolved to rebuild it in gypsum and fired brick." **The palaces of the governors.** The most spectacular case is al-Ḥajjāj's green-domed palace at the new city of Wāsiṭ, which delighted him "as no building ever had." The episode is preserved with a punchline that no commentary could improve: a captured Khārijite, brought before al-Ḥajjāj and gazing at the construction, throws the Qurʾān's own anti-building verse in his face. أُتِيَ الْحَجَّاجُ بِرَجُلٍ مِنَ الْخَوَارِجِ وَهُوَ فِي خَضْرَاءِ وَاسِطٍ، فَلَمَّا مَثُلَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ وَنَظَرَ إِلَى بُنْيَانِهِ فَقَالَ: ﴿أَتَبْنُونَ بِكُلِّ رِيعٍ آيَةً تَعْبَثُونَ وَتَتَّخِذُونَ مَصَانِعَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَخْلُدُونَ﴾ … وَكَانَ الْحَجَّاجُ قَدْ بَنَى خَضْرَاءَ وَاسِطٍ فَأَعْجَبَتْهُ مَا لَمْ يُعْجِبْهُ بِنَاءٌ قَطُّ، فَقَالَ لِمَنْ حَوْلَهُ: كَيْفَ تَرَوْنَ قُبَّتِي هَذِهِ؟ A man of the Khārijites was brought before al-Ḥajjāj while he was in the Green Palace of Wāsiṭ. When he stood before him and looked at his building, he recited: "Do you build on every hill a monument for vanity's sake, and take for yourselves strongholds, as if you will last forever?" … al-Ḥajjāj had built the Green Palace of Wāsiṭ, and it pleased him as no building ever had, so he asked those around him: "How do you see this dome of mine?" This single anecdote ties the whole argument into a knot. Here is an Iraqi governor of exactly the era and the cities in question, gazing with pride at the most lavish building of his life, and here is a pious opponent answering him with the very Qurʾānic verse (26:128 to 129) that condemns monumental building as the mark of the doomed. The "barefoot shepherds competing in tall buildings" report is the hadith form of that Khārijite's recitation. It is the ascetic and pietist reaction to the Umayyad-Iraqi building boom, turned into an omen and projected back onto the Prophet. **The motif had deep roots in Iraq.** The Arabs of Iraq did not even need to invent the idea that monumental building is vanity doomed to ruin. It was the most famous local legend they had. Beside Kūfa stood the Lakhmid palaces of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr, and the proverbial tale of their builder-king, al-Nuʿmān, who looked out from his tower over all his wealth and dominion and was struck by its transience, then renounced the world. The poet ʿAdī b. Zayd fixed it as a maxim: وَتَذَكَّرَ رَبَّ الْخَوَرْنَقِ إِذْ أَشْـ ـرَفَ يَوْمًا وَلِلْهُدَى تَفْكِيرُ سَرَّهُ مَالُهُ وَكَثْرَةُ مَا يَمْـ ـلِكُ وَالْبَحْرُ مُعْرِضٌ وَالسَّدِيرُ "And remember the lord of al-Khawarnaq, when he looked out one day, and was moved to think on guidance: his wealth had delighted him, and the abundance of his possessions, with the sea stretched before him and al-Sadīr." The lesson that the proud builder's monument is vanity was, quite literally, the view from the edge of Kūfa. When a Kūfan or Baṣran moralist of the first century watched the conquest fortunes rise into brick and dome around him, he had both a live target and a ready cultural script. The "tall buildings" sign is what he produced. Verdict The report that "barefoot, naked shepherds will compete in tall buildings" is not a prophecy of Gulf skyscrapers. It is a piece of first-century Iraqi ascetic preaching, condemning the wealth and monumental building that the conquests poured into Kūfa and Baṣra, and projected back onto the Prophet in the Gabriel scene. It fails the apologists' own criteria: building was never beyond the Arabs (Petra, al-Ḥijr), the claim fixes no testable detail, and the tradition's own commentator, Ibn Ḥajar, says the sign already occurred near the Prophet's time. Its matn will not hold still, sliding between camels, black beasts, and sheep, and between "heads of the people" and "kings of the earth," which is the signature of a paraphrased homiletic motif, not a fixed dictum. Its two "independent" Companion attestations collapse into a single source: the Kūfan common link Abū Zurʿa al-Bajalī (in the name of Abū Hurayra), paralleled by the Baṣran common link Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar (in the name of ʿUmar), an exact contemporary who supplied a fresh chain to ʿUmar and wrapped it in the anti-qadarī Maʿbad al-Juhanī frame of the 80s AH, manufacturing the look of corroboration. What the saying actually condemns is documented history: the spoils of Ctesiphon, Ziyād rebuilding Baṣra's residence in fired brick, and al-Ḥajjāj's green dome at Wāsiṭ, against which a Khārijite recited the Qurʾān's own rebuke of vain building (26:128 to 129). The same Kūfan circle that produced the omen also preserved Khabbāb b. al-Aratt's lament, through the Kūfan chain Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid from Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim, that the believers had acquired wealth they could only sink "into the dust." The hadith is the sermon of the ascetics, not the foresight of a prophet. [^families]: The two families used here. **Abū Hurayra (Kūfan common link Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr al-Bajalī):** Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 50 (Musaddad ← Ismāʿīl b. ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān al-Taymī ← Abū Zurʿa), "camels"; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8e (Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba and Zuhayr ← Ibn ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa), "black beasts," "heads of the people"; Muslim 9 (Ibn Numayr ← Muḥammad b. Bishr ← Abū Ḥayyān), with the concubine gloss on the slave-girl sign; Muslim 10 (Zuhayr ← Jarīr ← ʿUmāra b. al-Qaʿqāʿ ← Abū Zurʿa), "deaf and dumb kings of the earth"; Sunan Ibn Mājah 64 and 4044 (Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba ← Ibn ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa), "sheep"; Sunan al-Nasāʾī 4991 (Muḥammad b. Qudāma ← Jarīr ← Abū Farwa ← Abū Zurʿa ← Abū Hurayra and Abū Dharr), with the "clay bench" frame; Musnad Aḥmad 9501 (Ismāʿīl b. ʿUlayya ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa); Ibn Ḥibbān 159 (Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm ← Jarīr ← Abū Ḥayyān ← Abū Zurʿa). A separate Companion route with a paraphrased matn ("the hungry vie in building") is Aḥmad 9128 (Shahr b. Ḥawshab ← Abū Hurayra). [^umar]: **ʿUmar (Baṣran/Mervi common link Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar), all carrying the Maʿbad al-Juhanī / qadar frame:** Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 8 and 8a (Zuhayr ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda ← Yaḥyā; and ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muʿādh ← Muʿādh ← Kahmas); Sunan Abī Dāwūd 4695 (ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muʿādh ← Muʿādh ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 2610 (Abū ʿAmmār al-Ḥusayn b. Ḥurayth ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Sunan al-Nasāʾī 4990 (Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm ← al-Naḍr b. Shumayl ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Sunan Ibn Mājah 63 (ʿAlī b. Muḥammad ← Wakīʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda); Musnad Aḥmad 184 (Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd ← ʿUthmān b. Ghiyāth ← Ibn Burayda); Ibn Ḥibbān 168 (Muḥammad b. al-Minhāl ← Yazīd b. Zurayʿ ← Kahmas ← Ibn Burayda). Maʿbad al-Juhanī's qadar agitation and his death in the aftermath of the revolt of Ibn al-Ashʿath place the narrative frame in the 80s AH. [^rijal]: Gradings from Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb: Abū Zurʿa b. ʿAmr b. Jarīr al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa, third ṭabaqa," with his given name unstable across the sources (Haram / ʿAmr / ʿAbd Allāh / ʿAbd al-Raḥmān / Jarīr); Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar al-Baṣrī, judge of Merv, "thiqa, eloquent, used to transmit mursal, third ṭabaqa, died before/after 100"; Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa, second ṭabaqa, mukhaḍram"; Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid al-Aḥmasī al-Bajalī al-Kūfī, "thiqa thabt, fourth ṭabaqa, died 146." [^khabbab]: The Khabbāb wealth-and-building lament, Kūfan chain Ismāʿīl b. Abī Khālid ← Qays b. Abī Ḥāzim ← Khabbāb: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 5672 (Ādam ← Shuʿba), with both the "wealth we find nowhere to put but the dust" and the wall-building clause; Bukhārī 6431 (Muḥammad b. al-Muthannā ← Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays), "building a wall of his"; Bukhārī 6349 to 6350 (the "do not wish for death" portion); Musnad Aḥmad 21059 (Wakīʿ ← Ibn Abī Khālid ← Qays), "the Muslim is rewarded in everything except what he puts in this dust," again while building a wall; al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr 3635 (ʿAlī b. al-Jaʿd ← Shuʿba ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays), the full version. Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2681a (ʿAbd Allāh b. Idrīs ← Ismāʿīl ← Qays) preserves only the death-wish portion without the building clause, showing the anti-building moral to be a clause that some Kūfan narrators raised and others did not. al-Bazzār notes that the building-condemnation wording was raised from the Ismāʿīl-Qays-Khabbāb chain only by Abū Muʿāwiya. [^zuhd]: The wider zuhd-against-building cluster: Sunan Ibn Mājah 4161 (ḥasan), the Anṣārī's dome which he demolishes after the Prophet's rebuke, "every wealth like this is a burden on its owner"; Sunan Abī Dāwūd 5237 (← Anas), the raised dome (qubba mushrifa) the Prophet shuns until it is leveled, ending "every building is a burden on its owner except what is indispensable (illā mā lā budda minhu)"; with parallels in Abū Yaʿlā, al-Ṭaḥāwī's Sharḥ Mushkil al-Āthār, and al-Bayhaqī's Shuʿab al-Īmān. The Qurʾānic frame is Sūrat al-Takāthur 102:1 to 2 and the rebuke of ʿĀd in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:128 to 129. [^iraq]: On the conquest wealth and the Iraqi building boom: the spoils of al-Madāʾin (Ctesiphon), the carpet and crown of Khusraw, and the "White Palace," in al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh, al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, and Ibn Faḍl Allāh al-ʿUmarī, Masālik al-Abṣār; the rebuilding of Baṣra's Dār al-Imāra by Ziyād b. Abīhi in gypsum and fired brick, al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān; al-Ḥajjāj's Green Palace (al-Khaḍrāʾ) at Wāsiṭ and the Khārijite's recitation of Q 26:128 to 129, Ibn ʿAsākir, Tārīkh Dimashq, and al-Tadhkira al-Ḥamdūniyya; the legend of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr and al-Nuʿmān's renunciation, in the verse of ʿAdī b. Zayd preserved by Ibn ʿAsākir and others.

title: How Masrūq Wrote a Hadith Against the Mourners of Ḥusayn
description: Masrūq b. al-Ajdaʿ did not merely relay the prohibition of mourning-lamentation. He originated it — as a deliberate juristic polemic against the Ḥusaynid mourning practices emerging in Kūfa between 61 and 64 AH — and then falsely attributed it to Ibn Masʿūd and ʿĀʾisha to give it prophetic authority it never had.
