A hadith attributed to the Prophet says that a fire will emerge from the Hijaz and illuminate the necks of camels at Buṣrā in Syria. In 654 AH / 1256 CE, a major eruption occurred near Medina, and medieval historians later identified that event with the report. The modern miracle claim then says: the Prophet predicted a volcanic eruption more than six centuries in advance. That argument sounds strong only if the report is treated as a free-floating sentence, isolated from its transmission, its matn relatives, and the way the 1256 eruption was interpreted by people who already knew the hadith. Once the report is placed back into its tradition-history, the case changes. The exact Prophetic version is not transmitted through many independent early witnesses. It converges on one Medinan-Syrian channel: > **al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra** The most revealing early-looking witness is even more direct. ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves the same sentence from Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī, but without Abū Hurayra and without the Prophet: قَالَ عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ، قَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ: تَخْرُجُ نَارٌ بِأَرْضِ الْحِجَازِ تُضِيءُ أَعْنَاقَ الْإِبِلِ بِبُصْرَى. ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Maʿmar said: al-Zuhrī said: “A fire will emerge in the land of the Hijaz, illuminating the necks of the camels at Buṣrā.” That mursal or unattributed form is not a minor curiosity. It shows that the phrase circulated as an al-Zuhrī saying before, or at least alongside, the full Saʿīd → Abū Hurayra Prophetic version. The safer reconstruction is not that every later narrator lied. It is that the recoverable wording becomes historically visible at al-Zuhrī, and the Prophetic isnād is part of the report’s later authoritative packaging. The “fire from Hijaz” report is best explained as an al-Zuhrī-centered apocalyptic localization of older Arabian fire lore. The 1256 eruption is real, but the miracle claim depends on treating later fulfillment-shaped reception as if it were independent proof of a first/seventh-century prophecy. ## The Isnād: One Real Bottleneck, Many Lower Routes The canonical form appears in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Al-Bukhārī gives it through Abū al-Yamān → Shuʿayb → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd → Abū Hurayra. Muslim gives it through Yūnus and ʿUqayl from Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī through the same upper line. Ibn Ḥibbān repeats the Yūnus route. Al-Bazzār and al-Ḥākim preserve ʿUqayl-side forms. The lower routes differ, but the upper structure does not. The diagram does not “disprove” the report by itself. It tells us where the historical question belongs. If a report appears in many books but every usable line passes through al-Zuhrī, then al-Zuhrī’s milieu is the place to ask why this sentence took its final form. The answer is not difficult to see. Al-Zuhrī stands at the meeting-point of Medinan authority, Syrian-Umayyad circulation, and apocalyptic interest in the geography of Syria. The Bukhārī/Muslim wording also has a very polished form. It is not an open-ended volcano notice. It is a sign-of-the-Hour formula: “The Hour will not come until…” That formula belongs to a much wider end-time repertoire in which places, rulers, invasions, fires, earthquakes, and migrations are turned into chronological signs. ## The Older Fire Lore: Kaʿb, Yemen, and Syria The strongest collateral evidence is the Kaʿb report preserved in Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād’s *Kitāb al-Fitan*: عَنْ كَعْبٍ قَالَ: يُوشِكُ نَارٌ تَخْرُجُ بِالْيَمَنِ تَسُوقُ النَّاسَ إِلَى الشَّامِ، تَغْدُو إِذَا غَدَوْا، وَتَقِيلُ إِذَا قَالُوا، وَتَرُوحُ إِذَا رَاحُوا، تُضِيءُ مِنْهَا أَعْنَاقُ الْإِبِلِ بِبُصْرَى، فَإِذَا سَمِعْتَ ذَلِكَ فَاخْرُجُوا إِلَى الشَّامِ. Kaʿb said: “A fire will soon emerge in Yemen, driving people to al-Shām. It will go with them when they go in the morning, rest when they rest at midday, and go with them when they go in the evening. From it the necks of the camels at Buṣrā will be illuminated. When you hear of that, go out to al-Shām.” This is not the same report as the al-Zuhrī hadith. It says Yemen, not Hijaz. It drives people to Syria, rather than merely shining toward Buṣrā. It is placed on Kaʿb, not on the Prophet. But the shared phrase is too specific to ignore: **“the necks of the camels at Buṣrā will be illuminated.”** That phrase is the distinctive image in the canonical report. Nuʿaym also places this Kaʿb material beside other Yemen/Aden fire traditions, including reports in which the fire drives people and travels with them by day and night. The Kaʿb report should not be treated as a secure transcript of Kaʿb’s own words. Nuʿaym’s book is a later apocalyptic compilation. The point is narrower: the Buṣrā camel-neck image is attested in non-Prophetic apocalyptic fire lore, and the al-Zuhrī report looks like a Hijaz-localized version of that same symbolic geography. The shift from **Yemen → al-Shām** to **Hijaz → Buṣrā** is exactly the sort of localization one expects in early Islamic apocalyptic tradition. Syria is the destination and viewing horizon. The Hijaz supplies a more concrete Arabian fire landscape, because Medina sits beside volcanic harrats. The final form then turns that localized sign into a Prophetic prediction through Abū Hurayra. ## Why Abū Hurayra Was the Right Companion Frame Abū Hurayra is not incidental. In the tradition literature, he is one of the Companions most often placed near Kaʿb al-Aḥbār. Muslim even preserves a report in which Abū Hurayra says something to Kaʿb, and Kaʿb asks him whether he heard it from the Prophet. Whatever one thinks of that individual report, it shows that early transmitters could imagine Abū Hurayra and Kaʿb exchanging religious lore. That matters here because the fire-from-Hijaz report is exactly the kind of material that could migrate across the boundary between Companion hadith and Kaʿb-style apocalyptic interpretation. A non-Prophetic end-time motif about a fire from Arabia toward Syria becomes more authoritative if it is attached to Abū Hurayra, then passed through Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī. This is also why the report’s geography makes sense in al-Zuhrī’s world. Al-Zuhrī is a Medinan scholar whose transmission travelled strongly through Syrian and Umayyad channels. A sign that begins in the Hijaz but shines toward Buṣrā gives both regions a role. It is Medinan enough to be tied to Abū Hurayra and Saʿīd. It is Syrian enough to interest an audience for whom al-Shām was the center of apocalyptic expectation. ## The 641 Problem Has to Be Handled Carefully The old version of the argument leaned heavily on a first/seventh-century eruption around 640 or 641 CE. That part should be made more careful. There are medieval reports, transmitted much later, that during the caliphate of ʿUmar a small fire rose from the lava field of Medina and then died out. Modern geological discussions have sometimes connected those reports with a 640/641 eruption near Medina. NASA’s Earth Observatory article, for example, presents the 1256 flow as Harrat Rahat’s youngest lava flow and says that an earlier eruption in 641 CE created finger-like flows east of the 1256 flow. But newer USGS mapping complicates this. The USGS geologic map of northern Harrat Rahat says that a cluster of cones and small lava flows in the western outskirts of Medina, previously ascribed to 641 CE, actually dates to **13.3 ± 1.9 ka**, near the Pleistocene-Holocene boundary. The same study identifies the historically described 1256 basalt of al-Lābah as the secure Holocene eruption in the mapped area. This does not mean there was no remembered earthquake or small fire in the early Islamic period. It does mean that the 641 eruption cannot be used as a simple proven geological anchor. That is why the argument should not depend on saying, “Kaʿb saw the 641 eruption, therefore he invented the report.” The stronger argument is more modest and more durable: > The fire-from-Hijaz hadith belongs to an early apocalyptic fire complex, and the exact Prophetic form becomes visible through al-Zuhrī. A remembered early fire or earthquake may help explain why the Hijaz became the chosen location, but the transmission evidence does not require a fully verified 641 lava flow. ## The 1256 Eruption Was Real, But the Fulfillment Claim Is a Reception Event The 1256 eruption near Medina is not imaginary. It is one of the best documented historical eruptions in Arabia. Modern geological sources describe the 1256 event as a basaltic eruption from aligned vents in northern Harrat Rahat. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program says that the best-known eruption took place in 1256 CE, when a lava flow of about 0.5 cubic kilometers erupted from six aligned scoria cones and travelled 23 km to within 4 km of Medina. USGS summaries likewise identify Harrat Rahat as the largest Saudi lava field and describe the 1256 eruption as the most recent historical eruption in the mapped region. Medieval historians also recorded the event in detail. Ibn Kathīr, summarizing Abū Shāma’s contemporary material, says that letters reached Damascus from Medina describing a mighty event in 654 AH. Those letters described earthquakes, a fire in the lava field near Qurayẓa, lava-like streams, smoke, sparks, and a terrifying glow. Later in the same entry, Ibn Kathīr reports that a Damascene judge heard from a Bedouin at Buṣrā that they saw the necks of their camels in the light of the fire. That last detail is the apologetic centerpiece. It should be read with care. The Buṣrā camel-neck phrase is already the hadith’s own phrase. The 1256 reports do not give us a neutral instrument reading from southern Syria. They give us a medieval religious interpretation of an eruption by people who already knew the report and were actively reading the event as its fulfillment. Ibn Kathīr’s chapter says this directly: the event was understood as a confirmation of the hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. The result is not independent confirmation. It is a feedback loop: Before the canon Apocalyptic fire lore Yemen, Aden, Hijaz, and Syria appear in fire-and-gathering traditions. Kaʿb-style material already uses the Buṣrā illumination image. al-Zuhrī layer Hijaz localized The exact sentence appears from al-Zuhrī. In one early witness it is simply his statement; in the canonical form it is raised through Saʿīd and Abū Hurayra. 654 AH / 1256 CE Medina eruption A real eruption occurs near Medina. Contemporary letters and later histories describe earthquakes, fire, smoke, lava, and distant light. Later reception Fulfillment reading Historians identify the eruption with the hadith. The Buṣrā camel-neck phrase re-enters the historical narrative as proof that the report came true. This is the core problem. A religious community experiences a volcanic disaster. Its scholars already possess a hadith about a fire in the Hijaz. They then describe the disaster in the hadith’s own language. Modern apologists take that reception language and use it as proof that the hadith predicted the disaster. The source-critical question is not whether the eruption happened. It did. The question is whether the report’s transmission proves a first/seventh-century prophecy. It does not. ## The Quranic Problem The Quran repeatedly frames the Prophet as a warner whose mission is tied to revelation, not independent fortune-telling. The most direct verse is 7:188: That verse does not deny that God knows the future. It denies that the Prophet possessed future knowledge as a personal power. The same pattern appears when people demand signs and are redirected to the Quran itself as the sufficient sign: This matters because the fire-from-Hijaz miracle claim is not merely saying, “God knows all things.” It is using a later hadith complex to give the Prophet a catalogue of precise future predictions, then using those predictions to validate the hadith corpus. That is exactly the move the Quranic evidence resists. The Prophet’s authorized miracle is the message, not a portfolio of volcanic forecasts. ## The Matn Tells the Story The matn development is easier to see when the reports are placed side by side. | Form | Source profile | Fire origin | Direction / function | Buṣrā phrase | Attribution | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Yemen fire drives people to al-Shām | Nuʿaym, Kaʿb report | Yemen | Drives people to Syria; travels and rests with them | Yes | Kaʿb, not the Prophet | | Yemen/Aden final gathering fire | Nuʿaym and broader apocalyptic reports | Yemen / Aden | Gathers people at the end | Sometimes absent, sometimes with travel/rest motif | Mixed | | Hijaz fire illuminates Buṣrā | ʿAbd al-Razzāq / Nuʿaym through Maʿmar | Hijaz | Illumination only | Yes | al-Zuhrī statement | | Hijaz fire as sign of the Hour | Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Bazzār, al-Ḥākim | Hijaz | Sign before the Hour | Yes | Prophet through Abū Hurayra | | 1256 fulfillment narrative | Abū Shāma, Ibn Kathīr, later historians | Medina lava field | Historical eruption interpreted as sign | Reused as fulfillment language | Historiographical reception | The shared Buṣrā phrase is the thread. The geography changes. The function changes. The attribution changes. But the visual image remains. ## Objections ### “But al-Bukhārī and Muslim both transmit it.” They do, but both collections still depend on the same upper transmission. The issue is not whether later collectors accepted the report. The issue is whether the report has independent early roots. The usable forms converge on al-Zuhrī. That is a narrow historical base for a claim of supernatural prediction. ### “But the 1256 eruption really happened.” Yes. The eruption is real and well documented. The critique is not geological denial. The critique is that the hadith existed before the eruption and shaped the way the eruption was described afterward. A fulfillment narrative is not automatically independent evidence. ### “But people in Buṣrā reportedly saw the camel necks illuminated.” The report exists, but it reaches us inside the very fulfillment literature that cites the hadith. Ibn Kathīr’s entry explicitly frames the event as the realization of the hadith, then reports the Buṣrā detail in that context. That makes it weak as independent confirmation. The phrase may be true, exaggerated, or formulaically repeated. It cannot carry the miracle claim by itself. ### “Could the eruption’s light reach far away?” Volcanic glow, smoke, aerosols, and atmospheric scattering can affect skies far from an eruption. The 1256 historical accounts mention light as far as Taymāʾ, Mecca, and, in later summaries, Buṣrā. The problem is not that distant atmospheric effects are impossible. The problem is that the precise Buṣrā-camel wording is already the hadith’s wording, so its appearance in the eruption narratives is not neutral. ### “Does the 641 eruption prove the hadith was made after the fact?” Not by itself. The 641 eruption is not secure enough to bear the full argument. Some modern summaries mention it, but USGS mapping challenges earlier identifications of the supposed 641 cones near Medina. The article’s stronger claim is about transmission and matn: the report is al-Zuhrī-centered and belongs to a broader apocalyptic fire motif. The possible early Islamic fire memory is contextual support, not the foundation. ## The Most Likely Reconstruction The report probably did not begin as a precise volcanic prophecy. It began in a wider apocalyptic imagination in which fires emerge from Arabia and drive or signal people toward Syria. Kaʿb-style material preserves one version of that lore: a Yemen fire, a movement toward al-Shām, and the striking Buṣrā camel-neck image. Al-Zuhrī’s circle gives the motif its Hijaz form. The wording is shortened, localized, and made more elegant: a fire from the land of the Hijaz illuminates the necks of camels at Buṣrā. In Maʿmar’s route, this appears as al-Zuhrī’s own statement. In the canonical route, it is raised through Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and Abū Hurayra to the Prophet. The 1256 eruption then gives the report its afterlife. A dramatic volcanic event occurs near Medina. Letters reach Damascus. Historians describe the event through the lens of the hadith. The phrase “necks of camels at Buṣrā” becomes part of the event’s religious memory. Later readers mistake that memory-loop for proof of prediction. The fire-from-Hijaz hadith is not best explained as a clean supernatural forecast of the 1256 eruption. Its recoverable transmission is narrow, centered on al-Zuhrī; its imagery is already present in Kaʿb-style Arabian fire lore; and the 1256 eruption was interpreted through the hadith after the fact. The eruption happened. The miracle claim is the later identification of that eruption with an al-Zuhrī-shaped apocalyptic report. ## Sources consulted 1. **Main Prophetic fire-from-Hijaz report.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7118; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2902; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6839; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 7770; al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8369. 2. **Unattributed al-Zuhrī form.** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 20788: Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī, “A fire will emerge in the land of the Hijaz, illuminating the necks of the camels at Buṣrā”; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1764, preserving the same Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī form. 3. **Kaʿb and the wider Arabian fire motif.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1754, Kaʿb’s Yemen-fire report; compare nos. 1755, 1763, 1765–1767 and related Aden/Yemen fire traditions. 4. **1256 eruption historical reception.** Abū Shāma, *al-Dhayl ʿalā al-Rawḍatayn*; Ibn Kathīr, *al-Bidāya wa-l-nihāya*, events of 654 AH; al-Qurṭubī, *al-Tadhkira*; al-Nawawī, *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*; al-Samhūdī, *Wafāʾ al-wafā bi-akhbār dār al-Muṣṭafā*. 5. **Modern volcanology and historical eruption studies.** Drew T. Downs et al., “Volcanic history of the northernmost part of the Harrat Rahat volcanic field, Saudi Arabia,” *Geosphere* 14.3 (2018): 1253–1282; David T. Downs et al., *Geologic Map of the Northern Harrat Rahat Volcanic Field, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia*, USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3428 (2019); Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, “Harrat Rahat”; NASA Earth Observatory, “Living on Lava”; Nabil Nasr El-Masry et al., “Historical Accounts of the AD 1256 Eruption near Al-Madinah” (VORISA, 2013). 6. **Apocalyptic method and context.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *The Book of Tribulations: The Syrian Muslim Apocalyptic Tradition*, ed. and trans. That argument sounds strong only if the report is treated as a free-floating sentence, isolated from its transmission, its matn relatives, and the way the 1256 eruption was interpreted by people who already knew the hadith. Once the report is placed back into its tradition-history, the case changes. The exact Prophetic version is not transmitted through many independent early witnesses. It converges on one Medinan-Syrian channel: > **al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra** The most revealing early-looking witness is even more direct. ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves the same sentence from Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī, but without Abū Hurayra and without the Prophet: قَالَ عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ، قَالَ الزُّهْرِيُّ: تَخْرُجُ نَارٌ بِأَرْضِ الْحِجَازِ تُضِيءُ أَعْنَاقَ الْإِبِلِ بِبُصْرَى. ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Maʿmar said: al-Zuhrī said: “A fire will emerge in the land of the Hijaz, illuminating the necks of the camels at Buṣrā.” That mursal or unattributed form is not a minor curiosity. It shows that the phrase circulated as an al-Zuhrī saying before, or at least alongside, the full Saʿīd → Abū Hurayra Prophetic version. The safer reconstruction is not that every later narrator lied. It is that the recoverable wording becomes historically visible at al-Zuhrī, and the Prophetic isnād is part of the report’s later authoritative packaging. The “fire from Hijaz” report is best explained as an al-Zuhrī-centered apocalyptic localization of older Arabian fire lore. The 1256 eruption is real, but the miracle claim depends on treating later fulfillment-shaped reception as if it were independent proof of a first/seventh-century prophecy. The Isnād: One Real Bottleneck, Many Lower Routes The canonical form appears in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. Al-Bukhārī gives it through Abū al-Yamān → Shuʿayb → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd → Abū Hurayra. Muslim gives it through Yūnus and ʿUqayl from Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī through the same upper line. Ibn Ḥibbān repeats the Yūnus route. Al-Bazzār and al-Ḥākim preserve ʿUqayl-side forms. The lower routes differ, but the upper structure does not. The diagram does not “disprove” the report by itself. It tells us where the historical question belongs. If a report appears in many books but every usable line passes through al-Zuhrī, then al-Zuhrī’s milieu is the place to ask why this sentence took its final form. The answer is not difficult to see. Al-Zuhrī stands at the meeting-point of Medinan authority, Syrian-Umayyad circulation, and apocalyptic interest in the geography of Syria. The Bukhārī/Muslim wording also has a very polished form. It is not an open-ended volcano notice. It is a sign-of-the-Hour formula: “The Hour will not come until…” That formula belongs to a much wider end-time repertoire in which places, rulers, invasions, fires, earthquakes, and migrations are turned into chronological signs. The Older Fire Lore: Kaʿb, Yemen, and Syria The strongest collateral evidence is the Kaʿb report preserved in Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād’s *Kitāb al-Fitan*: عَنْ كَعْبٍ قَالَ: يُوشِكُ نَارٌ تَخْرُجُ بِالْيَمَنِ تَسُوقُ النَّاسَ إِلَى الشَّامِ، تَغْدُو إِذَا غَدَوْا، وَتَقِيلُ إِذَا قَالُوا، وَتَرُوحُ إِذَا رَاحُوا، تُضِيءُ مِنْهَا أَعْنَاقُ الْإِبِلِ بِبُصْرَى، فَإِذَا سَمِعْتَ ذَلِكَ فَاخْرُجُوا إِلَى الشَّامِ. Kaʿb said: “A fire will soon emerge in Yemen, driving people to al-Shām. It will go with them when they go in the morning, rest when they rest at midday, and go with them when they go in the evening. From it the necks of the camels at Buṣrā will be illuminated. When you hear of that, go out to al-Shām.” This is not the same report as the al-Zuhrī hadith. It says Yemen, not Hijaz. It drives people to Syria, rather than merely shining toward Buṣrā. It is placed on Kaʿb, not on the Prophet. But the shared phrase is too specific to ignore: **“the necks of the camels at Buṣrā will be illuminated.”** That phrase is the distinctive image in the canonical report. Nuʿaym also places this Kaʿb material beside other Yemen/Aden fire traditions, including reports in which the fire drives people and travels with them by day and night. The Kaʿb report should not be treated as a secure transcript of Kaʿb’s own words. Nuʿaym’s book is a later apocalyptic compilation. The point is narrower: the Buṣrā camel-neck image is attested in non-Prophetic apocalyptic fire lore, and the al-Zuhrī report looks like a Hijaz-localized version of that same symbolic geography. The shift from **Yemen → al-Shām** to **Hijaz → Buṣrā** is exactly the sort of localization one expects in early Islamic apocalyptic tradition. Syria is the destination and viewing horizon. The Hijaz supplies a more concrete Arabian fire landscape, because Medina sits beside volcanic harrats. The final form then turns that localized sign into a Prophetic prediction through Abū Hurayra. Why Abū Hurayra Was the Right Companion Frame Abū Hurayra is not incidental. In the tradition literature, he is one of the Companions most often placed near Kaʿb al-Aḥbār. Muslim even preserves a report in which Abū Hurayra says something to Kaʿb, and Kaʿb asks him whether he heard it from the Prophet. Whatever one thinks of that individual report, it shows that early transmitters could imagine Abū Hurayra and Kaʿb exchanging religious lore. That matters here because the fire-from-Hijaz report is exactly the kind of material that could migrate across the boundary between Companion hadith and Kaʿb-style apocalyptic interpretation. A non-Prophetic end-time motif about a fire from Arabia toward Syria becomes more authoritative if it is attached to Abū Hurayra, then passed through Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī. This is also why the report’s geography makes sense in al-Zuhrī’s world. Al-Zuhrī is a Medinan scholar whose transmission travelled strongly through Syrian and Umayyad channels. A sign that begins in the Hijaz but shines toward Buṣrā gives both regions a role. It is Medinan enough to be tied to Abū Hurayra and Saʿīd. It is Syrian enough to interest an audience for whom al-Shām was the center of apocalyptic expectation. The 641 Problem Has to Be Handled Carefully The old version of the argument leaned heavily on a first/seventh-century eruption around 640 or 641 CE. That part should be made more careful. There are medieval reports, transmitted much later, that during the caliphate of ʿUmar a small fire rose from the lava field of Medina and then died out. Modern geological discussions have sometimes connected those reports with a 640/641 eruption near Medina. NASA’s Earth Observatory article, for example, presents the 1256 flow as Harrat Rahat’s youngest lava flow and says that an earlier eruption in 641 CE created finger-like flows east of the 1256 flow. But newer USGS mapping complicates this. The USGS geologic map of northern Harrat Rahat says that a cluster of cones and small lava flows in the western outskirts of Medina, previously ascribed to 641 CE, actually dates to **13.3 ± 1.9 ka**, near the Pleistocene-Holocene boundary. The same study identifies the historically described 1256 basalt of al-Lābah as the secure Holocene eruption in the mapped area. This does not mean there was no remembered earthquake or small fire in the early Islamic period. It does mean that the 641 eruption cannot be used as a simple proven geological anchor. That is why the argument should not depend on saying, “Kaʿb saw the 641 eruption, therefore he invented the report.” The stronger argument is more modest and more durable: > The fire-from-Hijaz hadith belongs to an early apocalyptic fire complex, and the exact Prophetic form becomes visible through al-Zuhrī. A remembered early fire or earthquake may help explain why the Hijaz became the chosen location, but the transmission evidence does not require a fully verified 641 lava flow. The 1256 Eruption Was Real, But the Fulfillment Claim Is a Reception Event The 1256 eruption near Medina is not imaginary. It is one of the best documented historical eruptions in Arabia. Modern geological sources describe the 1256 event as a basaltic eruption from aligned vents in northern Harrat Rahat. The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program says that the best-known eruption took place in 1256 CE, when a lava flow of about 0.5 cubic kilometers erupted from six aligned scoria cones and travelled 23 km to within 4 km of Medina. USGS summaries likewise identify Harrat Rahat as the largest Saudi lava field and describe the 1256 eruption as the most recent historical eruption in the mapped region. Medieval historians also recorded the event in detail. Ibn Kathīr, summarizing Abū Shāma’s contemporary material, says that letters reached Damascus from Medina describing a mighty event in 654 AH. Those letters described earthquakes, a fire in the lava field near Qurayẓa, lava-like streams, smoke, sparks, and a terrifying glow. Later in the same entry, Ibn Kathīr reports that a Damascene judge heard from a Bedouin at Buṣrā that they saw the necks of their camels in the light of the fire. That last detail is the apologetic centerpiece. It should be read with care. The Buṣrā camel-neck phrase is already the hadith’s own phrase. The 1256 reports do not give us a neutral instrument reading from southern Syria. They give us a medieval religious interpretation of an eruption by people who already knew the report and were actively reading the event as its fulfillment. Ibn Kathīr’s chapter says this directly: the event was understood as a confirmation of the hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. The result is not independent confirmation. It is a feedback loop: Before the canon Apocalyptic fire lore Yemen, Aden, Hijaz, and Syria appear in fire-and-gathering traditions. Kaʿb-style material already uses the Buṣrā illumination image. al-Zuhrī layer Hijaz localized The exact sentence appears from al-Zuhrī. In one early witness it is simply his statement; in the canonical form it is raised through Saʿīd and Abū Hurayra. 654 AH / 1256 CE Medina eruption A real eruption occurs near Medina. Contemporary letters and later histories describe earthquakes, fire, smoke, lava, and distant light. Later reception Fulfillment reading Historians identify the eruption with the hadith. The Buṣrā camel-neck phrase re-enters the historical narrative as proof that the report came true. This is the core problem. A religious community experiences a volcanic disaster. Its scholars already possess a hadith about a fire in the Hijaz. They then describe the disaster in the hadith’s own language. Modern apologists take that reception language and use it as proof that the hadith predicted the disaster. The source-critical question is not whether the eruption happened. It did. The question is whether the report’s transmission proves a first/seventh-century prophecy. It does not. The Quranic Problem The Quran repeatedly frames the Prophet as a warner whose mission is tied to revelation, not independent fortune-telling. The most direct verse is 7:188: That verse does not deny that God knows the future. It denies that the Prophet possessed future knowledge as a personal power. The same pattern appears when people demand signs and are redirected to the Quran itself as the sufficient sign: This matters because the fire-from-Hijaz miracle claim is not merely saying, “God knows all things.” It is using a later hadith complex to give the Prophet a catalogue of precise future predictions, then using those predictions to validate the hadith corpus. That is exactly the move the Quranic evidence resists. The Prophet’s authorized miracle is the message, not a portfolio of volcanic forecasts. The Matn Tells the Story The matn development is easier to see when the reports are placed side by side. | Form | Source profile | Fire origin | Direction / function | Buṣrā phrase | Attribution | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Yemen fire drives people to al-Shām | Nuʿaym, Kaʿb report | Yemen | Drives people to Syria; travels and rests with them | Yes | Kaʿb, not the Prophet | | Yemen/Aden final gathering fire | Nuʿaym and broader apocalyptic reports | Yemen / Aden | Gathers people at the end | Sometimes absent, sometimes with travel/rest motif | Mixed | | Hijaz fire illuminates Buṣrā | ʿAbd al-Razzāq / Nuʿaym through Maʿmar | Hijaz | Illumination only | Yes | al-Zuhrī statement | | Hijaz fire as sign of the Hour | Bukhārī, Muslim, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Bazzār, al-Ḥākim | Hijaz | Sign before the Hour | Yes | Prophet through Abū Hurayra | | 1256 fulfillment narrative | Abū Shāma, Ibn Kathīr, later historians | Medina lava field | Historical eruption interpreted as sign | Reused as fulfillment language | Historiographical reception | The shared Buṣrā phrase is the thread. The geography changes. The function changes. The attribution changes. But the visual image remains. Objections “But al-Bukhārī and Muslim both transmit it.” They do, but both collections still depend on the same upper transmission. The issue is not whether later collectors accepted the report. The issue is whether the report has independent early roots. The usable forms converge on al-Zuhrī. That is a narrow historical base for a claim of supernatural prediction. “But the 1256 eruption really happened.” Yes. The eruption is real and well documented. The critique is not geological denial. The critique is that the hadith existed before the eruption and shaped the way the eruption was described afterward. A fulfillment narrative is not automatically independent evidence. “But people in Buṣrā reportedly saw the camel necks illuminated.” The report exists, but it reaches us inside the very fulfillment literature that cites the hadith. Ibn Kathīr’s entry explicitly frames the event as the realization of the hadith, then reports the Buṣrā detail in that context. That makes it weak as independent confirmation. The phrase may be true, exaggerated, or formulaically repeated. It cannot carry the miracle claim by itself. “Could the eruption’s light reach far away?” Volcanic glow, smoke, aerosols, and atmospheric scattering can affect skies far from an eruption. The 1256 historical accounts mention light as far as Taymāʾ, Mecca, and, in later summaries, Buṣrā. The problem is not that distant atmospheric effects are impossible. The problem is that the precise Buṣrā-camel wording is already the hadith’s wording, so its appearance in the eruption narratives is not neutral. “Does the 641 eruption prove the hadith was made after the fact?” Not by itself. The 641 eruption is not secure enough to bear the full argument. Some modern summaries mention it, but USGS mapping challenges earlier identifications of the supposed 641 cones near Medina. The article’s stronger claim is about transmission and matn: the report is al-Zuhrī-centered and belongs to a broader apocalyptic fire motif. The possible early Islamic fire memory is contextual support, not the foundation. The Most Likely Reconstruction The report probably did not begin as a precise volcanic prophecy. It began in a wider apocalyptic imagination in which fires emerge from Arabia and drive or signal people toward Syria. Kaʿb-style material preserves one version of that lore: a Yemen fire, a movement toward al-Shām, and the striking Buṣrā camel-neck image. Al-Zuhrī’s circle gives the motif its Hijaz form. The wording is shortened, localized, and made more elegant: a fire from the land of the Hijaz illuminates the necks of camels at Buṣrā. In Maʿmar’s route, this appears as al-Zuhrī’s own statement. In the canonical route, it is raised through Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and Abū Hurayra to the Prophet. The 1256 eruption then gives the report its afterlife. A dramatic volcanic event occurs near Medina. Letters reach Damascus. Historians describe the event through the lens of the hadith. The phrase “necks of camels at Buṣrā” becomes part of the event’s religious memory. Later readers mistake that memory-loop for proof of prediction. The fire-from-Hijaz hadith is not best explained as a clean supernatural forecast of the 1256 eruption. Its recoverable transmission is narrow, centered on al-Zuhrī; its imagery is already present in Kaʿb-style Arabian fire lore; and the 1256 eruption was interpreted through the hadith after the fact. The eruption happened. The miracle claim is the later identification of that eruption with an al-Zuhrī-shaped apocalyptic report. Sources consulted 1. **Main Prophetic fire-from-Hijaz report.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7118; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2902; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6839; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 7770; al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8369. 2. **Unattributed al-Zuhrī form.** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 20788: Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī, “A fire will emerge in the land of the Hijaz, illuminating the necks of the camels at Buṣrā”; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1764, preserving the same Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī form. 3. **Kaʿb and the wider Arabian fire motif.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1754, Kaʿb’s Yemen-fire report; compare nos. 1755, 1763, 1765–1767 and related Aden/Yemen fire traditions. 4. **1256 eruption historical reception.** Abū Shāma, *al-Dhayl ʿalā al-Rawḍatayn*; Ibn Kathīr, *al-Bidāya wa-l-nihāya*, events of 654 AH; al-Qurṭubī, *al-Tadhkira*; al-Nawawī, *Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*; al-Samhūdī, *Wafāʾ al-wafā bi-akhbār dār al-Muṣṭafā*. 5. **Modern volcanology and historical eruption studies.** Drew T. Downs et al., “Volcanic history of the northernmost part of the Harrat Rahat volcanic field, Saudi Arabia,” *Geosphere* 14.3 (2018): 1253–1282; David T. Downs et al., *Geologic Map of the Northern Harrat Rahat Volcanic Field, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia*, USGS Scientific Investigations Map 3428 (2019); Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, “Harrat Rahat”; NASA Earth Observatory, “Living on Lava”; Nabil Nasr El-Masry et al., “Historical Accounts of the AD 1256 Eruption near Al-Madinah” (VORISA, 2013). 6. **Apocalyptic method and context.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *The Book of Tribulations: The Syrian Muslim Apocalyptic Tradition*, ed. and trans. David Cook (Edinburgh University Press, 2017); Harald Motzki, “Dating Muslim Traditions: A Survey,” *Arabica* 52.2 (2005); David Cook, *Studies in Muslim Apocalyptic*. { .fireTimeline { margin: 2.25rem 0; padding: clamp(1rem, 2vw, 1.4rem); border: 1px solid rgba(216, 183, 97, 0.28); border-radius: 22px; background: radial-gradient(circle at 22% 18%, rgba(255, 117, 52, 0.13), transparent 30%), radial-gradient(circle at 78% 12%, rgba(216, 183, 97, 0.10), transparent 28%), linear-gradient(135deg, rgba(34, 13, 6, 0.84), rgba(10, 10, 10, 0.94)); display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: 0.9rem; } .fireTimeline__card { position: relative; min-height: 225px; padding: 1.15rem 1rem 1rem; border: 1px solid rgba(216, 183, 97, 0.24); border-radius: 18px; background: rgba(12, 12, 12, 0.74); box-shadow: inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.025); } .fireTimeline__card--hot { border-color: rgba(232, 129, 68, 0.58); background: linear-gradient(180deg, rgba(105, 39, 16, 0.48), rgba(12, 12, 12, 0.78)); } .fireTimeline__card span { display: inline-flex; margin-bottom: 0.75rem; padding: 0.28rem 0.58rem; border: 1px solid rgba(216, 183, 97, 0.3); border-radius: 999px; color: rgba(216, 183, 97, 0.92); font-size: 0.76rem; letter-spacing: 0.08em; text-transform: uppercase; background: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.28); } .fireTimeline__card h3 { margin: 0 0 0.65rem; color: var(--hc-gold, #d8b761); font-size: clamp(1.05rem, 1.4vw, 1.28rem); line-height: 1.2; } .fireTimeline__card p { margin: 0; color: rgba(245, 238, 220, 0.84); font-size: 0.98rem; line-height: 1.6; } @media (max-width: 1050px) { .fireTimeline { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } } }

title: The Green Arabia Hadith: Suhayl, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and the Umayyad Reclamation World
description: A revised isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that the land of the Arabs will return to meadows and rivers: Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ as the common link, Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān al-Zayyāt as the more plausible motive-layer, and the late Umayyad world of land reclamation behind the image.

Arabia was once greener in the distant past, parts of it are greener today after rain, and the report says the land of the Arabs will “return” to meadows and rivers. The claim then treats the sentence as a scientifically precise prediction of modern climate change. That framing skips the older historical problem. The report is not a free-floating climate statement. It is a small eschatological clause embedded in changing bundles about wealth, zakāt, safe travel, killing, and the signs of the Hour. Its transmission does not spread from many independent Companions. It converges on one family line: **Abū Hurayra → Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān → Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ**. The point is not merely that Suhayl appears in the chain. The point is that every recoverable line containing the distinctive “meadows and rivers” clause runs through Suhayl, and the earliest technical notice we have, from al-Bazzār, already says so. The “Green Arabia” report is best explained as a late Umayyad agrarian-apocalyptic tradition. Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ is the demonstrable common link and disseminator. The better motive, however, points one generation earlier to his father, Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt: a Medinan client-scholar, a Medina-to-Kufa trader in ghee and oil, and an ʿUthmānī transmitter whose world was materially tied to pasture, irrigation, and the political imagination of land reclamation. That is more accurate than the older version of this blog. The old argument treated Suhayl as if the entire case depended on proving that he personally fabricated the report. The stronger argument is subtler. In isnād-cum-matn analysis, the common link is the point from which the report becomes visible and organized. He is not automatically the inventor. Here the matn, the family biography, and the historical setting make Abū Ṣāliḥ’s world the more plausible place to locate the kernel. ## The report in its best-known form لاَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْمَالُ وَيَفِيضَ، حَتَّى يَخْرُجَ الرَّجُلُ بِزَكَاةِ مَالِهِ فَلاَ يَجِدُ أَحَدًا يَقْبَلُهَا مِنْهُ، وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا. > “The Hour will not be established until wealth becomes abundant and overflows, so that a man will go out with the zakāt of his wealth and find no one to accept it from him, and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 157c, through Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qārī → Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ → his father → Abū Hurayra. Aḥmad preserves a near-identical form through the same Qutayba–Yaʿqūb route, but with the added clause that killing will become widespread: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْمَالُ وَيَفِيضَ ... وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا، وَحَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ. قَالُوا: وَمَا الْهَرْجُ يَا رَسُولَ اللهِ؟ قَالَ: الْقَتْلُ، الْقَتْلُ. > “The Hour will not be established until wealth becomes abundant and overflows ... and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers, and until killing becomes widespread.” They said, “What is killing, Messenger of God?” He said, “Killing, killing.” > > **Source:** Aḥmad, *Musnad*, no. 9395, through Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Another Aḥmad version changes the surrounding material. The greening clause comes first, then safe travel between Iraq and Mecca, then *harj*: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا، وَحَتَّى يَسِيرَ الرَّاكِبُ بَيْنَ الْعِرَاقِ وَمَكَّةَ لَا يَخَافُ إِلَّا ضَلَالَ الطَّرِيقِ، وَحَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ. > “The Hour will not be established until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers, until a rider travels between Iraq and Mecca fearing nothing except losing the road, and until killing becomes widespread.” > > **Source:** Aḥmad, *Musnad*, no. 8833, through Muḥammad b. al-Ṣabbāḥ → Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Ibn Ḥibbān has a shorter form with only *harj* and greening: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ، وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا. > “The Hour will not be established until killing becomes widespread and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6700, through Muḥammad b. Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm → Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Al-Ḥākim preserves the bare clause through Sufyān al-Thawrī, but his form contains an important hesitation: قَالَ سُفْيَانُ: لَا أَعْلَمُ إِلَّا قَدْ رَفَعَهُ. قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: «لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا». > Sufyān said: “I only know that he raised it.” He said: the Messenger of God said, “The Hour will not be established until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8472, through al-Ḥusayn b. Ḥafṣ → Sufyān al-Thawrī → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Sufyān’s hesitation matters. It does not destroy the report by itself, but it does show that the attribution was not as effortless as later apologetic citation makes it sound. The transmitter himself pauses over whether he knows it as a raised Prophetic statement. ## The isnād: not a wide prophetic memory, but a Suhayl bundle The diagram corrects two common mistakes. The first mistake is the apologetic one: treating the existence of multiple later citations as if they were independent prophetic witnesses. They are not. Muslim, Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, al-Bazzār, and Abū ʿAwāna preserve different recensions, but the distinctive clause does not escape the line **Suhayl → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra**. The second mistake is the crude skeptical one: treating this as if there were no real transmission bundle at all. There is a bundle. After Suhayl, we have several students in different regional settings: Yaʿqūb al-Qārī in the Medinan line, Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā and Sufyān al-Thawrī in Kufan lines, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār in the Basran line. The problem is not that the whole thing is a single late citation. The problem is that the bundle begins only at Suhayl. That distinction is important. The correct conclusion is not “one weak liar invented it.” The correct conclusion is that the report becomes visible as a structured tradition in Suhayl’s lifetime, while the content and family context point one generation earlier. ## al-Bazzār already noticed the bottleneck The most important early critical note comes from al-Bazzār. After transmitting the fullest form through ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār from Suhayl, he says: وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ قَدْ رُوِيَ بَعْضُهُ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ، وَلَا نَعْلَمُ أَخَذَهُ إِلَّا سُهَيْلٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ. > “Part of this ḥadīth has been narrated from Abū Hurayra by more than one route, but we do not know anyone who took it except Suhayl from his father from Abū Hurayra.” > > **Source:** al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 9071. This is the key to the whole case. al-Bazzār is not saying that every surrounding theme is unique to Suhayl. The motifs of overflowing wealth, refused zakāt, *harj*, and secure travel have other lives in the hadith corpus. What is distinctive here is the way those motifs are joined to the clause that **the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers**. That clause is the family’s contribution. The apologetic argument often points to Muslim or al-Ḥākim and stops there. But al-Bazzār’s note shows that the bottleneck was visible to early hadith critics themselves. This is not a modern hostile invention. ## Suhayl is the disseminator, not necessarily the author Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ was not an unknown nobody. He was a known Medinan transmitter, and several authorities accepted him. That has to be stated clearly because the older blog’s rijāl section leaned too hard on selective negative judgments. At the same time, he was not above criticism. Ibn Ḥajar summarizes him as truthful, but says his memory changed late. Critics also report that his Iraqi transmission was affected by forgetfulness. Abū Ḥātim’s formula is especially useful: his ḥadīth may be written, but is not used as proof. This is not a total rejection. It is a warning against building a miracle claim on a unique Suhayl-family clause. The route profile matches that warning. The “Green Arabia” clause does not come through Mālik b. Anas, even though Mālik transmits from Suhayl elsewhere. It comes through later non-Medinan lines: Kufan, Basran, and routes tied to Suhayl’s wider post-Medina circulation. That is precisely the layer where the report becomes movable as an eschatological unit. The point is methodological. If a report has a respectable common link, that does not make it Prophetic. A common link can be the systematic disseminator of a report that formed in his family, school, or social world. The isnād tells us where the report becomes recoverable. The matn and historical setting tell us why it would have been meaningful there. ## Why Abū Ṣāliḥ matters more than Suhayl The real improvement in the argument is to move the motive one generation upstream. Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt, Suhayl’s father, is the figure whose profile most closely fits the report. He was a major transmitter from Abū Hurayra, and the chain **Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra** was one of the most useful ways to give Medinan authority to a report. But his biography adds details that make the “meadows and rivers” clause unusually intelligible. First, he was called **al-Sammān**, the ghee-seller, and **al-Zayyāt**, the oil-seller. Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he used to bring ghee and oil from Medina to Kufa. These are not random products. Ghee presupposes pastoral abundance. Oil presupposes agricultural and irrigated production. The report’s central imagery is precisely the world of pasture and irrigated land. Second, he moved along the Medina-Kufa corridor. That matters because the Umayyad and early Marwānid period was an age of estates, canals, land grants, and reclamation projects across Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the Hijaz. A transmitter who regularly moved between Medina and Kufa did not need a modern satellite image to imagine “Arab land” becoming productive. He lived in the commercial orbit of that transformation. Third, he was remembered as an ʿUthmānī. al-Mizzī reports that when ʿUthmān was mentioned, Abū Ṣāliḥ wept until his beard trembled. Some reports also place him among those who witnessed the siege of ʿUthmān’s house. This does not prove that he was a Marwānid propagandist. It does mean that his political temperament was not anti-Umayyad in the way a Kūfan anti-Marwānid rebel’s would be. A providential reading of agrarian abundance under the Umayyad order fits his world better than it fits a neutral Bedouin memory from the Prophet’s lifetime. The report therefore makes sense as an al-Sammān household tradition. Abū Ṣāliḥ supplies the Abū Hurayra authority and the commercial-ideological setting. Suhayl supplies the later hadith bundle. ## The matn is not about hidden paleoclimate Modern apologetics tends to read the phrase **“returns to meadows and rivers”** through prehistoric climate studies. But the pre-modern reception points in another direction. The commentators did not need to invoke a lost green Arabia tens of thousands of years in the past. They read the report as a sign of settlement, cultivation, and irrigation. Al-Qurṭubī’s explanation is especially useful. He says the Arabs would turn away from their old habit of seeking rain-pastures and moving for war and raids, and would instead occupy themselves with planting the land, developing it, and channeling its waters. He even says this had already been seen in many of their lands and circumstances. That matters because it destroys the modern claim that the report is impressive only if interpreted as geological or paleoclimatic foresight. A major medieval commentator read it as social and agrarian transformation, not a scientific prediction about deep-time climate cycles. Ibn Kathīr also files the report among the signs of the Hour as a sign of abundance. In the hadith families themselves, the greening clause sits beside wealth overflowing, zakāt becoming hard to distribute, and the earth producing treasures. The point is not meteorology. The point is ominous abundance. ## The historical setting: reviving dead land The late Umayyad period had a legal and fiscal language for making land productive: **iḥyāʾ al-mawāt**, the reviving of dead land. In legal theory, someone who revived dead land could acquire it, and such land could be taxed more lightly. The imam could also grant land. In practice, this created both opportunity and grievance. Reclamation could reward loyal elites and increase revenue, while also concentrating land and putting pressure on cultivators. This historical setting gives the report a motive. The phrase “the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers” is not just a climate image. It is a religiously charged version of a real social process: canals, reclaimed land, estates, produce, taxation, and the transformation of frontier or marginal land into productive property. That also explains why the report is ambivalent. It is framed as a sign of the Hour, so abundance is ominous. But the imagery itself is positive: pasture, water, fertility, wealth. It sacralizes an agrarian transformation while keeping it inside apocalyptic warning. ## What does “the land of the Arabs” mean? A major weakness in the modern miracle reading is that it quietly assumes **arḍ al-ʿarab** means the modern Arabian Peninsula in a narrow geographical sense. That is not how the phrase always worked. Classical geographers could define the land or peninsula of the Arabs elastically. al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition, preserved by al-Bakrī, runs from the farthest south to the marches of Syria, while other boundary descriptions reach toward the Sawād of Iraq and the Baṭāʾiḥ. This matters because the documented agrarian transformations of the Umayyad period were not limited to the interior of today’s Saudi Arabia. They were especially visible in Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the frontier zones. So even if one takes the report literally, it does not have to mean “Riyadh becomes Switzerland.” In the world of early Arabic geography, “Arab land” could include the very regions where reclamation and irrigation were historically active. This is why the paper’s reconstruction is stronger than both modern apologetics and simplistic skepticism. It does not deny that landscapes changed. It asks whose world produced a prophecy in which Arab land became irrigated, pastoral, and productive. ## Why the surrounding clauses look borrowed The Bazzār note matters because the greening clause does not float alone. It gets attached to other eschatological motifs. The **overflowing wealth** motif has wider attestation. So does the image of a man offering zakāt and finding no one to accept it. The **harj** motif, defined as killing, is also widely known. The **safe travel between Iraq and Mecca** motif belongs to a recognizable political-security imagination. These motifs could circulate independently and be joined to new local material. What the Suhayl bundle appears to have done is attach the distinctive agrarian image to familiar eschatological furniture. The report becomes more credible because it sounds like other end-times reports. But the distinctive line still points back to one family bundle. This is how retrospective prophecy often works. A new historical concern is framed with older recognized motifs so that it sounds like inherited sacred memory. ## Why it is not enough to say “Muslim narrated it” The report is in Muslim, and that matters for later Sunni reception. But canonical placement is not a time machine. Muslim’s version is still a later collection-level witness to a report whose transmission history runs through Suhayl. al-Ḥākim’s grading also does not solve the problem, because his own cited route through Sufyān contains hesitation over the raised attribution. The issue is not whether the report can be made formally acceptable within later Sunni hadith grading. The issue is whether it is a clean miracle claim. It is not. A clean miracle claim would need an early, broad, independent transmission profile and a matn that cannot be better explained by the transmitter’s world. Here we have the opposite: a recoverable bottleneck, a family profile that fits the imagery, and a historical setting that explains the motive. ## The revised verdict The older blog focused too much on whether Suhayl’s narrations are “weak.” That is not the best case. The best case is that the report is historically located. Suhayl is the common link and disseminator. Abū Ṣāliḥ is the probable origin-layer. The surrounding clauses are standard eschatological pieces. The distinctive greening clause fits the al-Sammān family’s commercial world and the late Umayyad reclamation order. Classical commentary reads the report through settlement and irrigation, not modern paleoclimate. The phrase “land of the Arabs” itself is geographically elastic enough to include the very regions undergoing transformation. The “Green Arabia” report is best understood as an eschatological interpretation of late Umayyad agrarian transformation. It is not a clean prophecy of modern climate change. The distinctive clause enters the recoverable tradition through Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ, while the motive points to Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān al-Zayyāt’s Medina-Kufa commercial world of pasture, oil, irrigation, and ʿUthmānī political memory. A land-reclamation world became an end-times sign. ## Sources consulted 1. **Core hadith variants.** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 157c; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, nos. 8833 and 9395; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6700; al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8472; al-Bazzār, *al-Baḥr al-zakhkhār / Musnad*, no. 9071; Abū ʿAwāna, *al-Mustakhraj*, no. 3449. 2. **al-Bazzār’s common-link notice.** al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 9071: “part of this ḥadīth has been narrated from Abū Hurayra by more than one route, but we know it only through Suhayl from his father from Abū Hurayra.” 3. **Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ in rijāl.** al-Dhahabī, *Mīzān al-iʿtidāl*, entry on Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ; Ibn Ḥajar, *Tahdhīb al-tahdhīb* and *Taqrīb al-tahdhīb*, entry on Suhayl; Ibn Abī Ḥātim, *al-Jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl*, material on the Suhayl → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra channel. 4. **Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt.** Ibn Abī Ḥātim, *al-Jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl*, entry on Dhakwān Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān al-Zayyāt; Ibn Abī Khaythama, *al-Tārīkh al-kabīr*, report that he was al-Sammān, al-Zayyāt, a mawlā of Ghaṭafān, and narrated from the Kufans; al-Samʿānī, *al-Ansāb*, entry on al-Zayyāt; al-Mizzī, *Tahdhīb al-kamāl*, entry on Dhakwān; al-Dhahabī, *Tārīkh al-Islām*, entry on Dhakwān. 5. **Classical commentary on the meaning of “meadows and rivers.”** al-Qurṭubī, *al-Mufhim li-mā ashkala min talkhīṣ kitāb Muslim*, commentary on the abundance reports; Qiwām al-Sunna al-Aṣbahānī, *al-Taḥrīr fī sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim*, gloss of *murūjan wa-anhāran*; ʿIyāḍ b. Mūsā, *Ikmāl al-muʿlim bi-fawāʾid Muslim*; Ibn Kathīr, *al-Nihāya fī al-fitan wa-l-malāḥim*. 6. **Land reclamation, estates, and fiscal setting.** Abū Yūsuf, *Kitāb al-kharāj*, discussions of reviving dead land and dredging canals in the Sawād; al-Ṭabarī, *Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk*, reports used in discussions of al-Ḥajjāj’s taxation and rural policy; Harry Munt, “Caliphal Estates and Properties around Medina in the Umayyad Period”; Peter Verkinderen, “Land Reclamation and Irrigation Programs in Early Islamic Southern Mesopotamia”; Michele Campopiano, “Land Tenure, Land Tax and Social Conflictuality in Iraq.” 7. **The boundaries of arḍ al-ʿarab.** al-Bakrī, *Muʿjam mā istaʿjam*, preserving al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition of Jazīrat al-ʿArab; al-Bakrī, *al-Masālik wa-l-mamālik*, descriptions extending the boundary toward the Sawād and the Iraqi Baṭāʾiḥ. 8. **Method and modern framing.** G. H. A. Juynboll, *Muslim Tradition* and *Encyclopedia of Canonical Ḥadīth*, for common-link terminology and debate; Fred Donner, *Narratives of Islamic Origins*, and David Cook, *Studies in Muslim Apocalyptic*, for the political and communal use of apocalyptic material; Patricia Crone, “Were the Qays and Yemen of the Umayyad Period Political Parties?” for caution against flattening Qays/Yaman into ideological parties.

Arabia was once greener in the distant past, parts of it are greener today after rain, and the report says the land of the Arabs will “return” to meadows and rivers. The claim then treats the sentence as a scientifically precise prediction of modern climate change. That framing skips the older historical problem. The report is not a free-floating climate statement. It is a small eschatological clause embedded in changing bundles about wealth, zakāt, safe travel, killing, and the signs of the Hour. Its transmission does not spread from many independent Companions. It converges on one family line: **Abū Hurayra → Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān → Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ**. The point is not merely that Suhayl appears in the chain. The point is that every recoverable line containing the distinctive “meadows and rivers” clause runs through Suhayl, and the earliest technical notice we have, from al-Bazzār, already says so. The “Green Arabia” report is best explained as a late Umayyad agrarian-apocalyptic tradition. Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ is the demonstrable common link and disseminator. The better motive, however, points one generation earlier to his father, Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt: a Medinan client-scholar, a Medina-to-Kufa trader in ghee and oil, and an ʿUthmānī transmitter whose world was materially tied to pasture, irrigation, and the political imagination of land reclamation. That is more accurate than the older version of this blog. The old argument treated Suhayl as if the entire case depended on proving that he personally fabricated the report. The stronger argument is subtler. In isnād-cum-matn analysis, the common link is the point from which the report becomes visible and organized. He is not automatically the inventor. Here the matn, the family biography, and the historical setting make Abū Ṣāliḥ’s world the more plausible place to locate the kernel. The report in its best-known form لاَ تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْمَالُ وَيَفِيضَ، حَتَّى يَخْرُجَ الرَّجُلُ بِزَكَاةِ مَالِهِ فَلاَ يَجِدُ أَحَدًا يَقْبَلُهَا مِنْهُ، وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا. > “The Hour will not be established until wealth becomes abundant and overflows, so that a man will go out with the zakāt of his wealth and find no one to accept it from him, and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 157c, through Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Qārī → Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ → his father → Abū Hurayra. Aḥmad preserves a near-identical form through the same Qutayba–Yaʿqūb route, but with the added clause that killing will become widespread: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْمَالُ وَيَفِيضَ ... وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا، وَحَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ. قَالُوا: وَمَا الْهَرْجُ يَا رَسُولَ اللهِ؟ قَالَ: الْقَتْلُ، الْقَتْلُ. > “The Hour will not be established until wealth becomes abundant and overflows ... and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers, and until killing becomes widespread.” They said, “What is killing, Messenger of God?” He said, “Killing, killing.” > > **Source:** Aḥmad, *Musnad*, no. 9395, through Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Another Aḥmad version changes the surrounding material. The greening clause comes first, then safe travel between Iraq and Mecca, then *harj*: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا، وَحَتَّى يَسِيرَ الرَّاكِبُ بَيْنَ الْعِرَاقِ وَمَكَّةَ لَا يَخَافُ إِلَّا ضَلَالَ الطَّرِيقِ، وَحَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ. > “The Hour will not be established until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers, until a rider travels between Iraq and Mecca fearing nothing except losing the road, and until killing becomes widespread.” > > **Source:** Aḥmad, *Musnad*, no. 8833, through Muḥammad b. al-Ṣabbāḥ → Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Ibn Ḥibbān has a shorter form with only *harj* and greening: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى يَكْثُرَ الْهَرْجُ، وَحَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا. > “The Hour will not be established until killing becomes widespread and until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6700, through Muḥammad b. Isḥāq b. Ibrāhīm → Qutayba b. Saʿīd → Yaʿqūb b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Al-Ḥākim preserves the bare clause through Sufyān al-Thawrī, but his form contains an important hesitation: قَالَ سُفْيَانُ: لَا أَعْلَمُ إِلَّا قَدْ رَفَعَهُ. قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: «لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَعُودَ أَرْضُ الْعَرَبِ مُرُوجًا وَأَنْهَارًا». > Sufyān said: “I only know that he raised it.” He said: the Messenger of God said, “The Hour will not be established until the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers.” > > **Source:** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8472, through al-Ḥusayn b. Ḥafṣ → Sufyān al-Thawrī → Suhayl → his father → Abū Hurayra. Sufyān’s hesitation matters. It does not destroy the report by itself, but it does show that the attribution was not as effortless as later apologetic citation makes it sound. The transmitter himself pauses over whether he knows it as a raised Prophetic statement. The isnād: not a wide prophetic memory, but a Suhayl bundle The diagram corrects two common mistakes. The first mistake is the apologetic one: treating the existence of multiple later citations as if they were independent prophetic witnesses. They are not. Muslim, Aḥmad, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, al-Bazzār, and Abū ʿAwāna preserve different recensions, but the distinctive clause does not escape the line **Suhayl → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra**. The second mistake is the crude skeptical one: treating this as if there were no real transmission bundle at all. There is a bundle. After Suhayl, we have several students in different regional settings: Yaʿqūb al-Qārī in the Medinan line, Ismāʿīl b. Zakariyyā and Sufyān al-Thawrī in Kufan lines, and ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār in the Basran line. The problem is not that the whole thing is a single late citation. The problem is that the bundle begins only at Suhayl. That distinction is important. The correct conclusion is not “one weak liar invented it.” The correct conclusion is that the report becomes visible as a structured tradition in Suhayl’s lifetime, while the content and family context point one generation earlier. al-Bazzār already noticed the bottleneck The most important early critical note comes from al-Bazzār. After transmitting the fullest form through ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. al-Mukhtār from Suhayl, he says: وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ قَدْ رُوِيَ بَعْضُهُ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ مِنْ غَيْرِ وَجْهٍ، وَلَا نَعْلَمُ أَخَذَهُ إِلَّا سُهَيْلٌ عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ. > “Part of this ḥadīth has been narrated from Abū Hurayra by more than one route, but we do not know anyone who took it except Suhayl from his father from Abū Hurayra.” > > **Source:** al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 9071. This is the key to the whole case. al-Bazzār is not saying that every surrounding theme is unique to Suhayl. The motifs of overflowing wealth, refused zakāt, *harj*, and secure travel have other lives in the hadith corpus. What is distinctive here is the way those motifs are joined to the clause that **the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers**. That clause is the family’s contribution. The apologetic argument often points to Muslim or al-Ḥākim and stops there. But al-Bazzār’s note shows that the bottleneck was visible to early hadith critics themselves. This is not a modern hostile invention. Suhayl is the disseminator, not necessarily the author Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ was not an unknown nobody. He was a known Medinan transmitter, and several authorities accepted him. That has to be stated clearly because the older blog’s rijāl section leaned too hard on selective negative judgments. At the same time, he was not above criticism. Ibn Ḥajar summarizes him as truthful, but says his memory changed late. Critics also report that his Iraqi transmission was affected by forgetfulness. Abū Ḥātim’s formula is especially useful: his ḥadīth may be written, but is not used as proof. This is not a total rejection. It is a warning against building a miracle claim on a unique Suhayl-family clause. The route profile matches that warning. The “Green Arabia” clause does not come through Mālik b. Anas, even though Mālik transmits from Suhayl elsewhere. It comes through later non-Medinan lines: Kufan, Basran, and routes tied to Suhayl’s wider post-Medina circulation. That is precisely the layer where the report becomes movable as an eschatological unit. The point is methodological. If a report has a respectable common link, that does not make it Prophetic. A common link can be the systematic disseminator of a report that formed in his family, school, or social world. The isnād tells us where the report becomes recoverable. The matn and historical setting tell us why it would have been meaningful there. Why Abū Ṣāliḥ matters more than Suhayl The real improvement in the argument is to move the motive one generation upstream. Abū Ṣāliḥ Dhakwān al-Sammān al-Zayyāt, Suhayl’s father, is the figure whose profile most closely fits the report. He was a major transmitter from Abū Hurayra, and the chain **Abū Ṣāliḥ → Abū Hurayra** was one of the most useful ways to give Medinan authority to a report. But his biography adds details that make the “meadows and rivers” clause unusually intelligible. First, he was called **al-Sammān**, the ghee-seller, and **al-Zayyāt**, the oil-seller. Ibn Abī Ḥātim says he used to bring ghee and oil from Medina to Kufa. These are not random products. Ghee presupposes pastoral abundance. Oil presupposes agricultural and irrigated production. The report’s central imagery is precisely the world of pasture and irrigated land. Second, he moved along the Medina-Kufa corridor. That matters because the Umayyad and early Marwānid period was an age of estates, canals, land grants, and reclamation projects across Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the Hijaz. A transmitter who regularly moved between Medina and Kufa did not need a modern satellite image to imagine “Arab land” becoming productive. He lived in the commercial orbit of that transformation. Third, he was remembered as an ʿUthmānī. al-Mizzī reports that when ʿUthmān was mentioned, Abū Ṣāliḥ wept until his beard trembled. Some reports also place him among those who witnessed the siege of ʿUthmān’s house. This does not prove that he was a Marwānid propagandist. It does mean that his political temperament was not anti-Umayyad in the way a Kūfan anti-Marwānid rebel’s would be. A providential reading of agrarian abundance under the Umayyad order fits his world better than it fits a neutral Bedouin memory from the Prophet’s lifetime. The report therefore makes sense as an al-Sammān household tradition. Abū Ṣāliḥ supplies the Abū Hurayra authority and the commercial-ideological setting. Suhayl supplies the later hadith bundle. The matn is not about hidden paleoclimate Modern apologetics tends to read the phrase **“returns to meadows and rivers”** through prehistoric climate studies. But the pre-modern reception points in another direction. The commentators did not need to invoke a lost green Arabia tens of thousands of years in the past. They read the report as a sign of settlement, cultivation, and irrigation. Al-Qurṭubī’s explanation is especially useful. He says the Arabs would turn away from their old habit of seeking rain-pastures and moving for war and raids, and would instead occupy themselves with planting the land, developing it, and channeling its waters. He even says this had already been seen in many of their lands and circumstances. That matters because it destroys the modern claim that the report is impressive only if interpreted as geological or paleoclimatic foresight. A major medieval commentator read it as social and agrarian transformation, not a scientific prediction about deep-time climate cycles. Ibn Kathīr also files the report among the signs of the Hour as a sign of abundance. In the hadith families themselves, the greening clause sits beside wealth overflowing, zakāt becoming hard to distribute, and the earth producing treasures. The point is not meteorology. The point is ominous abundance. The historical setting: reviving dead land The late Umayyad period had a legal and fiscal language for making land productive: **iḥyāʾ al-mawāt**, the reviving of dead land. In legal theory, someone who revived dead land could acquire it, and such land could be taxed more lightly. The imam could also grant land. In practice, this created both opportunity and grievance. Reclamation could reward loyal elites and increase revenue, while also concentrating land and putting pressure on cultivators. This historical setting gives the report a motive. The phrase “the land of the Arabs returns to meadows and rivers” is not just a climate image. It is a religiously charged version of a real social process: canals, reclaimed land, estates, produce, taxation, and the transformation of frontier or marginal land into productive property. That also explains why the report is ambivalent. It is framed as a sign of the Hour, so abundance is ominous. But the imagery itself is positive: pasture, water, fertility, wealth. It sacralizes an agrarian transformation while keeping it inside apocalyptic warning. What does “the land of the Arabs” mean? A major weakness in the modern miracle reading is that it quietly assumes **arḍ al-ʿarab** means the modern Arabian Peninsula in a narrow geographical sense. That is not how the phrase always worked. Classical geographers could define the land or peninsula of the Arabs elastically. al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition, preserved by al-Bakrī, runs from the farthest south to the marches of Syria, while other boundary descriptions reach toward the Sawād of Iraq and the Baṭāʾiḥ. This matters because the documented agrarian transformations of the Umayyad period were not limited to the interior of today’s Saudi Arabia. They were especially visible in Iraq, the Jazīra, Syria, and the frontier zones. So even if one takes the report literally, it does not have to mean “Riyadh becomes Switzerland.” In the world of early Arabic geography, “Arab land” could include the very regions where reclamation and irrigation were historically active. This is why the paper’s reconstruction is stronger than both modern apologetics and simplistic skepticism. It does not deny that landscapes changed. It asks whose world produced a prophecy in which Arab land became irrigated, pastoral, and productive. Why the surrounding clauses look borrowed The Bazzār note matters because the greening clause does not float alone. It gets attached to other eschatological motifs. The **overflowing wealth** motif has wider attestation. So does the image of a man offering zakāt and finding no one to accept it. The **harj** motif, defined as killing, is also widely known. The **safe travel between Iraq and Mecca** motif belongs to a recognizable political-security imagination. These motifs could circulate independently and be joined to new local material. What the Suhayl bundle appears to have done is attach the distinctive agrarian image to familiar eschatological furniture. The report becomes more credible because it sounds like other end-times reports. But the distinctive line still points back to one family bundle. This is how retrospective prophecy often works. A new historical concern is framed with older recognized motifs so that it sounds like inherited sacred memory. Why it is not enough to say “Muslim narrated it” The report is in Muslim, and that matters for later Sunni reception. But canonical placement is not a time machine. Muslim’s version is still a later collection-level witness to a report whose transmission history runs through Suhayl. al-Ḥākim’s grading also does not solve the problem, because his own cited route through Sufyān contains hesitation over the raised attribution. The issue is not whether the report can be made formally acceptable within later Sunni hadith grading. The issue is whether it is a clean miracle claim. It is not. A clean miracle claim would need an early, broad, independent transmission profile and a matn that cannot be better explained by the transmitter’s world. Here we have the opposite: a recoverable bottleneck, a family profile that fits the imagery, and a historical setting that explains the motive. The revised verdict The older blog focused too much on whether Suhayl’s narrations are “weak.” That is not the best case. The best case is that the report is historically located. Suhayl is the common link and disseminator. Abū Ṣāliḥ is the probable origin-layer. The surrounding clauses are standard eschatological pieces. The distinctive greening clause fits the al-Sammān family’s commercial world and the late Umayyad reclamation order. Classical commentary reads the report through settlement and irrigation, not modern paleoclimate. The phrase “land of the Arabs” itself is geographically elastic enough to include the very regions undergoing transformation. The “Green Arabia” report is best understood as an eschatological interpretation of late Umayyad agrarian transformation. It is not a clean prophecy of modern climate change. The distinctive clause enters the recoverable tradition through Suhayl b. Abī Ṣāliḥ, while the motive points to Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān al-Zayyāt’s Medina-Kufa commercial world of pasture, oil, irrigation, and ʿUthmānī political memory. Mūsā, *Ikmāl al-muʿlim bi-fawāʾid Muslim*; Ibn Kathīr, *al-Nihāya fī al-fitan wa-l-malāḥim*. 6. **Land reclamation, estates, and fiscal setting.** Abū Yūsuf, *Kitāb al-kharāj*, discussions of reviving dead land and dredging canals in the Sawād; al-Ṭabarī, *Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk*, reports used in discussions of al-Ḥajjāj’s taxation and rural policy; Harry Munt, “Caliphal Estates and Properties around Medina in the Umayyad Period”; Peter Verkinderen, “Land Reclamation and Irrigation Programs in Early Islamic Southern Mesopotamia”; Michele Campopiano, “Land Tenure, Land Tax and Social Conflictuality in Iraq.” 7. **The boundaries of arḍ al-ʿarab.** al-Bakrī, *Muʿjam mā istaʿjam*, preserving al-Aṣmaʿī’s definition of Jazīrat al-ʿArab; al-Bakrī, *al-Masālik wa-l-mamālik*, descriptions extending the boundary toward the Sawād and the Iraqi Baṭāʾiḥ. 8. **Method and modern framing.** G. H. A. Juynboll, *Muslim Tradition* and *Encyclopedia of Canonical Ḥadīth*, for common-link terminology and debate; Fred Donner, *Narratives of Islamic Origins*, and David Cook, *Studies in Muslim Apocalyptic*, for the political and communal use of apocalyptic material; Patricia Crone, “Were the Qays and Yemen of the Umayyad Period Political Parties?” for caution against flattening Qays/Yaman into ideological parties.

title: The Killing of ʿUmar and the Afflictions: Ḥudhayfa, the Door, and Kufan Fitna Memory
description: A full isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that ʿUmar was the closed door before the sea-like afflictions: the Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī transmission families, the al-Aʿmash problem, the broken-door motif, and the historical motive behind turning ʿUmar’s murder into prophecy.
