Since ʿUmar was assassinated and the Muslim community later entered civil war, apologists treat the narration as a prediction that could only have come from revelation. That reading is too simple. The report is better understood as a **Kūfan retrospective theology of the first civil war**. It takes three things everyone already knew by the late first and early second century: ʿUmar was murdered, the political order after him became unstable, and the first civil war shattered the memory of communal unity. It then turns those known facts into a symbolic scene in which Ḥudhayfa, the famous Companion of secrets and afflictions, explains the whole future by means of a closed door. The “closed door” report is not best attacked by saying merely, “al-Aʿmash was a mudallis, therefore the hadith is false.” The stronger argument is that the report is a carefully shaped Kūfan fitna narrative. Its strongest forms run through late first-century Kūfan transmitters from Ḥudhayfa. The matn itself shows retrospective construction: the fatal detail is not a public Prophetic prediction, but a later dialogue in which Ḥudhayfa turns ʿUmar’s already-known death into the moment when the door of civil strife was broken. ## The report in question The narrative has a memorable shape, but that is precisely the point. It is not merely a loose prediction of trouble. It is a staged interpretive scene. ʿUmar asks. Ḥudhayfa answers indirectly. The door is broken rather than opened. The audience is too afraid to ask the meaning. Masrūq finally asks. The hidden answer is ʿUmar. This dramatic structure is not incidental decoration. It is how the report turns remembered political history into a prophetic-seeming riddle. ## What the report actually predicts The first mistake is to treat every sentence in the narration as a direct statement from the Prophet. In the report itself, the most secure Prophetic saying is the opening material about ordinary afflictions in a man’s family, wealth, child, and neighbor being expiated by acts of devotion. The “sea-like afflictions” are introduced as something ʿUmar asks about, and the door explanation is given by Ḥudhayfa in the later conversation. This matters because the apologetic version usually says, “The Prophet predicted the assassination of ʿUmar.” The report does not actually give a public scene in which the Prophet names ʿUmar, names his killer, gives the year, or describes the assassination. The decisive identification appears only at the end, through a later disclosure: the group asks Ḥudhayfa, and Masrūq is sent to ask him directly. The report is therefore built like a remembered explanation of history, not like a public prediction before the event. In some variants Ḥudhayfa says, “I told him that between you and it there is a closed door.” That wording makes the door explanation Ḥudhayfa’s disclosure to ʿUmar. The prophecy claim rests less on a public Prophetic statement than on Ḥudhayfa’s private interpretation of what the coming afflictions meant for ʿUmar’s place in history. This is already enough to weaken the miracle claim. The report does not have to be read as a pre-644 CE prediction. It can be read as a post-644 CE, post-fitna explanation of why later Muslim history seemed to collapse after ʿUmar’s death. ## The transmission map The old version of this article leaned too heavily on al-Aʿmash as if he alone were the common link and therefore the obvious fabricator. That needs correcting. Al-Aʿmash is a major proliferator of the most famous form, but he is not the only route through which the story circulates. The material also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil, through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil, and through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. That does not save the prophecy claim. It sharpens the problem. The report is not a broad public Companion memory. It is a **Kūfan Ḥudhayfa dossier**. Its recoverable early centers are Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī, both Kūfan transmitters, and its major later spread is through Kūfan figures such as al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Jāmiʿ. The most important result is that the evidence does not point to a miraculous public prediction. It points to a set of Kūfan and Iraqi transmitters preserving, shaping, and expanding a Ḥudhayfa-centered explanation of post-ʿUmar civil strife. ## The Abū Wāʾil family: the famous form The famous version runs through Abū Wāʾil, whose name is Shuqayq b. Salama. From him the report branches mainly through al-Aʿmash. Bukhārī repeats this family several times. Muslim also preserves it through Abū Muʿāwiya from al-Aʿmash. Ibn Ḥibbān gives essentially the same form through Musaddad → Yaḥyā → al-Aʿmash → Shuqayq. This is the family in which the report is most polished. It contains the full staged sequence: ʿUmar asks, Ḥudhayfa distinguishes personal fitna from sea-like fitna, Ḥudhayfa speaks of a closed door, ʿUmar asks if it will be broken or opened, and Masrūq later asks who the door was. The answer is ʿUmar. The presence of several routes inside this family does not make them independent witnesses to the original event. Bukhārī’s multiple citations are not five separate origins. They are repetitions and branches of a shared Abū Wāʾil-Kūfan report. The center of gravity remains the same. ## The Jāmiʿ and ʿĀṣim routes: support, but still the same Kūfan world The report also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil in Bukhārī. This is useful because it prevents the analysis from being reduced to “al-Aʿmash alone made it up.” The story was larger than one man. But it is still the same Abū Wāʾil channel from Ḥudhayfa. Another supporting line goes through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil. Al-Tirmidhī’s route is especially interesting because Shuʿba reports from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala, all saying they heard Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa. That looks like a cluster of Kūfan students who knew a report attached to Abū Wāʾil. Al-Bazzār also preserves a strange route through ʿĀṣim from Zirr from Ḥudhayfa. But al-Bazzār himself flags the problem. He says that a group narrated the report from ʿĀṣim from Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa, and that he did not know anyone who narrated it from ʿĀṣim from Zirr except Muṭarrif. This means the Zirr route should not be treated as a clean independent Companion-transmitter path. It is probably a displacement or confusion within the wider ʿĀṣim material. The problem is not that every route is weak. Many of the named transmitters are respectable. The problem is that the report’s independent-looking spread remains concentrated inside Kūfan Ḥudhayfa fitna lore. Multiple branches after Abū Wāʾil do not prove that the Prophet publicly predicted ʿUmar’s assassination. They show that a powerful explanatory story circulated through Kūfan transmitters. ## The Ribʿī family: a different matn complex The second major family runs through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. Muslim preserves it through Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq from Ribʿī. Aḥmad and al-Bazzār preserve similar material. This family is not just a duplicate of the Abū Wāʾil version. It includes the famous image of afflictions being presented to hearts like a mat, one strand after another, until hearts become either white and resistant or black and overturned. This matters because it shows that the “door” motif is embedded inside a larger Ḥudhayfa fitna complex. In the Ribʿī family, Ḥudhayfa says that he told ʿUmar there was a closed door between him and those afflictions, and that the door was a man who would be killed or die. This version explains the metaphor without needing the final Masrūq scene as strongly as the Abū Wāʾil form does. The Ribʿī family therefore looks like a parallel development, not a pristine independent confirmation. It has the same historical logic: ʿUmar’s removal marks the transition from controlled order to uncontrolled fitna. But it packages the idea inside a different sermon on hearts and moral testing. ## The ʿAbd al-Razzāq report: early circulation without a full chain ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves a version through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī. It says that ʿUmar asked who would tell them about the afflictions, Ḥudhayfa answered, and the broken-door exchange followed. This is important because it is early and shows the story circulating beyond the exact al-Aʿmash line. But it also lacks the full Companion-to-Successor chain that would make it independent proof. Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī are not presented as hearing this scene from Ḥudhayfa. The report is a piece of early Basran-Iraqi fitna lore in Maʿmar’s material. Its value is not that it proves the prophecy. Its value is that it shows the “ʿUmar as door” story had become memorable and portable by the time these Iraqi transmitters were active. That is exactly what one would expect from a retrospective explanation of the first civil war. It becomes a compact moral formula: the door was ʿUmar; the door was broken; therefore the community never returned to its earlier unity. ## The matn is built like retrospective history The matn has several layers. The first layer is a common moral teaching: a person faces trials through family, wealth, children, and neighbors, and acts of worship expiate these trials. This is general religious advice. It does not require knowledge of the future. The second layer is the “waves of the sea.” This is vague, but it is not meaningless. After the murder of ʿUthmān, the battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, the rise of factional politics, and later Umayyad and anti-Umayyad violence, “fitna like the waves of the sea” was exactly the language one would use to describe the past. The third layer is the door. A door can be opened or broken. If opened, it might be closed again. If broken, the rupture is permanent. This distinction only becomes powerful after one already knows how ʿUmar died. He was not replaced by a normal administrative transition. He was murdered. The door was not opened; it was broken. The fourth layer is the later identification. The transmitters are afraid to ask Ḥudhayfa who the door is. Masrūq is sent. Ḥudhayfa answers: ʿUmar. That is a dramatic device. It makes the answer feel hidden, dangerous, and authoritative. It also makes the meaning appear to be discovered rather than invented. ## Why ʿUmar? The motive becomes clearer once we ask what the report accomplishes. It does not merely predict that a person will die. Everyone dies. Nor does it merely predict that fitna will happen. The Qurʾān already says that believers will be tested, and early Muslims had no shortage of real political turmoil to interpret. The report does something more specific. It makes ʿUmar the barrier between the community and the age of civil strife. That is an extremely useful memory. It sanctifies ʿUmar’s rule as the last intact door of communal order. It also explains later chaos without having to say bluntly that the Companions failed. The fitna was not simply bad policy, factional ambition, or tribal conflict. It was the destiny of a broken door. The Qurʾān does not require a hidden prophecy to explain trials. It treats testing as a basic condition of faith. The hadith report adds something else: a political chronology. ʿUmar becomes the threshold. Before him, the door is closed. After him, the waves begin. ## Why Ḥudhayfa? Ḥudhayfa is the perfect narrator for this kind of material. In Islamic memory he is not just another Companion. He is the Companion associated with secrets, hypocrisy, and future afflictions. A report placed through Ḥudhayfa can sound like privileged knowledge even when its historical setting is vague. He also fits the geography. The report’s recoverable transmission is heavily Kūfan, and Ḥudhayfa’s memory was important in Iraqi fitna discourse. The first civil war mattered intensely in Kūfa. ʿAlī’s capital, the battle of Ṣiffīn, the Khārijites, pro-ʿAlid and anti-ʿAlid currents, and later anti-Umayyad movements all made Iraq a natural place for traditions that explained how fitna began. A report through Ḥudhayfa lets later transmitters speak about civil war while avoiding direct factional accusation. Instead of saying “this party caused the disaster” or “that Companion caused the disaster,” the report says that the door was broken and the sea-like afflictions came. It turns political blame into sacred chronology. ## The historical pressure behind the story The murder of ʿUmar was not a simple isolated event. Historical sources preserve the immediate shock and its aftermath. Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ places ʿUmar’s stabbing near the end of Dhū al-Ḥijja in 23 AH and says he lived several days after being stabbed. Al-Ṭabarī gives the same basic chronological memory. The aftermath was politically charged. Al-Balādhurī reports that ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar, in response to his father’s murder, killed al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, and the daughter of Abū Luʾluʾa after accusing them of involvement. This became a dispute under ʿUthmān. That means the murder of ʿUmar already generated a moral and legal crisis before the later civil wars even began. Then came the ʿUthmān crisis. Historical reports describe complaints against ʿUthmān, the mobilization of provincial opposition, and eventually his killing. Whether one accepts every detail of later historiography or not, the larger memory is unmistakable: the post-ʿUmar order was remembered as the beginning of a chain of unresolved crises. The “door” report gives later Muslims a clean explanation for a messy transition. ʿUmar’s murder, ʿUthmān’s contested rule, ʿUthmān’s murder, the battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, and later factional violence become a single sequence. The door was broken, so the waves came. This is why the report would be attractive in Kūfan circles. Kūfa was not a neutral archive. It was one of the main theaters of early Islamic political memory. A compact Ḥudhayfa report explaining why fitna became unstoppable would have been useful across multiple groups: quietists could use it to discourage participation in civil war; Sunnis could use it to elevate ʿUmar; and later transmitters could use it to narrate early chaos as fate rather than as the failure of their heroes. ## The self-authenticating line One line deserves special attention: > “I narrated to him a report that was not from the errors.” This is not a neutral phrase. It functions like a built-in guarantee. The report knows that it is asking the audience to accept a hidden interpretation of history. So the narrative gives the interpretation a seal of certainty: Ḥudhayfa says he told ʿUmar a report free of mistakes. That line does not make the report stronger historically. It makes it more revealing literarily. It is exactly the kind of sentence that appears when a report is aware that its claim rests on private knowledge that cannot be checked. The audience is being told not only what happened, but how confidently it should believe what happened. ## The “broken” door is the giveaway The door could have been opened. Instead, it is broken. The difference matters. An opened door can be shut again. A broken door cannot. The report therefore explains why later history did not return to the idealized age before the first civil war. This is ex eventu logic. Once the narrator knows that ʿUmar was assassinated, and once he knows that the subsequent period was remembered as irreversible political rupture, “broken” becomes the perfect word. It is not just a prediction of death. It is an interpretation of the assassination as the irreversible destruction of the communal barrier. Some variants sharpen the point even more by saying that the door would not be closed until the Day of Resurrection. That looks like later apocalyptic inflation. The more the community’s history appears permanently fractured, the more the report can stretch the broken door into an end-times condition. ## The report is not weak in the simplistic way A careful critique should not pretend that the whole report collapses because every transmitter is unreliable. That is not true. Ibn Ḥajar describes Abū Wāʾil as trustworthy, Kūfan, and a mukhadram. He describes Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh as trustworthy, devout, and a mukhadram. He describes Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid and Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq as trustworthy. Even al-Aʿmash is described as trustworthy, a ḥāfiẓ, and a recitation expert, though he practiced tadlīs. The tadlīs point must be used carefully. In several core versions al-Aʿmash uses explicit hearing language from Shuqayq or Abū Wāʾil, so it is not enough to dismiss the report by saying “al-Aʿmash was a mudallis.” The stronger point is methodological: reliable transmitters can still preserve a retrospective political interpretation as if it were early sacred memory. ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala is a more mixed figure. Ibn Ḥajar calls him truthful but with mistakes, a proof in Qurʾānic recitation, and says his ḥadīth in the two Ṣaḥīḥs comes in supporting form. That fits the evidence here. His Abū Wāʾil route supports the existence of the story in Kūfan transmission, but the anomalous Zirr route in al-Bazzār shows how easily the report could shift within the Ḥudhayfa transmitter network. The issue is not that the isnād is obviously worthless. The issue is that a politically meaningful, post-event explanation of early Islamic history has been transmitted through exactly the kind of Iraqi fitna network in which such an explanation would be expected to form. ## How the report should be classified The report is not a simple one-man invention at al-Aʿmash’s level. That claim is too narrow. It is also not a clean miracle prophecy. The best classification is: 1. **Base saying:** a general Prophetic or early moral saying about ordinary trials in family, wealth, children, and neighbors. 2. **Fitna expansion:** Ḥudhayfa-centered Iraqi material about the sea-like afflictions. 3. **Historical interpretation:** ʿUmar is made the closed door between the community and those afflictions. 4. **Narrative dramatization:** Masrūq’s later question reveals the hidden meaning. 5. **Canonical reception:** Bukhārī and Muslim preserve the report as part of a larger Sunni memory of ʿUmar, fitna, and moral decline. The miracle claim depends on collapsing all five layers into one public Prophetic prediction. The report itself does not require that reading. ## Why this narrative was useful The report was useful because it solved several problems at once. First, it elevated ʿUmar. He becomes the door that kept catastrophic fitna away. This is a powerful piece of Sunni memory. ʿUmar is not merely the second caliph. He is the barrier between order and chaos. Second, it explained why the community fell into civil war without directly blaming revered figures. The door was broken. Once that happened, the waves came. The metaphor reduces the need to assign political blame. Third, it served quietist purposes. If the fitna after ʿUmar is an irreversible sea, then the pious response is caution, withdrawal, and suspicion of political mobilization. That is why the report sits naturally among other fitan reports warning against civil conflict. Fourth, it gave Kūfan transmitters a way to make sense of their own inherited trauma. Kūfa was a city of civil-war memory. The report does not come from nowhere. It comes from the world that most needed a sacred explanation for why the early community fractured. ## What a fulfillment argument misses A fulfillment argument says: ʿUmar died, fitna followed, therefore the Prophet knew the future. A historical-critical reading says: later Muslims knew ʿUmar died and fitna followed, so they told the story of ʿUmar as the broken door. The report is not impressive because it describes an unforeseeable detail. It is revealing because it captures how early Muslims turned trauma into theology. The report’s power is not precision. It does not name Abū Luʾluʾa. It does not name the date. It does not name the shūrā, ʿUthmān, the rebels, the battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, or the Umayyads. Its power is symbolic. ʿUmar’s death becomes a threshold. Everything after him becomes the sea. The ʿUmar-door report is best explained as a Kūfan retrospective fitna narrative. Its exact famous form clusters around Abū Wāʾil and al-Aʿmash, while parallel Kūfan lines through Jāmiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ribʿī show that the story was broader than one transmitter but still concentrated in Ḥudhayfa-centered Iraqi fitna memory. The report turns a known historical sequence, ʿUmar’s murder followed by political rupture, into sacred chronology. It is not a clean miracle claim. It is a broken-door theology of the first civil war. ## Sources consulted 1. **Main Abū Wāʾil / al-Aʿmash family.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 525, 1435, 3586, 7096; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 144d; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, no. 23412; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 5966; Ibn Abī Shayba, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 37129; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 60. 2. **Parallel Abū Wāʾil routes.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 1895, through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil; al-Tirmidhī, *Jāmiʿ*, no. 2258, through Shuʿba from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, nos. 2496, 2511, 2529, including his note that the Zirr route from ʿĀṣim is anomalous against the better-known Abū Wāʾil route. 3. **Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh family.** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 144a; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, nos. 23280, 23440; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 2472; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, nos. 65, 67; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, report through al-Shaʿbī / Mujālid from Ribʿī. 4. **Early collateral / mursal circulation.** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf / al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20753, through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-awsaṭ*, nos. 1774 and 4835, for later collateral forms of the same Abū Wāʾil material. 5. **Rijāl evidence.** Ibn Ḥajar, *Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb*, entries for Abū Wāʾil Shuqayq b. Salama, Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh, Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid, Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq, al-Aʿmash Sulaymān b. Mihrān, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala; Ibn Ḥibbān, *al-Majrūḥīn*, discussion of trustworthy mudallis transmitters and the need for explicit hearing. 6. **Historical context of ʿUmar’s murder and its aftermath.** Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ, *al-Tārīkh*, entry on the killing of ʿUmar; al-Ṭabarī, *Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk*, chronology of ʿUmar’s stabbing and death; al-Balādhurī, *Futūḥ al-buldān* and *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, Abū Luʾluʾa, ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar’s retaliatory killings, and the later ʿUthmān crisis.

Since ʿUmar was assassinated and the Muslim community later entered civil war, apologists treat the narration as a prediction that could only have come from revelation. That reading is too simple. The report is better understood as a **Kūfan retrospective theology of the first civil war**. It takes three things everyone already knew by the late first and early second century: ʿUmar was murdered, the political order after him became unstable, and the first civil war shattered the memory of communal unity. It then turns those known facts into a symbolic scene in which Ḥudhayfa, the famous Companion of secrets and afflictions, explains the whole future by means of a closed door. The “closed door” report is not best attacked by saying merely, “al-Aʿmash was a mudallis, therefore the hadith is false.” The stronger argument is that the report is a carefully shaped Kūfan fitna narrative. Its strongest forms run through late first-century Kūfan transmitters from Ḥudhayfa. The matn itself shows retrospective construction: the fatal detail is not a public Prophetic prediction, but a later dialogue in which Ḥudhayfa turns ʿUmar’s already-known death into the moment when the door of civil strife was broken. The report in question The narrative has a memorable shape, but that is precisely the point. It is not merely a loose prediction of trouble. It is a staged interpretive scene. ʿUmar asks. Ḥudhayfa answers indirectly. The door is broken rather than opened. The audience is too afraid to ask the meaning. Masrūq finally asks. The hidden answer is ʿUmar. This dramatic structure is not incidental decoration. It is how the report turns remembered political history into a prophetic-seeming riddle. What the report actually predicts The first mistake is to treat every sentence in the narration as a direct statement from the Prophet. In the report itself, the most secure Prophetic saying is the opening material about ordinary afflictions in a man’s family, wealth, child, and neighbor being expiated by acts of devotion. The “sea-like afflictions” are introduced as something ʿUmar asks about, and the door explanation is given by Ḥudhayfa in the later conversation. This matters because the apologetic version usually says, “The Prophet predicted the assassination of ʿUmar.” The report does not actually give a public scene in which the Prophet names ʿUmar, names his killer, gives the year, or describes the assassination. The decisive identification appears only at the end, through a later disclosure: the group asks Ḥudhayfa, and Masrūq is sent to ask him directly. The report is therefore built like a remembered explanation of history, not like a public prediction before the event. In some variants Ḥudhayfa says, “I told him that between you and it there is a closed door.” That wording makes the door explanation Ḥudhayfa’s disclosure to ʿUmar. The prophecy claim rests less on a public Prophetic statement than on Ḥudhayfa’s private interpretation of what the coming afflictions meant for ʿUmar’s place in history. This is already enough to weaken the miracle claim. The report does not have to be read as a pre-644 CE prediction. It can be read as a post-644 CE, post-fitna explanation of why later Muslim history seemed to collapse after ʿUmar’s death. The transmission map The old version of this article leaned too heavily on al-Aʿmash as if he alone were the common link and therefore the obvious fabricator. That needs correcting. Al-Aʿmash is a major proliferator of the most famous form, but he is not the only route through which the story circulates. The material also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil, through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil, and through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. That does not save the prophecy claim. It sharpens the problem. The report is not a broad public Companion memory. It is a **Kūfan Ḥudhayfa dossier**. Its recoverable early centers are Abū Wāʾil and Ribʿī, both Kūfan transmitters, and its major later spread is through Kūfan figures such as al-Aʿmash, ʿĀṣim, and Jāmiʿ. The most important result is that the evidence does not point to a miraculous public prediction. It points to a set of Kūfan and Iraqi transmitters preserving, shaping, and expanding a Ḥudhayfa-centered explanation of post-ʿUmar civil strife. The Abū Wāʾil family: the famous form The famous version runs through Abū Wāʾil, whose name is Shuqayq b. Salama. From him the report branches mainly through al-Aʿmash. Bukhārī repeats this family several times. Muslim also preserves it through Abū Muʿāwiya from al-Aʿmash. Ibn Ḥibbān gives essentially the same form through Musaddad → Yaḥyā → al-Aʿmash → Shuqayq. This is the family in which the report is most polished. It contains the full staged sequence: ʿUmar asks, Ḥudhayfa distinguishes personal fitna from sea-like fitna, Ḥudhayfa speaks of a closed door, ʿUmar asks if it will be broken or opened, and Masrūq later asks who the door was. The answer is ʿUmar. The presence of several routes inside this family does not make them independent witnesses to the original event. Bukhārī’s multiple citations are not five separate origins. They are repetitions and branches of a shared Abū Wāʾil-Kūfan report. The center of gravity remains the same. The Jāmiʿ and ʿĀṣim routes: support, but still the same Kūfan world The report also appears through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil in Bukhārī. This is useful because it prevents the analysis from being reduced to “al-Aʿmash alone made it up.” The story was larger than one man. But it is still the same Abū Wāʾil channel from Ḥudhayfa. Another supporting line goes through ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil. Al-Tirmidhī’s route is especially interesting because Shuʿba reports from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala, all saying they heard Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa. That looks like a cluster of Kūfan students who knew a report attached to Abū Wāʾil. Al-Bazzār also preserves a strange route through ʿĀṣim from Zirr from Ḥudhayfa. But al-Bazzār himself flags the problem. He says that a group narrated the report from ʿĀṣim from Abū Wāʾil from Ḥudhayfa, and that he did not know anyone who narrated it from ʿĀṣim from Zirr except Muṭarrif. This means the Zirr route should not be treated as a clean independent Companion-transmitter path. It is probably a displacement or confusion within the wider ʿĀṣim material. The problem is not that every route is weak. Many of the named transmitters are respectable. The problem is that the report’s independent-looking spread remains concentrated inside Kūfan Ḥudhayfa fitna lore. Multiple branches after Abū Wāʾil do not prove that the Prophet publicly predicted ʿUmar’s assassination. They show that a powerful explanatory story circulated through Kūfan transmitters. The Ribʿī family: a different matn complex The second major family runs through Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh from Ḥudhayfa. Muslim preserves it through Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq from Ribʿī. Aḥmad and al-Bazzār preserve similar material. This family is not just a duplicate of the Abū Wāʾil version. It includes the famous image of afflictions being presented to hearts like a mat, one strand after another, until hearts become either white and resistant or black and overturned. This matters because it shows that the “door” motif is embedded inside a larger Ḥudhayfa fitna complex. In the Ribʿī family, Ḥudhayfa says that he told ʿUmar there was a closed door between him and those afflictions, and that the door was a man who would be killed or die. This version explains the metaphor without needing the final Masrūq scene as strongly as the Abū Wāʾil form does. The Ribʿī family therefore looks like a parallel development, not a pristine independent confirmation. It has the same historical logic: ʿUmar’s removal marks the transition from controlled order to uncontrolled fitna. But it packages the idea inside a different sermon on hearts and moral testing. The ʿAbd al-Razzāq report: early circulation without a full chain ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves a version through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī. It says that ʿUmar asked who would tell them about the afflictions, Ḥudhayfa answered, and the broken-door exchange followed. This is important because it is early and shows the story circulating beyond the exact al-Aʿmash line. But it also lacks the full Companion-to-Successor chain that would make it independent proof. Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī are not presented as hearing this scene from Ḥudhayfa. The report is a piece of early Basran-Iraqi fitna lore in Maʿmar’s material. Its value is not that it proves the prophecy. Its value is that it shows the “ʿUmar as door” story had become memorable and portable by the time these Iraqi transmitters were active. That is exactly what one would expect from a retrospective explanation of the first civil war. It becomes a compact moral formula: the door was ʿUmar; the door was broken; therefore the community never returned to its earlier unity. The matn is built like retrospective history The matn has several layers. The first layer is a common moral teaching: a person faces trials through family, wealth, children, and neighbors, and acts of worship expiate these trials. This is general religious advice. It does not require knowledge of the future. The second layer is the “waves of the sea.” This is vague, but it is not meaningless. After the murder of ʿUthmān, the battles of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, the rise of factional politics, and later Umayyad and anti-Umayyad violence, “fitna like the waves of the sea” was exactly the language one would use to describe the past. The third layer is the door. A door can be opened or broken. If opened, it might be closed again. If broken, the rupture is permanent. This distinction only becomes powerful after one already knows how ʿUmar died. He was not replaced by a normal administrative transition. He was murdered. The door was not opened; it was broken. The fourth layer is the later identification. The transmitters are afraid to ask Ḥudhayfa who the door is. Masrūq is sent. Ḥudhayfa answers: ʿUmar. That is a dramatic device. It makes the answer feel hidden, dangerous, and authoritative. It also makes the meaning appear to be discovered rather than invented. Why ʿUmar? The motive becomes clearer once we ask what the report accomplishes. It does not merely predict that a person will die. Everyone dies. Nor does it merely predict that fitna will happen. The Qurʾān already says that believers will be tested, and early Muslims had no shortage of real political turmoil to interpret. The report does something more specific. It makes ʿUmar the barrier between the community and the age of civil strife. That is an extremely useful memory. It sanctifies ʿUmar’s rule as the last intact door of communal order. It also explains later chaos without having to say bluntly that the Companions failed. The fitna was not simply bad policy, factional ambition, or tribal conflict. It was the destiny of a broken door. The Qurʾān does not require a hidden prophecy to explain trials. It treats testing as a basic condition of faith. The hadith report adds something else: a political chronology. ʿUmar becomes the threshold. Before him, the door is closed. After him, the waves begin. Why Ḥudhayfa? Ḥudhayfa is the perfect narrator for this kind of material. In Islamic memory he is not just another Companion. He is the Companion associated with secrets, hypocrisy, and future afflictions. A report placed through Ḥudhayfa can sound like privileged knowledge even when its historical setting is vague. He also fits the geography. The report’s recoverable transmission is heavily Kūfan, and Ḥudhayfa’s memory was important in Iraqi fitna discourse. The first civil war mattered intensely in Kūfa. ʿAlī’s capital, the battle of Ṣiffīn, the Khārijites, pro-ʿAlid and anti-ʿAlid currents, and later anti-Umayyad movements all made Iraq a natural place for traditions that explained how fitna began. A report through Ḥudhayfa lets later transmitters speak about civil war while avoiding direct factional accusation. Instead of saying “this party caused the disaster” or “that Companion caused the disaster,” the report says that the door was broken and the sea-like afflictions came. It turns political blame into sacred chronology. The historical pressure behind the story The murder of ʿUmar was not a simple isolated event. Historical sources preserve the immediate shock and its aftermath. Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ places ʿUmar’s stabbing near the end of Dhū al-Ḥijja in 23 AH and says he lived several days after being stabbed. Al-Ṭabarī gives the same basic chronological memory. The aftermath was politically charged. Al-Balādhurī reports that ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar, in response to his father’s murder, killed al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, and the daughter of Abū Luʾluʾa after accusing them of involvement. This became a dispute under ʿUthmān. That means the murder of ʿUmar already generated a moral and legal crisis before the later civil wars even began. Then came the ʿUthmān crisis. Historical reports describe complaints against ʿUthmān, the mobilization of provincial opposition, and eventually his killing. Whether one accepts every detail of later historiography or not, the larger memory is unmistakable: the post-ʿUmar order was remembered as the beginning of a chain of unresolved crises. The “door” report gives later Muslims a clean explanation for a messy transition. ʿUmar’s murder, ʿUthmān’s contested rule, ʿUthmān’s murder, the battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, and later factional violence become a single sequence. The door was broken, so the waves came. This is why the report would be attractive in Kūfan circles. Kūfa was not a neutral archive. It was one of the main theaters of early Islamic political memory. A compact Ḥudhayfa report explaining why fitna became unstoppable would have been useful across multiple groups: quietists could use it to discourage participation in civil war; Sunnis could use it to elevate ʿUmar; and later transmitters could use it to narrate early chaos as fate rather than as the failure of their heroes. The self-authenticating line One line deserves special attention: > “I narrated to him a report that was not from the errors.” This is not a neutral phrase. It functions like a built-in guarantee. The report knows that it is asking the audience to accept a hidden interpretation of history. So the narrative gives the interpretation a seal of certainty: Ḥudhayfa says he told ʿUmar a report free of mistakes. That line does not make the report stronger historically. It makes it more revealing literarily. It is exactly the kind of sentence that appears when a report is aware that its claim rests on private knowledge that cannot be checked. The audience is being told not only what happened, but how confidently it should believe what happened. The “broken” door is the giveaway The door could have been opened. Instead, it is broken. The difference matters. An opened door can be shut again. A broken door cannot. The report therefore explains why later history did not return to the idealized age before the first civil war. This is ex eventu logic. Once the narrator knows that ʿUmar was assassinated, and once he knows that the subsequent period was remembered as irreversible political rupture, “broken” becomes the perfect word. It is not just a prediction of death. It is an interpretation of the assassination as the irreversible destruction of the communal barrier. Some variants sharpen the point even more by saying that the door would not be closed until the Day of Resurrection. That looks like later apocalyptic inflation. The more the community’s history appears permanently fractured, the more the report can stretch the broken door into an end-times condition. The report is not weak in the simplistic way A careful critique should not pretend that the whole report collapses because every transmitter is unreliable. That is not true. Ibn Ḥajar describes Abū Wāʾil as trustworthy, Kūfan, and a mukhadram. He describes Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh as trustworthy, devout, and a mukhadram. He describes Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid and Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq as trustworthy. Even al-Aʿmash is described as trustworthy, a ḥāfiẓ, and a recitation expert, though he practiced tadlīs. The tadlīs point must be used carefully. In several core versions al-Aʿmash uses explicit hearing language from Shuqayq or Abū Wāʾil, so it is not enough to dismiss the report by saying “al-Aʿmash was a mudallis.” The stronger point is methodological: reliable transmitters can still preserve a retrospective political interpretation as if it were early sacred memory. ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala is a more mixed figure. Ibn Ḥajar calls him truthful but with mistakes, a proof in Qurʾānic recitation, and says his ḥadīth in the two Ṣaḥīḥs comes in supporting form. That fits the evidence here. His Abū Wāʾil route supports the existence of the story in Kūfan transmission, but the anomalous Zirr route in al-Bazzār shows how easily the report could shift within the Ḥudhayfa transmitter network. The issue is not that the isnād is obviously worthless. The issue is that a politically meaningful, post-event explanation of early Islamic history has been transmitted through exactly the kind of Iraqi fitna network in which such an explanation would be expected to form. How the report should be classified The report is not a simple one-man invention at al-Aʿmash’s level. That claim is too narrow. It is also not a clean miracle prophecy. The best classification is: 1. **Base saying:** a general Prophetic or early moral saying about ordinary trials in family, wealth, children, and neighbors. 2. **Fitna expansion:** Ḥudhayfa-centered Iraqi material about the sea-like afflictions. 3. **Historical interpretation:** ʿUmar is made the closed door between the community and those afflictions. 4. **Narrative dramatization:** Masrūq’s later question reveals the hidden meaning. 5. **Canonical reception:** Bukhārī and Muslim preserve the report as part of a larger Sunni memory of ʿUmar, fitna, and moral decline. The miracle claim depends on collapsing all five layers into one public Prophetic prediction. The report itself does not require that reading. Why this narrative was useful The report was useful because it solved several problems at once. First, it elevated ʿUmar. He becomes the door that kept catastrophic fitna away. This is a powerful piece of Sunni memory. ʿUmar is not merely the second caliph. He is the barrier between order and chaos. Second, it explained why the community fell into civil war without directly blaming revered figures. The door was broken. Once that happened, the waves came. The metaphor reduces the need to assign political blame. Third, it served quietist purposes. If the fitna after ʿUmar is an irreversible sea, then the pious response is caution, withdrawal, and suspicion of political mobilization. That is why the report sits naturally among other fitan reports warning against civil conflict. Fourth, it gave Kūfan transmitters a way to make sense of their own inherited trauma. Kūfa was a city of civil-war memory. The report does not come from nowhere. It comes from the world that most needed a sacred explanation for why the early community fractured. What a fulfillment argument misses A fulfillment argument says: ʿUmar died, fitna followed, therefore the Prophet knew the future. A historical-critical reading says: later Muslims knew ʿUmar died and fitna followed, so they told the story of ʿUmar as the broken door. The report is not impressive because it describes an unforeseeable detail. It is revealing because it captures how early Muslims turned trauma into theology. The report’s power is not precision. It does not name Abū Luʾluʾa. It does not name the date. It does not name the shūrā, ʿUthmān, the rebels, the battle of the Camel, Ṣiffīn, or the Umayyads. Its power is symbolic. ʿUmar’s death becomes a threshold. Everything after him becomes the sea. The ʿUmar-door report is best explained as a Kūfan retrospective fitna narrative. Its exact famous form clusters around Abū Wāʾil and al-Aʿmash, while parallel Kūfan lines through Jāmiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ribʿī show that the story was broader than one transmitter but still concentrated in Ḥudhayfa-centered Iraqi fitna memory. The report turns a known historical sequence, ʿUmar’s murder followed by political rupture, into sacred chronology. It is not a clean miracle claim. It is a broken-door theology of the first civil war. Sources consulted 1. **Main Abū Wāʾil / al-Aʿmash family.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 525, 1435, 3586, 7096; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 144d; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, no. 23412; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 5966; Ibn Abī Shayba, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 37129; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 60. 2. **Parallel Abū Wāʾil routes.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 1895, through Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid from Abū Wāʾil; al-Tirmidhī, *Jāmiʿ*, no. 2258, through Shuʿba from al-Aʿmash, Ḥammād, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala from Abū Wāʾil; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, nos. 2496, 2511, 2529, including his note that the Zirr route from ʿĀṣim is anomalous against the better-known Abū Wāʾil route. 3. **Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh family.** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 144a; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, nos. 23280, 23440; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 2472; Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, nos. 65, 67; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, report through al-Shaʿbī / Mujālid from Ribʿī. 4. **Early collateral / mursal circulation.** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf / al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20753, through Maʿmar from Qatāda and Sulaymān al-Taymī; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-awsaṭ*, nos. 1774 and 4835, for later collateral forms of the same Abū Wāʾil material. 5. **Rijāl evidence.** Ibn Ḥajar, *Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb*, entries for Abū Wāʾil Shuqayq b. Salama, Ribʿī b. Ḥirāsh, Jāmiʿ b. Abī Rāshid, Abū Mālik Saʿd b. Ṭāriq, al-Aʿmash Sulaymān b. Mihrān, and ʿĀṣim b. Bahdala; Ibn Ḥibbān, *al-Majrūḥīn*, discussion of trustworthy mudallis transmitters and the need for explicit hearing. 6. **Historical context of ʿUmar’s murder and its aftermath.** Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ, *al-Tārīkh*, entry on the killing of ʿUmar; al-Ṭabarī, *Tārīkh al-rusul wa-l-mulūk*, chronology of ʿUmar’s stabbing and death; al-Balādhurī, *Futūḥ al-buldān* and *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on al-Hurmuzān, Jufayna, Abū Luʾluʾa, ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿUmar’s retaliatory killings, and the later ʿUthmān crisis.

title: The Dhū al-Khalaṣa Prophecy: Daws, Abū Hurayra, and the Shrine-Survival Problem
description: A full isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that the women of Daws will circle Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour: the al-Zuhrī bottleneck, Maʿmar’s house-over-the-stone clue, the separate Jarīr destruction family, and the reason Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected.

A pre-Islamic idol called **Dhū al-Khalaṣa** was destroyed in the Prophet’s lifetime. Centuries later, the shrine allegedly reappeared in southern Arabia and was destroyed again in the modern period. Therefore, the report in which the Prophet predicts that the women of Daws will one day circle Dhū al-Khalaṣa is presented as a fulfilled prophecy. The argument sounds impressive only if the report is treated as an isolated sentence. Once the sentence is placed back into its transmission history, its local geography, and its shrine-memory context, it looks less like supernatural foresight and more like a later apocalyptic interpretation of a sacred site that had never fully disappeared from memory. The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is best read as an **al-Zuhrī-shaped apocalyptic reworking of a persistent southern sanctuary memory**. The exact prophetic form runs through al-Zuhrī from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib from Abū Hurayra, while the destruction report is a separate Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh family. The motive is exposed by Maʿmar’s aside: someone in his world knew that a house already stood over the old stone. That means the modern “fulfillment” argument starts at the wrong end of the problem. The more important question is not whether some later building at the site can be found. The more important question is why a second/eighth-century transmitter already preserved a note that the old stone had a building over it. ## The report in question لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ أَلَيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ عَلَى ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَذُو الْخَلَصَةِ طَاغِيَةُ دَوْسٍ الَّتِي كَانُوا يَعْبُدُونَ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ. > “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. Dhū al-Khalaṣa was the idol of Daws which they used to worship in the Jāhiliyya.” > > **Source:** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7116, through Abū al-Yamān → Shuʿayb → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra. Muslim’s form has the same core, but adds a useful geographical gloss: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ أَلَيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ حَوْلَ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَكَانَتْ صَنَمًا تَعْبُدُهَا دَوْسٌ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ بِتَبَالَةَ. > “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. It was an idol worshiped by Daws in the Jāhiliyya at Tabāla.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2906, through ʿAbd al-Razzāq → Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra. The language is deliberately humiliating. It does not merely say that people will worship an idol. It says that **the women of Daws** will move their bodies around it. This is not neutral ethnography. It is tribal shame language placed into an end-times frame. ## The isnād: one polished prophetic stem The important point is not that al-Zuhrī, Saʿīd, or Abū Hurayra are “weak” in the ordinary Sunni rijāl sense. They are not. The point is that the exact prophecy has a narrow recoverable shape, and the most revealing variant comes through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. The branches after al-Zuhrī are not independent origins. Bukhārī has Shuʿayb from al-Zuhrī. Muslim and ʿAbd al-Razzāq have Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Al-Bazzār has ʿUqayl from al-Zuhrī. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim has Muḥammad b. Abī ʿAtīq from Ibn Shihāb. The spread begins **after** al-Zuhrī, not before him. That does not prove by itself that al-Zuhrī invented the report. It does mean that the famous prophetic form is recoverable to an al-Zuhrī-centered transmission environment, not to a public, multiply witnessed Prophetic statement. ## The smoking gun: the house over the stone The most important version is the Maʿmar route because it preserves an aside that Bukhārī’s shorter form does not foreground. أَخْبَرَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، عَنْ مَعْمَرٍ، عَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، عَنِ ابْنِ الْمُسَيَّبِ، عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ، قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ آلِيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ حَوْلَ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَكَانَتْ صَنَمًا تَعْبُدُهَا دَوْسٌ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ بِتَبَالَةَ. قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ: وَسَمِعْتُ غَيْرَ الزُّهْرِيِّ يَقُولُ: عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْحَجَرِ بَيْتٌ بُنِيَ الْيَوْمَ. > ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of God said: “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. It was an idol worshiped by Daws in the Jāhiliyya at Tabāla.” Maʿmar said: “I heard someone other than al-Zuhrī say: over that stone there is a house built today.” > > **Source:** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20795. Ibn Ḥibbān preserves the same clue in an even sharper form: قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ: إِنَّ عَلَيْهِ الْآنَ بَيْتًا مَبْنِيًّا مُغْلَقًا. > Maʿmar said: “There is now a built, closed house over it.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6749. This is the line that explains the report’s motive. The old idol had supposedly been destroyed. Yet Maʿmar’s world still knew of a **stone** and a **built house over it**. That is not a clean fulfilled prophecy appearing out of nowhere centuries later. It is a living site-memory problem already visible in the transmission itself. The hadith answers that problem by turning the site into an apocalyptic sign. The old sanctuary is not simply a ruin. It is a future relapse waiting to happen. ## The destruction report is separate The destruction story is often cited as if it supports the prophecy. It supports the existence and importance of the sanctuary, but it does not independently support the future prediction. It is a separate report family. قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: أَلَا تُرِيحُنِي مِنْ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ؟ وَكَانَ بَيْتًا فِي خَثْعَمَ يُسَمَّى كَعْبَةَ الْيَمَانِيَةِ. > Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh said: The Messenger of God said to me, “Will you not relieve me of Dhū al-Khalaṣa?” It was a house in Khathʿam called the Yemeni Kaʿba. > > **Source:** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 3020. Other versions say that Jarīr set out with cavalry from Aḥmas, demolished it, burned it, and killed those found around it. Muslim’s versions also call it the Yemeni Kaʿba and place it in the Khathʿam/Bajīla environment. Ibn Abī Shayba likewise preserves the form, “a house that belonged to Khathʿam in the Jāhiliyya, called the Yemeni Kaʿba.” Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Ḥibbān preserve an even more useful line in which the Prophet is made to say that nothing remained of the pre-Islamic idols except the house of Dhū al-Khalaṣa. That last idea is important because it matches the later shrine-survival problem. The narrative world itself remembers Dhū al-Khalaṣa as the idol that remained when the others had been demolished. ## Dhū al-Khalaṣa was not simply “the idol of Daws” This is where the apologetic reading becomes too flat. The prophecy version says Daws. But the broader historical memory does not restrict Dhū al-Khalaṣa to Daws. Ibn Hishām says that Dhū al-Khalaṣa belonged to **Daws, Khathʿam, Bajīla, and those Arabs who lived in their lands at Tabāla**. Al-Balādhurī describes it as **a white stone at Tabāla** and as an idol of **Bajīla, Khathʿam, and Azd al-Sarāt**. Ibn Ḥazm expands the associated groups even further, listing Bajīla, Khathʿam, al-Ḥārith b. Kaʿb, Jurm, Zubayd, al-Ghawth b. Murr, and Banū Hilāl b. ʿĀmir, and locating it between Mecca and Yemen. Ibn ʿAsākir preserves later legendary material in which the Arabs as a whole are said to have revered the site. Al-Hamdānī lists Dhū al-Khalaṣa among the sacred geographies of Arabia, alongside Mecca, Īliyāʾ, al-Lāt near Nakhlah, and the Kaʿba of Najrān. So why does the prophecy focus on Daws? The answer is almost certainly **Abū Hurayra**. The report becomes more rhetorically powerful when a Dawsi Companion reports the future relapse of his own tribal world. It is not an outsider saying, “Those southern tribes will return to paganism.” It is an internal tribal witness saying, in effect, “My own people’s women will one day circle the old idol.” That is why the wording is so humiliating. It does not say “Daws will worship.” It says “the buttocks of the women of Daws will move around it.” The report makes the future relapse bodily, tribal, and shameful. ## The Daws conversion template The selection of Daws also fits a pre-existing conversion story. Daws is remembered in the sīra and hadith material as a tribe whose guidance was difficult and required prophetic prayer. جَاءَ الطُّفَيْلُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو الدَّوْسِيُّ إِلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ فَقَالَ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، إِنَّ دَوْسًا قَدْ عَصَتْ وَأَبَتْ، فَادْعُ اللَّهَ عَلَيْهَا. فَقَالَ النَّاسُ: هَلَكَتْ دَوْسٌ. فَقَالَ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِ دَوْسًا وَأْتِ بِهِمْ. > Al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr al-Dawsī came to the Messenger of God and said: “Messenger of God, Daws has disobeyed and refused, so pray to God against them.” The people said, “Daws is destroyed.” But he said: “O God, guide Daws and bring them.” > > **Sources:** al-Shāfiʿī, *Musnad*; also preserved through related routes in Ibn Rāhawayh and the sīra material. That memory gives the Dhū al-Khalaṣa prophecy a narrative arc. Daws was once resistant, then guided by prophetic mercy, and now the eschatological report imagines Daws relapsing back into the cultic world from which it had been saved. Whether one treats that conversion story as historical or literary, it shows that Daws already carried a recognizable symbolic role in early Islamic memory. It was not random. ## What would push Saʿīd or al-Zuhrī to transmit such a report? The question of motive should not be flattened into one sentence: “al-Zuhrī fabricated it for the Umayyads.” That is too crude. The report’s motive becomes clearer when Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī are placed in their own worlds. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is not a clean candidate for simple Umayyad propaganda. Historical reports remember him refusing the Umayyad demand to pledge allegiance to al-Walīd and Sulaymān while ʿAbd al-Malik was still alive. He was beaten, dressed in rough garments, paraded, and imprisoned for that refusal. That memory matters. If the report entered at Saʿīd’s layer, it is better explained as **Medinan moral-apocalyptic commentary** than as a court-sponsored anti-Yemeni slogan. Saʿīd’s world had witnessed the collapse of the old order into civil war, coercive bayʿa politics, hereditary succession, and the transformation of religion into state control. In such an atmosphere, a report about Arabia eventually reverting to the religion of its fathers makes sense. It is a warning about post-Prophetic decline. Al-Zuhrī’s position is different. He is the perfect figure for the report’s polished circulation because he sits between **Saʿīd’s Medinan authority** and **Umayyad-era writing and diffusion**. Ibn Saʿd and al-Balādhurī preserve the famous report in which al-Zuhrī says that scholars disliked writing knowledge until the rulers compelled them, after which they thought it wrong to prevent Muslims from it. They also preserve the memory that after al-Walīd b. Yazīd was killed, written materials from al-Zuhrī’s knowledge were found in such quantity that they were carried on pack animals. Al-Zuhrī is also remembered as having sat with Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib for years. That makes al-Zuhrī the natural common-link for a report like this. He could attach a southern shrine-memory to Saʿīd, Saʿīd to Abū Hurayra, and Abū Hurayra to Daws. The result is an elegant prophetic form: a famous Dawsi Companion predicts a future Dawsi relapse around a site whose physical afterlife was already known. The report does not require a special Umayyad grudge against Daws. The stronger motive is sacred-site polemic. The old southern “Yemeni Kaʿba” is demoted into an end-times sign of pagan relapse, while Abū Hurayra’s Dawsi identity makes the warning sound like an internal tribal confession rather than outside slander. ## The “Yemeni Kaʿba” angle The phrase “Yemeni Kaʿba” is not just a geographical curiosity. It matters because it places Dhū al-Khalaṣa inside a sacred-political hierarchy. In the Islamic order, Mecca is the sanctuary. The Kaʿba is the center. A rival or quasi-rival sanctuary remembered as the **Yemeni Kaʿba** is not merely a local idol; it is a rival sacred memory. A report predicting the shameful return of people to this Yemeni sanctuary implicitly subordinates it to the Islamic Meccan order. It says: the true Kaʿba remains the center of worship, while the “Yemeni Kaʿba” becomes a sign of end-times degeneration. This is why the report’s southern geography, Dawsi framing, and Abū Hurayra attribution work so well together. The story is not simply “idols will return.” It is: a famous Dawsi authority predicts that his own tribal world will regress to a southern pagan sanctuary remembered as a rival Kaʿba. ## The collateral variants: a wider return-to-idols motif The exact Daws report is al-Zuhrī-shaped, but the motif is wider. Other reports imagine the end of time as a return to ancestral cults after Islam has declined. Muslim preserves a report from ʿĀʾisha in which the Prophet says that night and day will not pass away until al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā are worshiped. When ʿĀʾisha objects that she thought the Qurʾānic promise had ended such worship, the response is that God will send a good wind to take the believers, and those who remain will return to the religion of their fathers. Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād preserves a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr: إِذَا عُبِدَتْ ذُو الْخَلَصَةِ كَانَ ظُهُورُ الرُّومِ عَلَى الشَّامِ. > “When Dhū al-Khalaṣa is worshiped, the Romans will dominate al-Shām.” > > **Source:** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1333. This is not the same report. It is not even phrased as a Prophetic hadith here. But it shows how Dhū al-Khalaṣa could function inside a wider Syrian apocalyptic imagination: Arabia returns to paganism, Syria falls to Rome, and the final age begins. Nuʿaym also preserves a form in which, after Jesus and after a wind takes the believers, people return to the religion of their fathers. Then Abū Hurayra’s line appears almost as a vivid comment: “As if I can see the buttocks of the women of Daws...” That form is valuable because it suggests that the Daws phrase could circulate as an illustrative apocalyptic image inside a broader return-to-idols framework. There is also a striking variant in al-Ḥākim’s *Mustadrak*. In a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr, a man is asked his tribe and says he is from Banū ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. The reply then says: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَتَدَافَعَ نِسَاءُ بَنِي عَامِرٍ عَلَى ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَثَنٍ كَانَ يُسَمَّى فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ. > “The Hour will not be established until the women of Banū ʿĀmir push against one another at Dhū al-Khalaṣa, an idol that was named in the Jāhiliyya.” > > **Source:** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8653. This is extremely important. It shows that the formula “women of [tribe] around Dhū al-Khalaṣa” could be adapted. In Abū Hurayra’s version the tribe is Daws because Abū Hurayra is Dawsi. In the ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr variant, the target can become Banū ʿĀmir in response to a tribal exchange. That does not prove the Abū Hurayra version was copied from the Banū ʿĀmir version. It proves something more general: the report belongs to a flexible apocalyptic shame motif, not a single cleanly preserved public prophecy. ## The matn development The development looks like this: | Layer | Evidence | Function | |---|---|---| | Shrine memory | Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a white stone at Tabāla, linked to Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others | Establishes a real southern sacred site | | Destruction memory | Jarīr destroys the house called the Yemeni Kaʿba | Explains Islamic triumph over the old cult | | Survival problem | Reports that it remained, or that a house stood over the stone “today” | Creates the need for explanation | | Dawsi framing | Abū Hurayra is Dawsi, and Daws has a conversion-story template | Makes the prophecy an internal tribal warning | | Apocalyptic upgrade | The women of Daws return to Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour | Converts site survival into prophecy | | Later fulfillment claim | Modern stories of a revived shrine | Misread the report as a miracle instead of recognizing the earlier site afterlife | ## The rijāl question Sunni rijāl literature does not give a simple “weak transmitter” solution here. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is one of the most prestigious Medinan authorities. Al-Zuhrī is central to early Sunni transmission. Abū Hurayra is one of the most frequently used Companion authorities. That is precisely why the report is effective. The critique is not: > “The chain contains an obviously rejected liar.” The critique is: > “The exact prophetic form has a narrow al-Zuhrī stem, the matn selects Daws for a reason, and the Maʿmar version preserves the contemporary shrine-survival clue that explains why the prophecy was useful.” This is an isnād-cum-matn argument, not a one-line rijāl dismissal. ## Why the modern fulfillment claim fails The modern fulfillment claim usually says: Dhū al-Khalaṣa returned, people worshiped around it, and it was destroyed again. But the Maʿmar note already says there was a built house over the stone in his own period or in the memory available to him. That means the old cultic site had a visible afterlife long before the modern event. So the modern episode cannot function as a clean miracle. It is part of a longer pattern of shrine memory, local sacred geography, and recurrent attempts to interpret or suppress the site. The correct question is not: > “How could the Prophet know this shrine would return?” The correct question is: > “Why did a second/eighth-century transmission environment already know of a house over the old stone, and why did it preserve a prophecy saying people would one day return to it?” Once that question is asked, the report becomes intelligible without miracle. ## Conclusion The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is not a straightforward fulfilled prophecy. The exact prophetic wording is narrow and al-Zuhrī-centered. The destruction report is separate. The site is not consistently Dawsi in the historical memory. The old sanctuary is described as belonging to a wider southern tribal landscape: Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others. It is remembered as a white stone at Tabāla and as the Yemeni Kaʿba. The most important clue is Maʿmar’s note: there was already a built house over the stone. That makes the motive visible. The prophecy was not produced because the shrine unexpectedly reappeared centuries later. It was produced because the shrine, stone, or sacred memory had not disappeared cleanly in the first place. Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected because they made the report rhetorically stronger. Abū Hurayra was Dawsi, so the report becomes an internal tribal confession. A famous Muslim authority from Daws is made to predict that his own tribal world will return to an old pagan sanctuary. That is far more powerful than a generic warning that Arabs will worship idols again. The Dhū al-Khalaṣa prophecy is best explained as a second/eighth-century apocalyptic reinterpretation of a persistent southern sacred site. The report demotes the old “Yemeni Kaʿba” into an end-times sign, uses Abū Hurayra’s Dawsi identity to create an internal tribal witness, and turns the survival of a shrine memory into a prophecy. It is not a clean miracle claim. It is a shrine-survival problem dressed as foresight. ## Sources consulted 1. **Prophecy report: women of Daws and Dhū al-Khalaṣa.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7116; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2906; ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf / al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20795; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6749; Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, *al-Sunna*, nos. 77–78; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 7135. 2. **Jarīr’s destruction of Dhū al-Khalaṣa.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 3020, 3076, 3823, 4355, 4356, 4357; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2476; Ibn Abī Shayba, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 32342; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, reports under Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 7201–7202. 3. **Pre-Islamic shrine memory and the “Yemeni Kaʿba.”** Ibn Hishām, *al-Sīra al-nabawiyya*, report on Dhū al-Khalaṣa at Tabāla; al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, report on Jarīr and the white stone at Tabāla; Ibn Ḥazm, *Jamharat ansāb al-ʿArab*, entry on Dhū al-Khalaṣa; Ibn ʿAsākir, *Tārīkh Dimashq*, pre-Islamic reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa; al-Hamdānī, *Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab*, list of Arabian sacred sites. 4. **Reports that Dhū al-Khalaṣa remained a problem after the destruction of other idols.** Ibn Saʿd, *al-Ṭabaqāt al-kubrā*, report in which the Prophet asks what happened to Dhū al-Khalaṣa after tribes demolished their idols; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, related Dhū al-Khalaṣa reports; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, related reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a remaining pre-Islamic idol-house. 5. **Daws, al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr, and the memory of delayed tribal guidance.** al-Shāfiʿī, *Musnad*, report of al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr al-Dawsī and the Prophet’s prayer, “O God, guide Daws and bring them”; Ibn Rāhawayh, *Musnad*, related report; Ibn ʿAsākir, *Tārīkh Dimashq*, al-Ṭufayl/Daws material. 6. **Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī’s historical setting.** al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib’s refusal of the bayʿa to al-Walīd and Sulaymān; Ibn Saʿd, *al-Ṭabaqāt al-kubrā*, reports on al-Zuhrī, his relationship with Umayyad rulers, and the writing of knowledge; al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on al-Zuhrī and the ruler-driven writing of knowledge. 7. **Wider apocalyptic return-to-idols motif.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa, Roman dominance in al-Shām, and the return to ancestral religion; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2907, report on the renewed worship of al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā; Ibn Waḍḍāḥ, *al-Bidaʿ*, report on tribes joining the polytheists and worshiping idols; Hūd al-Hawwārī, *Tafsīr*, report from Ibn Sīrīn on Dhū al-Khalaṣa. 8. **Variant displacement of the motif.** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8653, variant in which the women of Banū ʿĀmir are attached to Dhū al-Khalaṣa instead of the women of Daws.
