A pre-Islamic idol called **Dhū al-Khalaṣa** was destroyed in the Prophet’s lifetime. Centuries later, the shrine allegedly reappeared in southern Arabia and was destroyed again in the modern period. Therefore, the report in which the Prophet predicts that the women of Daws will one day circle Dhū al-Khalaṣa is presented as a fulfilled prophecy. The argument sounds impressive only if the report is treated as an isolated sentence. Once the sentence is placed back into its transmission history, its local geography, and its shrine-memory context, it looks less like supernatural foresight and more like a later apocalyptic interpretation of a sacred site that had never fully disappeared from memory. The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is best read as an **al-Zuhrī-shaped apocalyptic reworking of a persistent southern sanctuary memory**. The exact prophetic form runs through al-Zuhrī from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib from Abū Hurayra, while the destruction report is a separate Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh family. The motive is exposed by Maʿmar’s aside: someone in his world knew that a house already stood over the old stone. That means the modern “fulfillment” argument starts at the wrong end of the problem. The more important question is not whether some later building at the site can be found. The more important question is why a second/eighth-century transmitter already preserved a note that the old stone had a building over it. The report in question لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ أَلَيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ عَلَى ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَذُو الْخَلَصَةِ طَاغِيَةُ دَوْسٍ الَّتِي كَانُوا يَعْبُدُونَ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ. > “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. Dhū al-Khalaṣa was the idol of Daws which they used to worship in the Jāhiliyya.” > > **Source:** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7116, through Abū al-Yamān → Shuʿayb → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra. Muslim’s form has the same core, but adds a useful geographical gloss: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ أَلَيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ حَوْلَ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَكَانَتْ صَنَمًا تَعْبُدُهَا دَوْسٌ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ بِتَبَالَةَ. > “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. It was an idol worshiped by Daws in the Jāhiliyya at Tabāla.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2906, through ʿAbd al-Razzāq → Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī → Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib → Abū Hurayra. The language is deliberately humiliating. It does not merely say that people will worship an idol. It says that **the women of Daws** will move their bodies around it. This is not neutral ethnography. It is tribal shame language placed into an end-times frame. The isnād: one polished prophetic stem The important point is not that al-Zuhrī, Saʿīd, or Abū Hurayra are “weak” in the ordinary Sunni rijāl sense. They are not. The point is that the exact prophecy has a narrow recoverable shape, and the most revealing variant comes through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. The branches after al-Zuhrī are not independent origins. Bukhārī has Shuʿayb from al-Zuhrī. Muslim and ʿAbd al-Razzāq have Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Al-Bazzār has ʿUqayl from al-Zuhrī. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim has Muḥammad b. Abī ʿAtīq from Ibn Shihāb. The spread begins **after** al-Zuhrī, not before him. That does not prove by itself that al-Zuhrī invented the report. It does mean that the famous prophetic form is recoverable to an al-Zuhrī-centered transmission environment, not to a public, multiply witnessed Prophetic statement. The smoking gun: the house over the stone The most important version is the Maʿmar route because it preserves an aside that Bukhārī’s shorter form does not foreground. أَخْبَرَنَا عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ، عَنْ مَعْمَرٍ، عَنِ الزُّهْرِيِّ، عَنِ ابْنِ الْمُسَيَّبِ، عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ، قَالَ: قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَضْطَرِبَ آلِيَاتُ نِسَاءِ دَوْسٍ حَوْلَ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَكَانَتْ صَنَمًا تَعْبُدُهَا دَوْسٌ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ بِتَبَالَةَ. قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ: وَسَمِعْتُ غَيْرَ الزُّهْرِيِّ يَقُولُ: عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْحَجَرِ بَيْتٌ بُنِيَ الْيَوْمَ. > ʿAbd al-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn al-Musayyib, from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of God said: “The Hour will not be established until the buttocks of the women of Daws move around Dhū al-Khalaṣa. It was an idol worshiped by Daws in the Jāhiliyya at Tabāla.” Maʿmar said: “I heard someone other than al-Zuhrī say: over that stone there is a house built today.” > > **Source:** ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20795. Ibn Ḥibbān preserves the same clue in an even sharper form: قَالَ مَعْمَرٌ: إِنَّ عَلَيْهِ الْآنَ بَيْتًا مَبْنِيًّا مُغْلَقًا. > Maʿmar said: “There is now a built, closed house over it.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6749. This is the line that explains the report’s motive. The old idol had supposedly been destroyed. Yet Maʿmar’s world still knew of a **stone** and a **built house over it**. That is not a clean fulfilled prophecy appearing out of nowhere centuries later. It is a living site-memory problem already visible in the transmission itself. The hadith answers that problem by turning the site into an apocalyptic sign. The old sanctuary is not simply a ruin. It is a future relapse waiting to happen. The destruction report is separate The destruction story is often cited as if it supports the prophecy. It supports the existence and importance of the sanctuary, but it does not independently support the future prediction. It is a separate report family. قَالَ لِي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: أَلَا تُرِيحُنِي مِنْ ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ؟ وَكَانَ بَيْتًا فِي خَثْعَمَ يُسَمَّى كَعْبَةَ الْيَمَانِيَةِ. > Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh said: The Messenger of God said to me, “Will you not relieve me of Dhū al-Khalaṣa?” It was a house in Khathʿam called the Yemeni Kaʿba. > > **Source:** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 3020. Other versions say that Jarīr set out with cavalry from Aḥmas, demolished it, burned it, and killed those found around it. Muslim’s versions also call it the Yemeni Kaʿba and place it in the Khathʿam/Bajīla environment. Ibn Abī Shayba likewise preserves the form, “a house that belonged to Khathʿam in the Jāhiliyya, called the Yemeni Kaʿba.” Al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Ḥibbān preserve an even more useful line in which the Prophet is made to say that nothing remained of the pre-Islamic idols except the house of Dhū al-Khalaṣa. That last idea is important because it matches the later shrine-survival problem. The narrative world itself remembers Dhū al-Khalaṣa as the idol that remained when the others had been demolished. Dhū al-Khalaṣa was not simply “the idol of Daws” This is where the apologetic reading becomes too flat. The prophecy version says Daws. But the broader historical memory does not restrict Dhū al-Khalaṣa to Daws. Ibn Hishām says that Dhū al-Khalaṣa belonged to **Daws, Khathʿam, Bajīla, and those Arabs who lived in their lands at Tabāla**. Al-Balādhurī describes it as **a white stone at Tabāla** and as an idol of **Bajīla, Khathʿam, and Azd al-Sarāt**. Ibn Ḥazm expands the associated groups even further, listing Bajīla, Khathʿam, al-Ḥārith b. Kaʿb, Jurm, Zubayd, al-Ghawth b. Murr, and Banū Hilāl b. ʿĀmir, and locating it between Mecca and Yemen. Ibn ʿAsākir preserves later legendary material in which the Arabs as a whole are said to have revered the site. Al-Hamdānī lists Dhū al-Khalaṣa among the sacred geographies of Arabia, alongside Mecca, Īliyāʾ, al-Lāt near Nakhlah, and the Kaʿba of Najrān. So why does the prophecy focus on Daws? The answer is almost certainly **Abū Hurayra**. The report becomes more rhetorically powerful when a Dawsi Companion reports the future relapse of his own tribal world. It is not an outsider saying, “Those southern tribes will return to paganism.” It is an internal tribal witness saying, in effect, “My own people’s women will one day circle the old idol.” That is why the wording is so humiliating. It does not say “Daws will worship.” It says “the buttocks of the women of Daws will move around it.” The report makes the future relapse bodily, tribal, and shameful. The Daws conversion template The selection of Daws also fits a pre-existing conversion story. Daws is remembered in the sīra and hadith material as a tribe whose guidance was difficult and required prophetic prayer. جَاءَ الطُّفَيْلُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو الدَّوْسِيُّ إِلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ فَقَالَ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، إِنَّ دَوْسًا قَدْ عَصَتْ وَأَبَتْ، فَادْعُ اللَّهَ عَلَيْهَا. فَقَالَ النَّاسُ: هَلَكَتْ دَوْسٌ. فَقَالَ: اللَّهُمَّ اهْدِ دَوْسًا وَأْتِ بِهِمْ. > Al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr al-Dawsī came to the Messenger of God and said: “Messenger of God, Daws has disobeyed and refused, so pray to God against them.” The people said, “Daws is destroyed.” But he said: “O God, guide Daws and bring them.” > > **Sources:** al-Shāfiʿī, *Musnad*; also preserved through related routes in Ibn Rāhawayh and the sīra material. That memory gives the Dhū al-Khalaṣa prophecy a narrative arc. Daws was once resistant, then guided by prophetic mercy, and now the eschatological report imagines Daws relapsing back into the cultic world from which it had been saved. Whether one treats that conversion story as historical or literary, it shows that Daws already carried a recognizable symbolic role in early Islamic memory. It was not random. What would push Saʿīd or al-Zuhrī to transmit such a report? The question of motive should not be flattened into one sentence: “al-Zuhrī fabricated it for the Umayyads.” That is too crude. The report’s motive becomes clearer when Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī are placed in their own worlds. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is not a clean candidate for simple Umayyad propaganda. Historical reports remember him refusing the Umayyad demand to pledge allegiance to al-Walīd and Sulaymān while ʿAbd al-Malik was still alive. He was beaten, dressed in rough garments, paraded, and imprisoned for that refusal. That memory matters. If the report entered at Saʿīd’s layer, it is better explained as **Medinan moral-apocalyptic commentary** than as a court-sponsored anti-Yemeni slogan. Saʿīd’s world had witnessed the collapse of the old order into civil war, coercive bayʿa politics, hereditary succession, and the transformation of religion into state control. In such an atmosphere, a report about Arabia eventually reverting to the religion of its fathers makes sense. It is a warning about post-Prophetic decline. Al-Zuhrī’s position is different. He is the perfect figure for the report’s polished circulation because he sits between **Saʿīd’s Medinan authority** and **Umayyad-era writing and diffusion**. Ibn Saʿd and al-Balādhurī preserve the famous report in which al-Zuhrī says that scholars disliked writing knowledge until the rulers compelled them, after which they thought it wrong to prevent Muslims from it. They also preserve the memory that after al-Walīd b. Yazīd was killed, written materials from al-Zuhrī’s knowledge were found in such quantity that they were carried on pack animals. Al-Zuhrī is also remembered as having sat with Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib for years. That makes al-Zuhrī the natural common-link for a report like this. He could attach a southern shrine-memory to Saʿīd, Saʿīd to Abū Hurayra, and Abū Hurayra to Daws. The result is an elegant prophetic form: a famous Dawsi Companion predicts a future Dawsi relapse around a site whose physical afterlife was already known. The report does not require a special Umayyad grudge against Daws. The stronger motive is sacred-site polemic. The old southern “Yemeni Kaʿba” is demoted into an end-times sign of pagan relapse, while Abū Hurayra’s Dawsi identity makes the warning sound like an internal tribal confession rather than outside slander. The “Yemeni Kaʿba” angle The phrase “Yemeni Kaʿba” is not just a geographical curiosity. It matters because it places Dhū al-Khalaṣa inside a sacred-political hierarchy. In the Islamic order, Mecca is the sanctuary. The Kaʿba is the center. A rival or quasi-rival sanctuary remembered as the **Yemeni Kaʿba** is not merely a local idol; it is a rival sacred memory. A report predicting the shameful return of people to this Yemeni sanctuary implicitly subordinates it to the Islamic Meccan order. It says: the true Kaʿba remains the center of worship, while the “Yemeni Kaʿba” becomes a sign of end-times degeneration. This is why the report’s southern geography, Dawsi framing, and Abū Hurayra attribution work so well together. The story is not simply “idols will return.” It is: a famous Dawsi authority predicts that his own tribal world will regress to a southern pagan sanctuary remembered as a rival Kaʿba. The collateral variants: a wider return-to-idols motif The exact Daws report is al-Zuhrī-shaped, but the motif is wider. Other reports imagine the end of time as a return to ancestral cults after Islam has declined. Muslim preserves a report from ʿĀʾisha in which the Prophet says that night and day will not pass away until al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā are worshiped. When ʿĀʾisha objects that she thought the Qurʾānic promise had ended such worship, the response is that God will send a good wind to take the believers, and those who remain will return to the religion of their fathers. Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād preserves a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr: إِذَا عُبِدَتْ ذُو الْخَلَصَةِ كَانَ ظُهُورُ الرُّومِ عَلَى الشَّامِ. > “When Dhū al-Khalaṣa is worshiped, the Romans will dominate al-Shām.” > > **Source:** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, no. 1333. This is not the same report. It is not even phrased as a Prophetic hadith here. But it shows how Dhū al-Khalaṣa could function inside a wider Syrian apocalyptic imagination: Arabia returns to paganism, Syria falls to Rome, and the final age begins. Nuʿaym also preserves a form in which, after Jesus and after a wind takes the believers, people return to the religion of their fathers. Then Abū Hurayra’s line appears almost as a vivid comment: “As if I can see the buttocks of the women of Daws...” That form is valuable because it suggests that the Daws phrase could circulate as an illustrative apocalyptic image inside a broader return-to-idols framework. There is also a striking variant in al-Ḥākim’s *Mustadrak*. In a report from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr, a man is asked his tribe and says he is from Banū ʿĀmir b. Ṣaʿṣaʿa. The reply then says: لَا تَقُومُ السَّاعَةُ حَتَّى تَتَدَافَعَ نِسَاءُ بَنِي عَامِرٍ عَلَى ذِي الْخَلَصَةِ، وَثَنٍ كَانَ يُسَمَّى فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ. > “The Hour will not be established until the women of Banū ʿĀmir push against one another at Dhū al-Khalaṣa, an idol that was named in the Jāhiliyya.” > > **Source:** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8653. This is extremely important. It shows that the formula “women of [tribe] around Dhū al-Khalaṣa” could be adapted. In Abū Hurayra’s version the tribe is Daws because Abū Hurayra is Dawsi. In the ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr variant, the target can become Banū ʿĀmir in response to a tribal exchange. That does not prove the Abū Hurayra version was copied from the Banū ʿĀmir version. It proves something more general: the report belongs to a flexible apocalyptic shame motif, not a single cleanly preserved public prophecy. The matn development The development looks like this: | Layer | Evidence | Function | |---|---|---| | Shrine memory | Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a white stone at Tabāla, linked to Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others | Establishes a real southern sacred site | | Destruction memory | Jarīr destroys the house called the Yemeni Kaʿba | Explains Islamic triumph over the old cult | | Survival problem | Reports that it remained, or that a house stood over the stone “today” | Creates the need for explanation | | Dawsi framing | Abū Hurayra is Dawsi, and Daws has a conversion-story template | Makes the prophecy an internal tribal warning | | Apocalyptic upgrade | The women of Daws return to Dhū al-Khalaṣa before the Hour | Converts site survival into prophecy | | Later fulfillment claim | Modern stories of a revived shrine | Misread the report as a miracle instead of recognizing the earlier site afterlife | The rijāl question Sunni rijāl literature does not give a simple “weak transmitter” solution here. Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib is one of the most prestigious Medinan authorities. Al-Zuhrī is central to early Sunni transmission. Abū Hurayra is one of the most frequently used Companion authorities. That is precisely why the report is effective. The critique is not: > “The chain contains an obviously rejected liar.” The critique is: > “The exact prophetic form has a narrow al-Zuhrī stem, the matn selects Daws for a reason, and the Maʿmar version preserves the contemporary shrine-survival clue that explains why the prophecy was useful.” This is an isnād-cum-matn argument, not a one-line rijāl dismissal. Why the modern fulfillment claim fails The modern fulfillment claim usually says: Dhū al-Khalaṣa returned, people worshiped around it, and it was destroyed again. But the Maʿmar note already says there was a built house over the stone in his own period or in the memory available to him. That means the old cultic site had a visible afterlife long before the modern event. So the modern episode cannot function as a clean miracle. It is part of a longer pattern of shrine memory, local sacred geography, and recurrent attempts to interpret or suppress the site. The correct question is not: > “How could the Prophet know this shrine would return?” The correct question is: > “Why did a second/eighth-century transmission environment already know of a house over the old stone, and why did it preserve a prophecy saying people would one day return to it?” Once that question is asked, the report becomes intelligible without miracle. Conclusion The Dhū al-Khalaṣa report is not a straightforward fulfilled prophecy. The exact prophetic wording is narrow and al-Zuhrī-centered. The destruction report is separate. The site is not consistently Dawsi in the historical memory. The old sanctuary is described as belonging to a wider southern tribal landscape: Khathʿam, Bajīla, Azd, Daws, and others. It is remembered as a white stone at Tabāla and as the Yemeni Kaʿba. The most important clue is Maʿmar’s note: there was already a built house over the stone. That makes the motive visible. The prophecy was not produced because the shrine unexpectedly reappeared centuries later. It was produced because the shrine, stone, or sacred memory had not disappeared cleanly in the first place. Daws and Abū Hurayra were selected because they made the report rhetorically stronger. Abū Hurayra was Dawsi, so the report becomes an internal tribal confession. A famous Muslim authority from Daws is made to predict that his own tribal world will return to an old pagan sanctuary. That is far more powerful than a generic warning that Arabs will worship idols again. The Dhū al-Khalaṣa prophecy is best explained as a second/eighth-century apocalyptic reinterpretation of a persistent southern sacred site. The report demotes the old “Yemeni Kaʿba” into an end-times sign, uses Abū Hurayra’s Dawsi identity to create an internal tribal witness, and turns the survival of a shrine memory into a prophecy. It is not a clean miracle claim. It is a shrine-survival problem dressed as foresight. Sources consulted 1. **Prophecy report: women of Daws and Dhū al-Khalaṣa.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 7116; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2906; ʿAbd al-Razzāq, *al-Muṣannaf / al-Jāmiʿ*, no. 20795; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 6749; Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, *al-Sunna*, nos. 77–78; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 7135. 2. **Jarīr’s destruction of Dhū al-Khalaṣa.** al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 3020, 3076, 3823, 4355, 4356, 4357; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2476; Ibn Abī Shayba, *al-Muṣannaf*, no. 32342; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, reports under Jarīr b. ʿAbd Allāh; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 7201–7202. 3. **Pre-Islamic shrine memory and the “Yemeni Kaʿba.”** Ibn Hishām, *al-Sīra al-nabawiyya*, report on Dhū al-Khalaṣa at Tabāla; al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, report on Jarīr and the white stone at Tabāla; Ibn Ḥazm, *Jamharat ansāb al-ʿArab*, entry on Dhū al-Khalaṣa; Ibn ʿAsākir, *Tārīkh Dimashq*, pre-Islamic reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa; al-Hamdānī, *Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab*, list of Arabian sacred sites. 4. **Reports that Dhū al-Khalaṣa remained a problem after the destruction of other idols.** Ibn Saʿd, *al-Ṭabaqāt al-kubrā*, report in which the Prophet asks what happened to Dhū al-Khalaṣa after tribes demolished their idols; al-Ṭabarānī, *al-Muʿjam al-kabīr*, related Dhū al-Khalaṣa reports; Ibn Ḥibbān, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, related reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa as a remaining pre-Islamic idol-house. 5. **Daws, al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr, and the memory of delayed tribal guidance.** al-Shāfiʿī, *Musnad*, report of al-Ṭufayl b. ʿAmr al-Dawsī and the Prophet’s prayer, “O God, guide Daws and bring them”; Ibn Rāhawayh, *Musnad*, related report; Ibn ʿAsākir, *Tārīkh Dimashq*, al-Ṭufayl/Daws material. 6. **Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib and al-Zuhrī’s historical setting.** al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib’s refusal of the bayʿa to al-Walīd and Sulaymān; Ibn Saʿd, *al-Ṭabaqāt al-kubrā*, reports on al-Zuhrī, his relationship with Umayyad rulers, and the writing of knowledge; al-Balādhurī, *Ansāb al-ashrāf*, reports on al-Zuhrī and the ruler-driven writing of knowledge. 7. **Wider apocalyptic return-to-idols motif.** Nuʿaym b. Ḥammād, *Kitāb al-Fitan*, reports on Dhū al-Khalaṣa, Roman dominance in al-Shām, and the return to ancestral religion; Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 2907, report on the renewed worship of al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā; Ibn Waḍḍāḥ, *al-Bidaʿ*, report on tribes joining the polytheists and worshiping idols; Hūd al-Hawwārī, *Tafsīr*, report from Ibn Sīrīn on Dhū al-Khalaṣa. 8. **Variant displacement of the motif.** al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, no. 8653, variant in which the women of Banū ʿĀmir are attached to Dhū al-Khalaṣa instead of the women of Daws.

title: The Zubayrid Mahdi: How Ibn al-Zubayr
description: A critical isnād-cum-matn analysis of the Meccan sanctuary reports: the refuge-seeker at the House, the army swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ, and how Ibn al-Zubayr’s failed Meccan caliphate became a Mahdī template.

A force will be sent against him. When they are at a desert plain, they will be swallowed.” This article is about one layer of the Mahdī tradition. It is not about every report ever attached to the Mahdī. It is about a specific Meccan cluster: a man takes refuge at the House, an army is sent against him, and God swallows that army at al-Bayḍāʾ before it reaches him. In later versions, the story grows. A caliph dies, a man flees from Medina to Mecca, people force him into allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām, a Syrian army marches against him, the army is swallowed, Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes come to him, a Kalbī enemy appears, and eventually the figure is named as the Mahdī. The claim here is not that the entire Mahdī corpus comes from Ibn al-Zubayr. The earlier Kaysānī layer belongs to a different world, centered around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. The black-banner material has its own Abbasid setting. The Sufyānī material has its own line of development. The point here is narrower and stronger: the Meccan sanctuary layer of the Mahdī narrative is best read as a Zubayrid memory, built around the failed Meccan caliphate of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr and later transformed into an eschatological reversal. The Zubayrid contribution to the Mahdī corpus is not the title “Mahdī” itself. It is the Meccan stage: the refuge-seeker at the House, the sanctuary, the Rukn and Maqām, the Syrian army, and the swallowed-army reversal at al-Bayḍāʾ. For a lay reader, the method is simple. We are not starting with later theology. We are starting with the shape of the reports. What is the repeated scene? Who is the unnamed figure? Why is Mecca central? Why is an army sent from Syria? Why is the army destroyed before reaching the sanctuary? And why do early versions explicitly say that people were asking about this report **in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr** or when **al-Ḥajjāj’s army** came? Once those clues are placed next to the historical record, the pattern becomes hard to ignore. ## The Historical Anchor: Ibn al-Zubayr Was the Refuge-Seeker The key to this cluster is not hidden inside the hadith books. It is in the chronicles. Ibn al-Zubayr was not merely a man who happened to be in Mecca. He was publicly known as **the refuge-seeker at the House** and **the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary**. This was not a vague title. It was a political and religious identity attached to him during his revolt against the Umayyads. Al-Masʿūdī says that Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge at the Sacred House and had named himself **العائذ بالبيت**, “the refuge-seeker at the House,” until poets mentioned him by that name. وَعَاذَ ابْنُ الزُّبَيْرِ بِالْبَيْتِ الْحَرَامِ، وَكَانَ قَدْ سَمَّى نَفْسَهُ الْعَائِذَ بِالْبَيْتِ، وَشُهِرَ بِهَذَا حَتَّى ذَكَرَتْهُ الشُّعَرَاءُ فِي أَشْعَارِهَا “Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge at the Sacred House. He had named himself ‘the refuge-seeker at the House,’ and he became known by this until the poets mentioned him in their verses.” Al-Ṭabarī preserves the same identification with even less ambiguity. A man calls people to **the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary**, and al-Ṭabarī glosses it directly: “meaning ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.” أَدْعُوكُمْ إِلَى الْعَائِذِ بِالْحَرَمِ — يَعْنِي عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ الزُّبَيْرِ “I call you to the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary — meaning ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.” Al-Balādhurī preserves the same title in several registers. Ibn al-Zubayr uses it for himself. His supporters use it to rally others. His opponents use it to dismiss him. One hostile statement says, “By God, Ibn al-Zubayr is not a caliph upon whom the community has agreed. He is only a man taking refuge at the House.” That is exactly why the title matters. It was not a later scholarly guess. It was a live political label. This is the historical anchor. Without it, the hadith reports sound like abstract prophecy. With it, the vocabulary becomes specific. The reports say “a refuge-seeker seeks refuge at the House.” The chronicles say Ibn al-Zubayr was known as “the refuge-seeker at the House.” The reports say an army comes against the sanctuary. The chronicles say Syrian armies came against Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca. The reports say God swallows the army. History says the army was not swallowed and Ibn al-Zubayr was killed. That gap between the report and the history is where the eschatological reversal happens. ## The Earliest Kernel: A Refuge-Seeker and a Swallowed Army The simplest form of the report is not yet a full Mahdī story. There is no caliph’s death, no forced bayʿa, no Iraqi bands, no Kalb enemy, and no explicit Mahdī. There is only the sanctuary refugee, the army, and the swallowing at al-Bayḍāʾ. The key Umm Salama version runs through: **The Prophet → Umm Salama → ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Qibṭiyya → ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Rufayʿ → Jarīr / Zuhayr → collectors.** The important part is not only the prediction. It is the scene around the prediction. In Ibn Abī Shayba’s version, al-Ḥārith b. Abī Rabīʿa and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān enter upon Umm Salama and ask her about the army that will be swallowed. The report then says this happened **in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr**. دَخَلَ الْحَارِثُ بْنُ أَبِي رَبِيعَةَ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ صَفْوَانَ عَلَى أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ ... فَسَأَلَاهَا عَنِ الْجَيْشِ الَّذِي يُخْسَفُ بِهِ، وَذَلِكَ فِي زَمَانِ ابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ “al-Ḥārith b. Abī Rabīʿa and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān entered upon Umm Salama ... and asked her about the army that would be swallowed. That was in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr.” This sentence is load-bearing. It tells us how the report was being heard. People in the Zubayrid crisis were asking about a swallowed-army prophecy because a real army was threatening a real refuge-seeker at the House. The report does not name Ibn al-Zubayr as the predicted figure, but the early interpretive frame points directly to him. There are also small wording variations. Some versions say the refuge-seeker takes refuge **at the House**. Some say **in the Sanctuary**. Aḥmad preserves a variant saying **at the Stone**. These differences do not weaken the identification. They all point to the same Meccan sacred space. What stays stable is the core image: a protected sanctuary figure and an army destroyed before reaching him. ## The Army-at-the-House Reports A second family removes the refuge-seeker and focuses on the army. In these reports, an army attacks the House and is swallowed. This is not a different world. It is the same memory with the camera moved. The first family focuses on the protected figure. This family focuses on the punished army. The strongest version is the Ḥafṣa report through the family of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān. That matters because ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān was not a random name. He was a Meccan Zubayrid loyalist and was killed defending Ibn al-Zubayr’s body. His family transmits a report about an army attacking the House, and Ibn Mājah preserves the crucial gloss: when the army of al-Ḥajjāj came, “we thought they were the ones.” فَلَمَّا جَاءَ جَيْشُ الْحَجَّاجِ ظَنَنَّا أَنَّهُمْ هُمْ “When the army of al-Ḥajjāj came, we thought they were the ones.” That is about as clear as an interpretive activation can get. The family transmitting the report thought al-Ḥajjāj’s army — the army that actually killed Ibn al-Zubayr — might be the army that the Prophet had foretold would be swallowed. The historical irony is the point. Al-Ḥajjāj’s army was not swallowed. It reached Mecca, defeated Ibn al-Zubayr, and killed him. So what does the hadith material do? It preserves the opposite outcome. It takes the army that succeeded historically and imagines the army being destroyed by God. It takes a political defeat and turns it into an eschatological expectation. That is why this cluster should not be read as a neutral prediction floating above history. It is embedded in the memory of the Meccan sieges. ## The Full Scenario: The Anonymous Meccan Redeemer The third family expands the kernel into a full eschatological scenario. Now the report says a caliph dies, people disagree, a man leaves Medina for Mecca, the Meccans bring him out unwillingly, they pledge allegiance to him between the Rukn and the Maqām, a Syrian army is sent against him, and that army is swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ. Then Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes come to him, a Quraysh man with Kalbī maternal uncles rises against him, the enemy is defeated, wealth is distributed, the sunna is restored, and the figure reigns seven or nine years. This is the familiar Mahdī template, but in the earlier versions the figure is usually still anonymous. He is “a man from Medina,” “a man from my community,” or, in one later route, “a man from Banū Hāshim.” The story is Mahdī-shaped before it is consistently Mahdī-named. The main route runs through Qatāda: **The Prophet → Umm Salama → unstable upper link → Ṣāliḥ Abū al-Khalīl → Qatāda → Hishām / Maʿmar / ʿImrān → collectors.** The ʿAbd al-Razzāq version is especially important because it is transmitted from Qatāda in mursal form. Qatāda raises it to the Prophet, but without a named Companion in the chain. That matters because it may preserve an earlier stage before the prophetic attribution was fully stabilized through a named Companion route. يَكُونُ اخْتِلَافٌ عِنْدَ مَوْتِ خَلِيفَةٍ، فَيَخْرُجُ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ فَيَأْتِي مَكَّةَ، فَيَسْتَخْرِجُهُ النَّاسُ مِنْ بَيْتِهِ وَهُوَ كَارِهٌ، فَيُبَايِعُونَهُ بَيْنَ الرُّكْنِ وَالْمَقَامِ، فَيُبْعَثُ إِلَيْهِ جَيْشٌ مِنَ الشَّامِ، حَتَّى إِذَا كَانُوا بِالْبَيْدَاءِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ “There will be disagreement at the death of a caliph. A man will leave Medina and come to Mecca. The people will bring him out from his house while he is unwilling, and they will pledge allegiance to him between the Rukn and the Maqām. An army from Syria will be sent against him, and when they are at al-Bayḍāʾ they will be swallowed.” This is where the Zubayrid memory becomes a full end-times story. Ibn al-Zubayr fled to Mecca after refusing the Umayyad order. He received allegiance there. Syrian armies came against him. His caliphate lasted roughly nine years. He had Iraqi support. His great enemy was the Umayyad-Syrian order, deeply tied to Kalbī power. The hadith version keeps the structure but changes the ending. The Meccan claimant is righteous and unwilling. The Syrian army is destroyed. The supporters arrive. The Kalbī enemy is defeated. The reign succeeds. That is not random similarity. It is narrative reversal. ## The Rukn-and-Maqām Motif Becomes Explicitly Mahdī The fourth layer is where the Meccan bayʿa motif becomes detached from the full story and explicitly attached to the Mahdī. Earlier versions say “a man” will be pledged allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām. Later versions say **the Mahdī** will be pledged allegiance there. يُبَايَعُ الْمَهْدِيُّ بَيْنَ الرُّكْنِ وَالْمَقَامِ، لَا يُوقِظُ نَائِمًا وَلَا يُهْرِيقُ دَمًا “The Mahdī will be pledged allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām. He will not wake a sleeping person and will not shed blood.” That detail is important. Ibn al-Zubayr’s Meccan claim ended in blood. The later Mahdī version imagines the same sacred space but removes the blood. The bayʿa becomes peaceful, purified, and eschatological. Fitr b. Khalīfa is important because he also appears in the earlier Kaysānī Mahdī material. He was a Kūfan Shīʿī transmitter, and some rijāl material connects him with extreme Khashabī tendencies. But that does not mean the whole Zubayrid sanctuary cluster is Kaysānī. The matn is not about Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya. The scene is not Kaysānī geography. It is Meccan: the Rukn, the Maqām, the sanctuary, the House. Fitr’s role is better understood as a later Kūfan channel through which the Meccan bayʿa motif was absorbed into the broader Mahdī corpus and explicitly named. ## The Development in One Picture The cluster develops in stages. First, there is the historical Ibn al-Zubayr: the refuge-seeker at the House, besieged by Syrian armies, finally killed at Mecca. Then comes the simple hadith kernel: a refuge-seeker at the House and an army swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ. Then comes the army-at-the-House family, where the focus shifts to divine punishment of the attackers. Then comes the full scenario through Qatāda, where the anonymous Meccan claimant is given a complete eschatological career. Finally, the Rukn-and-Maqām bayʿa is explicitly named as the Mahdī’s inauguration. This diagram is the simplest way to understand the argument. The tradition is not born fully formed as the standard Sunnī Mahdī narrative. It grows. The earliest pieces are simple and Meccan. Later pieces add narrative machinery. The final pieces name the Mahdī. ## The Motifs Line Up Too Well The strongest argument is not one isolated chain. It is the convergence of motifs. Historical Ibn al-Zubayr Hadith cluster reversal Ibn al-Zubayr is called the refuge-seeker at the House A refuge-seeker seeks refuge at the House Syrian armies attack Mecca A Syrian army is sent against the Meccan figure The Kaʿba is damaged and burned The attacking army is swallowed before reaching victory Ibn al-Zubayr receives contested allegiance in Mecca The future figure receives bayʿa between the Rukn and the Maqām Ibn al-Zubayr is killed by al-Ḥajjāj The future figure survives and triumphs Zubayrid supporters fail to save the cause Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes arrive to support the future figure Umayyad-Kalbī power triumphs The Quraysh-Kalbī enemy is defeated The historical reign ends in defeat after roughly nine years The future reign lasts seven or nine years and restores justice This is why the cluster looks Zubayrid. It does not merely mention Mecca. It takes the major elements of Ibn al-Zubayr’s failed sanctuary claim and turns them into the architecture of a successful future redeemer. The report does not preserve Ibn al-Zubayr by name. It preserves the structure of his defeat: refuge at Mecca, Syrian assault, sanctuary violation, contested bayʿa, and the hope that God would destroy the army before it could win. That is exactly how political memory often becomes eschatology. A failed claimant is not necessarily remembered directly. Instead, the shape of his claim is carried forward, purified, anonymized, and projected into the future. ## The Four Main Families Family Core route Main motif Historical function Simple refuge-seeker Umm Salama → ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Qibṭiyya → ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Rufayʿ Refuge-seeker at the House, army swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ Earliest kernel, explicitly activated in Ibn al-Zubayr’s time Army at the House Ḥafṣa / Ṣafiyya / Abū Hurayra routes Army attacks the House and is swallowed Punishment of the attacking army, with al-Ḥajjāj gloss in the Ḥafṣa strand Full scenario Qatāda → Ṣāliḥ Abū al-Khalīl → Umm Salama Caliph dies, man flees to Mecca, bayʿa, Syrian army swallowed, Kalb enemy defeated Zubayrid template expanded into a full eschatological narrative Rukn-and-Maqām Mahdī coding Fitr b. Khalīfa route and later reception The Mahdī is pledged allegiance between the Rukn and Maqām Anonymous Meccan claimant finally receives explicit Mahdī identity This table also prevents a common mistake. The cluster does not depend on proving that one person fabricated all the reports. That is not the argument. The argument is that related Meccan sanctuary motifs circulated in several families, and the earliest interpretive frames tie those motifs to the Zubayrid crisis. Later transmitters then expanded the material until it became the familiar Mahdī scenario. ## Why the Army Being Swallowed Matters Historically, the army was not swallowed. That is the point. Ḥuṣayn b. Numayr’s army besieged Mecca under Yazīd. The Kaʿba was damaged and burned. Al-Ḥajjāj’s army later besieged Mecca under ʿAbd al-Malik. Ibn al-Zubayr was killed. The sanctuary did not stop the army in the way Zubayrid supporters may have hoped. The hadith cluster rewrites that outcome. In the reports, the army never wins. It is swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ before it can complete its mission. The sanctuary is vindicated. The refuge-seeker is protected. The Umayyad victory is transformed into divine defeat. This is not simply “prediction.” It is reversal. The reports imagine the outcome that Zubayrid Mecca needed but did not receive in history. That makes the reports powerful. They allow the defeated memory to survive. Ibn al-Zubayr himself is not named, so the story is not trapped in the past. It becomes reusable. Any later Meccan redeemer can step into the template. ## Why the Figure Becomes Anonymous One of the most important features of the cluster is that the figure is often unnamed. He is a refuge-seeker, a man from Medina, a man from the community, a Meccan figure, or sometimes a man from Banū Hāshim. This anonymity is not weakness. It is how the template becomes portable. If the reports had simply named Ibn al-Zubayr, the tradition would have died with his defeat. But by removing his name and preserving the structure of his claim, the reports turn his story into a future pattern. The failed Meccan caliph becomes the prototype of the successful eschatological claimant. This is also how the Zubayrid layer can be absorbed into the broader Mahdī corpus. The figure is already anonymous enough to be renamed. Later transmitters can attach the Mahdī title to the Meccan bayʿa scene without needing to preserve Ibn al-Zubayr’s name. ## Why This Is Not the Same as the Kaysānī Layer The Kaysānī Mahdī material and the Zubayrid sanctuary material should not be collapsed into one origin. They solve different historical defeats. The Kaysānī layer centers around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya and the hope that a failed ʿAlid-Hāshimid figure did not truly disappear. Its logic is household, occultation, and return. The Zubayrid layer centers around Mecca, the sanctuary, the House, the Rukn and Maqām, and the army sent from Syria. Its logic is sacred geography and divine reversal of a violated sanctuary. Both layers are anti-Umayyad in broad structure. Both transform failure into future vindication. But they are not the same layer. Kaysānism contributes one kind of Mahdī material. Zubayrid Mecca contributes another. The later Mahdī figure is not a single clean origin. He is a composite. Kaysānī material contributes one layer. Zubayrid sanctuary memory contributes another. Later Abbasid, Sufyānī, and black-banner materials add still more layers. ## What Would Change This Analysis? This reading would be weakened if we found an early, independent, geographically diverse form of the sanctuary-refugee scenario that clearly predates the Zubayrid crisis, does not preserve Zubayrid interpretive activation, and does not share the Meccan political vocabulary. It would also be weakened if the title “refuge-seeker at the House” were not historically attached to Ibn al-Zubayr. But that is not what we have. We have the opposite. The historical sources explicitly identify Ibn al-Zubayr as the refuge-seeker at the House and in the Sanctuary. The simple hadith reports are asked about in his time. The Ḥafṣa strand says that when al-Ḥajjāj’s army came, they thought it was the army foretold. The full scenario then expands the same Meccan sanctuary template into a future redeemer story. Later still, the Rukn-and-Maqām scene is explicitly attached to the Mahdī. That is a coherent developmental sequence. ## Final Verdict The Zubayrid sanctuary cluster is best read as the Meccan layer of the Mahdī corpus. It begins with the historical memory of Ibn al-Zubayr, the man publicly known as the refuge-seeker at the House, who made Mecca the center of his anti-Umayyad claim and was ultimately killed there after the sanctuary was violated by Syrian armies. The hadith material takes the same elements and reverses them. The refuge-seeker survives. The army is swallowed. The bayʿa becomes peaceful. The Syrian enemy fails. The Meccan claimant becomes the future redeemer rather than the defeated rebel. This does not require claiming that every transmitter in the cluster was a Zubayrid partisan. The rijāl evidence does not support that. The stronger argument is tradition-historical: the vocabulary, setting, early interpretive comments, motif structure, and later Mahdī coding all point to the same development. The political memory of Ibn al-Zubayr’s failed Meccan caliphate was anonymized, purified, and projected into the future. That is why this cluster matters. It shows how history becomes prophecy. It shows how a failed claimant can survive as an eschatological template. And it shows how the Mahdī tradition absorbed the defeats of multiple anti-Umayyad movements until the later figure became a composite redeemer made from older political ghosts. The Zubayrid Mahdī is Ibn al-Zubayr without the name: the refuge-seeker whose army is finally swallowed before it can reach the House. ## Appendix: Comparative Motif Table Motif Simple refuge-seeker Army-at-the-House Full scenario Rukn/Maqām Mahdī coding Historical layer Refuge-seeker at sanctuary Explicit Usually absent Implicit, man flees to Mecca Absent Ibn al-Zubayr = العائذ بالبيت Army Yes Yes Yes, from Syria Absent Syrian/Umayyad armies Swallowing at al-Bayḍāʾ Yes Yes Yes Absent Did not occur historically; theological reversal Bayʿa between Rukn and Maqām Absent Absent Yes Yes Ibn al-Zubayr’s Meccan allegiance Reluctance Absent Absent Yes Implied by peaceful scene Ibn al-Zubayr framed himself first as refuge-seeker Iraqi / Syrian supporters Absent Absent Yes Sometimes Zubayrid Iraqi support and Syrian opposition Kalb enemy Absent Absent Yes Absent Umayyad-Kalbī alliance Seven/nine-year reign Absent Absent Yes Absent Ibn al-Zubayr ruled roughly nine years Mahdī named Absent Absent Usually absent Present Later coding Interpretive activation In the time of Ibn al-Zubayr When al-Ḥajjāj’s army came Absorbed Absorbed Zubayrid crisis ## Appendix: Key Variant Families and References Family Key references Notes Umm Salama refuge-seeker Ibn Abī Shayba 37219; Isḥāq b. A force will be sent against him. When they are at a desert plain, they will be swallowed.” This article is about one layer of the Mahdī tradition. It is not about every report ever attached to the Mahdī. It is about a specific Meccan cluster: a man takes refuge at the House, an army is sent against him, and God swallows that army at al-Bayḍāʾ before it reaches him. In later versions, the story grows. A caliph dies, a man flees from Medina to Mecca, people force him into allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām, a Syrian army marches against him, the army is swallowed, Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes come to him, a Kalbī enemy appears, and eventually the figure is named as the Mahdī. The claim here is not that the entire Mahdī corpus comes from Ibn al-Zubayr. The earlier Kaysānī layer belongs to a different world, centered around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya. The black-banner material has its own Abbasid setting. The Sufyānī material has its own line of development. The point here is narrower and stronger: the Meccan sanctuary layer of the Mahdī narrative is best read as a Zubayrid memory, built around the failed Meccan caliphate of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr and later transformed into an eschatological reversal. The Zubayrid contribution to the Mahdī corpus is not the title “Mahdī” itself. It is the Meccan stage: the refuge-seeker at the House, the sanctuary, the Rukn and Maqām, the Syrian army, and the swallowed-army reversal at al-Bayḍāʾ. For a lay reader, the method is simple. We are not starting with later theology. We are starting with the shape of the reports. What is the repeated scene? Who is the unnamed figure? Why is Mecca central? Why is an army sent from Syria? Why is the army destroyed before reaching the sanctuary? And why do early versions explicitly say that people were asking about this report **in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr** or when **al-Ḥajjāj’s army** came? Once those clues are placed next to the historical record, the pattern becomes hard to ignore. The Historical Anchor: Ibn al-Zubayr Was the Refuge-Seeker The key to this cluster is not hidden inside the hadith books. It is in the chronicles. Ibn al-Zubayr was not merely a man who happened to be in Mecca. He was publicly known as **the refuge-seeker at the House** and **the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary**. This was not a vague title. It was a political and religious identity attached to him during his revolt against the Umayyads. Al-Masʿūdī says that Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge at the Sacred House and had named himself **العائذ بالبيت**, “the refuge-seeker at the House,” until poets mentioned him by that name. وَعَاذَ ابْنُ الزُّبَيْرِ بِالْبَيْتِ الْحَرَامِ، وَكَانَ قَدْ سَمَّى نَفْسَهُ الْعَائِذَ بِالْبَيْتِ، وَشُهِرَ بِهَذَا حَتَّى ذَكَرَتْهُ الشُّعَرَاءُ فِي أَشْعَارِهَا “Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge at the Sacred House. He had named himself ‘the refuge-seeker at the House,’ and he became known by this until the poets mentioned him in their verses.” Al-Ṭabarī preserves the same identification with even less ambiguity. A man calls people to **the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary**, and al-Ṭabarī glosses it directly: “meaning ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.” أَدْعُوكُمْ إِلَى الْعَائِذِ بِالْحَرَمِ — يَعْنِي عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ الزُّبَيْرِ “I call you to the refuge-seeker in the Sanctuary — meaning ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr.” Al-Balādhurī preserves the same title in several registers. Ibn al-Zubayr uses it for himself. His supporters use it to rally others. His opponents use it to dismiss him. One hostile statement says, “By God, Ibn al-Zubayr is not a caliph upon whom the community has agreed. He is only a man taking refuge at the House.” That is exactly why the title matters. It was not a later scholarly guess. It was a live political label. This is the historical anchor. Without it, the hadith reports sound like abstract prophecy. With it, the vocabulary becomes specific. The reports say “a refuge-seeker seeks refuge at the House.” The chronicles say Ibn al-Zubayr was known as “the refuge-seeker at the House.” The reports say an army comes against the sanctuary. The chronicles say Syrian armies came against Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca. The reports say God swallows the army. History says the army was not swallowed and Ibn al-Zubayr was killed. That gap between the report and the history is where the eschatological reversal happens. The Earliest Kernel: A Refuge-Seeker and a Swallowed Army The simplest form of the report is not yet a full Mahdī story. There is no caliph’s death, no forced bayʿa, no Iraqi bands, no Kalb enemy, and no explicit Mahdī. There is only the sanctuary refugee, the army, and the swallowing at al-Bayḍāʾ. The key Umm Salama version runs through: **The Prophet → Umm Salama → ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Qibṭiyya → ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Rufayʿ → Jarīr / Zuhayr → collectors.** The important part is not only the prediction. It is the scene around the prediction. In Ibn Abī Shayba’s version, al-Ḥārith b. Abī Rabīʿa and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān enter upon Umm Salama and ask her about the army that will be swallowed. The report then says this happened **in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr**. دَخَلَ الْحَارِثُ بْنُ أَبِي رَبِيعَةَ وَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ صَفْوَانَ عَلَى أُمِّ سَلَمَةَ ... فَسَأَلَاهَا عَنِ الْجَيْشِ الَّذِي يُخْسَفُ بِهِ، وَذَلِكَ فِي زَمَانِ ابْنِ الزُّبَيْرِ “al-Ḥārith b. Abī Rabīʿa and ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān entered upon Umm Salama ... and asked her about the army that would be swallowed. That was in the time of Ibn al-Zubayr.” This sentence is load-bearing. It tells us how the report was being heard. People in the Zubayrid crisis were asking about a swallowed-army prophecy because a real army was threatening a real refuge-seeker at the House. The report does not name Ibn al-Zubayr as the predicted figure, but the early interpretive frame points directly to him. There are also small wording variations. Some versions say the refuge-seeker takes refuge **at the House**. Some say **in the Sanctuary**. Aḥmad preserves a variant saying **at the Stone**. These differences do not weaken the identification. They all point to the same Meccan sacred space. What stays stable is the core image: a protected sanctuary figure and an army destroyed before reaching him. The Army-at-the-House Reports A second family removes the refuge-seeker and focuses on the army. In these reports, an army attacks the House and is swallowed. This is not a different world. It is the same memory with the camera moved. The first family focuses on the protected figure. This family focuses on the punished army. The strongest version is the Ḥafṣa report through the family of ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān. That matters because ʿAbd Allāh b. Ṣafwān was not a random name. He was a Meccan Zubayrid loyalist and was killed defending Ibn al-Zubayr’s body. His family transmits a report about an army attacking the House, and Ibn Mājah preserves the crucial gloss: when the army of al-Ḥajjāj came, “we thought they were the ones.” فَلَمَّا جَاءَ جَيْشُ الْحَجَّاجِ ظَنَنَّا أَنَّهُمْ هُمْ “When the army of al-Ḥajjāj came, we thought they were the ones.” That is about as clear as an interpretive activation can get. The family transmitting the report thought al-Ḥajjāj’s army — the army that actually killed Ibn al-Zubayr — might be the army that the Prophet had foretold would be swallowed. The historical irony is the point. Al-Ḥajjāj’s army was not swallowed. It reached Mecca, defeated Ibn al-Zubayr, and killed him. So what does the hadith material do? It preserves the opposite outcome. It takes the army that succeeded historically and imagines the army being destroyed by God. It takes a political defeat and turns it into an eschatological expectation. That is why this cluster should not be read as a neutral prediction floating above history. It is embedded in the memory of the Meccan sieges. The Full Scenario: The Anonymous Meccan Redeemer The third family expands the kernel into a full eschatological scenario. Now the report says a caliph dies, people disagree, a man leaves Medina for Mecca, the Meccans bring him out unwillingly, they pledge allegiance to him between the Rukn and the Maqām, a Syrian army is sent against him, and that army is swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ. Then Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes come to him, a Quraysh man with Kalbī maternal uncles rises against him, the enemy is defeated, wealth is distributed, the sunna is restored, and the figure reigns seven or nine years. This is the familiar Mahdī template, but in the earlier versions the figure is usually still anonymous. He is “a man from Medina,” “a man from my community,” or, in one later route, “a man from Banū Hāshim.” The story is Mahdī-shaped before it is consistently Mahdī-named. The main route runs through Qatāda: **The Prophet → Umm Salama → unstable upper link → Ṣāliḥ Abū al-Khalīl → Qatāda → Hishām / Maʿmar / ʿImrān → collectors.** The ʿAbd al-Razzāq version is especially important because it is transmitted from Qatāda in mursal form. Qatāda raises it to the Prophet, but without a named Companion in the chain. That matters because it may preserve an earlier stage before the prophetic attribution was fully stabilized through a named Companion route. يَكُونُ اخْتِلَافٌ عِنْدَ مَوْتِ خَلِيفَةٍ، فَيَخْرُجُ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ فَيَأْتِي مَكَّةَ، فَيَسْتَخْرِجُهُ النَّاسُ مِنْ بَيْتِهِ وَهُوَ كَارِهٌ، فَيُبَايِعُونَهُ بَيْنَ الرُّكْنِ وَالْمَقَامِ، فَيُبْعَثُ إِلَيْهِ جَيْشٌ مِنَ الشَّامِ، حَتَّى إِذَا كَانُوا بِالْبَيْدَاءِ خُسِفَ بِهِمْ “There will be disagreement at the death of a caliph. A man will leave Medina and come to Mecca. The people will bring him out from his house while he is unwilling, and they will pledge allegiance to him between the Rukn and the Maqām. An army from Syria will be sent against him, and when they are at al-Bayḍāʾ they will be swallowed.” This is where the Zubayrid memory becomes a full end-times story. Ibn al-Zubayr fled to Mecca after refusing the Umayyad order. He received allegiance there. Syrian armies came against him. His caliphate lasted roughly nine years. He had Iraqi support. His great enemy was the Umayyad-Syrian order, deeply tied to Kalbī power. The hadith version keeps the structure but changes the ending. The Meccan claimant is righteous and unwilling. The Syrian army is destroyed. The supporters arrive. The Kalbī enemy is defeated. The reign succeeds. That is not random similarity. It is narrative reversal. The Rukn-and-Maqām Motif Becomes Explicitly Mahdī The fourth layer is where the Meccan bayʿa motif becomes detached from the full story and explicitly attached to the Mahdī. Earlier versions say “a man” will be pledged allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām. Later versions say **the Mahdī** will be pledged allegiance there. يُبَايَعُ الْمَهْدِيُّ بَيْنَ الرُّكْنِ وَالْمَقَامِ، لَا يُوقِظُ نَائِمًا وَلَا يُهْرِيقُ دَمًا “The Mahdī will be pledged allegiance between the Rukn and the Maqām. He will not wake a sleeping person and will not shed blood.” That detail is important. Ibn al-Zubayr’s Meccan claim ended in blood. The later Mahdī version imagines the same sacred space but removes the blood. The bayʿa becomes peaceful, purified, and eschatological. Fitr b. Khalīfa is important because he also appears in the earlier Kaysānī Mahdī material. He was a Kūfan Shīʿī transmitter, and some rijāl material connects him with extreme Khashabī tendencies. But that does not mean the whole Zubayrid sanctuary cluster is Kaysānī. The matn is not about Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya. The scene is not Kaysānī geography. It is Meccan: the Rukn, the Maqām, the sanctuary, the House. Fitr’s role is better understood as a later Kūfan channel through which the Meccan bayʿa motif was absorbed into the broader Mahdī corpus and explicitly named. The Development in One Picture The cluster develops in stages. First, there is the historical Ibn al-Zubayr: the refuge-seeker at the House, besieged by Syrian armies, finally killed at Mecca. Then comes the simple hadith kernel: a refuge-seeker at the House and an army swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ. Then comes the army-at-the-House family, where the focus shifts to divine punishment of the attackers. Then comes the full scenario through Qatāda, where the anonymous Meccan claimant is given a complete eschatological career. Finally, the Rukn-and-Maqām bayʿa is explicitly named as the Mahdī’s inauguration. This diagram is the simplest way to understand the argument. The tradition is not born fully formed as the standard Sunnī Mahdī narrative. It grows. The earliest pieces are simple and Meccan. Later pieces add narrative machinery. The final pieces name the Mahdī. The Motifs Line Up Too Well The strongest argument is not one isolated chain. It is the convergence of motifs. Historical Ibn al-Zubayr Hadith cluster reversal Ibn al-Zubayr is called the refuge-seeker at the House A refuge-seeker seeks refuge at the House Syrian armies attack Mecca A Syrian army is sent against the Meccan figure The Kaʿba is damaged and burned The attacking army is swallowed before reaching victory Ibn al-Zubayr receives contested allegiance in Mecca The future figure receives bayʿa between the Rukn and the Maqām Ibn al-Zubayr is killed by al-Ḥajjāj The future figure survives and triumphs Zubayrid supporters fail to save the cause Iraqi bands and Syrian substitutes arrive to support the future figure Umayyad-Kalbī power triumphs The Quraysh-Kalbī enemy is defeated The historical reign ends in defeat after roughly nine years The future reign lasts seven or nine years and restores justice This is why the cluster looks Zubayrid. It does not merely mention Mecca. It takes the major elements of Ibn al-Zubayr’s failed sanctuary claim and turns them into the architecture of a successful future redeemer. The report does not preserve Ibn al-Zubayr by name. It preserves the structure of his defeat: refuge at Mecca, Syrian assault, sanctuary violation, contested bayʿa, and the hope that God would destroy the army before it could win. That is exactly how political memory often becomes eschatology. A failed claimant is not necessarily remembered directly. Instead, the shape of his claim is carried forward, purified, anonymized, and projected into the future. The Four Main Families Family Core route Main motif Historical function Simple refuge-seeker Umm Salama → ʿUbayd Allāh b. al-Qibṭiyya → ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz b. Rufayʿ Refuge-seeker at the House, army swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ Earliest kernel, explicitly activated in Ibn al-Zubayr’s time Army at the House Ḥafṣa / Ṣafiyya / Abū Hurayra routes Army attacks the House and is swallowed Punishment of the attacking army, with al-Ḥajjāj gloss in the Ḥafṣa strand Full scenario Qatāda → Ṣāliḥ Abū al-Khalīl → Umm Salama Caliph dies, man flees to Mecca, bayʿa, Syrian army swallowed, Kalb enemy defeated Zubayrid template expanded into a full eschatological narrative Rukn-and-Maqām Mahdī coding Fitr b. Khalīfa route and later reception The Mahdī is pledged allegiance between the Rukn and Maqām Anonymous Meccan claimant finally receives explicit Mahdī identity This table also prevents a common mistake. The cluster does not depend on proving that one person fabricated all the reports. That is not the argument. The argument is that related Meccan sanctuary motifs circulated in several families, and the earliest interpretive frames tie those motifs to the Zubayrid crisis. Later transmitters then expanded the material until it became the familiar Mahdī scenario. Why the Army Being Swallowed Matters Historically, the army was not swallowed. That is the point. Ḥuṣayn b. Numayr’s army besieged Mecca under Yazīd. The Kaʿba was damaged and burned. Al-Ḥajjāj’s army later besieged Mecca under ʿAbd al-Malik. Ibn al-Zubayr was killed. The sanctuary did not stop the army in the way Zubayrid supporters may have hoped. The hadith cluster rewrites that outcome. In the reports, the army never wins. It is swallowed at al-Bayḍāʾ before it can complete its mission. The sanctuary is vindicated. The refuge-seeker is protected. The Umayyad victory is transformed into divine defeat. This is not simply “prediction.” It is reversal. The reports imagine the outcome that Zubayrid Mecca needed but did not receive in history. That makes the reports powerful. They allow the defeated memory to survive. Ibn al-Zubayr himself is not named, so the story is not trapped in the past. It becomes reusable. Any later Meccan redeemer can step into the template. Why the Figure Becomes Anonymous One of the most important features of the cluster is that the figure is often unnamed. He is a refuge-seeker, a man from Medina, a man from the community, a Meccan figure, or sometimes a man from Banū Hāshim. This anonymity is not weakness. It is how the template becomes portable. If the reports had simply named Ibn al-Zubayr, the tradition would have died with his defeat. But by removing his name and preserving the structure of his claim, the reports turn his story into a future pattern. The failed Meccan caliph becomes the prototype of the successful eschatological claimant. This is also how the Zubayrid layer can be absorbed into the broader Mahdī corpus. The figure is already anonymous enough to be renamed. Later transmitters can attach the Mahdī title to the Meccan bayʿa scene without needing to preserve Ibn al-Zubayr’s name. Why This Is Not the Same as the Kaysānī Layer The Kaysānī Mahdī material and the Zubayrid sanctuary material should not be collapsed into one origin. They solve different historical defeats. The Kaysānī layer centers around Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya and the hope that a failed ʿAlid-Hāshimid figure did not truly disappear. Its logic is household, occultation, and return. The Zubayrid layer centers around Mecca, the sanctuary, the House, the Rukn and Maqām, and the army sent from Syria. Its logic is sacred geography and divine reversal of a violated sanctuary. Both layers are anti-Umayyad in broad structure. Both transform failure into future vindication. But they are not the same layer. Kaysānism contributes one kind of Mahdī material. Zubayrid Mecca contributes another. The later Mahdī figure is not a single clean origin. He is a composite. Kaysānī material contributes one layer. Zubayrid sanctuary memory contributes another. Later Abbasid, Sufyānī, and black-banner materials add still more layers. What Would Change This Analysis? This reading would be weakened if we found an early, independent, geographically diverse form of the sanctuary-refugee scenario that clearly predates the Zubayrid crisis, does not preserve Zubayrid interpretive activation, and does not share the Meccan political vocabulary. It would also be weakened if the title “refuge-seeker at the House” were not historically attached to Ibn al-Zubayr. But that is not what we have. We have the opposite. The historical sources explicitly identify Ibn al-Zubayr as the refuge-seeker at the House and in the Sanctuary. The simple hadith reports are asked about in his time. The Ḥafṣa strand says that when al-Ḥajjāj’s army came, they thought it was the army foretold. The full scenario then expands the same Meccan sanctuary template into a future redeemer story. Later still, the Rukn-and-Maqām scene is explicitly attached to the Mahdī. That is a coherent developmental sequence. Final Verdict The Zubayrid sanctuary cluster is best read as the Meccan layer of the Mahdī corpus. It begins with the historical memory of Ibn al-Zubayr, the man publicly known as the refuge-seeker at the House, who made Mecca the center of his anti-Umayyad claim and was ultimately killed there after the sanctuary was violated by Syrian armies. The hadith material takes the same elements and reverses them. The refuge-seeker survives. The army is swallowed. The bayʿa becomes peaceful. The Syrian enemy fails. The Meccan claimant becomes the future redeemer rather than the defeated rebel. This does not require claiming that every transmitter in the cluster was a Zubayrid partisan. The rijāl evidence does not support that. The stronger argument is tradition-historical: the vocabulary, setting, early interpretive comments, motif structure, and later Mahdī coding all point to the same development. The political memory of Ibn al-Zubayr’s failed Meccan caliphate was anonymized, purified, and projected into the future. That is why this cluster matters. It shows how history becomes prophecy. It shows how a failed claimant can survive as an eschatological template. And it shows how the Mahdī tradition absorbed the defeats of multiple anti-Umayyad movements until the later figure became a composite redeemer made from older political ghosts. The Zubayrid Mahdī is Ibn al-Zubayr without the name: the refuge-seeker whose army is finally swallowed before it can reach the House. title: The Thirty-Year Reign Hadith: A Safīnah Bottleneck and an Anti-Umayyad Calculation
description: A full isnād-cum-matn analysis of the report that the caliphate after the Prophet would last thirty years, then become kingship. The report collapses through Saʿīd b. Jumhān from Safīnah and carries a visible anti-Umayyad polemical frame.
