The usual version says that Constantinople would be conquered, and that its commander and army would be excellent. Since the city fell to Mehmed II in 1453, the report is commonly read backward from that Ottoman victory. The problem is that the hadith evidence does not begin in 1453. The most famous report already contains a much earlier military setting. It says that Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik, the Umayyad prince who led the great siege of Constantinople in 98–99 AH / 717–718 CE, asked for the report and then campaigned against the city. That detail changes the entire argument. The report was not first heard as an Ottoman victory caption. In its transmitted form, it was already attached to an Umayyad attempt that failed. The Constantinople material does not behave like a broad, independently preserved prophecy. The famous “excellent commander and excellent army” report collapses into a narrow stem with name instability at the crucial transmitter and an explicit Maslama campaign frame. The newly checked material strengthens that conclusion: al-Baghawī preserves the Maslama note in a Companion-entry context, Ibn Abī Khaythama exposes the al-Ghanawī/al-Khathʿamī confusion, and Abū Zurʿa al-Dimashqī shows that Constantinople was already a living Syrian military memory under Muʿāwiya. The tasbih/takbir family rests on Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh, a transmitter fiercely rejected in the rijāl literature. The “Constantinople before Rome” report is stronger than the Kathīr family, but it is a different Egyptian apocalyptic stream and cannot rescue the famous commander report. This article is not arguing that Constantinople was never conquered. It obviously was. The question is narrower and more historical: do these reports independently preserve a prophetic prediction, or do they look like conquest-era and post-conquest traditions shaped by the military and political hopes of later Muslims? The report everyone quotes The most famous wording is the report found in Aḥmad, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, al-Bukhārī’s *al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr*, and Ibn ʿAsākir’s *Tārīkh Dimashq*. The wording is short, polished, and rhetorically powerful. لَتُفْتَحَنَّ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةُ، فَلَنِعْمَ الْأَمِيرُ أَمِيرُهَا، وَلَنِعْمَ الْجَيْشُ ذَلِكَ الْجَيْشُ. قَالَ: فَدَعَانِي مَسْلَمَةُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ فَسَأَلَنِي، فَحَدَّثْتُهُ، فَغَزَا الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ. “Constantinople will certainly be conquered. What an excellent commander its commander will be, and what an excellent army that army will be.” The transmitter then says: “Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik summoned me and asked me, so I narrated it to him, and he campaigned against Constantinople.” The added compilations give an even cleaner witness to the same problem. Al-Baghawī places the report under the Companion entry for Bishr al-Khathʿamī, while noting that he is also called al-Ghanawī and that he settled in Syria.[^added-compilations] His wording again includes the Maslama sequel: the report was narrated to Maslama, and Maslama then campaigned against that Constantinople. This is not a later critic forcing the siege context onto the hadith. The siege context is inside a transmitted version of the report. عَنْ أَبِيهِ أَنَّهُ سَمِعَ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ يَقُولُ: لَتُفْتَحَنَّ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةُ، وَلَنِعْمَ الْأَمِيرُ أَمِيرُهَا، وَلَنِعْمَ الْجَيْشُ ذَلِكَ الْجَيْشُ. فَحَدَّثْتُ بِهِ مَسْلَمَةَ بْنَ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ فَغَزَا تِلْكَ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ. From his father, who heard the Prophet say: “Constantinople will certainly be conquered. What an excellent commander its commander will be, and what an excellent army that army will be.” He then said: “So I narrated it to Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik, and he campaigned against that Constantinople.” This version is especially useful because al-Baghawī is not presenting a modern polemical reconstruction. He is listing a Companion and preserving the same unstable identity markers: Bishr is introduced as al-Khathʿamī, but the entry notes that he is also called al-Ghanawī and settled in Syria. The report then travels through al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra al-Maʿāfirī, an Egyptian transmitter, to Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb and then to the later collectors. Al-Baghawī calls al-Walīd “acceptable in hadith,” so the argument should not pretend that every man in the chain was dismissed. The real problem is narrower and stronger: even when the route is treated fairly, it still remains a single fragile stem with the same Maslama frame and the same instability at the son-of-Bishr link. The second half is often ignored in popular apologetics, but it is exactly where the historical problem appears. The report does not simply float in timeless prophetic space. It is attached to Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik. The report itself tells us that it was requested by an Umayyad prince in connection with a Constantinople campaign. If the report was already being deployed for Maslama’s expedition, then its first recoverable political use belongs to the early eighth-century Umayyad siege horizon, not to the fifteenth-century Ottoman conquest. The later Ottoman reading may be devotional and retrospective, but it is not the setting in which the report first becomes historically visible. The isnād bundle is narrower than it looks At first glance the report appears in several books, so it can look widely transmitted. When the chains are lined up, however, the spread happens late. The recoverable stem is the same: > Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra al-Maʿāfirī → the son of Bishr → Bishr → the Prophet. The branches into Aḥmad, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, al-Bukhārī’s *Tārīkh*, and Ibn ʿAsākir mostly occur above Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb. That is not independent early attestation. It is a late fan-out from a narrow stem. The most important rijāl detail is the instability at the son-of-Bishr link. Across the sources he appears as ʿUbayd, ʿUbayd Allāh, or ʿAbd Allāh b. Bishr. His nisba is also unstable: al-Ghanawī in some reports, al-Khathʿamī in others, and even al-ʿAbdī appears as an error in one route reported and corrected by Ibn ʿAsākir. This is exactly the wrong place for uncertainty, because this is the transmitter who connects the report to the alleged Companion father and to the Maslama frame. Source Critical chain segment What it shows Aḥmad 18957 Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿAbd Allāh b. Bishr al-Khathʿamī → his father Contains the famous wording and the Maslama campaign note. The supplied grading marks the chain weak. al-Ḥākim 8300 ʿAbdah b. ʿAbd Allāh → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿAbd Allāh b. Bishr al-Ghanawī → his father Al-Ḥākim declares it sound, but the same narrow stem and Maslama note remain. al-Ṭabarānī, al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿAbd Allāh b. Bishr al-Ghanawī → his father Another late collector branch, not a separate early origin. Ibn Abī Khaythama, al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr Abū Kurayb → Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿUbayd b. Bishr al-Ghanawī → his father Preserves the wording and explicitly flags the nisba problem: “thus he said al-Ghanawī; and it is said al-Khathʿamī.” He then notes Ibn Abī Shayba’s contrary form through Bishr al-Khathʿamī. al-Bukhārī, al-Tārīkh al-Kabīr Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿUbayd / ʿUbayd Allāh b. Bishr al-Ghanawī → his father Preserves the report but also exposes name instability at the crucial transmitter. al-Baghawī, Muʿjam al-Ṣaḥāba Abū Bakr and ʿUthmān, the sons of Abī Shayba → Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → ʿAbd Allāh b. Bishr al-Khathʿamī / al-Ghanawī → his father Independent source-form confirms the Maslama sequel and the Khathʿamī/Ghanawī instability in a Companion-entry setting. Ibn ʿAsākir, Tārīkh Dimashq Collects the variant names and nisbas around the same stem Notes the correction of al-ʿAbdī and reports the crucial observation: “No one transmitted it except Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb.” The point is not that every later collector copied from one book. The point is that the recoverable living isnād is thin before the late fan-out. The report does not come to us through several Companion routes, several Successor routes, or even several stable second-century regional channels. It comes through a single fragile stem and then spreads. The Maslama problem The Maslama note is not a harmless historical afterthought. It is part of the report’s function. Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik was not a random listener. He was the Umayyad prince associated with the massive siege of Constantinople under Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik and ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz. A report praising the commander and army destined to take Constantinople would be useful precisely in that environment. This creates a strong historical tension. If the report was meant for Maslama’s campaign, then it failed in its immediate setting. The city did not fall to him. Later Muslims could still reuse the wording after 1453, but that is a second life of the report, not proof of its original prophetic character. The wording also does not name Mehmed II, the Ottomans, the year 857 AH / 1453 CE, or any unmistakable Ottoman sign. It names no commander at all. Its specific historical anchor is not Mehmed; it is Maslama. The argument should not rest on whether Mehmed II was a good or bad ruler. That quickly becomes subjective and distracts from the hadith evidence. The stronger argument is textual and historical: the report is already tied to an earlier Umayyad siege, and its isnād does not show broad independent preservation before that political horizon. What the chronicle sources add The historical works make the Maslama frame much stronger. They show that Constantinople was not a distant, vague city waiting for an Ottoman fulfillment centuries later. It was a repeated Umayyad frontier obsession. Muʿāwiya’s forces pushed toward the straits. Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya led a campaign in which Abū Ayyūb al-Anṣārī died by the walls of the city. Then Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik turned the project into a massive state siege under his brother Maslama. This is the world in which a slogan praising the future commander and army would have real political value. Historical witness What it says Why it matters Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ, year 32 AH Muʿāwiya is said to have campaigned toward the strait near Constantinople. Constantinople appears as a military goal already in the first/seventh century frontier imagination. Ibn Qutayba and al-Balādhurī on Abū Ayyūb Abū Ayyūb went with Yazīd b. Muʿāwiya, died at Constantinople, and was buried near the base of its wall. The city already carried Companion-memory and Umayyad prestige before Maslama’s campaign. Khalīfa b. Khayyāṭ, year 98 AH Maslama wintered in Roman territory, moved against Constantinople by land and sea, crossed the gulf, and devastated the area between the gulf and the city. This is one of the earliest historical notices anchoring the great siege in the annalistic record. al-Ṭabarī, year 98 AH Sulaymān ordered Maslama to remain until he conquered the city or received new orders; the siege then collapses into food loss, hunger, and failure. The “excellent commander” report is not attached to a successful conquest in this historical setting. al-Masʿūdī The expedition is described as a land-and-sea operation in 97 AH with 120,000 fighters and ʿUmar b. Hubayra over the naval force. The siege was remembered as a major Umayyad imperial project, not a minor raid. Ibn ʿAsākir He preserves reports from men linked to the siege describing hunger, Byzantine negotiations, and ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s order for withdrawal. The local Syrian memory of the siege is a memory of strain, refusal to withdraw, and eventual recall. al-Dhahabī In the year-98 material, he places the hadith next to the Maslama siege notice, then immediately reports Ibn al-Madīnī’s judgment that its narrator is unknown. A later Sunni historian preserves both the political setting and the rijāl problem in one place. Two passages are especially important. In al-Ṭabarī, the siege is explicitly framed as an order from Sulaymān to Maslama to remain at the city until conquest or further instruction. The story then turns into an account of logistical overconfidence, deception by Leon, and near disaster. فَمِنْ ذَلِكَ مَا كَانَ مِنْ تَوْجِيهِ سُلَيْمَانَ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ أَخَاهُ مَسْلَمَةَ بْنَ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ إِلَى الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةِ، وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يُقِيمَ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى يَفْتَحَهَا أَوْ يَأْتِيَهُ ... فَضَاقَ الْمُسْلِمُونَ حَتَّى كَادُوا يَهْلِكُونَ. “Among the events was Sulaymān b. ʿAbd al-Malik’s dispatching of his brother Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik to Constantinople, ordering him to remain over it until he conquered it or until an order came to him … Then the Muslims were constricted until they nearly perished.” Al-Yaʿqūbī gives another compact version of the same siege logic. Sulaymān goes to Dābiq, sends Maslama into Byzantine territory, and orders him to aim for Constantinople and remain over it until conquest. Maslama reaches the city, stays long enough to plant and eat from what was planted, suffers hunger and cold with the Muslims, and receives reinforcements by land and sea. This is useful because it gives the political ambition in plain narrative form: the caliph was not merely raiding. He was trying to force the conquest. وَأَغْزَى مَسْلَمَةَ بْنَ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ بِلَادَ الرُّومِ، وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يَقْصِدَ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ فَيُقِيمَ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى يَفْتَحَهَا، فَسَارَ مَسْلَمَةُ حَتَّى بَلَغَ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ، وَأَقَامَ عَلَيْهَا حَتَّى زَرَعَ وَأَكَلَ مِمَّا زَرَعَ ... وَأَصَابَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ ضُرٌّ وَجُوعٌ وَبَرْدٌ. “He sent Maslama b. ʿAbd al-Malik into Byzantine territory and ordered him to aim for Constantinople and remain over it until he conquered it. Maslama traveled until he reached Constantinople and remained over it until he planted and ate from what he planted … and the Muslims were afflicted by hardship, hunger, and cold.” Ibn ʿAsākir’s material is even sharper because it preserves siege-memory from inside the Syrian military milieu. One report has a man say, “I was among those who besieged Constantinople.” He describes hunger, a signal-fire rumor, the arrival of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz’s messenger, Maslama’s initial refusal to withdraw, and then the caliph’s renewed order. كُنْتُ فِيمَنْ حَاصَرَ الْقُسْطَنْطِينَةَ ... فَجَاءَنَا رَسُولُ عُمَرَ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ فِي نَحْوٍ مِنْ أَرْبَعَةِ آلَافٍ بِكِتَابٍ إِلَى مَسْلَمَةَ يَأْمُرُهُ بِالْقُفُولِ، فَقَرَأَهُ مَسْلَمَةُ فَلَمْ يَقْفُلْ ... فَغَضِبَ وَقَالَ: مَسْلَمَةُ فِي أَمْرِهِ عَظِيمَةٌ يَكْرَهُ فِرَاقَهَا، وَرَدَّ الرَّسُولَ يَأْمُرُهُ بِالْقُفُولِ. “I was among those who besieged Constantinople … Then the messenger of ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz came to us with about four thousand men, carrying a letter to Maslama ordering him to return. Maslama read it and did not return … ʿUmar became angry and said: ‘Maslama is in the grip of a grave affair that he hates to leave,’ and he sent the messenger back ordering him to return.” This evidence changes the force of the famous report. If the report were a clean, free-floating prediction of the Ottoman conquest, we would not expect the earliest recoverable historical frame to pull us into the failed Umayyad siege of 98–100 AH. Yet that is exactly where the report points. Its preserved narrative world is not Mehmed II’s Istanbul. It is Sulaymān’s Dābiq, Maslama’s encampment, Syrian troops, naval support, food stores, negotiations, hunger, and withdrawal. The chronicle evidence does not prove by itself that the report was fabricated. What it does prove is that the hadith had a concrete early use-context. It made sense as morale language for an Umayyad siege. That is far more historically specific than the modern claim that the report simply waited, unattached and unpoliticized, until 1453. The pre-Ottoman afterlife of the slogan The later historical sources also show how flexible the slogan became before the Ottoman conquest. Ibn Khaldūn preserves a pre-1453 apocalyptic reading in which the “excellent commander” is not Mehmed II at all but a future expected figure tied to Mahdī speculation, the destruction of Caesar, and the capture of Constantinople. He then criticizes this kind of timed apocalyptic speculation as built on weak proofs and arbitrary claims. وَالَّذِي يُهْلِكُ قَيْصَرَ وَيُنْفِقُ كُنُوزَهُ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ هُوَ هَذَا الْمُنْتَظَرُ حِينَ يَفْتَحُ الْقُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةَ: فَنِعْمَ الْأَمِيرُ أَمِيرُهَا وَنِعْمَ الْجَيْشُ ذَلِكَ الْجَيْشُ ... يَعَيِّنُونَ فِيهِ الْوَقْتَ وَالرَّجُلَ وَالْمَكَانَ بِأَدِلَّةٍ وَاهِيَةٍ وَتَحَكُّمَاتٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ، فَيَنْقَضِي الزَّمَانُ وَلَا أَثَرَ لِشَيْءٍ مِنْ ذَلِكَ، فَيَرْجِعُونَ إِلَى تَجْدِيدِ رَأْيٍ آخَرَ مُنْتَحَلٍ. “The one who will destroy Caesar and spend his treasures in God’s path is this awaited one when he conquers Constantinople: ‘What an excellent commander its commander will be, and what an excellent army that army will be’ … They specify in this the time, the man, and the place with weak proofs and differing arbitrary claims. Then time passes and no trace of any of it appears, so they return to inventing another opinion.” This is useful because it shows that the Ottoman identification was not the only way the report was read before 1453. The same wording could be redirected toward new apocalyptic expectations when earlier hopes failed. That is exactly how politically useful prophecy language often survives: it is not falsified by one failed campaign, because later readers can detach it from the failed setting and attach it to another expected conqueror. The “City of Caesar” reports show the Umayyad campaign setting The added compilations also supply collateral evidence from the Umm Ḥarām sea-campaign tradition. This material should not be collapsed into the “excellent commander” report, because it is a different family with a different chain. But it is historically important because it shows the same kind of campaign-merit language being attached to early Byzantine warfare. The report promises merit to the first army that rides the sea and then to the first army that reaches the “City of Caesar.” In the early Islamic historical imagination, that language points naturally to the first naval campaigns under Muʿāwiya and to the Umayyad assaults on Constantinople, not to the Ottomans centuries later. أَوَّلُ جَيْشٍ مِنْ أُمَّتِي يَغْزُونَ هَذَا الْبَحْرَ قَدْ أَوْجَبُوا ... أَوَّلُ جَيْشٍ مِنْ أُمَّتِي يَغْزُونَ مَدِينَةَ قَيْصَرَ مَغْفُورٌ لَهُمْ. “The first army of my community to campaign on this sea has made Paradise obligatory for themselves … The first army of my community to campaign against the City of Caesar will be forgiven.” Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm’s *Fawāʾid* gives a closely related wording: “The first army of my community to ride the sea have made Paradise obligatory,” followed by “the first army of my community to set foot in the City of Caesar will be forgiven.” The chain runs through a Syrian-Egyptian frontier network: Ayyūb b. Ḥassān → Thawr b. Yazīd → Khālid b. Maʿdān → ʿAmr b. al-Aswad → Umm Ḥarām. Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim gives the related form through Yaḥyā b. Ḥamza → Thawr b. Yazīd → Khālid b. Maʿdān → ʿAmr b. al-Aswad. Witness Wording Historical value Ibn Abī ʿĀṣim, al-Āḥād wa-l-Mathānī “The first army to campaign on this sea” and “the first army to campaign against the City of Caesar will be forgiven.” Shows early campaign-merit language tied to the sea and Caesar’s city in the Umm Ḥarām tradition. Muḥammad b. Ibrāhīm, al-Fawāʾid “The first army to ride the sea” and “the first army to set foot in the City of Caesar will be forgiven.” Preserves the same two-stage structure through a Syrian route, with the Cyprus/sea context immediately nearby. al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-buldān Muʿāwiya’s first naval campaign to Cyprus, with ʿUbāda b. al-Ṣāmit and Umm Ḥarām present. Gives the historical setting that made the first sea-army report politically meaningful. This does not prove that the famous “excellent commander” report was copied from the Umm Ḥarām report. It proves something more modest and more useful: praise reports about Byzantine campaigns were already circulating in exactly the Umayyad frontier world in which Constantinople was a repeated military obsession. When the famous report’s own text says that it was narrated to Maslama and then used for his expedition, that detail fits a broader pattern rather than standing alone. The tasbih and takbir conquest report A second family says that the Muslims will fight Banū al-Aṣfar, then conquer Constantinople through *tasbīḥ* and *takbīr*. This appears in Sunan Ibn Mājah and in several Ṭabarānī variants. إِنَّكُمْ سَتُقَاتِلُونَ بَنِي الأَصْفَرِ، وَيُقَاتِلُهُمُ الَّذِينَ مِنْ بَعْدِكُمْ، حَتَّى تَخْرُجَ إِلَيْهِمْ رُوقَةُ الإِسْلَامِ أَهْلُ الْحِجَازِ، الَّذِينَ لَا يَخَافُونَ فِي اللَّهِ لَوْمَةَ لَائِمٍ، فَيَفْتَحُونَ الْقُسْطُنْطِينِيَّةَ بِالتَّسْبِيحِ وَالتَّكْبِيرِ. “You will fight Banū al-Aṣfar, and those after you will fight them, until the choicest Muslims, the people of the Ḥijāz who do not fear the blame of any blamer for God’s sake, go out against them. They will conquer Constantinople with glorification and magnification.” This family is much weaker than the famous commander report. Its chains are built around Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. ʿAwf → his father → his grandfather. That family chain is exactly the pattern condemned in the rijāl sources. The rijāl verdicts on Kathīr are not minor caution flags. They are severe. كَثِيرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ عَمْرِو بْنِ عَوْفٍ الْمُزَنِيُّ ... مُنْكَرُ الْحَدِيثِ جِدًّا، يَرْوِي عَنْ أَبِيهِ، عَنْ جَدِّهِ بِنُسْخَةٍ مَوْضُوعَةٍ، لَا يَحِلُّ ذِكْرُهَا فِي الْكُتُبِ وَلَا الرِّوَايَةُ عَنْهُ إِلَّا عَلَى جِهَةِ التَّعَجُّبِ. وَكَانَ الشَّافِعِيُّ يَقُولُ: كَثِيرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ الْمُزَنِيُّ رُكْنٌ مِنْ أَرْكَانِ الْكَذِبِ. “Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr b. ʿAwf al-Muzanī … is extremely rejected in hadith. He narrates from his father from his grandfather a fabricated copy. It is not lawful to mention it in books or narrate from him except by way of astonishment. Al-Shāfiʿī used to say: Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh al-Muzanī is one of the pillars of falsehood.” Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports Aḥmad’s judgment that Kathīr is *munkar al-ḥadīth* and “nothing,” Yaḥyā b. Maʿīn’s judgment that he is weak, Abū Zurʿa’s judgment that he is frail in hadith and not strong, and Abū Ḥātim’s judgment that he is not firm. Ibn Ḥajar’s short summary in the *Taqrīb* is also cautious: Kathīr is weak, and those who accused him of lying went too far. That last moderation matters, but it still leaves the report unusable as proof of a prophecy. Even under the softer verdict, the chain is weak; under the harsher verdicts, the exact father-from-grandfather pattern is treated as fabricated material. The result is simple: the tasbih/takbir family is not an independent witness that strengthens the famous report. It is a separate weak family built on a transmitter whose family-copy reports were attacked by the hadith critics themselves. The “Constantinople before Rome” report A third report asks which city will be conquered first: Constantinople or Rome. The Prophet is made to answer: the city of Heraclius first. This report is different from the Kathīr family and should not be dismissed in the same way. بَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ حَوْلَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ نَكْتُبُ، إِذْ سُئِلَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: أَيُّ الْمَدِينَتَيْنِ تُفْتَحُ أَوَّلًا، قُسْطَنْطِينِيَّةُ أَوْ رُومِيَّةُ؟ فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ: لَا، بَلْ مَدِينَةُ هِرَقْلَ أَوَّلًا. “While we were around the Messenger of God writing, the Messenger of God was asked: ‘Which of the two cities will be conquered first, Constantinople or Rome?’ The Prophet said: ‘No, rather the city of Heraclius first.’” The chain runs through Abū Qabīl, whose name is Ḥuyayy b. Hāniʾ al-Maʿāfirī al-Miṣrī, from ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr. This is not Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh. The rijāl profile is also not the same. Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports Aḥmad, Ibn Maʿīn, Abū Zurʿa, and others calling Abū Qabīl reliable or acceptable. Ibn Ḥajar summarizes him as truthful but prone to error. That means the critique has to be more careful. The issue is not that Abū Qabīl is a notorious liar. The issue is that the report remains a single Egyptian apocalyptic stream with a distinctive literary frame: ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr produces a written book or scroll, and from it comes a conquest ordering between Constantinople and Rome. This is not an independent confirmation of the “excellent commander” report. It is a different tradition family with a different function. This report should therefore be separated from the popular Ottoman apologetic claim. It might show that some early transmitters expected Constantinople to fall before Rome. It does not show that the famous “excellent commander” report was independently known through multiple early channels. It also leaves an obvious problem: Rome itself has not been conquered by a Muslim army in the way the broader eschatological imagination expects. Collateral apocalyptic reports do not rescue the famous report The wider corpus contains additional Constantinople material: reports connecting the first sea army, the City of Caesar, the great battle, the fall of Constantinople, and the Dajjāl; reports about the prosperity or ruin of Jerusalem and Medina; and reports in which the Romans, the city of Heraclius, or the Byzantine frontier appear in end-times sequences. These are valuable for mapping Muslim apocalyptic expectations, but they should not be conflated with the “excellent commander” report. A hadith about the *malḥama*, Constantinople, and the Dajjāl is not the same as the Maslama-linked report praising the commander and army. A report through Abū Qabīl is not a second chain for Kathīr’s tasbih/takbir wording. A mawqūf or apocalyptic report from Abū Hurayra or Ibn Masʿūd does not repair name instability in the Bishr stem. Variant control matters because without it every mention of Constantinople gets counted as support for every other mention of Constantinople. A prophecy dossier should not count “same city” as “same report.” The first task is to separate tradition families. Only after the families are separated can we ask which ones are independently transmitted, which ones share common links, which ones are weak by rijāl standards, and which ones look tied to concrete political use. What the variants actually prove The variant map gives us three different levels of evidence. Family Main wording Transmission profile Historical assessment Family A “Constantinople will be conquered. Excellent commander; excellent army.” Narrow stem through Zayd b. al-Ḥubāb → al-Walīd b. al-Mughīra → unstable son of Bishr → Bishr. Most important family, but historically suspicious because of the Maslama frame and the weakly spread early stem. Family B First sea army; first army to the City of Caesar forgiven. Umm Ḥarām stream through Syrian-Egyptian transmitters such as Thawr b. Yazīd, Khālid b. Maʿdān, and ʿAmr b. al-Aswad. Not a chain for the excellent-commander report, but strong contextual evidence that Byzantine campaign-merit reports circulated in the early Umayyad frontier setting. Family C Banū al-Aṣfar; Constantinople conquered by tasbīḥ and takbīr. Kathīr b. ʿAbd Allāh → his father → his grandfather. Very weak. The exact family-copy channel is heavily condemned in the rijāl literature. Family D Constantinople or Rome first? “The city of Heraclius first.” Egyptian stream through Abū Qabīl → ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr. Not the same problem as Kathīr, but also not independent support for Family A. It belongs to a different apocalyptic question. This is why the popular claim is overstated. The evidence does not say: several independent prophetic reports precisely predicted Mehmed II. It says: several later books preserve Constantinople traditions, but the famous praise report is tied to Maslama’s failed siege, the City of Caesar material belongs to a separate early Byzantine campaign-merit stream, the miracle-conquest report is built on a condemned transmitter, and the Rome-ordering report belongs to a separate Egyptian apocalyptic stream. Verdict The Constantinople conquest reports are better explained as layered conquest-era and apocalyptic traditions than as a clean, independently preserved prediction of the Ottoman conquest in 1453. The famous “excellent commander” report is the only one that directly gives the apologetic slogan, but its recoverable form points back to Maslama’s Umayyad siege environment. The newly checked historical and hadith material makes that setting harder to dismiss: Constantinople was already a Syrian-Umayyad military memory, and praise reports about sea campaigns and Caesar’s city were already being transmitted in that world. Later fulfillment claims depend on rereading that earlier siege tradition after the city finally fell centuries later. The strongest version of the argument is not that every Constantinople report is equally worthless. That would be careless. The stronger argument is that the reports must be separated. Once separated, the famous apologetic use of the hadith loses most of its force. The Ottoman conquest may have been historically significant, but this hadith dossier does not give us a clean prophecy fulfilled by Mehmed II. It gives us a politically useful report, a weak miracle-conquest family, and a separate apocalyptic ordering tradition. title: The Dajjāl and the Antichrist: How Christian apocalyptic lore entered the hadith corpus
description: A matn comparison between the Islamic Dajjāl reports and Christian Antichrist apocalyptic traditions, with special attention to Pseudo-John, false miracles, marked faces, drought, altered time, and Jesus’ final defeat of the deceiver.

It never gives him an eye defect, a written mark between his eyes, a paradise and hell, a power over rain and vegetation, a forty-day career with altered days, or a final defeat by Jesus at Ludd. All of that comes from hadith. That does not automatically prove the reports are fabricated. But it tells us where the question begins. The full Dajjāl profile is not Qur’anic. It is a hadith-era apocalyptic portrait, and when we place that portrait next to Christian Antichrist traditions, the overlap is too strong to ignore. The Dajjāl reports do not look like Qur’anic prophecy. They look like Christian Antichrist folklore translated into Islamic hadith form. This article is not arguing that Muslim transmitters copied one surviving Pseudo-John manuscript word for word. That would be too strong, and it would create a dating problem. The safer argument is that the Dajjāl material belongs to the same apocalyptic world as Christian Antichrist lore. The Apocalypse of Pseudo-John, or more precisely the Pseudo-Johannine Antichrist tradition, gives us a useful comparison point because it preserves several of the same motifs: the monstrous deceiver, abnormal eyes, a face inscription, false wonders, drought, compressed time, and final exposure. That is the point. The Dajjāl does not appear in the Qur’an. He appears in hadith looking like the Antichrist of late antique and medieval Christian imagination. ## The Dajjāl in Hadith The hadith corpus gives the Dajjāl a detailed profile. He is not merely a generic deceiver. He has a marked body, a visible sign of disbelief, supernatural powers of deception, and a fixed role in the end-times drama. رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا جَعْدًا قَطِطًا أَعْوَرَ الْعَيْنِ الْيُمْنَى كَأَنَّهَا عِنَبَةٌ طَافِيَةٌ، قُلْتُ: مَنْ هَذَا؟ قَالُوا: هَذَا الدَّجَّالُ “I saw a man with very curly hair, blind in the right eye, as if his eye were a protruding grape. I said, ‘Who is this?’ They said, ‘This is the Dajjāl.’” In another version, the Dajjāl is marked between the eyes. The mark tells the believer what he is. إِنَّهُ مَكْتُوبٌ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ كَافِرٌ يَقْرَؤُهُ كُلُّ مُؤْمِنٍ “Written between his eyes is ‘disbeliever,’ and every believer will read it.” He also comes with deceptive opposites. What he calls paradise is hell, and what he calls hell is paradise. What people think is water is fire, and what they think is fire is cool water. إِنَّ مَعَهُ جَنَّةً وَنَارًا، فَنَارُهُ جَنَّةٌ، وَجَنَّتُهُ نَارٌ “He will have with him a paradise and a fire. His fire is paradise, and his paradise is fire.” The long al-Nawwās b. Samʿān report gives the Dajjāl a strange time structure. One day is like a year, another like a month, another like a week, and the rest are like normal days. يَوْمٌ كَسَنَةٍ، وَيَوْمٌ كَشَهْرٍ، وَيَوْمٌ كَجُمُعَةٍ، وَسَائِرُ أَيَّامِهِ كَأَيَّامِكُمْ “A day like a year, a day like a month, a day like a week, and the rest of his days like your days.” The same general complex gives him false signs over nature and life. He can command the sky and the earth, create the appearance of resurrection, and deceive people through what looks like divine power. فَيَأْمُرُ السَّمَاءَ فَتُمْطِرُ، وَالْأَرْضَ فَتُنْبِتُ “He will command the sky and it will rain, and the earth and it will bring forth vegetation.” If we were dealing with one vague similarity, that would not mean much. But this is a full profile: abnormal body, facial inscription, false miracles, command over nature, distorted time, and defeat in an end-times confrontation. That profile has a close cousin in Christian Antichrist lore. ## What Pseudo-John Says The online text commonly called the Apocalypse of Pseudo-John gives a dramatic description of Antichrist. The text says that John asks what Antichrist is like, and the answer describes a monstrous figure. His face is dusky. His hair is sharp like darts. His eyebrows are like a wild beast’s. One eye is like the morning star, the other like a lion’s. His mouth, teeth, fingers, and feet are grotesquely exaggerated. Most important for our comparison, the text says that on his face is an inscription: “Antichrist.” > “The appearance of his face is dusky; the hairs of his head are sharp, like darts; his eyebrows like a wild beast’s; his right eye like the star which rises in the morning, and the other like a lion’s ... and on his face an inscription, Antichrist.” The same text says that Antichrist makes false displays. It says the heaven becomes brazen so that it gives no moisture, the clouds are hidden so that they bring no moisture, and the wind is stopped. It also says the time of Antichrist is three years, but then compresses the years into months, weeks, days, hours, and seconds. > “Three years shall those times be; and I will make the three years like three months, and the three months like three weeks, and the three weeks like three days, and the three days like three hours, and the three hours like three seconds.” Those are not minor parallels. They are the same kind of apocalyptic imagination. The deceiver has an abnormal body. His identity is written on him. He performs false wonders. Nature collapses around his career. Time itself becomes strange. The dating must be handled carefully. The surviving Pseudo-John / Latin Revelation of John about Antichrist material should not be presented as a certain second- or third-century source for the hadith. The safer claim is that it preserves a Christian Antichrist motif-complex that overlaps strongly with the Dajjāl material. ## The Motif Genealogy The Dajjāl does not emerge in a vacuum. Christian Antichrist lore itself grew from older biblical roots. Daniel gives beastly kingdoms and anti-divine rulers. Revelation gives beasts, false signs, persecution, and a limited period of authority. Later Christian apocalyptic imagination then expands these ideas into a full Antichrist portrait. Pseudo-John is one witness to that expanded tradition. The hadith Dajjāl profile fits this larger stream much better than it fits the Qur’an. This diagram is deliberately not a claim of direct copying from one manuscript. It is a map of motif transmission. Apocalyptic motifs do not always move like a book being copied line by line. They move through sermons, debates, oral storytelling, monastic lore, sectarian polemics, translations, local Christian communities, and converts. That is exactly the kind of environment in which the Dajjāl material could have formed. ## The Strongest Parallels The comparison becomes clearer when the motifs are placed side by side. Motif Dajjāl Hadith Pseudo-John / Antichrist Lore Abnormal eye The Dajjāl is one-eyed, with one eye like a protruding grape. Antichrist has strange asymmetrical eyes, one like the morning star and the other like a lion’s. Written mark “Disbeliever” or the letters k-f-r are written between his eyes. “Antichrist” is inscribed on his face. False miracles He presents paradise and hell, water and fire, and deceptive resurrection-like signs. He makes false displays and deceives through apparent signs. Drought / nature Dajjāl-related reports describe rain withheld, vegetation withheld, and nature responding to him. The heaven becomes brazen, clouds bring no moisture, and wind is stopped. Altered time One day is like a year, one like a month, one like a week, then ordinary days. Three years become three months, then weeks, days, hours, and seconds. Final exposure Jesus descends and destroys the Dajjāl. Enoch and Elijah expose Antichrist, and the final judgment defeats evil. This is not a perfect one-to-one correspondence, and it does not need to be. The point is not that every word matches. The point is that the same profile exists: a marked end-times deceiver with a monstrous body, supernatural deception, control over nature, altered time, and final defeat by divine intervention. ## The Facial Mark The facial mark is one of the strongest parallels because it is so specific. In the hadith, the Dajjāl does not merely behave like a disbeliever. His identity is written between his eyes. In Pseudo-John, Antichrist does not merely behave like Antichrist. His identity is written on his face. That is a distinctive literary device. The deceiver is dangerous, but God gives the faithful a sign by which he can be recognized. His identity is hidden from the deceived but legible to the elect. مَكْتُوبٌ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ كَافِرٌ “Written between his eyes is: disbeliever.” This is the kind of motif that travels easily. A preacher can tell it. A storyteller can adapt it. One community can make the mark say “Antichrist,” another can make it say “disbeliever.” The function remains the same: the false savior carries his condemnation on his face. ## The Eye Motif The eye motif is also strong, but it should be framed carefully. Pseudo-John does not simply say Antichrist is one-eyed in the same way the hadith says the Dajjāl is one-eyed. It gives him strange, monstrous, asymmetrical eyes. Hadith often describes the Dajjāl as one-eyed, with one eye defective or protruding. The exact wording differs, but the visual logic overlaps. The deceiver is bodily marked. His eye is not normal. His appearance gives away his inner corruption. This matters because apocalyptic literature often makes moral corruption visible in the body. The villain is not only evil. He is physically wrong. The Dajjāl reports and the Pseudo-John Antichrist portrait both use that same symbolic grammar. ## False Wonders and Deceptive Power The Dajjāl’s signs are deceptive inversions. What looks like paradise is hell. What looks like water is fire. He appears to bring life, food, and rain, but the entire performance is a test. The point is not simply that he has power. The point is that his power is counterfeit divine authority. Pseudo-John uses the same kind of language. Antichrist makes false displays. Related Christian Antichrist traditions often give him false miracles and healing claims. The figure is not just a military tyrant. He is a religious deceiver. That is exactly what the Dajjāl becomes in hadith: not a normal king, but a counterfeit lord. ## Drought and Famine The drought parallel is especially important because it is not merely visual. It is environmental. In the Dajjāl material, the time around the Dajjāl is linked with famine and withheld rain. In some reports, he commands the sky and earth. In others, there are years of progressive drought before him. Pseudo-John says the heaven becomes brazen, the clouds are hidden so they do not bring moisture, and the wind is stopped. That is the same apocalyptic atmosphere. Creation itself becomes part of the trial. The idea is simple: when Antichrist or Dajjāl appears, the world becomes unstable. Rain, crops, time, and life all become signs in the deception. ## Altered Time The altered-time motif is another major overlap. In Muslim’s long Dajjāl report, the Companions ask how long the Dajjāl will remain. The answer says forty days, but one day is like a year, another like a month, another like a week, and the rest are like ordinary days. Pseudo-John gives a different structure but the same imaginative mechanism. The time of Antichrist is three years, then the years become months, the months become weeks, the weeks become days, the days become hours, and the hours become seconds. These are not identical chronologies. But they share the same apocalyptic intuition: at the end of time, time itself breaks. The career of the deceiver is measured in distorted units. That is too specific to dismiss as a generic coincidence. ## The Dating Problem The dating of Pseudo-John has to be handled carefully. It is tempting to treat the text as a direct source for the Dajjāl reports and then argue that Muslim transmitters simply copied it. But that would be too blunt. The surviving Pseudo-John or Latin Revelation of John about Antichrist material should not be treated as a securely early source that directly predates the hadith corpus in the exact form available to us today. Its extant manuscript and publication history belong to a later Christian apocryphal tradition, and that means direct dependence on the surviving text itself would be difficult to prove. That does not weaken the comparison. It actually makes the argument more precise. Christian Antichrist lore was not born in one book. It developed through Daniel, Revelation, the “man of lawlessness” tradition, sermons, monastic storytelling, apocalyptic speculation, oral lore, and local Christian communities across the Near East. Pseudo-John is useful because it preserves a concentrated form of motifs that were already part of that wider Antichrist imagination: the marked deceiver, monstrous body, abnormal eyes, false wonders, drought, distorted time, and final exposure. So the question is not whether a Muslim transmitter sat with the exact Pseudo-John text we now possess and copied it line by line. That is not necessary. The better question is why the hadith Dajjāl looks like he belongs to the same Antichrist world. The Qur’an does not name him. It does not describe his eye. It does not place k-f-r between his eyes. It does not give him paradise and hell, water and fire, altered days, or a detailed career before Jesus kills him. Those features appear in hadith, and they overlap strongly with Christian apocalyptic motifs. The safest conclusion is therefore not direct copying from the extant Pseudo-John text. The safer conclusion is shared apocalyptic transmission. The Dajjāl reports absorbed the same Christian Antichrist motif-complex that Pseudo-John also preserves. The argument is not “the hadith copied the extant Pseudo-John text.” The stronger argument is that the Dajjāl hadiths absorbed the same Christian Antichrist motif-complex that Pseudo-John also preserves. ## The Qur’anic Silence Matters If the Qur’an had given a detailed Dajjāl profile, the comparison with Christian Antichrist lore would be less important. But the Qur’an does not. The Dajjāl’s body, inscription, false paradise and hell, altered days, and defeat by Jesus all come from hadith. This is why the Dajjāl reports are vulnerable. They are not simply explaining a Qur’anic figure. They are importing a full apocalyptic character into Islam through hadith. The result is a figure that feels central to popular Islamic eschatology but has no Qur’anic name, no Qur’anic biography, and no Qur’anic doctrine behind him. ## More Parallels Beyond Pseudo-John Pseudo-John is useful because the parallels are concentrated in one text. But the broader background is even larger. Daniel gives the older pattern of arrogant anti-divine rulers and beastly kingdoms. Revelation gives the beast, false worship, limited authority, and war against the saints. The New Testament language of Antichrist and the man of lawlessness gives Christian communities a vocabulary for a final deceiver. Later apocalyptic traditions expand that figure into a monstrous religious impostor who performs wonders, persecutes believers, manipulates nature, and is finally exposed or destroyed by divine intervention. The Dajjāl reports look like they entered this stream and were Islamized. The Christian Antichrist becomes the Muslim Dajjāl. The final victory becomes the descent of Jesus in Muslim eschatology. The mark of Antichrist becomes k-f-r between the eyes. The false wonders become paradise and hell, water and fire, rain and vegetation. The apocalyptic time distortion becomes the Dajjāl’s abnormal days. This is not the Qur’an explaining itself. This is apocalyptic folklore being absorbed into hadith. ## What About Independent Islamic Development? A defender could argue that the similarities are natural because every end-times deceiver will share the same features: deception, false miracles, and defeat by God. Some overlap is indeed expected. A final deceiver will deceive. An apocalyptic villain will be defeated. Those generic features alone would not prove influence. But the case here is not built on generic features alone. It is built on a cluster: bodily abnormality, abnormal eyes, a written facial mark, false wonders, drought, altered time, and final defeat by Jesus or divine agents. When several unusual features gather around the same type of figure, the explanation of independent coincidence becomes weaker. The strongest explanation is not direct copying from one text. It is shared apocalyptic tradition. The Dajjāl reports are best explained as Islamic adaptations of a wider Antichrist folklore complex, not as independent Qur’anic doctrine and not necessarily as direct copying from the extant Pseudo-John text. ## What Would Change the Analysis? The analysis would change if the Qur’an named the Dajjāl and gave the same profile. It would also change if early, demonstrably independent Muslim material preserved the Dajjāl complex before contact with Christian apocalyptic communities. It would change further if the strongest motifs were not present in Christian Antichrist lore. But that is not what we have. The Qur’an is silent. The hadith literature supplies the full profile. Christian apocalyptic lore already contains the same kind of marked deceiver, monstrous body, false signs, drought, distorted time, and final defeat. Pseudo-John preserves many of these motifs in one place, even if its extant form is not a simple source text for hadith. So the conclusion should be careful but firm. The Dajjāl profile is best explained as hadith-era apocalyptic borrowing from the wider Antichrist tradition, not as an independent Qur’anic doctrine and not as proven word-for-word copying from one surviving Christian text. ## Final Verdict The Dajjāl is not a Qur’anic figure. He is a hadith figure, and his profile looks overwhelmingly like Christian Antichrist folklore in Islamic dress. The parallels with Pseudo-John and related apocalyptic traditions are too specific to dismiss: abnormal eyes, facial inscription, false wonders, drought, altered time, and final defeat. The dating problem means we should not claim that Muslim transmitters directly copied the surviving Pseudo-John text. That is unnecessary anyway. The stronger argument is that the Dajjāl reports belong to the same apocalyptic environment as Christian Antichrist lore. They preserve a shared motif-complex that moved across religious boundaries and was eventually naturalized inside hadith literature. That is why the Dajjāl matters. He shows how a figure absent from the Qur’an can become central in later religious imagination. He shows how hadith can import whole mythic biographies from surrounding traditions. And he shows why matn criticism is necessary. A chain may tell us who transmitted a report, but the text tells us what world the report came from. The Dajjāl came from the world of Antichrist. ## Appendix: Compact Motif Table | Motif | Dajjāl reports | Pseudo-John / Christian Antichrist tradition | Strength | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | | Qur’anic basis | Not named in the Qur’an | Antichrist is developed from biblical and post-biblical Christian apocalyptic interpretation | Background | | Abnormal eye | One-eyed, defective eye, protruding grape imagery | Strange/asymmetrical eyes, one like morning star, another like lion’s | Strong motif parallel | | Written mark | k-f-r / disbeliever written between his eyes | “Antichrist” inscribed on his face | Very strong | | False wonders | Paradise/hell inversion, water/fire inversion, apparent resurrection-like signs | False displays, deceptive signs, later false miracles | Strong | | Control over nature | Rain and vegetation tied to his command; famine/drought motifs | Heaven gives no moisture, clouds are hidden, wind stopped | Strong | | Altered time | Day like year, day like month, day like week | Three years compressed into months, weeks, days, hours, seconds | Strong motif parallel | | Final defeat | Jesus descends and kills the Dajjāl | Antichrist exposed by Enoch/Elias and defeated in final judgment | Medium-strong | | Religious function | Ultimate test for believers | Ultimate deceiver before judgment | Strong | ## Appendix: Key Hadith References Used | Source | Reference | Motif | | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī | 6999 | Dajjāl’s appearance, curly hair, defective eye | | Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī | 7130 | Water/fire inversion | | Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim | 166c | Written mark between his eyes | | Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim | 2934a | Paradise and hell inversion | | Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim | 2937a | Long Dajjāl report, altered time, Jesus’ descent | | Sunan Ibn Mājah | 4075 | Dajjāl and natural signs / end-times complex | | Sunan Ibn Mājah | 4077 | Deceptive resurrection-like sign through devils | | al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaghīr / later compilations | no. 7875 in common citation | Three-year drought motif before Dajjāl | ## Bibliography al-Bukhārī, Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl. *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī*. It never gives him an eye defect, a written mark between his eyes, a paradise and hell, a power over rain and vegetation, a forty-day career with altered days, or a final defeat by Jesus at Ludd. All of that comes from hadith. That does not automatically prove the reports are fabricated. But it tells us where the question begins. The full Dajjāl profile is not Qur’anic. It is a hadith-era apocalyptic portrait, and when we place that portrait next to Christian Antichrist traditions, the overlap is too strong to ignore. The Dajjāl reports do not look like Qur’anic prophecy. They look like Christian Antichrist folklore translated into Islamic hadith form. This article is not arguing that Muslim transmitters copied one surviving Pseudo-John manuscript word for word. That would be too strong, and it would create a dating problem. The safer argument is that the Dajjāl material belongs to the same apocalyptic world as Christian Antichrist lore. The Apocalypse of Pseudo-John, or more precisely the Pseudo-Johannine Antichrist tradition, gives us a useful comparison point because it preserves several of the same motifs: the monstrous deceiver, abnormal eyes, a face inscription, false wonders, drought, compressed time, and final exposure. That is the point. The Dajjāl does not appear in the Qur’an. He appears in hadith looking like the Antichrist of late antique and medieval Christian imagination. The Dajjāl in Hadith The hadith corpus gives the Dajjāl a detailed profile. He is not merely a generic deceiver. He has a marked body, a visible sign of disbelief, supernatural powers of deception, and a fixed role in the end-times drama. رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا جَعْدًا قَطِطًا أَعْوَرَ الْعَيْنِ الْيُمْنَى كَأَنَّهَا عِنَبَةٌ طَافِيَةٌ، قُلْتُ: مَنْ هَذَا؟ قَالُوا: هَذَا الدَّجَّالُ “I saw a man with very curly hair, blind in the right eye, as if his eye were a protruding grape. I said, ‘Who is this?’ They said, ‘This is the Dajjāl.’” In another version, the Dajjāl is marked between the eyes. The mark tells the believer what he is. إِنَّهُ مَكْتُوبٌ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ كَافِرٌ يَقْرَؤُهُ كُلُّ مُؤْمِنٍ “Written between his eyes is ‘disbeliever,’ and every believer will read it.” He also comes with deceptive opposites. What he calls paradise is hell, and what he calls hell is paradise. What people think is water is fire, and what they think is fire is cool water. إِنَّ مَعَهُ جَنَّةً وَنَارًا، فَنَارُهُ جَنَّةٌ، وَجَنَّتُهُ نَارٌ “He will have with him a paradise and a fire. His fire is paradise, and his paradise is fire.” The long al-Nawwās b. Samʿān report gives the Dajjāl a strange time structure. One day is like a year, another like a month, another like a week, and the rest are like normal days. يَوْمٌ كَسَنَةٍ، وَيَوْمٌ كَشَهْرٍ، وَيَوْمٌ كَجُمُعَةٍ، وَسَائِرُ أَيَّامِهِ كَأَيَّامِكُمْ “A day like a year, a day like a month, a day like a week, and the rest of his days like your days.” The same general complex gives him false signs over nature and life. He can command the sky and the earth, create the appearance of resurrection, and deceive people through what looks like divine power. فَيَأْمُرُ السَّمَاءَ فَتُمْطِرُ، وَالْأَرْضَ فَتُنْبِتُ “He will command the sky and it will rain, and the earth and it will bring forth vegetation.” If we were dealing with one vague similarity, that would not mean much. But this is a full profile: abnormal body, facial inscription, false miracles, command over nature, distorted time, and defeat in an end-times confrontation. That profile has a close cousin in Christian Antichrist lore. What Pseudo-John Says The online text commonly called the Apocalypse of Pseudo-John gives a dramatic description of Antichrist. The text says that John asks what Antichrist is like, and the answer describes a monstrous figure. His face is dusky. His hair is sharp like darts. His eyebrows are like a wild beast’s. One eye is like the morning star, the other like a lion’s. His mouth, teeth, fingers, and feet are grotesquely exaggerated. Most important for our comparison, the text says that on his face is an inscription: “Antichrist.” > “The appearance of his face is dusky; the hairs of his head are sharp, like darts; his eyebrows like a wild beast’s; his right eye like the star which rises in the morning, and the other like a lion’s ... and on his face an inscription, Antichrist.” The same text says that Antichrist makes false displays. It says the heaven becomes brazen so that it gives no moisture, the clouds are hidden so that they bring no moisture, and the wind is stopped. It also says the time of Antichrist is three years, but then compresses the years into months, weeks, days, hours, and seconds. > “Three years shall those times be; and I will make the three years like three months, and the three months like three weeks, and the three weeks like three days, and the three days like three hours, and the three hours like three seconds.” Those are not minor parallels. They are the same kind of apocalyptic imagination. The deceiver has an abnormal body. His identity is written on him. He performs false wonders. Nature collapses around his career. Time itself becomes strange. The dating must be handled carefully. The surviving Pseudo-John / Latin Revelation of John about Antichrist material should not be presented as a certain second- or third-century source for the hadith. The safer claim is that it preserves a Christian Antichrist motif-complex that overlaps strongly with the Dajjāl material. The Motif Genealogy The Dajjāl does not emerge in a vacuum. Christian Antichrist lore itself grew from older biblical roots. Daniel gives beastly kingdoms and anti-divine rulers. Revelation gives beasts, false signs, persecution, and a limited period of authority. Later Christian apocalyptic imagination then expands these ideas into a full Antichrist portrait. Pseudo-John is one witness to that expanded tradition. The hadith Dajjāl profile fits this larger stream much better than it fits the Qur’an. This diagram is deliberately not a claim of direct copying from one manuscript. It is a map of motif transmission. Apocalyptic motifs do not always move like a book being copied line by line. They move through sermons, debates, oral storytelling, monastic lore, sectarian polemics, translations, local Christian communities, and converts. That is exactly the kind of environment in which the Dajjāl material could have formed. The Strongest Parallels The comparison becomes clearer when the motifs are placed side by side. Motif Dajjāl Hadith Pseudo-John / Antichrist Lore Abnormal eye The Dajjāl is one-eyed, with one eye like a protruding grape. Antichrist has strange asymmetrical eyes, one like the morning star and the other like a lion’s. Written mark “Disbeliever” or the letters k-f-r are written between his eyes. “Antichrist” is inscribed on his face. False miracles He presents paradise and hell, water and fire, and deceptive resurrection-like signs. He makes false displays and deceives through apparent signs. Drought / nature Dajjāl-related reports describe rain withheld, vegetation withheld, and nature responding to him. The heaven becomes brazen, clouds bring no moisture, and wind is stopped. Altered time One day is like a year, one like a month, one like a week, then ordinary days. Three years become three months, then weeks, days, hours, and seconds. Final exposure Jesus descends and destroys the Dajjāl. Enoch and Elijah expose Antichrist, and the final judgment defeats evil. This is not a perfect one-to-one correspondence, and it does not need to be. The point is not that every word matches. The point is that the same profile exists: a marked end-times deceiver with a monstrous body, supernatural deception, control over nature, altered time, and final defeat by divine intervention. The Facial Mark The facial mark is one of the strongest parallels because it is so specific. In the hadith, the Dajjāl does not merely behave like a disbeliever. His identity is written between his eyes. In Pseudo-John, Antichrist does not merely behave like Antichrist. His identity is written on his face. That is a distinctive literary device. The deceiver is dangerous, but God gives the faithful a sign by which he can be recognized. His identity is hidden from the deceived but legible to the elect. مَكْتُوبٌ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ كَافِرٌ “Written between his eyes is: disbeliever.” This is the kind of motif that travels easily. A preacher can tell it. A storyteller can adapt it. One community can make the mark say “Antichrist,” another can make it say “disbeliever.” The function remains the same: the false savior carries his condemnation on his face. The Eye Motif The eye motif is also strong, but it should be framed carefully. Pseudo-John does not simply say Antichrist is one-eyed in the same way the hadith says the Dajjāl is one-eyed. It gives him strange, monstrous, asymmetrical eyes. Hadith often describes the Dajjāl as one-eyed, with one eye defective or protruding. The exact wording differs, but the visual logic overlaps. The deceiver is bodily marked. His eye is not normal. His appearance gives away his inner corruption. This matters because apocalyptic literature often makes moral corruption visible in the body. The villain is not only evil. He is physically wrong. The Dajjāl reports and the Pseudo-John Antichrist portrait both use that same symbolic grammar. False Wonders and Deceptive Power The Dajjāl’s signs are deceptive inversions. What looks like paradise is hell. What looks like water is fire. He appears to bring life, food, and rain, but the entire performance is a test. The point is not simply that he has power. The point is that his power is counterfeit divine authority. Pseudo-John uses the same kind of language. Antichrist makes false displays. Related Christian Antichrist traditions often give him false miracles and healing claims. The figure is not just a military tyrant. He is a religious deceiver. That is exactly what the Dajjāl becomes in hadith: not a normal king, but a counterfeit lord. Drought and Famine The drought parallel is especially important because it is not merely visual. It is environmental. In the Dajjāl material, the time around the Dajjāl is linked with famine and withheld rain. In some reports, he commands the sky and earth. In others, there are years of progressive drought before him. Pseudo-John says the heaven becomes brazen, the clouds are hidden so they do not bring moisture, and the wind is stopped. That is the same apocalyptic atmosphere. Creation itself becomes part of the trial. The idea is simple: when Antichrist or Dajjāl appears, the world becomes unstable. Rain, crops, time, and life all become signs in the deception. Altered Time The altered-time motif is another major overlap. In Muslim’s long Dajjāl report, the Companions ask how long the Dajjāl will remain. The answer says forty days, but one day is like a year, another like a month, another like a week, and the rest are like ordinary days. Pseudo-John gives a different structure but the same imaginative mechanism. The time of Antichrist is three years, then the years become months, the months become weeks, the weeks become days, the days become hours, and the hours become seconds. These are not identical chronologies. But they share the same apocalyptic intuition: at the end of time, time itself breaks. The career of the deceiver is measured in distorted units. That is too specific to dismiss as a generic coincidence. The Dating Problem The dating of Pseudo-John has to be handled carefully. It is tempting to treat the text as a direct source for the Dajjāl reports and then argue that Muslim transmitters simply copied it. But that would be too blunt. The surviving Pseudo-John or Latin Revelation of John about Antichrist material should not be treated as a securely early source that directly predates the hadith corpus in the exact form available to us today. Its extant manuscript and publication history belong to a later Christian apocryphal tradition, and that means direct dependence on the surviving text itself would be difficult to prove. That does not weaken the comparison. It actually makes the argument more precise. Christian Antichrist lore was not born in one book. It developed through Daniel, Revelation, the “man of lawlessness” tradition, sermons, monastic storytelling, apocalyptic speculation, oral lore, and local Christian communities across the Near East. Pseudo-John is useful because it preserves a concentrated form of motifs that were already part of that wider Antichrist imagination: the marked deceiver, monstrous body, abnormal eyes, false wonders, drought, distorted time, and final exposure. So the question is not whether a Muslim transmitter sat with the exact Pseudo-John text we now possess and copied it line by line. That is not necessary. The better question is why the hadith Dajjāl looks like he belongs to the same Antichrist world. The Qur’an does not name him. It does not describe his eye. It does not place k-f-r between his eyes. It does not give him paradise and hell, water and fire, altered days, or a detailed career before Jesus kills him. Those features appear in hadith, and they overlap strongly with Christian apocalyptic motifs. The safest conclusion is therefore not direct copying from the extant Pseudo-John text. The safer conclusion is shared apocalyptic transmission. The Dajjāl reports absorbed the same Christian Antichrist motif-complex that Pseudo-John also preserves. The argument is not “the hadith copied the extant Pseudo-John text.” The stronger argument is that the Dajjāl hadiths absorbed the same Christian Antichrist motif-complex that Pseudo-John also preserves. The Qur’anic Silence Matters If the Qur’an had given a detailed Dajjāl profile, the comparison with Christian Antichrist lore would be less important. But the Qur’an does not. The Dajjāl’s body, inscription, false paradise and hell, altered days, and defeat by Jesus all come from hadith. This is why the Dajjāl reports are vulnerable. They are not simply explaining a Qur’anic figure. They are importing a full apocalyptic character into Islam through hadith. The result is a figure that feels central to popular Islamic eschatology but has no Qur’anic name, no Qur’anic biography, and no Qur’anic doctrine behind him. More Parallels Beyond Pseudo-John Pseudo-John is useful because the parallels are concentrated in one text. But the broader background is even larger. Daniel gives the older pattern of arrogant anti-divine rulers and beastly kingdoms. Revelation gives the beast, false worship, limited authority, and war against the saints. The New Testament language of Antichrist and the man of lawlessness gives Christian communities a vocabulary for a final deceiver. Later apocalyptic traditions expand that figure into a monstrous religious impostor who performs wonders, persecutes believers, manipulates nature, and is finally exposed or destroyed by divine intervention. The Dajjāl reports look like they entered this stream and were Islamized. The Christian Antichrist becomes the Muslim Dajjāl. The final victory becomes the descent of Jesus in Muslim eschatology. The mark of Antichrist becomes k-f-r between the eyes. The false wonders become paradise and hell, water and fire, rain and vegetation. The apocalyptic time distortion becomes the Dajjāl’s abnormal days. This is not the Qur’an explaining itself. This is apocalyptic folklore being absorbed into hadith. What About Independent Islamic Development? A defender could argue that the similarities are natural because every end-times deceiver will share the same features: deception, false miracles, and defeat by God. Some overlap is indeed expected. A final deceiver will deceive. An apocalyptic villain will be defeated. Those generic features alone would not prove influence. But the case here is not built on generic features alone. It is built on a cluster: bodily abnormality, abnormal eyes, a written facial mark, false wonders, drought, altered time, and final defeat by Jesus or divine agents. When several unusual features gather around the same type of figure, the explanation of independent coincidence becomes weaker. The strongest explanation is not direct copying from one text. It is shared apocalyptic tradition. The Dajjāl reports are best explained as Islamic adaptations of a wider Antichrist folklore complex, not as independent Qur’anic doctrine and not necessarily as direct copying from the extant Pseudo-John text. What Would Change the Analysis? The analysis would change if the Qur’an named the Dajjāl and gave the same profile. It would also change if early, demonstrably independent Muslim material preserved the Dajjāl complex before contact with Christian apocalyptic communities. It would change further if the strongest motifs were not present in Christian Antichrist lore. But that is not what we have. The Qur’an is silent. The hadith literature supplies the full profile. Christian apocalyptic lore already contains the same kind of marked deceiver, monstrous body, false signs, drought, distorted time, and final defeat. Pseudo-John preserves many of these motifs in one place, even if its extant form is not a simple source text for hadith. So the conclusion should be careful but firm. The Dajjāl profile is best explained as hadith-era apocalyptic borrowing from the wider Antichrist tradition, not as an independent Qur’anic doctrine and not as proven word-for-word copying from one surviving Christian text. Final Verdict The Dajjāl is not a Qur’anic figure. He is a hadith figure, and his profile looks overwhelmingly like Christian Antichrist folklore in Islamic dress. The parallels with Pseudo-John and related apocalyptic traditions are too specific to dismiss: abnormal eyes, facial inscription, false wonders, drought, altered time, and final defeat. The dating problem means we should not claim that Muslim transmitters directly copied the surviving Pseudo-John text. That is unnecessary anyway. The stronger argument is that the Dajjāl reports belong to the same apocalyptic environment as Christian Antichrist lore. They preserve a shared motif-complex that moved across religious boundaries and was eventually naturalized inside hadith literature. That is why the Dajjāl matters. He shows how a figure absent from the Qur’an can become central in later religious imagination. He shows how hadith can import whole mythic biographies from surrounding traditions. And he shows why matn criticism is necessary. A chain may tell us who transmitted a report, but the text tells us what world the report came from. The Dajjāl came from the world of Antichrist. Kurayb', labelPos: 'right' }, { id: 'alqama', x: 650, y: 290, label: 'Kaʿb b. ʿAlqama al-Tanūkhī', labelPos: 'right' }, { id: 'ibnlahia', x: 650, y: 210, label: 'Ibn Lahīʿa', sublabel: '"confused after his books burned"', labelPos: 'right' }, { id: 'nuaym', x: 650, y: 100, label: 'Nuʿaym / al-Ṭabarānī', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'right' } ]; { from: 'event', to: 'muawiyah', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'muawiyah', to: 'hudayj', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'hudayj', to: 'ghost1', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'ghost1', to: 'ishaq', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'ishaq', to: 'abuyala' }, { from: 'muawiyah', to: 'dhikala', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'dhikala', to: 'kurayb' }, { from: 'kurayb', to: 'alqama' }, { from: 'alqama', to: 'ibnlahia' }, { from: 'ibnlahia', to: 'nuaym' } ]; { y: 660, label: 'Event' }, { y: 560, label: 'Companion' }, { y: 260, label: 'Two independent, individually weak routes' }, { y: 100, label: 'Compilers' } ]; { x: 400, y: 500, text: 'No shared transmitter below Muʿāwiyah — real multiple attestation, but each route is weak on its own', kind: 'note', anchor: 'middle' } ]; The Sunni canon preserves roughly two dozen reports in which the Prophet warns of a people with small eyes, red faces, and faces "like hammered shields," wearing sandals of hair, who will one day fight the Arabs and tie their horses somewhere they should not be. Every modern reader of these reports reaches for the same referent: the Mongols. That reading is chronologically impossible — Bukhārī and Muslim had already canonized this material some five centuries before Chinggis Khan was born — and it also misses what the isnāds themselves are trying to tell us. This corpus is not one hadith. It is five, attributed to five different Companions, transmitted through five different bottlenecks, none of whom can be checked against each other. Read as isnad-cum-matn evidence rather than as a single undifferentiated "Turks hadith," each cluster resolves into a specific transmitter with a specific regional stake, reporting on (or reformulating) a specific, datable seventh- or eighth-century frontier war. This piece walks through all five. The apocalyptic Turks corpus is not a single tradition with multiple chains. It is five independent companion-attributions — Abū Hurayra, Buraydah, ʿAmr b. Thaghlab, Abū Bakr, and Muʿāwiyah — each collapsing at its own bottleneck, each bottleneck situated in a real war on the eastern or northern frontier between 650 and 750 CE. The physiognomic vocabulary is shared because it is a floating ethnographic formula, not because the five clusters share an origin.
