title: The Salafi Paradox
description: A source-based critique of the modern Salafi claim that posthumous tawassul and istighatha are major shirk, measured against classical Sunni devotional manuals and the authorities Salafis still rely on.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Theology · Sunni Tradition · Internal Critique The paradox is not disagreement. The paradox is takfir. Salafis can disagree with al-Nawawi, al-Subki, Ibn al-Jazari, al-Shawkani, or later Sunni manuals. Disagreement by itself is normal. The problem begins when the disagreement is turned into a doctrine of major shirk while those same scholars remain part of the inherited Sunni library. If asking the Prophet or the righteous dead for intercession, aid, or mediation is major shirk in the obvious foundations of religion, then the historical implications do not stop with ordinary shrine visitors. They reach jurists, hadith commentators, Quran reciters, devotional authors, and legal authorities whom Salafis still read, cite, and depend on. This article is not defending posthumous tawassul or istighatha from the Quran. The Quranic standard remains God alone. The point here is narrower: the modern Salafi accusation of major shirk does not sit comfortably with the actual Sunni tradition that Salafis claim to preserve. ## Terms Before the Argument The debate becomes confused when several different practices are forced under one word. Classical writers, modern Salafis, and ordinary Muslims do not always mean the same thing by tawassul and istighatha . Tawassul Asking God by a means This usually means asking God through the Prophet, a righteous person, a good deed, a rank, a blessing, or a living person’s supplication. Salafis often treat some forms as bidʿa, but Ibn Baz himself says asking God by the rank, blessing, or right of someone is a bidʿa, not shirk.[^1] Istishfaʿ Seeking intercession This can mean asking God to grant the Prophet’s intercession, or directly addressing the Prophet after death and asking him to intercede. Ibn Baz classifies the latter as major shirk.[^2] Istighatha Seeking aid The word can mean asking a living person for help in what he can do, asking God by means of a beloved servant, or calling upon a dead or absent figure for aid. Salafi polemics often treat the last category as the controlling meaning. The article is about the place where those categories collide. If a man says, “O Messenger of God, intercede for me with your Lord,” is he a sinner, an innovator, a mistaken jurist, or a polytheist? Modern Salafi answers often move quickly to the last category. The older Sunni record is not that tidy. ## The Salafi Ruling Ibn Baz states the modern Salafi position clearly. Asking the Prophet, or any other dead figure, for intercession is not merely impermissible. It is major shirk. فَالْحَاصِلُ: أَنَّ طَلَبَ الشَّفَاعَةِ مِنَ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ، أَوْ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ مِنَ الأَمْوَاتِ؛ أَمْرٌ لا يَجُوزُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى القَاعِدَةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ مِنَ الشِّرْكِ الأَكْبَرِ؛ لأَنَّهُ طَلَبٌ مِنَ المَيِّتِ شَيْئًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ. “In summary, requesting intercession from the Prophet ﷺ, or from anyone else among the dead, is not permissible. According to the legal principle, it is major shirk, because it is asking the dead for something they cannot do.” The same fatwa says there is no difference between asking this from the Prophet, from ʿAbd al-Qadir, from al-Badawi, from al-Husayn, or from anyone else. Ibn Baz includes requests for aid, intercession, victory, and relief among the actions of pre-Islamic polytheism.[^2] This is not a small claim. If the category is **major shirk**, then the issue is no longer a disputed devotional etiquette. It becomes a boundary of Islam itself. Ibn Baz also speaks strongly about ignorance in creed. He says that a Muslim living among Muslims, hearing the Quran and hadith, is not excused in the foundations of the religion, and he places calling upon grave-dwellers, asking them for healing, and seeking their aid among the greatest forms of shirk.[^3] 1 Posthumous request for intercession or aid is major shirk. → 2 Ignorance is not easily excused in obvious foundations of tawhid. → 3 Classical Sunni authorities who endorsed the practice become a theological problem. That is the paradox. It is not enough to say, “They were wrong.” Salafi rhetoric often says much more than that. ## Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab Was More Careful About Tawassul There is a point that should not be skipped. Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab himself distinguished tawassul from direct supplication to created beings. In a response about asking God through the righteous, he says the difference is very clear. He describes tawassul through the righteous as a matter of fiqh, says the correct view for him is that it is disliked, and then says there is no harsh condemnation of the one who does it because disputed ijtihad matters are not treated that way.[^4] فَكَوْنُ بَعْضٍ يُرَخِّصُ بِالتَّوَسُّلِ بِالصَّالِحِينَ، وَبَعْضُهُمْ يَخُصُّهُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ، وَأَكْثَرُ العُلَمَاءِ يَنْهَى عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَيَكْرَهُهُ، فَهَذِهِ المَسْأَلَةُ مِنْ مَسَائِلِ الفِقْهِ ... فَلا نُنْكِرُ عَلَى مَنْ فَعَلَهُ؛ وَلا إِنْكَارَ فِي مَسَائِلِ الاجْتِهَادِ. “Some permit tawassul through the righteous, some restrict it to the Prophet ﷺ, and most scholars forbid it and dislike it. This issue is among the issues of fiqh ... We do not condemn the one who does it, for there is no condemnation in matters of ijtihad.” He then contrasts that with a person who goes to the grave of ʿAbd al-Qadir or someone else and asks for relief from distress, rescue, and worldly needs. For him, those are not the same case.[^4] This matters because it exposes a later tightening. Some modern Salafi speech collapses the distinction between disliked tawassul, asking a dead person to pray, and worshipful supplication to other than God. Once everything is called major shirk, the inherited Sunni record becomes almost impossible to handle honestly. ## The Classical Sunni Record The strongest argument is not that every Sunni scholar had the same view. They did not. The stronger argument is that posthumous tawassul, istishfaʿ, and related devotional language are found inside major Sunni manuals, not only in marginal folk practice. Shafiʿi law al-Nawawi ثُمَّ يَرْجِعُ إِلَى مَوْقِفِهِ الأَوَّلِ قُبَالَةَ وَجْهِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ وَيَتَوَسَّلُ بِهِ فِي حَقِّ نَفْسِهِ وَيَسْتَشْفِعُ بِهِ إِلَى رَبِّهِ In the visitation section of al-Majmuʿ , al-Nawawi says the visitor returns to face the Messenger of God, seeks tawassul through him for himself, and seeks his intercession with his Lord.[^5] Anti-Ibn Taymiyya polemic Taqi al-Din al-Subki يَجُوزُ وَيَحْسُنُ التَّوَسُّلُ وَالاسْتِغَاثَةُ وَالتَّشَفُّعُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ إِلَى رَبِّهِ In Shifa al-Siqam , al-Subki treats tawassul, istighatha, and seeking intercession through the Prophet as known and commendable, then criticizes Ibn Taymiyya for denying it.[^6] Supplication manual Ibn al-Jazari / al-Shawkani وَيَتَوَسَّلُ إِلَى اللهِ سُبْحَانَهُ بِأَنْبِيَائِهِ وَالصَّالِحِينَ Ibn al-Jazari’s devotional manual lists tawassul through God’s prophets and righteous servants among the etiquette of supplication. Al-Shawkani comments on this line and supports it through the blind man report and the Companions’ rain-prayer through al-ʿAbbas.[^7] Historical reception Ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَنْسِبُهُ إِلَى الزَّنْدَقَةِ لِقَوْلِهِ إِنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ لا يُسْتَغَاثُ بِهِ Ibn Hajar records that some of Ibn Taymiyya’s opponents accused him of heresy for saying that the Prophet is not sought for aid. That does not make the accusation true, but it shows how abnormal the denial sounded to some of his contemporaries.[^8] The point is not that every citation above proves the same legal category. The point is that the devotional world which modern Salafism condemns was not sitting outside Sunni scholarship. It was written into law books, visitation manuals, supplication manuals, and polemical works by scholars who are still treated as part of the Sunni inheritance. ## The al-Nawawi Problem Al-Nawawi is not an obscure Sufi storyteller. He is one of the most used Sunni scholars in hadith, law, and devotional literature. His commentary on Muslim, his Riyad al-Salihin , and his forty-hadith collection remain everywhere. That is why his visitation passage matters. The visitor is not told merely to send peace upon the Prophet and leave. He is told to face the Prophet, seek tawassul through him, and seek his intercession with God. Al-Nawawi then preserves the famous al-ʿUtbi story under Quran 4:64, where a Bedouin comes to the Prophet’s grave and says he has come seeking forgiveness and seeking intercession through him.[^5] وَقَدْ جِئْتُكَ مُسْتَغْفِرًا مِنْ ذَنْبِي مُسْتَشْفِعًا بِكَ إِلَى رَبِّي “I have come to you seeking forgiveness for my sin, seeking intercession through you with my Lord.” A hadith critic can say the al-ʿUtbi story is not a proof-text with a sound isnad. That is fair. But this article is not using the story as proof that the practice is true. It is using al-Nawawi’s legal placement of the story as evidence of what a major Sunni authority considered acceptable devotional language. If Ibn Baz’s category is applied without qualification, al-Nawawi’s manual has a major problem. ## The al-Subki Problem Al-Subki’s statement is even more direct. He explicitly names tawassul, istighatha, and tashaffuʿ through the Prophet and says that their permissibility and goodness are known in the religious community. He then says no one denied it until Ibn Taymiyya.[^6] اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ وَيَحْسُنُ التَّوَسُّلُ وَالاسْتِغَاثَةُ وَالتَّشَفُّعُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ إِلَى رَبِّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى ... وَلَمْ يُنْكِرْ أَحَدٌ ذَلِكَ ... حَتَّى جَاءَ ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّةَ “Know that it is permissible and good to seek tawassul, istighatha, and intercession through the Prophet ﷺ with his Lord, Glorified and Exalted ... No one denied this ... until Ibn Taymiyya came.” One can argue that al-Subki overstated the historical consensus. That is possible. But even if the consensus claim is reduced, the paradox remains. A major Shafiʿi authority publicly treated Ibn Taymiyya’s denial as a novelty, while modern Salafi discourse often treats the opposite practice as obvious major shirk. That is a serious gap in historical memory. ## The Ibn al-Jazari and al-Shawkani Problem Ibn al-Jazari is central to Quranic recitation. Sunni and Salafi circles do not discard him. Yet the devotional manual associated with him includes tawassul through the prophets and righteous among the etiquette of supplication. Al-Shawkani’s commentary is important because he was not simply repeating Shafiʿi grave-visit literature. He explains the line by citing the blind man report for tawassul through the Prophet and the rain-prayer through al-ʿAbbas for tawassul through the righteous.[^7] Al-Shawkani is useful here because many modern reformist and Salafi-leaning readers respect him. His discussion does not prove every later shrine practice. It does show that tawassul through prophets and righteous figures could remain inside serious hadith-legal discussion without being treated as major shirk. ## The Three Escape Routes Once these sources are on the table, the Salafi position has only a few ways out. Escape 1 Reinterpret the scholars One may argue that al-Nawawi, al-Subki, Ibn al-Jazari, and al-Shawkani meant only lawful tawassul, not direct calling upon the dead. Sometimes this works. Sometimes the wording resists it, especially when the visitor addresses the Prophet at the grave and seeks intercession through him. Escape 2 Excuse them One may say they were mistaken, confused, relying on weak stories, or using inherited language. But if the practice is major shirk in the obvious foundations of religion, the excuse has to be explained. Ibn Baz’s own framework makes that difficult. Escape 3 Downgrade the ruling One may say the issue is bidʿa, disliked tawassul, or a mistaken devotional practice unless the person believes the dead independently control benefit and harm. That is more historically workable, but it weakens the modern habit of calling the whole field major shirk. The third route is the most coherent historically. It allows a person to reject these practices from a Quranic or Salafi perspective without pretending that much of Sunni scholarship was sitting in obvious polytheism. ## The Real Paradox The paradox is not that Salafis reject some classical practices. Every reform movement does that. The paradox is that Salafis often claim to represent the saved Sunni inheritance while making theological accusations that, if applied consistently, would place major Sunni authorities under the shadow of major shirk. Claim Historical pressure Asking the Prophet after death for intercession is major shirk. Al-Nawawi’s visitation passage explicitly uses posthumous tawassul and istishfaʿ language. Istighatha through the Prophet was obviously forbidden. Al-Subki says its permissibility was known and that Ibn Taymiyya’s denial was a novelty. Tawassul through persons is a route to shirk. Ibn al-Jazari lists tawassul through prophets and righteous servants among supplication etiquette, and al-Shawkani explains it as a recognized devotional form. The issue was always obvious in Sunni Islam. Ibn Hajar records that some contemporaries viewed Ibn Taymiyya’s denial of istighatha through the Prophet as religiously shocking. This does not prove that al-Nawawi or al-Subki were right. It proves that the Salafi historical story is too clean. The practice was not merely the religion of ignorant grave-worshippers. It existed in the learned tradition, sometimes in places where Salafis still go for law, hadith, Quranic recitation, and devotional vocabulary. ## The Quranic Baseline From a Quran-centered perspective, there is a separate question: should any of this have authority over the believer? The Quran’s answer is simpler than the Sunni inheritance. Worship and supplication belong to God. These verses are why the article does not need to defend al-Nawawi or al-Subki as correct. The argument is about consistency. A Quranic critique can reject all devotional intermediaries without inheriting the Salafi need to protect Sunni authority. The Salafi has a harder task. He wants to reject the practice as major shirk while still claiming the tradition that preserved it as his own. The Salafi paradox is not solved by saying that some classical scholars were wrong. The problem is that modern Salafi rhetoric often calls these practices major shirk while continuing to depend on a Sunni scholarly inheritance where posthumous tawassul, istishfaʿ, and related devotional language were accepted, defended, or normalized by major authorities. A consistent position must either soften the takfir category, openly demote large parts of the Sunni tradition, or admit that the modern framing is historically much narrower than it claims. ## Conclusion The sources do not support the simple story that Salafism is just the old Sunni tradition stripped of later excess. On this issue, modern Salafi theology cuts against large parts of the classical record. Al-Nawawi’s visitor faces the Prophet and seeks intercession through him. Al-Subki defends tawassul, istighatha, and tashaffuʿ through the Prophet. Ibn al-Jazari places tawassul through prophets and righteous servants in a supplication manual. Al-Shawkani explains that line through hadith and Companion precedent. Ibn Hajar records how controversial Ibn Taymiyya’s denial of istighatha through the Prophet sounded to some in his own world. A Muslim may still reject all of this on Quranic grounds. That is a separate argument. But the Salafi claim is different. It says this rejection is the obvious Sunni position, the inherited way of the early community, and that the opposite is major shirk. The historical record does not make that claim easy to maintain. The cleaner conclusion is that modern Salafism is not simply preserving Sunni orthodoxy. On tawassul and istighatha, it is judging much of that orthodoxy. [^1]: Ibn Baz, “حكم الحجب والتوسل ببركة الصالحين والصلاة خلف من يفعله,” official Ibn Baz website. He states that tawassul by the rank, blessing, or right of a person is a bidʿa and not shirk. [^2]: Ibn Baz, “حكم طلب الشفاعة من النبي ﷺ,” official Ibn Baz website. The fatwa says asking the Prophet or other dead figures for intercession is major shirk because it asks the dead for what they cannot do. [^3]: Ibn Baz, “العذر بالجهل في مسائل الاعتقاد,” official Ibn Baz website. He says a Muslim among Muslims is not excused in such foundational matters and lists calling upon grave-dwellers, asking them for healing, and seeking their aid among the greatest forms of shirk. [^4]: Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab, Fatawa wa-Masa'il , question on tawassul through the righteous, printed in Mu'allafat al-Shaykh Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab , vol. 4. The Shamela text preserves the line: “This issue is among the issues of fiqh ... we do not condemn the one who does it; there is no condemnation in matters of ijtihad.” [^5]: al-Nawawi, al-Majmuʿ Sharh al-Muhadhdhab , vol. 8, p. 274, section on visiting the Prophet’s grave. The text says the visitor returns to face the Messenger of God and “seeks tawassul through him for himself and seeks his intercession with his Lord.” [^6]: Taqi al-Din al-Subki, Shifa al-Siqam fi Ziyarat Khayr al-Anam , chapter on tawassul and istighatha. The wording is quoted and debated in later polemical sources as well. [^7]: Ibn al-Jazari, al-Hisn al-Hasin , as commented upon by al-Shawkani in Tuhfat al-Dhakirin bi-ʿUddat al-Hisn al-Hasin , section “The manner of tawassul through the prophets and the righteous.” Al-Shawkani cites the blind man report and the Companions’ rain-prayer through al-ʿAbbas. [^8]: Ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina fi Aʿyan al-Mi'a al-Thamina , biography of Ibn Taymiyya. fullText: Theology · Sunni Tradition · Internal Critique The paradox is not disagreement. The paradox is takfir. Salafis can disagree with al-Nawawi, al-Subki, Ibn al-Jazari, al-Shawkani, or later Sunni manuals. Disagreement by itself is normal. The problem begins when the disagreement is turned into a doctrine of major shirk while those same scholars remain part of the inherited Sunni library. If asking the Prophet or the righteous dead for intercession, aid, or mediation is major shirk in the obvious foundations of religion, then the historical implications do not stop with ordinary shrine visitors. They reach jurists, hadith commentators, Quran reciters, devotional authors, and legal authorities whom Salafis still read, cite, and depend on. This article is not defending posthumous tawassul or istighatha from the Quran. The Quranic standard remains God alone. The point here is narrower: the modern Salafi accusation of major shirk does not sit comfortably with the actual Sunni tradition that Salafis claim to preserve. Terms Before the Argument The debate becomes confused when several different practices are forced under one word. Classical writers, modern Salafis, and ordinary Muslims do not always mean the same thing by tawassul and istighatha . Tawassul Asking God by a means This usually means asking God through the Prophet, a righteous person, a good deed, a rank, a blessing, or a living person’s supplication. Salafis often treat some forms as bidʿa, but Ibn Baz himself says asking God by the rank, blessing, or right of someone is a bidʿa, not shirk.[^1] Istishfaʿ Seeking intercession This can mean asking God to grant the Prophet’s intercession, or directly addressing the Prophet after death and asking him to intercede. Ibn Baz classifies the latter as major shirk.[^2] Istighatha Seeking aid The word can mean asking a living person for help in what he can do, asking God by means of a beloved servant, or calling upon a dead or absent figure for aid. Salafi polemics often treat the last category as the controlling meaning. The article is about the place where those categories collide. If a man says, “O Messenger of God, intercede for me with your Lord,” is he a sinner, an innovator, a mistaken jurist, or a polytheist? Modern Salafi answers often move quickly to the last category. The older Sunni record is not that tidy. The Salafi Ruling Ibn Baz states the modern Salafi position clearly. Asking the Prophet, or any other dead figure, for intercession is not merely impermissible. It is major shirk. فَالْحَاصِلُ: أَنَّ طَلَبَ الشَّفَاعَةِ مِنَ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ، أَوْ مِنْ غَيْرِهِ مِنَ الأَمْوَاتِ؛ أَمْرٌ لا يَجُوزُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى القَاعِدَةِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ مِنَ الشِّرْكِ الأَكْبَرِ؛ لأَنَّهُ طَلَبٌ مِنَ المَيِّتِ شَيْئًا لا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ. “In summary, requesting intercession from the Prophet ﷺ, or from anyone else among the dead, is not permissible. According to the legal principle, it is major shirk, because it is asking the dead for something they cannot do.” The same fatwa says there is no difference between asking this from the Prophet, from ʿAbd al-Qadir, from al-Badawi, from al-Husayn, or from anyone else. Ibn Baz includes requests for aid, intercession, victory, and relief among the actions of pre-Islamic polytheism.[^2] This is not a small claim. If the category is **major shirk**, then the issue is no longer a disputed devotional etiquette. It becomes a boundary of Islam itself. Ibn Baz also speaks strongly about ignorance in creed. He says that a Muslim living among Muslims, hearing the Quran and hadith, is not excused in the foundations of the religion, and he places calling upon grave-dwellers, asking them for healing, and seeking their aid among the greatest forms of shirk.[^3] 1 Posthumous request for intercession or aid is major shirk. → 2 Ignorance is not easily excused in obvious foundations of tawhid. → 3 Classical Sunni authorities who endorsed the practice become a theological problem. That is the paradox. It is not enough to say, “They were wrong.” Salafi rhetoric often says much more than that. Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab Was More Careful About Tawassul There is a point that should not be skipped. Muhammad b. Abd al-Wahhab himself distinguished tawassul from direct supplication to created beings. In a response about asking God through the righteous, he says the difference is very clear. He describes tawassul through the righteous as a matter of fiqh, says the correct view for him is that it is disliked, and then says there is no harsh condemnation of the one who does it because disputed ijtihad matters are not treated that way.[^4] فَكَوْنُ بَعْضٍ يُرَخِّصُ بِالتَّوَسُّلِ بِالصَّالِحِينَ، وَبَعْضُهُمْ يَخُصُّهُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ، وَأَكْثَرُ العُلَمَاءِ يَنْهَى عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَيَكْرَهُهُ، فَهَذِهِ المَسْأَلَةُ مِنْ مَسَائِلِ الفِقْهِ ... فَلا نُنْكِرُ عَلَى مَنْ فَعَلَهُ؛ وَلا إِنْكَارَ فِي مَسَائِلِ الاجْتِهَادِ. “Some permit tawassul through the righteous, some restrict it to the Prophet ﷺ, and most scholars forbid it and dislike it. This issue is among the issues of fiqh ... We do not condemn the one who does it, for there is no condemnation in matters of ijtihad.” He then contrasts that with a person who goes to the grave of ʿAbd al-Qadir or someone else and asks for relief from distress, rescue, and worldly needs. For him, those are not the same case.[^4] This matters because it exposes a later tightening. Some modern Salafi speech collapses the distinction between disliked tawassul, asking a dead person to pray, and worshipful supplication to other than God. Once everything is called major shirk, the inherited Sunni record becomes almost impossible to handle honestly. The Classical Sunni Record The strongest argument is not that every Sunni scholar had the same view. They did not. The stronger argument is that posthumous tawassul, istishfaʿ, and related devotional language are found inside major Sunni manuals, not only in marginal folk practice. Shafiʿi law al-Nawawi ثُمَّ يَرْجِعُ إِلَى مَوْقِفِهِ الأَوَّلِ قُبَالَةَ وَجْهِ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ وَيَتَوَسَّلُ بِهِ فِي حَقِّ نَفْسِهِ وَيَسْتَشْفِعُ بِهِ إِلَى رَبِّهِ In the visitation section of al-Majmuʿ , al-Nawawi says the visitor returns to face the Messenger of God, seeks tawassul through him for himself, and seeks his intercession with his Lord.[^5] Anti-Ibn Taymiyya polemic Taqi al-Din al-Subki يَجُوزُ وَيَحْسُنُ التَّوَسُّلُ وَالاسْتِغَاثَةُ وَالتَّشَفُّعُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ إِلَى رَبِّهِ In Shifa al-Siqam , al-Subki treats tawassul, istighatha, and seeking intercession through the Prophet as known and commendable, then criticizes Ibn Taymiyya for denying it.[^6] Supplication manual Ibn al-Jazari / al-Shawkani وَيَتَوَسَّلُ إِلَى اللهِ سُبْحَانَهُ بِأَنْبِيَائِهِ وَالصَّالِحِينَ Ibn al-Jazari’s devotional manual lists tawassul through God’s prophets and righteous servants among the etiquette of supplication. Al-Shawkani comments on this line and supports it through the blind man report and the Companions’ rain-prayer through al-ʿAbbas.[^7] Historical reception Ibn Hajar al-ʿAsqalani وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَنْسِبُهُ إِلَى الزَّنْدَقَةِ لِقَوْلِهِ إِنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ لا يُسْتَغَاثُ بِهِ Ibn Hajar records that some of Ibn Taymiyya’s opponents accused him of heresy for saying that the Prophet is not sought for aid. That does not make the accusation true, but it shows how abnormal the denial sounded to some of his contemporaries.[^8] The point is not that every citation above proves the same legal category. The point is that the devotional world which modern Salafism condemns was not sitting outside Sunni scholarship. It was written into law books, visitation manuals, supplication manuals, and polemical works by scholars who are still treated as part of the Sunni inheritance. The al-Nawawi Problem Al-Nawawi is not an obscure Sufi storyteller. He is one of the most used Sunni scholars in hadith, law, and devotional literature. His commentary on Muslim, his Riyad al-Salihin , and his forty-hadith collection remain everywhere. That is why his visitation passage matters. The visitor is not told merely to send peace upon the Prophet and leave. He is told to face the Prophet, seek tawassul through him, and seek his intercession with God. Al-Nawawi then preserves the famous al-ʿUtbi story under Quran 4:64, where a Bedouin comes to the Prophet’s grave and says he has come seeking forgiveness and seeking intercession through him.[^5] وَقَدْ جِئْتُكَ مُسْتَغْفِرًا مِنْ ذَنْبِي مُسْتَشْفِعًا بِكَ إِلَى رَبِّي “I have come to you seeking forgiveness for my sin, seeking intercession through you with my Lord.” A hadith critic can say the al-ʿUtbi story is not a proof-text with a sound isnad. That is fair. But this article is not using the story as proof that the practice is true. It is using al-Nawawi’s legal placement of the story as evidence of what a major Sunni authority considered acceptable devotional language. If Ibn Baz’s category is applied without qualification, al-Nawawi’s manual has a major problem. The al-Subki Problem Al-Subki’s statement is even more direct. He explicitly names tawassul, istighatha, and tashaffuʿ through the Prophet and says that their permissibility and goodness are known in the religious community. He then says no one denied it until Ibn Taymiyya.[^6] اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يَجُوزُ وَيَحْسُنُ التَّوَسُّلُ وَالاسْتِغَاثَةُ وَالتَّشَفُّعُ بِالنَّبِيِّ ﷺ إِلَى رَبِّهِ سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَى ... وَلَمْ يُنْكِرْ أَحَدٌ ذَلِكَ ... حَتَّى جَاءَ ابْنُ تَيْمِيَّةَ “Know that it is permissible and good to seek tawassul, istighatha, and intercession through the Prophet ﷺ with his Lord, Glorified and Exalted ... No one denied this ... until Ibn Taymiyya came.” One can argue that al-Subki overstated the historical consensus. That is possible. But even if the consensus claim is reduced, the paradox remains. A major Shafiʿi authority publicly treated Ibn Taymiyya’s denial as a novelty, while modern Salafi discourse often treats the opposite practice as obvious major shirk. That is a serious gap in historical memory. The Ibn al-Jazari and al-Shawkani Problem Ibn al-Jazari is central to Quranic recitation. Sunni and Salafi circles do not discard him. Yet the devotional manual associated with him includes tawassul through the prophets and righteous among the etiquette of supplication. Al-Shawkani’s commentary is important because he was not simply repeating Shafiʿi grave-visit literature. He explains the line by citing the blind man report for tawassul through the Prophet and the rain-prayer through al-ʿAbbas for tawassul through the righteous.[^7] Al-Shawkani is useful here because many modern reformist and Salafi-leaning readers respect him. His discussion does not prove every later shrine practice. It does show that tawassul through prophets and righteous figures could remain inside serious hadith-legal discussion without being treated as major shirk. The Three Escape Routes Once these sources are on the table, the Salafi position has only a few ways out. Escape 1 Reinterpret the scholars One may argue that al-Nawawi, al-Subki, Ibn al-Jazari, and al-Shawkani meant only lawful tawassul, not direct calling upon the dead. Sometimes this works. Sometimes the wording resists it, especially when the visitor addresses the Prophet at the grave and seeks intercession through him. Escape 2 Excuse them One may say they were mistaken, confused, relying on weak stories, or using inherited language. But if the practice is major shirk in the obvious foundations of religion, the excuse has to be explained. Ibn Baz’s own framework makes that difficult. Escape 3 Downgrade the ruling One may say the issue is bidʿa, disliked tawassul, or a mistaken devotional practice unless the person believes the dead independently control benefit and harm. That is more historically workable, but it weakens the modern habit of calling the whole field major shirk. The third route is the most coherent historically. It allows a person to reject these practices from a Quranic or Salafi perspective without pretending that much of Sunni scholarship was sitting in obvious polytheism. The Real Paradox The paradox is not that Salafis reject some classical practices. Every reform movement does that. The paradox is that Salafis often claim to represent the saved Sunni inheritance while making theological accusations that, if applied consistently, would place major Sunni authorities under the shadow of major shirk. Claim Historical pressure Asking the Prophet after death for intercession is major shirk. Al-Nawawi’s visitation passage explicitly uses posthumous tawassul and istishfaʿ language. Istighatha through the Prophet was obviously forbidden. Al-Subki says its permissibility was known and that Ibn Taymiyya’s denial was a novelty. Tawassul through persons is a route to shirk. Ibn al-Jazari lists tawassul through prophets and righteous servants among supplication etiquette, and al-Shawkani explains it as a recognized devotional form. The issue was always obvious in Sunni Islam. Ibn Hajar records that some contemporaries viewed Ibn Taymiyya’s denial of istighatha through the Prophet as religiously shocking. This does not prove that al-Nawawi or al-Subki were right. It proves that the Salafi historical story is too clean. The practice was not merely the religion of ignorant grave-worshippers. It existed in the learned tradition, sometimes in places where Salafis still go for law, hadith, Quranic recitation, and devotional vocabulary. The Quranic Baseline From a Quran-centered perspective, there is a separate question: should any of this have authority over the believer? The Quran’s answer is simpler than the Sunni inheritance. Worship and supplication belong to God. These verses are why the article does not need to defend al-Nawawi or al-Subki as correct. The argument is about consistency. A Quranic critique can reject all devotional intermediaries without inheriting the Salafi need to protect Sunni authority. The Salafi has a harder task. He wants to reject the practice as major shirk while still claiming the tradition that preserved it as his own. The Salafi paradox is not solved by saying that some classical scholars were wrong. The problem is that modern Salafi rhetoric often calls these practices major shirk while continuing to depend on a Sunni scholarly inheritance where posthumous tawassul, istishfaʿ, and related devotional language were accepted, defended, or normalized by major authorities. A consistent position must either soften the takfir category, openly demote large parts of the Sunni tradition, or admit that the modern framing is historically much narrower than it claims. Conclusion The sources do not support the simple story that Salafism is just the old Sunni tradition stripped of later excess. On this issue, modern Salafi theology cuts against large parts of the classical record. Al-Nawawi’s visitor faces the Prophet and seeks intercession through him. Al-Subki defends tawassul, istighatha, and tashaffuʿ through the Prophet. Ibn al-Jazari places tawassul through prophets and righteous servants in a supplication manual. Al-Shawkani explains that line through hadith and Companion precedent. Ibn Hajar records how controversial Ibn Taymiyya’s denial of istighatha through the Prophet sounded to some in his own world. A Muslim may still reject all of this on Quranic grounds. That is a separate argument. But the Salafi claim is different. It says this rejection is the obvious Sunni position, the inherited way of the early community, and that the opposite is major shirk. The historical record does not make that claim easy to maintain. The cleaner conclusion is that modern Salafism is not simply preserving Sunni orthodoxy. On tawassul and istighatha, it is judging much of that orthodoxy. [^1]: Ibn Baz, “حكم الحجب والتوسل ببركة الصالحين والصلاة خلف من يفعله,” official Ibn Baz website. He states that tawassul by the rank, blessing, or right of a person is a bidʿa and not shirk. [^2]: Ibn Baz, “حكم طلب الشفاعة من النبي ﷺ,” official Ibn Baz website. The fatwa says asking the Prophet or other dead figures for intercession is major shirk because it asks the dead for what they cannot do. [^3]: Ibn Baz, “العذر بالجهل في مسائل الاعتقاد,” official Ibn Baz website. He says a Muslim among Muslims is not excused in such foundational matters and lists calling upon grave-dwellers, asking them for healing, and seeking their aid among the greatest forms of shirk. title: The Prophet Did Not Know the Future
description: The Quran presents Muhammad as a messenger who follows revelation, not as a soothsayer with independent access to the unseen.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The Quran does not present Muhammad as a man who possessed the future. It presents him as a messenger who followed what was revealed to him. Those are not the same claim. A messenger can be given a specific announcement by God and still not possess independent access to the unseen. The Quran keeps that boundary in place repeatedly, especially in verses where Muhammad is commanded to deny knowledge of what lies ahead. This matters because many hadith prophecy claims depend on quietly changing the Prophet’s role. He is no longer treated as the one who conveys revelation from God. He becomes a figure who sees across history, speaks about empires, rulers, battles, and distant events, and later communities then search history for confirmations. The Quran gives us a different picture. Muhammad warns, recites, conveys, and follows revelation. He does not claim the standing power to know the unseen. God alone possesses the unseen Hidden past disclosed 3:44 · 11:49 · 12:102 These verses describe stories that Muhammad did not witness. They are revealed to him as Quranic instruction. Specific future announcements 30:2–4 · 48:27 · 54:45–46 These are not examples of personal clairvoyance. They are particular disclosures from God. Explicit limits on Muhammad 7:188 · 46:9 · 72:25 · 52:29 The Prophet is made to deny possession of the unseen, deny knowing what will happen, and deny being a soothsayer. The Quranic model is revelation, not prophetic fortune-telling. ## What the Quran Actually Denies The issue is not whether God can reveal future information. The Quran itself contains divine promises, warnings, and announcements. The issue is whether Muhammad possessed the unseen as his own knowledge, in the way a soothsayer or fortune-teller claims hidden access. The Quran answers that question directly. This verse does not leave the Prophet with a hidden reserve of future knowledge. He is commanded to say that if he knew the unseen, he would have increased good for himself and avoided harm. That is an argument from ordinary human limitation. If he possessed the unseen, his own life would have shown the benefits of such knowledge. The same limitation appears again in Surat al-Ahqaf: Here the Prophet is not merely denying knowledge of some distant apocalyptic date. He is denying knowledge of what will happen to himself and to his audience. He then defines his role positively: he follows what is revealed to him. That definition is the center of the whole matter. The Prophet’s knowledge is not independent possession. It is reception and transmission. The Quran also rejects the category of soothsaying. A soothsayer claims access to hidden matters through an occult or inspired faculty. The Quran rejects that description of Muhammad. He is not a kahin. He is not a man trading in hidden knowledge. He is a messenger reciting revelation. ## The Prophet’s Own Admission in Surat al-Jinn The clearest passage for this question is often quoted only halfway. Apologists usually cite 72:26–27, where God says He does not disclose the unseen except to a messenger He approves. But the verse immediately before it matters. Verse 25 has Muhammad say that he does not know whether what people are promised is near or whether his Lord will appoint for it a distant term. Then verses 26–27 explain that God controls the unseen and may disclose what He chooses to a messenger. Read together, the passage does not turn Muhammad into a possessor of the future. It says that the unseen belongs to God, and that any disclosure of it comes from God. 72:25 Muhammad says he does not know whether the promised event is near or delayed. ↓ 72:26–27 God says He controls the unseen and discloses it only by His choice. ↓ Result The passage protects God’s ownership of the unseen. It does not give the Prophet open access to the future. This also explains why the Quran can contain future announcements without contradicting 7:188 or 46:9. A disclosed message does not make the messenger the owner of the unseen. It means God revealed that particular matter to him. ## Hidden Stories from the Past Are Also Called Ghayb Another source of confusion is the word *ghayb*. Many readers hear “unseen” and immediately think “future,” but the Quran also uses this language for hidden events from the past. Muhammad did not witness Mary, Noah, or Joseph. When the Quran tells those stories, it calls them hidden news because they were outside his direct knowledge. These verses are important because they show how revelation works. Muhammad is told things he did not witness. The information comes to him from God. The same pattern applies when a future event is disclosed. The Prophet does not become a clairvoyant because God tells him a hidden matter. He remains the messenger who receives what God chooses to reveal. ## The Verses Used to Claim Muhammad Knew the Future The verses most often used to support prophetic foreknowledge do not actually show Muhammad possessing future knowledge. They show God disclosing specific matters. The distinction is not artificial. It comes from the Quran’s own wording, because the same Quran that contains these announcements also has Muhammad deny knowledge of the unseen. | Verse | Common claim | What the verse actually shows | |---|---|---| | **2:119** | Muhammad knew the future fate of people because he was a bearer of good news and a warner. | A messenger warns and gives good news by conveying God’s message. The title does not make him the source of future knowledge. | | **3:44** | Muhammad knew the unseen, so he could also know the future. | The verse says this is hidden news from the past. It proves revelation, not personal omniscience. | | **8:7** | Muhammad knew the military outcome before it happened. | The verse speaks of God’s promise and God’s plan. The knowledge belongs to God and is disclosed as guidance. | | **30:2–4** | Muhammad personally predicted Rome’s victory. | The passage says the command belongs to God before and after. The announcement is revelation, not independent foresight. | | **48:27** | Muhammad had a future vision and therefore knew the future. | The verse itself says God knew what the believers did not know. It presents the vision as divine disclosure. | | **54:45–46** | Muhammad predicted Quraysh’s defeat by his own knowledge. | The warning is part of revelation. Nothing in the passage gives Muhammad general access to future events. | | **72:26–27** | Messengers can know the unseen, so Muhammad knew the future. | The preceding verse has Muhammad deny knowing the timing of what is promised. The passage is about God’s control over disclosure. | ## Rome, Mecca, and Battle Warnings The Roman passage is usually treated as the strongest proof-text for prophetic prediction. But the passage itself frames the matter as God’s command. The prediction is not Muhammad speaking from a personal faculty of future knowledge. It is Quranic revelation. That is why this passage can stand alongside 7:188 and 46:9 without contradiction. The Prophet only knows the future matter because God revealed that specific matter. The same applies to the promise before battle: The verse does not say Muhammad looked into the future and saw the outcome. It says God promised one of the two groups. The believers still preferred the easier target. The scene reads like a human community being guided through revelation, not a group led by someone with constant future knowledge. The vision of entering the Sacred Mosque works the same way: The verse does not end by saying Muhammad knew what everyone else did not know. It says God knew what they did not know. The vision belongs inside divine disclosure, not prophetic possession. ## Al-Tabari on 7:188 Classical tafsir can be useful here because the plain reading of 7:188 is not a modern invention. Al-Tabari explains the verse as a command to Muhammad to answer those asking about the Hour. He paraphrases the Prophet’s position as one who cannot bring benefit to himself or ward off harm except by what God wills, and he reads “if I knew the unseen” as a denial of knowledge of what is yet to occur. He reports interpretations that if the Prophet knew hidden future matters, he would prepare for benefit and avoid harm, such as knowing when famine would occur or when death would come.[^1] Tafsir witness Al-Tabari on Quran 7:188 Al-Tabari reads the verse as a denial that Muhammad possessed knowledge of what would occur. If he had such knowledge, he would have prepared for benefit and avoided harm. The verse therefore treats ignorance of the future as part of the Prophet’s human condition. This reading matters because it does not treat 7:188 as a vague humility formula. It treats the verse as a real denial of future knowledge. Muhammad is not made to say, “I know the unseen but only by permission.” He is made to say that if he knew it, his life would be different. ## Why 11:49 Does Not Prove Future Knowledge One verse is often quoted without context: The verse says that these are news from the unseen which God reveals. But the surrounding passage is the story of Noah. Muhammad is being told an account of earlier history that neither he nor his people witnessed. This is the same pattern we saw in 3:44 and 12:102. The unseen here is hidden past information, not a license to turn Muhammad into a knower of future events. When a verse is about Noah’s story, it should not be used as if it were a general grant of future knowledge. The verse is making a claim about revelation. It is not changing the Prophet’s human limits. ## The Prophet Was Not a Soothsayer The Quran’s rejection of soothsaying is not a minor point. It blocks a whole way of imagining prophetic authority. Muhammad is not a religious fortune-teller whose authority comes from predicting future events. His authority comes from delivering God’s message. That means hadith prophecy claims have to be judged carefully. If a later report makes Muhammad speak like a political forecaster, naming future dynasties, cities, sects, rulers, battles, or far-off historical conditions, the Quranic baseline should make us cautious. The Quran does not deny that God can reveal an event before it happens. It denies that Muhammad possessed a standing knowledge of the unseen. The Quranic test A report about the future cannot be accepted merely because later history can be made to resemble it. The first question is whether the report fits the Quran’s portrayal of Muhammad as a messenger who follows revelation, not as a soothsayer who possesses the unseen. ## What This Means for Hadith Prophecies Many alleged hadith prophecies work by reading later history back into earlier reports. A vague statement is attached to a later dynasty, a city, a conquest, a sectarian conflict, or a natural event. The report then becomes proof that Muhammad knew the future. But the Quranic picture does not support that kind of argument. If a future statement is genuinely Quranic revelation, the Quran marks it as God’s disclosure. If a hadith report appears later through a suspicious transmission pattern, through a common link after the event, or through wording that fits a later political or legal setting, then its historical burden is much heavier. The Quran gives no permission to treat every successful-looking hadith prediction as proof of prophetic foresight. This is why each prophecy report has to be studied on its own terms. We have to ask where the report first appears, who spreads it, what historical setting it fits, and whether the wording looks like a prediction before the event or a memory written after the event. The Quran has already ruled out the easy answer: Muhammad did not possess the future. ## Further Case Studies The following studies examine specific hadith prophecy claims through transmission history, wording, and historical setting: The Thirty-Year Reign Hold On to These Six Things The Return of Dhul-Khalasa The Killing of Umar and the Afflictions The Green Arabia Hadith The Baghdad Prophecy The Fire from Hijaz Bedouins Building Tall Buildings ## Conclusion The Quran gives a consistent account of Muhammad’s role. He warns, gives good news, recites, and follows what is revealed to him. He does not claim possession of the unseen. He does not know what will happen to himself or to his people unless God reveals a particular matter. He is not a soothsayer. This framework does not deny revelation. It protects revelation from being confused with fortune-telling. When God discloses a hidden matter, the knowledge belongs to God and the messenger conveys it. That is the Quranic boundary. Any hadith that turns Muhammad into an open-ended predictor of future history has to be tested against that boundary before it is used as evidence. [^1]: Al-Tabari, *Jami al-Bayan fi Tafsir al-Quran*, commentary on Quran 7:188. That is why this passage can stand alongside 7:188 and 46:9 without contradiction. The Prophet only knows the future matter because God revealed that specific matter. The same applies to the promise before battle: The verse does not say Muhammad looked into the future and saw the outcome. It says God promised one of the two groups. The believers still preferred the easier target. The scene reads like a human community being guided through revelation, not a group led by someone with constant future knowledge. The vision of entering the Sacred Mosque works the same way: The verse does not end by saying Muhammad knew what everyone else did not know. It says God knew what they did not know. The vision belongs inside divine disclosure, not prophetic possession. Al-Tabari on 7:188 Classical tafsir can be useful here because the plain reading of 7:188 is not a modern invention. Al-Tabari explains the verse as a command to Muhammad to answer those asking about the Hour. He paraphrases the Prophet’s position as one who cannot bring benefit to himself or ward off harm except by what God wills, and he reads “if I knew the unseen” as a denial of knowledge of what is yet to occur. He reports interpretations that if the Prophet knew hidden future matters, he would prepare for benefit and avoid harm, such as knowing when famine would occur or when death would come.[^1] Tafsir witness Al-Tabari on Quran 7:188 Al-Tabari reads the verse as a denial that Muhammad possessed knowledge of what would occur. If he had such knowledge, he would have prepared for benefit and avoided harm. The verse therefore treats ignorance of the future as part of the Prophet’s human condition. This reading matters because it does not treat 7:188 as a vague humility formula. It treats the verse as a real denial of future knowledge. Muhammad is not made to say, “I know the unseen but only by permission.” He is made to say that if he knew it, his life would be different. Why 11:49 Does Not Prove Future Knowledge One verse is often quoted without context: The verse says that these are news from the unseen which God reveals. But the surrounding passage is the story of Noah. Muhammad is being told an account of earlier history that neither he nor his people witnessed. This is the same pattern we saw in 3:44 and 12:102. The unseen here is hidden past information, not a license to turn Muhammad into a knower of future events. When a verse is about Noah’s story, it should not be used as if it were a general grant of future knowledge. The verse is making a claim about revelation. It is not changing the Prophet’s human limits. The Prophet Was Not a Soothsayer The Quran’s rejection of soothsaying is not a minor point. It blocks a whole way of imagining prophetic authority. Muhammad is not a religious fortune-teller whose authority comes from predicting future events. His authority comes from delivering God’s message. That means hadith prophecy claims have to be judged carefully. If a later report makes Muhammad speak like a political forecaster, naming future dynasties, cities, sects, rulers, battles, or far-off historical conditions, the Quranic baseline should make us cautious. The Quran does not deny that God can reveal an event before it happens. It denies that Muhammad possessed a standing knowledge of the unseen. The Quranic test A report about the future cannot be accepted merely because later history can be made to resemble it. The first question is whether the report fits the Quran’s portrayal of Muhammad as a messenger who follows revelation, not as a soothsayer who possesses the unseen. What This Means for Hadith Prophecies Many alleged hadith prophecies work by reading later history back into earlier reports. A vague statement is attached to a later dynasty, a city, a conquest, a sectarian conflict, or a natural event. The report then becomes proof that Muhammad knew the future. But the Quranic picture does not support that kind of argument. If a future statement is genuinely Quranic revelation, the Quran marks it as God’s disclosure. If a hadith report appears later through a suspicious transmission pattern, through a common link after the event, or through wording that fits a later political or legal setting, then its historical burden is much heavier. The Quran gives no permission to treat every successful-looking hadith prediction as proof of prophetic foresight. This is why each prophecy report has to be studied on its own terms. We have to ask where the report first appears, who spreads it, what historical setting it fits, and whether the wording looks like a prediction before the event or a memory written after the event. The Quran has already ruled out the easy answer: Muhammad did not possess the future. Further Case Studies The following studies examine specific hadith prophecy claims through transmission history, wording, and historical setting: The Thirty-Year Reign Hold On to These Six Things The Return of Dhul-Khalasa The Killing of Umar and the Afflictions The Green Arabia Hadith The Baghdad Prophecy The Fire from Hijaz Bedouins Building Tall Buildings Conclusion The Quran gives a consistent account of Muhammad’s role. He warns, gives good news, recites, and follows what is revealed to him. He does not claim possession of the unseen. He does not know what will happen to himself or to his people unless God reveals a particular matter. He is not a soothsayer. This framework does not deny revelation. It protects revelation from being confused with fortune-telling. When God discloses a hidden matter, the knowledge belongs to God and the messenger conveys it. That is the Quranic boundary. Any hadith that turns Muhammad into an open-ended predictor of future history has to be tested against that boundary before it is used as evidence. [^1]: Al-Tabari, *Jami al-Bayan fi Tafsir al-Quran*, commentary on Quran 7:188. title: The Ten Promised Paradise Hadith: How a Kufan Polemic Became a Sunni Creed
description: A critical isnād-cum-matn analysis of the so-called Ten Promised Paradise hadith, its early Kufan transmission families, and the later polishing of the report into a Sunni creedal list.

It appears in Tirmidhī and later Sunni collections as a clean list of ten Companions who were already guaranteed Paradise. In that form the report sounds simple, stable, and harmless. أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعِيدُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ بْنُ الْجَرَّاحِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ is in Paradise, Saʿīd b. Zayd is in Paradise, and Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ is in Paradise.” If that polished form were the original form, we would expect it to be anchored in a wide and early network. We would expect multiple Companion routes, stable wording, and no obvious sign that the report was born inside a live political dispute. That is not what the evidence looks like. The early material does not begin with a serene, universally known list. It begins in Kūfa, in polemical settings, through Saʿīd b. Zayd. It begins with awkward details that later transmitters had every reason to smooth over. The real question is not how many later books quote the hadith. The real question is where the report first becomes historically recoverable, and what shape it had there. ## The Earliest Recoverable Layer Is Kufan and Saʿīd-Centered When the variants are grouped by isnād family and compared as texts, the early field does not scatter broadly across the Companions. It converges on one figure: **Saʿīd b. Zayd**. Three early families preserve the core material, and all three are tied to Kūfa. One family runs through **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Akhnas** and then **al-Ḥurr b. al-Ṣayyāḥ**. Another runs through **ʿAbd Allāh b. Ẓālim** and then **Hilāl b. Yasāf**. A third runs through **Riyāḥ b. al-Ḥārith** and then **Ṣadaqa b. al-Muthannā**. Those are not random side routes. They are the earliest field in which the tradition becomes visible. That structure matters because it changes the direction of the inquiry. Instead of asking whether later compilers liked the report, we ask why these three Kufan families are carrying it, why Saʿīd stands at the center, and why the earliest forms are so clumsy. ## The Earliest Forms Are Awkward for a Reason The old Saʿīd material does not read like the polished creed of later Sunni handbooks. It still shows the seams. In one important strand, Saʿīd rises after ʿAlī is disparaged in public and recites the list as a rebuttal. In that version the setting is not abstract piety. It is an argument inside a live political culture. شَهِدْتُ سَعِيدَ بْنَ زَيْدٍ عِنْدَ الْمُغِيرَةِ بْنِ شُعْبَةَ، فَذَكَرَ مِنْ عَلِيٍّ شَيْئًا، فَقَالَ سَعِيدٌ: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ يَقُولُ: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: النَّبِيُّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ. وَلَوْ شِئْتُ أَنْ أُسَمِّيَ الْعَاشِرَ لَسَمَّيْتُهُ “I witnessed Saʿīd b. Zayd in the presence of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba. Something was said against ʿAlī, so Saʿīd said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ten are in Paradise: the Prophet is in Paradise, Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, and Saʿd is in Paradise. If I wished, I would name the tenth.” This is already enough to make the historian pause. The Prophet is counted inside the ten. Abū ʿUbayda is absent. Saʿīd does not simply transmit a fixed and famous list. He recites nine names and then hints at the tenth. A report that later becomes a clean creed here still looks unstable and interested. The second early family preserves an even more revealing form. The setting shifts to Ḥirāʾ, the Prophet says the mountain carries only a prophet, a ṣiddīq, or martyrs, and Saʿīd again leaves the tenth hanging until he effectively identifies himself. أَشْهَدُ عَلَى التِّسْعَةِ أَنَّهُمْ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَلَوْ شَهِدْتُ عَلَى الْعَاشِرِ لَمْ آثَمْ ... كُنَّا مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِحِرَاءَ، فَقَالَ: اثْبُتْ حِرَاءُ، فَإِنَّمَا عَلَيْكَ نَبِيٌّ أَوْ صِدِّيقٌ أَوْ شَهِيدٌ “I bear witness for the nine that they are in Paradise, and if I were to bear witness for the tenth, I would not sin … We were with the Messenger of God ﷺ on Ḥirāʾ, and he said: Be still, Ḥirāʾ, for upon you is none but a prophet, a ṣiddīq, or a martyr.” Now the report shows another important feature. It is feeding on an older **mountain motif**. The Ḥirāʾ material did not originally need a full list of ten. It was a short virtue report about the mountain shaking and the Prophet identifying the people with him. The Saʿīd family fuses that motif into a broader ten-name claim. This is exactly why matn comparison matters. Once the versions are laid side by side, the polished creed begins to look secondary. The earlier forms still preserve the rough edges: the anti-ʿAlī setting, the Prophet counted inside the ten, the “nine then the tenth” device, and the fusion with the Ḥirāʾ report. ## What the Report Was Doing in Kūfa The early forms are not just textually awkward. They are historically useful. They appear in a city where ʿAlī was publicly reviled from the Umayyad minbar, and they place Saʿīd inside that fight. That matters because the report is not merely praising a set of Companions. It is performing reconciliation work. It says, in effect, that the key figures of the first civil war all belong inside the same salvific circle. ʿAlī is in Paradise. So are Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, who fought against him. So is ʿUthmān. So are Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. This is not neutral memory. It is a formula for healing, or suppressing, the political wounds of the first fitna. That also explains why Saʿīd’s role is so awkward. He is not just narrating a report about others. He is presenting a salvation list in which he himself belongs. The hesitation preserved in some variants is telling. It suggests that transmitters felt the discomfort and tried to manage it within the wording itself. ## How the List Was Polished The next major stage in the tradition appears in Medina through **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥumayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf**. He is the bridge figure. One branch still transmits the hadith from **Saʿīd b. Zayd**. Another branch attributes the hadith instead to **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf**. That is not a small detail. It is the point at which the report is being regularized. Here is the Saʿīd-side branch that still preserves the old hesitation: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ ... فَعَدَّ هَؤُلَاءِ التِّسْعَةَ، ثُمَّ سَكَتَ عَنِ الْعَاشِرِ ... فَقَالَ: أَبُو الْأَعْوَرِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Ten are in Paradise: Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿAlī and ʿUthmān are in Paradise, al-Zubayr and Ṭalḥa are in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū ʿUbayda, and Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ … He counted those nine, then was silent about the tenth … Then he said: Abū al-Aʿwar is in Paradise.” Abū al-Aʿwar here is Saʿīd b. Zayd. And here is the polished family form: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعِيدُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ بْنُ الْجَرَّاحِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Ten are in Paradise: Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ is in Paradise, Saʿīd b. Zayd is in Paradise, and Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ is in Paradise.” This is not what one expects if the ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf route were the untouched original and the Saʿīd material were later noise. The textual pressure runs the other way. The Saʿīd branch keeps the older, stranger features. The polished family route removes the strain, fixes the list, and supplies Abū ʿUbayda as the completed tenth name. Even classical criticism points in that direction. Tirmidhī reports that al-Bukhārī regarded the Saʿīd-form as stronger than the first, more polished report. Abū Ḥātim also treated the report as belonging to the Saʿīd stream rather than as a known report from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf. ## The Late Corroborative Routes Do Not Rescue the Report A reader may object that there are other Companion attributions, especially the Ibn ʿUmar route. The problem is that not every formally different isnād is historically independent. The Ibn ʿUmar material narrows very quickly into one late and fragile line: **Ibn ʿUmar → Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit → Suʿayr b. al-Khims → Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah → Ḥāmid b. Yaḥyā al-Balkhī → the collectors**. That is not an early broad bundle. It is a late spider. That distinction is important. The existence of another isnād on paper does not automatically create independent corroboration. The issue is whether the route has its own early spread, stable upper structure, and believable transmitter ecology. Here it does not. It looks like the sort of late corroborative scaffolding one expects after a report has already become desirable. ## Why This Became a Sunni Creed By the time the report reaches its familiar form, the politics have been hidden inside the piety. The anti-ʿAlī setting fades. The hesitation about the tenth name disappears. The Prophet is no longer counted in the ten. Abū ʿUbayda is inserted to complete the canonical number. What remains is a tidy virtue list that can function as a Sunni badge of orthodoxy. This development makes sense historically. Once the first fitna receded into memory, Sunni identity needed formulas that gathered the major early figures into a single legitimating frame. A report that simultaneously affirmed ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar was perfect for that work. What began as a Kufan polemical defense could therefore end as a transregional creed. ## A Quranic Problem There is also a broader theological problem. The Quran does not teach believers to hand out unconditional salvific guarantees to named individuals on the strength of later communal memory. It repeatedly returns judgment to God and does not present the Prophet as a public dispenser of final verdicts over the unseen future of specific people in this style. Even apart from theology, though, the historical problem is already enough. The report reaches us not as an early, stable, multiply anchored Prophetic declaration, but as a developing cluster of Saʿīd-centered Kufan virtue traditions later regularized into a clean Sunni list. The so-called Ten Promised Paradise hadith is best understood as a developing matn cluster, not as a single stable Prophetic report. Its earliest recoverable forms are Kufan, polemical, and centered on Saʿīd b. Zayd. The polished ten-name list associated with later Sunni creed is secondary. It is the endpoint of regularization, not the beginning of the tradition. ## Conclusion Once the variants are compared carefully, the report stops looking like a fixed Prophetic proclamation and starts looking like a historical process. The earliest families converge on Saʿīd b. Zayd in Kūfa. Their wording is uneven. Their settings are political. Their structure still shows discomfort about self-inclusion. One family fuses the report with the older Ḥirāʾ mountain motif. A later Medinan bridge narrator, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥumayd, stands at the point where the old Saʿīd material is reshaped into the smooth form that later readers know. That is why the familiar list should not be treated as the starting point. It is the result of editing, smoothing, and canonizing. In other words, the famous “Ten Promised Paradise” hadith did not begin as a timeless Sunni creed. It became one.
