It appears in Tirmidhī and later Sunni collections as a clean list of ten Companions who were already guaranteed Paradise. In that form the report sounds simple, stable, and harmless. أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعِيدُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ بْنُ الْجَرَّاحِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ is in Paradise, Saʿīd b. Zayd is in Paradise, and Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ is in Paradise.” If that polished form were the original form, we would expect it to be anchored in a wide and early network. We would expect multiple Companion routes, stable wording, and no obvious sign that the report was born inside a live political dispute. That is not what the evidence looks like. The early material does not begin with a serene, universally known list. It begins in Kūfa, in polemical settings, through Saʿīd b. Zayd. It begins with awkward details that later transmitters had every reason to smooth over. The real question is not how many later books quote the hadith. The real question is where the report first becomes historically recoverable, and what shape it had there. The Earliest Recoverable Layer Is Kufan and Saʿīd-Centered When the variants are grouped by isnād family and compared as texts, the early field does not scatter broadly across the Companions. It converges on one figure: **Saʿīd b. Zayd**. Three early families preserve the core material, and all three are tied to Kūfa. One family runs through **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. al-Akhnas** and then **al-Ḥurr b. al-Ṣayyāḥ**. Another runs through **ʿAbd Allāh b. Ẓālim** and then **Hilāl b. Yasāf**. A third runs through **Riyāḥ b. al-Ḥārith** and then **Ṣadaqa b. al-Muthannā**. Those are not random side routes. They are the earliest field in which the tradition becomes visible. That structure matters because it changes the direction of the inquiry. Instead of asking whether later compilers liked the report, we ask why these three Kufan families are carrying it, why Saʿīd stands at the center, and why the earliest forms are so clumsy. The Earliest Forms Are Awkward for a Reason The old Saʿīd material does not read like the polished creed of later Sunni handbooks. It still shows the seams. In one important strand, Saʿīd rises after ʿAlī is disparaged in public and recites the list as a rebuttal. In that version the setting is not abstract piety. It is an argument inside a live political culture. شَهِدْتُ سَعِيدَ بْنَ زَيْدٍ عِنْدَ الْمُغِيرَةِ بْنِ شُعْبَةَ، فَذَكَرَ مِنْ عَلِيٍّ شَيْئًا، فَقَالَ سَعِيدٌ: سَمِعْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ يَقُولُ: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: النَّبِيُّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ. وَلَوْ شِئْتُ أَنْ أُسَمِّيَ الْعَاشِرَ لَسَمَّيْتُهُ “I witnessed Saʿīd b. Zayd in the presence of al-Mughīra b. Shuʿba. Something was said against ʿAlī, so Saʿīd said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: ten are in Paradise: the Prophet is in Paradise, Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, and Saʿd is in Paradise. If I wished, I would name the tenth.” This is already enough to make the historian pause. The Prophet is counted inside the ten. Abū ʿUbayda is absent. Saʿīd does not simply transmit a fixed and famous list. He recites nine names and then hints at the tenth. A report that later becomes a clean creed here still looks unstable and interested. The second early family preserves an even more revealing form. The setting shifts to Ḥirāʾ, the Prophet says the mountain carries only a prophet, a ṣiddīq, or martyrs, and Saʿīd again leaves the tenth hanging until he effectively identifies himself. أَشْهَدُ عَلَى التِّسْعَةِ أَنَّهُمْ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَلَوْ شَهِدْتُ عَلَى الْعَاشِرِ لَمْ آثَمْ ... كُنَّا مَعَ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِحِرَاءَ، فَقَالَ: اثْبُتْ حِرَاءُ، فَإِنَّمَا عَلَيْكَ نَبِيٌّ أَوْ صِدِّيقٌ أَوْ شَهِيدٌ “I bear witness for the nine that they are in Paradise, and if I were to bear witness for the tenth, I would not sin … We were with the Messenger of God ﷺ on Ḥirāʾ, and he said: Be still, Ḥirāʾ, for upon you is none but a prophet, a ṣiddīq, or a martyr.” Now the report shows another important feature. It is feeding on an older **mountain motif**. The Ḥirāʾ material did not originally need a full list of ten. It was a short virtue report about the mountain shaking and the Prophet identifying the people with him. The Saʿīd family fuses that motif into a broader ten-name claim. This is exactly why matn comparison matters. Once the versions are laid side by side, the polished creed begins to look secondary. The earlier forms still preserve the rough edges: the anti-ʿAlī setting, the Prophet counted inside the ten, the “nine then the tenth” device, and the fusion with the Ḥirāʾ report. What the Report Was Doing in Kūfa The early forms are not just textually awkward. They are historically useful. They appear in a city where ʿAlī was publicly reviled from the Umayyad minbar, and they place Saʿīd inside that fight. That matters because the report is not merely praising a set of Companions. It is performing reconciliation work. It says, in effect, that the key figures of the first civil war all belong inside the same salvific circle. ʿAlī is in Paradise. So are Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, who fought against him. So is ʿUthmān. So are Abū Bakr and ʿUmar. This is not neutral memory. It is a formula for healing, or suppressing, the political wounds of the first fitna. That also explains why Saʿīd’s role is so awkward. He is not just narrating a report about others. He is presenting a salvation list in which he himself belongs. The hesitation preserved in some variants is telling. It suggests that transmitters felt the discomfort and tried to manage it within the wording itself. How the List Was Polished The next major stage in the tradition appears in Medina through **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥumayd b. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf**. He is the bridge figure. One branch still transmits the hadith from **Saʿīd b. Zayd**. Another branch attributes the hadith instead to **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf**. That is not a small detail. It is the point at which the report is being regularized. Here is the Saʿīd-side branch that still preserves the old hesitation: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ ... فَعَدَّ هَؤُلَاءِ التِّسْعَةَ، ثُمَّ سَكَتَ عَنِ الْعَاشِرِ ... فَقَالَ: أَبُو الْأَعْوَرِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Ten are in Paradise: Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿAlī and ʿUthmān are in Paradise, al-Zubayr and Ṭalḥa are in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū ʿUbayda, and Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ … He counted those nine, then was silent about the tenth … Then he said: Abū al-Aʿwar is in Paradise.” Abū al-Aʿwar here is Saʿīd b. Zayd. And here is the polished family form: عَشَرَةٌ فِي الْجَنَّةِ: أَبُو بَكْرٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُمَرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعُثْمَانُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَلِيٌّ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَطَلْحَةُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَالزُّبَيْرُ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَعَبْدُ الرَّحْمَنِ بْنُ عَوْفٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعْدُ بْنُ أَبِي وَقَّاصٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَسَعِيدُ بْنُ زَيْدٍ فِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَبُو عُبَيْدَةَ بْنُ الْجَرَّاحِ فِي الْجَنَّةِ “Ten are in Paradise: Abū Bakr is in Paradise, ʿUmar is in Paradise, ʿUthmān is in Paradise, ʿAlī is in Paradise, Ṭalḥa is in Paradise, al-Zubayr is in Paradise, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf is in Paradise, Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ is in Paradise, Saʿīd b. Zayd is in Paradise, and Abū ʿUbayda b. al-Jarrāḥ is in Paradise.” This is not what one expects if the ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf route were the untouched original and the Saʿīd material were later noise. The textual pressure runs the other way. The Saʿīd branch keeps the older, stranger features. The polished family route removes the strain, fixes the list, and supplies Abū ʿUbayda as the completed tenth name. Even classical criticism points in that direction. Tirmidhī reports that al-Bukhārī regarded the Saʿīd-form as stronger than the first, more polished report. Abū Ḥātim also treated the report as belonging to the Saʿīd stream rather than as a known report from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf. The Late Corroborative Routes Do Not Rescue the Report A reader may object that there are other Companion attributions, especially the Ibn ʿUmar route. The problem is that not every formally different isnād is historically independent. The Ibn ʿUmar material narrows very quickly into one late and fragile line: **Ibn ʿUmar → Ḥabīb b. Abī Thābit → Suʿayr b. al-Khims → Sufyān b. ʿUyaynah → Ḥāmid b. Yaḥyā al-Balkhī → the collectors**. That is not an early broad bundle. It is a late spider. That distinction is important. The existence of another isnād on paper does not automatically create independent corroboration. The issue is whether the route has its own early spread, stable upper structure, and believable transmitter ecology. Here it does not. It looks like the sort of late corroborative scaffolding one expects after a report has already become desirable. Why This Became a Sunni Creed By the time the report reaches its familiar form, the politics have been hidden inside the piety. The anti-ʿAlī setting fades. The hesitation about the tenth name disappears. The Prophet is no longer counted in the ten. Abū ʿUbayda is inserted to complete the canonical number. What remains is a tidy virtue list that can function as a Sunni badge of orthodoxy. This development makes sense historically. Once the first fitna receded into memory, Sunni identity needed formulas that gathered the major early figures into a single legitimating frame. A report that simultaneously affirmed ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar was perfect for that work. What began as a Kufan polemical defense could therefore end as a transregional creed. A Quranic Problem There is also a broader theological problem. The Quran does not teach believers to hand out unconditional salvific guarantees to named individuals on the strength of later communal memory. It repeatedly returns judgment to God and does not present the Prophet as a public dispenser of final verdicts over the unseen future of specific people in this style. Even apart from theology, though, the historical problem is already enough. The report reaches us not as an early, stable, multiply anchored Prophetic declaration, but as a developing cluster of Saʿīd-centered Kufan virtue traditions later regularized into a clean Sunni list. The so-called Ten Promised Paradise hadith is best understood as a developing matn cluster, not as a single stable Prophetic report. Its earliest recoverable forms are Kufan, polemical, and centered on Saʿīd b. Zayd. The polished ten-name list associated with later Sunni creed is secondary. It is the endpoint of regularization, not the beginning of the tradition. Conclusion Once the variants are compared carefully, the report stops looking like a fixed Prophetic proclamation and starts looking like a historical process. The earliest families converge on Saʿīd b. Zayd in Kūfa. Their wording is uneven. Their settings are political. Their structure still shows discomfort about self-inclusion. One family fuses the report with the older Ḥirāʾ mountain motif. A later Medinan bridge narrator, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥumayd, stands at the point where the old Saʿīd material is reshaped into the smooth form that later readers know. That is why the familiar list should not be treated as the starting point. It is the result of editing, smoothing, and canonizing. In other words, the famous “Ten Promised Paradise” hadith did not begin as a timeless Sunni creed. It became one.

title: Quran 22:15: Suicide or Salvation?
description: A close reading of Quran 22:15, the contested words sabab and sama, the classical strangulation reading, and the case for reading the verse as a call to sever dependence on anything besides God.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Translation Forensics · Quran 22:15 Did God tell a man to hang himself? That is how many readers first encounter Quran 22:15 in English. The verse is often rendered as a sarcastic command to tie a rope to the ceiling, strangle oneself, and see whether that removes one’s rage. The problem is not that the verse is simple and translators have ignored it. The problem is that a chain of interpretive choices has been turned into the verse itself. The Arabic can be read another way. The contested words are not obscure: sabab , sama , li-yaqtaʿ , kayd , and the pronoun in yanṣuruhu . Each one was discussed in the classical tradition. The question is whether the suicide reading is the only reading the language allows, and whether it is the reading that best fits the Quran’s own usage. This article is not arguing that the strangulation interpretation was invented by modern translators. It is old and widely transmitted. The argument is narrower: the same classical tradition also preserves the tools needed to read the verse without making God command suicide, and the Quran’s own use of the key words supports that cleaner reading. ## The Verse in One Sentence A literal word-for-word rendering can sound strange: “Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a means/rope toward the sky, then let him cut, then let him see whether his plan removes what enrages him.” The dispute begins because several words can be narrowed in more than one direction. If sabab is narrowed to “rope,” sama is narrowed to “ceiling,” and li-yaqtaʿ is supplied with “his breath” or “himself,” the verse becomes a hanging scene. If sabab is read as “means” or “connection,” sama as heaven, and li-yaqtaʿ as severing dependence, the verse becomes a challenge to the person who thinks God will not support him: turn upward to God and cut off the false attachments that feed your rage. Common strangulation reading Rope → ceiling → hang himself This reading depends on narrowing sabab to a rope, glossing sama as the ceiling of a house, and supplying the object of “cut” as the man’s breath, body, or connection to the ground. Quran-consistent reading Means → heaven → sever dependence This reading keeps the wider Quranic sense of sabab as a means or connection, keeps sama as heaven, and reads “cut” as severing the false dependencies that do not remove distress. ## Word-by-Word Map مَن whoever كَانَ يَظُنُّ thinks / assumes أَن لَّن يَنصُرَهُ اللَّهُ that God will not help him فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ in this world and the Hereafter فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ let him extend a means / connection إِلَى السَّمَاءِ toward the sky / heaven ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ then let him cut / sever فَلْيَنظُرْ then let him look هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ whether his plan removes مَا يَغِيظُ what enrages or distresses him ## Why the Suicide Reading Creates a Problem The Quran does not allow an interpretation to be judged in isolation from the rest of the Quran. It asks the reader to notice internal consistency: A reading of 22:15 that turns the verse into a literal command to hang oneself has to be measured against verses where the Quran says God does not command indecency and where self-killing is forbidden. This does not mean every violent or sarcastic image in the Quran must be softened. It means we should be careful before turning a rhetorical challenge into a divine instruction. The verse can mock the futility of the doubter’s rage without telling a human being to commit suicide. ## How the Strangulation Reading Entered Tafsir The strangulation reading is not a modern accident. It appears in classical tafsir and was inherited by many English translators. The strongest versions of that reading gloss sabab as a rope, sama as the ceiling of the house, and “cut” as strangling oneself. Tafsir al-Jalalayn Ceiling and strangulation Al-Jalalayn explains the “sky” as the ceiling of the house, the sabab as a rope tied to that ceiling and to the neck, and “cut” as choking oneself by cutting off connection to the ground. Ibn Kathir The inherited report Ibn Kathir transmits the familiar explanation through early authorities: the man stretches a rope to the ceiling of his house and strangles himself with it. Al-Fayruzabadi The same narrowing The verse is again explained as a man tying a rope to the ceiling and hanging himself because of rage over God’s support or over his own provision. This reading is old, so it should not be dismissed as a translation mistake. The better criticism is that it is a commentary-driven narrowing of the verse. The Arabic words can bear that reading only after several interpretive steps have been supplied. ## Popular English Translations Many English translations simply reproduce the strangulation reading. The result is that a reader encounters the tafsir as though it were the direct meaning of the verse. Dr. Mustafa Khattab “Let them stretch out a rope to the ceiling and strangle themselves.” Saheeh International “Let him extend a rope to the ceiling, then cut off [his breath].” Hilali & Khan “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and let him strangle himself.” M. Pickthall “Let him stretch a rope up to the roof ... and let him hang himself.” A. Yusuf Ali “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and cut himself off.” The same pattern keeps appearing: ceiling, hanging, strangling, cutting off breath. Those words are not all in the verse. They are a tradition of explanation that translators have allowed into the translation. ## What the Classical Sources Also Preserve The strangulation reading became dominant, but the classical sources preserve more than one interpretive tool. Once those tools are collected, the verse does not have to be read as a divine command to self-harm. ### The Pronoun Was Disputed The common reading assumes that the pronoun in yanṣuruhu means “God will not help Muhammad.” But exegetes also record another reading: the pronoun can return to man , the “whoever” at the beginning of the verse. On that reading, the verse addresses the person who thinks God will not help or provide for him in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Razi on 22:15 أَنَّ الْهَاءَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ، رَاجِعٌ إِلَى مَنْ فِي أَوَّلِ الْآيَةِ ... فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَرْزُقَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ “The pronoun in ‘God will not help him’ returns to ‘whoever’ at the start of the verse … as if it said: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter.” Al-Qurtubi records the same option, and al-Tabari preserves the explanation that “support” here means provision, with yanṣuruhu read in the sense of yarzuquhu . That reading changes the emotional scene. The verse is no longer about a man enraged by the Prophet’s victory. It can be read as a person who thinks God will not support him and is told to redirect his dependence upward. ### Sabab Means a Means or Connection The word sabab can mean a rope, but “rope” is not the only sense and not always the central sense. Al-Qurtubi defines it broadly: Al-Qurtubi السَّبَبُ مَا يُتَوَصَّلُ بِهِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ “A sabab is that by which one reaches a thing.” That is why “means,” “connection,” or “way” is often the better starting point. A rope is one kind of sabab , but not every sabab is a noose. ### The Quran Uses Sabab as a Way or Means The Quran’s own usage matters. In Surat Ghafir, Pharaoh tells Haman to build a tower so that he may reach the means to the heavens: Here the phrase asbab al-samawat cannot mean nooses to ceilings. It means ways, means, or routes of ascent toward the heavens. That makes it relevant to 22:15, where sabab and sama appear together. The Quran also uses the same root with cutting language: In 2:166, the asbab are cut off, meaning relationships, ties, or dependencies are severed. That is a stronger Quranic parallel for 22:15 than the idea of cutting off one’s breath. The Quran itself shows that sabab can be something relational that is severed. 22:15 bi-sababin ... thumma li-yaqtaʿ extend a means, then cut 2:166 wa-taqaṭṭaʿat bihim al-asbab the ties / means between them are cut off ### Sama Is Not Automatically a Ceiling The word in the verse is al-sama . Translating it as “the ceiling of his house” is a tafsir gloss. Commentators justify that gloss by saying that Arabs may call anything above a person sama . But the literal sense remains sky or heaven, and the real-sky reading is preserved in the exegetical tradition. Al-Qurtubi reports Ibn Zayd’s reading that it means the known sky. Al-Razi lists the real sky as an interpretive option. Ibn Ashur also reports the same broader possibility. So the reading “toward heaven” is not a modern rescue attempt. It is one of the possibilities already visible in the tradition. ### Even the Strangulation Reading Is Rhetorical Even when classical exegetes adopt the strangulation reading, they do not treat the verse as practical religious instruction. They treat it as a rhetorical challenge, a way of showing that the doubter’s rage cannot overturn God’s decree. Al-Razi states the logic of that kind of interpretation: Al-Razi كُلُّ مَا كَانَ الْمَذْكُورُ أَبْعَدَ مِنَ الْإِمْكَانِ كَانَ أَوْلَى بِأَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْمُرَادَ “The more impossible the mentioned act is, the more fitting it is as the intended figurative sense.” That means the worst English rendering is not merely “rope” or “ceiling.” It is the impression that the verse is a literal command to commit suicide. Even within the strangulation reading, the verse is a rhetorical taunt about futility, not a devotional instruction. ## The Reading That Makes the Most Sense Rashad Khalifa’s translation is unusual because it does not import the ceiling/noose scenario into the verse. He reads the verse through reliance on God: “If anyone thinks that GOD cannot support him in this life and in the Hereafter, let him turn completely to his Creator in heaven, and sever his dependence on anyone else. He will then see that this plan eliminates anything that bothers him.” This reading does not require pretending the classical strangulation interpretation never existed. It does something more useful. It notices that the key words have broader Quranic meanings and that the verse can be read as guidance for the person who doubts God’s support. 1 He thinks God will not support him. 2 He is told to extend his means toward heaven. 3 He cuts the false dependencies beneath him. 4 He sees whether that plan removes what troubles him. The reading is not just more comforting. Comfort by itself is not evidence. It is stronger because it makes better use of the Quran’s own language. Sabab is a means or connection. Asbab can be cut off as ties and dependencies. Sama can remain heaven without being reduced to a ceiling. The pronoun can refer to the doubter himself. The whole sentence can function as a challenge to misplaced dependence rather than a command to self-destruction. ## What the Verse Is Saying The verse is addressing a person who thinks God will not support him. It challenges him to test the logic of his own dependence. If he thinks support will not come from God, let him direct his means upward and cut the false attachments that keep him trapped in rage or despair. Then let him see whether that plan removes what is troubling him. This reading turns the verse back into Quranic guidance. The person is not told to end his life. He is told to stop imagining that his frustration can defeat God’s decree or that his support must come from somewhere other than God. Quran 22:15 is best read as a rhetorical challenge about support, dependence, and misplaced rage. The strangulation interpretation is old, but it relies on narrowing several Arabic words and flattening the verse into a literal hanging scene. The Quran’s own use of sabab , sama , and cutting language supports a reading in which the person turns toward God and severs dependence on anything else. ## A More Coherent Translation “Whoever thinks that God will not support him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a means toward heaven, then sever it, and let him see whether his plan removes what enrages him.” A fuller explanatory translation would be: “Whoever thinks that God will not support him in this life and in the Hereafter should turn his means upward to heaven and sever his dependence on anything else. Then let him see whether this plan removes what distresses him.” The shorter version stays closer to the Arabic. The fuller version explains the interpretation. What should not be done is to make “ceiling,” “noose,” “breath,” or “strangle himself” sound like words the verse itself required. ## Conclusion Quran 22:15 has often been read through a hanging scene: rope, ceiling, neck, strangulation. That reading is old, but age does not make every supplied detail part of the verse. The verse says sabab , not noose. It says sama , not ceiling. It says “cut,” without saying “cut off his breath.” It asks whether the person’s kayd , his plan or effort, will remove what enrages him. The Quran gives us better controls than inherited habit. It uses sabab for means, ways, and connections. It uses cutting of asbab for severed ties. It refuses the idea that God commands indecency or self-destruction. Read inside that larger pattern, 22:15 is not a divine command to suicide. It is a challenge to the person who doubts God’s support: turn upward, cut false reliance, and see whether rage survives when dependence is placed where it belongs. { .article-opening { margin: 0 0 2.6rem; fullText: Translation Forensics · Quran 22:15 Did God tell a man to hang himself? That is how many readers first encounter Quran 22:15 in English. The verse is often rendered as a sarcastic command to tie a rope to the ceiling, strangle oneself, and see whether that removes one’s rage. The problem is not that the verse is simple and translators have ignored it. The problem is that a chain of interpretive choices has been turned into the verse itself. The Arabic can be read another way. The contested words are not obscure: sabab , sama , li-yaqtaʿ , kayd , and the pronoun in yanṣuruhu . Each one was discussed in the classical tradition. The question is whether the suicide reading is the only reading the language allows, and whether it is the reading that best fits the Quran’s own usage. This article is not arguing that the strangulation interpretation was invented by modern translators. It is old and widely transmitted. The argument is narrower: the same classical tradition also preserves the tools needed to read the verse without making God command suicide, and the Quran’s own use of the key words supports that cleaner reading. The Verse in One Sentence A literal word-for-word rendering can sound strange: “Whoever thinks that God will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a means/rope toward the sky, then let him cut, then let him see whether his plan removes what enrages him.” The dispute begins because several words can be narrowed in more than one direction. If sabab is narrowed to “rope,” sama is narrowed to “ceiling,” and li-yaqtaʿ is supplied with “his breath” or “himself,” the verse becomes a hanging scene. If sabab is read as “means” or “connection,” sama as heaven, and li-yaqtaʿ as severing dependence, the verse becomes a challenge to the person who thinks God will not support him: turn upward to God and cut off the false attachments that feed your rage. Common strangulation reading Rope → ceiling → hang himself This reading depends on narrowing sabab to a rope, glossing sama as the ceiling of a house, and supplying the object of “cut” as the man’s breath, body, or connection to the ground. Quran-consistent reading Means → heaven → sever dependence This reading keeps the wider Quranic sense of sabab as a means or connection, keeps sama as heaven, and reads “cut” as severing the false dependencies that do not remove distress. Word-by-Word Map مَن whoever كَانَ يَظُنُّ thinks / assumes أَن لَّن يَنصُرَهُ اللَّهُ that God will not help him فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ in this world and the Hereafter فَلْيَمْدُدْ بِسَبَبٍ let him extend a means / connection إِلَى السَّمَاءِ toward the sky / heaven ثُمَّ لْيَقْطَعْ then let him cut / sever فَلْيَنظُرْ then let him look هَلْ يُذْهِبَنَّ كَيْدُهُ whether his plan removes مَا يَغِيظُ what enrages or distresses him Why the Suicide Reading Creates a Problem The Quran does not allow an interpretation to be judged in isolation from the rest of the Quran. It asks the reader to notice internal consistency: A reading of 22:15 that turns the verse into a literal command to hang oneself has to be measured against verses where the Quran says God does not command indecency and where self-killing is forbidden. This does not mean every violent or sarcastic image in the Quran must be softened. It means we should be careful before turning a rhetorical challenge into a divine instruction. The verse can mock the futility of the doubter’s rage without telling a human being to commit suicide. How the Strangulation Reading Entered Tafsir The strangulation reading is not a modern accident. It appears in classical tafsir and was inherited by many English translators. The strongest versions of that reading gloss sabab as a rope, sama as the ceiling of the house, and “cut” as strangling oneself. Tafsir al-Jalalayn Ceiling and strangulation Al-Jalalayn explains the “sky” as the ceiling of the house, the sabab as a rope tied to that ceiling and to the neck, and “cut” as choking oneself by cutting off connection to the ground. Ibn Kathir The inherited report Ibn Kathir transmits the familiar explanation through early authorities: the man stretches a rope to the ceiling of his house and strangles himself with it. Al-Fayruzabadi The same narrowing The verse is again explained as a man tying a rope to the ceiling and hanging himself because of rage over God’s support or over his own provision. This reading is old, so it should not be dismissed as a translation mistake. The better criticism is that it is a commentary-driven narrowing of the verse. The Arabic words can bear that reading only after several interpretive steps have been supplied. Popular English Translations Many English translations simply reproduce the strangulation reading. The result is that a reader encounters the tafsir as though it were the direct meaning of the verse. Dr. Mustafa Khattab “Let them stretch out a rope to the ceiling and strangle themselves.” Saheeh International “Let him extend a rope to the ceiling, then cut off [his breath].” Hilali & Khan “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and let him strangle himself.” M. Pickthall “Let him stretch a rope up to the roof ... and let him hang himself.” A. Yusuf Ali “Let him stretch out a rope to the ceiling and cut himself off.” The same pattern keeps appearing: ceiling, hanging, strangling, cutting off breath. Those words are not all in the verse. They are a tradition of explanation that translators have allowed into the translation. What the Classical Sources Also Preserve The strangulation reading became dominant, but the classical sources preserve more than one interpretive tool. Once those tools are collected, the verse does not have to be read as a divine command to self-harm. The Pronoun Was Disputed The common reading assumes that the pronoun in yanṣuruhu means “God will not help Muhammad.” But exegetes also record another reading: the pronoun can return to man , the “whoever” at the beginning of the verse. On that reading, the verse addresses the person who thinks God will not help or provide for him in this world and the Hereafter. Al-Razi on 22:15 أَنَّ الْهَاءَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: لَنْ يَنْصُرَهُ اللَّهُ، رَاجِعٌ إِلَى مَنْ فِي أَوَّلِ الْآيَةِ ... فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ: مَنْ كَانَ يَظُنُّ أَنْ لَنْ يَرْزُقَهُ اللَّهُ فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ “The pronoun in ‘God will not help him’ returns to ‘whoever’ at the start of the verse … as if it said: whoever thinks that God will not provide for him in this world and the Hereafter.” Al-Qurtubi records the same option, and al-Tabari preserves the explanation that “support” here means provision, with yanṣuruhu read in the sense of yarzuquhu . That reading changes the emotional scene. The verse is no longer about a man enraged by the Prophet’s victory. It can be read as a person who thinks God will not support him and is told to redirect his dependence upward. Sabab Means a Means or Connection The word sabab can mean a rope, but “rope” is not the only sense and not always the central sense. Al-Qurtubi defines it broadly: Al-Qurtubi السَّبَبُ مَا يُتَوَصَّلُ بِهِ إِلَى الشَّيْءِ “A sabab is that by which one reaches a thing.” That is why “means,” “connection,” or “way” is often the better starting point. A rope is one kind of sabab , but not every sabab is a noose. The Quran Uses Sabab as a Way or Means The Quran’s own usage matters. In Surat Ghafir, Pharaoh tells Haman to build a tower so that he may reach the means to the heavens: Here the phrase asbab al-samawat cannot mean nooses to ceilings. It means ways, means, or routes of ascent toward the heavens. That makes it relevant to 22:15, where sabab and sama appear together. The Quran also uses the same root with cutting language: In 2:166, the asbab are cut off, meaning relationships, ties, or dependencies are severed. That is a stronger Quranic parallel for 22:15 than the idea of cutting off one’s breath. The Quran itself shows that sabab can be something relational that is severed. 22:15 bi-sababin ... thumma li-yaqtaʿ extend a means, then cut 2:166 wa-taqaṭṭaʿat bihim al-asbab the ties / means between them are cut off Sama Is Not Automatically a Ceiling The word in the verse is al-sama . Translating it as “the ceiling of his house” is a tafsir gloss. Commentators justify that gloss by saying that Arabs may call anything above a person sama . But the literal sense remains sky or heaven, and the real-sky reading is preserved in the exegetical tradition. Al-Qurtubi reports Ibn Zayd’s reading that it means the known sky. Al-Razi lists the real sky as an interpretive option. Ibn Ashur also reports the same broader possibility. So the reading “toward heaven” is not a modern rescue attempt. It is one of the possibilities already visible in the tradition. Even the Strangulation Reading Is Rhetorical Even when classical exegetes adopt the strangulation reading, they do not treat the verse as practical religious instruction. They treat it as a rhetorical challenge, a way of showing that the doubter’s rage cannot overturn God’s decree. Al-Razi states the logic of that kind of interpretation: Al-Razi كُلُّ مَا كَانَ الْمَذْكُورُ أَبْعَدَ مِنَ الْإِمْكَانِ كَانَ أَوْلَى بِأَنْ يَكُونَ هُوَ الْمُرَادَ “The more impossible the mentioned act is, the more fitting it is as the intended figurative sense.” That means the worst English rendering is not merely “rope” or “ceiling.” It is the impression that the verse is a literal command to commit suicide. Even within the strangulation reading, the verse is a rhetorical taunt about futility, not a devotional instruction. The Reading That Makes the Most Sense Rashad Khalifa’s translation is unusual because it does not import the ceiling/noose scenario into the verse. He reads the verse through reliance on God: “If anyone thinks that GOD cannot support him in this life and in the Hereafter, let him turn completely to his Creator in heaven, and sever his dependence on anyone else. He will then see that this plan eliminates anything that bothers him.” This reading does not require pretending the classical strangulation interpretation never existed. It does something more useful. It notices that the key words have broader Quranic meanings and that the verse can be read as guidance for the person who doubts God’s support. 1 He thinks God will not support him. 2 He is told to extend his means toward heaven. 3 He cuts the false dependencies beneath him. 4 He sees whether that plan removes what troubles him. The reading is not just more comforting. Comfort by itself is not evidence. It is stronger because it makes better use of the Quran’s own language. Sabab is a means or connection. Asbab can be cut off as ties and dependencies. Sama can remain heaven without being reduced to a ceiling. The pronoun can refer to the doubter himself. The whole sentence can function as a challenge to misplaced dependence rather than a command to self-destruction. What the Verse Is Saying The verse is addressing a person who thinks God will not support him. It challenges him to test the logic of his own dependence. If he thinks support will not come from God, let him direct his means upward and cut the false attachments that keep him trapped in rage or despair. Then let him see whether that plan removes what is troubling him. This reading turns the verse back into Quranic guidance. The person is not told to end his life. He is told to stop imagining that his frustration can defeat God’s decree or that his support must come from somewhere other than God. Quran 22:15 is best read as a rhetorical challenge about support, dependence, and misplaced rage. The strangulation interpretation is old, but it relies on narrowing several Arabic words and flattening the verse into a literal hanging scene. The Quran’s own use of sabab , sama , and cutting language supports a reading in which the person turns toward God and severs dependence on anything else. A More Coherent Translation “Whoever thinks that God will not support him in this world and the Hereafter, let him extend a means toward heaven, then sever it, and let him see whether his plan removes what enrages him.” A fuller explanatory translation would be: “Whoever thinks that God will not support him in this life and in the Hereafter should turn his means upward to heaven and sever his dependence on anything else. Then let him see whether this plan removes what distresses him.” The shorter version stays closer to the Arabic. The fuller version explains the interpretation. What should not be done is to make “ceiling,” “noose,” “breath,” or “strangle himself” sound like words the verse itself required. Conclusion Quran 22:15 has often been read through a hanging scene: rope, ceiling, neck, strangulation. That reading is old, but age does not make every supplied detail part of the verse. The verse says sabab , not noose. It says sama , not ceiling. It says “cut,” without saying “cut off his breath.” It asks whether the person’s kayd , his plan or effort, will remove what enrages him. The Quran gives us better controls than inherited habit. It uses sabab for means, ways, and connections. It uses cutting of asbab for severed ties. It refuses the idea that God commands indecency or self-destruction. Read inside that larger pattern, 22:15 is not a divine command to suicide. It is a challenge to the person who doubts God’s support: turn upward, cut false reliance, and see whether rage survives when dependence is placed where it belongs. { .article-opening { margin: 0 0 2.6rem; title: The Traditional Distortion of 4:3 - Polygamy
description: A close reading of Quran 4:3 in its orphan-justice context, the traditional four-wife limit, the reports of the Prophet

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Quran 4:3 · Marriage · Orphan Justice The verse begins with orphans. Later law often begins with men. Quran 4:3 is usually introduced as “the polygamy verse.” That label already shifts the reader’s attention. The verse does not open with male desire, household expansion, or a general right to multiple wives. It opens with fear of injustice toward orphans. The traditional reading then creates a second problem. It treats 4:3 as a clear Quranic limit of four wives, while hadith and sira reports portray the Prophet with nine wives at the same time. The usual solution is to create a prophetic exception. But that solution has to be tested against the Quran's own language about the Prophet following revelation, not standing above it. The argument is not that every historical form of plural marriage is identical, or that 4:3 has no numerical force. The argument is that the verse is conditional, justice-centered, and tied to vulnerability. Turning it into a broad male entitlement already distorts the verse before the number four is even discussed. ## The Shape of the Verse The verse has a clear internal movement: Condition If you fear injustice toward orphans The opening concern is not sexual access or male privilege. It is fear of failing the vulnerable. Permission Then marry two, three, or four The permission appears inside a social problem, not as a detached marital ideal. Restriction If you fear injustice, then one The verse ends by pushing the reader back toward reduced harm, not expanded desire. That structure matters. If the fear of injustice is removed from the verse, the whole moral logic changes. The verse becomes a permission slip. Inside its own wording, however, the permission is surrounded by caution. ## The Early Tafsir Did Not Forget the Orphans The earliest exegetical record does not read 4:3 as a free-floating celebration of polygamy. It repeatedly connects the verse to orphan property, orphan girls, and fear of injustice. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Urwa asks Aisha about the verse. Her answer places the verse in the setting of an orphan girl under the care of a guardian who shares her property. Her wealth and beauty tempt the guardian to marry her without giving her the dowry she would receive from someone else.[^1] هَذِهِ الْيَتِيمَةُ تَكُونُ فِي حِجْرِ وَلِيِّهَا، تُشَارِكُهُ فِي مَالِهِ، فَيُعْجِبُهُ مَالُهَا وَجَمَالُهَا، فَيُرِيدُ وَلِيُّهَا أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَهَا بِغَيْرِ أَنْ يُقْسِطَ فِي صَدَاقِهَا “This is about the orphan girl who lives under her guardian and shares his property. Her wealth and beauty please him, so her guardian wants to marry her without being fair in her bridal gift.” Al-Tabari preserves several explanations. Some connect the verse to men taking orphan property to fund numerous marriages. Others say that just as people feared injustice with orphans, they should also fear injustice toward women. Qatada says men in the pre-Islamic period would marry ten or fewer women, and that God permitted four and reduced them to four. Al-Tabari's preferred explanation is that the verse warns against injustice in women just as the previous verse warned against injustice in orphan wealth.[^2] Aisha The verse addresses a guardian tempted to marry an orphan girl under his care without giving her a fair dowry. Ikrima / Ibn Abbas strand Some reports connect the verse to men taking orphan wealth while marrying many women. Qatada / al-Tabari The verse moves from fear of injustice toward orphans to fear of injustice toward women, limiting pre-Islamic excess. These are not identical interpretations. That is important. The early record itself shows that the verse was being explained through a cluster of justice concerns: orphan girls, orphan wealth, excessive wives, and unequal treatment of women. None of those readings makes the verse a simple general entitlement. ## Is “Two, Three, or Four” a Hard Limit? Traditional law treats the verse as establishing a maximum of four wives. It also uses reports in which men who entered Islam with more than four wives were told to keep four and separate from the rest. The report of Ghaylan b. Salama is the most famous example: he accepted Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet reportedly commanded him to choose four of them.[^3] أَنَّ غَيْلَانَ بْنَ سَلَمَةَ الثَّقَفِيَّ أَسْلَمَ وَلَهُ عَشْرُ نِسْوَةٍ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ، فَأَسْلَمْنَ مَعَهُ، فَأَمَرَهُ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ أَنْ يَتَخَيَّرَ أَرْبَعًا مِنْهُنَّ “Ghaylan b. Salama al-Thaqafi accepted Islam while he had ten wives from the pre-Islamic period, and they accepted Islam with him. The Prophet ﷺ commanded him to choose four of them.” There is a real debate here. The phrase mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ is distributive: twos, threes, and fours. The same pattern appears in 35:1 for the wings of angels. That parallel matters because 35:1 immediately says that God adds to creation what He wills. So the phrase itself is not always a mathematical ceiling by its own grammar. In 4:3, the traditional ceiling comes from the verse's legal reading, the justice condition, and the hadith reports used by jurists. It is not simply the grammar alone. Quran 4:3 mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ Plural marriage appears inside a warning about justice and orphans. Quran 35:1 mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ The same numerical form describes angelic wings, then adds that God increases creation as He wills. This creates a problem for simplistic traditional claims. If four is a Quranic ceiling, then the later reports about the Prophet's nine wives need a Quranic explanation. If four is not a ceiling by grammar alone, then traditionalists should stop pretending that 4:3 is a simple proof-text for their later legal package. ## The Hadith Problem: Nine Wives Sahih al-Bukhari preserves the report from Anas that the Prophet would go around to all his wives in one night and that he had nine wives.[^4] كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ يَدُورُ عَلَى نِسَائِهِ فِي اللَّيْلَةِ الْوَاحِدَةِ، وَلَهُ تِسْعُ نِسْوَةٍ “The Prophet ﷺ used to go around to his wives in one night, and he had nine wives.” This is where the tension becomes unavoidable. The same tradition that reads 4:3 as a four-wife limit also preserves reports in which the Prophet has nine wives. Traditional law answers by saying the Prophet had special rules. The Quran does give the Prophet some specific marriage rulings in 33:50. But 33:52 then says: Whatever one does with these verses, they do not allow a lazy answer. The Quran does not present the Prophet as an independent legislator who may simply override God's boundaries. The traditional solution therefore has to do more than say, “The Prophet is an exception.” It has to show that the exception is clear in the Quran itself, and that the reports about nine simultaneous wives match the Quran's own sequence and restrictions. ## The Actual Dilemma Option 1 4:3 is a hard Quranic cap of four. Then hadith reports of nine simultaneous wives require a clear Quranic exception. The burden is on the tradition to show that exception rather than assume it. Option 2 4:3 is not a cap by grammar alone. Then the familiar four-wife rule depends heavily on juristic tradition and reports like Ghaylan, not on an obvious standalone reading of the verse. Option 3 4:3 is conditional and justice-centered. This reading does not begin with male entitlement. It begins with vulnerability, fairness, and fear of harm. The third option is the one most faithful to the verse's moral movement. It does not need to solve every later legal question at once. fullText: Quran 4:3 · Marriage · Orphan Justice The verse begins with orphans. Later law often begins with men. Quran 4:3 is usually introduced as “the polygamy verse.” That label already shifts the reader’s attention. The verse does not open with male desire, household expansion, or a general right to multiple wives. It opens with fear of injustice toward orphans. The traditional reading then creates a second problem. It treats 4:3 as a clear Quranic limit of four wives, while hadith and sira reports portray the Prophet with nine wives at the same time. The usual solution is to create a prophetic exception. But that solution has to be tested against the Quran's own language about the Prophet following revelation, not standing above it. The argument is not that every historical form of plural marriage is identical, or that 4:3 has no numerical force. The argument is that the verse is conditional, justice-centered, and tied to vulnerability. Turning it into a broad male entitlement already distorts the verse before the number four is even discussed. The Shape of the Verse The verse has a clear internal movement: Condition If you fear injustice toward orphans The opening concern is not sexual access or male privilege. It is fear of failing the vulnerable. Permission Then marry two, three, or four The permission appears inside a social problem, not as a detached marital ideal. Restriction If you fear injustice, then one The verse ends by pushing the reader back toward reduced harm, not expanded desire. That structure matters. If the fear of injustice is removed from the verse, the whole moral logic changes. The verse becomes a permission slip. Inside its own wording, however, the permission is surrounded by caution. The Early Tafsir Did Not Forget the Orphans The earliest exegetical record does not read 4:3 as a free-floating celebration of polygamy. It repeatedly connects the verse to orphan property, orphan girls, and fear of injustice. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Urwa asks Aisha about the verse. Her answer places the verse in the setting of an orphan girl under the care of a guardian who shares her property. Her wealth and beauty tempt the guardian to marry her without giving her the dowry she would receive from someone else.[^1] هَذِهِ الْيَتِيمَةُ تَكُونُ فِي حِجْرِ وَلِيِّهَا، تُشَارِكُهُ فِي مَالِهِ، فَيُعْجِبُهُ مَالُهَا وَجَمَالُهَا، فَيُرِيدُ وَلِيُّهَا أَنْ يَتَزَوَّجَهَا بِغَيْرِ أَنْ يُقْسِطَ فِي صَدَاقِهَا “This is about the orphan girl who lives under her guardian and shares his property. Her wealth and beauty please him, so her guardian wants to marry her without being fair in her bridal gift.” Al-Tabari preserves several explanations. Some connect the verse to men taking orphan property to fund numerous marriages. Others say that just as people feared injustice with orphans, they should also fear injustice toward women. Qatada says men in the pre-Islamic period would marry ten or fewer women, and that God permitted four and reduced them to four. Al-Tabari's preferred explanation is that the verse warns against injustice in women just as the previous verse warned against injustice in orphan wealth.[^2] Aisha The verse addresses a guardian tempted to marry an orphan girl under his care without giving her a fair dowry. Ikrima / Ibn Abbas strand Some reports connect the verse to men taking orphan wealth while marrying many women. Qatada / al-Tabari The verse moves from fear of injustice toward orphans to fear of injustice toward women, limiting pre-Islamic excess. These are not identical interpretations. That is important. The early record itself shows that the verse was being explained through a cluster of justice concerns: orphan girls, orphan wealth, excessive wives, and unequal treatment of women. None of those readings makes the verse a simple general entitlement. Is “Two, Three, or Four” a Hard Limit? Traditional law treats the verse as establishing a maximum of four wives. It also uses reports in which men who entered Islam with more than four wives were told to keep four and separate from the rest. The report of Ghaylan b. Salama is the most famous example: he accepted Islam with ten wives, and the Prophet reportedly commanded him to choose four of them.[^3] أَنَّ غَيْلَانَ بْنَ سَلَمَةَ الثَّقَفِيَّ أَسْلَمَ وَلَهُ عَشْرُ نِسْوَةٍ فِي الْجَاهِلِيَّةِ، فَأَسْلَمْنَ مَعَهُ، فَأَمَرَهُ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ أَنْ يَتَخَيَّرَ أَرْبَعًا مِنْهُنَّ “Ghaylan b. Salama al-Thaqafi accepted Islam while he had ten wives from the pre-Islamic period, and they accepted Islam with him. The Prophet ﷺ commanded him to choose four of them.” There is a real debate here. The phrase mathna wa-thulatha wa-rubaʿ is distributive: twos, threes, and fours. The same pattern appears in 35:1 for the wings of angels. That parallel matters because 35:1 immediately says that God adds to creation what He wills. So the phrase itself is not always a mathematical ceiling by its own grammar. In 4:3, the traditional ceiling comes from the verse's legal reading, the justice condition, and the hadith reports used by jurists. It is not simply the grammar alone. title: Gabriel’s Six Hundred Wings and Qur’an 53:10
description: A critical look at the hadith claim that Gabriel had six hundred wings, its dependence on one Kūfan exegetical route through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī, and the Qur’anic problem around 53:10 and 35:1.

That number comes from hadith. The report is usually presented as if it were a broad, independent description of Gabriel’s created form. But when the isnāds are mapped, the picture is much narrower. The main “six hundred wings” reports pass through one Kūfan exegetical route: **Ibn Masʿūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī.** After al-Shaybānī, the report fans out through several later transmitters and enters Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī. That later spread can make the report look wider than it is. But above the spread, the tradition is compact. The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is not a mass-transmitted description of Gabriel. It is a Qur’an-exegesis report clustered through one Kūfan route: Ibn Masʿūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. This matters because the report is not just giving a detail about angels. It is explaining Qur’an 53:9–10. The hadith tells us that Ibn Masʿūd understood the passage as a reference to Muhammad seeing Gabriel. The problem is that this explanation pushes the verse away from its simpler Qur’anic grammar. ## The Verse Being Explained The verse says that **He** revealed to **His servant** what He revealed. The natural reading is that God is the revealer and Muhammad is the servant. The hadith explanation shifts the focus. It reads the surrounding scene as Muhammad seeing Gabriel in his true form, and then adds that Gabriel had six hundred wings. The issue is not only the number of wings. The issue is the exegetical move. The report turns a verse about revelation from God to His servant into a report about Gabriel’s appearance. قَالَ أَخْبَرَنِي ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ رَأَى جِبْرِيلَ لَهُ سِتُّمِائَةِ جَنَاحٍ “He said: Ibn Masʿūd informed me that the Prophet saw Gabriel, and he had six hundred wings.” The wording is simple, but its function is large. It is not a free-floating angelology report. It is a tafsīr report. Zirr is asked about Qur’an 53, and he answers by transmitting Ibn Masʿūd’s statement about Gabriel. That is why the chain and the context matter. ## The Isnād Map The diagram below replaces the older raw image with a cleaner route map. The important point is not how many boxes appear at the bottom. The important point is where all the lines meet. Every listed route comes down through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. For a lay reader, this means the report has a bottleneck. A bottleneck is the point in a transmission map where many later roads collapse into one earlier road. Here, the later collectors preserve several routes, but they are not independent at the level that matters. They all return to the same Kūfan exegetical strand. That does not automatically prove the report is invented. But it prevents an exaggerated claim. One cannot simply say, “Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī all have it, therefore it is broadly established.” The real question is where the report becomes recoverable before the collectors. The answer is al-Shaybānī from Zirr from Ibn Masʿūd. Reference Route below al-Shaybānī Shared upper route Bukhārī 3232 Qutaybah b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Tirmidhī 3277 Aḥmad b. Manīʿ → ʿAbbād b. al-ʿAwwām → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd This table shows why the report should be discussed as one exegetical family, not as a broad multi-origin tradition. The collector-facing routes differ. The upper route does not. ## The Matn Problem The matn is short. But the interpretive problem is large. سَأَلْتُ زِرَّ بْنَ حُبَيْشٍ عَنْ قَوْلِ اللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: فَكَانَ قَابَ قَوْسَيْنِ أَوْ أَدْنَى. قَالَ: أَخْبَرَنِي ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ رَأَى جِبْرِيلَ وَلَهُ سِتُّمِائَةِ جَنَاحٍ “I asked Zirr b. Ḥubaysh about the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ‘He was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer.’ He said: Ibn Masʿūd informed me that the Prophet saw Gabriel, and he had six hundred wings.” Notice the structure. The report begins with a question about a Qur’anic verse. It ends with a claim about Gabriel’s wings. That means the report is doing tafsīr work. It is telling the reader how to understand the vision scene in Sūrat al-Najm. The problem is that Qur’an 53:10 reads as God revealing to His servant. The servant is Muhammad. The revealer is God. The hadith explanation places Gabriel at the center and makes the point of the verse the Prophet’s vision of Gabriel. That is not the most natural reading of the verse itself. This does not mean a reader must deny that Gabriel appears elsewhere in Sūrat al-Najm. The point is narrower. The hadith report is not merely preserving a neutral historical memory. It is intervening in the meaning of a verse. It supplies an exegetical explanation and then builds angelology on top of that explanation. ## Qur’an 35:1 and the Wings of Angels Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as messengers with wings: two, three, and four. The same verse also says that God increases in creation what He wills. That last clause matters because it is often used as the traditional answer to the objection. A defender can say, “The verse mentions two, three, and four, but then says God increases in creation, so six hundred is possible.” That response is possible, but it does not remove the critical problem. The Qur’an itself does not say Gabriel has six hundred wings. The hadith supplies that number through one exegetical chain. The question is not whether God could create an angel with more wings. The question is whether this specific report has strong enough textual and transmission evidence to impose six hundred wings onto Gabriel and then use that as the explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The better argument is therefore precise. Qur’an 35:1 does not directly teach six hundred wings. Qur’an 53:10 does not naturally require Gabriel as the subject of “His servant.” The six-hundred-wings claim comes from a narrow hadith-tafsīr strand, not from the Qur’an itself. ## Why the Bottleneck Matters Hadith reports can look stronger than they are when later branches are counted as if each branch were an independent origin. Here, the report appears in Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī, but the major routes converge through al-Shaybānī. That means the collector spread is real, but the early spread is limited. The key question is not, “How many books contain this?” The key question is, “Where does the report become recoverable?” For this family, the answer is: **Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd.** That makes al-Shaybānī the visible bottleneck of the preserved family. Zirr is also central because he is the one being asked about the verse. Ibn Masʿūd is the Companion authority used to anchor the explanation. But the later literary spread does not create multiple independent Companion-level witnesses. The report’s strength should not be exaggerated by counting Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī as though they were separate early origins. They are separate collector witnesses to one shared upper route. ## The Report as Exegesis, Not Independent Angelology The most important correction is conceptual. The report is often treated as if it were mainly about the physical form of Gabriel. But the report itself begins as an explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The question is about Qur’anic wording. The answer is a hadith explanation. That changes how the report should be evaluated. If it were an independent report from multiple Companions saying, “The Prophet saw Gabriel with six hundred wings,” the issue would be one thing. But the recoverable family is specifically Ibn Masʿūd’s interpretation transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī. The number belongs to that exegetical tradition. It is also important that the Qur’an does not need the six-hundred-wings report to make sense. Qur’an 53:10 can be read as God revealing to His servant. Qur’an 35:1 already gives a restrained description of angels as winged messengers. The hadith adds a dramatic number and then attaches it to a disputed reading of the vision passage. ## What the Diagram Shows The diagram does not show that every individual in the chain was unreliable. That is not the point. It shows that the report is structurally narrow. The chain does not branch at Ibn Masʿūd into multiple students. It does not branch at Zirr into many independent transmitters. It branches below al-Shaybānī. That means the “six hundred wings” tradition is not a broad early memory. It is a compact Kūfan tafsīr report that later became widely cited because major compilers preserved its branches. The same pattern appears in many hadith studies. A report can have many later witnesses but still depend on one earlier bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is identified, the report has to be argued from that bottleneck, not from the number of later books. ## Final Verdict The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is best understood as a narrow exegetical hadith family, not as Qur’anic angelology. Its main preserved routes all converge through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī from Zirr b. Ḥubaysh from Ibn Masʿūd. The later branches into Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī show that the report circulated well below al-Shaybānī, but they do not create independent early origins above him. The Qur’anic issue is also important. Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as having wings in twos, threes, and fours, while also saying God increases in creation what He wills. That means the verse should not be used in a simplistic way, as if it mechanically forbids all increase. But it also does not teach six hundred wings. The six-hundred number is supplied by hadith, not by the Qur’an. Qur’an 53:10 is even more central. The verse naturally reads as God revealing to His servant. The hadith turns the passage into a statement about Muhammad seeing Gabriel and then adds the six-hundred-wings detail. That is an exegetical move, and the isnād map shows that the move is preserved through one compact Kūfan route. So the strongest conclusion is careful but clear: the Qur’an does not require the six-hundred-wings doctrine, and the hadith evidence for it depends on a narrow tafsīr bottleneck. The report is not a broad independent memory of Gabriel’s form. It is Ibn Masʿūd’s Qur’an-exegesis tradition as transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī. ## Appendix: Main References | Reference | Route | | ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Bukhārī 3232 | Qutaybah b. vs. hadith expansion', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'above' } ]; export const wingComparisonEdges = [ { from: 'quran35', to: 'twoThreeFour', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'quran35', to: 'increase' }, { from: 'twoThreeFour', to: 'hadithClaim' }, { from: 'increase', to: 'hadithClaim', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'hadithClaim', to: 'criticalPoint', kind: 'trunk' } ]; export const wingComparisonTiers = [ { y: 120, label: 'Interpretive problem' }, { y: 285, label: 'Hadith expansion' }, { y: 460, label: 'Qur’anic wording' }, { y: 620, label: 'Primary text' } ]; export const wingComparisonAnnotations = [ { x: 500, y: 220, text: 'the hadith moves far beyond the Qur’anic description', anchor: 'middle', kind: 'note' }, { x: 785, y: 445, text: 'traditional escape clause, but not a direct 600-wing claim', anchor: 'start', kind: 'dive' } ]; The Problem The Qur’an describes angels as messengers with wings, but it does not say that Gabriel has six hundred wings. That number comes from hadith. The report is usually presented as if it were a broad, independent description of Gabriel’s created form. But when the isnāds are mapped, the picture is much narrower. The main “six hundred wings” reports pass through one Kūfan exegetical route: **Ibn Masʿūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī.** After al-Shaybānī, the report fans out through several later transmitters and enters Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī. That later spread can make the report look wider than it is. But above the spread, the tradition is compact. The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is not a mass-transmitted description of Gabriel. It is a Qur’an-exegesis report clustered through one Kūfan route: Ibn Masʿūd → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. This matters because the report is not just giving a detail about angels. It is explaining Qur’an 53:9–10. The hadith tells us that Ibn Masʿūd understood the passage as a reference to Muhammad seeing Gabriel. The problem is that this explanation pushes the verse away from its simpler Qur’anic grammar. The Verse Being Explained The verse says that **He** revealed to **His servant** what He revealed. The natural reading is that God is the revealer and Muhammad is the servant. The hadith explanation shifts the focus. It reads the surrounding scene as Muhammad seeing Gabriel in his true form, and then adds that Gabriel had six hundred wings. The issue is not only the number of wings. The issue is the exegetical move. The report turns a verse about revelation from God to His servant into a report about Gabriel’s appearance. قَالَ أَخْبَرَنِي ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ رَأَى جِبْرِيلَ لَهُ سِتُّمِائَةِ جَنَاحٍ “He said: Ibn Masʿūd informed me that the Prophet saw Gabriel, and he had six hundred wings.” The wording is simple, but its function is large. It is not a free-floating angelology report. It is a tafsīr report. Zirr is asked about Qur’an 53, and he answers by transmitting Ibn Masʿūd’s statement about Gabriel. That is why the chain and the context matter. The Isnād Map The diagram below replaces the older raw image with a cleaner route map. The important point is not how many boxes appear at the bottom. The important point is where all the lines meet. Every listed route comes down through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī. For a lay reader, this means the report has a bottleneck. A bottleneck is the point in a transmission map where many later roads collapse into one earlier road. Here, the later collectors preserve several routes, but they are not independent at the level that matters. They all return to the same Kūfan exegetical strand. That does not automatically prove the report is invented. But it prevents an exaggerated claim. One cannot simply say, “Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī all have it, therefore it is broadly established.” The real question is where the report becomes recoverable before the collectors. The answer is al-Shaybānī from Zirr from Ibn Masʿūd. Reference Route below al-Shaybānī Shared upper route Bukhārī 3232 Qutaybah b. Saʿīd → Abū ʿAwānah al-Waḍḍāḥ b. ʿAbd Allāh → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Bukhārī 4856 Abū al-Nuʿmān Muḥammad b. al-Faḍl → ʿAbd al-Wāḥid b. Ziyād → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Bukhārī 4857 Ṭalq b. Ghannām → Zāʾidah b. Qudāmah al-Thaqafī → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Muslim 174a Abū al-Rabīʿ al-Zahrānī → ʿAbbād b. al-ʿAwwām → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Muslim 174b Abū Bakr b. Abī Shaybah → Ḥafṣ b. Ghiyāth → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Muslim 174c ʿUbayd Allāh b. Muʿādh al-ʿAnbarī → Muʿādh b. Muʿādh b. Naṣr → Shuʿbah b. al-Ḥajjāj → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd Tirmidhī 3277 Aḥmad b. Manīʿ → ʿAbbād b. al-ʿAwwām → al-Shaybānī al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd This table shows why the report should be discussed as one exegetical family, not as a broad multi-origin tradition. The collector-facing routes differ. The upper route does not. The Matn Problem The matn is short. But the interpretive problem is large. سَأَلْتُ زِرَّ بْنَ حُبَيْشٍ عَنْ قَوْلِ اللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ: فَكَانَ قَابَ قَوْسَيْنِ أَوْ أَدْنَى. قَالَ: أَخْبَرَنِي ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ رَأَى جِبْرِيلَ وَلَهُ سِتُّمِائَةِ جَنَاحٍ “I asked Zirr b. Ḥubaysh about the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: ‘He was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer.’ He said: Ibn Masʿūd informed me that the Prophet saw Gabriel, and he had six hundred wings.” Notice the structure. The report begins with a question about a Qur’anic verse. It ends with a claim about Gabriel’s wings. That means the report is doing tafsīr work. It is telling the reader how to understand the vision scene in Sūrat al-Najm. The problem is that Qur’an 53:10 reads as God revealing to His servant. The servant is Muhammad. The revealer is God. The hadith explanation places Gabriel at the center and makes the point of the verse the Prophet’s vision of Gabriel. That is not the most natural reading of the verse itself. This does not mean a reader must deny that Gabriel appears elsewhere in Sūrat al-Najm. The point is narrower. The hadith report is not merely preserving a neutral historical memory. It is intervening in the meaning of a verse. It supplies an exegetical explanation and then builds angelology on top of that explanation. Qur’an 35:1 and the Wings of Angels Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as messengers with wings: two, three, and four. The same verse also says that God increases in creation what He wills. That last clause matters because it is often used as the traditional answer to the objection. A defender can say, “The verse mentions two, three, and four, but then says God increases in creation, so six hundred is possible.” That response is possible, but it does not remove the critical problem. The Qur’an itself does not say Gabriel has six hundred wings. The hadith supplies that number through one exegetical chain. The question is not whether God could create an angel with more wings. The question is whether this specific report has strong enough textual and transmission evidence to impose six hundred wings onto Gabriel and then use that as the explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The better argument is therefore precise. Qur’an 35:1 does not directly teach six hundred wings. Qur’an 53:10 does not naturally require Gabriel as the subject of “His servant.” The six-hundred-wings claim comes from a narrow hadith-tafsīr strand, not from the Qur’an itself. Why the Bottleneck Matters Hadith reports can look stronger than they are when later branches are counted as if each branch were an independent origin. Here, the report appears in Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī, but the major routes converge through al-Shaybānī. That means the collector spread is real, but the early spread is limited. The key question is not, “How many books contain this?” The key question is, “Where does the report become recoverable?” For this family, the answer is: **Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī → Zirr b. Ḥubaysh → Ibn Masʿūd.** That makes al-Shaybānī the visible bottleneck of the preserved family. Zirr is also central because he is the one being asked about the verse. Ibn Masʿūd is the Companion authority used to anchor the explanation. But the later literary spread does not create multiple independent Companion-level witnesses. The report’s strength should not be exaggerated by counting Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī as though they were separate early origins. They are separate collector witnesses to one shared upper route. The Report as Exegesis, Not Independent Angelology The most important correction is conceptual. The report is often treated as if it were mainly about the physical form of Gabriel. But the report itself begins as an explanation of Sūrat al-Najm. The question is about Qur’anic wording. The answer is a hadith explanation. That changes how the report should be evaluated. If it were an independent report from multiple Companions saying, “The Prophet saw Gabriel with six hundred wings,” the issue would be one thing. But the recoverable family is specifically Ibn Masʿūd’s interpretation transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī. The number belongs to that exegetical tradition. It is also important that the Qur’an does not need the six-hundred-wings report to make sense. Qur’an 53:10 can be read as God revealing to His servant. Qur’an 35:1 already gives a restrained description of angels as winged messengers. The hadith adds a dramatic number and then attaches it to a disputed reading of the vision passage. What the Diagram Shows The diagram does not show that every individual in the chain was unreliable. That is not the point. It shows that the report is structurally narrow. The chain does not branch at Ibn Masʿūd into multiple students. It does not branch at Zirr into many independent transmitters. It branches below al-Shaybānī. That means the “six hundred wings” tradition is not a broad early memory. It is a compact Kūfan tafsīr report that later became widely cited because major compilers preserved its branches. The same pattern appears in many hadith studies. A report can have many later witnesses but still depend on one earlier bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is identified, the report has to be argued from that bottleneck, not from the number of later books. Final Verdict The “Gabriel had six hundred wings” report is best understood as a narrow exegetical hadith family, not as Qur’anic angelology. Its main preserved routes all converge through Abū Isḥāq al-Shaybānī from Zirr b. Ḥubaysh from Ibn Masʿūd. The later branches into Bukhārī, Muslim, and Tirmidhī show that the report circulated well below al-Shaybānī, but they do not create independent early origins above him. The Qur’anic issue is also important. Qur’an 35:1 describes angels as having wings in twos, threes, and fours, while also saying God increases in creation what He wills. That means the verse should not be used in a simplistic way, as if it mechanically forbids all increase. But it also does not teach six hundred wings. The six-hundred number is supplied by hadith, not by the Qur’an. Qur’an 53:10 is even more central. The verse naturally reads as God revealing to His servant. The hadith turns the passage into a statement about Muhammad seeing Gabriel and then adds the six-hundred-wings detail. That is an exegetical move, and the isnād map shows that the move is preserved through one compact Kūfan route. So the strongest conclusion is careful but clear: the Qur’an does not require the six-hundred-wings doctrine, and the hadith evidence for it depends on a narrow tafsīr bottleneck. The report is not a broad independent memory of Gabriel’s form. It is Ibn Masʿūd’s Qur’an-exegesis tradition as transmitted through Zirr and al-Shaybānī.
