title: The Sunni-Quranic Abrogation Dilemma
description: A source-based critique of Quranic abrogation in Sunni legal theory, showing how the doctrine creates an unstable index of supposedly inactive verses and conflicts with the Quran

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Quranic Epistemology · Abrogation · Sunni Legal Theory The problem is not merely that scholars disagreed. The problem is that the doctrine gives them permission to retire revelation. The Sunni doctrine of Quranic abrogation says that some Quranic rulings were replaced by later rulings. In its narrowest form, it means that a later revealed command cancels an earlier command when both cannot be practiced together. In its wider historical use, however, it became a way to explain away verses that sat uneasily with later law, later warfare theory, or inherited legal assumptions. That is where the dilemma begins. If a verse from God can remain in the mushaf while its ruling is treated as no longer operative, then ordinary believers need a reliable way to know which verses still bind them. The classical tradition never produced a universally agreed Quranic index of abrogated verses. It produced lists, counter-lists, reductions, reclassifications, and debates over whether many alleged cases were abrogation at all. The argument is not that no Muslim scholar ever tried to define naskh carefully. Some did. The argument is that once intra-Quranic abrogation is accepted, the believer is forced to rely on contested post-Quranic scholarship to know which Quranic commands are still operative. ## The Quranic Baseline The Quran repeatedly describes God's words as complete, true, just, and not subject to alteration. Any doctrine that says a verse is present in recitation but no longer operative has to be measured against that baseline. These verses do not disappear because later scholars developed a technical category called naskh. A Muslim can try to argue that abrogation is not "changing God's words" because God Himself replaces one ruling with another. But then the evidence must be clear. It cannot rest on later discomfort, broad contradiction claims, or an inherited habit of declaring difficult verses mansukh. Quranic claim God's words are complete and unalterable. The text presents itself as guidance, not as a book whose operative parts must later be sorted by conflicting scholarly lists. Sunni naskh claim Some verses remain recited but no longer rule. That claim requires an external method for identifying inactive verses with certainty. The dilemma The method is disputed. The classical tradition preserves disagreement over which verses are abrogated and even over what should count as abrogation. ## The Verses Usually Used for Abrogation The two verses most often invoked are 2:106 and 16:101. These verses mention replacing or causing an aya to be forgotten. The traditional argument reads aya here as a Quranic verse. That reading is possible, but it is not the only possible reading of the word. In the Quran, aya can mean a sign, proof, miracle, or revealed communication. The context of 16:101 also includes the accusation that Muhammad is fabricating, which means the verse is defending God's authority over revelation rather than giving later jurists a blank license to cancel difficult verses. The safer reading is this: if God replaces one aya with another, that is God's action. It does not follow that later scholars may take every apparent tension, every historical sequence, or every legal inconvenience and declare one Quranic passage inactive. ## Al-Suyuti Tried to Narrow the Chaos Al-Suyuti did not invent the abrogation problem. He inherited a field already swollen with claims. In al-Itqan fi Ulum al-Quran , he reports that people had greatly multiplied the number of alleged abrogated verses, then he gives a reduced list. He says the refined list has twenty cases and puts it into verse so it can be remembered.[^1] قَدْ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسُ فِي الْمَنْسُوخِ مِنْ عَدَدٍ وَأَدْخَلُوا فِيهِ آيًا لَيْسَ تَنْحَصِرُ وَهَاكَ تَحْرِيرَ آيٍ لَا مَزِيدَ لَهَا عِشْرِينَ حَرَّرَهَا الْحُذَّاقُ وَالْكُبَرُ “People have greatly multiplied the number of abrogated verses and have included verses beyond counting. Here is a refined list of verses, with no addition to it: twenty, refined by the skilled and senior scholars.” This reduction is often presented as a sign of discipline. It is also evidence of the problem. If earlier scholars could multiply abrogation claims beyond measure, and a later scholar has to reduce them, then the method was never self-evident. The Quran did not come with a visible label on each verse saying "operative" or "abrogated." Al-Suyuti also preserves a stricter methodological warning from Ibn al-Hassar: abrogation should only be known through an explicit report from the Messenger, a Companion saying that one verse abrogated another, or a clear historical contradiction where the earlier and later rulings are known. He says that one does not rely on the opinions of common exegetes or on mere juristic reasoning, because abrogation involves removing one established ruling and affirming another.[^2] The standard al-Suyuti preserves Abrogation requires explicit transmission or clear chronological contradiction. It is not supposed to be a tool for every exegete who sees tension between two verses. The problem is that this stricter standard undercuts many casual abrogation claims. If the proof must be explicit and historically controlled, then most claims become doubtful. If the proof can be loose and interpretive, then the Quran becomes vulnerable to legal editing by later scholars. ## Ibn al-Jawzi Shows the Same Problem from Another Angle Ibn al-Jawzi wrote a full work on the abrogating and abrogated verses, Nawasikh al-Quran . The book does not present a simple, universally agreed list. It discusses a large field of alleged abrogation cases. In the printed arrangement available online, the section on verses claimed to be abrogated introduces a discussion of **247 issues across 62 surahs**.[^3] That number should not be confused with the number of cases Ibn al-Jawzi finally accepts. A serious reader has to distinguish between: Claimed cases Many Verses earlier writers or interpreters alleged to be abrogated. Accepted cases Fewer Cases a given scholar actually accepts after applying his criteria. Rejected cases Many again Cases later scholars deny because they are better explained as specification, context, exception, or no conflict at all. This distinction actually strengthens the critique. The tradition itself testifies that large numbers of abrogation claims were made, contested, reduced, and corrected. The doctrine did not simply clarify the Quran. It generated a second-order discipline whose job was to decide which verses people had wrongly retired. Ibn al-Jawzi himself lists conditions for valid abrogation. One of them is that the two rulings must truly contradict in a way that makes combined practice impossible. Another is that the later ruling must be established by a path equal to or stronger than the earlier one. He also rejects the idea that ordinary custom being replaced by revelation counts as abrogation.[^4] That matters because many alleged abrogations are not real abrogations even by classical standards. A verse may be general and later specified. It may be conditional. It may describe one circumstance while another verse describes another. Calling all of that naskh turns interpretation into cancellation. ## The Categories Make the Dilemma Worse The doctrine did not stop at ordinary legal replacement. Classical manuals discuss several kinds of abrogation, including: Type Meaning Why it creates pressure Ruling abrogated, recitation remains The verse is still in the Quran, but its legal force is gone. The reader encounters God's words but is told not to apply the apparent ruling. Recitation abrogated, ruling remains The words are no longer recited as Quran, but the law supposedly remains. A binding law is attached to wording no longer present in the mushaf. Both recitation and ruling abrogated The words and ruling are both said to have been removed. The doctrine depends almost entirely on reports outside the present Quranic text. Al-Suyuti preserves these categories and gives examples, including the famous report attributed to Aisha about ten known sucklings being abrogated by five known sucklings, while some people still recited the latter after the Prophet's death.[^5] He also reports examples of material said to have been revealed and then lifted from recitation, such as reports about the people of Bir Mauna and other alleged missing or lifted passages.[^6] This is not just a legal theory. It becomes a theory about the history of the Quranic text itself. For a Quran-centered theology, that is not a small matter. ## The Table Problem The difficulty becomes visible when later scholars and editors build tables of alleged abrogated verses. In one table attached to Ibn al-Jawzi's work, a verse such as 2:109 is listed with scholars who claimed abrogation and scholars who denied it. The same table identifies al-Nahhas among those who claimed abrogation while listing Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Suyuti, and others among those who denied it.[^7] Quran 2:109 Claimed abrogation Some treated “forgive and overlook until God brings His command” as abrogated by the fighting verses. Counter-reading Others denied abrogation because the verse contains its own limit: “until God brings His command.” A time-limited command is not necessarily cancelled by contradiction. This kind of case shows why the doctrine is unstable in practice. One scholar sees abrogation. Another sees a verse with a built-in endpoint. Another sees specification. Another sees contextual sequencing. The result is not a revealed index. It is a scholastic sorting process. ## The Epistemological Crisis A doctrine about divine guidance should not make divine guidance harder to identify. If God intended some verses to remain in the Quran while their rulings no longer apply, then the believer needs more than scholarly confidence. He needs certainty. The classical tradition often answers by saying that only qualified scholars can know these matters. But that answer shifts the problem. The scholars themselves disagreed. Some expanded the list. Others reduced it. Some called cases abrogation. Others called the same cases specification, restriction, explanation, or time-limited command. Option 1 Accept broad abrogation The Quran becomes dependent on later scholarly lists to know which commands still operate. Option 2 Accept narrow abrogation Most classical claims collapse, and many famous examples have to be reclassified. Option 3 Reject intra-Quranic cancellation The Quran remains internally binding, while apparent tensions must be solved by context, scope, and careful reading. The third option fits the Quranic self-description best. It does not require pretending that scholars never noticed tension. It simply refuses to let later inherited tension cancel God's words. ## What Naskh Often Does in Practice In practice, many abrogation claims do not solve contradictions. They avoid interpretation. A verse about patience is treated as cancelled by a verse about fighting. A verse about forgiveness is treated as cancelled by a verse about combat. A verse about bequest is treated as cancelled by inheritance law. A verse about private consultation is treated as cancelled after one incident. Sometimes this is defended through chronology. Sometimes it is defended by legal need. Sometimes the proof is much weaker than the claim. The Quran gives a different reading discipline: If the Quran contains no contradiction, the first task is reconciliation, not cancellation. A contradiction should not be manufactured by ignoring conditions, context, audience, genre, and scope. If falsehood does not come to it from before it or behind it, the burden is on the person who claims that one Quranic statement has legally neutralized another. That burden is rarely met with the kind of certainty the doctrine requires. The Sunni doctrine of Quranic abrogation creates a theological and epistemic problem. It asks believers to accept that some Quranic verses remain recited while no longer ruling, but it does not provide a universally agreed Quranic index for identifying them. The classical tradition preserves reduction, disagreement, and reclassification. A Quran-centered approach should treat every verse as binding within its proper context unless the Quran itself clearly limits it. ## Conclusion The doctrine of abrogation was supposed to protect the coherence of revelation. In practice, it often made the Quran dependent on later scholarly sorting. Al-Suyuti had to reduce inflated lists. Ibn al-Jawzi had to discuss and sift through large numbers of alleged cases. Classical authorities warned that abrogation cannot rest on loose opinion. Yet the doctrine continued to be used as a way to retire verses from active force. A book that calls itself complete and unalterable should not require believers to wonder which of God's words are no longer operative. Apparent tension should be handled through context, qualification, and careful interpretation. It should not be handled by building a second book beside the Quran, one that tells the reader which parts of the first book no longer count. fullText: Quranic Epistemology · Abrogation · Sunni Legal Theory The problem is not merely that scholars disagreed. The problem is that the doctrine gives them permission to retire revelation. The Sunni doctrine of Quranic abrogation says that some Quranic rulings were replaced by later rulings. In its narrowest form, it means that a later revealed command cancels an earlier command when both cannot be practiced together. In its wider historical use, however, it became a way to explain away verses that sat uneasily with later law, later warfare theory, or inherited legal assumptions. That is where the dilemma begins. If a verse from God can remain in the mushaf while its ruling is treated as no longer operative, then ordinary believers need a reliable way to know which verses still bind them. The classical tradition never produced a universally agreed Quranic index of abrogated verses. It produced lists, counter-lists, reductions, reclassifications, and debates over whether many alleged cases were abrogation at all. The argument is not that no Muslim scholar ever tried to define naskh carefully. Some did. The argument is that once intra-Quranic abrogation is accepted, the believer is forced to rely on contested post-Quranic scholarship to know which Quranic commands are still operative. The Quranic Baseline The Quran repeatedly describes God's words as complete, true, just, and not subject to alteration. Any doctrine that says a verse is present in recitation but no longer operative has to be measured against that baseline. These verses do not disappear because later scholars developed a technical category called naskh. A Muslim can try to argue that abrogation is not "changing God's words" because God Himself replaces one ruling with another. But then the evidence must be clear. It cannot rest on later discomfort, broad contradiction claims, or an inherited habit of declaring difficult verses mansukh. Quranic claim God's words are complete and unalterable. The text presents itself as guidance, not as a book whose operative parts must later be sorted by conflicting scholarly lists. Sunni naskh claim Some verses remain recited but no longer rule. That claim requires an external method for identifying inactive verses with certainty. The dilemma The method is disputed. The classical tradition preserves disagreement over which verses are abrogated and even over what should count as abrogation. The Verses Usually Used for Abrogation The two verses most often invoked are 2:106 and 16:101. These verses mention replacing or causing an aya to be forgotten. The traditional argument reads aya here as a Quranic verse. That reading is possible, but it is not the only possible reading of the word. In the Quran, aya can mean a sign, proof, miracle, or revealed communication. The context of 16:101 also includes the accusation that Muhammad is fabricating, which means the verse is defending God's authority over revelation rather than giving later jurists a blank license to cancel difficult verses. The safer reading is this: if God replaces one aya with another, that is God's action. It does not follow that later scholars may take every apparent tension, every historical sequence, or every legal inconvenience and declare one Quranic passage inactive. Al-Suyuti Tried to Narrow the Chaos Al-Suyuti did not invent the abrogation problem. He inherited a field already swollen with claims. In al-Itqan fi Ulum al-Quran , he reports that people had greatly multiplied the number of alleged abrogated verses, then he gives a reduced list. He says the refined list has twenty cases and puts it into verse so it can be remembered.[^1] قَدْ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسُ فِي الْمَنْسُوخِ مِنْ عَدَدٍ وَأَدْخَلُوا فِيهِ آيًا لَيْسَ تَنْحَصِرُ وَهَاكَ تَحْرِيرَ آيٍ لَا مَزِيدَ لَهَا عِشْرِينَ حَرَّرَهَا الْحُذَّاقُ وَالْكُبَرُ “People have greatly multiplied the number of abrogated verses and have included verses beyond counting. Here is a refined list of verses, with no addition to it: twenty, refined by the skilled and senior scholars.” This reduction is often presented as a sign of discipline. It is also evidence of the problem. If earlier scholars could multiply abrogation claims beyond measure, and a later scholar has to reduce them, then the method was never self-evident. The Quran did not come with a visible label on each verse saying "operative" or "abrogated." Al-Suyuti also preserves a stricter methodological warning from Ibn al-Hassar: abrogation should only be known through an explicit report from the Messenger, a Companion saying that one verse abrogated another, or a clear historical contradiction where the earlier and later rulings are known. He says that one does not rely on the opinions of common exegetes or on mere juristic reasoning, because abrogation involves removing one established ruling and affirming another.[^2] The standard al-Suyuti preserves Abrogation requires explicit transmission or clear chronological contradiction. It is not supposed to be a tool for every exegete who sees tension between two verses. The problem is that this stricter standard undercuts many casual abrogation claims. If the proof must be explicit and historically controlled, then most claims become doubtful. If the proof can be loose and interpretive, then the Quran becomes vulnerable to legal editing by later scholars. Ibn al-Jawzi Shows the Same Problem from Another Angle Ibn al-Jawzi wrote a full work on the abrogating and abrogated verses, Nawasikh al-Quran . The book does not present a simple, universally agreed list. It discusses a large field of alleged abrogation cases. In the printed arrangement available online, the section on verses claimed to be abrogated introduces a discussion of **247 issues across 62 surahs**.[^3] That number should not be confused with the number of cases Ibn al-Jawzi finally accepts. A serious reader has to distinguish between: Claimed cases Many Verses earlier writers or interpreters alleged to be abrogated. Accepted cases Fewer Cases a given scholar actually accepts after applying his criteria. Rejected cases Many again Cases later scholars deny because they are better explained as specification, context, exception, or no conflict at all. This distinction actually strengthens the critique. The tradition itself testifies that large numbers of abrogation claims were made, contested, reduced, and corrected. The doctrine did not simply clarify the Quran. It generated a second-order discipline whose job was to decide which verses people had wrongly retired. Ibn al-Jawzi himself lists conditions for valid abrogation. One of them is that the two rulings must truly contradict in a way that makes combined practice impossible. Another is that the later ruling must be established by a path equal to or stronger than the earlier one. He also rejects the idea that ordinary custom being replaced by revelation counts as abrogation.[^4] That matters because many alleged abrogations are not real abrogations even by classical standards. A verse may be general and later specified. It may be conditional. It may describe one circumstance while another verse describes another. Calling all of that naskh turns interpretation into cancellation. The Categories Make the Dilemma Worse The doctrine did not stop at ordinary legal replacement. Classical manuals discuss several kinds of abrogation, including: Type Meaning Why it creates pressure Ruling abrogated, recitation remains The verse is still in the Quran, but its legal force is gone. The reader encounters God's words but is told not to apply the apparent ruling. Recitation abrogated, ruling remains The words are no longer recited as Quran, but the law supposedly remains. A binding law is attached to wording no longer present in the mushaf. Both recitation and ruling abrogated The words and ruling are both said to have been removed. The doctrine depends almost entirely on reports outside the present Quranic text. Al-Suyuti preserves these categories and gives examples, including the famous report attributed to Aisha about ten known sucklings being abrogated by five known sucklings, while some people still recited the latter after the Prophet's death.[^5] He also reports examples of material said to have been revealed and then lifted from recitation, such as reports about the people of Bir Mauna and other alleged missing or lifted passages.[^6] This is not just a legal theory. It becomes a theory about the history of the Quranic text itself. For a Quran-centered theology, that is not a small matter. The Table Problem The difficulty becomes visible when later scholars and editors build tables of alleged abrogated verses. In one table attached to Ibn al-Jawzi's work, a verse such as 2:109 is listed with scholars who claimed abrogation and scholars who denied it. The same table identifies al-Nahhas among those who claimed abrogation while listing Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Suyuti, and others among those who denied it.[^7] Quran 2:109 Claimed abrogation Some treated “forgive and overlook until God brings His command” as abrogated by the fighting verses. Counter-reading Others denied abrogation because the verse contains its own limit: “until God brings His command.” A time-limited command is not necessarily cancelled by contradiction. This kind of case shows why the doctrine is unstable in practice. One scholar sees abrogation. Another sees a verse with a built-in endpoint. Another sees specification. Another sees contextual sequencing. The result is not a revealed index. It is a scholastic sorting process. The Epistemological Crisis A doctrine about divine guidance should not make divine guidance harder to identify. If God intended some verses to remain in the Quran while their rulings no longer apply, then the believer needs more than scholarly confidence. He needs certainty. The classical tradition often answers by saying that only qualified scholars can know these matters. But that answer shifts the problem. The scholars themselves disagreed. Some expanded the list. Others reduced it. Some called cases abrogation. Others called the same cases specification, restriction, explanation, or time-limited command. Option 1 Accept broad abrogation The Quran becomes dependent on later scholarly lists to know which commands still operate. Option 2 Accept narrow abrogation Most classical claims collapse, and many famous examples have to be reclassified. Option 3 Reject intra-Quranic cancellation The Quran remains internally binding, while apparent tensions must be solved by context, scope, and careful reading. The third option fits the Quranic self-description best. It does not require pretending that scholars never noticed tension. It simply refuses to let later inherited tension cancel God's words. What Naskh Often Does in Practice In practice, many abrogation claims do not solve contradictions. They avoid interpretation. A verse about patience is treated as cancelled by a verse about fighting. A verse about forgiveness is treated as cancelled by a verse about combat. A verse about bequest is treated as cancelled by inheritance law. A verse about private consultation is treated as cancelled after one incident. Sometimes this is defended through chronology. Sometimes it is defended by legal need. Sometimes the proof is much weaker than the claim. The Quran gives a different reading discipline: If the Quran contains no contradiction, the first task is reconciliation, not cancellation. A contradiction should not be manufactured by ignoring conditions, context, audience, genre, and scope. If falsehood does not come to it from before it or behind it, the burden is on the person who claims that one Quranic statement has legally neutralized another. That burden is rarely met with the kind of certainty the doctrine requires. The Sunni doctrine of Quranic abrogation creates a theological and epistemic problem. It asks believers to accept that some Quranic verses remain recited while no longer ruling, but it does not provide a universally agreed Quranic index for identifying them. The classical tradition preserves reduction, disagreement, and reclassification. A Quran-centered approach should treat every verse as binding within its proper context unless the Quran itself clearly limits it. Conclusion The doctrine of abrogation was supposed to protect the coherence of revelation. In practice, it often made the Quran dependent on later scholarly sorting. Al-Suyuti had to reduce inflated lists. Ibn al-Jawzi had to discuss and sift through large numbers of alleged cases. Classical authorities warned that abrogation cannot rest on loose opinion. Yet the doctrine continued to be used as a way to retire verses from active force. A book that calls itself complete and unalterable should not require believers to wonder which of God's words are no longer operative. Apparent tension should be handled through context, qualification, and careful interpretation. It should not be handled by building a second book beside the Quran, one that tells the reader which parts of the first book no longer count. title: How Long Did the Prophet Stay in Mecca?
description: A hadith-critical study of the conflicting reports that place the Prophet’s post-revelation Meccan period at ten, thirteen, or fifteen years, and what their isnāds reveal about early sīra chronology.

This sounds like a basic historical question. It should not be difficult. The common outline says the Prophet received revelation at around forty, preached in Mecca, migrated to Medina, and then lived in Medina for about ten years. On that outline, the Meccan period after revelation is usually counted as roughly thirteen years. But when we turn to the hadith corpus, the answer is not stable. Reports in major accepted collections give different numbers: ten years, thirteen years, and fifteen years. Some of these reports are attached to the same Companion, Ibn ʿAbbās. That creates a real historical problem. If accepted reports disagree on a basic chronological question, then “it is in Bukhārī” or “it is in Muslim” cannot by itself settle the matter. The problem is not that one weak report disagrees with a strong report. The problem is that accepted hadith collections preserve multiple incompatible durations for the Prophet’s Meccan period after revelation. This article does not argue that we know nothing about the Prophet’s Meccan period. It argues something more precise. The hadith transmission of this chronological detail is unstable. The reports preserve competing calculations, and the isnād map shows that the disagreement is not a simple matter of one isolated error. The reports are not merely contradictory. They preserve competing chronological systems. ## The Three Durations The basic conflict is simple. أَقَامَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً، وَتُوُفِّيَ وَهُوَ ابْنُ ثَلَاثٍ وَسِتِّينَ “The Messenger of God stayed in Mecca for thirteen years, and he died when he was sixty-three.” That is the familiar version. But it is not the only version. مَكَثَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ يُنْزَلُ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ، وَبِالْمَدِينَةِ عَشْرًا “The Prophet stayed in Mecca for ten years while the Qur’an was being revealed to him, and in Medina for ten years.” Another report gives fifteen years. أَقَامَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ خَمْسَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً، يَسْمَعُ الصَّوْتَ وَيَرَى الضَّوْءَ سَبْعَ سِنِينَ، وَلَا يَرَى شَيْئًا، وَثَمَانِيَ سِنِينَ يُوحَى إِلَيْهِ، وَأَقَامَ بِالْمَدِينَةِ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ “The Messenger of God stayed in Mecca for fifteen years. For seven years he heard the voice and saw the light but saw no visible form, and for eight years revelation was sent to him. He stayed in Medina for ten years.” These are not tiny variations. Ten, thirteen, and fifteen years are different chronologies. They cannot all be the same straightforward count unless someone changes what is being counted. Reported duration Meaning if taken literally Historical pressure 10 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for ten years after revelation while Qur’an was being revealed. This is shorter than the common sīra chronology unless the count begins from a later public or Qur’anic phase. 13 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for thirteen years after the first revelation. This best matches the common outline: revelation around age forty, migration before the Medinan decade, death at sixty-three. 15 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for fifteen years, sometimes divided into early visionary experience and later revelation. This requires a broader counting scheme and appears to preserve developed explanations of the Prophet’s earliest prophetic experience. The issue is not whether one can invent harmonizations. One can always say one report counts public preaching, another counts Qur’anic revelation, another counts visionary preparation, and another rounds the numbers. The issue is that the reports themselves do not present one clean chronology. The harmonization is imposed after the fact. ## Seeing the Problem at a Glance The disagreement is easier to understand when the reports are set beside one another. The issue is not merely that one transmitter said ten and another said thirteen. The issue is that the corpus preserves different chronological models for the Prophet’s life. The value of this comparison is that it prevents the discussion from being reduced to simple arithmetic. These numbers are doing interpretive work. They are not merely counting years. They are organizing the Prophet’s life into meaningful stages. 10 The symmetrical model This count gives Mecca and Medina the same length. It is elegant, but it creates tension with the more familiar age-of-death traditions. 13 The sīra model This is the count that best fits the standard narrative framework: revelation around forty, migration after about thirteen years, and death at sixty-three. 15 The expanded Meccan model This count seems to preserve a broader Meccan phase, one that can include hidden preaching, preparatory revelation, or other early narrative material. ## Rubin’s Point: These Are Chronological Models, Not Just Dates Uri Rubin’s discussion is important because it helps us describe the problem with more precision. The reports are not simply scattered memories of a date. They preserve models. The simplest model is **10–10**: ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. This creates a neat symmetry between the two periods of Qur’anic revelation. It also fits a broader typological scheme in which revelation begins at forty and the Prophet dies at sixty. That means the ten-year Meccan report should not be treated as a simple historical memory in isolation. It belongs to a schematic way of arranging the Prophet’s career. The two halves of his prophetic life are made equal: ten years of revelation in Mecca, then ten years in Medina. The problem is that this model collides with the more common age calculation of revelation beginning at forty and death at sixty-three. Once the death age becomes sixty-three, the old symmetry has to be repaired. One repair is the **13–10 model**: thirteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-three. This is the model that best fits the standard sīra outline. But the important point is that it looks like a correction of the earlier symmetry, not simply a neutral datum floating by itself. Three years are added to the Meccan period in order to preserve the age boundary of sixty-three. Rubin also notes that those extra three years could be filled with sīra material about non-Qur’anic revelations before Gabriel’s normal Qur’anic revelation. In some reports, between the ages of forty and forty-three, the Prophet receives a preliminary kind of revelation through Michael or Isrāfīl. Then, at forty-three, Gabriel begins bringing the proper Qur’anic revelation for ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. This preserves the 10–10 model for Qur’anic revelation while still allowing the Prophet to die at sixty-three. That is exactly the kind of thing a historian should notice. The traditions are not only reporting durations. They are solving chronological problems by inserting stages: pre-Qur’anic revelation, secret preaching, public preaching, Qur’anic revelation, and Medinan revelation. The chronology is being built out of interpretive material. This also explains the fifteen-year reports. The fifteen-year Meccan model is not just a bigger number. It absorbs additional sīra motifs. In some versions, five years are assigned to hidden preaching and ten years to public preaching. In another version, seven years are assigned to hearing voices and seeing light, while eight years are assigned to revelation. The number fifteen therefore functions as an expanded Meccan chronology that gives more room to the Prophet’s early prophetic preparation. The point is not that every version is equally plausible. The point is that the corpus preserves multiple chronological systems. Ten years creates symmetry. Thirteen years preserves the standard death age of sixty-three. Fifteen years expands the Meccan period by inserting earlier stages of preparation, hidden preaching, or non-Qur’anic revelation. These are not three clean eyewitness memories. They are competing ways of organizing the Prophet’s life. ## How the Different Models Were Built Once the reports are read together, a second pattern becomes visible. Each number appears to solve a slightly different problem. One model preserves symmetry. Another preserves the age of sixty-three. Another expands the Meccan period by drawing in poetry and early sīra motifs. That is why the disagreement should not be treated as a trivial discrepancy. The reports are not merely contradictory. They preserve competing chronological systems. ## A Useful Modern Study The modern study that helps bring this into focus most clearly is Uri Rubin’s *The Eye of the Beholder: The Life of Muḥammad as Viewed by the Early Muslims*. Rubin’s broader approach is useful because he is not treating the early Muslim texts as a simple window into “what happened.” He studies how the texts tell the story of Muḥammad’s life and what those evolving versions reveal about the image of the Prophet among the communities that transmitted them. STUDIES IN LATE ANTIQUITY AND EARLY ISLAM 5 THE EYE OF THE BEHOLDER THE LIFE OF MUḤAMMAD AS VIEWED BY THE EARLY MUSLIMS A Textual Analysis EJ Why it matters: Rubin shows that the chronology is not a flat list of remembered dates. It is shaped by literary models, poetic evidence, and competing conceptions of revelation, preaching, and prophetic beginnings. ## Poetry and the “Some Ten Years” Problem Rubin also draws attention to the role of poetry. Ibn Isḥāq preserves verses attributed to the Medinan poet Abū Qays Ṣirma b. Abī Anas. In those verses, the Prophet is said to have spent “some ten years” among Quraysh, preaching and seeking support before finding refuge among the Anṣār. This poetic line later enters the chronological discussion. That matters because **bidʿa ʿashrata hijjatan** does not mean a precise ten years. It means “some ten years,” or “a number over ten.” In later transmission, this poetic expression could be read in more than one way. Some transmitters used it to support a Meccan period longer than ten years. In one Ibn ʿAbbās-linked tradition, the wording becomes fifteen years rather than “some ten years.” This is important because it shows how chronological reports absorbed material from outside strict historical calculation. A poetic phrase about the Prophet’s long and unsuccessful preaching among Quraysh was pulled into hadith chronology and then used to support a larger Meccan period. The date was not simply remembered. It was argued from poetry, sīra motifs, and inherited models. That makes the conflict more serious. The reports are not just disagreeing over arithmetic. They are preserving different attempts to make sense of the Prophet’s early career. ## What the Corpus Adds A wider scan of the corpus strengthens the point. The disagreement is not just Bukhārī versus Muslim. Earlier and broader compilers already preserve the competing systems side by side. The scan produced five useful models: Model Meaning Why it matters 10 + 10, death at 60 Ten years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty. This is the cleanest symmetrical model, especially in Anas-linked material. 10 + 10, death at 63 Ten years of Qur’anic revelation in Mecca and ten in Medina, while still preserving death at sixty-three. This requires an extra pre-Qur’anic or preparatory phase before normal Qur’anic revelation. 13 + 10, death at 63 Thirteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-three. This is the standard sīra-compatible model and the strongest historical reconstruction. 15 + 10, death at 65 Fifteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-five. This expands the Meccan period and changes the age calculation. 15 with internal sub-stages Fifteen years in Mecca, sometimes divided into hidden preaching, early visionary experience, or later public revelation. This shows the number becoming a narrative framework rather than a bare date. This is the strongest version of the argument. The problem is not simply that “some hadith disagree.” The problem is that the tradition preserves multiple chronological systems trying to organize the same life period. ## Ibn Abī Shayba: The Conflict in One Early Chapter Ibn Abī Shayba is especially useful because he preserves several versions close together in a chapter on how old the Prophet was when revelation came to him. This makes the contradiction visible inside one early compilation rather than only through modern comparison. The early corpus itself preserves the competing systems. Ibn Abī Shayba does not give us one neat date. He gives us the problem. ## ʿAbd al-Razzāq: The Early Layer ʿAbd al-Razzāq is also important because he preserves several of the models in an early compilation. His material shows the same instability: ten plus ten, thirteen plus ten, and explanations that preserve ten years of Qur’anic revelation in Mecca by inserting a preparatory phase before Gabriel’s normal Qur’anic revelation. Ḥassān → Ibn Sīrīn → Ibn ʿAbbās Revelation at forty; Mecca thirteen; Medina ten; death at sixty-three. ʿAbd al-Razzāq 6785 Ismāʿīl b. ʿAbd Allāh → Dāwūd b. Abī Hind → al-Shaʿbī Michael or Isrāfīl assigned to him at forty for three years; Gabriel at forty-three; Qur’an in Mecca ten and Medina ten; death at sixty-three. ʿAbd al-Razzāq 6786 ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿUmar → Rabīʿah b. Abī ʿAbd al-Raḥmān → Anas Revelation at forty; Mecca ten; Medina ten; death at sixty. ʿAbd al-Razzāq 9734 Maʿmar → someone who heard ʿIkrimah Mecca fifteen, with four or five years of hidden preaching before the public command. The al-Shaʿbī version is especially revealing. It keeps the 10–10 structure for Qur’anic revelation, but it adds a three-year preparatory period before Gabriel. That is not raw memory. That is a harmonizing model. It answers a chronological problem by distinguishing between different kinds of revelation. ## The Internal Dispute The most important evidence is not merely that different reports give different numbers. It is that some reports already know about the disagreement. In the Saʿīd b. Jubayr route, a man tells Ibn ʿAbbās that revelation lasted ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. Ibn ʿAbbās asks where he heard this. The man says he heard people saying it. Ibn ʿAbbās then rejects the claim and gives a longer Meccan period. قِيلَ لِابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ: إِنَّهُ أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ بِمَكَّةَ، وَعَشْرَ سِنِينَ بِالْمَدِينَةِ. فَقَالَ: مَنْ يَقُولُ هَذَا؟ لَقَدْ أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ بِمَكَّةَ عَشْرًا وَخَمْسًا، وَأَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ “It was said to Ibn ʿAbbās: ‘Revelation was sent to him for ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina.’ He said: ‘Who says this? Revelation was sent to him in Mecca for ten and five, and more than that.’” This means the chronological dispute was not created by modern comparison. It was already present inside the early transmission environment. The ten-year view was circulating as a popular claim, and another Ibn ʿAbbās-linked tradition pushes back against it. That makes the argument much stronger. The issue is not only contradiction. It is recognized contradiction. ## The Isnād Map The old way to present this issue is to list the reports and then say they contradict. That is true, but it is not enough. The better way is to map the chains and ask where each number travels. For a lay reader, the diagram shows two things. First, the reports are not one chain with one obvious mistake. They are several route families. Second, the same Companion authority, Ibn ʿAbbās, appears behind conflicting numbers. That is the core historical problem. If Ibn ʿAbbās really gave one fixed chronological answer, then later transmission has not preserved it cleanly. Either different transmitters counted different things and later attached those counts to him, or variant chronological traditions were already circulating under his authority. In either case, the hadith record is not giving one stable memory. ## Why Ibn ʿAbbās Is Central Ibn ʿAbbās is the main Companion authority in the cluster. That is itself interesting. He was young during the Prophet’s lifetime and was not a direct adult witness to the earliest Meccan preaching. So when a report through Ibn ʿAbbās gives a chronology for the Meccan period, it is already a transmitted historical calculation, not his personal adult memory of those years. This does not make Ibn ʿAbbās useless as a source. It simply means his reports need to be treated as early historical tradition, not eyewitness diary material. The problem is that the same early historical authority is used for multiple answers. The issue is not Ibn ʿAbbās as a person. The issue is the later transmission of chronological claims under his authority. The reports make him support more than one duration. That is exactly the kind of place where isnād-cum-matn analysis matters. A hadith can have a respected Companion name at the top and still preserve a later calculation, harmonization, or exegetical scheme. ## The Thirteen-Year Reports The thirteen-year reports are the most historically comfortable. They match the common chronology: the Prophet receives revelation around forty, stays in Mecca until the Hijrah, then lives in Medina for about ten years, and dies at sixty-three. That does not mean every thirteen-year report is automatically original. It means the thirteen-year number fits the standard chronological framework better than the ten- or fifteen-year reports. The thirteen-year routes appear through several lines, including the ʿAmr b. Dīnār route, the Abū Jamrah route, the Ibn Sīrīn route, the ʿIkrimah route, and the ʿĀʾishah route through Abū Salamah. That gives the number broader support than the other counts. But even here, the existence of competing reports means we should not pretend the corpus is perfectly clean. ## The Ten-Year Reports The ten-year reports are the hardest if read literally. If the Prophet began receiving revelation at forty and died at sixty-three after ten years in Medina, then a ten-year Meccan revelation period does not fit the common arithmetic. It leaves only twenty years after forty, not twenty-three. A defender might say the ten-year reports count only the period of Qur’anic revelation after a preparatory phase, or that they count only the public phase, or that they round the number. Those are possible harmonizations. In fact, some reports already do this kind of work by inserting a three-year period involving Michael or Isrāfīl before Gabriel begins the proper Qur’anic revelation. That matters because it means the ten-year model is not just “bad math.” It became part of a larger harmonizing scheme. The ten years can be protected if the first three years after forty are made into another kind of prophetic preparation. ## The Fifteen-Year Reports The fifteen-year reports are different because they often include an explanatory structure. One version says the Prophet stayed in Mecca fifteen years: seven years hearing a voice and seeing light without seeing a visible form, then eight years of revelation, then ten years in Medina. This is not just a number. It is a narrative scheme. It divides the Meccan period into stages and explains early prophetic experience before regular revelation. That may preserve a real attempt to account for earlier visionary phenomena, but it also looks like a developed chronological explanation. The fifteen-year report should therefore be treated carefully. It may not be simply “wrong.” It may be counting a different kind of pre-revelation or pre-public prophetic experience. But if so, it is not answering the same question as the thirteen-year report. That means the hadith corpus is mixing different counting systems under the same general historical question. ## The Conflict in One Picture This is the main point. The conflict is real. It does not disappear because the reports are famous. It does not disappear because some of them are in Bukhārī or Muslim. Authentication tells us that later hadith critics accepted the chains according to their criteria. It does not turn three different numbers into one number. ## Why This Matters This question seems small, but it exposes a bigger problem. The Prophet’s Meccan period is foundational. It is the period of the first revelation, early preaching, persecution, migration, and the formation of the first community. If hadith reports disagree over something as basic as how long the period lasted, then we should be cautious about using hadith as if it gives direct access to a perfectly preserved biography. The reports are not useless. They are evidence. But they are evidence that must be analyzed, compared, and historically weighed. A report in an accepted collection can preserve a real early tradition and still conflict with another accepted report. That is why “ṣaḥīḥ” should not be confused with “historically settled.” A ṣaḥīḥ chain may mean the transmitters met the standards of later hadith critics. It does not guarantee that every chronological detail is historically exact. When accepted reports disagree on a basic chronological question, the historian cannot simply quote one and ignore the others. The reports have to be mapped, compared, and judged as historical traditions. ## What Is the Most Plausible Duration? The most plausible duration remains thirteen years. It fits the common chronological structure best: revelation begins around age forty, the Prophet migrates to Medina, remains there about ten years, and dies at sixty-three. That basic arithmetic supports thirteen years in Mecca after revelation. But the important point is not simply “thirteen wins.” The important point is how the hadith corpus preserves the disagreement. The ten-year and fifteen-year reports show that chronological traditions about the Meccan period were being counted and transmitted in different ways. Some reports may count only Qur’anic revelation. Others may count public preaching. Others may include a preparation phase before normal revelation. Others may round or compress. So the answer is: **Historically, thirteen years is the strongest reconstruction. Textually, the hadith corpus preserves conflicting accepted reports.** That distinction matters. ## Final Verdict The Prophet most likely remained in Mecca for about thirteen years after the beginning of revelation. That is the count that best fits the standard sīra chronology: revelation around forty, migration before the Medinan decade, and death at sixty-three. But the hadith record does not preserve this chronology cleanly. It preserves competing chronological systems. The **10–10 model** creates symmetry between Meccan and Medinan revelation. The **13–10 model** preserves the death age of sixty-three and fits the common sīra outline. The **15-year model** expands the Meccan period by absorbing stories of hidden preaching, early visionary experience, or non-Qur’anic revelation before Gabriel’s regular Qur’anic revelation. Poetry also enters the discussion, especially the phrase that the Prophet remained among Quraysh for “some ten years,” which could be used to push the Meccan period beyond a literal ten. That means the disagreement is not accidental. It is not just one bad transmitter getting a number wrong. The corpus preserves different ways of organizing the Prophet’s early career. Some reports count Qur’anic revelation. Others count public preaching. Others include a preparation phase before normal revelation. Others preserve a schematic symmetry between Mecca and Medina. So the historical conclusion and the hadith-critical conclusion must be kept separate. Historically, thirteen years remains the strongest reconstruction. Hadith-critically, the accepted corpus preserves more than one chronology, and later transmitters tried to solve the problem by building models around the numbers. The issue is therefore larger than a date. It shows that even basic sīra chronology was shaped through transmission, interpretation, poetry, symbolic numbering, and harmonization. This sounds like a basic historical question. It should not be difficult. The common outline says the Prophet received revelation at around forty, preached in Mecca, migrated to Medina, and then lived in Medina for about ten years. On that outline, the Meccan period after revelation is usually counted as roughly thirteen years. But when we turn to the hadith corpus, the answer is not stable. Reports in major accepted collections give different numbers: ten years, thirteen years, and fifteen years. Some of these reports are attached to the same Companion, Ibn ʿAbbās. That creates a real historical problem. If accepted reports disagree on a basic chronological question, then “it is in Bukhārī” or “it is in Muslim” cannot by itself settle the matter. The problem is not that one weak report disagrees with a strong report. The problem is that accepted hadith collections preserve multiple incompatible durations for the Prophet’s Meccan period after revelation. This article does not argue that we know nothing about the Prophet’s Meccan period. It argues something more precise. The hadith transmission of this chronological detail is unstable. The reports preserve competing calculations, and the isnād map shows that the disagreement is not a simple matter of one isolated error. The reports are not merely contradictory. They preserve competing chronological systems. The Three Durations The basic conflict is simple. أَقَامَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً، وَتُوُفِّيَ وَهُوَ ابْنُ ثَلَاثٍ وَسِتِّينَ “The Messenger of God stayed in Mecca for thirteen years, and he died when he was sixty-three.” That is the familiar version. But it is not the only version. مَكَثَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ يُنْزَلُ عَلَيْهِ الْقُرْآنُ، وَبِالْمَدِينَةِ عَشْرًا “The Prophet stayed in Mecca for ten years while the Qur’an was being revealed to him, and in Medina for ten years.” Another report gives fifteen years. أَقَامَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِمَكَّةَ خَمْسَ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً، يَسْمَعُ الصَّوْتَ وَيَرَى الضَّوْءَ سَبْعَ سِنِينَ، وَلَا يَرَى شَيْئًا، وَثَمَانِيَ سِنِينَ يُوحَى إِلَيْهِ، وَأَقَامَ بِالْمَدِينَةِ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ “The Messenger of God stayed in Mecca for fifteen years. For seven years he heard the voice and saw the light but saw no visible form, and for eight years revelation was sent to him. He stayed in Medina for ten years.” These are not tiny variations. Ten, thirteen, and fifteen years are different chronologies. They cannot all be the same straightforward count unless someone changes what is being counted. Reported duration Meaning if taken literally Historical pressure 10 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for ten years after revelation while Qur’an was being revealed. This is shorter than the common sīra chronology unless the count begins from a later public or Qur’anic phase. 13 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for thirteen years after the first revelation. This best matches the common outline: revelation around age forty, migration before the Medinan decade, death at sixty-three. 15 years The Prophet stayed in Mecca for fifteen years, sometimes divided into early visionary experience and later revelation. This requires a broader counting scheme and appears to preserve developed explanations of the Prophet’s earliest prophetic experience. The issue is not whether one can invent harmonizations. One can always say one report counts public preaching, another counts Qur’anic revelation, another counts visionary preparation, and another rounds the numbers. The issue is that the reports themselves do not present one clean chronology. The harmonization is imposed after the fact. Seeing the Problem at a Glance The disagreement is easier to understand when the reports are set beside one another. The issue is not merely that one transmitter said ten and another said thirteen. The issue is that the corpus preserves different chronological models for the Prophet’s life. The value of this comparison is that it prevents the discussion from being reduced to simple arithmetic. These numbers are doing interpretive work. They are not merely counting years. They are organizing the Prophet’s life into meaningful stages. 10 The symmetrical model This count gives Mecca and Medina the same length. It is elegant, but it creates tension with the more familiar age-of-death traditions. 13 The sīra model This is the count that best fits the standard narrative framework: revelation around forty, migration after about thirteen years, and death at sixty-three. 15 The expanded Meccan model This count seems to preserve a broader Meccan phase, one that can include hidden preaching, preparatory revelation, or other early narrative material. Rubin’s Point: These Are Chronological Models, Not Just Dates Uri Rubin’s discussion is important because it helps us describe the problem with more precision. The reports are not simply scattered memories of a date. They preserve models. The simplest model is **10–10**: ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. This creates a neat symmetry between the two periods of Qur’anic revelation. It also fits a broader typological scheme in which revelation begins at forty and the Prophet dies at sixty. That means the ten-year Meccan report should not be treated as a simple historical memory in isolation. It belongs to a schematic way of arranging the Prophet’s career. The two halves of his prophetic life are made equal: ten years of revelation in Mecca, then ten years in Medina. The problem is that this model collides with the more common age calculation of revelation beginning at forty and death at sixty-three. Once the death age becomes sixty-three, the old symmetry has to be repaired. One repair is the **13–10 model**: thirteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-three. This is the model that best fits the standard sīra outline. But the important point is that it looks like a correction of the earlier symmetry, not simply a neutral datum floating by itself. Three years are added to the Meccan period in order to preserve the age boundary of sixty-three. Rubin also notes that those extra three years could be filled with sīra material about non-Qur’anic revelations before Gabriel’s normal Qur’anic revelation. In some reports, between the ages of forty and forty-three, the Prophet receives a preliminary kind of revelation through Michael or Isrāfīl. Then, at forty-three, Gabriel begins bringing the proper Qur’anic revelation for ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. This preserves the 10–10 model for Qur’anic revelation while still allowing the Prophet to die at sixty-three. That is exactly the kind of thing a historian should notice. The traditions are not only reporting durations. They are solving chronological problems by inserting stages: pre-Qur’anic revelation, secret preaching, public preaching, Qur’anic revelation, and Medinan revelation. The chronology is being built out of interpretive material. This also explains the fifteen-year reports. The fifteen-year Meccan model is not just a bigger number. It absorbs additional sīra motifs. In some versions, five years are assigned to hidden preaching and ten years to public preaching. In another version, seven years are assigned to hearing voices and seeing light, while eight years are assigned to revelation. The number fifteen therefore functions as an expanded Meccan chronology that gives more room to the Prophet’s early prophetic preparation. The point is not that every version is equally plausible. The point is that the corpus preserves multiple chronological systems. Ten years creates symmetry. Thirteen years preserves the standard death age of sixty-three. Fifteen years expands the Meccan period by inserting earlier stages of preparation, hidden preaching, or non-Qur’anic revelation. These are not three clean eyewitness memories. They are competing ways of organizing the Prophet’s life. How the Different Models Were Built Once the reports are read together, a second pattern becomes visible. Each number appears to solve a slightly different problem. One model preserves symmetry. Another preserves the age of sixty-three. Another expands the Meccan period by drawing in poetry and early sīra motifs. That is why the disagreement should not be treated as a trivial discrepancy. The reports are not merely contradictory. They preserve competing chronological systems. A Useful Modern Study The modern study that helps bring this into focus most clearly is Uri Rubin’s *The Eye of the Beholder: The Life of Muḥammad as Viewed by the Early Muslims*. Rubin’s broader approach is useful because he is not treating the early Muslim texts as a simple window into “what happened.” He studies how the texts tell the story of Muḥammad’s life and what those evolving versions reveal about the image of the Prophet among the communities that transmitted them. STUDIES IN LATE ANTIQUITY AND EARLY ISLAM 5 THE EYE OF THE BEHOLDER THE LIFE OF MUḤAMMAD AS VIEWED BY THE EARLY MUSLIMS A Textual Analysis EJ Why it matters: Rubin shows that the chronology is not a flat list of remembered dates. It is shaped by literary models, poetic evidence, and competing conceptions of revelation, preaching, and prophetic beginnings. Poetry and the “Some Ten Years” Problem Rubin also draws attention to the role of poetry. Ibn Isḥāq preserves verses attributed to the Medinan poet Abū Qays Ṣirma b. Abī Anas. In those verses, the Prophet is said to have spent “some ten years” among Quraysh, preaching and seeking support before finding refuge among the Anṣār. This poetic line later enters the chronological discussion. That matters because **bidʿa ʿashrata hijjatan** does not mean a precise ten years. It means “some ten years,” or “a number over ten.” In later transmission, this poetic expression could be read in more than one way. Some transmitters used it to support a Meccan period longer than ten years. In one Ibn ʿAbbās-linked tradition, the wording becomes fifteen years rather than “some ten years.” This is important because it shows how chronological reports absorbed material from outside strict historical calculation. A poetic phrase about the Prophet’s long and unsuccessful preaching among Quraysh was pulled into hadith chronology and then used to support a larger Meccan period. The date was not simply remembered. It was argued from poetry, sīra motifs, and inherited models. That makes the conflict more serious. The reports are not just disagreeing over arithmetic. They are preserving different attempts to make sense of the Prophet’s early career. What the Corpus Adds A wider scan of the corpus strengthens the point. The disagreement is not just Bukhārī versus Muslim. Earlier and broader compilers already preserve the competing systems side by side. The scan produced five useful models: Model Meaning Why it matters 10 + 10, death at 60 Ten years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty. This is the cleanest symmetrical model, especially in Anas-linked material. 10 + 10, death at 63 Ten years of Qur’anic revelation in Mecca and ten in Medina, while still preserving death at sixty-three. This requires an extra pre-Qur’anic or preparatory phase before normal Qur’anic revelation. 13 + 10, death at 63 Thirteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-three. This is the standard sīra-compatible model and the strongest historical reconstruction. 15 + 10, death at 65 Fifteen years in Mecca, ten in Medina, death at sixty-five. This expands the Meccan period and changes the age calculation. 15 with internal sub-stages Fifteen years in Mecca, sometimes divided into hidden preaching, early visionary experience, or later public revelation. This shows the number becoming a narrative framework rather than a bare date. This is the strongest version of the argument. The problem is not simply that “some hadith disagree.” The problem is that the tradition preserves multiple chronological systems trying to organize the same life period. Ibn Abī Shayba: The Conflict in One Early Chapter Ibn Abī Shayba is especially useful because he preserves several versions close together in a chapter on how old the Prophet was when revelation came to him. This makes the contradiction visible inside one early compilation rather than only through modern comparison. The al-Shaʿbī version is especially revealing. It keeps the 10–10 structure for Qur’anic revelation, but it adds a three-year preparatory period before Gabriel. That is not raw memory. That is a harmonizing model. It answers a chronological problem by distinguishing between different kinds of revelation. The Internal Dispute The most important evidence is not merely that different reports give different numbers. It is that some reports already know about the disagreement. In the Saʿīd b. Jubayr route, a man tells Ibn ʿAbbās that revelation lasted ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina. Ibn ʿAbbās asks where he heard this. The man says he heard people saying it. Ibn ʿAbbās then rejects the claim and gives a longer Meccan period. قِيلَ لِابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ: إِنَّهُ أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ عَشْرَ سِنِينَ بِمَكَّةَ، وَعَشْرَ سِنِينَ بِالْمَدِينَةِ. فَقَالَ: مَنْ يَقُولُ هَذَا؟ لَقَدْ أُنْزِلَ عَلَيْهِ بِمَكَّةَ عَشْرًا وَخَمْسًا، وَأَكْثَرَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ “It was said to Ibn ʿAbbās: ‘Revelation was sent to him for ten years in Mecca and ten years in Medina.’ He said: ‘Who says this? Revelation was sent to him in Mecca for ten and five, and more than that.’” This means the chronological dispute was not created by modern comparison. It was already present inside the early transmission environment. The ten-year view was circulating as a popular claim, and another Ibn ʿAbbās-linked tradition pushes back against it. That makes the argument much stronger. The issue is not only contradiction. It is recognized contradiction. The Isnād Map The old way to present this issue is to list the reports and then say they contradict. That is true, but it is not enough. The better way is to map the chains and ask where each number travels. For a lay reader, the diagram shows two things. First, the reports are not one chain with one obvious mistake. They are several route families. Second, the same Companion authority, Ibn ʿAbbās, appears behind conflicting numbers. That is the core historical problem. If Ibn ʿAbbās really gave one fixed chronological answer, then later transmission has not preserved it cleanly. Either different transmitters counted different things and later attached those counts to him, or variant chronological traditions were already circulating under his authority. In either case, the hadith record is not giving one stable memory. Why Ibn ʿAbbās Is Central Ibn ʿAbbās is the main Companion authority in the cluster. That is itself interesting. He was young during the Prophet’s lifetime and was not a direct adult witness to the earliest Meccan preaching. So when a report through Ibn ʿAbbās gives a chronology for the Meccan period, it is already a transmitted historical calculation, not his personal adult memory of those years. This does not make Ibn ʿAbbās useless as a source. It simply means his reports need to be treated as early historical tradition, not eyewitness diary material. The problem is that the same early historical authority is used for multiple answers. The issue is not Ibn ʿAbbās as a person. The issue is the later transmission of chronological claims under his authority. The reports make him support more than one duration. That is exactly the kind of place where isnād-cum-matn analysis matters. A hadith can have a respected Companion name at the top and still preserve a later calculation, harmonization, or exegetical scheme. The Thirteen-Year Reports The thirteen-year reports are the most historically comfortable. They match the common chronology: the Prophet receives revelation around forty, stays in Mecca until the Hijrah, then lives in Medina for about ten years, and dies at sixty-three. That does not mean every thirteen-year report is automatically original. It means the thirteen-year number fits the standard chronological framework better than the ten- or fifteen-year reports. The thirteen-year routes appear through several lines, including the ʿAmr b. Dīnār route, the Abū Jamrah route, the Ibn Sīrīn route, the ʿIkrimah route, and the ʿĀʾishah route through Abū Salamah. That gives the number broader support than the other counts. But even here, the existence of competing reports means we should not pretend the corpus is perfectly clean. The Ten-Year Reports The ten-year reports are the hardest if read literally. If the Prophet began receiving revelation at forty and died at sixty-three after ten years in Medina, then a ten-year Meccan revelation period does not fit the common arithmetic. It leaves only twenty years after forty, not twenty-three. A defender might say the ten-year reports count only the period of Qur’anic revelation after a preparatory phase, or that they count only the public phase, or that they round the number. Those are possible harmonizations. In fact, some reports already do this kind of work by inserting a three-year period involving Michael or Isrāfīl before Gabriel begins the proper Qur’anic revelation. That matters because it means the ten-year model is not just “bad math.” It became part of a larger harmonizing scheme. The ten years can be protected if the first three years after forty are made into another kind of prophetic preparation. The Fifteen-Year Reports The fifteen-year reports are different because they often include an explanatory structure. One version says the Prophet stayed in Mecca fifteen years: seven years hearing a voice and seeing light without seeing a visible form, then eight years of revelation, then ten years in Medina. This is not just a number. It is a narrative scheme. It divides the Meccan period into stages and explains early prophetic experience before regular revelation. That may preserve a real attempt to account for earlier visionary phenomena, but it also looks like a developed chronological explanation. The fifteen-year report should therefore be treated carefully. It may not be simply “wrong.” It may be counting a different kind of pre-revelation or pre-public prophetic experience. But if so, it is not answering the same question as the thirteen-year report. That means the hadith corpus is mixing different counting systems under the same general historical question. The Conflict in One Picture This is the main point. The conflict is real. It does not disappear because the reports are famous. It does not disappear because some of them are in Bukhārī or Muslim. Authentication tells us that later hadith critics accepted the chains according to their criteria. It does not turn three different numbers into one number. Why This Matters This question seems small, but it exposes a bigger problem. The Prophet’s Meccan period is foundational. It is the period of the first revelation, early preaching, persecution, migration, and the formation of the first community. If hadith reports disagree over something as basic as how long the period lasted, then we should be cautious about using hadith as if it gives direct access to a perfectly preserved biography. The reports are not useless. They are evidence. But they are evidence that must be analyzed, compared, and historically weighed. A report in an accepted collection can preserve a real early tradition and still conflict with another accepted report. That is why “ṣaḥīḥ” should not be confused with “historically settled.” A ṣaḥīḥ chain may mean the transmitters met the standards of later hadith critics. It does not guarantee that every chronological detail is historically exact. When accepted reports disagree on a basic chronological question, the historian cannot simply quote one and ignore the others. The reports have to be mapped, compared, and judged as historical traditions. What Is the Most Plausible Duration? The most plausible duration remains thirteen years. It fits the common chronological structure best: revelation begins around age forty, the Prophet migrates to Medina, remains there about ten years, and dies at sixty-three. That basic arithmetic supports thirteen years in Mecca after revelation. But the important point is not simply “thirteen wins.” The important point is how the hadith corpus preserves the disagreement. The ten-year and fifteen-year reports show that chronological traditions about the Meccan period were being counted and transmitted in different ways. Some reports may count only Qur’anic revelation. Others may count public preaching. Others may include a preparation phase before normal revelation. Others may round or compress. So the answer is: **Historically, thirteen years is the strongest reconstruction. Textually, the hadith corpus preserves conflicting accepted reports.** That distinction matters. Final Verdict The Prophet most likely remained in Mecca for about thirteen years after the beginning of revelation. That is the count that best fits the standard sīra chronology: revelation around forty, migration before the Medinan decade, and death at sixty-three. But the hadith record does not preserve this chronology cleanly. It preserves competing chronological systems. The **10–10 model** creates symmetry between Meccan and Medinan revelation. The **13–10 model** preserves the death age of sixty-three and fits the common sīra outline. The **15-year model** expands the Meccan period by absorbing stories of hidden preaching, early visionary experience, or non-Qur’anic revelation before Gabriel’s regular Qur’anic revelation. Poetry also enters the discussion, especially the phrase that the Prophet remained among Quraysh for “some ten years,” which could be used to push the Meccan period beyond a literal ten. That means the disagreement is not accidental. It is not just one bad transmitter getting a number wrong. The corpus preserves different ways of organizing the Prophet’s early career. Some reports count Qur’anic revelation. Others count public preaching. Others include a preparation phase before normal revelation. Others preserve a schematic symmetry between Mecca and Medina. So the historical conclusion and the hadith-critical conclusion must be kept separate. Historically, thirteen years remains the strongest reconstruction. Hadith-critically, the accepted corpus preserves more than one chronology, and later transmitters tried to solve the problem by building models around the numbers. The issue is therefore larger than a date. It shows that even basic sīra chronology was shaped through transmission, interpretation, poetry, symbolic numbering, and harmonization. The reports are evidence, but they are not a single preserved stopwatch for the Prophet’s life.
