fullText: **QuranTalk** wrote a brilliant article arguing the case that the various accounts of Jesus in the Gospels constantly reflect a priestly figure, as opposed to the traditional warrior-king messiah that the Israelites were expecting. The genealogies in Matthew and Luke trace Jesus through Joseph, who by the virgin birth is not his biological father, which means those genealogies cannot actually establish a Davidic claim. Elizabeth, a relative of Mary, is called a descendant of Aaron in Luke 1:5. The Quran names Mary’s father Amram and calls Mary herself a ‘descendant of Aaron.’ And the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve a real Jewish expectation of two messiahs rather than one, a royal Messiah from David and a priestly Messiah from Aaron. Taken together, this pointed toward Jesus fulfilling the priestly role rather than the royal one. The argument of this study is that the Aaronic material surrounding Jesus is not merely an incidental set of Gospel details. It forms a coherent priestly pattern when read against the House of Amram, Second Temple messianic expectations, and the technical duties of the Aaronic priesthood. Tanakh and other Jewish source quotations in this piece are drawn from Sefaria.org and follow THE JPS TANAKH: Gender-Sensitive Edition (Philadelphia: Jewish Publication Society, 2023) unless a footnote specifies otherwise. New Testament quotations follow the NRSVUE and have been checked by hand, since the New Testament is outside Sefaria's library. This article asks why the name Amram was chosen at all, what that name meant to the people who first heard it, and what was actually happening to the Aaronic priesthood in the centuries before Jesus was born. QuranTalk's argument also left the 'Jesus as priest' case mostly at the level of teaching and temperament, resting on the Sermon on the Mount, the temple cleansing, and the language of Hebrews. There is a great deal more textual evidence sitting inside the Gospels themselves, evidence that has nothing to do with tone or teaching style and everything to do with specific priestly law. --- Amram Was Never *Just* a Man’s Name Amram, according to Exodus 6:20, was a specific individual. “Amram took to wife his father's sister Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses; and the span of Amram's life was 137 years.”[^1] Amram was the father of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam, roughly thirteen centuries before Mary, the mother of Jesus. If the Quran is naming Mary’s father Amram, the objection goes, it has simply confused Miriam (Moses’s sister) with Mary, the mother of Jesus; two names that happen to be identical in Arabic. This objection assumes Amram functions in the text the way a modern first name functions, as a label for one man and no one else. The Torah itself does not use it that way. Numbers 3:27 and 1 Chronicles 26:23 both list ‘the Amramites’ as one of four clans making up the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, alongside the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites. “To Kohath belonged the clan of the Amramites, the clan of the Izharites, the clan of the Hebronites, and the clan of the Uzzielites; those were the clans of the Kohathites.”[^2] “Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, the Uzzielites: Shebuel son of Gershom son of Moses was the chief officer over the treasuries.”[^3] The Kohathite clan of Levi was divided into four families—the Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites—numbering 8,600 males who camped on the south side of the tabernacle. Their privileged and weighty duty was to care for and transport the sanctuary’s most sacred furnishings, including the ark, table, lampstand, altars, and holy utensils, all under the oversight of Eleazar, Aaron’s son and chief over the Levite leaders. The Amramites are noted as the family from which Moses and Aaron descended.[^4] The Amramites in this passage were 8,600 men, one generation after the Exodus, all counted under a single ancestor’s name. This is the same pattern the Torah uses everywhere else for priestly lineage. The term “sons of Aaron” throughout Exodus and Leviticus does not mean Aaron’s literal children; it means the priestly house descending from him. The term “sons of Amram” is functioning the same way here—an ancestor’s name converted into the name of his house. There is a smaller detail worth noticing inside the Torah’s own text. Exodus 6:20 calls Aaron ‘an Amramite’ rather than stating plainly that Amram fathered him in that clause, and as already noted, the clan numbers in the thousands within a single generation. The term is already doing double duty as a household name within the Torah’s own priestly material, not functioning as strict biological paternity even there. Centuries later, in 1 Chronicles 26:23-28, the Amramite clan reappears in David’s reorganization of temple service, specifically placed in charge of the treasuries of the house of the Lord, which shows the clan designation was still an active administrative category long after the wilderness period, not a one-time census label that disappeared later in history. Read Q. 3:33 with this in mind. The third chapter in the Quran entitled “*Al Imran,*” the family of Amram, is named in the same verse as ‘the family of Abraham,’ a phrase nobody reads as Abraham’s literal household rather than the whole line descending from him. The verse reads, “*GOD has chosen Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Amram (as messengers) to the people.*”[^5] If “family of Amram” is doing the same work, the verse is not claiming Mary’s father was the thirteenth-century BCE man who fathered Aaron. It is identifying Mary as belonging to the Amramite house, the same Aaronic priestly clan the Torah names after that ancestor. Read this way, the name functions the way “House of David” functions elsewhere, marking lineage by clan founder rather than by a literal father one generation back. --- What the Name Itself Carried Imran (Amram) carries no independent meaning as an Arabic word; it functions purely as a proper name. It is most plausibly an Arabization of the Hebrew עַמְרָם (ʿAmrām), itself a compound of עַם (ʿam, “*people*”) and רָם (rām, “*exalted, high*”), yielding a sense along the lines of “*the people are exalted.*”[^6] Muhammad Hamidullah has suggested the term may function more like a title than a strict personal name, which fits comfortably with the clan reading above.[^7] Amram was not a forgettable name in the centuries before the Quran. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a text called *The Visions of Amram*, preserved in at least five separate Aramaic copies at Qumran (4Q543–4Q549), a real indication of how much the community that kept it valued this composition.[^8] In the Hebrew Bible, Amram is barely a character, a name in a census list. In *The Visions of Amram*, he becomes a dying patriarch who gathers his children, describes a vision in which two angelic powers contend for him, and blesses a son—almost certainly Aaron—in language of divine election and priestly commissioning.[^9] The text explicitly frames Amram as the third link in a chain of priestly succession running from Levi, to Kohath, to Amram, to Aaron. By the time Q. 3:33 says God ‘chose’ (istafa) Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham, and the family of Amram, using the exact vocabulary of divine election, it is applying that word to a name that already carried priestly weight in the surrounding tradition. --- A Priesthood Already Broken QuranTalk established that a priestly messiah, a Messiah ben Aaron, was a live expectation in certain Jewish communities by the first century. It is worth asking why. The Aaronic high priesthood had not simply been sitting quietly for centuries waiting for a Davidic king to show up alongside it. By the time Jesus was born, it had been broken, bought, and reassigned so many times that a large faction of religious Jews considered the office illegitimate. The argument here depends on distinguishing the broader Aaronic priesthood from the narrower Zadokite/Oniad succession dispute. The two overlap historically, but they are not interchangeable claims of lineage or legitimacy. The Prophetic Root of Two Messiahs Qumran’s two-messiah scheme did not appear from nowhere. It has a direct scriptural anchor in Zechariah, written in the early Persian period as the exiles rebuilt the temple. Zechariah 3 shows Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest, standing in filthy garments before the angel of the Lord, who has them stripped off him and replaced with clean priestly robes and a pure diadem, restoring him to office. The angel then tells Joshua directly that this is a sign of someone still to come. “Hearken well, O High Priest Joshua, you and your fellow priests sitting before you! For those men are a sign that I am going to bring My servant the Branch.”[^20] “The Branch” is Zechariah’s standing title for the future Davidic king, the same term Jeremiah uses for the ruler God will “raise up for David” (Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15). Three chapters later, Zechariah stages the coronation itself, and the priest and the Branch appear side by side rather than merged into one office. “Thus said GOD of Hosts: Behold, a man called the Branch shall branch out from the place where he is, and he shall build the Temple of GOD. He shall build the Temple of GOD and shall assume majesty, and he shall sit on his throne and rule. And there shall also be a priest seated on his throne, and harmonious understanding shall prevail between them.”[^21] Two figures, two thrones, one covenant of “harmonious understanding” between them, a royal Branch and a seated priest, ruling in tandem rather than in competition. This is the textual seed of exactly the two-messiah expectation Qumran later formalized: a Davidic king and an Aaronic priest as separate, coordinate offices, not one man wearing both crowns. Whatever else the Gospels are doing with Jesus, they are doing it against a scriptural background that had already imagined two anointed figures standing together in the same scene. The High Priesthood For Sale The line ran continuously from Solomon down to Onias III, high priest when Antiochus IV Epiphanes took the Seleucid throne around 175 BCE. Onias III’s own brother Jason bribed Antiochus to depose him and take the office for himself. Menelaus then outbid Jason for it, and according to 2 Maccabees 4:23-26, Menelaus was not even from a legitimate priestly family. Onias III was assassinated around 171 BCE. The office was already being bought and sold before the Maccabean revolt even began. In 167 BCE Antiochus desecrated the temple outright. By 159 BCE the high priest Alcimus was dead and the office sat vacant for seven years. In 152 BCE the Seleucid king Alexander Balas appointed Jonathan Maccabee, a Hasmonean with no Zadokite or Oniad ancestry, as high priest. Jonathan’s brother Simon made the office hereditary in the Hasmonean family shortly after, meaning the same family now held both the kingship and the high priesthood at once—a separation of powers that had held since David and Zadok. This is what triggered the formation of the Qumran community. Their ‘Teacher of Righteousness’ clashed directly with a Hasmonean high priest they called the “Wicked Priest,” and their self-designation as ‘sons of Zadok’ was a direct polemical claim. They argued that they were the legitimate priesthood; the Hasmoneans are usurpers. A remnant of the older Oniad line fled to Egypt and built a rival temple at Leontopolis rather than serve under the new arrangement. Herod the Great made things worse. An Idumean with no interest in a hereditary high priest accumulating independent legitimacy, Herod began appointing and deposing high priests at will, sometimes importing Diaspora priestly families with no ancestral claim to Jerusalem at all. Rome continued the same practice under the procurators. By Jesus’s lifetime, Annas, appointed high priest in 6 CE, and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office as a revolving political appointment rather than an unbroken sacred inheritance. By any older Israelite standard, the high priesthood had already lost legitimate succession roughly two centuries before Jesus’s ministry—which is precisely the establishment he confronted in the temple courts. Aaronic Is Not Zadokite The Zadokite lineage claim is not the same claim as an Aaronic one. Zadok is one specific high priestly branch descending from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas, not the entire Aaronic priesthood. Luke’s claim about Elizabeth is the broader Aaronic claim, ‘daughters of Aaron,’ not a narrower Zadokite one. A solid Aaronic descent claim for Mary’s side does not by itself place Jesus inside the specific Zadokite legitimacy dispute that Qumran and the Oniads were fighting over, though the two claims sit close together and both point toward the same underlying problem of a priesthood that badly needed correcting by the time Jesus arrived. Where the Pharisees Fit In It is also worth noting where the Pharisees fit into this picture, since they are so often treated as Jesus’s main opponents without explaining where their authority came from in the first place. The Pharisees were not priests contesting the priesthood; they were largely laymen and scribes who built a separate authority on legal scholarship and the transmission of oral tradition. Josephus dates their emergence as a distinct movement to the Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus, the same period the Zadokite priesthood was being displaced.[^10] As confidence in the priestly establishment eroded, the Pharisees filled the resulting vacuum through interpretive authority instead of hereditary office. The Sadducees, by contrast, stayed closer to the priestly aristocracy and temple administration, rejected the oral law, and were seen as more accommodating toward Rome—which is part of why both the Gospels and the Qumran texts treat the Sadducee-controlled temple establishment as compromised. --- Zeal for Your House Against that backdrop, the temple cleansing reads differently. It is the one moment across all four Gospels where Jesus takes forceful physical action, in a ministry otherwise defined by verbal rebuke, weeping, and healing rather than violence. John’s Gospel glosses the scene with a direct citation of Psalm 69:9, “*zeal for your house will consume me.*”[^11] Zeal, *qinah* in Hebrew, *zelos* in Greek, is covenantal jealousy language in biblical usage. It is reserved for defending something that already belongs to you, not generic outrage at wrongdoing in general. The precedent for that specific language is Phinehas, Aaron’s grandson, an Amramite by direct descent, who in Numbers 25:6-13 sees covenant defilement happening at the entrance to the sanctuary and acts violently to stop it. “I grant him My pact of friendship. It shall be for him and his descendants after him a pact of priesthood for all time, because he took impassioned action for his God, thus making expiation for the Israelites.”[^12] Two Covenants in the Same Breath This was not a one-time episode that faded from memory. Ben Sira, writing in the second century BCE, devotes a hymn to Israel's ancestors, and gives Phinehas his own place in it, a third portion of glory after Moses and Aaron, earned by his zeal at the exact moment the covenant itself was most exposed. “And also Phinehas son of Eleazar, in his strength, a third portion, in his zealousness to the God of all, stood at the people's breach. In his nobility and his heart he atoned for the children of Israel, so he too was given a law, an eternal covenant to administer the Sanctuary, that it would be his and his seed's, a great priesthood for all time. And also his covenant with David son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah.”[^22] The two covenants sit in the same sentence, one clause apart: an eternal priesthood for Phinehas's line, and immediately after it, the covenant with David. Ben Sira is not choosing between a royal messianic hope and a priestly one. He names both in the same breath, as though it would not occur to him that a reader might expect only one. Later Jewish memory kept treating Phinehas's zeal as a live legal precedent rather than an antiquarian detail. When Mattathias kills a Jew about to comply with a royal decree to sacrifice on a pagan altar, along with the king’s officer enforcing it, 1 Maccabees makes the citation explicit, saying “*he burned with zeal for the law, just as Phinehas did against Zimri son of Salu*” (1 Maccabees 2:26). Mattathias later invokes Phinehas by name on his deathbed while blessing his sons, telling them “*Phinehas our father, in return for his burning zeal, received the covenant of everlasting priesthood*” (1 Maccabees 2:54).[^13] By Jesus’s era, zeal like Phinehas was an established script—a recognized way for a priestly figure to assert authority over sacred space by force. Placing the temple cleansing inside that script changes what kind of act it is. The cleansing is not an outsider’s protest against the temple establishment; it is insider correction, someone with a legitimate stake cleaning his own house. --- The Priestly Fingerprints in the Gospels Once you start looking for it, the priestly material in the Gospels is not limited to the temple cleansing and a handful of teaching passages. It runs through details most readers pass over without noticing, and it is worth walking through several of them directly. A Priestly Reading of the Baptism Mark opens his Gospel with a citation attributed to Isaiah that is actually a splice. Only the second half, “*the voice of one crying out in the wilderness,*” comes from Isaiah 40:3. The first half, “*see, I am sending my messenger ahead of you,*” is Malachi 3:1 (Mark 1:2-3), a well-known textual crux that later scribes tried to smooth over by changing the attribution to “the prophets” in plural. Malachi 3:2-3, two verses later in the same passage, supplies the frame Mark is quietly borrowing. “But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can hold out when he appears? For he is like a smelter's fire and like fuller's lye. He shall act like a smelter and purger of silver; and he shall purify the descendants of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, so that they shall present offerings in righteousness.”[^14] Mark plants the priestly purification frame in his opening sentence, before either John or Jesus even appears on the page, and then immediately follows it with John—a priest’s own son—baptizing, and Jesus undergoing that washing. Leviticus 8:6 and Exodus 29:4 both require Aaron and his sons to be washed with water at the entrance to the tent of meeting before being vested and anointed for priestly service. “Lead Aaron and his sons up to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting, and wash them with water.” Moses said to the community, “This is what GOD has commanded to be done.” Then Moses brought Aaron and his sons forward and washed them with water. Jesus’s baptism—an immersion into water, performed no less by a priest’s son (John)—immediately preceding the start of his public ministry, mirrors that exact inaugural washing more than it mirrors the traditional reading of a repentance-based baptism. This is worth noting given John’s own priestly pedigree, which makes him the needed officiant for such a rite. Priestly Law in the Grain-Plucking Dispute Another occurrence of priestly function is found when the Pharisees challenge the disciples for plucking grain on the Sabbath. Jesus defends his disciples by citing David eating the bread of the Presence, “*which is not lawful for any but the priests to eat.*”[^15] This argument is preserved in Matthew and Luke as well, which is notable given how technical and specific it is, an argument that presumes real familiarity with priestly dietary restriction rather than general moral teaching. Even Matthew, the most Davidic-focused of the four Gospels, reaches independently for priestly language when he expands the grain-plucking dispute, adding a line absent from both Mark and Luke. He asks, “*have you not read in the law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are guiltless?... something greater than the temple is here*” (Matthew 12:5-6). That the evangelist most invested in building a Davidic case still reaches for a priest and temple comparison when he has room to elaborate suggests the underlying priestly association in the tradition was strong enough that even his own redactional instincts kept returning to it. The Reverse-Contagion Healings There is also a healing pattern that places Jesus under a priestly designation. Under normal Levitical logic, an impure person contaminates whoever touches them. Three separate healing episodes in Mark reverse that direction instead: 1. **The leper** is touched and declared clean rather than the reverse (Mark 1:40-45; cf. Leviticus 13-14, where only a priest may diagnose or declare someone clean). 2. **The woman with the chronic hemorrhage** touches Jesus and is healed rather than transmitting her impurity to him (Mark 5:25-34; cf. Leviticus 15:25-30). 3. **Jairus’s daughter**, already dead—the strongest source of ritual impurity under Numbers 19:11—is touched and restored to life rather than contaminating whoever handles the body (Mark 5:35-43). This reversal shows up three separate times and is never narrated as remarkable in the text itself, which is exactly what you would expect if it reflects an underlying assumption rather than an argued theological point. Blood Theology at the Last Supper The words at the Last Supper draw directly on priestly blood theology as well. Mark records Jesus saying “this is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many” (Mark 14:24), and that line sits on top of two distinct priestly texts rather than one. “Moses took the blood and dashed it on the people and said, ‘This is the blood of the covenant that GOD now makes with you concerning all these commands.’” This is the original covenant-ratification ceremony at Sinai. The exact phrase “blood of the covenant” is otherwise rare in the Hebrew Bible, which is what makes its near-identical reappearance at the Supper read as a direct citation rather than loose sacrificial language. “For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have assigned it to you for making expiation for your lives upon the altar; it is the blood, as life, that effects expiation.” This verse supplies the reasoning behind the Sinai ceremony. Blood atones because, in the text’s own terms, blood simply is life, and that life-bearing substance has been assigned to one place and one function, the altar and atonement, administered by one class of person alone. “He said to them, ‘This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.’” Element Old Testament source Mark 14:24 Demonstrative opener “This is the blood of the covenant...” (Exodus 24:8) “This is my blood of the covenant...” Core phrase “the blood of the covenant,” a construction almost unique to Exodus 24:8 “my blood of the covenant” Rationale for atoning power “the life of the flesh is in the blood... it is the blood, as life, that effects expiation” (Leviticus 17:11) Blood offered as his own life, poured out for many Where the act belongs The altar, applied by a consecrated priest alone The supper table, applied by Jesus himself Blood manipulation in Leviticus is the priestly action above all others, performed liturgically by no one but a priest. Here Jesus performs it over his own body, in his own words, at a meal he himself is hosting. There is no altar in the room, no priestly vestment, and no Aaronic office in the conventional sense. He speaks the covenant-ratification formula of Exodus 24:8, applies the atonement logic of Leviticus 17:11 to his own blood, and carries out the very act Leviticus reserves for a priest’s hands alone. The one who offers, the one who is offered, and the one who pronounces the ritual words over the offering collapse into a single person at the table. The Untorn Robe One further detail of priestly vestment law is easy to miss because it is buried in a construction specification rather than a narrative scene. Exodus is unusually precise about the high priest's robe, to the point of specifying how the neck opening must be reinforced so the garment cannot rip. “The opening for the head shall be in the middle of it; the opening shall have a binding of woven work round about—it shall be like the opening of a coat of mail—so that it does not tear.”[^19] John's crucifixion account describes the soldiers dividing Jesus's clothes among themselves, then stopping short of his tunic for a specific reason. “Now the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top; so they said to one another, ‘Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see who will get it.’” The vocabulary lines up directly: the one priestly garment the Torah legislates against tearing is the one garment of Jesus's the men standing at the cross go out of their way not to tear, casting lots instead. John does not explain the detail or draw the comparison himself; he simply reports that the soldiers, for their own practical reasons, preserved intact the one item of clothing that priestly law singles out for that exact protection. The Torn Veil and the Infancy Rites The temple veil tears at the moment of Jesus’s death in Mark 15:38—the earliest of the three Synoptic crucifixion accounts—not a detail added later by Matthew or Luke, both of whom simply follow Mark here. Read next to the untorn robe above, the two details run in opposite directions at the same moment: the barrier that stood between the people and the sanctuary is destroyed, while the one garment priestly law protects from tearing survives intact. And in Luke’s infancy narrative, Mary undergoes the purification required by Leviticus 12, and the family performs the firstborn redemption rite of Exodus 13 and Numbers 18:15-16, both technically priest-administered cultic transactions (Luke 2:22-24). Nothing in the text calls attention to this; the family is simply shown operating correctly inside priestly law from Jesus’s infancy onward. --- Which Came First, David or Aaron? If both a Davidic claim and an Aaronic claim sit inside the Gospels, which one is more likely to be the earlier, underlying tradition, and which is more likely to be a later addition by the writers themselves? Asserted Versus Assumed The Davidic material is always asserted outright, stated plainly and repeated. It appears as “*an account of the genealogy of Jesus the Messiah, the son of David*” (Matthew 1:1), “*the throne of his ancestor David*” (Luke 1:32), and “*Hosanna to the Son of David*” (Matthew 21:9), among other places. The Aaronic material, by contrast, is never argued for explicitly. It simply sits inside the structure of the narrative, in Elizabeth described as one of ‘the daughters of Aaron’ almost in passing, Zechariah’s priestly division named administratively, the zeal citation at the temple, and the blood theology at the supper. Nobody in the Gospels ever states outright that Jesus is a priest the way Matthew and Luke repeatedly state that he is David’s son. Contradictions in the Davidic Genealogies The genealogies themselves show real seams. As QuranTalk has previously demonstrated, the genealogies of Joseph found in Matthew and Luke cannot be reconciled with each other. They assign different fathers to Joseph, a different number of generations, and contradictory lines back to David, a problem noticed as early as the third century by Julius Africanus, who attempted a levirate marriage explanation that still leaves real difficulties. And as already established in the previous piece, both trace descent through Joseph, whom both authors themselves say is not the biological father, which means the Davidic claim already requires a legal fiction according to its own authors, not a genetic record. Mark's Earliest Silence Mark, the earliest Gospel, has none of this Davidic scaffolding at all. No genealogy, no Bethlehem birth narrative; the account simply opens with John’s baptism of Jesus. The entire Davidic apparatus is a later addition layered on by Matthew and Luke. Mark also preserves a scene that a church invested in Jesus’s Davidic credentials had every reason to omit and apparently could not. In Mark 12:35-37, Jesus asks in the temple, “*how can the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David,*” quotes Psalm 110, and presses the question further, asking “*David himself calls him Lord; so how can he be his son.*” “GOD said to my lord, ‘Sit at My right hand while I make your enemies your footstool.’” The text never resolves this; Jesus poses it as an open puzzle and moves on. A community heavily invested in the Davidic credential has no obvious motive to preserve a scene of Jesus publicly relativizing that credential inside the temple itself, in the earliest of the four Gospels. It survived because it was apparently already too well known in the tradition to leave out. John's Unresolved Objection John’s Gospel shows the same fault line from a different angle. In John 7:41-43, the crowd in Jerusalem splits over whether the Messiah can come from Galilee at all, since “*scripture has said that the Messiah is descended from David and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David lived,*” and John never resolves the objection inside the narrative. The latest and most theologically developed of the four Gospels leaves the Davidic and Bethlehem question openly contested, while independently developing heavy priestly and temple imagery of its own—the Lamb of God, “*something greater than the temple,*” the high priestly prayer of chapter 17, the seamless robe—none of which requires a genealogy to work. Taken together, this points toward the Davidic material being the later, constructed layer, self-contradictory even within its own sources and self-undermining given the virgin birth, while the Aaronic material behaves like the older substrate underneath it. It is early attested, embedded in incidental detail rather than argued claims, and recurring independently in John without any genealogical scaffolding at all. Feature Davidic claim Aaronic claim Explicitness Repeatedly asserted as “Son of David” Usually embedded in priestly narrative details Genealogical basis Matthew and Luke trace through Joseph Mary and Elizabeth are connected to Aaronic tradition Narrative pattern Royal, Davidic, Bethlehem-centered claims Temple, purity, sacrifice, blessing, teaching, and priestly action Early Gospel witness Absent from Mark’s opening Priestly motifs are present from Mark’s opening through the Passion --- Priestly Duties, Point by Point Jesus behaved more like a priest than a warrior king. It is possible to be considerably more specific than that. Levitical priestly duty splits into two tiers. The narrower tier is the Kohathite and Amramite-specific transport duty described in Numbers 4, and the broader tier covers the Aaronic functions of teaching, blessing, purity adjudication, atonement, guarding sacred space, and judging disputes. Teaching and the Judgment of Purity Deuteronomy 33:10 and Leviticus 10:11 assign the priesthood the specific duty to “*teach Your laws to Jacob and Your instructions to Israel,*”[^23] and teaching is Jesus’s single most dominant activity across all four Gospels, a specifically priestly assignment at this stage of Israelite religion rather than generic rabbinic instruction, since the later rabbinic teaching class itself developed after the temple’s destruction, partly to fill the vacuum left by a compromised priesthood. The strongest fit of all is the priestly duty to distinguish holy from common, clean from unclean, assigned in Leviticus 10:10. Jesus does not merely heal lepers; he pronounces them clean, “*be made clean*” (Mark 1:41-42), using the same declarative authority Leviticus 13-14 assigns specifically to priests. He rules on food purity, “*there is nothing outside a person that by going in can defile, but the things that come out are what defile*” (Mark 7:15), and on Sabbath versus mercy conflicts, exercising the adjudicating authority Leviticus 10:10 assigns to the priesthood. Combined with the reverse contagion healings already discussed above, the pattern is coherent. Jesus repeatedly occupies the priestly judgment seat on questions of purity. The Blessing Formula Numbers 6:22-27 sets out the priestly benediction, the specific words God commands Aaron and his sons to pronounce over the people. The instruction is explicit about who is authorized to perform it. “GOD spoke to Moses: Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless the people of Israel. Say to them: GOD bless you and protect you!” Leviticus 9:22 then shows Aaron actually carrying this out, immediately after his ordination as high priest, in the same physical posture the text keeps returning to. “Aaron lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them; and he stepped down after offering the purgation offering, the burnt offering, and the offering of well-being.” Luke’s ascension scene reproduces that exact gesture, hands raised over the people, and assigns it to Jesus rather than to a priest of Aaron’s line. “Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them.” Element Priestly source Gospel occurrence Hands raised in blessing Aaron “lifted his hands toward the people and blessed them” (Leviticus 9:22) Jesus, “lifting up his hands, blessed them” (Luke 24:50) Who is authorized to bless “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus shall you bless” (Numbers 6:22-23) Jesus pronounces the blessing himself, without a priestly intermediary There is a separate, smaller pattern worth noting alongside this one, though it is not itself drawn from Aaronic law. At the feeding of the 5,000 and again at the Last Supper, Mark records Jesus performing the identical four-step action of taking bread, blessing it, breaking it, and giving it out. “Taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven, and blessed and broke the loaves, and gave them to his disciples to set before the people.” “While they were eating, he took a loaf of bread, and after blessing it he broke it, gave it to them, and said, ‘Take; this is my body.’” That four-verb sequence is not a priestly formula from Numbers or Leviticus. It is the ordinary Jewish table blessing, the *berakah* any head of a household would recite over bread at an everyday meal, with no restriction to Aaron's line at all. What is notable is not its priestly origin, since it has none, but its exact repetition. Mark uses the same four verbs, in the same order, for both the feeding miracle and the supper, tying the two scenes together as a matched pair rather than two unrelated meals. Read alongside the hands-raised blessing gesture above, the two patterns point in the same general direction without being the same kind of evidence: one shows Jesus occupying a role Aaronic law reserves for the priesthood, and the other shows Mark deliberately linking two meals through a shared, ordinary liturgical action. --- The Davidic Motivation Davidic messianism was the dominant, pre-existing expectation—Aaronic wasn’t. By the Second Temple period, the scriptural apparatus for a coming Davidic ruler was enormous and already fixed in the popular imagination.[^16] A priestly-messianic expectation existed (Qumran’s two-messiah scheme), but it was a minority, largely sectarian strand. The Rhetorical Advantage of David If you’re a Gospel writer trying to persuade an audience—Jewish or God-fearing Gentile—that this specific man is the promised deliverer, “son of David” is the category with instant recognition and a citation apparatus ten times deeper than anything Aaronic material offers. Matthew’s whole formula-quotation structure (“*this was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet…*”) is only viable because the Davidic prophetic corpus is that rich. You couldn’t build the same rhetorical machine out of Aaronic material, since there isn’t enough of it, and what exists doesn’t point as cleanly at an individual coming figure. A Title Fixed Before the Gospels Were Written The title “Messiah” itself was already Davidic-coded before any Gospel was written. Paul—writing in the 50s CE, decades before Mark—already passes on a received tradition that Jesus is descended from David, embedded in what looks like a pre-Pauline confessional formula.[^17] That means “Messiah = Davidic” was locked into the earliest post-Easter kerygma before a single Gospel narrative existed. The Gospel writers aren’t neutrally investigating Jesus’s ancestry and discovering he’s Davidic; they’re writing narratives that have to service this specific title-claim the movement had already adopted as its core confession. The conclusion came first, and the genealogies and birth narratives were built to support it afterward, which is precisely why they contradict each other and require a legal fiction (descent through Joseph, despite the virgin birth) to work at all. Writing to a Post-Temple Audience Matthew is almost certainly writing after 70 CE, to a community watching the entire cultic infrastructure—altar, sacrifice, functioning priesthood—cease to exist. A messianic claim rooted in Davidic kingship needs no operative Temple to remain meaningful; “kingdom” language ports over easily into something spiritual/eschatological. A messianic claim rooted in priestly office is much harder to sustain rhetorically once there’s no altar left to serve at. The Davidic framing is simply more durable messaging for the audience these texts are being written for. The actual Aaronic institution was the antagonist, not a plausible identity to claim. By Jesus’s lifetime the high priesthood was Rome-appointed, Sadducee-controlled, and, per the Passion narratives themselves, the institution that orchestrates his death (Annas, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin’s priestly faction). Claiming Jesus continues or fulfills that specific line would be self-defeating in a text whose climax depicts that same line condemning him. Melchizedek as a Way Around the Broken Line This is likely a real part of why Hebrews goes a different direction entirely rather than doubling down on Aaronic descent. It roots Jesus’s priesthood in Melchizedek, a figure from before Levi even existed (Genesis 14, older than Sinai, outside the tribal system altogether).[^18] Hebrews does not invent this connection; it draws it from the same psalm already at the center of the Davidic puzzle in Mark 12. The verse Jesus quotes to relativize his own Davidic sonship, “GOD said to my lord,” comes from Psalm 110:1. Four verses later, the same psalm supplies the priestly credential Hebrews builds its entire argument on. “GOD has sworn and will not relent, ‘You are a priest forever, a rightful king by My decree.’”[^25] The psalm that destabilizes the Davidic label in Mark's earliest Gospel is the same psalm that, four verses on, grounds a priesthood older than Levi. Hebrews is not reaching outside scripture for a workaround; it is following the same text to a different verse. This lets the author claim priestly authority for Jesus while owing nothing to, and carrying no contamination from, the corrupted Hasmonean-then-Herodian-then-Roman-appointed high priesthood the same broader tradition treats as illegitimate. Melchizedek isn’t necessarily a rejection of priestly Christology; it was simply a way to get priestly Christology without touching the compromised institutional line. A Rabbinic Parallel to the Same Two Verses Hebrews is not the only tradition that fastens onto this psalm to settle a question about priesthood. The Babylonian Talmud, discussing why the priesthood belongs to Abraham's line rather than to Melchizedek himself, cites the same two verses in the same order, Psalm 110:1 and then Psalm 110:4, to make its own, unrelated argument. The Holy One, Blessed be He, wanted the priesthood to emerge from Shem, so that his children would be priests, as it is stated: "And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine; and he was priest of God the Most High" (Genesis 14:18). Once Melchizedek placed the blessing of Abraham before the blessing of the Omnipresent, He had the priesthood emerge from Abraham instead, as it is stated: "The Lord says to my lord: Sit at My right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool" (Psalms 110:1), and afterward it is written: "The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: you shall be a priest forever, because you are a king of righteousness" (Psalms 110:4).[^24] Two very different traditions, writing centuries apart and for entirely different purposes, both stop at the same pair of verses when a text needs to explain why the priesthood in question does not run through the ordinary Aaronic line. The Talmud is not a source for Hebrews; the Babylonian Talmud was redacted centuries after the New Testament and cannot be read backward as its influence. What the parallel shows instead is that the two verses in Psalm 110 were, independently, recognized in both traditions as the place to go when a priesthood needed grounding outside the hereditary system. It also puts on display exactly how flexible the Hebrew of verse 4 is: the Talmud renders the same phrase as "a king of righteousness," the Gender-Sensitive JPS renders it "a rightful king by My decree," and the reading Hebrews depends on takes it as the proper name Melchizedek. All three are legitimate readings of מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק; which one a text prefers depends entirely on what argument it is trying to make with it. The Political Danger of a Davidic Claim A straightforwardly Davidic royal claim was politically live and dangerous. Rome executed Jesus under a titulus reading “King of the Jews,” reading the claim as insurrectionary regardless of how the Gospels wanted to spiritualize it. But rhetorically, casting Jesus as the fulfillment of the nationalist hope while redefining its politics (“my kingdom is not from this world”) let the writers inherit the emotional and scriptural power of Davidic hope while defusing its revolutionary content. That’s a very different kind of narrative labor than an Aaronic claim would require, since nobody needed to defuse a priestly claim politically, because it was never going to read as a threat to Rome the way “son of David” did. Davidic identity was the load-bearing confessional premise the whole movement needed—recognizable, prophetically over-determined, politically useful once reframed, and durable past 70 CE. Aaronic material had none of those institutional pressures pushing it forward, which is exactly why it shows up unforced, structurally, and without argument. Nobody needed it to do apologetic work, so nobody made it into a claim. --- Conclusion The previous piece established that Jesus’s Davidic credentials rest on a genealogy through a man who was not his biological father, that Elizabeth and Mary were both connected to Aaron’s line, and that Second Temple Judaism had a real category for a priestly messiah standing alongside a Davidic king. This piece adds on to the argument with positive support toward the Aaronic claim. Amram was never simply the name of one man a thousand years removed from Mary; it was already functioning as a clan name inside the Torah’s own priestly source, the same way “sons of Aaron” functions throughout Exodus and Leviticus, and by the Second Temple period it carried its own weight as a name associated with priestly election. The priesthood that Amram’s line was supposed to steward had, by Jesus’s own lifetime, been bought, deposed, and reassigned so many times over two centuries that a significant part of the religious community considered it illegitimate—which is the actual context the temple cleansing and its language of zeal belong to. And once the Gospels are read for specifically priestly detail rather than general moral tone, the pattern runs far deeper than the temple cleansing alone. It reaches into the blood theology of the Last Supper, the reversed contagion of the healing narratives, the blessing formula repeated at two separate meals, the priestly judgment language Jesus repeatedly uses when he pronounces people clean, and the priestly ceremony of water baptism conducted by one of Levitic descent. Taken as a whole, the case for Jesus as Messiah ben Aaron looks considerably stronger once it rests on more than temperament and teaching style—once it rests on the actual mechanics of a broken priesthood, a name that meant more than a single father, and a set of textual details in the Gospels that line up with Aaronic law far too specifically to be accidental. The strongest form of the argument is cumulative. Amram functions as a house-name, Aaronic messianism was a real Second Temple category, the inherited priesthood was deeply contested by Jesus’s era, and the Gospel narratives repeatedly place Jesus inside specifically priestly patterns. The Davidic claim may be the movement’s explicit confessional layer, but the Aaronic material provides a strikingly coherent underlying substrate. title: The Case for the Plural of Participation
description: A survey of classical Sunni scholarship showing that the Quranic divine plural

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: In Appendix 10 of his Quran translation, Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that God's use of "We" in the Quran is not a plural of majesty.[^1] He states the rule directly, writing that "*whenever the first person plural form is used by the Almighty, it invariably indicates participation of other entities, such as the angels.*"[^2] The claim is not that the plural *can* mark participation. It is that the plural *always* does. When the Quran says "We revealed" (15:9), the plural reflects Gabriel and Muhammad, an angel and a man, both taking part in delivering the message.[^3] The reading Rashad Khalifa gives in Appendix 10, that the Quran's divine "We" marks real participation by angels or agents rather than a plural of majesty, is not a modern invention. It is a live, named, continuously attested position in mainstream Sunni scholarship running from the third Islamic century forward, including inside the work of Ibn Taymiyyah, the very scholar most often cited against it. When God blows the breath of life into Adam, a creation that happens directly in heaven with no intermediary at all, the Quran shifts to the singular, "*I blew into Adam from My spirit.*"[^4][^5] When the same act happens to Jesus, mediated through Gabriel on earth, the plural returns.[^6][^7] This is not a reading imposed backward onto the text by a modern translator. Ibn Kathir (d. 774 AH) says exactly this about Mary's conception, in his own words, with no polemical occasion prompting it. His tafsir is the single most widely used in the Sunni tradition after al-Tabari's. Commenting on 21:91, he draws the same distinction. That exact phrase, بِوَاسِطَةِ الْمَلَكِ وَهُوَ جِبْرِيلُ — "by the mediation of the angel, namely Gabriel" — recurs word for word across every printed edition of his tafsir. Khalifa's Adam-versus-Mary contrast is not an inference. It is Ibn Kathir's own stated reading of the same two passages. When God addresses Moses directly, with no go-between of any kind, the pronoun drops to singular again (20:12–14).[^9] The pattern tracks participation, not majesty. And on Khalifa's reading, the agent behind the plural is not restricted to one category of being. The standard traditionalist response is that this reading is a modern invention — something Dr. Khalifa introduced with no real footing in classical scholarship. That response does not survive contact with the sources. The idea that divine "We" marks literal participation by an agent carrying out God's command is not a fringe reading born in the twentieth century. It runs continuously through mainstream Sunni tafsir across five centuries. It runs through the classical lexicographers of Quranic vocabulary. It runs through the encyclopedists of Quranic rhetoric. It even shows up inside the work of Ibn Taymiyyah, the same scholar modern traditionalists cite as the authority for the opposite position. This piece documents where the participatory reading appears in the classical record and how consistently it recurs. It does not adjudicate, verse by verse, which of the two explanations is correct wherever both remain possible; several of the scholars cited below hold both readings open at once, and this survey follows their lead rather than resolving it for them. --- ## Two Explanations, Not One Classical scholarship on the Quranic "We" splits into two recognized camps, not one. The first is جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم , the plural of majesty, an honorific borrowed from royal speech. A king says "we decree" while remaining one person. This is the explanation most people encounter today, and it is treated as though it were the only explanation that ever existed. The second is جَمْعٌ لِمُشَارَكَةِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالْأَعْوَانِ , the plural of participation by angels or agents. On this reading, the act described is carried out through whoever God assigns to it, acting under His command. The plural covers God and that agent together, not as partners in His essence, but as an instrument carrying out His decree. Angels are the most frequently cited example, since most of the verses in question describe revelation, death, and cosmic events where angels are the obvious operators. A good example is found in what happens at the time of death.[^10][^11] The first verse, 15:23, uses نَحْنُ نُمِيتُ ("We" cause death) — the plural. The second, 47:27, uses تَوَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ / يَتَوَفَّى الْمَلَائِكَةُ ("the angels" put them to death). It is the exact same verb, تَوَفَّى , "to take [a soul]," but now with a real plural subject, الْمَلَائِكَةُ , explicitly named. Since the Quran uses the identical verb for the identical act in both cases, the pairing shows that the "We" of 15:23 is not empty grammatical majesty. It is a real plural that includes the angels as God's executing agents. This does not amount to shirk, because the angels act only by God's command, as the Quran itself specifies that "*they do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command*" (Q 21:27).[^12] That clause is the theological hinge. It keeps the reading from becoming multiple independent agents. This is delegated causation, not co-equal causation. Ibn Kathir applies precisely this reasoning to the neighboring death-and-nearness verses. Commenting on "*and We are nearer to him than you*" (56:85), he glosses it flatly as "*by Our angels.*" He extends the identical gloss to "*and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein*" (50:16), citing 56:85 and 15:9 together as three instances of the same pattern.[^13] The نَحْنُ of causing death and the مَلَائِكَةُ of taking souls sit inside one continuous exegetical habit. This is not an isolated coincidence Dr. Khalifa alone noticed. ### A Standing Grammatical Option, Not a Hunch Classical exegetes had a standing name for exactly this either/or, applied routinely to first-person-plural verbs that had nothing to do with revelation or the Trinity. Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 542 AH) explains a Quranic reading variant as "*either the nūn of magnification, or it belongs to the angels.*"[^14] Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi (d. 745 AH) gives the identical two options, "*the nūn of magnification, or the nūn of the company of angels*," for a plural verb in Surat al-'Ankabut (29:55).[^15] Ibn 'Adil al-Hanbali (d. 775 AH) repeats the same formula for the same verse.[^16] Mujir al-Din al-'Ulaymi (d. 927 AH) repeats it again, word for word, a century and a half later.[^17] These are four scholars across four different centuries, a Maliki, a grammarian, a Hanbali, and a Shafi'i, and none of them is arguing with anyone. "Maybe it's the angels" is simply the routine second reading whenever a divine or near-divine verb shows up in the plural. --- ## Ibn Taymiyyah Names Both, On the Record Ibn Taymiyyah is a good example of this, because he is usually invoked as the champion of the majesty-only reading. In *Bayan Talbis al-Jahmiyya*, responding to a Christian who cited the Quran's "We" as proof of the Trinity, his actual argument is more precise than a simple "there are two options," and more useful to this case. He writes that the word نَحْنُ can be used "*for the One who has [real] partners, and for the singular, magnified, obeyed one who has subjects (mamālīk) that obey him,*" and that this is exactly the ambiguity ( تَشَابُه ) the Christians exploited.[^18] His resolution is not "it's just majesty." It is that God's claim to the majestic plural is stronger than any king's, precisely because His subordinates are real, and "*everything besides Him is created and owned by Him — from among the angels and others — so He has more right to the nūn of magnification than those kings who use this expression for it.*"[^19] He repeats and sharpens this at least four more times across *Majmu' al-Fatawa*. Discussing the occasion of the argument — the Najran Christian delegation who cited the Quran's " إِنَّا " and " نَحْنُ " as evidence for three gods — he writes that these terms fit a specific pattern. "*[These terms] are only said of a singular one who has helpers, either they are partners with him, or they are his property/subjects... and He, glory be to Him, governs the affair of the world by Himself and by His angels, who are His messengers in His creation and command, and He has the most right of anyone to say 'innā' and 'naḥnu' on this consideration.*"[^20] That is the participatory reading stated as an argument for God's greater claim to the plural, not a concession that the plural is empty honorific. Both readings rule out the Trinity, since real partners are impossible for God, while owned and commanded subordinates are not. Ibn Taymiyyah does not choose one over the other. He uses both, together, in the same breath. --- ## The Earliest Confirmed Layer The claim that this is a late theological improvisation runs into trouble as soon as you look at how early scholars handled the Quran's habit of shifting between singular and plural in divine speech at all. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH) takes up this exact problem in *al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya wa'l-Zanadiqa*. He answers doubters who pointed to God saying "*Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing*" (20:46, to Moses and Aaron) alongside "*Indeed We are with you, listening*" (26:15, the same event), as if the shift were a contradiction.[^21] His answer treats the alternation as ordinary linguistic idiom, not evidence of anything suspicious and not something requiring embarrassment. That establishes, in the third Islamic century, that the Quran's pronoun variation had already been noticed, questioned by skeptics, and answered by the tradition's founding jurists — centuries before anyone was debating Trinity proof-texts with Christian missionaries. Later Hanbali jurists, among them al-Qadi Abu Ya'la, read Ahmad's brief comment as reported by Ibn Taymiyyah to mean exactly what the participatory reading argues, that "*it is permissible in the language for a single great one who has agents (a'wan) to say 'we did such-and-such.'*"[^22] The specific two-explanation structure — majesty as one live option, agency as the other, named side by side rather than fought over — is on record by the fifth century AH. Makki ibn Abi Talib (d. 437 AH) explains the shift from singular to plural in "*My Lord, send me back*" (23:99) exactly this way in *al-Hidaya ila Bulugh al-Nihaya*. The disbeliever addresses God alone in the singular, then turns to address the angels who seize his soul, hence the plural.[^23] Both explanations are offered as ordinary, uncontroversial options, in a work of Quranic grammar with no theological argument to win. --- ## The Clearest Classical Statement — Al-Raghib al-Isfahani The clearest confirmation that this was never a marginal position comes directly from al-Raghib al-Isfahani (d. c. 502 AH), in his own dictionary of Quranic vocabulary, *al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an*. Al-Raghib records both explanations as live options in his own time, majesty being one. He then states the second explanation in language almost identical to Khalifa's. "*Some of the scholars said, God, exalted is He, mentions such expressions when the act named afterward is done through the mediation of some of His angels, or some of His agents, so that 'We' becomes an expression for Him together with them.*"[^24] He applies this exact framework to 15:9, tracing the descent of the Quran through the Pen, the Tablet, and Gabriel, and to 56:85, where "We are nearer to him than you" refers to the moment of death, when the angels are the ones present taking the soul.[^25] This is a lexical reference work, not a polemical tract. Al-Raghib is not defending Islam from an outside challenge. He is defining how a specific grammatical form functions across the text, and angelic participation is one of the two definitions on record, stated as plainly as the majesty reading sitting right next to it. Two later lexicographers carried the same passage forward almost word for word, al-Samin al-Halabi (d. 756 AH), in *'Umdat al-Huffaz*, and al-Firuzabadi (d. 817 AH) — author of the standard Arabic dictionary *al-Qamus al-Muhit* — in his own *Basa'ir Dhawi al-Tamyiz*.[^26] Al-Firuzabadi's version adds a genuine refinement rather than simply copying. He explicitly rules the agentive reading out for "*and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein*" (50:16), insisting that verse has to be read as plain majesty instead.[^27] Three lexicographers across three centuries kept this reading alive, and they kept arguing over exactly where its boundary falls. That is the mark of a real, working grammatical category. --- ## Ibn Kathir Draws the Line Himself Beyond Mary's conception, Ibn Kathir ties the reading together across the Quran in his own words. Commenting on "*and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein*" (50:16), he draws the same connection out loud. He is not being asked to defend this against a Christian, a Mu'tazilite, or anyone else. He is simply reading the Quran, verse by verse, and reaching for the same explanation each time three of Khalifa's own key verses come up. ### Two More Scholars, Same Verses Two later scholars independently apply the identical reading to Mary's conception specifically. Al-Khatib al-Sharbini (d. 977 AH) fuses majesty and mediation into a single clause on 66:12 in *al-Siraj al-Munir*, writing that the plural belongs there "*by virtue of what belongs to Us of majesty, through the mediation of Our angel Gabriel.*"[^29] He does not treat these as competing theories. The plural is majestic because it proceeds through the angel. Al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH) treats angelic mediation as a live, unremarkable reading of the same verse, 21:91, not in his famous *al-Durr al-Manthur* but in a separate work specifically on Quranic inimitability, *Mu'tarak al-Aqran fi I'jaz al-Qur'an*, where he states plainly that "*that casting was either through the mediation of the angel referred to by 'the spirit,' or without it.*"[^30] --- ## The Mechanism Behind the Pronoun ### Al-Razi on the Order of Belief None of this works unless revelation itself actually runs through angelic mediation as a matter of course, and that premise is not asserted only by implication. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 606 AH) states it as settled doctrine in *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, grounded in the Quran's own ordering of belief-objects at the end of Surat al-Baqara, "*the believers — all have believed in God, and His angels, and His books, and His messengers*" (2:285). He argues the order is not accidental. "*Revelation's arrival from God to the prophets never occurs except by the mediation of the angels... He began with God, then the angels, because they are the ones who receive the revelation from God directly, without mediation, and then convey it to the prophets.*"[^31] This is the mechanism the participatory reading of 15:9 depends on. It is stated independently by one of the tradition's most influential rationalist exegetes, without reference to the pronoun question at all. ### Al-Zarkashi States It as a General Rule Badr al-Din al-Zarkashi (d. 794 AH) goes a step further and states the pronoun's connection to that mechanism as a general rule. His *al-Burhan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an* is one of the two or three most authoritative reference works ever written on Quranic science. In his chapter on اِلْتِفَات , the grammatical device of shifting between persons, he explains why the Quran moves from third person to first person in "*God, who sent the winds, so they raise a cloud... then We drove it to a dead land*" (35:9). "*It is His habitual practice, glory be to Him, in all these acts, to speak of them with the nūn of magnification that indicates He has troops and creation whom He has subjected to that end.*"[^32] He backs this "habitual practice" claim by pointing to the same first-person shift elsewhere in the Quran, including "*so when We recite it, follow its recitation*" (75:18), which he glosses as "*when Our messenger Gabriel recites it.*"[^33] Al-Zarkashi works this out in direct conversation with 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani and al-Zamakhshari on the mechanics of اِلْتِفَات . This is mainstream Arabic rhetorical scholarship on the Quran treating the participatory plural as a working assumption about how the language functions, not a theological special plea. ### Where Al-Zamakhshari Holds Back Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) himself does not make this exact grammatical argument on 15:9 in *al-Kashshaf*. His emphatic reading of " إِنَّا نَحْنُ " there is built around underscoring God's own decisive responsibility for sending the Quran down, not an explicit joint pronoun. But even so, he takes Gabriel's active role in the event for granted as part of what the verse describes, writing that "*He is the one who dispatched Gabriel with it to Muhammad, with watchers before him and behind him, until it descended... preserved from the devils.*"[^34] Even where an exegete's own emphasis lands on majesty, Gabriel's participation in the act is never in question. --- ## Not Only Angels Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's own definition already names the category as "*some of His angels or some of His agents,*" a phrase that opens the door beyond angelic beings without anyone having to stretch it there. Ibn Taymiyyah's version of the same joint explanation uses the same pairing in *Bayan Talbis al-Jahmiyya*, a sovereign speaking in the plural because he has subordinates under his real ownership and command, not because those subordinates are all one kind of creature.[^35] Khalifa's own reading already reflects this. His example for 15:9 names Gabriel and Muhammad together, an angel and a man, both credited inside the same plural pronoun. That is not an inconsistency in the classical category. It is the category working as designed. The relevant division in the sources was never angel versus human. It was single divine actor versus divine actor plus whoever carries the task out, whatever that agent happens to be. --- ## What the Objection Actually Assumes The idea that Dr. Khalifa invented this reading rests on the assumption that جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم was always the only serious explanation, and everything else is a recent workaround invented to answer Christians. The sources above make that assumption hard to hold. Ahmad ibn Hanbal was answering doubts about the Quran's pronoun shifts in the third Islamic century, long before organized polemics with Christian missionaries over the Trinity became a live genre. Makki ibn Abi Talib and al-Raghib al-Isfahani were writing grammar and lexicography, not apologetics, and they named the agentive reading as a live option with no argument to win. Al-Zarkashi built a standard reference work on Quranic rhetoric still assigned in seminaries today, and he states the participatory reading as a general rule, not a defensive maneuver. Ibn Kathir, the most-read tafsir in the Sunni world after al-Tabari's, reaches for the identical explanation unprompted, every time one of Khalifa's key verses comes up. And Ibn Taymiyyah — the scholar most often cited as the source of the majesty-only position — is on record naming both explanations and using them together against a Christian interlocutor, arguing that God has the greater claim to the plural precisely because His subordinates are real. What actually happened, if the sources are read in order, is closer to the reverse of the traditionalist claim. The angelic-participation reading is attested, explicitly and by name, in mainstream Sunni scholarship continuously from the fifth century AH forward. It appears in lexicons. It appears in the two or three most important Quranic-science encyclopedias in the tradition. It appears in the most widely read tafsir after al-Tabari's. And its underlying puzzle — why does the Quran's divine speech vary between singular and plural at all — was already being seriously answered in the third century. The plural-of-majesty reading, borrowed from the vocabulary of kings, became the more repeated answer in later popular use, partly because it is shorter and easier to deploy in a live argument than tracing which verses involve angelic mediation and which do not. Convenience is not the same thing as precedent. On the sources that survive scrutiny, the precedent runs the other way. --- ## Where Khalifa's Reading Goes Further Dr. Khalifa's specific contribution is not the existence of the agentic reading. The sources above already establish that. His contribution is the precision with which he applies it, and the absoluteness of the rule he states. Al-Raghib names 15:9 and 56:85. Ibn Kathir names 50:16, 56:85, and 15:9, tying them together himself. Al-Sharbini and al-Suyuti independently apply the same reading to 21:91 and 66:12. None of them lay out the full pattern across the whole Quran the way Khalifa does, and none of them claim, as he does, that the plural *invariably* signals participation rather than sometimes doing so.[^36] It is singular where God acts alone and directly, as with Adam and with Moses. It is plural wherever an angel is textually involved in carrying the act out, as with Jesus's creation and the Quran's descent. That is not a new theological claim. It is the same classical grammatical category, جَمْعٌ لِمُشَارَكَةِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ , checked systematically against every relevant verse instead of a handful of proof texts scattered across a dozen different books written centuries apart. The grammatical machinery underneath it is not modern at all. ### A Contemporary Scholar Confirms It Independently Contemporary scholars of Quranic rhetoric still teach a version of it. Fadel Saleh al-Samarra'i, in a recorded lecture series on Quranic eloquence, independently lays out the identical Adam-versus-Mary contrast, stating that "*when God's command is delivered through the mediation of an angel, it comes with the plural pronoun; and when it is not, it is singular.*"[^37] He cites 21:91 against 38:72 by name — the same pairing Khalifa uses in Appendix 10 — arrived at independently by a scholar working inside the classical tradition rather than defending it. --- ## Conclusion The claim that God's plural "We" reflects agentic participation rather than royal self-reference is not a twentieth-century apologetic invention. Its underlying puzzle was already being answered by Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the third Islamic century. The specific two-explanation structure — majesty as one reading, angelic or agentive participation as the other, offered side by side — is on record by the fifth century in Makki ibn Abi Talib. It is stated in its clearest and most explicit form by al-Raghib al-Isfahani, and carried forward faithfully by al-Samin al-Halabi and al-Firuzabadi across three more centuries. It is applied verse by verse to exactly Khalifa's own examples by Ibn Kathir. It is restated as a general principle of Quranic rhetoric by al-Zarkashi, in dialogue with al-Jurjani and al-Zamakhshari. It is grounded in its theological mechanism by al-Razi. And, the sharpest confirmation of all, it is named explicitly — alongside the majesty reading rather than instead of it — by Ibn Taymiyyah himself, the very scholar modern traditionalists invoke as the authority against it. The modern insistence that جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم is the only classical position does not describe the actual history of the question. It describes which answer became easiest to repeat. Khalifa's reading in Appendix 10 sits inside a real, well-documented, cross-generational tradition. He applies it with more textual consistency, and states it in more absolute terms, than most of the scholars who articulated it ever had occasion to. The participatory plural ( جَمْعُ الْمُشَارَكَةِ ) is not a modern invention. It is a live, named, continuously attested reading in mainstream Sunni scholarship from the 3rd/9th century forward. Khalifa's contribution is not creating the category but applying it with systematic consistency across the entire Quranic text. --- --- ## Notes [^1]: Rashad Khalifa, trans., *Quran: The Final Testament: Authorized English Version*, rev. ed.
