fullText: In Appendix 10 of his Quran translation, Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that God's use of "We" in the Quran is not a plural of majesty.[^1] He states the rule directly, writing that "*whenever the first person plural form is used by the Almighty, it invariably indicates participation of other entities, such as the angels.*"[^2] The claim is not that the plural *can* mark participation. It is that the plural *always* does. When the Quran says "We revealed" (15:9), the plural reflects Gabriel and Muhammad, an angel and a man, both taking part in delivering the message.[^3] The reading Rashad Khalifa gives in Appendix 10, that the Quran's divine "We" marks real participation by angels or agents rather than a plural of majesty, is not a modern invention. It is a live, named, continuously attested position in mainstream Sunni scholarship running from the third Islamic century forward, including inside the work of Ibn Taymiyyah, the very scholar most often cited against it. When God blows the breath of life into Adam, a creation that happens directly in heaven with no intermediary at all, the Quran shifts to the singular, "*I blew into Adam from My spirit.*"[^4][^5] When the same act happens to Jesus, mediated through Gabriel on earth, the plural returns.[^6][^7] This is not a reading imposed backward onto the text by a modern translator. Ibn Kathir (d. 774 AH) says exactly this about Mary's conception, in his own words, with no polemical occasion prompting it. His tafsir is the single most widely used in the Sunni tradition after al-Tabari's. Commenting on 21:91, he draws the same distinction. That exact phrase, بِوَاسِطَةِ الْمَلَكِ وَهُوَ جِبْرِيلُ — "by the mediation of the angel, namely Gabriel" — recurs word for word across every printed edition of his tafsir. Khalifa's Adam-versus-Mary contrast is not an inference. It is Ibn Kathir's own stated reading of the same two passages. When God addresses Moses directly, with no go-between of any kind, the pronoun drops to singular again (20:12–14).[^9] The pattern tracks participation, not majesty. And on Khalifa's reading, the agent behind the plural is not restricted to one category of being. The standard traditionalist response is that this reading is a modern invention — something Dr. Khalifa introduced with no real footing in classical scholarship. That response does not survive contact with the sources. The idea that divine "We" marks literal participation by an agent carrying out God's command is not a fringe reading born in the twentieth century. It runs continuously through mainstream Sunni tafsir across five centuries. It runs through the classical lexicographers of Quranic vocabulary. It runs through the encyclopedists of Quranic rhetoric. It even shows up inside the work of Ibn Taymiyyah, the same scholar modern traditionalists cite as the authority for the opposite position. This piece documents where the participatory reading appears in the classical record and how consistently it recurs. It does not adjudicate, verse by verse, which of the two explanations is correct wherever both remain possible; several of the scholars cited below hold both readings open at once, and this survey follows their lead rather than resolving it for them. --- Two Explanations, Not One Classical scholarship on the Quranic "We" splits into two recognized camps, not one. The first is جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم , the plural of majesty, an honorific borrowed from royal speech. A king says "we decree" while remaining one person. This is the explanation most people encounter today, and it is treated as though it were the only explanation that ever existed. The second is جَمْعٌ لِمُشَارَكَةِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ وَالْأَعْوَانِ , the plural of participation by angels or agents. On this reading, the act described is carried out through whoever God assigns to it, acting under His command. The plural covers God and that agent together, not as partners in His essence, but as an instrument carrying out His decree. Angels are the most frequently cited example, since most of the verses in question describe revelation, death, and cosmic events where angels are the obvious operators. A good example is found in what happens at the time of death.[^10][^11] The first verse, 15:23, uses نَحْنُ نُمِيتُ ("We" cause death) — the plural. The second, 47:27, uses تَوَفَّتْهُمُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ / يَتَوَفَّى الْمَلَائِكَةُ ("the angels" put them to death). It is the exact same verb, تَوَفَّى , "to take [a soul]," but now with a real plural subject, الْمَلَائِكَةُ , explicitly named. Since the Quran uses the identical verb for the identical act in both cases, the pairing shows that the "We" of 15:23 is not empty grammatical majesty. It is a real plural that includes the angels as God's executing agents. This does not amount to shirk, because the angels act only by God's command, as the Quran itself specifies that "*they do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command*" (Q 21:27).[^12] That clause is the theological hinge. It keeps the reading from becoming multiple independent agents. This is delegated causation, not co-equal causation. Ibn Kathir applies precisely this reasoning to the neighboring death-and-nearness verses. Commenting on "*and We are nearer to him than you*" (56:85), he glosses it flatly as "*by Our angels.*" He extends the identical gloss to "*and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein*" (50:16), citing 56:85 and 15:9 together as three instances of the same pattern.[^13] The نَحْنُ of causing death and the مَلَائِكَةُ of taking souls sit inside one continuous exegetical habit. This is not an isolated coincidence Dr. Khalifa alone noticed. A Standing Grammatical Option, Not a Hunch Classical exegetes had a standing name for exactly this either/or, applied routinely to first-person-plural verbs that had nothing to do with revelation or the Trinity. Ibn 'Atiyya (d. 542 AH) explains a Quranic reading variant as "*either the nūn of magnification, or it belongs to the angels.*"[^14] Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi (d. 745 AH) gives the identical two options, "*the nūn of magnification, or the nūn of the company of angels*," for a plural verb in Surat al-'Ankabut (29:55).[^15] Ibn 'Adil al-Hanbali (d. 775 AH) repeats the same formula for the same verse.[^16] Mujir al-Din al-'Ulaymi (d. 927 AH) repeats it again, word for word, a century and a half later.[^17] These are four scholars across four different centuries, a Maliki, a grammarian, a Hanbali, and a Shafi'i, and none of them is arguing with anyone. "Maybe it's the angels" is simply the routine second reading whenever a divine or near-divine verb shows up in the plural. --- Ibn Taymiyyah Names Both, On the Record Ibn Taymiyyah is a good example of this, because he is usually invoked as the champion of the majesty-only reading. In *Bayan Talbis al-Jahmiyya*, responding to a Christian who cited the Quran's "We" as proof of the Trinity, his actual argument is more precise than a simple "there are two options," and more useful to this case. He writes that the word نَحْنُ can be used "*for the One who has [real] partners, and for the singular, magnified, obeyed one who has subjects (mamālīk) that obey him,*" and that this is exactly the ambiguity ( تَشَابُه ) the Christians exploited.[^18] His resolution is not "it's just majesty." It is that God's claim to the majestic plural is stronger than any king's, precisely because His subordinates are real, and "*everything besides Him is created and owned by Him — from among the angels and others — so He has more right to the nūn of magnification than those kings who use this expression for it.*"[^19] He repeats and sharpens this at least four more times across *Majmu' al-Fatawa*. Discussing the occasion of the argument — the Najran Christian delegation who cited the Quran's " إِنَّا " and " نَحْنُ " as evidence for three gods — he writes that these terms fit a specific pattern. "*[These terms] are only said of a singular one who has helpers, either they are partners with him, or they are his property/subjects... and He, glory be to Him, governs the affair of the world by Himself and by His angels, who are His messengers in His creation and command, and He has the most right of anyone to say 'innā' and 'naḥnu' on this consideration.*"[^20] That is the participatory reading stated as an argument for God's greater claim to the plural, not a concession that the plural is empty honorific. Both readings rule out the Trinity, since real partners are impossible for God, while owned and commanded subordinates are not. Ibn Taymiyyah does not choose one over the other. He uses both, together, in the same breath. --- The Earliest Confirmed Layer The claim that this is a late theological improvisation runs into trouble as soon as you look at how early scholars handled the Quran's habit of shifting between singular and plural in divine speech at all. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (d. 241 AH) takes up this exact problem in *al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya wa'l-Zanadiqa*. He answers doubters who pointed to God saying "*Indeed I am with you both, hearing and seeing*" (20:46, to Moses and Aaron) alongside "*Indeed We are with you, listening*" (26:15, the same event), as if the shift were a contradiction.[^21] His answer treats the alternation as ordinary linguistic idiom, not evidence of anything suspicious and not something requiring embarrassment. That establishes, in the third Islamic century, that the Quran's pronoun variation had already been noticed, questioned by skeptics, and answered by the tradition's founding jurists — centuries before anyone was debating Trinity proof-texts with Christian missionaries. Later Hanbali jurists, among them al-Qadi Abu Ya'la, read Ahmad's brief comment as reported by Ibn Taymiyyah to mean exactly what the participatory reading argues, that "*it is permissible in the language for a single great one who has agents (a'wan) to say 'we did such-and-such.'*"[^22] The specific two-explanation structure — majesty as one live option, agency as the other, named side by side rather than fought over — is on record by the fifth century AH. Makki ibn Abi Talib (d. 437 AH) explains the shift from singular to plural in "*My Lord, send me back*" (23:99) exactly this way in *al-Hidaya ila Bulugh al-Nihaya*. The disbeliever addresses God alone in the singular, then turns to address the angels who seize his soul, hence the plural.[^23] Both explanations are offered as ordinary, uncontroversial options, in a work of Quranic grammar with no theological argument to win. --- The Clearest Classical Statement — Al-Raghib al-Isfahani The clearest confirmation that this was never a marginal position comes directly from al-Raghib al-Isfahani (d. c. 502 AH), in his own dictionary of Quranic vocabulary, *al-Mufradat fi Gharib al-Qur'an*. Al-Raghib records both explanations as live options in his own time, majesty being one. He then states the second explanation in language almost identical to Khalifa's. "*Some of the scholars said, God, exalted is He, mentions such expressions when the act named afterward is done through the mediation of some of His angels, or some of His agents, so that 'We' becomes an expression for Him together with them.*"[^24] He applies this exact framework to 15:9, tracing the descent of the Quran through the Pen, the Tablet, and Gabriel, and to 56:85, where "We are nearer to him than you" refers to the moment of death, when the angels are the ones present taking the soul.[^25] This is a lexical reference work, not a polemical tract. Al-Raghib is not defending Islam from an outside challenge. He is defining how a specific grammatical form functions across the text, and angelic participation is one of the two definitions on record, stated as plainly as the majesty reading sitting right next to it. Two later lexicographers carried the same passage forward almost word for word, al-Samin al-Halabi (d. 756 AH), in *'Umdat al-Huffaz*, and al-Firuzabadi (d. 817 AH) — author of the standard Arabic dictionary *al-Qamus al-Muhit* — in his own *Basa'ir Dhawi al-Tamyiz*.[^26] Al-Firuzabadi's version adds a genuine refinement rather than simply copying. He explicitly rules the agentive reading out for "*and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein*" (50:16), insisting that verse has to be read as plain majesty instead.[^27] Three lexicographers across three centuries kept this reading alive, and they kept arguing over exactly where its boundary falls. That is the mark of a real, working grammatical category. --- Ibn Kathir Draws the Line Himself Beyond Mary's conception, Ibn Kathir ties the reading together across the Quran in his own words. Commenting on "*and We are nearer to him than the jugular vein*" (50:16), he draws the same connection out loud. He is not being asked to defend this against a Christian, a Mu'tazilite, or anyone else. He is simply reading the Quran, verse by verse, and reaching for the same explanation each time three of Khalifa's own key verses come up. Two More Scholars, Same Verses Two later scholars independently apply the identical reading to Mary's conception specifically. Al-Khatib al-Sharbini (d. 977 AH) fuses majesty and mediation into a single clause on 66:12 in *al-Siraj al-Munir*, writing that the plural belongs there "*by virtue of what belongs to Us of majesty, through the mediation of Our angel Gabriel.*"[^29] He does not treat these as competing theories. The plural is majestic because it proceeds through the angel. Al-Suyuti (d. 911 AH) treats angelic mediation as a live, unremarkable reading of the same verse, 21:91, not in his famous *al-Durr al-Manthur* but in a separate work specifically on Quranic inimitability, *Mu'tarak al-Aqran fi I'jaz al-Qur'an*, where he states plainly that "*that casting was either through the mediation of the angel referred to by 'the spirit,' or without it.*"[^30] --- The Mechanism Behind the Pronoun Al-Razi on the Order of Belief None of this works unless revelation itself actually runs through angelic mediation as a matter of course, and that premise is not asserted only by implication. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 606 AH) states it as settled doctrine in *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, grounded in the Quran's own ordering of belief-objects at the end of Surat al-Baqara, "*the believers — all have believed in God, and His angels, and His books, and His messengers*" (2:285). He argues the order is not accidental. "*Revelation's arrival from God to the prophets never occurs except by the mediation of the angels... He began with God, then the angels, because they are the ones who receive the revelation from God directly, without mediation, and then convey it to the prophets.*"[^31] This is the mechanism the participatory reading of 15:9 depends on. It is stated independently by one of the tradition's most influential rationalist exegetes, without reference to the pronoun question at all. Al-Zarkashi States It as a General Rule Badr al-Din al-Zarkashi (d. 794 AH) goes a step further and states the pronoun's connection to that mechanism as a general rule. His *al-Burhan fi 'Ulum al-Qur'an* is one of the two or three most authoritative reference works ever written on Quranic science. In his chapter on اِلْتِفَات , the grammatical device of shifting between persons, he explains why the Quran moves from third person to first person in "*God, who sent the winds, so they raise a cloud... then We drove it to a dead land*" (35:9). "*It is His habitual practice, glory be to Him, in all these acts, to speak of them with the nūn of magnification that indicates He has troops and creation whom He has subjected to that end.*"[^32] He backs this "habitual practice" claim by pointing to the same first-person shift elsewhere in the Quran, including "*so when We recite it, follow its recitation*" (75:18), which he glosses as "*when Our messenger Gabriel recites it.*"[^33] Al-Zarkashi works this out in direct conversation with 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani and al-Zamakhshari on the mechanics of اِلْتِفَات . This is mainstream Arabic rhetorical scholarship on the Quran treating the participatory plural as a working assumption about how the language functions, not a theological special plea. Where Al-Zamakhshari Holds Back Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) himself does not make this exact grammatical argument on 15:9 in *al-Kashshaf*. His emphatic reading of " إِنَّا نَحْنُ " there is built around underscoring God's own decisive responsibility for sending the Quran down, not an explicit joint pronoun. But even so, he takes Gabriel's active role in the event for granted as part of what the verse describes, writing that "*He is the one who dispatched Gabriel with it to Muhammad, with watchers before him and behind him, until it descended... preserved from the devils.*"[^34] Even where an exegete's own emphasis lands on majesty, Gabriel's participation in the act is never in question. --- Not Only Angels Al-Raghib al-Isfahani's own definition already names the category as "*some of His angels or some of His agents,*" a phrase that opens the door beyond angelic beings without anyone having to stretch it there. Ibn Taymiyyah's version of the same joint explanation uses the same pairing in *Bayan Talbis al-Jahmiyya*, a sovereign speaking in the plural because he has subordinates under his real ownership and command, not because those subordinates are all one kind of creature.[^35] Khalifa's own reading already reflects this. His example for 15:9 names Gabriel and Muhammad together, an angel and a man, both credited inside the same plural pronoun. That is not an inconsistency in the classical category. It is the category working as designed. The relevant division in the sources was never angel versus human. It was single divine actor versus divine actor plus whoever carries the task out, whatever that agent happens to be. --- What the Objection Actually Assumes The idea that Dr. Khalifa invented this reading rests on the assumption that جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم was always the only serious explanation, and everything else is a recent workaround invented to answer Christians. The sources above make that assumption hard to hold. Ahmad ibn Hanbal was answering doubts about the Quran's pronoun shifts in the third Islamic century, long before organized polemics with Christian missionaries over the Trinity became a live genre. Makki ibn Abi Talib and al-Raghib al-Isfahani were writing grammar and lexicography, not apologetics, and they named the agentive reading as a live option with no argument to win. Al-Zarkashi built a standard reference work on Quranic rhetoric still assigned in seminaries today, and he states the participatory reading as a general rule, not a defensive maneuver. Ibn Kathir, the most-read tafsir in the Sunni world after al-Tabari's, reaches for the identical explanation unprompted, every time one of Khalifa's key verses comes up. And Ibn Taymiyyah — the scholar most often cited as the source of the majesty-only position — is on record naming both explanations and using them together against a Christian interlocutor, arguing that God has the greater claim to the plural precisely because His subordinates are real. What actually happened, if the sources are read in order, is closer to the reverse of the traditionalist claim. The angelic-participation reading is attested, explicitly and by name, in mainstream Sunni scholarship continuously from the fifth century AH forward. It appears in lexicons. It appears in the two or three most important Quranic-science encyclopedias in the tradition. It appears in the most widely read tafsir after al-Tabari's. And its underlying puzzle — why does the Quran's divine speech vary between singular and plural at all — was already being seriously answered in the third century. The plural-of-majesty reading, borrowed from the vocabulary of kings, became the more repeated answer in later popular use, partly because it is shorter and easier to deploy in a live argument than tracing which verses involve angelic mediation and which do not. Convenience is not the same thing as precedent. On the sources that survive scrutiny, the precedent runs the other way. --- Where Khalifa's Reading Goes Further Dr. Khalifa's specific contribution is not the existence of the agentic reading. The sources above already establish that. His contribution is the precision with which he applies it, and the absoluteness of the rule he states. Al-Raghib names 15:9 and 56:85. Ibn Kathir names 50:16, 56:85, and 15:9, tying them together himself. Al-Sharbini and al-Suyuti independently apply the same reading to 21:91 and 66:12. None of them lay out the full pattern across the whole Quran the way Khalifa does, and none of them claim, as he does, that the plural *invariably* signals participation rather than sometimes doing so.[^36] It is singular where God acts alone and directly, as with Adam and with Moses. It is plural wherever an angel is textually involved in carrying the act out, as with Jesus's creation and the Quran's descent. That is not a new theological claim. It is the same classical grammatical category, جَمْعٌ لِمُشَارَكَةِ الْمَلَائِكَةِ , checked systematically against every relevant verse instead of a handful of proof texts scattered across a dozen different books written centuries apart. The grammatical machinery underneath it is not modern at all. A Contemporary Scholar Confirms It Independently Contemporary scholars of Quranic rhetoric still teach a version of it. Fadel Saleh al-Samarra'i, in a recorded lecture series on Quranic eloquence, independently lays out the identical Adam-versus-Mary contrast, stating that "*when God's command is delivered through the mediation of an angel, it comes with the plural pronoun; and when it is not, it is singular.*"[^37] He cites 21:91 against 38:72 by name — the same pairing Khalifa uses in Appendix 10 — arrived at independently by a scholar working inside the classical tradition rather than defending it. --- Conclusion The claim that God's plural "We" reflects agentic participation rather than royal self-reference is not a twentieth-century apologetic invention. Its underlying puzzle was already being answered by Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the third Islamic century. The specific two-explanation structure — majesty as one reading, angelic or agentive participation as the other, offered side by side — is on record by the fifth century in Makki ibn Abi Talib. It is stated in its clearest and most explicit form by al-Raghib al-Isfahani, and carried forward faithfully by al-Samin al-Halabi and al-Firuzabadi across three more centuries. It is applied verse by verse to exactly Khalifa's own examples by Ibn Kathir. It is restated as a general principle of Quranic rhetoric by al-Zarkashi, in dialogue with al-Jurjani and al-Zamakhshari. It is grounded in its theological mechanism by al-Razi. And, the sharpest confirmation of all, it is named explicitly — alongside the majesty reading rather than instead of it — by Ibn Taymiyyah himself, the very scholar modern traditionalists invoke as the authority against it. The modern insistence that جَمْعُ التَّعْظِيم is the only classical position does not describe the actual history of the question. It describes which answer became easiest to repeat. Khalifa's reading in Appendix 10 sits inside a real, well-documented, cross-generational tradition. He applies it with more textual consistency, and states it in more absolute terms, than most of the scholars who articulated it ever had occasion to. The participatory plural ( جَمْعُ الْمُشَارَكَةِ ) is not a modern invention. It is a live, named, continuously attested reading in mainstream Sunni scholarship from the 3rd/9th century forward. Khalifa's contribution is not creating the category but applying it with systematic consistency across the entire Quranic text. --- --- Notes [^1]: Rashad Khalifa, trans., *Quran: The Final Testament: Authorized English Version*, rev. ed. title: The Wisdom of Solomon and the End of Jesus
description: A close reading of Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 against the Wisdom of Solomon

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Sean Anthony has proposed that the Qur'an's account of the end of Jesus's earthly mission is best read against late ancient Jewish polemics against, and parody of, the life of Jesus of Nazareth.[^1] His case rests on a simple observation: Q 4:157 does not argue with a Christian confession. It answers a hostile claim placed in the mouths of Jesus's own opponents — "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God." Anthony shows that the shape of this claim, and of the Qur'an's rebuttal, tracks the anti-Passion narrative preserved in the earliest Aramaic recensions of the *Toledot Yeshu*, the Jewish counter-Gospel in which the sages of Israel try, execute, and bury Jesus, then produce his corpse before Pilate to refute his followers' claim that he ascended to heaven.[^2] This piece extends Anthony's reorientation of the discussion toward Jewish sources by turning to a different kind of text: the Wisdom of Solomon, a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book composed centuries before Muḥammad's mission and read as scripture by both Jewish and Christian communities of the late antique Near East. Wisdom 2–5 supplies a scriptural grammar in which the elements of the qur'anic dispute over Jesus's end already appear together, in sequence, applied to an unnamed righteous man rather than to a fictionalized biography of Jesus. Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, five criteria drawn directly from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end: hostile plotting, testing of divine sonship, condemnation to a shameful death, hostile misperception mistaken for knowledge, and divine taking beyond hostile reach. Since Wisdom 2's mockery scene is also the acknowledged literary source of the Synoptic crucifixion taunt in Matthew 27:39–43, the Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157 can be read as answering both a Jewish anti-Gospel narrative of Jesus's execution and the older scriptural idiom in which that execution scene was first cast as a test of divine sonship. Wisdom of Solomon and the Toledot Yeshu traditions are not competing sources — they are two moments in a single stream of Jewish righteous-sufferer literature that the Gospel Passion narratives drew on and that the Qur'an independently answers. Qur'anic citations below follow Rashad Khalifa's translation, matching the Arabic and English pulled directly from this site's own verified Qur'an data. Wisdom of Solomon and New Testament citations follow the NRSV tradition unless a footnote specifies otherwise, consistent with how the wider scholarship on Wisdom's relationship to the Gospel Passion narratives quotes it.

sections.heading: The Qur'anic Criteria
sections.text: Q 3:54–55 supplies the earlier of the Qur'an's two accounts of the end of Jesus's mission, in compressed form: the Israelites plot against Jesus, God plots in response and plots best of all, and God then tells Jesus that He will take him, raise him to Himself, and purify him from the disbelievers. Q 4:156–159 supplies the second account, embedded in an extended polemic against the People of Scripture in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Here the Qur'an cites the hostile claim directly, denies both the killing and the crucifixion, states that the matter was made to appear otherwise to the opponents, that those who differed over it were in doubt with no real knowledge, and concludes that God raised Jesus to Himself. Q 5:117 supplies a third, retrospective fragment in Jesus's own voice: as long as he remained among his people he was a witness over them, and once God took him, God alone remained watchful over them. Read together, these three passages yield five criteria a Jewish-scriptural analogue to the Qur'an's account should satisfy.[^3] These criteria deliberately set aside Q 4:156's slander against Mary (*buhtān ʿaẓīm*) and its connection to the Panthera legend, since Wisdom of Solomon has no analogue to a charge of adultery against the righteous man's mother — that motif belongs to a different polemical tradition already traced in detail by Anthony.[^4] ### 1. Hostile Plotting against the Righteous Figure Q 3:54 opens with the plot itself — "*they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters.*" The verse gives no content to the Israelites' scheme and lets the divine response define its shape. A relevant analogue needs a righteous figure opposed by hostile agents whose violence or intrigue becomes the occasion for a divine reversal rather than a defeat. ### 2. The Testing of Divine Sonship or Protection His opponents elsewhere dismiss Jesus's signs as sorcery: which is to say they contest the divine source of his authority rather than merely his person. Anthony reads these two verses as the Qur'an's rebuttal of a specific accusation preserved in the *Toledot Yeshu*, where Jesus's miracles are explained away as learned sorcery.[^5] The two readings are not exclusive — discrediting a claimant's miracles as sorcery and discrediting his claim to divine sonship are two ways of attacking the same thing, since a miracle is precisely the evidence a claim to divine sonship would call on. Wisdom's wicked test the righteous man's sonship through torture and death rather than by explaining away a miracle, but the target in both cases is the same: the reality of the figure's relationship to God, not just his safety or the facts of his biography. Wisdom's wicked never accuse the righteous man of sorcery — the charge has no place in Wisdom 2's anthropology of predation. The sorcery charge belongs to the *Toledot* line of transmission alone; Wisdom supplies the sonship-testing logic behind Q 5:110 and 61:6. ### 3. Condemnation to a Shameful Death The addition of crucifixion beyond mere killing matters. Crucifixion in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East was a punishment built for public humiliation as much as for death, and the opponents' claim asserts mastery over Jesus's body and reputation together. A relevant analogue needs the wicked to condemn the righteous figure specifically to a shameful, public death. ### 4. Hostile Misperception Mistaken for Knowledge Q 4:157 moves from *shubbiha lahum* ("it was made to appear so to them") to *shakk* ("doubt"), *ʿilm* ("knowledge"), *ẓann* ("conjecture"), and *yaqīn* ("certainty"), stripping the opponents' claim of the status of knowledge and reducing it to conjecture. A relevant analogue needs observers who take an appearance for certainty and are shown, within the text itself, to have mistaken the one for the other. ### 5. Divine Taking and Preservation beyond Hostile Reach Q 3:55 gives the fuller triad of taking, raising, and purification, and Q 5:117 supplies Jesus's own retrospective description of the moment God took him. Q 39:42 anchors the sense of the verb *tawaffī* used throughout this material, naming God's taking of souls both at death and during sleep and leaving the precise mode of the taking to context rather than to the verb itself. Plotting, testing, shameful death, misperception, and preservation each recur separately across a wide range of Second Temple and rabbinic literature, and on their own they prove little. What licenses treating a text as a genuine analogue, rather than a coincidental parallel, is that it supplies all five elements in the same sequence, applied to the same kind of figure, within one continuous unit — not scattered across independent compositions.

sections.heading: Control Texts: Other Candidates for the Righteous-Sufferer Analogue
sections.text: Four other texts belong to the same broad current of Second Temple and post-Temple Jewish literature and have each been proposed as background to the Gospel Passion or related qur'anic material: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, the court tales of Daniel 3 and 6, and the martyrdom narratives of 2 and 4 Maccabees. Running each against the five criteria shows why none is a rival candidate to Wisdom of Solomon. **Isaiah 53** satisfies the shameful-death and misperception criteria more clearly than any other candidate. The servant is "cut off from the land of the living" and given "his grave... with the wicked" (Isa 53:8–9), and the community's initial judgment — "we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted" (Isa 53:4) — is corrected within the poem itself. But Isaiah 53 supplies no equivalent to the first and second criteria: no named hostile agents are shown plotting against the servant, and his status as God's son is never at issue. Isaiah 53 has no sonship language at all.[^6] **Psalm 22** comes closer than Isaiah 53 to the sonship-testing criterion, since the psalmist's tormentors mock him in terms that anticipate both Wisdom 2 and the Gospel taunt at the cross: "He committed his cause to the Lord, let him deliver him, let him rescue him, for he delights in him" (Ps 22:8) — the same logic that organizes Wisdom 2:18 and Matthew 27:43, a connection well established in Passion-narrative scholarship.[^7] The psalm stages hostile plotting too, with the psalmist encircled by "a company of evildoers" (Ps 22:16). What it lacks is a narrated misperception for the text to correct — the psalm moves directly from lament to vindication — and its resolution is deliverance within the psalmist's own lifetime, not a taking or raising after the fact. **Daniel 3 and 6** supply the hostile-plot criterion as directly as any text considered here, and something like the sonship-testing criterion, since the officials' scheme doubles as a test of whether the protagonists' God can and will save them (Dan 3:15, 6:20).[^8] But Nebuchadnezzar and Darius witness the deliverance directly and in real time — a fourth figure in the furnace, the lions' mouths shut before onlookers — rather than a hidden reality later revealed. There is no death, no misperception, and no taking. **2 and 4 Maccabees** supply the hostile-plot and shameful-death criteria as fully as Wisdom does. Antiochus's persecution is a sustained hostile plot, and the martyrs voice a hope for bodily resurrection — "the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life" (2 Macc 7:9) — gesturing toward the fifth criterion.[^9] But the martyrs are tested on fidelity to the ancestral law, not on a claim to be God's son, and the narrative never stages a reversal of perception; Antiochus is never shown mistaking apparent defeat for real defeat. Text Plot Sonship test Shameful death Misperception corrected Taking / preservation Isaiah 53 No No Yes Yes Partial Psalm 22 Yes Partial Partial No No Daniel 3 / 6 Yes Partial No No No 2 & 4 Maccabees Yes No Yes No Partial Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes No single control text satisfies more than three of the five criteria, and none combines the sonship test with corrected misperception — the pairing structurally closest to the Qur'an's own rhetorical move in Q 4:157, where the opponents' claim is dismantled by stripping their certainty of the status of knowledge. Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 is the only text that supplies all five elements together, in the same sequence, applied to the same figure, within a single continuous unit.

sections.heading: The Wisdom of Solomon as Jewish-Scriptural Analogue
sections.text: The Wisdom of Solomon is a work of Alexandrian diaspora Judaism, composed in literary Greek and voiced through the persona of Solomon, most often dated to the late first century BCE or early first century CE.[^10] Its author combines biblical narrative, wisdom exhortation, and Hellenistic philosophical vocabulary in service of a single argument: the righteous who appear to suffer and die are in fact secure in God, while the wicked who appear to triumph over them are already living under judgment.[^11] Karina Hogan has shown that the book's retelling of Israel's history treats biblical narratives as paradigms of righteous and wicked conduct rather than continuous history tied to a single ethnic community, which gives its opening chapters a portable, generalized cast rather than a biography of a named hero.[^12] Larry Wills describes chapters 2–5 as staging a contest between two worldviews — the wicked, vocal and violent, and the righteous man, who says nothing and waits for a reversal that arrives only after his apparent defeat.[^13] That structure is what makes the passage useful for the Qur'an's account, since Q 4:157–158 is likewise organized around a hostile claim, an unanswering silence on its target's part, and a divine reversal delivered after the fact rather than staged as a real-time rescue. ### Wisdom 2: The Wicked Plot and Test the Righteous Man Wisdom 2 opens with the reasoning of the ungodly: life is short, death final, the soul no more than breath that disperses. From this anthropology the wicked derive an ethic of predation. Their hostility settles on one figure in particular — a righteous man who exposes their conduct as sin against the law, calls himself a child of God, and boasts that God is his father. "Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life, for if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him, and will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries." They move from proposition to action, deciding to examine his patience with insult and torture and to condemn him to a shameful death, reasoning that his own claim of divine protection will be tested by whether that protection actually arrives (Wis 2:19–20). The sequence answers the first three criteria at once. The wicked plot, as the Israelites plot against Jesus in Q 3:54. Their test targets the righteous man's claim to be God's son, not simply his life — the same way the sorcery charge in Q 5:110 and Q 61:6 targets Jesus's claim to divine backing rather than simply his safety. Their chosen instrument is a shameful death, exactly the qualifier the Qur'an adds in Q 4:157 by naming crucifixion alongside killing. ### Sonship Reworded: The Wicked's Boast in the Qur'an Wisdom's wicked do not attack an anonymous holy man. They quote him: he "professes to have knowledge of God, and calls himself a child of the Lord" (Wis 2:13), and "boasts that God is his father" (Wis 2:16). The wicked's own summary of his claim supplies the theology they intend to test — sonship of God, stated as directly as Hellenistic Greek allows. The Qur'an's opponents make the same structural move in Q 4:157 — they too are quoted boasting about a man they claim to have killed — but the content of the boast has changed. They do not say "we killed the son of God." They say "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God." The title that would answer to Wisdom's "child of the Lord" is absent. Two other titles stand in its place: son of Mary, and messenger of God. This is not an isolated turn of phrase. Q 4:171 makes the identical substitution outside any hostile speech, addressing the People of Scripture directly. The formula the Qur'an places in the mouths of Jesus's killers is the same formula the Qur'an uses for its own confession of Jesus. Element Wisdom of Solomon 2 Q 4:157 / 4:171 Self-description quoted by the hostile party "Calls himself a child of the Lord" (2:13); "boasts that God is his father" (2:16) "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God" What is being tested Literal divine sonship Prophetic office and human parentage Function of the substitution — Retains the accusatory shape of the boast while correcting its theology This kind of move — folding a doctrinal correction into a reported claim rather than refuting it afterward — is a documented feature of how the Qur'an handles material drawn from Jewish and Christian tradition. Much of the Qur'an's engagement with biblical narrative proceeds by subtext: it assumes the audience already knows a prior text, then reshapes that text's details to make a theological point rather than arguing with it directly, as Gabriel Reynolds has shown.[^14] Neal Robinson's study of qur'anic Christology treats "son of Mary" as a title chosen in deliberate contrast to Christian confessional language about Jesus, not a neutral genealogical marker.[^15] Sidney Griffith's account of the Bible's presence in the Qur'an's Arabic environment describes the same pattern: a text speaking in the vocabulary of the biblical tradition it addresses while redirecting that vocabulary toward its own claims.[^16] Set against Wisdom 2's "child of the Lord" and "God is his father," the Qur'an's "son of Mary, the messenger of God" reads as exactly this kind of move. ### Wisdom 3: Apparent Death and the Reversal of Perception Wisdom 3 opens by placing the fate of the righteous beyond the reach of the wicked's test. "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was thought to be an affliction, and their going from us to be their destruction, but they are at peace." The chapter states its opposition between perception and reality as plainly as any text in Second Temple literature could state it — the foolish read a departure as a death and a death as a destruction, and the text corrects them from outside their own perspective, in the same gesture by which Q 4:157 moves from denying the hostile act to denying that the opponents possessed any knowledge of what they claimed to have witnessed. Wisdom 3 Q 4:157–158 Shared move "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them" (3:1) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine possession overrules hostile interpretation "In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died" (3:2) "They did not kill him... but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157) Hostile or foolish observers mistake appearance for fact "Their departure was thought to be an affliction, and their going from us to be their destruction" (3:2–3) "We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary" (4:157) Apparent defeat is misread as real defeat "But they are at peace" (3:3) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine reality reverses the public reading of events Karina Hogan's study of what she calls the "ambiguity of death" in Wisdom, building on Michael Kolarcik's earlier analysis of the book's literary structure, shows this reversal is deliberate rather than incidental. Wisdom exploits the same vocabulary of death for two audiences at once: for the wicked, physical death confirms their belief in annihilation; for the righteous, the identical event marks the end of suffering and the beginning of nearness to God.[^17] That ambiguity is the interpretive space the Qur'an occupies in Q 4:157, where the opponents' certainty about Jesus's death is exposed as conjecture rather than corrected by a competing set of facts. ### Wisdom 4: The Righteous Man Taken from among Sinners Wisdom 4 turns from apparent death to the logic of removal: the one who pleases God is loved by Him and taken away while still living among sinners. "There was one who pleased God and was loved by him, and while living among sinners was taken up. He was caught up so that evil might not change his understanding or guile deceive his soul." The people who witness this fail to understand it, unaware that grace and mercy belong to God's elect and that He watches over His holy ones (Wis 4:14–15). This passage corresponds most closely to Q 3:55. Wisdom 4 Q 3:55 Shared move The one who pleases God is loved by him (4:10) "I am taking you" Divine favor defines the figure from the outset Taken while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (4:10–11) "And raising you to Myself" A verb of taking marks the removal The removal is protective, not punitive (4:11) "And purifying you from those who disbelieve" The removal separates the righteous figure from the hostile community Onlookers "see and do not understand" (4:14) Opponents have "no knowledge... only conjecture" (4:157) Onlookers witness the event without grasping it Grace and mercy belong to God's elect (4:15) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine favor, not hostile action, defines the outcome Qur'anic criterion Wisdom of Solomon Passage Hostile plotting The wicked lie in wait for the righteous man Wis 2:12 Testing of divine sonship They test whether God will deliver him as His son Wis 2:17–18 Shameful death They condemn him to a shameful death Wis 2:20 Misperception as false knowledge The foolish think he has died and mistake his departure for destruction Wis 3:2–3 Divine taking and preservation His soul is in God's hand; he is taken from among sinners Wis 3:1; 4:10–14

sections.heading: Wisdom 2 and the Gospel Passion Narrative
sections.text: The correspondence between Wisdom and the Qur'an's Jesus material gains a further layer once Wisdom 2's place in the New Testament's own Passion tradition is taken into account. Matthew's account of the mockery at the cross has long been read as drawing directly on Wisdom 2's scene of the wicked testing a self-proclaimed son of God. "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants to; for he said, 'I am God's Son.'" This reproduces the logic, and much of the vocabulary, of Wisdom 2:18. Douglas Moo's study of the Old Testament and deuterocanonical background of the Gospel Passion narratives treats the Matthean taunt as dependent on Wisdom 2 alongside Psalm 22, and commentators on Matthew have long placed the two texts side by side for exactly this reason.[^18] This connection changes what a comparison between the Qur'an and Wisdom of Solomon can claim. The Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 boast that they killed and crucified Jesus in circumstances that, on the Gospel's own telling, were narrated in the language Wisdom 2 had already supplied for the mockery of a righteous man tested as God's son. Anthony's *Toledot Yeshu* material gives the Qur'an's audience a Jewish counter-narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel's account of Jesus's death and resurrection.[^19] Wisdom of Solomon gives the same audience the older scriptural idiom in which the Gospel's own crucifixion scene had first been cast. The Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157–158 therefore reaches, whether directly or through the mediation of the Passion tradition it was answering, back to the same righteous-sufferer grammar standing behind both the Christian narrative of Jesus's death and the Jewish narrative built to mock and invert it.

sections.heading: Wisdom 3, 5, and the Motifs Absent from the Toledot Yeshu
sections.text: Anthony's own comparison supplies a further test of this argument. He scores nine motifs shared by the *Toledot Yeshu*, Q 3:54–55, and Q 4:156–159, and three of the qur'anic motifs take a minus sign under *Toledot Yeshu*: God's cleansing of Jesus from his disbelieving opponents, the exaltation of Jesus's followers over the disbelieving Israelites, and Jesus's role as an eschatological witness against his own community.[^20] Anthony's Jewish source does not account for these three motifs. Wisdom of Solomon does. Qur'anic motif Toledot Yeshu Wisdom of Solomon God cleanses Jesus of his disbelieving opponents (Q 3:55) Absent The righteous man is taken away while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (Wis 4:10–11) Followers of Jesus are exalted over the disbelieving Israelites (Q 3:55) Absent "They will govern nations and rule over peoples, and the Lord will reign over them forever" (Wis 3:8) Jesus is an eschatological witness against his ummah (Q 4:159; Q 5:117) Absent The righteous man stands before those who once condemned him, who confess, "we fools! We accounted his life madness" (Wis 5:1–5) Wisdom 3:8 answers the second gap only in a qualified sense — the verse belongs to the poem's shift from the singular righteous man of chapter 2 to the collective "righteous" of chapters 3 through 5, so its promise exalts the righteous as a class rather than naming a teacher's own followers.[^21] The structural correspondence nonetheless holds: in both texts, a hostile plot against a righteous figure ends in the elevation of those aligned with him over those who opposed him, a widening of scope Q 3:55 itself performs when it moves from Jesus's individual purification to the promise that God will place those who follow him above those who disbelieve. The third gap calls for Wisdom 5:1–8, which completes the confrontation staged in chapter 2. The wicked, who had condemned the righteous man to a shameful death, now stand before him at the reckoning. "Then the righteous will stand with great confidence in the presence of those who have oppressed them... When they see him, they will shudder with terrible dread, and they will be amazed at his unexpected salvation. They will speak to one another in repentance, and in anguish of spirit they will groan, and say, 'This is the one whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach — fools that we were! We thought that his life was madness and that his end was without honor. Why has he been numbered among the sons of God? And why is his lot among the saints?'" Q 4:159 states that "not one of the People of Scripture will fail to believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he shall bear witness against them," and Q 5:117 has Jesus describe his own role among his people in the same terms — a witness present while he remained among them and absent once God took him. Wisdom 5 stages this same reversal: the people who condemned the righteous man are made to stand before him, recognize him, and confess in his presence that their earlier judgment was wrong. The *Toledot Yeshu*, built to prove the sages' judgment of Jesus correct, supplies no such scene — its disciples claim only that God rescued Jesus by raising him to heaven, and the sages who condemned him are never made to recognize their error.[^22] Wisdom of Solomon supplies it because vindication before one's accusers, not merely rescue from them, is the outcome its argument has been building toward since chapter 2.

sections.heading: The Wisdom of Solomon in the Palestinian-Syriac Scriptural Contact Zone
sections.text: A comparison of this kind depends on Wisdom of Solomon having a plausible route into the Qur'an's late antique environment. The book's transmission history supplies one. Wisdom of Solomon began as a Greek Jewish composition from Hellenistic Alexandria, written in a monotheistic, Exodus-centered idiom for a Greek-reading Jewish community for whom the Septuagint already functioned as scripture.[^23] Its later transmission moved that idiom into the Christian biblical world. J. A. Emerton's study of the Peshitta Wisdom remains the standard account of that Syriac textual history.[^24] A second, later channel is Paul of Tella's Syro-Hexaplar translation, datable by its subscriptions to 613–617 CE, rendering Wisdom from Greek into Syriac within a generation of the Qur'an's own proclamation — evidence of active Syriac Christian scholarly investment in the book at exactly the relevant horizon.[^25] Reinhart Ceulemans and Gertjan Verhasselt have published Greek fragments of Wisdom 10 recovered from Khirbet Mird, the monastery of Kastellion in the Judean Desert, alongside other biblical fragments from the same site including portions of Mark, John, Matthew, and Acts.[^26] The find places a Septuagint copy of Wisdom inside a Palestinian monastic library of the kind that also transmitted Gospel texts. A separate Semitic Palestinian witness survives in Christian Palestinian Aramaic, attested in fragments of Wisdom 9–10 preserved in a Cairo Geniza palimpsest.[^27] This Palestinian-Syriac contact zone already carries weight elsewhere in the study of the Qur'an's Jesus and Mary traditions. Stephen Shoemaker has argued that the nativity scene in Q 19, with Mary sent to a remote place, resting beneath a palm, and given water from a spring, intersects with Palestinian local tradition connected to the Kathisma church between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where late antique Christian memory had already linked Mary's rest, a spring, and a palm tree at a single site.[^28] Nicolai Sinai's survey of the debate over Dye, Tesei, and Shoemaker's work identifies exactly this kind of Palestinian Christian material as central to reconstructing the Qur'an's rhetorical environment.[^29] Anthony's *Toledot Yeshu* argument occupies the Jewish side of the same contact zone, proposing that the Qur'an's account of Jesus's final days answers a narrative that had likely circulated orally among the Jews of the Hijaz by the early seventh century.[^30] The Kathisma church supplies the material anchor for that intersection: built in the mid-fifth century on the Jerusalem–Bethlehem road and enlarged with an octagonal plan in the sixth, it commemorated the tradition that Mary rested there during her journey to Bethlehem, and Byzantine pilgrim accounts and liturgical calendars associate the same location with a spring and, eventually, a palm tree said to have bent down to offer her its fruit.[^31] Kathisma's location matters beyond its relevance to Shoemaker's thesis: the shrine sat on the same Jerusalem–Bethlehem–Judean Desert corridor as Khirbet Mird, where the Greek fragments of Wisdom 10 were recovered, less than a day's journey apart. This is not evidence any single community read both texts side by side, but two separate lines of access converge on the same ground — Shoemaker's reconstruction places the qur'anic milieu within reach of Palestinian Christian sacred geography, and the evidence assembled here places it within reach of Palestinian Christian scriptural transmission.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, all five criteria drawn from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end. The wicked plot against the righteous man. They test whether his claim to be God's son is genuine by condemning him to insult, torture, and a shameful death. They believe, once he is gone, that they have destroyed him. The text answers them from outside their own perspective, placing the righteous man's soul in God's hand and describing his removal as protection rather than defeat. Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 move through the same sequence: hostile plotting, a claim of killing and crucifixion, the exposure of that claim as conjecture rather than knowledge, and God's own taking and raising of Jesus. The *Toledot Yeshu* supplies a hostile narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel directly, scene by scene, and it is this narrative, or something like it, that the Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 appear to be citing. Wisdom of Solomon supplies the older interpretive grammar that had already shaped how a scene of that kind could be told and understood, since it is Wisdom 2's mockery of a righteous son of God that stands behind Matthew's own account of the taunting at the cross. What the Qur'an adds to this inherited grammar is its own account of what Jesus was in the first place. Wisdom lets its righteous man call God his father and claim sonship as his own boast; the Qur'an gives Jesus none of that language, having the wicked in the text say only that they killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God. The wicked in Wisdom are wrong to think a righteous son of God can be destroyed by a shameful death. The Qur'an's opponents are wrong for the same reason and for a further one — even if a death had occurred, it would have marked the end of a servant's mission rather than the defeat of a divine son. Wisdom of Solomon and the Toledot Yeshu are not competing explanations for Q 4:157. They are two layers of the same tradition. The Toledot Yeshu gives the Qur'an's audience a scene-by-scene Jewish rebuttal of the Christian Passion. Wisdom of Solomon gives that same audience the older scriptural grammar — a righteous son of God, tested by a hostile crowd, condemned to a shameful death the crowd mistakes for victory, and secretly preserved in God's own hand — in which both the Gospel's crucifixion scene and its Jewish inversion were already cast. The Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157–158 answers a claim with a history reaching past the Gospel Passion narrative itself, into the wisdom literature that gave Second Temple Judaism its language for how a story like this was supposed to end.
