fullText: Sean Anthony has proposed that the Qur'an's account of the end of Jesus's earthly mission is best read against late ancient Jewish polemics against, and parody of, the life of Jesus of Nazareth.[^1] His case rests on a simple observation: Q 4:157 does not argue with a Christian confession. It answers a hostile claim placed in the mouths of Jesus's own opponents — "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God." Anthony shows that the shape of this claim, and of the Qur'an's rebuttal, tracks the anti-Passion narrative preserved in the earliest Aramaic recensions of the *Toledot Yeshu*, the Jewish counter-Gospel in which the sages of Israel try, execute, and bury Jesus, then produce his corpse before Pilate to refute his followers' claim that he ascended to heaven.[^2] This piece extends Anthony's reorientation of the discussion toward Jewish sources by turning to a different kind of text: the Wisdom of Solomon, a Hellenistic Jewish wisdom book composed centuries before Muḥammad's mission and read as scripture by both Jewish and Christian communities of the late antique Near East. Wisdom 2–5 supplies a scriptural grammar in which the elements of the qur'anic dispute over Jesus's end already appear together, in sequence, applied to an unnamed righteous man rather than to a fictionalized biography of Jesus. Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, five criteria drawn directly from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end: hostile plotting, testing of divine sonship, condemnation to a shameful death, hostile misperception mistaken for knowledge, and divine taking beyond hostile reach. Since Wisdom 2's mockery scene is also the acknowledged literary source of the Synoptic crucifixion taunt in Matthew 27:39–43, the Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157 can be read as answering both a Jewish anti-Gospel narrative of Jesus's execution and the older scriptural idiom in which that execution scene was first cast as a test of divine sonship. Wisdom of Solomon and the Toledot Yeshu traditions are not competing sources — they are two moments in a single stream of Jewish righteous-sufferer literature that the Gospel Passion narratives drew on and that the Qur'an independently answers. Qur'anic citations below follow Rashad Khalifa's translation, matching the Arabic and English pulled directly from this site's own verified Qur'an data. Wisdom of Solomon and New Testament citations follow the NRSV tradition unless a footnote specifies otherwise, consistent with how the wider scholarship on Wisdom's relationship to the Gospel Passion narratives quotes it. The Qur'anic Criteria Q 3:54–55 supplies the earlier of the Qur'an's two accounts of the end of Jesus's mission, in compressed form: the Israelites plot against Jesus, God plots in response and plots best of all, and God then tells Jesus that He will take him, raise him to Himself, and purify him from the disbelievers. Q 4:156–159 supplies the second account, embedded in an extended polemic against the People of Scripture in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. Here the Qur'an cites the hostile claim directly, denies both the killing and the crucifixion, states that the matter was made to appear otherwise to the opponents, that those who differed over it were in doubt with no real knowledge, and concludes that God raised Jesus to Himself. Q 5:117 supplies a third, retrospective fragment in Jesus's own voice: as long as he remained among his people he was a witness over them, and once God took him, God alone remained watchful over them. Read together, these three passages yield five criteria a Jewish-scriptural analogue to the Qur'an's account should satisfy.[^3] These criteria deliberately set aside Q 4:156's slander against Mary (*buhtān ʿaẓīm*) and its connection to the Panthera legend, since Wisdom of Solomon has no analogue to a charge of adultery against the righteous man's mother — that motif belongs to a different polemical tradition already traced in detail by Anthony.[^4] 1. Hostile Plotting against the Righteous Figure Q 3:54 opens with the plot itself — "*they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters.*" The verse gives no content to the Israelites' scheme and lets the divine response define its shape. A relevant analogue needs a righteous figure opposed by hostile agents whose violence or intrigue becomes the occasion for a divine reversal rather than a defeat. 2. The Testing of Divine Sonship or Protection His opponents elsewhere dismiss Jesus's signs as sorcery: which is to say they contest the divine source of his authority rather than merely his person. Anthony reads these two verses as the Qur'an's rebuttal of a specific accusation preserved in the *Toledot Yeshu*, where Jesus's miracles are explained away as learned sorcery.[^5] The two readings are not exclusive — discrediting a claimant's miracles as sorcery and discrediting his claim to divine sonship are two ways of attacking the same thing, since a miracle is precisely the evidence a claim to divine sonship would call on. Wisdom's wicked test the righteous man's sonship through torture and death rather than by explaining away a miracle, but the target in both cases is the same: the reality of the figure's relationship to God, not just his safety or the facts of his biography. Wisdom's wicked never accuse the righteous man of sorcery — the charge has no place in Wisdom 2's anthropology of predation. The sorcery charge belongs to the *Toledot* line of transmission alone; Wisdom supplies the sonship-testing logic behind Q 5:110 and 61:6. 3. Condemnation to a Shameful Death The addition of crucifixion beyond mere killing matters. Crucifixion in the ancient Mediterranean and Near East was a punishment built for public humiliation as much as for death, and the opponents' claim asserts mastery over Jesus's body and reputation together. A relevant analogue needs the wicked to condemn the righteous figure specifically to a shameful, public death. 4. Hostile Misperception Mistaken for Knowledge Q 4:157 moves from *shubbiha lahum* ("it was made to appear so to them") to *shakk* ("doubt"), *ʿilm* ("knowledge"), *ẓann* ("conjecture"), and *yaqīn* ("certainty"), stripping the opponents' claim of the status of knowledge and reducing it to conjecture. A relevant analogue needs observers who take an appearance for certainty and are shown, within the text itself, to have mistaken the one for the other. 5. Divine Taking and Preservation beyond Hostile Reach Q 3:55 gives the fuller triad of taking, raising, and purification, and Q 5:117 supplies Jesus's own retrospective description of the moment God took him. Q 39:42 anchors the sense of the verb *tawaffī* used throughout this material, naming God's taking of souls both at death and during sleep and leaving the precise mode of the taking to context rather than to the verb itself. Plotting, testing, shameful death, misperception, and preservation each recur separately across a wide range of Second Temple and rabbinic literature, and on their own they prove little. What licenses treating a text as a genuine analogue, rather than a coincidental parallel, is that it supplies all five elements in the same sequence, applied to the same kind of figure, within one continuous unit — not scattered across independent compositions. Control Texts: Other Candidates for the Righteous-Sufferer Analogue Four other texts belong to the same broad current of Second Temple and post-Temple Jewish literature and have each been proposed as background to the Gospel Passion or related qur'anic material: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, the court tales of Daniel 3 and 6, and the martyrdom narratives of 2 and 4 Maccabees. Running each against the five criteria shows why none is a rival candidate to Wisdom of Solomon. **Isaiah 53** satisfies the shameful-death and misperception criteria more clearly than any other candidate. The servant is "cut off from the land of the living" and given "his grave... with the wicked" (Isa 53:8–9), and the community's initial judgment — "we accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted" (Isa 53:4) — is corrected within the poem itself. But Isaiah 53 supplies no equivalent to the first and second criteria: no named hostile agents are shown plotting against the servant, and his status as God's son is never at issue. Isaiah 53 has no sonship language at all.[^6] **Psalm 22** comes closer than Isaiah 53 to the sonship-testing criterion, since the psalmist's tormentors mock him in terms that anticipate both Wisdom 2 and the Gospel taunt at the cross: "He committed his cause to the Lord, let him deliver him, let him rescue him, for he delights in him" (Ps 22:8) — the same logic that organizes Wisdom 2:18 and Matthew 27:43, a connection well established in Passion-narrative scholarship.[^7] The psalm stages hostile plotting too, with the psalmist encircled by "a company of evildoers" (Ps 22:16). What it lacks is a narrated misperception for the text to correct — the psalm moves directly from lament to vindication — and its resolution is deliverance within the psalmist's own lifetime, not a taking or raising after the fact. **Daniel 3 and 6** supply the hostile-plot criterion as directly as any text considered here, and something like the sonship-testing criterion, since the officials' scheme doubles as a test of whether the protagonists' God can and will save them (Dan 3:15, 6:20).[^8] But Nebuchadnezzar and Darius witness the deliverance directly and in real time — a fourth figure in the furnace, the lions' mouths shut before onlookers — rather than a hidden reality later revealed. There is no death, no misperception, and no taking. **2 and 4 Maccabees** supply the hostile-plot and shameful-death criteria as fully as Wisdom does. Antiochus's persecution is a sustained hostile plot, and the martyrs voice a hope for bodily resurrection — "the King of the universe will raise us up to an everlasting renewal of life" (2 Macc 7:9) — gesturing toward the fifth criterion.[^9] But the martyrs are tested on fidelity to the ancestral law, not on a claim to be God's son, and the narrative never stages a reversal of perception; Antiochus is never shown mistaking apparent defeat for real defeat. Text Plot Sonship test Shameful death Misperception corrected Taking / preservation Isaiah 53 No No Yes Yes Partial Psalm 22 Yes Partial Partial No No Daniel 3 / 6 Yes Partial No No No 2 & 4 Maccabees Yes No Yes No Partial Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes No single control text satisfies more than three of the five criteria, and none combines the sonship test with corrected misperception — the pairing structurally closest to the Qur'an's own rhetorical move in Q 4:157, where the opponents' claim is dismantled by stripping their certainty of the status of knowledge. Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 is the only text that supplies all five elements together, in the same sequence, applied to the same figure, within a single continuous unit. The Wisdom of Solomon as Jewish-Scriptural Analogue The Wisdom of Solomon is a work of Alexandrian diaspora Judaism, composed in literary Greek and voiced through the persona of Solomon, most often dated to the late first century BCE or early first century CE.[^10] Its author combines biblical narrative, wisdom exhortation, and Hellenistic philosophical vocabulary in service of a single argument: the righteous who appear to suffer and die are in fact secure in God, while the wicked who appear to triumph over them are already living under judgment.[^11] Karina Hogan has shown that the book's retelling of Israel's history treats biblical narratives as paradigms of righteous and wicked conduct rather than continuous history tied to a single ethnic community, which gives its opening chapters a portable, generalized cast rather than a biography of a named hero.[^12] Larry Wills describes chapters 2–5 as staging a contest between two worldviews — the wicked, vocal and violent, and the righteous man, who says nothing and waits for a reversal that arrives only after his apparent defeat.[^13] That structure is what makes the passage useful for the Qur'an's account, since Q 4:157–158 is likewise organized around a hostile claim, an unanswering silence on its target's part, and a divine reversal delivered after the fact rather than staged as a real-time rescue. Wisdom 2: The Wicked Plot and Test the Righteous Man Wisdom 2 opens with the reasoning of the ungodly: life is short, death final, the soul no more than breath that disperses. From this anthropology the wicked derive an ethic of predation. Their hostility settles on one figure in particular — a righteous man who exposes their conduct as sin against the law, calls himself a child of God, and boasts that God is his father. "Let us see if his words are true, and let us test what will happen at the end of his life, for if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him, and will deliver him from the hand of his adversaries." They move from proposition to action, deciding to examine his patience with insult and torture and to condemn him to a shameful death, reasoning that his own claim of divine protection will be tested by whether that protection actually arrives (Wis 2:19–20). The sequence answers the first three criteria at once. The wicked plot, as the Israelites plot against Jesus in Q 3:54. Their test targets the righteous man's claim to be God's son, not simply his life — the same way the sorcery charge in Q 5:110 and Q 61:6 targets Jesus's claim to divine backing rather than simply his safety. Their chosen instrument is a shameful death, exactly the qualifier the Qur'an adds in Q 4:157 by naming crucifixion alongside killing. Sonship Reworded: The Wicked's Boast in the Qur'an Wisdom's wicked do not attack an anonymous holy man. They quote him: he "professes to have knowledge of God, and calls himself a child of the Lord" (Wis 2:13), and "boasts that God is his father" (Wis 2:16). The wicked's own summary of his claim supplies the theology they intend to test — sonship of God, stated as directly as Hellenistic Greek allows. The Qur'an's opponents make the same structural move in Q 4:157 — they too are quoted boasting about a man they claim to have killed — but the content of the boast has changed. They do not say "we killed the son of God." They say "we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God." The title that would answer to Wisdom's "child of the Lord" is absent. Two other titles stand in its place: son of Mary, and messenger of God. This is not an isolated turn of phrase. Q 4:171 makes the identical substitution outside any hostile speech, addressing the People of Scripture directly. The formula the Qur'an places in the mouths of Jesus's killers is the same formula the Qur'an uses for its own confession of Jesus. Element Wisdom of Solomon 2 Q 4:157 / 4:171 Self-description quoted by the hostile party "Calls himself a child of the Lord" (2:13); "boasts that God is his father" (2:16) "The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God" What is being tested Literal divine sonship Prophetic office and human parentage Function of the substitution — Retains the accusatory shape of the boast while correcting its theology This kind of move — folding a doctrinal correction into a reported claim rather than refuting it afterward — is a documented feature of how the Qur'an handles material drawn from Jewish and Christian tradition. Much of the Qur'an's engagement with biblical narrative proceeds by subtext: it assumes the audience already knows a prior text, then reshapes that text's details to make a theological point rather than arguing with it directly, as Gabriel Reynolds has shown.[^14] Neal Robinson's study of qur'anic Christology treats "son of Mary" as a title chosen in deliberate contrast to Christian confessional language about Jesus, not a neutral genealogical marker.[^15] Sidney Griffith's account of the Bible's presence in the Qur'an's Arabic environment describes the same pattern: a text speaking in the vocabulary of the biblical tradition it addresses while redirecting that vocabulary toward its own claims.[^16] Set against Wisdom 2's "child of the Lord" and "God is his father," the Qur'an's "son of Mary, the messenger of God" reads as exactly this kind of move. Wisdom 3: Apparent Death and the Reversal of Perception Wisdom 3 opens by placing the fate of the righteous beyond the reach of the wicked's test. "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them. In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died, and their departure was thought to be an affliction, and their going from us to be their destruction, but they are at peace." The chapter states its opposition between perception and reality as plainly as any text in Second Temple literature could state it — the foolish read a departure as a death and a death as a destruction, and the text corrects them from outside their own perspective, in the same gesture by which Q 4:157 moves from denying the hostile act to denying that the opponents possessed any knowledge of what they claimed to have witnessed. Wisdom 3 Q 4:157–158 Shared move "The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them" (3:1) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine possession overrules hostile interpretation "In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died" (3:2) "They did not kill him... but it was made to appear so to them" (4:157) Hostile or foolish observers mistake appearance for fact "Their departure was thought to be an affliction, and their going from us to be their destruction" (3:2–3) "We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary" (4:157) Apparent defeat is misread as real defeat "But they are at peace" (3:3) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine reality reverses the public reading of events Karina Hogan's study of what she calls the "ambiguity of death" in Wisdom, building on Michael Kolarcik's earlier analysis of the book's literary structure, shows this reversal is deliberate rather than incidental. Wisdom exploits the same vocabulary of death for two audiences at once: for the wicked, physical death confirms their belief in annihilation; for the righteous, the identical event marks the end of suffering and the beginning of nearness to God.[^17] That ambiguity is the interpretive space the Qur'an occupies in Q 4:157, where the opponents' certainty about Jesus's death is exposed as conjecture rather than corrected by a competing set of facts. Wisdom 4: The Righteous Man Taken from among Sinners Wisdom 4 turns from apparent death to the logic of removal: the one who pleases God is loved by Him and taken away while still living among sinners. "There was one who pleased God and was loved by him, and while living among sinners was taken up. He was caught up so that evil might not change his understanding or guile deceive his soul." The people who witness this fail to understand it, unaware that grace and mercy belong to God's elect and that He watches over His holy ones (Wis 4:14–15). This passage corresponds most closely to Q 3:55. Wisdom 4 Q 3:55 Shared move The one who pleases God is loved by him (4:10) "I am taking you" Divine favor defines the figure from the outset Taken while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (4:10–11) "And raising you to Myself" A verb of taking marks the removal The removal is protective, not punitive (4:11) "And purifying you from those who disbelieve" The removal separates the righteous figure from the hostile community Onlookers "see and do not understand" (4:14) Opponents have "no knowledge... only conjecture" (4:157) Onlookers witness the event without grasping it Grace and mercy belong to God's elect (4:15) "Rather, God raised him to Himself" (4:158) Divine favor, not hostile action, defines the outcome Qur'anic criterion Wisdom of Solomon Passage Hostile plotting The wicked lie in wait for the righteous man Wis 2:12 Testing of divine sonship They test whether God will deliver him as His son Wis 2:17–18 Shameful death They condemn him to a shameful death Wis 2:20 Misperception as false knowledge The foolish think he has died and mistake his departure for destruction Wis 3:2–3 Divine taking and preservation His soul is in God's hand; he is taken from among sinners Wis 3:1; 4:10–14 Wisdom 2 and the Gospel Passion Narrative The correspondence between Wisdom and the Qur'an's Jesus material gains a further layer once Wisdom 2's place in the New Testament's own Passion tradition is taken into account. Matthew's account of the mockery at the cross has long been read as drawing directly on Wisdom 2's scene of the wicked testing a self-proclaimed son of God. "He trusts in God; let God deliver him now, if he wants to; for he said, 'I am God's Son.'" This reproduces the logic, and much of the vocabulary, of Wisdom 2:18. Douglas Moo's study of the Old Testament and deuterocanonical background of the Gospel Passion narratives treats the Matthean taunt as dependent on Wisdom 2 alongside Psalm 22, and commentators on Matthew have long placed the two texts side by side for exactly this reason.[^18] This connection changes what a comparison between the Qur'an and Wisdom of Solomon can claim. The Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 boast that they killed and crucified Jesus in circumstances that, on the Gospel's own telling, were narrated in the language Wisdom 2 had already supplied for the mockery of a righteous man tested as God's son. Anthony's *Toledot Yeshu* material gives the Qur'an's audience a Jewish counter-narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel's account of Jesus's death and resurrection.[^19] Wisdom of Solomon gives the same audience the older scriptural idiom in which the Gospel's own crucifixion scene had first been cast. The Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157–158 therefore reaches, whether directly or through the mediation of the Passion tradition it was answering, back to the same righteous-sufferer grammar standing behind both the Christian narrative of Jesus's death and the Jewish narrative built to mock and invert it. Wisdom 3, 5, and the Motifs Absent from the Toledot Yeshu Anthony's own comparison supplies a further test of this argument. He scores nine motifs shared by the *Toledot Yeshu*, Q 3:54–55, and Q 4:156–159, and three of the qur'anic motifs take a minus sign under *Toledot Yeshu*: God's cleansing of Jesus from his disbelieving opponents, the exaltation of Jesus's followers over the disbelieving Israelites, and Jesus's role as an eschatological witness against his own community.[^20] Anthony's Jewish source does not account for these three motifs. Wisdom of Solomon does. Qur'anic motif Toledot Yeshu Wisdom of Solomon God cleanses Jesus of his disbelieving opponents (Q 3:55) Absent The righteous man is taken away while still living among sinners, "lest wickedness change his understanding" (Wis 4:10–11) Followers of Jesus are exalted over the disbelieving Israelites (Q 3:55) Absent "They will govern nations and rule over peoples, and the Lord will reign over them forever" (Wis 3:8) Jesus is an eschatological witness against his ummah (Q 4:159; Q 5:117) Absent The righteous man stands before those who once condemned him, who confess, "we fools! We accounted his life madness" (Wis 5:1–5) Wisdom 3:8 answers the second gap only in a qualified sense — the verse belongs to the poem's shift from the singular righteous man of chapter 2 to the collective "righteous" of chapters 3 through 5, so its promise exalts the righteous as a class rather than naming a teacher's own followers.[^21] The structural correspondence nonetheless holds: in both texts, a hostile plot against a righteous figure ends in the elevation of those aligned with him over those who opposed him, a widening of scope Q 3:55 itself performs when it moves from Jesus's individual purification to the promise that God will place those who follow him above those who disbelieve. The third gap calls for Wisdom 5:1–8, which completes the confrontation staged in chapter 2. The wicked, who had condemned the righteous man to a shameful death, now stand before him at the reckoning. "Then the righteous will stand with great confidence in the presence of those who have oppressed them... When they see him, they will shudder with terrible dread, and they will be amazed at his unexpected salvation. They will speak to one another in repentance, and in anguish of spirit they will groan, and say, 'This is the one whom we once held in derision and made a byword of reproach — fools that we were! We thought that his life was madness and that his end was without honor. Why has he been numbered among the sons of God? And why is his lot among the saints?'" Q 4:159 states that "not one of the People of Scripture will fail to believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he shall bear witness against them," and Q 5:117 has Jesus describe his own role among his people in the same terms — a witness present while he remained among them and absent once God took him. Wisdom 5 stages this same reversal: the people who condemned the righteous man are made to stand before him, recognize him, and confess in his presence that their earlier judgment was wrong. The *Toledot Yeshu*, built to prove the sages' judgment of Jesus correct, supplies no such scene — its disciples claim only that God rescued Jesus by raising him to heaven, and the sages who condemned him are never made to recognize their error.[^22] Wisdom of Solomon supplies it because vindication before one's accusers, not merely rescue from them, is the outcome its argument has been building toward since chapter 2. The Wisdom of Solomon in the Palestinian-Syriac Scriptural Contact Zone A comparison of this kind depends on Wisdom of Solomon having a plausible route into the Qur'an's late antique environment. The book's transmission history supplies one. Wisdom of Solomon began as a Greek Jewish composition from Hellenistic Alexandria, written in a monotheistic, Exodus-centered idiom for a Greek-reading Jewish community for whom the Septuagint already functioned as scripture.[^23] Its later transmission moved that idiom into the Christian biblical world. J. A. Emerton's study of the Peshitta Wisdom remains the standard account of that Syriac textual history.[^24] A second, later channel is Paul of Tella's Syro-Hexaplar translation, datable by its subscriptions to 613–617 CE, rendering Wisdom from Greek into Syriac within a generation of the Qur'an's own proclamation — evidence of active Syriac Christian scholarly investment in the book at exactly the relevant horizon.[^25] Reinhart Ceulemans and Gertjan Verhasselt have published Greek fragments of Wisdom 10 recovered from Khirbet Mird, the monastery of Kastellion in the Judean Desert, alongside other biblical fragments from the same site including portions of Mark, John, Matthew, and Acts.[^26] The find places a Septuagint copy of Wisdom inside a Palestinian monastic library of the kind that also transmitted Gospel texts. A separate Semitic Palestinian witness survives in Christian Palestinian Aramaic, attested in fragments of Wisdom 9–10 preserved in a Cairo Geniza palimpsest.[^27] This Palestinian-Syriac contact zone already carries weight elsewhere in the study of the Qur'an's Jesus and Mary traditions. Stephen Shoemaker has argued that the nativity scene in Q 19, with Mary sent to a remote place, resting beneath a palm, and given water from a spring, intersects with Palestinian local tradition connected to the Kathisma church between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, where late antique Christian memory had already linked Mary's rest, a spring, and a palm tree at a single site.[^28] Nicolai Sinai's survey of the debate over Dye, Tesei, and Shoemaker's work identifies exactly this kind of Palestinian Christian material as central to reconstructing the Qur'an's rhetorical environment.[^29] Anthony's *Toledot Yeshu* argument occupies the Jewish side of the same contact zone, proposing that the Qur'an's account of Jesus's final days answers a narrative that had likely circulated orally among the Jews of the Hijaz by the early seventh century.[^30] The Kathisma church supplies the material anchor for that intersection: built in the mid-fifth century on the Jerusalem–Bethlehem road and enlarged with an octagonal plan in the sixth, it commemorated the tradition that Mary rested there during her journey to Bethlehem, and Byzantine pilgrim accounts and liturgical calendars associate the same location with a spring and, eventually, a palm tree said to have bent down to offer her its fruit.[^31] Kathisma's location matters beyond its relevance to Shoemaker's thesis: the shrine sat on the same Jerusalem–Bethlehem–Judean Desert corridor as Khirbet Mird, where the Greek fragments of Wisdom 10 were recovered, less than a day's journey apart. This is not evidence any single community read both texts side by side, but two separate lines of access converge on the same ground — Shoemaker's reconstruction places the qur'anic milieu within reach of Palestinian Christian sacred geography, and the evidence assembled here places it within reach of Palestinian Christian scriptural transmission. Conclusion Wisdom of Solomon 2–5 satisfies, in a single continuous unit, all five criteria drawn from the Qur'an's own account of Jesus's end. The wicked plot against the righteous man. They test whether his claim to be God's son is genuine by condemning him to insult, torture, and a shameful death. They believe, once he is gone, that they have destroyed him. The text answers them from outside their own perspective, placing the righteous man's soul in God's hand and describing his removal as protection rather than defeat. Q 3:54–55, Q 4:157–159, and Q 5:117 move through the same sequence: hostile plotting, a claim of killing and crucifixion, the exposure of that claim as conjecture rather than knowledge, and God's own taking and raising of Jesus. The *Toledot Yeshu* supplies a hostile narrative built to answer the Christian Gospel directly, scene by scene, and it is this narrative, or something like it, that the Qur'an's opponents in Q 4:157 appear to be citing. Wisdom of Solomon supplies the older interpretive grammar that had already shaped how a scene of that kind could be told and understood, since it is Wisdom 2's mockery of a righteous son of God that stands behind Matthew's own account of the taunting at the cross. What the Qur'an adds to this inherited grammar is its own account of what Jesus was in the first place. Wisdom lets its righteous man call God his father and claim sonship as his own boast; the Qur'an gives Jesus none of that language, having the wicked in the text say only that they killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of God. The wicked in Wisdom are wrong to think a righteous son of God can be destroyed by a shameful death. The Qur'an's opponents are wrong for the same reason and for a further one — even if a death had occurred, it would have marked the end of a servant's mission rather than the defeat of a divine son. Wisdom of Solomon and the Toledot Yeshu are not competing explanations for Q 4:157. They are two layers of the same tradition. The Toledot Yeshu gives the Qur'an's audience a scene-by-scene Jewish rebuttal of the Christian Passion. Wisdom of Solomon gives that same audience the older scriptural grammar — a righteous son of God, tested by a hostile crowd, condemned to a shameful death the crowd mistakes for victory, and secretly preserved in God's own hand — in which both the Gospel's crucifixion scene and its Jewish inversion were already cast. The Qur'an's denial in Q 4:157–158 answers a claim with a history reaching past the Gospel Passion narrative itself, into the wisdom literature that gave Second Temple Judaism its language for how a story like this was supposed to end. title: The First Revelation Story: A Zubayrid Call Narrative?
description: A hadith-critical and source-critical study of the iqraʾ narrative, its Zubayrid transmission setting, the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, al-Zuhrī’s canonical stream, Ibn Isḥāq’s Rayy-recension stream in al-Ṭabarī, and the Cædmon comparison.

Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel appears. The angel commands him, “Read.” Muhammad says, “I cannot read.” The command is repeated. The opening verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are revealed. Muhammad returns to Khadījah in fear. Khadījah consoles him. Waraqah b. Nawfal, the learned Christian relative, confirms that the visitor is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. The story is powerful. It explains the beginning of revelation, the first Qurʾānic words, Khadījah’s role, Waraqah’s scriptural validation, and Muhammad’s first confrontation with the terror of prophecy. But the question for a historian is not whether the story is powerful. The question is where the story becomes visible, what its transmissions look like, and why its narrative structure resembles a known Christian call-story so closely. The iqraʾ narrative is early as Islamic tradition, but weak as direct cave-memory. Its recoverable forms point strongly into Zubayrid-linked transmission, with one stream through ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī and another through the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr at the court of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr. The goal here is not to deny that Muhammad had a revelatory beginning. The goal is narrower. The polished “Read!” story, as it survives in hadith and sīrah, looks like a crafted call narrative. It has an isnād history. It has a literary shape. It has Qurʾānic interests. And it has a striking parallel in Bede’s story of Cædmon. ## The Canonical Hadith Form The most influential form is the ʿĀʾishah report. Its upper route is: **ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī.** After al-Zuhrī, the report spreads through later transmitters and compilers. One early witness is ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh preserves the same broad form through ʿAbd al-Razzāq. Bukhārī then gives the version that becomes the standard form at the opening of his Ṣaḥīḥ. أَوَّلُ مَا بُدِئَ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ مِنَ الْوَحْيِ الرُّؤْيَا الصَّادِقَةُ، فَكَانَ لَا يَرَى رُؤْيَا إِلَّا جَاءَتْ مِثْلَ فَلَقِ الصُّبْحِ، ثُمَّ حُبِّبَ إِلَيْهِ الْخَلَاءُ، فَكَانَ يَأْتِي حِرَاءً فَيَتَحَنَّثُ فِيهِ... “The first thing with which the Messenger of God was begun from revelation was the true dream. He would not see a dream except that it came like the break of dawn. Then seclusion was made beloved to him, and he would go to Ḥirāʾ and worship there...” The report then gives the famous scene. فَجَاءَهُ الْمَلَكُ فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ. فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ. قَالَ: فَأَخَذَنِي فَغَطَّنِي حَتَّى بَلَغَ مِنِّي الْجَهْدَ، ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَنِي فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ... “The angel came to him and said, ‘Read.’ The Messenger of God said, ‘I am not one who reads.’ He said, ‘Then he seized me and pressed me until I was exhausted, then released me and said, ‘Read.’” This version is not simply a memory of a cave. It is a structured call narrative. It begins with true dreams, moves to seclusion, brings an angelic command, repeats the refusal, attaches the scene to Qurʾān 96:1–5, and ends with Khadījah and Waraqah validating the experience. ## The Rayy Recension in al-Ṭabarī The most important source for the storyteller hypothesis is the Rayy-recension material preserved in al-Ṭabarī. The practical way to find this material is by filtering for the isnād: **Ibn Ḥumayd → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Isḥāq.** In the first-revelation passage, Ṭabarī gives the chain: **Muḥammad b. Ḥumayd al-Rāzī → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Muḥammad b. Isḥāq → Wahb b. Kaysān, mawlā of the House of al-Zubayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr.** That chain matters because it does not merely transmit the story. It frames the story as a Zubayrid court event. Wahb b. Kaysān says that he heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr ask ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to tell them how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him. سَمِعْتُ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ الزُّبَيْرِ، وَهُوَ يَقُولُ لِعُبَيْدِ بْنِ عُمَيْرِ بْنِ قَتَادَةَ اللَّيْثِيِّ: حَدِّثْنَا يَا عُبَيْدُ، كَيْفَ كَانَ بَدْءُ مَا ابْتُدِئَ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ مِنَ النُّبُوَّةِ، حِينَ جَاءَهُ جِبْرِيلُ؟ “I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr saying to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr b. Qatādah al-Laythī: ‘Tell us, O ʿUbayd, how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him.’” This is the core of the argument. The dramatic iqraʾ story is not merely floating in Ibn Isḥāq. In this stream, it is attached to a Meccan storyteller, in a Zubayrid court setting, transmitted by a client of the House of al-Zubayr. ## The Two Zubayrid Exits The diagram below shows the two major exits from the Zubayrid memory world. One stream goes through ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr’s court to Wahb b. Kaysān and Ibn Isḥāq. The other goes through ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr to al-Zuhrī and then into the hadith collections. For a lay reader, the important point is simple. The story does not appear as a broad Companion memory with many independent early roots. Its most influential forms concentrate around Zubayrid-linked transmitters. ʿUrwah is a central figure of the Zubayrid household. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr is the Zubayrid claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān is attached to the House of al-Zubayr. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr is the Meccan storyteller in the scene. This does not prove that one person invented the story. It means the earliest recoverable forms of the polished iqraʾ narrative are not socially neutral. They cluster in a Zubayrid memory network. ## Why ʿĀʾishah Is Not an Eyewitness Here The ʿĀʾishah attribution is important, but it must be handled carefully. ʿĀʾishah was not present at Ḥirāʾ. She was not an eyewitness to the first revelation. The report attributed to her is therefore not a direct memory of the event. It is a report about the event transmitted through family and teaching networks. That does not make the report worthless. But it changes the question. We are not asking, “What did ʿĀʾishah see?” We are asking, “What form of the first-revelation story circulated through ʿUrwah and al-Zuhrī under ʿĀʾishah’s authority?” That distinction matters. A report can carry an early Companion name while still being a later household narrative, shaped by theological, Qurʾānic, and literary needs. ## The Meccan Storyteller Hypothesis The strongest candidate for the narrative crystallizer is ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That does not mean he definitely fabricated the story. It means he fits the social role better than almost anyone else in the surviving record. He is not merely a transmitter. He is a **qāṣṣ**, a storyteller-preacher. His function was to narrate sacred material in public, to make hidden beginnings vivid, and to turn religious memory into memorable moral instruction. The first-revelation story has exactly that kind of shape. It dramatizes an otherwise hidden event. It turns the first revelation into dialogue. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with **iqraʾ**. It gives Muhammad fear, crisis, and validation. It brings in Khadījah as moral witness and Waraqah as scriptural witness. Schoeler’s reconstruction is important here. He argues that ʿUbayd combined a set of motifs that circulated around the beginnings of revelation: Ḥirāʾ devotion, Khadījah, iqraʾ, the horizon vision, and Waraqah. In that reconstruction, the result was a coherent, edifying, and entertaining story. As a qāṣṣ, ʿUbayd may have embellished and extended some elements. The story then spread through the Zubayrid family as a family tradition.[^1] This is the most careful way to state the theory: ʿUbayd is not proven to be the inventor, but he is the best candidate for the narrative organizer of the dramatic form. ## The Source-Critical Debate The qāṣṣ hypothesis is not just a modern suspicion. Görke and Schoeler explicitly discuss the possibility that ʿUrwah’s source was the same family tradition that Ibn Isḥāq transmits through Wahb b. Kaysān from ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. They point out that ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, ʿUrwah’s elder brother, asks ʿUbayd in a meeting to report the Prophet’s first revelation. They then state that the al-Zuhrī / Hishām b. ʿUrwah tradition from ʿUrwah and the Ibn Isḥāq tradition from Wahb b. Kaysān and ʿUbayd are so close that they must have the same origin.[^2] That is the key. The two streams are not identical, but they are too close to be treated as fully independent. One can debate where the Qurʾānic elements entered. They may come from ʿUbayd, Wahb, Ibn Isḥāq, al-Zuhrī, or several stages together. But the broad conclusion remains: the story is a Zubayrid-linked call narrative, not a simple transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Shoemaker is the main methodological counterweight. He argues that many attempts to reconstruct ʿUrwah’s sīrah push the evidence too far. In his view, al-Zuhrī and sometimes figures of his generation can be linked to traditions, but the reach back to ʿUrwah is often less secure.[^3] This warning matters. It prevents overclaiming. But even on a more skeptical reading, the story remains early, al-Zuhrī-linked, and Zubayrid-adjacent. That is enough for the argument here. The safest conclusion is not “ʿUbayd invented the story.” The safer conclusion is that the dramatic iqraʾ narrative likely crystallized in a Meccan-Zubayrid storytelling environment and then spread through two related Zubayrid exits: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb → Ibn Isḥāq, and ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. ## Ibn Isḥāq’s Dramatic Form The Ibn Isḥāq / Ṭabarī form is more vivid than the shorter canonical hadith form. Muhammad is at Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel comes while he is asleep. The angel brings a written object. The command is “Read.” Muhammad resists. The words of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are placed into his heart. He wakes frightened and considers whether he is a poet or possessed. He thinks of throwing himself from the mountain, until Gabriel appears again and confirms his prophethood. فَجَاءَنِي جِبْرِيلُ وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ بِنَمَطٍ مِنْ دِيبَاجٍ، فِيهِ كِتَابٌ، فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ. فَقُلْتُ: مَا أَقْرَأُ؟ “Gabriel came to me while I was asleep with a brocade cloth in which there was writing. He said, ‘Read.’ I said, ‘What shall I read?’” This version matters because it is the form most closely resembling the Cædmon pattern. The visitor comes in sleep. There is a command. There is an inability response. Sacred speech follows. The content concerns creation. The experience is later validated by authorities. ## The Cædmon Story Bede’s story of Cædmon appears in the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. Cædmon is an unlearned man who cannot sing. At feasts, when the harp is passed around, he leaves in shame because he has no song. One night, after leaving a feast, he goes to the cattle stable and falls asleep. In a dream, someone calls him by name and commands him to sing. Cædmon says he cannot sing. The figure insists. Cædmon asks what he should sing about. The answer is: sing about the beginning of created things. He then sings verses praising God the Creator, words he had never learned before. In the morning, he remembers the song and is taken to religious authorities who test and validate the gift. The resemblance to the iqraʾ narrative is not just one shared motif. It is a sequence. This is why the comparison matters. Both stories are about an unprepared recipient who receives a supernatural command to perform sacred speech in his own language and then has the experience validated by religious authorities. The exact theological setting differs, but the narrative skeleton is strikingly similar. ## The Similarities Motif Cædmon in Bede Muhammad in the iqraʾ narrative Unlearned / unable figure Cædmon cannot sing and leaves the feast when the harp approaches. Muhammad responds to the command with “I cannot read” or “What shall I read?” Liminal retreat Cædmon withdraws from the feast and sleeps near the animals. Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ for solitary devotion. Night / sleep setting The command comes in a dream while Cædmon sleeps. In Ibn Isḥāq’s form, Gabriel comes while Muhammad is asleep. Supernatural visitor A mysterious figure stands by Cædmon and calls him by name. Gabriel comes to Muhammad with the command of God. Command to perform sacred speech “Sing me something.” “Read / recite.” Refusal of ability “I cannot sing.” “I am not one who reads” or “What shall I read?” Creation theme Cædmon is told to sing of the beginning of created things. The revealed passage begins with God creating man from a clot. Miraculous vernacular gift Cædmon receives the ability to sing sacred poetry in English. Muhammad receives the ability to recite revealed Arabic scripture. Validation after the event Cædmon is brought to the reeve, abbess, and learned men. Muhammad is reassured by Khadījah and validated by Waraqah. This is not a loose comparison between two religious people receiving inspiration. It is a specific story type. The recipient cannot perform sacred speech. A visitor commands it anyway. The inability is overcome by divine gift. The first speech concerns creation. A community authority confirms the gift afterward. ## Which Direction Did the Influence Run? The direction is debated. Older comparisons often raised the possibility that the Islamic iqraʾ narrative and the Cædmon story share a direct relationship. Some scholars argued for Muhammad’s call influencing Cædmon. Others were more cautious and preferred a shared call-story pattern. Richard North has recently argued directly for the direction **Muhammad story → Bede’s Cædmon story**. His model is that Arculf heard the Muhammad call story around Jerusalem around 680, transmitted it to Adomnán in Iona in 683–686, and Adomnán passed it to Bede with *De locis sanctis* in Jarrow in 688.[^4] Whether one accepts North’s full route or not, it matters because it shows that the Cædmon comparison is not merely a fringe observation. It is now a serious scholarly proposal. The reverse direction, Cædmon → Meccan storyteller, is much weaker. Cædmon belongs to the Whitby world under Abbess Hild in the later seventh century, and Bede writes the story around 731. It is possible that a Cædmon-like oral story circulated before Bede, but we do not have evidence that it travelled from Northumbria to the Hijaz before the Zubayrid court. So the Meccan qāṣṣ did not need Cædmon specifically. He needed access to a broader call-story repertoire. That broader repertoire is older. Biblical and Christian traditions already contain scenes where a chosen but inadequate person is commanded, resists, receives divine speech, or is validated by an authority. The Cædmon story and the iqraʾ story are best read inside that late antique world of sacred speech and visionary commissioning. ## The Qurʾānization of the Story The iqraʾ story is also exegetical. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with the command **iqraʾ**. The Qurʾānic word becomes the engine of the narrative. Gabriel says “iqraʾ.” Muhammad replies with a phrase built from the same root. The repeated command becomes the dramatic setup for the revelation of 96:1–5. اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ، خَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ، اقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ الْأَكْرَمُ “Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is Most Generous.” This matters because the first-revelation story may not simply preserve the first moment of revelation. It may be a narrative built around a Qurʾānic opening. Anthony notes that the iqraʾ narrative claims Q. 96 is the first revelation, but modern Qurʾānic chronology has often rejected that claim on internal literary grounds. He treats the iqraʾ narrative as early and valuable for studying how sīrah traditions formed, but not as historically trustworthy for reconstructing the earliest Qurʾānic revelation.[^5] That is a very important distinction. The story is early as tradition. It is not necessarily early as event-memory. ## Khadījah and Waraqah Khadījah and Waraqah are not decorative figures. They solve the narrative problem. Muhammad is terrified and uncertain. Khadījah provides moral reassurance. Waraqah provides scriptural validation. He is the learned figure who says that the being who came to Muhammad is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. فَقَالَتْ خَدِيجَةُ: كَلَّا وَاللَّهِ لَا يُخْزِيكَ اللَّهُ أَبَدًا، إِنَّكَ لَتَصِلُ الرَّحِمَ، وَتَصْدُقُ الْحَدِيثَ، وَتَحْمِلُ الْكَلَّ، وَتُقْرِي الضَّيْفَ، وَتُعِينُ عَلَى نَوَائِبِ الْحَقِّ “Khadījah said: ‘No, by God, God will never disgrace you. You maintain kinship, speak truthfully, bear the burdens of others, host the guest, and help in the hardships of truth.’” Waraqah then moves the experience into biblical history. هَذَا النَّامُوسُ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَى مُوسَى “This is the heavenly messenger whom God sent down to Moses.” This is exactly what a call narrative needs. The chosen figure does not understand the event at first. A recognized authority interprets it. The frightening experience becomes a prophetic mission. ## The Attempted-Suicide Motif One of the most striking features of some versions is Muhammad’s crisis after the first encounter. In Ibn Isḥāq’s version, he fears that he is a poet or possessed and considers throwing himself from the mountain. In some al-Zuhrī-related biographical variants, the attempted-suicide motif appears in connection with the lapse of revelation. In the canonical hadith collections, the most troubling forms are softened or excluded. This pattern matters. It suggests that the story circulated in more dramatic forms before later tradition stabilized the more acceptable version. The raw literary form includes fear, doubt, and a near-catastrophic crisis. Later hadith transmission preserves a cleaner version: terror, yes, but not the same full dramatic despair. The attempted-suicide motif is not needed for the theology of prophethood. It is needed for the drama of a call narrative. Its presence in some streams and absence in others shows that the matn was being shaped. ## What the Corpus Shows The available corpus supports a two-stream model. The first stream is the canonical hadith family: **ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / later transmitters.** This stream gives the form that becomes dominant in hadith. It contains true dreams, seclusion, Ḥirāʾ, the angelic command, the refusal, the pressing, Q. 96:1–5, return to Khadījah, reassurance, and Waraqah’s validation. The second stream is the Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq family preserved in al-Ṭabarī: **ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb b. Kaysān → Ibn Isḥāq → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Ḥumayd → al-Ṭabarī.** This stream gives the dramatic storyteller form. It explicitly places the story in a Zubayrid court context. It contains the sleep setting, the written object, the repeated command, the “What shall I read?” reply, the placing of the words into Muhammad’s heart, and the mountain-crisis motif. Stream Main route Why it matters Canonical hadith stream ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / others This is the form that becomes dominant in hadith. It is Zubayrid through ʿUrwah and ʿĀʾishah’s household authority. ʿAbd al-Razzāq / Maʿmar stream ʿAbd al-Razzāq → Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī → ʿUrwah → ʿĀʾishah One of the earliest surviving written witnesses to the full canonical form. Bukhārī stream al-Zuhrī → ʿUrwah → ʿĀʾishah, through later canonical transmission The most famous stabilized form, placed at the beginning of the Ṣaḥīḥ. Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq stream in al-Ṭabarī ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb b. Kaysān → Ibn Isḥāq → Salamah → Ibn Ḥumayd → al-Ṭabarī The strongest evidence for a Meccan qāṣṣ and Zubayrid court setting. Hishām b. ʿUrwah-related material ʿUrwah → Hishām b. ʿUrwah and related shorter forms Important because some versions stop with ʿUrwah or preserve more dramatic elements in abridged form. ## Why the Zubayrid Setting Matters The Zubayrid household was not just a private family. It was one of the major memory-making circles of early Islam. ʿĀʾishah was a central transmitter of prophetic household memory. ʿUrwah, her nephew, became one of the great early authorities for sīrah and maghāzī material. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr was a political claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān was attached to the House of al-Zubayr. This is a powerful social setting for the formation of early prophetic biography. Anthony stresses that the Ibn Isḥāq frame places the story during the Second Civil War, when ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr and the Zubayrids were competing with the Umayyads for the leadership of the early Islamic polity.[^6] That context does not prove propaganda by itself, but it matters. A court claiming religious legitimacy has a strong reason to preserve, perform, and authorize stories about prophetic beginnings. The first-revelation story does important work in that setting. It makes Khadījah the first human validator. It makes Waraqah, a Christian scriptural authority connected to the Meccan household world, the biblical witness. It turns Muhammad’s terrifying experience into a recognized prophetic mission. It also makes the beginning of the Qurʾān intelligible through narrative. This does not mean the Zubayrids “invented Islam.” It means the polished first-revelation story, as a story, becomes recoverable in their memory network. ## Why the Story Looks Literary A historical memory can be literary, but this story is highly literary. It has repeated dialogue. It has a threefold pressure scene. It has dramatic fear. It has a return home. It has a wise spouse. It has a learned scriptural interpreter. It has a prediction of rejection and victory. It has a Qurʾānic keyword turned into the center of the plot. That is not how raw memory usually survives. It is how a community tells the origin of revelation. The comparison with Cædmon makes this clearer. Bede’s story is not about Islamic history. It is a Christian hagiographical call story. Yet its structure matches the Ibn Isḥāq iqraʾ narrative at too many points: sleep, inability, command, sacred speech, creation theme, miraculous vernacular performance, validation. This does not prove a simple line of borrowing in every detail. But it does show that the iqraʾ story belongs to a recognizable literary world. ## What Would Change the Analysis? This analysis would be weakened if we found many independent early Companion-level routes for the iqraʾ story that did not pass through ʿUrwah / al-Zuhrī or the Zubayrid storytelling environment. It would also be weakened if Ibn Isḥāq’s Zubayrid court frame were isolated and unrelated to the larger narrative shape. It would be weakened further if Cædmon only shared one generic motif, such as “a holy person receives inspiration.” But that is not what we have. The canonical hadith form concentrates through ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. The Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq form is tied to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, and Wahb b. Kaysān. The Cædmon comparison is not one shared idea but a shared narrative sequence. The result is a strong cumulative case. ## Final Verdict The famous first-revelation story is best understood as an early Islamic call narrative, not as a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Its most influential hadith form runs through ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr, and al-Zuhrī. Its most dramatic sīrah form, preserved in the Rayy-recension material inside al-Ṭabarī, is explicitly tied to a Zubayrid court setting: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr asks the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to narrate the beginning of prophecy, and Wahb b. Kaysān, a client of the House of al-Zubayr, transmits the scene. The matn is also not neutral. It is shaped around Qurʾān 96:1–5. The word **iqraʾ** becomes a scene. Gabriel commands. Muhammad refuses. The command is repeated. The revelation is attached to the first verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. Khadījah and Waraqah then validate the experience. The story explains revelation, scripture, prophethood, and biblical attestation all at once. The Cædmon parallel shows why the story cannot be treated as simple memory. Bede’s Cædmon and Ibn Isḥāq’s Muhammad both receive a nighttime visionary command to perform sacred speech despite claiming inability. Both are given a creation-themed utterance. Both are validated afterward by religious authorities. Whether one follows North’s proposal that Bede modelled Cædmon on the Muhammad story, or the more cautious view that both stories belong to a shared late antique call-story repertoire, the conclusion is similar: the iqraʾ narrative is literary and comparative, not raw cave-memory. So the strongest conclusion is careful but pointed: the iqraʾ narrative is early, Zubayrid-linked, Qurʾānized, and literary. It may preserve the memory that Muhammad’s prophetic career began with a terrifying revelatory experience. But the polished story of Gabriel saying “Read,” as preserved in the canonical hadith and sīrah tradition, is a crafted origin narrative shaped by household transmission, Meccan storytelling, scriptural exegesis, and the wider call-story patterns of the late antique world. The first-revelation story should be treated as an early Zubayrid-linked call narrative. The most plausible source-critical model is not a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ, but a story that crystallized in a Meccan qāṣṣ setting and then spread through Zubayrid household channels into al-Zuhrī and Ibn Isḥāq. ## Appendix: Core Motif Table | Motif | ʿĀʾishah / al-Zuhrī form | Ibn Isḥāq / Ṭabarī Rayy form | Cædmon form | | ---------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | | Night or dream setting | Begins with true dreams like dawn | Gabriel comes while Muhammad is asleep | Visitor comes while Cædmon sleeps | | Solitary setting | Ḥirāʾ retreat | Ḥirāʾ retreat | Cattle stable after leaving feast | | Command | “Read” | “Read” | “Sing” | | Inability response | “I am not one who reads” | “What shall I read?” | “I cannot sing” | | Repetition | Command and pressure repeated | Command repeated with intense pressure | Command insisted upon after refusal | | Creation theme | Q. 96: God created man | Q. 96: God created man | Sing of the beginning of created things | | Miraculous speech | Qurʾān recited in Arabic | Scripture placed in heart | English sacred poetry sung | | Validation | Khadījah and Waraqah | Khadījah and Waraqah | Reeve, abbess, and learned men | | Later function | Canonical first revelation | Dramatic sīrah call story | Christian hagiographical call story | ## Appendix: Main Transmission Families | Family | Route | Notes | | ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | al-Zuhrī canonical family | ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / others | Dominant hadith form, preserved through ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Isḥāq b.
