Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel appears. The angel commands him, “Read.” Muhammad says, “I cannot read.” The command is repeated. The opening verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are revealed. Muhammad returns to Khadījah in fear. Khadījah consoles him. Waraqah b. Nawfal, the learned Christian relative, confirms that the visitor is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. The story is powerful. It explains the beginning of revelation, the first Qurʾānic words, Khadījah’s role, Waraqah’s scriptural validation, and Muhammad’s first confrontation with the terror of prophecy. But the question for a historian is not whether the story is powerful. The question is where the story becomes visible, what its transmissions look like, and why its narrative structure resembles a known Christian call-story so closely. The iqraʾ narrative is early as Islamic tradition, but weak as direct cave-memory. Its recoverable forms point strongly into Zubayrid-linked transmission, with one stream through ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī and another through the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr at the court of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr. The goal here is not to deny that Muhammad had a revelatory beginning. The goal is narrower. The polished “Read!” story, as it survives in hadith and sīrah, looks like a crafted call narrative. It has an isnād history. It has a literary shape. It has Qurʾānic interests. And it has a striking parallel in Bede’s story of Cædmon. The Canonical Hadith Form The most influential form is the ʿĀʾishah report. Its upper route is: **ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī.** After al-Zuhrī, the report spreads through later transmitters and compilers. One early witness is ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Maʿmar from al-Zuhrī. Isḥāq b. Rāhawayh preserves the same broad form through ʿAbd al-Razzāq. Bukhārī then gives the version that becomes the standard form at the opening of his Ṣaḥīḥ. أَوَّلُ مَا بُدِئَ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ مِنَ الْوَحْيِ الرُّؤْيَا الصَّادِقَةُ، فَكَانَ لَا يَرَى رُؤْيَا إِلَّا جَاءَتْ مِثْلَ فَلَقِ الصُّبْحِ، ثُمَّ حُبِّبَ إِلَيْهِ الْخَلَاءُ، فَكَانَ يَأْتِي حِرَاءً فَيَتَحَنَّثُ فِيهِ... “The first thing with which the Messenger of God was begun from revelation was the true dream. He would not see a dream except that it came like the break of dawn. Then seclusion was made beloved to him, and he would go to Ḥirāʾ and worship there...” The report then gives the famous scene. فَجَاءَهُ الْمَلَكُ فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ. فَقَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: مَا أَنَا بِقَارِئٍ. قَالَ: فَأَخَذَنِي فَغَطَّنِي حَتَّى بَلَغَ مِنِّي الْجَهْدَ، ثُمَّ أَرْسَلَنِي فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ... “The angel came to him and said, ‘Read.’ The Messenger of God said, ‘I am not one who reads.’ He said, ‘Then he seized me and pressed me until I was exhausted, then released me and said, ‘Read.’” This version is not simply a memory of a cave. It is a structured call narrative. It begins with true dreams, moves to seclusion, brings an angelic command, repeats the refusal, attaches the scene to Qurʾān 96:1–5, and ends with Khadījah and Waraqah validating the experience. The Rayy Recension in al-Ṭabarī The most important source for the storyteller hypothesis is the Rayy-recension material preserved in al-Ṭabarī. The practical way to find this material is by filtering for the isnād: **Ibn Ḥumayd → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Isḥāq.** In the first-revelation passage, Ṭabarī gives the chain: **Muḥammad b. Ḥumayd al-Rāzī → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Muḥammad b. Isḥāq → Wahb b. Kaysān, mawlā of the House of al-Zubayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr.** That chain matters because it does not merely transmit the story. It frames the story as a Zubayrid court event. Wahb b. Kaysān says that he heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr ask ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to tell them how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him. سَمِعْتُ عَبْدَ اللَّهِ بْنَ الزُّبَيْرِ، وَهُوَ يَقُولُ لِعُبَيْدِ بْنِ عُمَيْرِ بْنِ قَتَادَةَ اللَّيْثِيِّ: حَدِّثْنَا يَا عُبَيْدُ، كَيْفَ كَانَ بَدْءُ مَا ابْتُدِئَ بِهِ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ مِنَ النُّبُوَّةِ، حِينَ جَاءَهُ جِبْرِيلُ؟ “I heard ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr saying to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr b. Qatādah al-Laythī: ‘Tell us, O ʿUbayd, how the Messenger of God first began prophethood when Gabriel came to him.’” This is the core of the argument. The dramatic iqraʾ story is not merely floating in Ibn Isḥāq. In this stream, it is attached to a Meccan storyteller, in a Zubayrid court setting, transmitted by a client of the House of al-Zubayr. The Two Zubayrid Exits The diagram below shows the two major exits from the Zubayrid memory world. One stream goes through ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr’s court to Wahb b. Kaysān and Ibn Isḥāq. The other goes through ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr to al-Zuhrī and then into the hadith collections. For a lay reader, the important point is simple. The story does not appear as a broad Companion memory with many independent early roots. Its most influential forms concentrate around Zubayrid-linked transmitters. ʿUrwah is a central figure of the Zubayrid household. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr is the Zubayrid claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān is attached to the House of al-Zubayr. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr is the Meccan storyteller in the scene. This does not prove that one person invented the story. It means the earliest recoverable forms of the polished iqraʾ narrative are not socially neutral. They cluster in a Zubayrid memory network. Why ʿĀʾishah Is Not an Eyewitness Here The ʿĀʾishah attribution is important, but it must be handled carefully. ʿĀʾishah was not present at Ḥirāʾ. She was not an eyewitness to the first revelation. The report attributed to her is therefore not a direct memory of the event. It is a report about the event transmitted through family and teaching networks. That does not make the report worthless. But it changes the question. We are not asking, “What did ʿĀʾishah see?” We are asking, “What form of the first-revelation story circulated through ʿUrwah and al-Zuhrī under ʿĀʾishah’s authority?” That distinction matters. A report can carry an early Companion name while still being a later household narrative, shaped by theological, Qurʾānic, and literary needs. The Meccan Storyteller Hypothesis The strongest candidate for the narrative crystallizer is ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. That does not mean he definitely fabricated the story. It means he fits the social role better than almost anyone else in the surviving record. He is not merely a transmitter. He is a **qāṣṣ**, a storyteller-preacher. His function was to narrate sacred material in public, to make hidden beginnings vivid, and to turn religious memory into memorable moral instruction. The first-revelation story has exactly that kind of shape. It dramatizes an otherwise hidden event. It turns the first revelation into dialogue. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with **iqraʾ**. It gives Muhammad fear, crisis, and validation. It brings in Khadījah as moral witness and Waraqah as scriptural witness. Schoeler’s reconstruction is important here. He argues that ʿUbayd combined a set of motifs that circulated around the beginnings of revelation: Ḥirāʾ devotion, Khadījah, iqraʾ, the horizon vision, and Waraqah. In that reconstruction, the result was a coherent, edifying, and entertaining story. As a qāṣṣ, ʿUbayd may have embellished and extended some elements. The story then spread through the Zubayrid family as a family tradition.[^1] This is the most careful way to state the theory: ʿUbayd is not proven to be the inventor, but he is the best candidate for the narrative organizer of the dramatic form. The Source-Critical Debate The qāṣṣ hypothesis is not just a modern suspicion. Görke and Schoeler explicitly discuss the possibility that ʿUrwah’s source was the same family tradition that Ibn Isḥāq transmits through Wahb b. Kaysān from ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr. They point out that ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, ʿUrwah’s elder brother, asks ʿUbayd in a meeting to report the Prophet’s first revelation. They then state that the al-Zuhrī / Hishām b. ʿUrwah tradition from ʿUrwah and the Ibn Isḥāq tradition from Wahb b. Kaysān and ʿUbayd are so close that they must have the same origin.[^2] That is the key. The two streams are not identical, but they are too close to be treated as fully independent. One can debate where the Qurʾānic elements entered. They may come from ʿUbayd, Wahb, Ibn Isḥāq, al-Zuhrī, or several stages together. But the broad conclusion remains: the story is a Zubayrid-linked call narrative, not a simple transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Shoemaker is the main methodological counterweight. He argues that many attempts to reconstruct ʿUrwah’s sīrah push the evidence too far. In his view, al-Zuhrī and sometimes figures of his generation can be linked to traditions, but the reach back to ʿUrwah is often less secure.[^3] This warning matters. It prevents overclaiming. But even on a more skeptical reading, the story remains early, al-Zuhrī-linked, and Zubayrid-adjacent. That is enough for the argument here. The safest conclusion is not “ʿUbayd invented the story.” The safer conclusion is that the dramatic iqraʾ narrative likely crystallized in a Meccan-Zubayrid storytelling environment and then spread through two related Zubayrid exits: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb → Ibn Isḥāq, and ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. Ibn Isḥāq’s Dramatic Form The Ibn Isḥāq / Ṭabarī form is more vivid than the shorter canonical hadith form. Muhammad is at Ḥirāʾ. Gabriel comes while he is asleep. The angel brings a written object. The command is “Read.” Muhammad resists. The words of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq are placed into his heart. He wakes frightened and considers whether he is a poet or possessed. He thinks of throwing himself from the mountain, until Gabriel appears again and confirms his prophethood. فَجَاءَنِي جِبْرِيلُ وَأَنَا نَائِمٌ بِنَمَطٍ مِنْ دِيبَاجٍ، فِيهِ كِتَابٌ، فَقَالَ: اقْرَأْ. فَقُلْتُ: مَا أَقْرَأُ؟ “Gabriel came to me while I was asleep with a brocade cloth in which there was writing. He said, ‘Read.’ I said, ‘What shall I read?’” This version matters because it is the form most closely resembling the Cædmon pattern. The visitor comes in sleep. There is a command. There is an inability response. Sacred speech follows. The content concerns creation. The experience is later validated by authorities. The Cædmon Story Bede’s story of Cædmon appears in the *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*. Cædmon is an unlearned man who cannot sing. At feasts, when the harp is passed around, he leaves in shame because he has no song. One night, after leaving a feast, he goes to the cattle stable and falls asleep. In a dream, someone calls him by name and commands him to sing. Cædmon says he cannot sing. The figure insists. Cædmon asks what he should sing about. The answer is: sing about the beginning of created things. He then sings verses praising God the Creator, words he had never learned before. In the morning, he remembers the song and is taken to religious authorities who test and validate the gift. The resemblance to the iqraʾ narrative is not just one shared motif. It is a sequence. This is why the comparison matters. Both stories are about an unprepared recipient who receives a supernatural command to perform sacred speech in his own language and then has the experience validated by religious authorities. The exact theological setting differs, but the narrative skeleton is strikingly similar. The Similarities Motif Cædmon in Bede Muhammad in the iqraʾ narrative Unlearned / unable figure Cædmon cannot sing and leaves the feast when the harp approaches. Muhammad responds to the command with “I cannot read” or “What shall I read?” Liminal retreat Cædmon withdraws from the feast and sleeps near the animals. Muhammad withdraws to Ḥirāʾ for solitary devotion. Night / sleep setting The command comes in a dream while Cædmon sleeps. In Ibn Isḥāq’s form, Gabriel comes while Muhammad is asleep. Supernatural visitor A mysterious figure stands by Cædmon and calls him by name. Gabriel comes to Muhammad with the command of God. Command to perform sacred speech “Sing me something.” “Read / recite.” Refusal of ability “I cannot sing.” “I am not one who reads” or “What shall I read?” Creation theme Cædmon is told to sing of the beginning of created things. The revealed passage begins with God creating man from a clot. Miraculous vernacular gift Cædmon receives the ability to sing sacred poetry in English. Muhammad receives the ability to recite revealed Arabic scripture. Validation after the event Cædmon is brought to the reeve, abbess, and learned men. Muhammad is reassured by Khadījah and validated by Waraqah. This is not a loose comparison between two religious people receiving inspiration. It is a specific story type. The recipient cannot perform sacred speech. A visitor commands it anyway. The inability is overcome by divine gift. The first speech concerns creation. A community authority confirms the gift afterward. Which Direction Did the Influence Run? The direction is debated. Older comparisons often raised the possibility that the Islamic iqraʾ narrative and the Cædmon story share a direct relationship. Some scholars argued for Muhammad’s call influencing Cædmon. Others were more cautious and preferred a shared call-story pattern. Richard North has recently argued directly for the direction **Muhammad story → Bede’s Cædmon story**. His model is that Arculf heard the Muhammad call story around Jerusalem around 680, transmitted it to Adomnán in Iona in 683–686, and Adomnán passed it to Bede with *De locis sanctis* in Jarrow in 688.[^4] Whether one accepts North’s full route or not, it matters because it shows that the Cædmon comparison is not merely a fringe observation. It is now a serious scholarly proposal. The reverse direction, Cædmon → Meccan storyteller, is much weaker. Cædmon belongs to the Whitby world under Abbess Hild in the later seventh century, and Bede writes the story around 731. It is possible that a Cædmon-like oral story circulated before Bede, but we do not have evidence that it travelled from Northumbria to the Hijaz before the Zubayrid court. So the Meccan qāṣṣ did not need Cædmon specifically. He needed access to a broader call-story repertoire. That broader repertoire is older. Biblical and Christian traditions already contain scenes where a chosen but inadequate person is commanded, resists, receives divine speech, or is validated by an authority. The Cædmon story and the iqraʾ story are best read inside that late antique world of sacred speech and visionary commissioning. The Qurʾānization of the Story The iqraʾ story is also exegetical. It explains why Sūrat al-ʿAlaq begins with the command **iqraʾ**. The Qurʾānic word becomes the engine of the narrative. Gabriel says “iqraʾ.” Muhammad replies with a phrase built from the same root. The repeated command becomes the dramatic setup for the revelation of 96:1–5. اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ، خَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ، اقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ الْأَكْرَمُ “Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clot. Read, and your Lord is Most Generous.” This matters because the first-revelation story may not simply preserve the first moment of revelation. It may be a narrative built around a Qurʾānic opening. Anthony notes that the iqraʾ narrative claims Q. 96 is the first revelation, but modern Qurʾānic chronology has often rejected that claim on internal literary grounds. He treats the iqraʾ narrative as early and valuable for studying how sīrah traditions formed, but not as historically trustworthy for reconstructing the earliest Qurʾānic revelation.[^5] That is a very important distinction. The story is early as tradition. It is not necessarily early as event-memory. Khadījah and Waraqah Khadījah and Waraqah are not decorative figures. They solve the narrative problem. Muhammad is terrified and uncertain. Khadījah provides moral reassurance. Waraqah provides scriptural validation. He is the learned figure who says that the being who came to Muhammad is the same heavenly messenger who came to Moses. فَقَالَتْ خَدِيجَةُ: كَلَّا وَاللَّهِ لَا يُخْزِيكَ اللَّهُ أَبَدًا، إِنَّكَ لَتَصِلُ الرَّحِمَ، وَتَصْدُقُ الْحَدِيثَ، وَتَحْمِلُ الْكَلَّ، وَتُقْرِي الضَّيْفَ، وَتُعِينُ عَلَى نَوَائِبِ الْحَقِّ “Khadījah said: ‘No, by God, God will never disgrace you. You maintain kinship, speak truthfully, bear the burdens of others, host the guest, and help in the hardships of truth.’” Waraqah then moves the experience into biblical history. هَذَا النَّامُوسُ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَى مُوسَى “This is the heavenly messenger whom God sent down to Moses.” This is exactly what a call narrative needs. The chosen figure does not understand the event at first. A recognized authority interprets it. The frightening experience becomes a prophetic mission. The Attempted-Suicide Motif One of the most striking features of some versions is Muhammad’s crisis after the first encounter. In Ibn Isḥāq’s version, he fears that he is a poet or possessed and considers throwing himself from the mountain. In some al-Zuhrī-related biographical variants, the attempted-suicide motif appears in connection with the lapse of revelation. In the canonical hadith collections, the most troubling forms are softened or excluded. This pattern matters. It suggests that the story circulated in more dramatic forms before later tradition stabilized the more acceptable version. The raw literary form includes fear, doubt, and a near-catastrophic crisis. Later hadith transmission preserves a cleaner version: terror, yes, but not the same full dramatic despair. The attempted-suicide motif is not needed for the theology of prophethood. It is needed for the drama of a call narrative. Its presence in some streams and absence in others shows that the matn was being shaped. What the Corpus Shows The available corpus supports a two-stream model. The first stream is the canonical hadith family: **ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / later transmitters.** This stream gives the form that becomes dominant in hadith. It contains true dreams, seclusion, Ḥirāʾ, the angelic command, the refusal, the pressing, Q. 96:1–5, return to Khadījah, reassurance, and Waraqah’s validation. The second stream is the Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq family preserved in al-Ṭabarī: **ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb b. Kaysān → Ibn Isḥāq → Salamah b. al-Faḍl → Ibn Ḥumayd → al-Ṭabarī.** This stream gives the dramatic storyteller form. It explicitly places the story in a Zubayrid court context. It contains the sleep setting, the written object, the repeated command, the “What shall I read?” reply, the placing of the words into Muhammad’s heart, and the mountain-crisis motif. Stream Main route Why it matters Canonical hadith stream ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr → al-Zuhrī → Maʿmar / Yūnus / others This is the form that becomes dominant in hadith. It is Zubayrid through ʿUrwah and ʿĀʾishah’s household authority. ʿAbd al-Razzāq / Maʿmar stream ʿAbd al-Razzāq → Maʿmar → al-Zuhrī → ʿUrwah → ʿĀʾishah One of the earliest surviving written witnesses to the full canonical form. Bukhārī stream al-Zuhrī → ʿUrwah → ʿĀʾishah, through later canonical transmission The most famous stabilized form, placed at the beginning of the Ṣaḥīḥ. Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq stream in al-Ṭabarī ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr → ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr → Wahb b. Kaysān → Ibn Isḥāq → Salamah → Ibn Ḥumayd → al-Ṭabarī The strongest evidence for a Meccan qāṣṣ and Zubayrid court setting. Hishām b. ʿUrwah-related material ʿUrwah → Hishām b. ʿUrwah and related shorter forms Important because some versions stop with ʿUrwah or preserve more dramatic elements in abridged form. Why the Zubayrid Setting Matters The Zubayrid household was not just a private family. It was one of the major memory-making circles of early Islam. ʿĀʾishah was a central transmitter of prophetic household memory. ʿUrwah, her nephew, became one of the great early authorities for sīrah and maghāzī material. ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr was a political claimant in Mecca. Wahb b. Kaysān was attached to the House of al-Zubayr. This is a powerful social setting for the formation of early prophetic biography. Anthony stresses that the Ibn Isḥāq frame places the story during the Second Civil War, when ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr and the Zubayrids were competing with the Umayyads for the leadership of the early Islamic polity.[^6] That context does not prove propaganda by itself, but it matters. A court claiming religious legitimacy has a strong reason to preserve, perform, and authorize stories about prophetic beginnings. The first-revelation story does important work in that setting. It makes Khadījah the first human validator. It makes Waraqah, a Christian scriptural authority connected to the Meccan household world, the biblical witness. It turns Muhammad’s terrifying experience into a recognized prophetic mission. It also makes the beginning of the Qurʾān intelligible through narrative. This does not mean the Zubayrids “invented Islam.” It means the polished first-revelation story, as a story, becomes recoverable in their memory network. Why the Story Looks Literary A historical memory can be literary, but this story is highly literary. It has repeated dialogue. It has a threefold pressure scene. It has dramatic fear. It has a return home. It has a wise spouse. It has a learned scriptural interpreter. It has a prediction of rejection and victory. It has a Qurʾānic keyword turned into the center of the plot. That is not how raw memory usually survives. It is how a community tells the origin of revelation. The comparison with Cædmon makes this clearer. Bede’s story is not about Islamic history. It is a Christian hagiographical call story. Yet its structure matches the Ibn Isḥāq iqraʾ narrative at too many points: sleep, inability, command, sacred speech, creation theme, miraculous vernacular performance, validation. This does not prove a simple line of borrowing in every detail. But it does show that the iqraʾ story belongs to a recognizable literary world. What Would Change the Analysis? This analysis would be weakened if we found many independent early Companion-level routes for the iqraʾ story that did not pass through ʿUrwah / al-Zuhrī or the Zubayrid storytelling environment. It would also be weakened if Ibn Isḥāq’s Zubayrid court frame were isolated and unrelated to the larger narrative shape. It would be weakened further if Cædmon only shared one generic motif, such as “a holy person receives inspiration.” But that is not what we have. The canonical hadith form concentrates through ʿĀʾishah → ʿUrwah → al-Zuhrī. The Rayy / Ibn Isḥāq form is tied to ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr, ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr, and Wahb b. Kaysān. The Cædmon comparison is not one shared idea but a shared narrative sequence. The result is a strong cumulative case. Final Verdict The famous first-revelation story is best understood as an early Islamic call narrative, not as a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ. Its most influential hadith form runs through ʿĀʾishah, ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr, and al-Zuhrī. Its most dramatic sīrah form, preserved in the Rayy-recension material inside al-Ṭabarī, is explicitly tied to a Zubayrid court setting: ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Zubayr asks the Meccan storyteller ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr to narrate the beginning of prophecy, and Wahb b. Kaysān, a client of the House of al-Zubayr, transmits the scene. The matn is also not neutral. It is shaped around Qurʾān 96:1–5. The word **iqraʾ** becomes a scene. Gabriel commands. Muhammad refuses. The command is repeated. The revelation is attached to the first verses of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq. Khadījah and Waraqah then validate the experience. The story explains revelation, scripture, prophethood, and biblical attestation all at once. The Cædmon parallel shows why the story cannot be treated as simple memory. Bede’s Cædmon and Ibn Isḥāq’s Muhammad both receive a nighttime visionary command to perform sacred speech despite claiming inability. Both are given a creation-themed utterance. Both are validated afterward by religious authorities. Whether one follows North’s proposal that Bede modelled Cædmon on the Muhammad story, or the more cautious view that both stories belong to a shared late antique call-story repertoire, the conclusion is similar: the iqraʾ narrative is literary and comparative, not raw cave-memory. So the strongest conclusion is careful but pointed: the iqraʾ narrative is early, Zubayrid-linked, Qurʾānized, and literary. It may preserve the memory that Muhammad’s prophetic career began with a terrifying revelatory experience. But the polished story of Gabriel saying “Read,” as preserved in the canonical hadith and sīrah tradition, is a crafted origin narrative shaped by household transmission, Meccan storytelling, scriptural exegesis, and the wider call-story patterns of the late antique world. The first-revelation story should be treated as an early Zubayrid-linked call narrative. The most plausible source-critical model is not a direct transcript from Ḥirāʾ, but a story that crystallized in a Meccan qāṣṣ setting and then spread through Zubayrid household channels into al-Zuhrī and Ibn Isḥāq. title: The Hadith of the Drought: How al-Albani
description: A strengthened refutation of the attempt to weaken the Malik al-Dar drought report, showing how the narration survives by hadith standards while colliding with the Qur

(Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ)', kind: 'root', labelPos: 'above' }, { id: 'isaba', x: 650, y: 550, label: 'al-Iṣābah', kind: 'cl', labelPos: 'right' }, { id: 'ibnHajar', x: 650, y: 50, label: 'Ibn Ḥajar', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'above' } ]; { from: 'episode', to: 'malik1', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'malik1', to: 'abuSalih' }, { from: 'abuSalih', to: 'amash' }, { from: 'amash', to: 'abuMuawiya' }, { from: 'abuMuawiya', to: 'ibnAbiShayba' }, { from: 'servedUmar', to: 'malik2', kind: 'dive' }, { from: 'malik2', to: 'isaba', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'isaba', to: 'ibnHajar' } ]; Fatwa 73 tries to neutralize the report of Mālik al-Dār by treating the narration as defective: Mālik is allegedly unknown, Ibn Ḥajar allegedly authenticated only part of the route, the normal drought practice was ṣalāt al-istisqāʾ, and the man at the grave is unnamed. Those objections only work if the standards are tightened exactly where the report becomes theologically embarrassing. By the ordinary Sunni hadith method, the report has enough support to survive. By the Qurʾān, however, the practice described in it is a direct appeal to a dead messenger for posthumous intervention, which is precisely why the report creates a problem. If the Sunni hadith method is applied consistently, the Mālik al-Dār report is difficult to dismiss. If the Qurʾānic standard is applied consistently, the report is religiously unacceptable. The contradiction is produced by the hadith framework itself: it authenticates a story that later theology has to weaken. The wording at issue is not a vague appeal to the Prophet’s status. The man goes to the Prophet’s grave and addresses him directly: “O Messenger of God, ask God for rain for your community.” The request is directed to a dead prophet after his death. The story then presents the Prophet as appearing in a dream, instructing the man to go to ʿUmar, and ʿUmar responding emotionally rather than condemning the act. ## The Report in Its Earliest Accessible Form The report is also transmitted through al-Bayhaqī’s route as cited by Ibn Kathīr. After giving the chain through Abū Muʿāwiya, al-Aʿmash, Abū Ṣāliḥ, and Mālik, Ibn Kathīr states: “This chain is authentic” (وهذا إسناد صحيح). Ibn Ḥajar likewise cites Ibn Abī Shayba’s route in _Fatḥ al-Bārī_ with the phrase “with an authentic chain” (بإسناد صحيح). The attempt to escape those two assessments is the center of the dispute. ## What Fatwa 73 Tries to Do Fatwa 73's move What the move needs to prove Why it fails internally Mālik al-Dār is unknown. That Mālik is so obscure that the report cannot be used. The biographical record does not treat him as a blank figure: he is identified as Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ, attached to ʿUmar, described as having met the early period, and remembered in multiple rijāl and historical notices. Ibn Ḥajar only authenticated up to Abū Ṣāliḥ. That “from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Mālik” is a deliberate technical limit. The wording naturally identifies the transmitted route. Ibn Ḥajar uses the report as a unit in his chapter discussion, and Ibn Kathīr’s full-chain wording removes the escape route anyway. The Sunnah in drought is istisqāʾ prayer. That one accepted drought practice cancels every other report. Hadith law routinely preserves multiple practices. The ʿAbbās report proves one practice in Bukhārī; it does not by itself falsify the Mālik report. The man at the grave is unnamed. That an anonymous actor inside the story invalidates the report. Hadith criticism evaluates the transmitters carrying the report. Anonymous characters appear throughout accepted hadith literature without collapsing the isnād. The fatwa’s structure reveals the pressure point. It does not merely say, “This report is weak.” It has to explain why two major later hadith authorities could speak of an authentic chain while still preserving a theology in which direct address to the dead is impermissible. The result is a set of objections that would become destructive if applied consistently across hadith literature. ## Mālik al-Dār Was Not a Blank Narrator The first objection is that Mālik al-Dār is unknown and that only Ibn Ḥibbān treated him as reliable. This is too narrow. Ibn Ḥajar identifies him as Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ, the freedman of ʿUmar, known as Mālik al-Dār. He states that Mālik had _idrāk_, heard from Abū Bakr, narrated from Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and Abū ʿUbayda, and was narrated from by Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān and his two sons ʿAwn and ʿAbd Allāh. Ibn Ḥajar also preserves reports that he served in trusted administrative capacities under ʿUmar and then under ʿUthmān. Administrative service is not the same thing as a formal hadith grading. A person can be trusted with money and still be weak in transmission. The problem is that Fatwa 73 does more than deny a formal grading; it rhetorically turns Mālik into an unknown nobody. The biographical notices do not allow that. He is named, located, connected to senior Companions, attached to ʿUmar’s administration, and known to later transmitters. Al-Khalīlī’s notice is even harder for the fatwa to absorb. He describes Mālik al-Dār as an early tābiʿī, “agreed upon” (متفق عليه), praised by the tābiʿūn, and not abundant in narration. A critic can debate how much force to give this wording, but it cannot be reduced to “only Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him.” The statement “only Ibn Ḥibbān authenticated him” leaves out the broader evidence that made later scholars comfortable citing the report. This matters because the fatwa’s argument depends on a strong form of ignorance. If Mālik were only a name floating in the chain with no profile, the objection would have force. Once he is a known client of ʿUmar, connected to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, noticed by Ibn Saʿd, al-Khalīlī, Ibn Ḥajar, and others, the objection becomes more selective. It may still be possible to argue that he falls below the highest hadith standard, but it becomes much harder to explain why Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Kathīr treated this exact route as sound. ## Ibn Ḥajar’s Statement Is Being Rewritten The second objection is the most strained one. Ibn Ḥajar says that Ibn Abī Shayba narrated the report “with an authentic chain from the narration of Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān from Mālik al-Dār.” Fatwa 73 turns this into a claim that Ibn Ḥajar authenticated the route only up to Abū Ṣāliḥ, leaving Mālik outside the authenticated portion. That reading asks the phrase to do too much. Ibn Ḥajar is not giving a full isnād line by line. He is summarizing the report and identifying the route by its lower link: Abū Ṣāliḥ from Mālik al-Dār. In Arabic hadith prose, “from the narration of X from Y” names the route through which the report is known. It does not automatically mean that the authentication stops before Y. If Ibn Ḥajar had wanted to flag Mālik as the unresolved problem, this was the obvious place to do so. Instead, he calls the route authentic and continues to use the report in the chapter discussion. Even if someone insists on forcing a “partial authentication” reading onto Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Kathīr blocks that maneuver. Ibn Kathīr cites the Bayhaqī chain and then says, without this alleged grammatical ambiguity, “This chain is authentic.” The fatwa therefore has to escape both Ibn Ḥajar’s wording and Ibn Kathīr’s wording. The escape becomes less like technical precision and more like theological damage control. ## The ʿAbbās Report Does Not Cancel the Mālik Report The fatwa appeals to the established practice of asking God for rain through the living, especially through al-ʿAbbās, the Prophet’s uncle. That report is genuinely important, but it does not prove what the fatwa needs it to prove. This report can be used to argue that ʿUmar’s public and formal method was to ask a living righteous person to supplicate. It cannot automatically erase a separate report in which a man goes to the Prophet’s grave. Hadith collections regularly preserve parallel practices, exceptional incidents, private actions, public rituals, and reports that sit uneasily beside one another. The existence of one accepted practice does not, by itself, disprove another report. A contradiction has to be argued, not assumed. The real issue is theological. The ʿAbbās report is safe for Sunni theology because the supplication is addressed to God and the intermediary is alive. The Mālik al-Dār report is dangerous because the man addresses the dead Prophet at the grave and asks him to act. The fatwa therefore treats the safe report as “the Sunnah” and the dangerous report as an error. That move may protect doctrine, but it is not a neutral hadith-critical argument. ## The Anonymous Man Objection Would Destroy Too Much The fourth objection asks: who was the man who went to the grave? What was his rank? What was his status? This sounds serious until the same standard is applied elsewhere. Hadith literature constantly contains unnamed actors: a man came to the Prophet, a Bedouin asked, a woman complained, a person saw a dream, a man recited a sūrah, and so on. Their anonymity does not automatically weaken the report because they are not the transmitters carrying the narration. The evaluation concerns the chain that reports the story. If an unnamed character inside a matn invalidated the report, a large portion of accepted hadith literature would become unstable. Some later discussions identify the man as Bilāl b. al-Ḥārith al-Muzanī, a Companion. That identification is not necessary for the argument and should not carry the weight of the proof, since it is tied to the problematic route through Sayf. The stronger point is simpler: the report’s validity does not depend on knowing the visitor’s name. The report is carried by Mālik al-Dār from an event in ʿUmar’s time, and the story itself says the matter reached ʿUmar. The fatwa’s question about the man’s status is therefore a distraction. The story does not ask the anonymous visitor to function as an independent legal authority. It says he performed the act, received a dream-message, and informed ʿUmar. If the chain is accepted, the report places ʿUmar inside the episode as the recipient of the information, weeping and responding rather than condemning the act as shirk. That is precisely why the narration is inconvenient. ## The al-Aʿmash Objection Does Not Rescue the Fatwa Some later critics add an objection not emphasized in Fatwa 73: al-Aʿmash narrates with ʿanʿana, and al-Aʿmash is known for tadlīs. This objection sounds more technical than the Mālik objection, but it still fails to explain the later authentications. Al-Aʿmash’s route through Abū Ṣāliḥ is not an obscure or isolated pairing. The Bukhārī corpus itself contains numerous reports through al-Aʿmash from Abū Ṣāliḥ, sometimes with explicit hearing and sometimes with ʿanʿana. A critic can raise tadlīs in individual cases, but he cannot pretend that the mere presence of al-Aʿmash → Abū Ṣāliḥ is automatically disqualifying in Sunni hadith practice. Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Kathīr knew al-Aʿmash’s profile. Their authentication of this route therefore cannot be dismissed by reciting the word “tadlīs” after the fact. This is where the problem becomes methodological. When the content supports ordinary Sunni law or virtue literature, the system has room for narrators like al-Aʿmash and routes like Abū Ṣāliḥ. When the content depicts a man appealing to the Prophet at his grave, the same system suddenly needs extra caution, extra suspicion, and extra reinterpretation. ## The Qurʾānic Problem: The Dead Are Not a Channel of Appeal The hadith dispute is only half the issue. The deeper problem is that the narration, if accepted, normalizes a practice the Qurʾān does not permit. The Qurʾān repeatedly denies that messengers or invoked beings possess independent access to the unseen, control over harm and benefit, or the ability to respond to the calls of the living after death. The scene in 5:109 is devastating for later saint-veneration logic. The messengers are asked about their communities and answer by disclaiming knowledge: God alone knows the unseen. The Qurʾān does not present dead messengers as supervising the requests of their communities from the grave. The Prophet is commanded to announce that he possesses no power to harm or guide. This is the Qurʾānic frame for prophetic authority: he delivers the message; he does not become a posthumous object of invocation. Death places a barrier between the deceased and the world until resurrection. The Mālik al-Dār report moves in the opposite direction. It depicts a man addressing the Prophet after death and receiving a dream-response that validates the appeal. This verse is especially direct: those called upon besides God do not hear the call, and even if they heard it, they could not respond. The verse then says they will disown that shirk on the Day of Resurrection. The report at the center of this article describes a man doing exactly what this verse warns against: calling upon someone other than God for assistance in a crisis, even if the assistance is framed as “ask God for us.” The hadith method can preserve the report because the chain can be defended. The Qurʾānic standard rejects the practice because the request is directed to the dead. Al-Albani’s school senses the theological danger, so it tightens the hadith method at the exact point where the narration becomes damaging. ## What This Shows About Hadith Authentication This report is a useful case study because it exposes how theological commitments shape hadith criticism. The narration has a recognizable chain, known transmitters, classical defenders, and explicit later authentication from Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Ḥajar. The objections raised against it are not impossible, but they are applied with unusual urgency because the content threatens a later doctrinal boundary. A Qurʾān-alone critique has no reason to defend the practice in the report. The man’s act is not made acceptable because a hadith chain can be defended. The point is that Sunni hadith methodology, when pressed on its own terms, can authenticate a story that depicts behavior the Qurʾān condemns. The later scholar then faces a choice: follow the chain and inherit the theological problem, or protect the theology by weakening the chain through selective criteria. The second option is what Fatwa 73 does. Mālik al-Dār becomes “unknown” despite substantial biographical notices. Ibn Ḥajar’s phrase becomes “partial” despite its normal reading and despite Ibn Kathīr’s fuller statement. The ʿAbbās report becomes a cancellation mechanism instead of a separate practice. The unnamed man becomes a fatal problem despite the routine presence of anonymous characters in accepted narrations. The Mālik al-Dār drought report should not be used to justify calling upon the dead. It should be used to expose the instability of hadith authentication. By Sunni hadith standards, the report is defensible. By the Qurʾān, the act it describes is indefensible. Fatwa 73 tries to solve the contradiction by weakening the report, but its arguments depend on standards that are not applied consistently elsewhere. ## Sources Consulted Source Use in this article Ibn Abī Shayba, al-Muṣannaf , no. 32002 Earliest accessible form of the report: Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Mālik al-Dār. al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa ; cited by Ibn Kathīr in al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya Parallel route through the same lower chain; Ibn Kathīr’s statement: “This chain is authentic.” Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī Classical citation of Ibn Abī Shayba’s route “with an authentic chain.” Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba fī Tamyīz al-Ṣaḥāba , entry on Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ Biographical profile of Mālik al-Dār: his identity, senior contacts, narrators, and administrative role. al-Khalīlī, al-Irshād fī Maʿrifat ʿUlamāʾ al-Ḥadīth Notice describing Mālik al-Dār as an early tābiʿī, agreed upon, praised by the tābiʿūn, and not prolific. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1010 and 3710 ʿUmar’s public drought appeal through al-ʿAbbās, used to show the difference between a safe living-intermediary report and the dangerous grave report. Qurʾān 5:109; 72:20-21; 23:99-100; 35:14 The Qurʾānic standard used to evaluate the theological content of the report.

It does not merely say, “This report is weak.” It has to explain why two major later hadith authorities could speak of an authentic chain while still preserving a theology in which direct address to the dead is impermissible. The result is a set of objections that would become destructive if applied consistently across hadith literature. Mālik al-Dār Was Not a Blank Narrator The first objection is that Mālik al-Dār is unknown and that only Ibn Ḥibbān treated him as reliable. This is too narrow. Ibn Ḥajar identifies him as Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ, the freedman of ʿUmar, known as Mālik al-Dār. He states that Mālik had _idrāk_, heard from Abū Bakr, narrated from Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, Muʿādh, and Abū ʿUbayda, and was narrated from by Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān and his two sons ʿAwn and ʿAbd Allāh. Ibn Ḥajar also preserves reports that he served in trusted administrative capacities under ʿUmar and then under ʿUthmān. Administrative service is not the same thing as a formal hadith grading. A person can be trusted with money and still be weak in transmission. The problem is that Fatwa 73 does more than deny a formal grading; it rhetorically turns Mālik into an unknown nobody. The biographical notices do not allow that. He is named, located, connected to senior Companions, attached to ʿUmar’s administration, and known to later transmitters. Al-Khalīlī’s notice is even harder for the fatwa to absorb. He describes Mālik al-Dār as an early tābiʿī, “agreed upon” (متفق عليه), praised by the tābiʿūn, and not abundant in narration. A critic can debate how much force to give this wording, but it cannot be reduced to “only Ibn Ḥibbān mentioned him.” The statement “only Ibn Ḥibbān authenticated him” leaves out the broader evidence that made later scholars comfortable citing the report. This matters because the fatwa’s argument depends on a strong form of ignorance. If Mālik were only a name floating in the chain with no profile, the objection would have force. Once he is a known client of ʿUmar, connected to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, noticed by Ibn Saʿd, al-Khalīlī, Ibn Ḥajar, and others, the objection becomes more selective. It may still be possible to argue that he falls below the highest hadith standard, but it becomes much harder to explain why Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Kathīr treated this exact route as sound. Ibn Ḥajar’s Statement Is Being Rewritten The second objection is the most strained one. Ibn Ḥajar says that Ibn Abī Shayba narrated the report “with an authentic chain from the narration of Abū Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān from Mālik al-Dār.” Fatwa 73 turns this into a claim that Ibn Ḥajar authenticated the route only up to Abū Ṣāliḥ, leaving Mālik outside the authenticated portion. That reading asks the phrase to do too much. Ibn Ḥajar is not giving a full isnād line by line. He is summarizing the report and identifying the route by its lower link: Abū Ṣāliḥ from Mālik al-Dār. In Arabic hadith prose, “from the narration of X from Y” names the route through which the report is known. It does not automatically mean that the authentication stops before Y. If Ibn Ḥajar had wanted to flag Mālik as the unresolved problem, this was the obvious place to do so. Instead, he calls the route authentic and continues to use the report in the chapter discussion. Even if someone insists on forcing a “partial authentication” reading onto Ibn Ḥajar, Ibn Kathīr blocks that maneuver. Ibn Kathīr cites the Bayhaqī chain and then says, without this alleged grammatical ambiguity, “This chain is authentic.” The fatwa therefore has to escape both Ibn Ḥajar’s wording and Ibn Kathīr’s wording. The escape becomes less like technical precision and more like theological damage control. The ʿAbbās Report Does Not Cancel the Mālik Report The fatwa appeals to the established practice of asking God for rain through the living, especially through al-ʿAbbās, the Prophet’s uncle. That report is genuinely important, but it does not prove what the fatwa needs it to prove. This report can be used to argue that ʿUmar’s public and formal method was to ask a living righteous person to supplicate. It cannot automatically erase a separate report in which a man goes to the Prophet’s grave. Hadith collections regularly preserve parallel practices, exceptional incidents, private actions, public rituals, and reports that sit uneasily beside one another. The existence of one accepted practice does not, by itself, disprove another report. A contradiction has to be argued, not assumed. The real issue is theological. The ʿAbbās report is safe for Sunni theology because the supplication is addressed to God and the intermediary is alive. The Mālik al-Dār report is dangerous because the man addresses the dead Prophet at the grave and asks him to act. The fatwa therefore treats the safe report as “the Sunnah” and the dangerous report as an error. That move may protect doctrine, but it is not a neutral hadith-critical argument. The Anonymous Man Objection Would Destroy Too Much The fourth objection asks: who was the man who went to the grave? What was his rank? What was his status? This sounds serious until the same standard is applied elsewhere. Hadith literature constantly contains unnamed actors: a man came to the Prophet, a Bedouin asked, a woman complained, a person saw a dream, a man recited a sūrah, and so on. Their anonymity does not automatically weaken the report because they are not the transmitters carrying the narration. The evaluation concerns the chain that reports the story. If an unnamed character inside a matn invalidated the report, a large portion of accepted hadith literature would become unstable. Some later discussions identify the man as Bilāl b. al-Ḥārith al-Muzanī, a Companion. That identification is not necessary for the argument and should not carry the weight of the proof, since it is tied to the problematic route through Sayf. The stronger point is simpler: the report’s validity does not depend on knowing the visitor’s name. The report is carried by Mālik al-Dār from an event in ʿUmar’s time, and the story itself says the matter reached ʿUmar. The fatwa’s question about the man’s status is therefore a distraction. The story does not ask the anonymous visitor to function as an independent legal authority. It says he performed the act, received a dream-message, and informed ʿUmar. If the chain is accepted, the report places ʿUmar inside the episode as the recipient of the information, weeping and responding rather than condemning the act as shirk. That is precisely why the narration is inconvenient. The al-Aʿmash Objection Does Not Rescue the Fatwa Some later critics add an objection not emphasized in Fatwa 73: al-Aʿmash narrates with ʿanʿana, and al-Aʿmash is known for tadlīs. This objection sounds more technical than the Mālik objection, but it still fails to explain the later authentications. Al-Aʿmash’s route through Abū Ṣāliḥ is not an obscure or isolated pairing. The Bukhārī corpus itself contains numerous reports through al-Aʿmash from Abū Ṣāliḥ, sometimes with explicit hearing and sometimes with ʿanʿana. A critic can raise tadlīs in individual cases, but he cannot pretend that the mere presence of al-Aʿmash → Abū Ṣāliḥ is automatically disqualifying in Sunni hadith practice. Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Kathīr knew al-Aʿmash’s profile. Their authentication of this route therefore cannot be dismissed by reciting the word “tadlīs” after the fact. This is where the problem becomes methodological. When the content supports ordinary Sunni law or virtue literature, the system has room for narrators like al-Aʿmash and routes like Abū Ṣāliḥ. When the content depicts a man appealing to the Prophet at his grave, the same system suddenly needs extra caution, extra suspicion, and extra reinterpretation. The Qurʾānic Problem: The Dead Are Not a Channel of Appeal The hadith dispute is only half the issue. The deeper problem is that the narration, if accepted, normalizes a practice the Qurʾān does not permit. The Qurʾān repeatedly denies that messengers or invoked beings possess independent access to the unseen, control over harm and benefit, or the ability to respond to the calls of the living after death. The scene in 5:109 is devastating for later saint-veneration logic. The messengers are asked about their communities and answer by disclaiming knowledge: God alone knows the unseen. The Qurʾān does not present dead messengers as supervising the requests of their communities from the grave. The Prophet is commanded to announce that he possesses no power to harm or guide. This is the Qurʾānic frame for prophetic authority: he delivers the message; he does not become a posthumous object of invocation. Death places a barrier between the deceased and the world until resurrection. The Mālik al-Dār report moves in the opposite direction. It depicts a man addressing the Prophet after death and receiving a dream-response that validates the appeal. This verse is especially direct: those called upon besides God do not hear the call, and even if they heard it, they could not respond. The verse then says they will disown that shirk on the Day of Resurrection. The report at the center of this article describes a man doing exactly what this verse warns against: calling upon someone other than God for assistance in a crisis, even if the assistance is framed as “ask God for us.” The hadith method can preserve the report because the chain can be defended. The Qurʾānic standard rejects the practice because the request is directed to the dead. Al-Albani’s school senses the theological danger, so it tightens the hadith method at the exact point where the narration becomes damaging. What This Shows About Hadith Authentication This report is a useful case study because it exposes how theological commitments shape hadith criticism. The narration has a recognizable chain, known transmitters, classical defenders, and explicit later authentication from Ibn Kathīr and Ibn Ḥajar. The objections raised against it are not impossible, but they are applied with unusual urgency because the content threatens a later doctrinal boundary. A Qurʾān-alone critique has no reason to defend the practice in the report. The man’s act is not made acceptable because a hadith chain can be defended. The point is that Sunni hadith methodology, when pressed on its own terms, can authenticate a story that depicts behavior the Qurʾān condemns. The later scholar then faces a choice: follow the chain and inherit the theological problem, or protect the theology by weakening the chain through selective criteria. The second option is what Fatwa 73 does. Mālik al-Dār becomes “unknown” despite substantial biographical notices. Ibn Ḥajar’s phrase becomes “partial” despite its normal reading and despite Ibn Kathīr’s fuller statement. The ʿAbbās report becomes a cancellation mechanism instead of a separate practice. The unnamed man becomes a fatal problem despite the routine presence of anonymous characters in accepted narrations. The Mālik al-Dār drought report should not be used to justify calling upon the dead. It should be used to expose the instability of hadith authentication. By Sunni hadith standards, the report is defensible. By the Qurʾān, the act it describes is indefensible. Fatwa 73 tries to solve the contradiction by weakening the report, but its arguments depend on standards that are not applied consistently elsewhere. Sources Consulted Source Use in this article Ibn Abī Shayba, al-Muṣannaf , no. 32002 Earliest accessible form of the report: Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Abū Ṣāliḥ → Mālik al-Dār. al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa ; cited by Ibn Kathīr in al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya Parallel route through the same lower chain; Ibn Kathīr’s statement: “This chain is authentic.” Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī Classical citation of Ibn Abī Shayba’s route “with an authentic chain.” Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba fī Tamyīz al-Ṣaḥāba , entry on Mālik b. ʿIyāḍ Biographical profile of Mālik al-Dār: his identity, senior contacts, narrators, and administrative role. al-Khalīlī, al-Irshād fī Maʿrifat ʿUlamāʾ al-Ḥadīth Notice describing Mālik al-Dār as an early tābiʿī, agreed upon, praised by the tābiʿūn, and not prolific. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1010 and 3710 ʿUmar’s public drought appeal through al-ʿAbbās, used to show the difference between a safe living-intermediary report and the dangerous grave report. Qurʾān 5:109; 72:20-21; 23:99-100; 35:14 The Qurʾānic standard used to evaluate the theological content of the report.

title: The Hadith of Angels Cursing Women: Common Links, False Independence, and Propheticized Obedience
description: A detailed isnād-cum-matn analysis of the Abū Hurayrah report that angels curse a wife who refuses or abandons her husband’s bed, arguing that the tradition is better explained as a Q. 4:34 legal-exegetical idea propheticized at the common-link level.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The report is famous because of what it says, but its transmission history is more revealing than the line usually quoted in sermons. In its most familiar form, the Prophet is made to say that when a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, the angels curse her until morning. That is how many readers know the hadith from Bukhārī and Muslim. Yet when all the early variants are placed beside one another, the report does not look like a single Prophetic teaching preserved through two independent routes from Abū Hurayrah. It looks like a **matn cluster**: one marital-obedience idea, formulated through two common links in two different centers, then attached to Abū Hurayrah through plausible but uncontrolled Successor links. The question is not whether one can simply point to Abū Hurayrah, Abū Ḥāzim, Qatādah, or al-Aʿmash and declare the report false. The case has to be structural. The report becomes visible only at the level of **Qatādah b. Diʿāmah** in Baṣra and **al-Aʿmash** in Kūfa. Above them, the chains narrow into single strands. Below them, the reports proliferate. That is exactly the zone where isnād-cum-matn analysis has to do its work. ## The two canonical forms The first form is the one most people recognize. The husband is the grammatical subject. He calls. She refuses. He sleeps angry. The angels curse until morning. إِذَا دَعَا الرَّجُلُ امْرَأَتَهُ إِلَى فِرَاشِهِ فَأَبَتْ، فَبَاتَ غَضْبَانَ عَلَيْهَا، لَعَنَتْهَا الْمَلَائِكَةُ حَتَّى تُصْبِحَ. “When a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, so he spends the night angry with her, the angels curse her until morning.” The second form is less famous but earlier in physical attestation and simpler in shape. The woman is the grammatical subject. She abandons the husband’s bed. The angels curse until she returns. إِذَا بَاتَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ هَاجِرَةً لِفِرَاشِ زَوْجِهَا، لَعَنَتْهَا الْمَلَائِكَةُ حَتَّى تَرْجِعَ. “When a woman spends the night abandoning her husband’s bed, the angels curse her until she returns.” There are variations inside each family. Some Qatādah lines say “until morning,” some say “until she returns,” and one preserves a bare maxim with no summons, no anger, and no time-limit: “A woman does not abandon her husband’s bed except that the angels of God curse her.” But the two basic forms are stable enough to analyze. The Qatādah form is broad, aphoristic, and woman-focused. The al-Aʿmash form is narrower, legal-casuistic, and husband-focused. ## What ICMA can and cannot prove Isnād-cum-matn analysis does not begin by asking whether a transmitter could have met another transmitter. That is only a background condition. A man may have met his teacher and still not have heard a particular report from him. The real question is whether the report is independently controlled above the common link. A common link is the transmitter at whose level the report begins to spread through multiple students. If several independent students transmit a report from Qatādah, then Qatādah is recoverable as the point from which that version proliferated. But if the chain above Qatādah is only Qatādah → Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah, with no other student of Zurārah transmitting the same report, then Zurārah is not independently controlled for this report. His general reliability and his general possibility of hearing from Abū Hurayrah do not prove that this specific hadith came from him. The same rule applies to al-Aʿmash. Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī was a real transmitter from Abū Hurayrah. al-Aʿmash really did transmit from Abū Ḥāzim. But if every early Abū Ḥāzim version of this report passes through al-Aʿmash, then Abū Ḥāzim is not an independent control for this report. The report is recoverable at al-Aʿmash, not securely above him. This is the central point. The issue is not whether the upper links are **possible**. They are possible. The issue is whether they are **proved for this specific report**. They are not. Method note: Classical hadith criticism often treats the general possibility of hearing, narrator reliability, and canonical acceptance as sufficient for accepting a report. ICMA asks a different historical question. It asks where the report first becomes visible in a branching transmission network and whether the pre-branching strand is independently controlled. ## The isnād diagram The two bundles can be drawn very simply. They both end at Abū Hurayrah, but each reaches him through a different uncontrolled Successor. The real proliferation occurs lower, at Qatādah and al-Aʿmash. Two apparent Abū Hurayrah routes, two real common-link formulations Baṣra · Cluster B Abū Hurayrah single strand · uncontrolled Zurārah b. Awfā single strand · no non-Qatādah control QATĀDAH b. Diʿāmah common link Shuʿbah Hammām Ṭayālisī · Aḥmad · Dārimī · Bukhārī · Muslim · Nasāʾī · Bayhaqī “A woman abandons her husband’s bed … until she returns.” Kūfa · Cluster A Abū Hurayrah single strand · uncontrolled Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī single strand · no non-al-Aʿmash control AL-AʿMASH common link Abū Muʿāwiyah Wakīʿ Jarīr Abū ʿAwānah Ibn Numayr Shuʿbah Ibn Abī Shaybah · Ibn Rāhawayh · Aḥmad · Bukhārī · Muslim · Abū Dāwūd · Nasāʾī “A man calls his wife … she refuses … he sleeps angry … until morning.” The diagram does not deny that Zurārah or Abū Ḥāzim could transmit from Abū Hurayrah. It shows that, for this specific report, neither upper strand is independently controlled. The recoverable transmission begins at Qatādah and al-Aʿmash. ## The variant corpus in brief A corpus search of 1,221 hadith collections, about 1.33 million records, and twenty rijāl and ʿilal works produced 194 raw matches for the curse motif, using normalized searches around “angels,” “curse,” “bed,” “abandoning,” and “a man calls his wife.” The analysis below is based on the early and primary witnesses, especially collectors up to Bayhaqī.[^1] The Qatādah bundle is the earlier recoverable family. Its earliest physical witness is al-Ṭayālisī, who gives the chain Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī → Shuʿbah → Qatādah → Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah. Aḥmad preserves multiple lines through Shuʿbah and Hammām. Dārimī places it under the husband’s right over the wife. Bukhārī and Muslim also preserve the Qatādah form, though Muslim contains a line with “until morning” beside the more native “until she returns.”[^2] The al-Aʿmash bundle appears in Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Rāhawayh, Aḥmad, Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān, and Bayhaqī. Its partial common links include Abū Muʿāwiyah, Wakīʿ, Jarīr, Abū ʿAwānah, Ibn Numayr, ʿAlī b. Mushir, and Shuʿbah through Sulaymān, which is al-Aʿmash. This is a strong common-link bundle below al-Aʿmash, but above al-Aʿmash the report is only al-Aʿmash → Abū Ḥāzim → Abū Hurayrah.[^3] The distribution is therefore not: Abū Hurayrah taught the same hadith independently to Zurārah and Abū Ḥāzim. It is more accurately: Qatādah and al-Aʿmash each produced recoverable common-link formulations of the same marital-obedience threat motif and each attached it to Abū Hurayrah through a plausible but uncontrolled Successor. ## The matn tells the story The two clusters are not the same wording randomly paraphrased. They are two different legal shapes. | Feature | Qatādah / Zurārah bundle | al-Aʿmash / Abū Ḥāzim bundle | |---|---:|---:| | Woman is the grammatical subject | Yes | No | | Husband is the grammatical subject | No | Yes | | “Abandoning / migrating from the husband’s bed” | Yes | No | | Husband summons the wife to bed | No | Yes | | Wife explicitly refuses | No | Yes | | Husband sleeps angry or displeased | No | Yes | | Curse ends “until she returns” | Dominant | No | | Curse ends “until morning” | Minority / contamination | Dominant | | Bare maxim form | Yes, through Hammām | No | The Qatādah form sounds like a moral warning: if she abandons the bed, the angels curse until she returns. The al-Aʿmash form sounds like a legal case: if he summons, she refuses, and he sleeps angry, then the curse lasts until morning. The direction of development is not difficult to see. A broad warning can easily be narrowed into a legal scenario. A fully casuistic scenario is less likely to generate the shorter maxim. The most primitive-looking form is the Hammām line from Qatādah: لاَ تَهْجُرُ امْرَأَةٌ فِرَاشَ زَوْجِهَا إِلاَّ لَعَنَتْهَا مَلاَئِكَةُ اللهِ. “No woman abandons her husband’s bed except that the angels of God curse her.” This is not yet the fully developed Bukhārī/Muslim form of the husband calling and the wife refusing. It is a short threat formula. That matters because short legal-moral maxims are exactly the kind of material that could be “propheticized” in early legal discourse. ## The upper links fail the control test This is the decisive point. Zurārah b. Awfā is not an unknown man. He is a Baṣran qāḍī and a plausible transmitter from Abū Hurayrah. But for this report, a scan of the corpus found no non-Qatādah student of Zurārah transmitting the bed-curse hadith. In the report corpus, the Zurārah-route matches are overwhelmingly through Qatādah, and the apparent exceptions are late compilations re-citing Bukhārī and Muslim rather than independent early lines.[^4] Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī is also not an unknown man. He is a real Kūfan transmitter from Abū Hurayrah, and al-Aʿmash is known to transmit from him. But for this report, every early Abū Ḥāzim line passes through al-Aʿmash. No non-al-Aʿmash student of Abū Ḥāzim preserves the report in an early source.[^5] That silence is not a small detail. Both Successors had other students. | Successor | Other well-attested students | Who carries this report? | |---|---|---| | Zurārah b. Awfā | Bahz b. Ḥakīm, ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī, ʿAbdallāh b. ʿUbayd, al-Mulaykī, others | Qatādah only | | Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī | Yazīd b. Kaysān, Manṣūr b. al-Muʿtamir, Abū Mālik al-Ashjaʿī, others | al-Aʿmash only | If the report had genuinely belonged to Zurārah as a known Abū Hurayrah teaching, we would expect at least one other Zurārah student to preserve it. If it had genuinely belonged to Abū Ḥāzim as a known Abū Hurayrah teaching, we would expect at least one other Abū Ḥāzim student to preserve it. Instead, each report appears only through the common link who made it proliferate. This is what I mean by **false independence at the Companion level**. The two reports both end at Abū Hurayrah, but that does not prove two independent Abū Hurayrah transmissions. It proves two common-link formations attached to Abū Hurayrah. ## Why Qatādah is the likeliest origin point The strongest scenario is that the Qatādah version is the earliest recoverable form. That does not mean we can prove Qatādah sat down and consciously forged it. The historical claim should be more careful. The report cannot be shown to predate Qatādah, and Qatādah’s legal-exegetical environment gives us the most natural reason for the report to exist. The key background is Q. 4:34. This verse supplied early exegetes with a legal grammar of male authority, female obedience, nushūz, admonition, bed-separation, and discipline. Qatādah’s preserved tafsīr of the verse is especially important. In ʿAbd al-Razzāq’s Tafsīr, Maʿmar transmits from Qatādah that a man struck his wife. She came to the Prophet. The Prophet wanted retaliation from him, but then the verse “Men are qawwāmūn over women” was revealed.[^6] عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ قَالَ: أَنَا مَعْمَرٌ، عَنْ قَتَادَةَ، قَالَ: صَكَّ رَجُلٌ امْرَأَتَهُ، فَأَتَتِ النَّبِيَّ، فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يُقِيدَهَا مِنْهُ، فَأَنْزَلَ اللهُ تَعَالَى: الرِّجَالُ قَوَّامُونَ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ. ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Maʿmar informed us from Qatādah: A man struck his wife, so she came to the Prophet. He wanted to exact retaliation for her against him, but God revealed: “Men are qawwāmūn over women.” This is not a neutral explanation of marriage. In Qatādah’s version, the verse enters the story precisely to block retaliation against a husband and to establish male authority as the controlling rule. In the same passage, Qatādah explains “qānitāt” as “obedient.” Ṭabarī preserves the fuller wording: “obedient to God and to their husbands.”[^7] عَنْ قَتَادَةَ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: قَانِتَاتٌ، قَالَ: مُطِيعَاتٌ. وَفِي رِوَايَةِ الطَّبَرِيِّ: أَيْ مُطِيعَاتٌ لِلَّهِ وَلِأَزْوَاجِهِنَّ. From Qatādah concerning “qānitāt”: he said, “obedient.” In Ṭabarī’s version: “obedient to God and to their husbands.” Then Qatādah explains the disciplinary sequence. If the husband fears nushūz, he admonishes her. If she accepts, that ends the matter. If not, he abandons her bed. If she accepts, that ends the matter. If not, he strikes her with a non-severe beating.[^8] إِذَا خَافَ نُشُوزَهَا وَعَظَهَا، فَإِنْ أَقْبَلَتْ وَإِلَّا هَجَرَ مَضْجَعَهَا، فَإِنْ أَقْبَلَتْ وَإِلَّا ضَرَبَهَا ضَرْبًا غَيْرَ مُبَرِّحٍ. وَفِي رِوَايَةٍ أُخْرَى عَنْ قَتَادَةَ: تَبْدَأُ يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ فَتَعِظُهَا، فَإِنْ أَبَتْ عَلَيْكَ فَاهْجُرْهَا، يَعْنِي بِهِ: فِرَاشَهَا. “If he fears her nushūz, he admonishes her. If she accepts, then fine; otherwise he abandons her bed. If she accepts, then fine; otherwise he strikes her with a non-severe beating.” In another Qatādah version: “You begin, son of Adam, by admonishing her. If she refuses you, then abandon her, meaning: her bed.” Now compare that exegetical logic to the Qatādah hadith form: Q. 4:34 in Qatādah’s tafsīr female nushūz → admonition → bed/firāsh discipline → return/obedience Qatādah’s hadith form woman abandons husband’s bed → angels curse her → until she returns The conceptual fit is exact. The hadith does not need to begin as a remembered saying from the Prophet. It reads naturally as a propheticized warning built from the Q. 4:34 exegetical-legal world. Qatādah’s tafsīr gives the motive profile: male authority, female obedience, bed-abandonment, and return to compliance. There is also an important non-Qatādah control. Mujāhid, in Ibn Abī Ḥātim’s Tafsīr, explains Q. 4:34 in terms very close to the hadith’s logic: if a woman commits nushūz away from her husband’s bed, he tells her, “Fear God and return to your bed; this is the admonition.”[^9] عَنْ مُجَاهِدٍ: فَعِظُوهُنَّ، قَالَ: إِذَا نَشَزَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ عَنْ فِرَاشِ زَوْجِهَا، فَإِنَّهُ يَقُولُ لَهَا: اتَّقِي اللهَ وَارْجِعِي إِلَى فِرَاشِكِ، وَهَذِهِ الْمَوْعِظَةُ. From Mujāhid concerning “admonish them”: “If the woman commits nushūz away from her husband’s bed, he says to her: Fear God and return to your bed. This is the admonition.” This is extremely important. It shows that the idea did not need the hadith in order to exist. The exegetical maxim was already there: wife, nushūz, husband’s bed, admonition, return. The hadith intensifies the same idea by adding angels and curse. That is why the Qatādah form is best explained as a **propheticized tarhīb**: a warning formula that attaches divine threat to a legal-exegetical norm. ## Why Zurārah is probably not the motive source Zurārah b. Awfā should not be made the villain of the argument. A scan of his wider transmission profile does not show him as a specialist in reports that elevate men over women. His preserved material is dominated by prayer, Qurʾān, night worship, moral reports, legal cases, and devotional material. The gender-control theme does not appear as his clear personal signature. That matters because the best historical explanation should locate motive where the evidence locates it. For this report, the motive does not appear clearly at Zurārah’s level. It appears at Qatādah’s level. Qatādah is the recoverable common link, and Qatādah’s tafsīr of Q. 4:34 supplies the full legal grammar of the report. So the argument should not be: Zurārah invented an anti-woman report. It should be: Qatādah, or the Basran legal-exegetical environment visible through Qatādah, propheticized a Q. 4:34 marital-obedience maxim and routed it through a plausible Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah strand. This distinction keeps the case precise. It does not overstate what we can prove. ## al-Aʿmash and the problem of false independence The al-Aʿmash bundle is not the earliest form. It is more developed. It supplies the details that a jurist would want: the husband initiates, the wife refuses, the husband sleeps angry, and the curse lasts until morning. It transforms a broad warning into a more actionable legal scenario. One could argue that al-Aʿmash independently formulated a Kūfan version of the same Q. 4:34 idea. That is possible. But al-Aʿmash should not be treated as a neutral transmitter in this dossier. There is a prior pattern problem. In the bewitchment dossier, al-Aʿmash appears in the same kind of structural role. A report centered elsewhere around Hishām b. ʿUrwah appears through a Kūfan al-Aʿmash route that lacks Hishām in the isnād while preserving the same narrative world. The earlier analysis argued that the most plausible explanation is not independent origin, but source-obscuring or route substitution in a politically charged Kufan environment.[^10] In an unpublished Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī study, the same structural tendency appears again. The study argues that al-Aʿmash produced a Kūfan cluster that reproduces the rhetorical architecture of an earlier al-Shaʿbī construction while changing the authority structure, contents, and polemical function. The point is not that the Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī case proves this hadith by itself. The point is that al-Aʿmash repeatedly appears as a common-link reformulator whose versions can look independent in isnād while being structurally dependent in matn architecture.[^11] That prior pattern changes how we judge the al-Aʿmash form here. The standalone evidence proves only that al-Aʿmash is the common link of the Kūfan version. The wider pattern makes genuine independence less attractive. The al-Aʿmash version preserves the same core threat as Qatādah’s earlier Baṣran form but recasts it into a sharper legal case and attaches it to a different plausible Abū Hurayrah Successor, Abū Ḥāzim. This is exactly how false independence works. The route is believable because Abū Ḥāzim really can transmit from Abū Hurayrah. But believability is not proof. A successful rerouted isnād normally uses plausible links. Careful claim: I am not claiming that this dossier alone proves al-Aʿmash stole Qatādah’s wording. The stronger claim is that al-Aʿmash’s bundle should be treated as suspect independence. It is a second common-link formulation, not independent proof that the report reaches Abū Hurayrah. ## What about al-Aʿmash hearing from Abū Ḥāzim? This point needs correction from some earlier polemical treatments. al-Aʿmash did transmit from Abū Ḥāzim in general, and direct-hearing language exists in other reports. Therefore, the argument should not rest on the claim that al-Aʿmash could not have heard from Abū Ḥāzim at all.[^12] The weak link is more specific. For **this report**, Abū Ḥāzim is uncontrolled. His other students do not preserve it. The only early route through him is al-Aʿmash. So the chain does not prove Abū Ḥāzim taught this report from Abū Hurayrah. It proves al-Aʿmash taught a report and placed it through Abū Ḥāzim to Abū Hurayrah. This is an important difference. Classical isnād criticism often asks: could al-Aʿmash have heard from Abū Ḥāzim? ICMA asks: does any independent Abū Ḥāzim student transmit this report? The answer, so far, is no. ## The legal setting: husband-rights literature By the time the report enters legal collections, it is already being read as a husband-rights text. Dārimī places the Qatādah form under a chapter on the husband’s right over the woman. Abū Dāwūd places the al-Aʿmash form under the same kind of chapter. Ibn Abī Shaybah places the al-Aʿmash report in a dense legal-ethical environment with reports about the wife being commanded to observe the husband’s right, women hypothetically prostrating to husbands, a wife coming to the husband even if at the oven, and extreme statements about never fully repaying the husband’s right.[^13] That environment does not prove where the report began, but it shows why it survived. It was useful. It gave jurists and preachers a Prophetic threat formula for enforcing a one-sided marital duty. The Q. 4:34 exegetical logic supplied the legal grammar. The hadith supplied the divine terror. Later tafsīr also recognizes the fit. Suyūṭī places the al-Aʿmash/Bukhārī-Muslim version directly inside discussion of Q. 4:34.[^14] That is exactly where the report belongs conceptually. ## The false companion-level support Bazzār notes that similar wording was also narrated from Zayd b. Arqam and Ibn Abī Awfā.[^15] This sounds, at first, like broader Companion support. But in the corpus search, those non-Abū Hurayrah versions do not appear in the major early core collections as independent controls. They surface in peripheral or later works. They are better understood as **deep dives**: later Companion-level strands that emerge after the report is already circulating. Deep dives do not independently prove an early Companion origin. They often show the opposite. Once a report becomes useful, it can acquire additional Companion routes. That creates the appearance of wider attestation while leaving the earliest recoverable common links unchanged. ## So who fabricated it? The clean answer is: we cannot prove a personal confession, so we should not pretend to have one. The better historical language is **propheticization**, **common-link formulation**, and **false independence**. Still, if we ask where the likeliest origin lies, the answer is Qatādah’s Basran environment. The Qatādah form is earlier, simpler, closer to the non-prophetic Q. 4:34 exegetical idea, and recoverable before the al-Aʿmash form. It is therefore the best candidate for the first propheticized version. al-Aʿmash then represents a second-stage problem. His version may be an independent Kūfan propheticization of the same Q. 4:34 motif, but his prior pattern makes route-rerouting or common-link reformulation especially plausible. The al-Aʿmash form is not proof of a second Abū Hurayrah transmission. It is proof of a second common-link formulation. ## The final reconstruction 1 Q. 4:34 exegetical world: male authority, female obedience, nushūz, bed/firāsh, admonition, return. 2 Non-prophetic legal maxim: if a woman leaves the husband’s bed, she is admonished and told to return. 3 Qatādah’s Baṣran formulation: the maxim becomes a Prophetic tarhīb report: angels curse her until she returns. 4 al-Aʿmash’s Kūfan formulation: the broad warning becomes a legal case: the husband calls, she refuses, he sleeps angry, angels curse until morning. 5 Canonical reception: Bukhārī and Muslim preserve both families, making the report classically ṣaḥīḥ while leaving its historical origin above the common links unproven. The report is therefore classically strong but historically weak above the common links. That distinction is essential. A classical scholar may say the report is ṣaḥīḥ because Bukhārī and Muslim transmit it through acceptable men. An ICMA analysis asks a different question: can the report be shown to predate Qatādah or al-Aʿmash? At present, the answer is no. ## Verdict The hadith is best understood as a first-/second-century legal-exegetical warning projected onto the Prophet. The earliest recoverable version is Qatādah’s Baṣran form. Its content fits his Q. 4:34 tafsīr almost too well: men’s authority, women’s obedience, nushūz, bed-abandonment, and return. The report turns that framework into a divine threat. The al-Aʿmash version is a later or secondary Kūfan formulation. It is not independent proof of Abū Hurayrah’s teaching. It is a second common-link bundle through an uncontrolled Abū Ḥāzim strand, produced by a transmitter who elsewhere appears capable of creating independent-looking routes for inherited report-architecture. So the strongest conclusion is not that one can name the exact moment of forgery. It is that the report **cannot be shown to come from the Prophet**, cannot be shown to come from Abū Hurayrah, and is better explained as a propheticized marital-obedience maxim from the early legal-exegetical tradition. The angels in this hadith are not evidence of heaven speaking. They are evidence of law learning how to speak with heaven’s voice. --- ## Notes [^1]: The corpus report used for this article searched 1,221 locally extracted Shamela hadith collections, approximately 1.33 million records, plus twenty rijāl and ʿilal works, for normalized combinations of ملائكة, لعن, فراش, هاجرة, and دعا امرأته.
