fullText: The report is famous because of what it says, but its transmission history is more revealing than the line usually quoted in sermons. In its most familiar form, the Prophet is made to say that when a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, the angels curse her until morning. That is how many readers know the hadith from Bukhārī and Muslim. Yet when all the early variants are placed beside one another, the report does not look like a single Prophetic teaching preserved through two independent routes from Abū Hurayrah. It looks like a **matn cluster**: one marital-obedience idea, formulated through two common links in two different centers, then attached to Abū Hurayrah through plausible but uncontrolled Successor links. The question is not whether one can simply point to Abū Hurayrah, Abū Ḥāzim, Qatādah, or al-Aʿmash and declare the report false. The case has to be structural. The report becomes visible only at the level of **Qatādah b. Diʿāmah** in Baṣra and **al-Aʿmash** in Kūfa. Above them, the chains narrow into single strands. Below them, the reports proliferate. That is exactly the zone where isnād-cum-matn analysis has to do its work. The two canonical forms The first form is the one most people recognize. The husband is the grammatical subject. He calls. She refuses. He sleeps angry. The angels curse until morning. إِذَا دَعَا الرَّجُلُ امْرَأَتَهُ إِلَى فِرَاشِهِ فَأَبَتْ، فَبَاتَ غَضْبَانَ عَلَيْهَا، لَعَنَتْهَا الْمَلَائِكَةُ حَتَّى تُصْبِحَ. “When a man calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, so he spends the night angry with her, the angels curse her until morning.” The second form is less famous but earlier in physical attestation and simpler in shape. The woman is the grammatical subject. She abandons the husband’s bed. The angels curse until she returns. إِذَا بَاتَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ هَاجِرَةً لِفِرَاشِ زَوْجِهَا، لَعَنَتْهَا الْمَلَائِكَةُ حَتَّى تَرْجِعَ. “When a woman spends the night abandoning her husband’s bed, the angels curse her until she returns.” There are variations inside each family. Some Qatādah lines say “until morning,” some say “until she returns,” and one preserves a bare maxim with no summons, no anger, and no time-limit: “A woman does not abandon her husband’s bed except that the angels of God curse her.” But the two basic forms are stable enough to analyze. The Qatādah form is broad, aphoristic, and woman-focused. The al-Aʿmash form is narrower, legal-casuistic, and husband-focused. What ICMA can and cannot prove Isnād-cum-matn analysis does not begin by asking whether a transmitter could have met another transmitter. That is only a background condition. A man may have met his teacher and still not have heard a particular report from him. The real question is whether the report is independently controlled above the common link. A common link is the transmitter at whose level the report begins to spread through multiple students. If several independent students transmit a report from Qatādah, then Qatādah is recoverable as the point from which that version proliferated. But if the chain above Qatādah is only Qatādah → Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah, with no other student of Zurārah transmitting the same report, then Zurārah is not independently controlled for this report. His general reliability and his general possibility of hearing from Abū Hurayrah do not prove that this specific hadith came from him. The same rule applies to al-Aʿmash. Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī was a real transmitter from Abū Hurayrah. al-Aʿmash really did transmit from Abū Ḥāzim. But if every early Abū Ḥāzim version of this report passes through al-Aʿmash, then Abū Ḥāzim is not an independent control for this report. The report is recoverable at al-Aʿmash, not securely above him. This is the central point. The issue is not whether the upper links are **possible**. They are possible. The issue is whether they are **proved for this specific report**. They are not. Method note: Classical hadith criticism often treats the general possibility of hearing, narrator reliability, and canonical acceptance as sufficient for accepting a report. ICMA asks a different historical question. It asks where the report first becomes visible in a branching transmission network and whether the pre-branching strand is independently controlled. The isnād diagram The two bundles can be drawn very simply. They both end at Abū Hurayrah, but each reaches him through a different uncontrolled Successor. The real proliferation occurs lower, at Qatādah and al-Aʿmash. Two apparent Abū Hurayrah routes, two real common-link formulations Baṣra · Cluster B Abū Hurayrah single strand · uncontrolled Zurārah b. Awfā single strand · no non-Qatādah control QATĀDAH b. Diʿāmah common link Shuʿbah Hammām Ṭayālisī · Aḥmad · Dārimī · Bukhārī · Muslim · Nasāʾī · Bayhaqī “A woman abandons her husband’s bed … until she returns.” Kūfa · Cluster A Abū Hurayrah single strand · uncontrolled Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī single strand · no non-al-Aʿmash control AL-AʿMASH common link Abū Muʿāwiyah Wakīʿ Jarīr Abū ʿAwānah Ibn Numayr Shuʿbah Ibn Abī Shaybah · Ibn Rāhawayh · Aḥmad · Bukhārī · Muslim · Abū Dāwūd · Nasāʾī “A man calls his wife … she refuses … he sleeps angry … until morning.” The diagram does not deny that Zurārah or Abū Ḥāzim could transmit from Abū Hurayrah. It shows that, for this specific report, neither upper strand is independently controlled. The recoverable transmission begins at Qatādah and al-Aʿmash. The variant corpus in brief A corpus search of 1,221 hadith collections, about 1.33 million records, and twenty rijāl and ʿilal works produced 194 raw matches for the curse motif, using normalized searches around “angels,” “curse,” “bed,” “abandoning,” and “a man calls his wife.” The analysis below is based on the early and primary witnesses, especially collectors up to Bayhaqī.[^1] The Qatādah bundle is the earlier recoverable family. Its earliest physical witness is al-Ṭayālisī, who gives the chain Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī → Shuʿbah → Qatādah → Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah. Aḥmad preserves multiple lines through Shuʿbah and Hammām. Dārimī places it under the husband’s right over the wife. Bukhārī and Muslim also preserve the Qatādah form, though Muslim contains a line with “until morning” beside the more native “until she returns.”[^2] The al-Aʿmash bundle appears in Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn Rāhawayh, Aḥmad, Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān, and Bayhaqī. Its partial common links include Abū Muʿāwiyah, Wakīʿ, Jarīr, Abū ʿAwānah, Ibn Numayr, ʿAlī b. Mushir, and Shuʿbah through Sulaymān, which is al-Aʿmash. This is a strong common-link bundle below al-Aʿmash, but above al-Aʿmash the report is only al-Aʿmash → Abū Ḥāzim → Abū Hurayrah.[^3] The distribution is therefore not: Abū Hurayrah taught the same hadith independently to Zurārah and Abū Ḥāzim. It is more accurately: Qatādah and al-Aʿmash each produced recoverable common-link formulations of the same marital-obedience threat motif and each attached it to Abū Hurayrah through a plausible but uncontrolled Successor. The matn tells the story The two clusters are not the same wording randomly paraphrased. They are two different legal shapes. | Feature | Qatādah / Zurārah bundle | al-Aʿmash / Abū Ḥāzim bundle | |---|---:|---:| | Woman is the grammatical subject | Yes | No | | Husband is the grammatical subject | No | Yes | | “Abandoning / migrating from the husband’s bed” | Yes | No | | Husband summons the wife to bed | No | Yes | | Wife explicitly refuses | No | Yes | | Husband sleeps angry or displeased | No | Yes | | Curse ends “until she returns” | Dominant | No | | Curse ends “until morning” | Minority / contamination | Dominant | | Bare maxim form | Yes, through Hammām | No | The Qatādah form sounds like a moral warning: if she abandons the bed, the angels curse until she returns. The al-Aʿmash form sounds like a legal case: if he summons, she refuses, and he sleeps angry, then the curse lasts until morning. The direction of development is not difficult to see. A broad warning can easily be narrowed into a legal scenario. A fully casuistic scenario is less likely to generate the shorter maxim. The most primitive-looking form is the Hammām line from Qatādah: لاَ تَهْجُرُ امْرَأَةٌ فِرَاشَ زَوْجِهَا إِلاَّ لَعَنَتْهَا مَلاَئِكَةُ اللهِ. “No woman abandons her husband’s bed except that the angels of God curse her.” This is not yet the fully developed Bukhārī/Muslim form of the husband calling and the wife refusing. It is a short threat formula. That matters because short legal-moral maxims are exactly the kind of material that could be “propheticized” in early legal discourse. The upper links fail the control test This is the decisive point. Zurārah b. Awfā is not an unknown man. He is a Baṣran qāḍī and a plausible transmitter from Abū Hurayrah. But for this report, a scan of the corpus found no non-Qatādah student of Zurārah transmitting the bed-curse hadith. In the report corpus, the Zurārah-route matches are overwhelmingly through Qatādah, and the apparent exceptions are late compilations re-citing Bukhārī and Muslim rather than independent early lines.[^4] Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī is also not an unknown man. He is a real Kūfan transmitter from Abū Hurayrah, and al-Aʿmash is known to transmit from him. But for this report, every early Abū Ḥāzim line passes through al-Aʿmash. No non-al-Aʿmash student of Abū Ḥāzim preserves the report in an early source.[^5] That silence is not a small detail. Both Successors had other students. | Successor | Other well-attested students | Who carries this report? | |---|---|---| | Zurārah b. Awfā | Bahz b. Ḥakīm, ʿAwf al-Aʿrābī, ʿAbdallāh b. ʿUbayd, al-Mulaykī, others | Qatādah only | | Abū Ḥāzim al-Ashjaʿī | Yazīd b. Kaysān, Manṣūr b. al-Muʿtamir, Abū Mālik al-Ashjaʿī, others | al-Aʿmash only | If the report had genuinely belonged to Zurārah as a known Abū Hurayrah teaching, we would expect at least one other Zurārah student to preserve it. If it had genuinely belonged to Abū Ḥāzim as a known Abū Hurayrah teaching, we would expect at least one other Abū Ḥāzim student to preserve it. Instead, each report appears only through the common link who made it proliferate. This is what I mean by **false independence at the Companion level**. The two reports both end at Abū Hurayrah, but that does not prove two independent Abū Hurayrah transmissions. It proves two common-link formations attached to Abū Hurayrah. Why Qatādah is the likeliest origin point The strongest scenario is that the Qatādah version is the earliest recoverable form. That does not mean we can prove Qatādah sat down and consciously forged it. The historical claim should be more careful. The report cannot be shown to predate Qatādah, and Qatādah’s legal-exegetical environment gives us the most natural reason for the report to exist. The key background is Q. 4:34. This verse supplied early exegetes with a legal grammar of male authority, female obedience, nushūz, admonition, bed-separation, and discipline. Qatādah’s preserved tafsīr of the verse is especially important. In ʿAbd al-Razzāq’s Tafsīr, Maʿmar transmits from Qatādah that a man struck his wife. She came to the Prophet. The Prophet wanted retaliation from him, but then the verse “Men are qawwāmūn over women” was revealed.[^6] عَبْدُ الرَّزَّاقِ قَالَ: أَنَا مَعْمَرٌ، عَنْ قَتَادَةَ، قَالَ: صَكَّ رَجُلٌ امْرَأَتَهُ، فَأَتَتِ النَّبِيَّ، فَأَرَادَ أَنْ يُقِيدَهَا مِنْهُ، فَأَنْزَلَ اللهُ تَعَالَى: الرِّجَالُ قَوَّامُونَ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ. ʿAbd al-Razzāq said: Maʿmar informed us from Qatādah: A man struck his wife, so she came to the Prophet. He wanted to exact retaliation for her against him, but God revealed: “Men are qawwāmūn over women.” This is not a neutral explanation of marriage. In Qatādah’s version, the verse enters the story precisely to block retaliation against a husband and to establish male authority as the controlling rule. In the same passage, Qatādah explains “qānitāt” as “obedient.” Ṭabarī preserves the fuller wording: “obedient to God and to their husbands.”[^7] عَنْ قَتَادَةَ فِي قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: قَانِتَاتٌ، قَالَ: مُطِيعَاتٌ. وَفِي رِوَايَةِ الطَّبَرِيِّ: أَيْ مُطِيعَاتٌ لِلَّهِ وَلِأَزْوَاجِهِنَّ. From Qatādah concerning “qānitāt”: he said, “obedient.” In Ṭabarī’s version: “obedient to God and to their husbands.” Then Qatādah explains the disciplinary sequence. If the husband fears nushūz, he admonishes her. If she accepts, that ends the matter. If not, he abandons her bed. If she accepts, that ends the matter. If not, he strikes her with a non-severe beating.[^8] إِذَا خَافَ نُشُوزَهَا وَعَظَهَا، فَإِنْ أَقْبَلَتْ وَإِلَّا هَجَرَ مَضْجَعَهَا، فَإِنْ أَقْبَلَتْ وَإِلَّا ضَرَبَهَا ضَرْبًا غَيْرَ مُبَرِّحٍ. وَفِي رِوَايَةٍ أُخْرَى عَنْ قَتَادَةَ: تَبْدَأُ يَا ابْنَ آدَمَ فَتَعِظُهَا، فَإِنْ أَبَتْ عَلَيْكَ فَاهْجُرْهَا، يَعْنِي بِهِ: فِرَاشَهَا. “If he fears her nushūz, he admonishes her. If she accepts, then fine; otherwise he abandons her bed. If she accepts, then fine; otherwise he strikes her with a non-severe beating.” In another Qatādah version: “You begin, son of Adam, by admonishing her. If she refuses you, then abandon her, meaning: her bed.” Now compare that exegetical logic to the Qatādah hadith form: Q. 4:34 in Qatādah’s tafsīr female nushūz → admonition → bed/firāsh discipline → return/obedience Qatādah’s hadith form woman abandons husband’s bed → angels curse her → until she returns The conceptual fit is exact. The hadith does not need to begin as a remembered saying from the Prophet. It reads naturally as a propheticized warning built from the Q. 4:34 exegetical-legal world. Qatādah’s tafsīr gives the motive profile: male authority, female obedience, bed-abandonment, and return to compliance. There is also an important non-Qatādah control. Mujāhid, in Ibn Abī Ḥātim’s Tafsīr, explains Q. 4:34 in terms very close to the hadith’s logic: if a woman commits nushūz away from her husband’s bed, he tells her, “Fear God and return to your bed; this is the admonition.”[^9] عَنْ مُجَاهِدٍ: فَعِظُوهُنَّ، قَالَ: إِذَا نَشَزَتِ الْمَرْأَةُ عَنْ فِرَاشِ زَوْجِهَا، فَإِنَّهُ يَقُولُ لَهَا: اتَّقِي اللهَ وَارْجِعِي إِلَى فِرَاشِكِ، وَهَذِهِ الْمَوْعِظَةُ. From Mujāhid concerning “admonish them”: “If the woman commits nushūz away from her husband’s bed, he says to her: Fear God and return to your bed. This is the admonition.” This is extremely important. It shows that the idea did not need the hadith in order to exist. The exegetical maxim was already there: wife, nushūz, husband’s bed, admonition, return. The hadith intensifies the same idea by adding angels and curse. That is why the Qatādah form is best explained as a **propheticized tarhīb**: a warning formula that attaches divine threat to a legal-exegetical norm. Why Zurārah is probably not the motive source Zurārah b. Awfā should not be made the villain of the argument. A scan of his wider transmission profile does not show him as a specialist in reports that elevate men over women. His preserved material is dominated by prayer, Qurʾān, night worship, moral reports, legal cases, and devotional material. The gender-control theme does not appear as his clear personal signature. That matters because the best historical explanation should locate motive where the evidence locates it. For this report, the motive does not appear clearly at Zurārah’s level. It appears at Qatādah’s level. Qatādah is the recoverable common link, and Qatādah’s tafsīr of Q. 4:34 supplies the full legal grammar of the report. So the argument should not be: Zurārah invented an anti-woman report. It should be: Qatādah, or the Basran legal-exegetical environment visible through Qatādah, propheticized a Q. 4:34 marital-obedience maxim and routed it through a plausible Zurārah → Abū Hurayrah strand. This distinction keeps the case precise. It does not overstate what we can prove. al-Aʿmash and the problem of false independence The al-Aʿmash bundle is not the earliest form. It is more developed. It supplies the details that a jurist would want: the husband initiates, the wife refuses, the husband sleeps angry, and the curse lasts until morning. It transforms a broad warning into a more actionable legal scenario. One could argue that al-Aʿmash independently formulated a Kūfan version of the same Q. 4:34 idea. That is possible. But al-Aʿmash should not be treated as a neutral transmitter in this dossier. There is a prior pattern problem. In the bewitchment dossier, al-Aʿmash appears in the same kind of structural role. A report centered elsewhere around Hishām b. ʿUrwah appears through a Kūfan al-Aʿmash route that lacks Hishām in the isnād while preserving the same narrative world. The earlier analysis argued that the most plausible explanation is not independent origin, but source-obscuring or route substitution in a politically charged Kufan environment.[^10] In an unpublished Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī study, the same structural tendency appears again. The study argues that al-Aʿmash produced a Kūfan cluster that reproduces the rhetorical architecture of an earlier al-Shaʿbī construction while changing the authority structure, contents, and polemical function. The point is not that the Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī case proves this hadith by itself. The point is that al-Aʿmash repeatedly appears as a common-link reformulator whose versions can look independent in isnād while being structurally dependent in matn architecture.[^11] That prior pattern changes how we judge the al-Aʿmash form here. The standalone evidence proves only that al-Aʿmash is the common link of the Kūfan version. The wider pattern makes genuine independence less attractive. The al-Aʿmash version preserves the same core threat as Qatādah’s earlier Baṣran form but recasts it into a sharper legal case and attaches it to a different plausible Abū Hurayrah Successor, Abū Ḥāzim. This is exactly how false independence works. The route is believable because Abū Ḥāzim really can transmit from Abū Hurayrah. But believability is not proof. A successful rerouted isnād normally uses plausible links. Careful claim: I am not claiming that this dossier alone proves al-Aʿmash stole Qatādah’s wording. The stronger claim is that al-Aʿmash’s bundle should be treated as suspect independence. It is a second common-link formulation, not independent proof that the report reaches Abū Hurayrah. What about al-Aʿmash hearing from Abū Ḥāzim? This point needs correction from some earlier polemical treatments. al-Aʿmash did transmit from Abū Ḥāzim in general, and direct-hearing language exists in other reports. Therefore, the argument should not rest on the claim that al-Aʿmash could not have heard from Abū Ḥāzim at all.[^12] The weak link is more specific. For **this report**, Abū Ḥāzim is uncontrolled. His other students do not preserve it. The only early route through him is al-Aʿmash. So the chain does not prove Abū Ḥāzim taught this report from Abū Hurayrah. It proves al-Aʿmash taught a report and placed it through Abū Ḥāzim to Abū Hurayrah. This is an important difference. Classical isnād criticism often asks: could al-Aʿmash have heard from Abū Ḥāzim? ICMA asks: does any independent Abū Ḥāzim student transmit this report? The answer, so far, is no. The legal setting: husband-rights literature By the time the report enters legal collections, it is already being read as a husband-rights text. Dārimī places the Qatādah form under a chapter on the husband’s right over the woman. Abū Dāwūd places the al-Aʿmash form under the same kind of chapter. Ibn Abī Shaybah places the al-Aʿmash report in a dense legal-ethical environment with reports about the wife being commanded to observe the husband’s right, women hypothetically prostrating to husbands, a wife coming to the husband even if at the oven, and extreme statements about never fully repaying the husband’s right.[^13] That environment does not prove where the report began, but it shows why it survived. It was useful. It gave jurists and preachers a Prophetic threat formula for enforcing a one-sided marital duty. The Q. 4:34 exegetical logic supplied the legal grammar. The hadith supplied the divine terror. Later tafsīr also recognizes the fit. Suyūṭī places the al-Aʿmash/Bukhārī-Muslim version directly inside discussion of Q. 4:34.[^14] That is exactly where the report belongs conceptually. The false companion-level support Bazzār notes that similar wording was also narrated from Zayd b. Arqam and Ibn Abī Awfā.[^15] This sounds, at first, like broader Companion support. But in the corpus search, those non-Abū Hurayrah versions do not appear in the major early core collections as independent controls. They surface in peripheral or later works. They are better understood as **deep dives**: later Companion-level strands that emerge after the report is already circulating. Deep dives do not independently prove an early Companion origin. They often show the opposite. Once a report becomes useful, it can acquire additional Companion routes. That creates the appearance of wider attestation while leaving the earliest recoverable common links unchanged. So who fabricated it? The clean answer is: we cannot prove a personal confession, so we should not pretend to have one. The better historical language is **propheticization**, **common-link formulation**, and **false independence**. Still, if we ask where the likeliest origin lies, the answer is Qatādah’s Basran environment. The Qatādah form is earlier, simpler, closer to the non-prophetic Q. 4:34 exegetical idea, and recoverable before the al-Aʿmash form. It is therefore the best candidate for the first propheticized version. al-Aʿmash then represents a second-stage problem. His version may be an independent Kūfan propheticization of the same Q. 4:34 motif, but his prior pattern makes route-rerouting or common-link reformulation especially plausible. The al-Aʿmash form is not proof of a second Abū Hurayrah transmission. It is proof of a second common-link formulation. The final reconstruction 1 Q. 4:34 exegetical world: male authority, female obedience, nushūz, bed/firāsh, admonition, return. 2 Non-prophetic legal maxim: if a woman leaves the husband’s bed, she is admonished and told to return. 3 Qatādah’s Baṣran formulation: the maxim becomes a Prophetic tarhīb report: angels curse her until she returns. 4 al-Aʿmash’s Kūfan formulation: the broad warning becomes a legal case: the husband calls, she refuses, he sleeps angry, angels curse until morning. 5 Canonical reception: Bukhārī and Muslim preserve both families, making the report classically ṣaḥīḥ while leaving its historical origin above the common links unproven. The report is therefore classically strong but historically weak above the common links. That distinction is essential. A classical scholar may say the report is ṣaḥīḥ because Bukhārī and Muslim transmit it through acceptable men. An ICMA analysis asks a different question: can the report be shown to predate Qatādah or al-Aʿmash? At present, the answer is no. Verdict The hadith is best understood as a first-/second-century legal-exegetical warning projected onto the Prophet. The earliest recoverable version is Qatādah’s Baṣran form. Its content fits his Q. 4:34 tafsīr almost too well: men’s authority, women’s obedience, nushūz, bed-abandonment, and return. The report turns that framework into a divine threat. The al-Aʿmash version is a later or secondary Kūfan formulation. It is not independent proof of Abū Hurayrah’s teaching. It is a second common-link bundle through an uncontrolled Abū Ḥāzim strand, produced by a transmitter who elsewhere appears capable of creating independent-looking routes for inherited report-architecture. So the strongest conclusion is not that one can name the exact moment of forgery. It is that the report **cannot be shown to come from the Prophet**, cannot be shown to come from Abū Hurayrah, and is better explained as a propheticized marital-obedience maxim from the early legal-exegetical tradition. The angels in this hadith are not evidence of heaven speaking. They are evidence of law learning how to speak with heaven’s voice. --- Notes [^1]: The corpus report used for this article searched 1,221 locally extracted Shamela hadith collections, approximately 1.33 million records, plus twenty rijāl and ʿilal works, for normalized combinations of ملائكة, لعن, فراش, هاجرة, and دعا امرأته. sections.text: The most ubiquitous defense of the Sunni hadith corpus is a simple, rhetorical question: *"How would you know how to pray without hadith?"* Traditionalists present early collections, such as the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* of Imam Malik, as essential, step-by-step instructional manuals without which the Islamic Contact Prayers (*Ṣalāh*) would have been lost. However, a critical analysis of these early narrations reveals the exact opposite. The hadith collections do not provide a comprehensive instructional framework. Instead, they presuppose a communal, living familiarity with *Ṣalāh*—an inherited Abrahamic tradition that existed long before the compilers were even born. When hadith narrators did attempt to document the specifics of the prayer, they introduced devastating contradictions, admitted to unauthorized political innovations, and documented the loss of original practices. We will use Imam Malik's *Muwaṭṭaʾ* (the earliest major Sunni compilation) as a case study to dismantle the myth that "hadith teach us how to pray." ## The *Muwaṭṭaʾ* is Not a Prayer Manual The *Muwaṭṭaʾ* was compiled roughly 160 years after the Prophet's death. This massive chronological gap immediately raises a logical problem: How did Muslims pray during those 160 years before this "instruction manual" was written? Furthermore, the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* is barely even a record of the Prophet's words. **The Contents of the Muwaṭṭaʾ:** According to Dr. Jonathan Brown in Hadith: Muhammad’s Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World , the famous Andalusian transmission of the Muwaṭṭaʾ contains 1,720 reports. Of these, only **527 are Prophetic hadiths**. The rest are composed of 613 statements of the Companions, 285 from Successors, and the remainder are Malik’s own personal opinions. If we look at the 61 chapters of the *Muwaṭṭaʾ*, only two chapters ("The Times of Prayer" and "Prayer") deal with the daily obligatory mechanics. And within those chapters, you will not find a single, unified, step-by-step guide from *Takbīr* to *Taslīm*. Instead, you find a chaotic assembly of contradictory rulings. ## Contradictions in the "Manual" If the hadith corpus is supposed to perfectly preserve the exact physical and verbal mechanics of the Prophet's prayer, the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* fails this test dramatically. ### Contradiction 1: When to Pray Asr? Early Asr (Before Decline) Late Asr (After Decline) Hadith 2: ʿĀʾisha reports praying Asr while sunlight was still pouring into her room, before the sun became visible (meaning the sun was still high in the sky). Hadith 9: Abu Hurayra says Asr is "When your shadow is twice the length of your height," a sign that the sun has passed its zenith and is heading towards sunset. ### Contradiction 2: Should You Rush to the Mosque? Rushing is Permitted Rushing is Forbidden Hadith 10: Ibn ʿUmar heard the iqāma while he was in Baqi, so he increased his pace of walking to the mosque. Hadith 4: Abu Hurayra reports the Prophet said, "When the iqāma is called for prayer, do not come to it running, but come with calmness. " ### Contradiction 3: What Do We Say in Tashahhud? The *Tashahhud* (the sitting testimony) is a fundamental pillar of the Sunni prayer. Yet, the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* records three entirely different versions from three major Companions (Book 3, Hadiths 56, 57, 58). - **ʿUmar's Version:** *"At-tahiyatu lillah, az-zakiyatu lillah, at-tayibatu wa's-salawatu lillah..."* - **Ibn ʿUmar's Version:** Starts with *"Bismillah"* (which his father didn't do) and rearranges the order of the praises. - **ʿĀʾisha's Version:** Radically alters the testimony of faith, adding *"wahdahu la sharika lah"* (alone without partner) and ends with *"As-salamu alaykum"*. If the Prophet taught a single, strict, ritualistic recitation for the *Tashahhud*, why did his closest companions disagree on the exact wording, the order of praises, and the testimony of faith itself? ## Admitted Innovations and Losses Perhaps the most damaging evidence against using hadith as a divine prayer manual is that the *Muwaṭṭaʾ* openly admits that the early Caliphs altered the ritual. **Adding to the Adhan:** > Malik heard that the muadhdhin came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to call him to the fajr prayer and found him sleeping, so he said, "Prayer is better than sleep," and **ʿUmar ordered him to put that in the adhan for fajr.** (Book 3, Hadith 8) **Skipping Quranic Verses:** > Anas ibn Malik said, "I stood behind Abu Bakr and ʿUmar and ʿUthman and **none of them used to recite 'In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate' [Bismillah]** when they began the prayer." (Book 3, Hadith 31) If the first three Caliphs of Sunnism skipped the very first verse of Al-Fātiḥah (which is universally considered obligatory today), and the second Caliph arbitrarily added words to the Adhan because he was woken from a nap, how can traditionalists claim the hadith perfectly preserved the Prophet's exact prayer? ## The Abrahamic Reality The reality is simple: Muslims do not learn to pray from reading Sahih al-Bukhari or the *Muwaṭṭaʾ*. They learn by standing next to their parents, who learned from their parents, in a continuous living tradition. This tradition did not start with Muhammad. It started with Abraham. The Quran explicitly states that the Children of Israel were commanded to observe the exact same Contact Prayers (*Ṣalāh*): However, over centuries, previous nations corrupted the ritual: Muhammad's mission was not to invent a new ritual prayer to be documented in Abbasid textbooks 200 years later. His mission was to follow the purified religion of Abraham, scrubbing away the polytheistic innovations that the Quraysh had introduced over the centuries. The claim that "we need hadith to know how to pray" is a historical and theological fallacy. The earliest hadith collections fail as instructional manuals, contradicting each other on timings, mechanics, and recitations, while openly documenting the Caliphs' unauthorized alterations to the ritual. The Ṣalāh is a living, continuous Abrahamic tradition, passed down physically through generations, and validated by the Quran. The hadith corpus did not preserve the prayer—in many cases, it merely documented its early corruption.

The report under review tells a woman to answer her husband’s sexual summons even if she is occupied at the oven. Later polemical and legal uses of the report often treat it as a clean prophetic command, but the transmission does not behave like a broad communal memory. It behaves like a narrow Yamāmī family report that becomes stronger in social effect as it passes through later collectors and jurists. The tannūr report should not be treated as an independent prophetic rule about marital access. Its recoverable lines converge on Qays b. Ṭalq from his father, and the strongest branch places the coercive wording in a path whose decisive lower link, Qays, was disputed by major critics. The matn also changes in a revealing direction: one branch says the husband should go to his wife, while the more cited branch makes the wife come or respond to him. ## The report in question The phrase “ḥasan gharīb” already tells the reader that this is not a mass-transmitted marital ethic. It is a report with a narrow route that later received legal and moral weight far beyond the strength of its historical base. The issue is not that every transmitter above Qays is automatically rejected. The issue is that the report’s moral burden rests on a disputed individual link, and the matn itself shows pressure toward a more coercive reading. ## The variants do not create independent corroboration Source Route Wording Critical Value al-Tirmidhī 1160 Hannād → Mulāzim → ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْتَأْتِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ عَلَى التَّنُّورِ The woman is commanded to come to him. al-Tirmidhī calls the report ḥasan gharīb . Ibn Ḥibbān / al-Ṭabarānī Mulāzim → ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْتُجِبْهُ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ عَلَى التَّنُّورِ The wording shifts from “let her come” to “let her respond,” but the same Qays-centered structure remains. Aḥmad / al-Ṭabarānī Muḥammad b. Jābir → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْيَأْتِهَا وَلَوْ كَانَتْ عَلَى تَنُّورٍ The subject changes: the husband should go to her. This branch runs through Muḥammad b. Jābir, who is weaker than the Mulāzim route. The table matters because a list of six citations can look like six independent witnesses. The transmission map shows something more limited. The major printed sources are mostly different exits from the same narrow corridor. Several collectors preserve the report, but the report keeps returning to Qays b. Ṭalq from his father. A repeated report is not automatically a multiplied report. The report has two social forms. In the Muḥammad b. Jābir branch, the husband is the grammatical subject: if he wants something from his wife, “let him go to her.” In the Mulāzim branch, the wife becomes the obligated subject: if he calls her, “let her come” or “let her respond.” Even if one does not accuse a specific narrator of intentional fabrication, the variant movement shows how a private desire can be transformed into a command placed upon the woman. ## Qays b. Ṭalq is the pressure point The criticism should focus where the chain actually narrows. Mulāzim b. ʿAmr and ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr are generally treated positively in the rijāl material. The problem is Qays b. Ṭalq. He is not a companion, and the report’s authority depends on accepting his claim from his father. Sunni critics themselves disagreed over whether he could carry this kind of legal burden. Authority Assessment Implication for This Report al-Tirmidhī Calls the tannūr report ḥasan gharīb . Useful for showing circulation, but the label admits narrowness. al-Shāfiʿī Reportedly said he did not find anyone who knew Qays in a way that would let him accept his report. A major early jurist did not regard Qays as a secure proof-carrier. Abū Ḥātim and Abū Zurʿa Reportedly said Qays was not someone by whom proof is established. The criticism targets the exact point on which the tannūr report depends. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal Reportedly said others were firmer than him. Aḥmad does not erase Qays, but he does not make him a strong independent legal pillar either. al-Dāraquṭnī Reportedly said Qays was “not strong.” This makes the report a fragile basis for a coercive marital doctrine. al-ʿIjlī, Ibn Ḥibbān, and some reports from Ibn Maʿīn More favorable assessments are preserved. The narrator is disputed, which is exactly the point: a disputed transmitter should not be used to impose an abusive rule. This is where the popular apologetic response often becomes circular. The report is treated as acceptable because later compilers cited it, and those citations are then treated as proof that the report should shape marriage ethics. The actual rijāl profile is mixed. Once the report is placed beside the Qurʾān’s standard for marriage, the burden of proof becomes even heavier. ## The Qurʾānic marital standard is not coercion The Qurʾān speaks about marriage in terms of kindness, mutual protection, and affection. It does not frame a wife as an instrument obligated to abandon her immediate circumstance whenever the husband expresses desire. A report that can be used to suspend a woman’s agency in the most intimate part of marriage needs extremely strong evidence. This report has the opposite profile: a narrow transmission, a disputed common link, variant wording, and a social afterlife that presses the wife into unilateral availability. This case does not require the claim that Qays sat down and consciously invented the report for personal lust. The more careful conclusion is that the earliest recoverable transmission already sits in a narrow patriarchal corridor, and the stronger later wording is the one that intensifies the wife’s obligation. Hadith criticism should be able to notice that pattern instead of hiding it behind the prestige of later compilation. ## Why this became useful A short, memorable report like this is convenient because it turns a social expectation into a prophetic sentence. It removes negotiation from marriage, treats male desire as legally urgent, and makes refusal appear religiously suspect. That is why its transmission history matters. The report did not merely preserve a sentence; it helped manufacture a moral atmosphere in which one spouse’s demand could be sacralized over the other spouse’s dignity. The Qurʾān warns that false religious speech becomes attractive precisely because it is useful to people who want authority. That warning applies especially when a report gives one group power over another. The tannūr report should be rejected as a basis for coercive marital doctrine. Its chains do not provide broad independent attestation, its decisive link is disputed, and its matn variants show a movement toward placing the burden on the wife. Whatever one makes of Qays b. Ṭalq personally, the report is too narrow and too morally dangerous to override the Qurʾān’s language of kindness, mercy, and mutual garment-like protection. ## Sources Consulted Source Use in This Article Jāmiʿ al-Tirmidhī 1160 Primary wording and al-Tirmidhī’s grading: https://www.islamweb.net/ar/library/content/2/1080/ Aḥmad and al-Ṭabarānī route through Muḥammad b. Jābir Secondary wording where the husband is the subject: https://dorar.net/h/5Jm3tJuq?osoul=1 Qays b. Ṭalq rijāl profile Mixed evaluations, including al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥātim, Aḥmad, al-Dāraquṭnī, and more favorable assessments: https://shamela.ws/narrator/5250 Mulāzim b. ʿAmr and ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr Used to distinguish the stronger upper branch from the Qays problem: https://muslimscholars.info/manage.php?ID=20743&submit=scholar and https://beta.sunnah.com/narrator/4737 Qurʾān 4:19; 30:21; 2:187; 6:112-113 Qurʾānic moral standard for marriage and warning against fabricated religious speech.

The report under review tells a woman to answer her husband’s sexual summons even if she is occupied at the oven. Later polemical and legal uses of the report often treat it as a clean prophetic command, but the transmission does not behave like a broad communal memory. It behaves like a narrow Yamāmī family report that becomes stronger in social effect as it passes through later collectors and jurists. The tannūr report should not be treated as an independent prophetic rule about marital access. Its recoverable lines converge on Qays b. Ṭalq from his father, and the strongest branch places the coercive wording in a path whose decisive lower link, Qays, was disputed by major critics. The matn also changes in a revealing direction: one branch says the husband should go to his wife, while the more cited branch makes the wife come or respond to him. The report in question The phrase “ḥasan gharīb” already tells the reader that this is not a mass-transmitted marital ethic. It is a report with a narrow route that later received legal and moral weight far beyond the strength of its historical base. The issue is not that every transmitter above Qays is automatically rejected. The issue is that the report’s moral burden rests on a disputed individual link, and the matn itself shows pressure toward a more coercive reading. The variants do not create independent corroboration Source Route Wording Critical Value al-Tirmidhī 1160 Hannād → Mulāzim → ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْتَأْتِهِ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ عَلَى التَّنُّورِ The woman is commanded to come to him. al-Tirmidhī calls the report ḥasan gharīb . Ibn Ḥibbān / al-Ṭabarānī Mulāzim → ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْتُجِبْهُ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ عَلَى التَّنُّورِ The wording shifts from “let her come” to “let her respond,” but the same Qays-centered structure remains. Aḥmad / al-Ṭabarānī Muḥammad b. Jābir → Qays → Ṭalq فَلْيَأْتِهَا وَلَوْ كَانَتْ عَلَى تَنُّورٍ The subject changes: the husband should go to her. This branch runs through Muḥammad b. Jābir, who is weaker than the Mulāzim route. The table matters because a list of six citations can look like six independent witnesses. The transmission map shows something more limited. The major printed sources are mostly different exits from the same narrow corridor. Several collectors preserve the report, but the report keeps returning to Qays b. Ṭalq from his father. A repeated report is not automatically a multiplied report. The report has two social forms. In the Muḥammad b. Jābir branch, the husband is the grammatical subject: if he wants something from his wife, “let him go to her.” In the Mulāzim branch, the wife becomes the obligated subject: if he calls her, “let her come” or “let her respond.” Even if one does not accuse a specific narrator of intentional fabrication, the variant movement shows how a private desire can be transformed into a command placed upon the woman. Qays b. Ṭalq is the pressure point The criticism should focus where the chain actually narrows. Mulāzim b. ʿAmr and ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr are generally treated positively in the rijāl material. The problem is Qays b. Ṭalq. He is not a companion, and the report’s authority depends on accepting his claim from his father. Sunni critics themselves disagreed over whether he could carry this kind of legal burden. Authority Assessment Implication for This Report al-Tirmidhī Calls the tannūr report ḥasan gharīb . Useful for showing circulation, but the label admits narrowness. al-Shāfiʿī Reportedly said he did not find anyone who knew Qays in a way that would let him accept his report. A major early jurist did not regard Qays as a secure proof-carrier. Abū Ḥātim and Abū Zurʿa Reportedly said Qays was not someone by whom proof is established. The criticism targets the exact point on which the tannūr report depends. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal Reportedly said others were firmer than him. Aḥmad does not erase Qays, but he does not make him a strong independent legal pillar either. al-Dāraquṭnī Reportedly said Qays was “not strong.” This makes the report a fragile basis for a coercive marital doctrine. al-ʿIjlī, Ibn Ḥibbān, and some reports from Ibn Maʿīn More favorable assessments are preserved. The narrator is disputed, which is exactly the point: a disputed transmitter should not be used to impose an abusive rule. This is where the popular apologetic response often becomes circular. The report is treated as acceptable because later compilers cited it, and those citations are then treated as proof that the report should shape marriage ethics. The actual rijāl profile is mixed. Once the report is placed beside the Qurʾān’s standard for marriage, the burden of proof becomes even heavier. The Qurʾānic marital standard is not coercion The Qurʾān speaks about marriage in terms of kindness, mutual protection, and affection. It does not frame a wife as an instrument obligated to abandon her immediate circumstance whenever the husband expresses desire. A report that can be used to suspend a woman’s agency in the most intimate part of marriage needs extremely strong evidence. This report has the opposite profile: a narrow transmission, a disputed common link, variant wording, and a social afterlife that presses the wife into unilateral availability. This case does not require the claim that Qays sat down and consciously invented the report for personal lust. The more careful conclusion is that the earliest recoverable transmission already sits in a narrow patriarchal corridor, and the stronger later wording is the one that intensifies the wife’s obligation. Hadith criticism should be able to notice that pattern instead of hiding it behind the prestige of later compilation. Why this became useful A short, memorable report like this is convenient because it turns a social expectation into a prophetic sentence. It removes negotiation from marriage, treats male desire as legally urgent, and makes refusal appear religiously suspect. That is why its transmission history matters. The report did not merely preserve a sentence; it helped manufacture a moral atmosphere in which one spouse’s demand could be sacralized over the other spouse’s dignity. The Qurʾān warns that false religious speech becomes attractive precisely because it is useful to people who want authority. That warning applies especially when a report gives one group power over another. The tannūr report should be rejected as a basis for coercive marital doctrine. Its chains do not provide broad independent attestation, its decisive link is disputed, and its matn variants show a movement toward placing the burden on the wife. Whatever one makes of Qays b. Ṭalq personally, the report is too narrow and too morally dangerous to override the Qurʾān’s language of kindness, mercy, and mutual garment-like protection. Jābir Secondary wording where the husband is the subject: https://dorar.net/h/5Jm3tJuq?osoul=1 Qays b. Ṭalq rijāl profile Mixed evaluations, including al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥātim, Aḥmad, al-Dāraquṭnī, and more favorable assessments: https://shamela.ws/narrator/5250 Mulāzim b. ʿAmr and ʿAbd Allāh b. Badr Used to distinguish the stronger upper branch from the Qays problem: https://muslimscholars.info/manage.php?ID=20743&submit=scholar and https://beta.sunnah.com/narrator/4737 Qurʾān 4:19; 30:21; 2:187; 6:112-113 Qurʾānic moral standard for marriage and warning against fabricated religious speech.

title: Exposing the False Use of
description: A transmission-critical study of two hadith clusters that turn the Qurʾānic category ummiyyūn into a doctrine of illiteracy.

/ ʿAffān', labelPos: 'right' }, { id: 'ahmad2', x: 650, y: 0, label: 'Aḥmad', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'above' } ]; { from: 'prophet', to: 'ubayy', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'prophet', to: 'hudhayfah', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'ubayy', to: 'zirr' }, { from: 'hudhayfah', to: 'zirr' }, { from: 'zirr', to: 'asim', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'asim', to: 'shayban' }, { from: 'shayban', to: 'hasanMusa' }, { from: 'hasanMusa', to: 'ahmadMani' }, { from: 'ahmadMani', to: 'tirmidhi' }, { from: 'asim', to: 'hammadSal' }, { from: 'hammadSal', to: 'abdSamad' }, { from: 'abdSamad', to: 'ahmad2' } ]; The word **ummiyyūn** is often translated as “illiterates,” and later hadith literature uses that meaning to build religious claims about the Prophet’s community. This article examines two hadith clusters where the term is made to mean a people who do not write, calculate, or read books. The first appears in the fasting material: “We are an ummī nation; we neither write nor calculate.” The second appears in the seven-aḥruf material: “I was sent to an ummī nation” made up of old men, women, children, and people who never read a book. The argument here is narrower than a general discussion of whether the Prophet could read or write. The Qurʾān uses **ummiyyūn** in contrast with scriptural communities, especially the People of the Book. These hadiths move the term into a different register: social illiteracy. That shift matters because it creates doctrines that the Qurʾān itself does not state. The fasting and seven-aḥruf reports do not simply translate a Qurʾānic word. They reframe it. In the Qurʾān, **ummiyyūn** functions primarily as a scriptural identity category, meaning those outside a prior scripture-bearing community or those without real knowledge of the Book. In these hadith clusters, the word is turned into a claim about the community’s inability to write, calculate, or read. The transmission maps show that this interpretive shift travels through identifiable narrow corridors. ## The Qurʾānic baseline: ummiyyūn against the People of the Book Before reading the hadiths, the Qurʾānic usage should be placed on the table. In 3:20, the Prophet is told to address “those given the Book” and “the ummiyyūn.” That pairing makes best sense as a contrast between scriptural communities and those outside them. The same contrast appears more explicitly in 3:75, where some among the People of the Book are described as saying they have no liability toward the **ummiyyūn**. Several translators render the term here as “Gentiles,” because the sentence is about how a scriptural community speaks about outsiders. The mission verse in Sūrat al-Jumuʿah also says the messenger was raised among the **ummiyyīn** and then immediately explains his work as reciting God’s verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom. The issue is scriptural instruction, not a census claim that the whole population could not decode letters. Qurʾān 2:78 uses **ummiyyūn** for people who do not truly know the Book except through wishful claims. That verse can be read as “unlettered” in the sense of unlearned in scripture, but it still does not require the meaning “biologically or socially unable to read and write.” It is about relation to the Book. The later hadiths examined below move beyond that and attach the word to writing, calculation, and the need for multiple recitation modes. ## Cluster One: “We are an ummī nation; we do not write or calculate” The important point is that this is not a weak report by later Sunni standards. It is canonically strong in the traditional system because it appears in Bukhārī and Muslim. The critique therefore has to be more precise. The report gives a legal reason for lunar practice: the community allegedly does not write or calculate. The word **ummiyyah** is no longer merely a Qurʾānic contrast with scripture-bearing peoples. It is now glossed by the report itself as **lā naktub wa-lā naḥsub**: we do not write and we do not calculate. Source Route Form of the Claim Why It Matters Bukhārī 1913 Ādam → Shuʿbah → al-Aswad → Saʿīd → Ibn ʿUmar إِنَّا أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيَّةٌ، لَا نَكْتُبُ وَلَا نَحْسُبُ The term is explicitly tied to non-writing and non-calculation. Muslim 1080 Ghundar / Ibn Mahdī → Shuʿbah or Sufyān → al-Aswad → Saʿīd → Ibn ʿUmar Same formula with gesture details about twenty-nine and thirty days. Multiple exits preserve the same al-Aswad–Saʿīd corridor. Abū Dāwūd / al-Nasāʾī / al-Bayhaqī Mostly through al-Aswad b. Qays from Saʿīd b. ʿAmr Minor ordering and gesture variations. The variants show circulation of a legal maxim, not independent Qurʾānic semantics. Aḥmad 6041-type path Hāshim → Isḥāq b. Saʿīd → his father → Ibn ʿUmar نَحْنُ أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيُّونَ لَا نَحْسُبُ وَلَا نَكْتُبُ A family route through Saʿīd’s house, not a new companion base. Classical commentators understood the phrase in exactly the way the hadith pushes them to understand it. Ibn Ḥajar’s discussion in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* treats “ummī” here as non-writing and non-calculation, including explanations that connect it to remaining upon the original state in which people were born. That confirms the point: this hadith became a proof-text for a social meaning of **ummī**, not merely a lexical translation. This report is often cited in debates over lunar calculation. The deeper linguistic issue is that a Qurʾānic identity term is made to carry a legal anthropology: the Prophet’s community supposedly does not write or calculate, so religious timekeeping should avoid calculation. Whether a jurist accepts or rejects astronomical calculation is a separate question. The hadith’s definition of **ummī** is the problem under review here. ## Cluster Two: “I was sent to an ummī nation” and the seven aḥruf The second cluster makes the semantic shift even more visible. Here the Prophet is made to say that he was sent to an **ummī** nation consisting of old men, old women, boys, girls, and people who have never read a book. Gabriel then answers that the Qurʾān was revealed in seven aḥruf. The logic depends on **ummī** meaning “unable to read,” because the report uses that alleged illiteracy to explain recitational accommodation. Source Companion Authority Shared Lower Corridor Critical Note al-Tirmidhī 2944 Ubayy b. Kaʿb ʿĀṣim → Zirr al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ and says it has other routes from Ubayy, but this cited form still runs through ʿĀṣim and Zirr. Aḥmad 23447 / 23398-type reports Ḥudhayfah Ḥammād → ʿĀṣim → Zirr The companion changes, but the lower transmitter pair remains the same. Ibn Ḥibbān and related listings Related seven-aḥruf material Often preserves the same explanation of an ummī audience. The motif circulates as an explanation for recitational plurality. The seven-aḥruf report has a more obvious motive than the fasting report because the explanation is built into the matn. The Prophet says he was sent to an **ummī** nation, and the examples immediately define that as people who would struggle with a written or fixed recitational form: elderly people, children, and someone who has never read a book. Gabriel’s answer then supplies seven aḥruf as a solution. If **ummiyyūn** means “Gentiles” or “non-scriptural people,” the list that follows becomes awkward. Being outside a previous scripture-bearing community does not make an elderly man, a woman, a child, or a man who never read a book require seven aḥruf. The report only works smoothly if **ummī** is already being read as illiterate or untrained in reading. That is why this hadith is valuable evidence for the later interpretive shift. ## ʿĀṣim is important, but the argument should stay disciplined The draft version of this article blamed ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd directly for fabricating the seven-aḥruf report. That is possible as a hypothesis, but it is stronger to state what the evidence can support. ʿĀṣim is a major Kūfan reciter and a central lower transmitter in these cited forms. He is praised in the rijāl literature, but he is also criticized for mistakes in ḥadīth. Ibn Saʿd reportedly called him trustworthy while saying he made many errors in his hadith, and other critics commented on his memory. That means the report’s seven-aḥruf explanation should be treated with caution. A reciter-linked Kūfan channel is not neutral evidence for why the Qurʾān allegedly came in seven aḥruf. It is exactly the type of channel in which one would expect later recitational theology to be explained, defended, and projected backward. Figure Evidence Interpretive Use ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd Major Kūfan reciter; praised by some critics but described by Ibn Saʿd as trustworthy with many hadith mistakes. He is not dismissed wholesale, but a recitational-theology report through him deserves scrutiny. Zirr b. Ḥubaysh Shared transmitter above ʿĀṣim in the Ubayy and Ḥudhayfah forms. The companion attribution varies while the lower explanatory corridor remains stable. al-Aswad b. Qays Central transmitter in the moon-sighting formula through Saʿīd b. ʿAmr from Ibn ʿUmar. The fasting cluster’s semantic move is tied to a narrow Kufan path. ## Epigraphy also weakens the “illiterate Arabia” assumption The hadith picture often depends on an older civilizational myth: pre-Islamic Arabia as overwhelmingly oral and textless. Modern Arabian epigraphy has complicated that picture. Ahmad al-Jallad’s work on Safaitic and other Ancient North Arabian inscriptions has emphasized the scale and variety of writing in pre-Islamic Arabia. The existence of tens of thousands of inscriptions does not prove that every Arab was literate, and it does not by itself prove the Prophet’s literacy. It does, however, make the blanket phrase “we do not write” historically suspicious when treated as a description of the whole community. Epigraphy does not turn every nomad into a scribe. It shows that writing was present, diverse, and culturally meaningful in parts of Arabia before Islam. That is enough to challenge a later religious slogan that makes non-writing part of the community’s identity. ## What the two clusters share Cluster Key Phrase Function of “Ummī” Resulting Doctrine Moon-sighting / fasting أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيَّةٌ، لَا نَكْتُبُ وَلَا نَحْسُبُ Ummī is defined by non-writing and non-calculation. Calculation is pushed aside in favor of visible lunar signs. Seven aḥruf أُمَّةٍ أُمِّيِّينَ ... وَالرَّجُلُ الَّذِي لَمْ يَقْرَأْ كِتَابًا قَطُّ Ummī is defined by inability or lack of reading practice. Multiple recitation modes are justified as accommodation for an allegedly unlettered audience. Qurʾānic usage الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ وَالْأُمِّيِّينَ Ummiyyūn are contrasted with scripture-bearing communities. The Prophet’s mission is framed as bringing scripture to a non-scriptural people. The pattern is clear. The Qurʾān uses **ummiyyūn** inside a scriptural map. The hadith clusters use the term to produce later legal and recitational doctrines. The reports are therefore not harmless translations. They are interpretive engines. The two hadith clusters should be treated as later interpretive uses of **ummiyyūn**, not as the Qurʾān’s own definition of the term. The fasting report turns the word into non-writing and non-calculation. The seven-aḥruf report turns it into lack of reading ability and then uses that meaning to justify recitational plurality. Both moves are traceable through narrow transmitter corridors, and both sit uneasily beside the Qurʾān’s scriptural contrast between the People of the Book and the ummiyyūn. ## Sources Consulted Source Use in This Article Qurʾān 3:20, 3:75, 62:2, 2:78 Baseline Qurʾānic usage of **ummiyyūn** in relation to scripture and the People of the Book. See also Quran.com 3:75, which renders the term as “Gentiles”: https://quran.com/en/ali-imran/75 Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1913 Primary moon-sighting wording and al-Aswad → Saʿīd → Ibn ʿUmar chain: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1913 Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1080 parallels Parallel transmission through al-Aswad b. This article examines two hadith clusters where the term is made to mean a people who do not write, calculate, or read books. The first appears in the fasting material: “We are an ummī nation; we neither write nor calculate.” The second appears in the seven-aḥruf material: “I was sent to an ummī nation” made up of old men, women, children, and people who never read a book. The argument here is narrower than a general discussion of whether the Prophet could read or write. The Qurʾān uses **ummiyyūn** in contrast with scriptural communities, especially the People of the Book. These hadiths move the term into a different register: social illiteracy. That shift matters because it creates doctrines that the Qurʾān itself does not state. The fasting and seven-aḥruf reports do not simply translate a Qurʾānic word. They reframe it. In the Qurʾān, **ummiyyūn** functions primarily as a scriptural identity category, meaning those outside a prior scripture-bearing community or those without real knowledge of the Book. In these hadith clusters, the word is turned into a claim about the community’s inability to write, calculate, or read. The transmission maps show that this interpretive shift travels through identifiable narrow corridors. The Qurʾānic baseline: ummiyyūn against the People of the Book Before reading the hadiths, the Qurʾānic usage should be placed on the table. In 3:20, the Prophet is told to address “those given the Book” and “the ummiyyūn.” That pairing makes best sense as a contrast between scriptural communities and those outside them. The same contrast appears more explicitly in 3:75, where some among the People of the Book are described as saying they have no liability toward the **ummiyyūn**. Several translators render the term here as “Gentiles,” because the sentence is about how a scriptural community speaks about outsiders. The mission verse in Sūrat al-Jumuʿah also says the messenger was raised among the **ummiyyīn** and then immediately explains his work as reciting God’s verses, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom. The issue is scriptural instruction, not a census claim that the whole population could not decode letters. Qurʾān 2:78 uses **ummiyyūn** for people who do not truly know the Book except through wishful claims. That verse can be read as “unlettered” in the sense of unlearned in scripture, but it still does not require the meaning “biologically or socially unable to read and write.” It is about relation to the Book. The later hadiths examined below move beyond that and attach the word to writing, calculation, and the need for multiple recitation modes. Cluster One: “We are an ummī nation; we do not write or calculate” The important point is that this is not a weak report by later Sunni standards. It is canonically strong in the traditional system because it appears in Bukhārī and Muslim. The critique therefore has to be more precise. The report gives a legal reason for lunar practice: the community allegedly does not write or calculate. The word **ummiyyah** is no longer merely a Qurʾānic contrast with scripture-bearing peoples. It is now glossed by the report itself as **lā naktub wa-lā naḥsub**: we do not write and we do not calculate. Source Route Form of the Claim Why It Matters Bukhārī 1913 Ādam → Shuʿbah → al-Aswad → Saʿīd → Ibn ʿUmar إِنَّا أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيَّةٌ، لَا نَكْتُبُ وَلَا نَحْسُبُ The term is explicitly tied to non-writing and non-calculation. Muslim 1080 Ghundar / Ibn Mahdī → Shuʿbah or Sufyān → al-Aswad → Saʿīd → Ibn ʿUmar Same formula with gesture details about twenty-nine and thirty days. Multiple exits preserve the same al-Aswad–Saʿīd corridor. Abū Dāwūd / al-Nasāʾī / al-Bayhaqī Mostly through al-Aswad b. Qays from Saʿīd b. ʿAmr Minor ordering and gesture variations. The variants show circulation of a legal maxim, not independent Qurʾānic semantics. Aḥmad 6041-type path Hāshim → Isḥāq b. Saʿīd → his father → Ibn ʿUmar نَحْنُ أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيُّونَ لَا نَحْسُبُ وَلَا نَكْتُبُ A family route through Saʿīd’s house, not a new companion base. Classical commentators understood the phrase in exactly the way the hadith pushes them to understand it. Ibn Ḥajar’s discussion in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* treats “ummī” here as non-writing and non-calculation, including explanations that connect it to remaining upon the original state in which people were born. That confirms the point: this hadith became a proof-text for a social meaning of **ummī**, not merely a lexical translation. This report is often cited in debates over lunar calculation. The deeper linguistic issue is that a Qurʾānic identity term is made to carry a legal anthropology: the Prophet’s community supposedly does not write or calculate, so religious timekeeping should avoid calculation. Whether a jurist accepts or rejects astronomical calculation is a separate question. The hadith’s definition of **ummī** is the problem under review here. Cluster Two: “I was sent to an ummī nation” and the seven aḥruf The second cluster makes the semantic shift even more visible. Here the Prophet is made to say that he was sent to an **ummī** nation consisting of old men, old women, boys, girls, and people who have never read a book. Gabriel then answers that the Qurʾān was revealed in seven aḥruf. The logic depends on **ummī** meaning “unable to read,” because the report uses that alleged illiteracy to explain recitational accommodation. Source Companion Authority Shared Lower Corridor Critical Note al-Tirmidhī 2944 Ubayy b. Kaʿb ʿĀṣim → Zirr al-Tirmidhī grades it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ and says it has other routes from Ubayy, but this cited form still runs through ʿĀṣim and Zirr. Aḥmad 23447 / 23398-type reports Ḥudhayfah Ḥammād → ʿĀṣim → Zirr The companion changes, but the lower transmitter pair remains the same. Ibn Ḥibbān and related listings Related seven-aḥruf material Often preserves the same explanation of an ummī audience. The motif circulates as an explanation for recitational plurality. The seven-aḥruf report has a more obvious motive than the fasting report because the explanation is built into the matn. The Prophet says he was sent to an **ummī** nation, and the examples immediately define that as people who would struggle with a written or fixed recitational form: elderly people, children, and someone who has never read a book. Gabriel’s answer then supplies seven aḥruf as a solution. If **ummiyyūn** means “Gentiles” or “non-scriptural people,” the list that follows becomes awkward. Being outside a previous scripture-bearing community does not make an elderly man, a woman, a child, or a man who never read a book require seven aḥruf. The report only works smoothly if **ummī** is already being read as illiterate or untrained in reading. That is why this hadith is valuable evidence for the later interpretive shift. ʿĀṣim is important, but the argument should stay disciplined The draft version of this article blamed ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd directly for fabricating the seven-aḥruf report. That is possible as a hypothesis, but it is stronger to state what the evidence can support. ʿĀṣim is a major Kūfan reciter and a central lower transmitter in these cited forms. He is praised in the rijāl literature, but he is also criticized for mistakes in ḥadīth. Ibn Saʿd reportedly called him trustworthy while saying he made many errors in his hadith, and other critics commented on his memory. That means the report’s seven-aḥruf explanation should be treated with caution. A reciter-linked Kūfan channel is not neutral evidence for why the Qurʾān allegedly came in seven aḥruf. It is exactly the type of channel in which one would expect later recitational theology to be explained, defended, and projected backward. Figure Evidence Interpretive Use ʿĀṣim b. Abī al-Najūd Major Kūfan reciter; praised by some critics but described by Ibn Saʿd as trustworthy with many hadith mistakes. He is not dismissed wholesale, but a recitational-theology report through him deserves scrutiny. Zirr b. Ḥubaysh Shared transmitter above ʿĀṣim in the Ubayy and Ḥudhayfah forms. The companion attribution varies while the lower explanatory corridor remains stable. al-Aswad b. Qays Central transmitter in the moon-sighting formula through Saʿīd b. ʿAmr from Ibn ʿUmar. The fasting cluster’s semantic move is tied to a narrow Kufan path. Epigraphy also weakens the “illiterate Arabia” assumption The hadith picture often depends on an older civilizational myth: pre-Islamic Arabia as overwhelmingly oral and textless. Modern Arabian epigraphy has complicated that picture. Ahmad al-Jallad’s work on Safaitic and other Ancient North Arabian inscriptions has emphasized the scale and variety of writing in pre-Islamic Arabia. The existence of tens of thousands of inscriptions does not prove that every Arab was literate, and it does not by itself prove the Prophet’s literacy. It does, however, make the blanket phrase “we do not write” historically suspicious when treated as a description of the whole community. Epigraphy does not turn every nomad into a scribe. It shows that writing was present, diverse, and culturally meaningful in parts of Arabia before Islam. That is enough to challenge a later religious slogan that makes non-writing part of the community’s identity. What the two clusters share Cluster Key Phrase Function of “Ummī” Resulting Doctrine Moon-sighting / fasting أُمَّةٌ أُمِّيَّةٌ، لَا نَكْتُبُ وَلَا نَحْسُبُ Ummī is defined by non-writing and non-calculation. Calculation is pushed aside in favor of visible lunar signs. Seven aḥruf أُمَّةٍ أُمِّيِّينَ ... وَالرَّجُلُ الَّذِي لَمْ يَقْرَأْ كِتَابًا قَطُّ Ummī is defined by inability or lack of reading practice. Multiple recitation modes are justified as accommodation for an allegedly unlettered audience. Qurʾānic usage الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ وَالْأُمِّيِّينَ Ummiyyūn are contrasted with scripture-bearing communities. The Prophet’s mission is framed as bringing scripture to a non-scriptural people. The pattern is clear. The Qurʾān uses **ummiyyūn** inside a scriptural map. The hadith clusters use the term to produce later legal and recitational doctrines. The reports are therefore not harmless translations. They are interpretive engines. The two hadith clusters should be treated as later interpretive uses of **ummiyyūn**, not as the Qurʾān’s own definition of the term. The fasting report turns the word into non-writing and non-calculation. The seven-aḥruf report turns it into lack of reading ability and then uses that meaning to justify recitational plurality. Both moves are traceable through narrow transmitter corridors, and both sit uneasily beside the Qurʾān’s scriptural contrast between the People of the Book and the ummiyyūn. title: Isnād Politics: al-Aʿmash, Hishām b. ʿUrwa, and the Bewitchment Report
description: A source-critical study of the bewitchment narrative, its Medinan family dossier, its thin Kūfan collateral route, and the rijāl problem created by Hishām’s Iraqi phase and al-Aʿmash’s ʿanʿana.
