{ y: 690, label: 'Narrated event' }, { y: 585, label: 'Companion / early authority' }, { y: 395, label: 'Second-century bottleneck' }, { y: 250, label: 'Iraqi transmitters' }, { y: 75, label: 'Compilers' } ]; { x: 410, y: 345, text: 'Dashed line: plausible Iraqi contact, not an attested isnād', kind: 'dive', anchor: 'middle' } ]; The bewitchment report is usually defended by pointing to two different Companion authorities. One route comes through ʿĀʾisha by way of ʿUrwa and Hishām b. ʿUrwa. Another route comes through Zayd b. Arqam by way of Yazīd b. Ḥayyān and al-Aʿmash. On the surface, this looks like corroboration: a Medinan household route and a Kūfan Companion route both remember the Prophet being bewitched by a Jewish man. That surface impression is too neat. The transmission map does not give us two equally strong independent memories. It gives us a broad Hishām-family dossier, a shorter mursal/collective al-Zuhrī layer, and a much thinner Kūfan collateral route whose recoverable form runs through al-Aʿmash and, below him, through Abū Muʿāwiya. The key question is not whether the report entered the canonical collections. It did. The key question is whether the Kūfan route truly reaches behind the Hishām dossier or whether it represents a secondary Iraqi reshaping of the same story-world. The Zayd b. Arqam route should not be treated as clean independent confirmation of the Hishām b. ʿUrwa bewitchment report. Its matn shares the same narrative skeleton but removes the diagnostic Medinan details, anonymizes the Jewish agent, inserts ʿAlī as the one who retrieves and unties the knots, and is transmitted through al-Aʿmash by ʿanʿana. The strongest conclusion is careful: direct borrowing from Hishām cannot be proven, but the Kūfan route is too thin, too late in recoverable form, and too exposed to Iraqi cross-contamination to function as an independent second witness. ## The Two Reports Are Not the Same Kind of Evidence The longest and most influential version is the ʿĀʾisha report through Hishām b. ʿUrwa. Its most revealing form is not simply “Hishām from his father from ʿĀʾisha.” In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿUyayna says that Ibn Jurayj first narrated it from **the family of ʿUrwa** before he asked Hishām about it. That small isnād note matters. It shows that the story was already functioning as an ʿUrwa-family dossier, and that Hishām became the main transmitter who regularized it into the famous father-from-ʿĀʾisha chain.[^1] The Zayd b. Arqam route is a different kind of artifact. It is shorter. It has no ʿĀʾisha interior scene, no named Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, no Banū Zurayq frame, no comb-and-hair detail, no male date-palm spathe, no named Dharwān well, and no dialogue between two bedside visitors. Instead, Gabriel directly diagnoses the magic, the object is described as knots in an unnamed well, and ʿAlī is sent to retrieve and undo them.[^2] The two reports therefore do not stand as two full narrative witnesses saying the same thing. They share a **story grammar**, not a stable detailed memory. The grammar is simple: a Jewish agent, hidden magic in a well, divine disclosure, physical removal, recovery, and no retaliation. Everything else shifts. Route A ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām A Medinan household report with diagnostic detail: Labīd, Banū Zurayq, comb, hair-remnants, date-palm spathe, Dharwān well, two visitors, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the matter. Broadly diffused below Hishām Route B Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash A compact Kūfan version: anonymous Jewish man, unnamed well, knots, Gabriel, ʿAlī as retriever, recovery “as if released from a tether,” and no confrontation. Thin recoverable lower conduit Route C al-Zuhrī → Ibn al-Musayyib / ʿUrwa An early legal/mursal memory in ʿAbd al-Razzāq: Banū Zurayq, well, knots, no killing. This shows the story circulated in legal discussions before the long Hishām version became the canonical form. Collective and non-musnad ## The Early Non-Hishām Layer: al-Zuhrī, ʿUrwa, and Legal Memory One reason the old “Hishām versus al-Aʿmash” framing is incomplete is that Hishām is not the only pre-canonical Medinan entry point. ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves reports from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn al-Musayyib and ʿUrwa, in legal chapters on whether a sorcerer from the People of the Book is killed. These reports do not give the full bedside narrative. They preserve the legal residue of the story: the Jews of Banū Zurayq bewitched the Prophet, the magic was placed in a well, knots were extracted, and no one is reported to have been killed.[^3] This al-Zuhrī layer is important because it complicates both apologetic and polemical readings. It does not prove the event. It does prove that the story had already entered a **Medinan legal-memory environment** before the later canonical form. In that environment, the issue was not primarily “can a prophet be bewitched?” but “if a Jewish group bewitched the Prophet, why was no sorcerer killed?” That is why ʿAbd al-Razzāq places it under chapters about killing the sorcerer of the People of the Book. The same Muṣannaf also preserves a loose report through Maʿmar from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī from Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar: the Prophet was held back from ʿĀʾisha for a year, two angels diagnosed the magic, the well is unnamed, and the magic is extracted.[^4] This is not a strong musnad report, but it shows that the story’s parts were circulating in modular form: ʿĀʾisha, angelic diagnosis, a well, extraction, and knots could be rearranged without the full Hishām wording. A report can be early in circulation and still historically unstable. The al-Zuhrī and Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar material shows that the bewitchment story was not born only in Bukhārī’s final form. It also shows that the narrative was fluid: legal memory, family memory, angelic diagnosis, and well-magic motifs circulated in separable pieces. ## The Isnād Map This diagram should not be read as a claim that al-Aʿmash definitely heard the story from Hishām and then falsified the isnād. That would outrun the evidence. The better claim is narrower and stronger: the Zayd route cannot be used as an unproblematic independent control because the same Iraqi scholarly world supplied the conditions for cross-contamination, compression, and regional reshaping. ## Matn Analysis: Same Skeleton, Different Narrative Politics The matn comparison is where the problem becomes visible. If the Zayd route were simply an independent Companion memory of the same event, one might expect some of the highly diagnostic details to survive: Labīd’s name, Banū Zurayq, the comb, the hair-remnants, the male date-palm spathe, the well of Dharwān, or the two visitors speaking at the Prophet’s bedside. Instead, the Zayd route preserves the broad skeleton and replaces the details most tied to the ʿĀʾisha household setting. Motif Hishām dossier Zayd / al-Aʿmash route Source-critical implication Perpetrator Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, Banū Zurayq, ally of Jews Anonymous Jewish man The Kūfan version keeps the polemical category but drops the Medinan identification. Object Comb, hair-remnants, male date-palm spathe Knots The Zayd report preserves the magic-removal motif in a simplified form. Location Dharwān / Dhī Arwān well Such-and-such a well The named local setting disappears outside the family dossier. Revelation scene Two men or angels converse at the Prophet’s head and feet Gabriel directly informs him The diagnostic scene is compressed into a simpler angelic notice. Human actor The Prophet and unnamed companions go to the well, or the object is extracted ʿAlī is sent, extracts it, and unties it The Kūfan version becomes easier to hear in an ʿAlid-friendly environment. Duration / effect Imagines doing what he did not do; some variants specify women or six months He suffers for some days, then rises as if freed from a tether The psychologically difficult element is softened and shortened. This is not random drift. The Zayd version looks like a **Kūfanized digest** of the broader story: shorter, less sexually explicit, less tied to ʿĀʾisha’s domestic vantage point, and more ʿAlī-centered. That does not make it automatically fabricated, but it prevents it from functioning as a clean independent witness to the Hishām report. ## Hishām b. ʿUrwa: Reliable, but the Iraqi Phase Matters Hishām b. ʿUrwa is not a weak narrator in the simple sense. Ibn Saʿd and al-ʿIjlī called him trustworthy; Abū Ḥātim called him a trustworthy imām in hadith; Ibn Ḥibbān described him as precise, devout, virtuous, and a memorizer.[^5] The question is not whether Hishām is disposable. The question is whether the exact type of report under study fits the precise zone classical critics themselves flagged: his later Iraqi transmission from his father. Ibn Ḥajar’s entry in Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb preserves the problem clearly. Yaʿqūb b. Shayba says that nothing was criticized from Hishām except after he went to Iraq, where he expanded his narration from his father. Ibn Kharrāsh reports that Mālik objected to Hishām’s reports for the Iraqis and describes a shift over three Kufan visits: first “my father told me: I heard ʿĀʾisha,” then “my father informed me from ʿĀʾisha,” then simply “my father from ʿĀʾisha.”[^6] وقال يعقوب بن شيبة: ثقة ثبت لم ينكر عليه شيء إلا بعد ما صار إلى العراق، فإنه انبسط في الرواية عن أبيه، فأنكر ذلك عليه أهل بلده ... وقال ابن خراش: كان مالك لا يرضاه ... قدم الكوفة ثلاث مرات: قدمة كان يقول: حدثني أبي قال: سمعت عائشة، وقدم الثانية فكان يقول: أخبرني أبي عن عائشة، وقدم الثالثة فكان يقول: أبي عن عائشة. Yaʿqūb b. Shayba said: “He was trustworthy and firm; nothing was criticized from him except after he went to Iraq, for he expanded in narrating from his father, and the people of his region objected to that.” Ibn Kharrāsh said that Mālik did not approve of him, and that Hishām came to Kūfa three times: on one visit he said, “my father narrated to me: I heard ʿĀʾisha”; on the second, “my father informed me from ʿĀʾisha”; and on the third, “my father from ʿĀʾisha.” That quotation should be handled carefully. It does not mean Hishām was a liar. It means the family route cannot be treated as though every father-from-ʿĀʾisha report is equally early, equally stable, and equally insulated from Iraqi transmission dynamics. The bewitchment dossier is exactly the kind of report where that matters: it is a vivid household narrative, transmitted through the ʿUrwa family, then widely diffused in Iraq through students such as Ibn Numayr, Abū Usāma, Ibn ʿUyayna, ʿĪsā b. Yūnus, and others. There is also a crucial internal clue in Bukhārī’s own version. Ibn Jurayj says he first heard it from **Āl ʿUrwa**, the family of ʿUrwa, and then asked Hishām about it. That is not a defect by itself. It is a sign of provenance. The report’s home is not “many Companions independently remembered this.” Its home is the ʿUrwa household memory-world. ## al-Aʿmash: Reliable, Kūfan, and a Real Tadlīs Problem Al-Aʿmash is also not a weak narrator in the crude sense. The same rijāl tradition praises him sharply. Al-ʿIjlī calls him trustworthy and firm, the hadith authority of Kūfa in his time, a head in Qurʾān, and notes that he had some Shīʿī leaning. Ibn Maʿīn called him trustworthy. Al-Nasāʾī called him trustworthy and firm. The issue is narrower: al-Aʿmash was also known as a mudallis, and classical critics repeatedly limited or questioned some of his claimed links when the formula was only ʿan.[^7] Ibn Ḥajar preserves Ibn Ḥibbān’s statement that al-Aʿmash saw Anas but heard from him only a few letters and “was a mudallis.” He also preserves Yaʿqūb b. Shayba’s report that al-Aʿmash’s reports from Mujāhid are only established when he says “I heard,” and that much of his Mujāhid material actually came through another intermediary.[^8] وقال العجلي: كان ثقة ثبتا في الحديث، وكان محدث أهل الكوفة في زمانه ... وكان فيه تشيع ... وذكره ابن حبان في ثقات التابعين، وقال ... وكان مدلسا ... وقال يعقوب بن شيبة ... ليس يصح للأعمش عن مجاهد إلا أحاديث يسيرة ... لا يثبت منها إلا ما قال: سمعت. Al-ʿIjlī said: “He was trustworthy and firm in hadith, and he was the hadith authority of Kūfa in his time ... and there was some Shīʿī leaning in him.” Ibn Ḥibbān included him among the trustworthy Successors and said: “He was a mudallis.” Yaʿqūb b. Shayba reports regarding his Mujāhid material: “Only a few hadiths are sound from al-Aʿmash from Mujāhid ... none is established except what he said, ‘I heard.’” In the Zayd b. Arqam bewitchment route, al-Aʿmash does not say “I heard Yazīd b. Ḥayyān.” The chain is **al-Aʿmash ʿan Yazīd b. Ḥayyān**. This does not automatically falsify the report. Yazīd b. Ḥayyān was a real Kūfan transmitter from Zayd b. Arqam, and Ibn Ḥajar’s entry explicitly says that al-Aʿmash narrated from him.[^9] Chronology is not the problem. The problem is source-critical: a mudallis using ʿan in a report that suspiciously overlaps with a famous Hishām family dossier cannot be used as a clean independent control. ## The Abū Muʿāwiya Bottleneck The lower isnād of the Zayd route intensifies the problem. In the recoverable versions consulted here, the report from al-Aʿmash is not widely diffused through many independent pupils of al-Aʿmash. It comes through **Abū Muʿāwiya**. Aḥmad has Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Yazīd → Zayd. Al-Nasāʾī has Hannād b. al-Sarī → Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Ibn Ḥayyān, meaning Yazīd, → Zayd. Al-Ṭabarānī has Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba → Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Yazīd → Zayd.[^10] That means the apparent spread through Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Ṭabarānī is partly an illusion created by compilation. It is the same lower conduit being collected in several books. Multiple books are not multiple early witnesses. Recoverable Kūfan route Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash → Abū Muʿāwiya Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Ṭabarānī preserve the report, but the lower strand repeatedly returns to Abū Muʿāwiya. This is not a broad al-Aʿmash fan-out; it is a narrow conduit that later compilers copied into separate collections. One lower conduit ≠ independent corroboration This is especially relevant because Abū Muʿāwiya also belonged to the same wider Iraqi transmission world as Hishām. Ibn Ḥajar lists Abū Muʿāwiya among those who narrated from Hishām b. ʿUrwa, and the Zayd route itself places Abū Muʿāwiya as the pupil of al-Aʿmash in this very report.[^11] This does not prove that Abū Muʿāwiya contaminated the chain. It does show that the two dossiers were not sealed off from one another. ## What Could Have Happened? There are three realistic models. Model 1 True independent memory Zayd b. Arqam independently remembered the same event in a compact Kūfan form, and al-Aʿmash preserved it accurately from Yazīd b. Ḥayyān. Possible, but least explanatory Model 2 Shared story-world Different Medinan legal and family memories circulated early; the Kūfan route absorbed the broad skeleton and stabilized it with local features. Best fits the fluid matn evidence Model 3 Direct Iraqi borrowing Al-Aʿmash, or a lower Iraqi transmitter, encountered the Hishām-family report during Hishām’s Iraqi period and transmitted a reshaped version through a more Kūfan-friendly chain. Plausible, not directly provable The first model is the apologetic one, but it leaves too much unexplained: why the diagnostic details vanish, why ʿAlī appears, why the route is so narrow below al-Aʿmash, and why a known mudallis transmits the crucial link with ʿan. The third model is attractive, especially because Hishām and al-Aʿmash were contemporaries, because Hishām came to Kūfa, and because his Iraqi transmission from his father was specifically criticized. But it should be presented as a historical hypothesis, not as a documented confession. The second model is the strongest. The story was already circulating in multiple forms: legal residue through al-Zuhrī, family dossier through ʿUrwa/Hishām, and loose angelic-diagnosis material through Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar. The Zayd/al-Aʿmash route then looks like a Kūfan collateral crystallization of that shared story-world, not an independent second anchor. ## The Political Layer: Why ʿAlī Appears in the Kūfan Version The Zayd route is not merely shorter. It is differently staged. In the Hishām report, the scene belongs to ʿĀʾisha’s room and the Prophet’s private exchange with her. In the Zayd route, ʿĀʾisha disappears, and ʿAlī becomes the operative who retrieves and unties the knots. That shift matters in Kūfa. Zayd b. Arqam settled in Kūfa, transmitted there, and is described in Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb as having witnessed Ṣiffīn with ʿAlī and as having been among his close associates.[^12] Al-Aʿmash, the Kūfan transmitter of the report, is described by al-ʿIjlī as having some Shīʿī leaning.[^13] Neither fact proves forgery. But together they explain why a Kūfan version of the story would be more likely to preserve an ʿAlī-centered action scene than an ʿĀʾisha-centered domestic scene. This is where the older anti-Jewish polemic does not disappear, but it becomes only one layer. The Hishām dossier names a Jewish-allied Medinan culprit and situates the story in a Banū Zurayq setting. The Zayd route preserves the Jewish culprit but makes the salvation mechanics more Kūfan and ʿAlid: Gabriel discloses, ʿAlī retrieves, knots are undone, and the Prophet rises freed. Calling the Zayd route “Kūfan” does not mean every Kūfan report is Shīʿī propaganda, and noting al-Aʿmash’s Shīʿī leaning does not mean he was a sectarian fabricator. The point is subtler: regional audiences shape which details survive. A report tied to ʿĀʾisha’s household could be retold in a form where ʿAlī becomes the decisive agent without the whole story being invented from nothing. ## The Classical Critics Saw the Pieces, but Not the Whole Problem Classical rijāl criticism gives us the materials needed for the critique, even if it does not always draw the source-critical conclusion. It tells us that Hishām was trustworthy but that his Iraqi father-reports drew criticism. It tells us that al-Aʿmash was trustworthy but a mudallis. It tells us that Yazīd b. Ḥayyān was a real Kūfan transmitter from Zayd and that al-Aʿmash narrated from him. It tells us that Abū Muʿāwiya transmitted from both worlds. What it does not do is ask the modern source-critical question: does the Zayd route independently confirm the Hishām dossier, or does it sit inside the same second-century Iraqi-Medinan circulation network? The answer is that it does not independently confirm it in any strong sense. It is a collateral route, but a compromised one. It may preserve a real Kūfan memory of a known story. It may be a reshaped digest. It may even go back to something Zayd said. But as evidence, it does not do the work apologists often assign to it. What is strong The Hishām dossier is widely collected and has multiple lower transmitters below Hishām. What is weak Above Hishām, the main canonical report still returns to the ʿUrwa family line, and Bukhārī’s own note points to Āl ʿUrwa as an early family-memory source. What is suspicious The Zayd route shares the skeleton but not the diagnostic details, travels through al-Aʿmash’s ʿanʿana, and is narrow below al-Aʿmash. What follows The Zayd route should be treated as a secondary Kūfan collateral, not as a secure independent witness. ## Conclusion The bewitchment narrative is not supported by two equal pillars. Its main pillar is the ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām family dossier, with an earlier Medinan legal residue visible through al-Zuhrī and ʿAbd al-Razzāq. The supposed second pillar, Zayd b. Arqam through Yazīd b. Ḥayyān and al-Aʿmash, is too narrow and too contextually exposed to carry the weight of independent corroboration. The most responsible conclusion is not that al-Aʿmash has been caught beyond doubt fabricating an isnād. The evidence does not prove that. The responsible conclusion is more damaging to the apologetic use of the report: the Kūfan route cannot rescue the historicity of the Hishām dossier. It is exactly the kind of route source criticism should hesitate over — a vivid story already circulating in Medinan family and legal contexts, a known Iraqi expansion environment around Hishām, a Kūfan mudallis transmitting with ʿan, and a secondary matn that conveniently replaces ʿĀʾisha’s room with ʿAlī’s action. If the report is defended, it should be defended honestly as a report canonized through Hishām’s family transmission and accepted by later hadith compilers. It should not be presented as if the Zayd b. Arqam route gives independent, multi-regional historical certainty. export const hishamArabic = حَدَّثَنِي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ بْنُ مُحَمَّدٍ قَالَ سَمِعْتُ ابْنَ عُيَيْنَةَ يَقُولُ: أَوَّلُ مَنْ حَدَّثَنَا بِهِ ابْنُ جُرَيْجٍ يَقُولُ: حَدَّثَنِي آلُ عُرْوَةَ عَنْ عُرْوَةَ، فَسَأَلْتُ هِشَامًا عَنْهُ، فَحَدَّثَنَا عَنْ أَبِيهِ عَنْ عَائِشَةَ رضي الله عنها قَالَتْ: كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ سُحِرَ حَتَّى كَانَ يَرَى أَنَّهُ يَأْتِي النِّسَاءَ وَلَا يَأْتِيهِنَّ ... فَقَالَ: يَا عَائِشَةُ، أَعَلِمْتِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ قَدْ أَفْتَانِي فِيمَا اسْتَفْتَيْتُهُ فِيهِ؟ أَتَانِي رَجُلَانِ ... فَقَالَ: مَا بَالُ الرَّجُلِ؟ قَالَ: مَطْبُوبٌ. قَالَ: وَمَنْ طَبَّهُ؟ قَالَ: لَبِيدُ بْنُ أَعْصَمَ، رَجُلٌ مِنْ بَنِي زُرَيْقٍ حَلِيفٌ لِيَهُودَ، كَانَ مُنَافِقًا ... فِي مُشْطٍ وَمُشَاقَةٍ ... فِي جُفِّ طَلْعَةٍ ذَكَرٍ تَحْتَ رَعُوفَةٍ فِي بِئْرِ ذَرْوَانَ ... فَقَالَ: أَمَا وَاللَّهِ فَقَدْ شَفَانِي، وَأَكْرَهُ أَنْ أُثِيرَ عَلَى أَحَدٍ مِنَ النَّاسِ شَرًّا.; export const hishamTranslation = ʿAbd Allāh b. export const sihrAnnotations = [ { x: 410, y: 345, text: 'Dashed line: plausible Iraqi contact, not an attested isnād', kind: 'dive', anchor: 'middle' } ]; The bewitchment report is usually defended by pointing to two different Companion authorities. One route comes through ʿĀʾisha by way of ʿUrwa and Hishām b. ʿUrwa. Another route comes through Zayd b. Arqam by way of Yazīd b. Ḥayyān and al-Aʿmash. On the surface, this looks like corroboration: a Medinan household route and a Kūfan Companion route both remember the Prophet being bewitched by a Jewish man. That surface impression is too neat. The transmission map does not give us two equally strong independent memories. It gives us a broad Hishām-family dossier, a shorter mursal/collective al-Zuhrī layer, and a much thinner Kūfan collateral route whose recoverable form runs through al-Aʿmash and, below him, through Abū Muʿāwiya. The key question is not whether the report entered the canonical collections. It did. The key question is whether the Kūfan route truly reaches behind the Hishām dossier or whether it represents a secondary Iraqi reshaping of the same story-world. The Zayd b. Arqam route should not be treated as clean independent confirmation of the Hishām b. ʿUrwa bewitchment report. Its matn shares the same narrative skeleton but removes the diagnostic Medinan details, anonymizes the Jewish agent, inserts ʿAlī as the one who retrieves and unties the knots, and is transmitted through al-Aʿmash by ʿanʿana. The strongest conclusion is careful: direct borrowing from Hishām cannot be proven, but the Kūfan route is too thin, too late in recoverable form, and too exposed to Iraqi cross-contamination to function as an independent second witness. The Two Reports Are Not the Same Kind of Evidence The longest and most influential version is the ʿĀʾisha report through Hishām b. ʿUrwa. Its most revealing form is not simply “Hishām from his father from ʿĀʾisha.” In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Ibn ʿUyayna says that Ibn Jurayj first narrated it from **the family of ʿUrwa** before he asked Hishām about it. That small isnād note matters. It shows that the story was already functioning as an ʿUrwa-family dossier, and that Hishām became the main transmitter who regularized it into the famous father-from-ʿĀʾisha chain.[^1] The Zayd b. Arqam route is a different kind of artifact. It is shorter. It has no ʿĀʾisha interior scene, no named Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, no Banū Zurayq frame, no comb-and-hair detail, no male date-palm spathe, no named Dharwān well, and no dialogue between two bedside visitors. Instead, Gabriel directly diagnoses the magic, the object is described as knots in an unnamed well, and ʿAlī is sent to retrieve and undo them.[^2] The two reports therefore do not stand as two full narrative witnesses saying the same thing. They share a **story grammar**, not a stable detailed memory. The grammar is simple: a Jewish agent, hidden magic in a well, divine disclosure, physical removal, recovery, and no retaliation. Everything else shifts. Route A ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām A Medinan household report with diagnostic detail: Labīd, Banū Zurayq, comb, hair-remnants, date-palm spathe, Dharwān well, two visitors, and the Prophet’s refusal to publicize the matter. Broadly diffused below Hishām Route B Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash A compact Kūfan version: anonymous Jewish man, unnamed well, knots, Gabriel, ʿAlī as retriever, recovery “as if released from a tether,” and no confrontation. Thin recoverable lower conduit Route C al-Zuhrī → Ibn al-Musayyib / ʿUrwa An early legal/mursal memory in ʿAbd al-Razzāq: Banū Zurayq, well, knots, no killing. This shows the story circulated in legal discussions before the long Hishām version became the canonical form. Collective and non-musnad The Early Non-Hishām Layer: al-Zuhrī, ʿUrwa, and Legal Memory One reason the old “Hishām versus al-Aʿmash” framing is incomplete is that Hishām is not the only pre-canonical Medinan entry point. ʿAbd al-Razzāq preserves reports from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, from Ibn al-Musayyib and ʿUrwa, in legal chapters on whether a sorcerer from the People of the Book is killed. These reports do not give the full bedside narrative. They preserve the legal residue of the story: the Jews of Banū Zurayq bewitched the Prophet, the magic was placed in a well, knots were extracted, and no one is reported to have been killed.[^3] This al-Zuhrī layer is important because it complicates both apologetic and polemical readings. It does not prove the event. It does prove that the story had already entered a **Medinan legal-memory environment** before the later canonical form. In that environment, the issue was not primarily “can a prophet be bewitched?” but “if a Jewish group bewitched the Prophet, why was no sorcerer killed?” That is why ʿAbd al-Razzāq places it under chapters about killing the sorcerer of the People of the Book. The same Muṣannaf also preserves a loose report through Maʿmar from ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī from Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar: the Prophet was held back from ʿĀʾisha for a year, two angels diagnosed the magic, the well is unnamed, and the magic is extracted.[^4] This is not a strong musnad report, but it shows that the story’s parts were circulating in modular form: ʿĀʾisha, angelic diagnosis, a well, extraction, and knots could be rearranged without the full Hishām wording. A report can be early in circulation and still historically unstable. The al-Zuhrī and Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar material shows that the bewitchment story was not born only in Bukhārī’s final form. It also shows that the narrative was fluid: legal memory, family memory, angelic diagnosis, and well-magic motifs circulated in separable pieces. The Isnād Map This diagram should not be read as a claim that al-Aʿmash definitely heard the story from Hishām and then falsified the isnād. That would outrun the evidence. The better claim is narrower and stronger: the Zayd route cannot be used as an unproblematic independent control because the same Iraqi scholarly world supplied the conditions for cross-contamination, compression, and regional reshaping. Matn Analysis: Same Skeleton, Different Narrative Politics The matn comparison is where the problem becomes visible. If the Zayd route were simply an independent Companion memory of the same event, one might expect some of the highly diagnostic details to survive: Labīd’s name, Banū Zurayq, the comb, the hair-remnants, the male date-palm spathe, the well of Dharwān, or the two visitors speaking at the Prophet’s bedside. Instead, the Zayd route preserves the broad skeleton and replaces the details most tied to the ʿĀʾisha household setting. Motif Hishām dossier Zayd / al-Aʿmash route Source-critical implication Perpetrator Labīd b. al-Aʿṣam, Banū Zurayq, ally of Jews Anonymous Jewish man The Kūfan version keeps the polemical category but drops the Medinan identification. Object Comb, hair-remnants, male date-palm spathe Knots The Zayd report preserves the magic-removal motif in a simplified form. Location Dharwān / Dhī Arwān well Such-and-such a well The named local setting disappears outside the family dossier. Revelation scene Two men or angels converse at the Prophet’s head and feet Gabriel directly informs him The diagnostic scene is compressed into a simpler angelic notice. Human actor The Prophet and unnamed companions go to the well, or the object is extracted ʿAlī is sent, extracts it, and unties it The Kūfan version becomes easier to hear in an ʿAlid-friendly environment. Duration / effect Imagines doing what he did not do; some variants specify women or six months He suffers for some days, then rises as if freed from a tether The psychologically difficult element is softened and shortened. This is not random drift. The Zayd version looks like a **Kūfanized digest** of the broader story: shorter, less sexually explicit, less tied to ʿĀʾisha’s domestic vantage point, and more ʿAlī-centered. That does not make it automatically fabricated, but it prevents it from functioning as a clean independent witness to the Hishām report. Hishām b. ʿUrwa: Reliable, but the Iraqi Phase Matters Hishām b. ʿUrwa is not a weak narrator in the simple sense. Ibn Saʿd and al-ʿIjlī called him trustworthy; Abū Ḥātim called him a trustworthy imām in hadith; Ibn Ḥibbān described him as precise, devout, virtuous, and a memorizer.[^5] The question is not whether Hishām is disposable. The question is whether the exact type of report under study fits the precise zone classical critics themselves flagged: his later Iraqi transmission from his father. Ibn Ḥajar’s entry in Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb preserves the problem clearly. Yaʿqūb b. Shayba says that nothing was criticized from Hishām except after he went to Iraq, where he expanded his narration from his father. Ibn Kharrāsh reports that Mālik objected to Hishām’s reports for the Iraqis and describes a shift over three Kufan visits: first “my father told me: I heard ʿĀʾisha,” then “my father informed me from ʿĀʾisha,” then simply “my father from ʿĀʾisha.”[^6] وقال يعقوب بن شيبة: ثقة ثبت لم ينكر عليه شيء إلا بعد ما صار إلى العراق، فإنه انبسط في الرواية عن أبيه، فأنكر ذلك عليه أهل بلده ... وقال ابن خراش: كان مالك لا يرضاه ... قدم الكوفة ثلاث مرات: قدمة كان يقول: حدثني أبي قال: سمعت عائشة، وقدم الثانية فكان يقول: أخبرني أبي عن عائشة، وقدم الثالثة فكان يقول: أبي عن عائشة. Yaʿqūb b. Shayba said: “He was trustworthy and firm; nothing was criticized from him except after he went to Iraq, for he expanded in narrating from his father, and the people of his region objected to that.” Ibn Kharrāsh said that Mālik did not approve of him, and that Hishām came to Kūfa three times: on one visit he said, “my father narrated to me: I heard ʿĀʾisha”; on the second, “my father informed me from ʿĀʾisha”; and on the third, “my father from ʿĀʾisha.” That quotation should be handled carefully. It does not mean Hishām was a liar. It means the family route cannot be treated as though every father-from-ʿĀʾisha report is equally early, equally stable, and equally insulated from Iraqi transmission dynamics. The bewitchment dossier is exactly the kind of report where that matters: it is a vivid household narrative, transmitted through the ʿUrwa family, then widely diffused in Iraq through students such as Ibn Numayr, Abū Usāma, Ibn ʿUyayna, ʿĪsā b. Yūnus, and others. There is also a crucial internal clue in Bukhārī’s own version. Ibn Jurayj says he first heard it from **Āl ʿUrwa**, the family of ʿUrwa, and then asked Hishām about it. That is not a defect by itself. It is a sign of provenance. The report’s home is not “many Companions independently remembered this.” Its home is the ʿUrwa household memory-world. al-Aʿmash: Reliable, Kūfan, and a Real Tadlīs Problem Al-Aʿmash is also not a weak narrator in the crude sense. The same rijāl tradition praises him sharply. Al-ʿIjlī calls him trustworthy and firm, the hadith authority of Kūfa in his time, a head in Qurʾān, and notes that he had some Shīʿī leaning. Ibn Maʿīn called him trustworthy. Al-Nasāʾī called him trustworthy and firm. The issue is narrower: al-Aʿmash was also known as a mudallis, and classical critics repeatedly limited or questioned some of his claimed links when the formula was only ʿan.[^7] Ibn Ḥajar preserves Ibn Ḥibbān’s statement that al-Aʿmash saw Anas but heard from him only a few letters and “was a mudallis.” He also preserves Yaʿqūb b. Shayba’s report that al-Aʿmash’s reports from Mujāhid are only established when he says “I heard,” and that much of his Mujāhid material actually came through another intermediary.[^8] وقال العجلي: كان ثقة ثبتا في الحديث، وكان محدث أهل الكوفة في زمانه ... وكان فيه تشيع ... وذكره ابن حبان في ثقات التابعين، وقال ... وكان مدلسا ... وقال يعقوب بن شيبة ... ليس يصح للأعمش عن مجاهد إلا أحاديث يسيرة ... لا يثبت منها إلا ما قال: سمعت. Al-ʿIjlī said: “He was trustworthy and firm in hadith, and he was the hadith authority of Kūfa in his time ... and there was some Shīʿī leaning in him.” Ibn Ḥibbān included him among the trustworthy Successors and said: “He was a mudallis.” Yaʿqūb b. Shayba reports regarding his Mujāhid material: “Only a few hadiths are sound from al-Aʿmash from Mujāhid ... none is established except what he said, ‘I heard.’” In the Zayd b. Arqam bewitchment route, al-Aʿmash does not say “I heard Yazīd b. Ḥayyān.” The chain is **al-Aʿmash ʿan Yazīd b. Ḥayyān**. This does not automatically falsify the report. Yazīd b. Ḥayyān was a real Kūfan transmitter from Zayd b. Arqam, and Ibn Ḥajar’s entry explicitly says that al-Aʿmash narrated from him.[^9] Chronology is not the problem. The problem is source-critical: a mudallis using ʿan in a report that suspiciously overlaps with a famous Hishām family dossier cannot be used as a clean independent control. The Abū Muʿāwiya Bottleneck The lower isnād of the Zayd route intensifies the problem. In the recoverable versions consulted here, the report from al-Aʿmash is not widely diffused through many independent pupils of al-Aʿmash. It comes through **Abū Muʿāwiya**. Aḥmad has Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Yazīd → Zayd. Al-Nasāʾī has Hannād b. al-Sarī → Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Ibn Ḥayyān, meaning Yazīd, → Zayd. Al-Ṭabarānī has Abū Bakr b. Abī Shayba → Abū Muʿāwiya → al-Aʿmash → Yazīd → Zayd.[^10] That means the apparent spread through Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Ṭabarānī is partly an illusion created by compilation. It is the same lower conduit being collected in several books. Multiple books are not multiple early witnesses. Recoverable Kūfan route Zayd → Yazīd → al-Aʿmash → Abū Muʿāwiya Aḥmad, al-Nasāʾī, and al-Ṭabarānī preserve the report, but the lower strand repeatedly returns to Abū Muʿāwiya. This is not a broad al-Aʿmash fan-out; it is a narrow conduit that later compilers copied into separate collections. One lower conduit ≠ independent corroboration This is especially relevant because Abū Muʿāwiya also belonged to the same wider Iraqi transmission world as Hishām. Ibn Ḥajar lists Abū Muʿāwiya among those who narrated from Hishām b. ʿUrwa, and the Zayd route itself places Abū Muʿāwiya as the pupil of al-Aʿmash in this very report.[^11] This does not prove that Abū Muʿāwiya contaminated the chain. It does show that the two dossiers were not sealed off from one another. What Could Have Happened? There are three realistic models. Model 1 True independent memory Zayd b. Arqam independently remembered the same event in a compact Kūfan form, and al-Aʿmash preserved it accurately from Yazīd b. Ḥayyān. Possible, but least explanatory Model 2 Shared story-world Different Medinan legal and family memories circulated early; the Kūfan route absorbed the broad skeleton and stabilized it with local features. Best fits the fluid matn evidence Model 3 Direct Iraqi borrowing Al-Aʿmash, or a lower Iraqi transmitter, encountered the Hishām-family report during Hishām’s Iraqi period and transmitted a reshaped version through a more Kūfan-friendly chain. Plausible, not directly provable The first model is the apologetic one, but it leaves too much unexplained: why the diagnostic details vanish, why ʿAlī appears, why the route is so narrow below al-Aʿmash, and why a known mudallis transmits the crucial link with ʿan. The third model is attractive, especially because Hishām and al-Aʿmash were contemporaries, because Hishām came to Kūfa, and because his Iraqi transmission from his father was specifically criticized. But it should be presented as a historical hypothesis, not as a documented confession. The second model is the strongest. The story was already circulating in multiple forms: legal residue through al-Zuhrī, family dossier through ʿUrwa/Hishām, and loose angelic-diagnosis material through Yaḥyā b. Maʿmar. The Zayd/al-Aʿmash route then looks like a Kūfan collateral crystallization of that shared story-world, not an independent second anchor. The Political Layer: Why ʿAlī Appears in the Kūfan Version The Zayd route is not merely shorter. It is differently staged. In the Hishām report, the scene belongs to ʿĀʾisha’s room and the Prophet’s private exchange with her. In the Zayd route, ʿĀʾisha disappears, and ʿAlī becomes the operative who retrieves and unties the knots. That shift matters in Kūfa. Zayd b. Arqam settled in Kūfa, transmitted there, and is described in Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb as having witnessed Ṣiffīn with ʿAlī and as having been among his close associates.[^12] Al-Aʿmash, the Kūfan transmitter of the report, is described by al-ʿIjlī as having some Shīʿī leaning.[^13] Neither fact proves forgery. But together they explain why a Kūfan version of the story would be more likely to preserve an ʿAlī-centered action scene than an ʿĀʾisha-centered domestic scene. This is where the older anti-Jewish polemic does not disappear, but it becomes only one layer. The Hishām dossier names a Jewish-allied Medinan culprit and situates the story in a Banū Zurayq setting. The Zayd route preserves the Jewish culprit but makes the salvation mechanics more Kūfan and ʿAlid: Gabriel discloses, ʿAlī retrieves, knots are undone, and the Prophet rises freed. Calling the Zayd route “Kūfan” does not mean every Kūfan report is Shīʿī propaganda, and noting al-Aʿmash’s Shīʿī leaning does not mean he was a sectarian fabricator. The point is subtler: regional audiences shape which details survive. A report tied to ʿĀʾisha’s household could be retold in a form where ʿAlī becomes the decisive agent without the whole story being invented from nothing. The Classical Critics Saw the Pieces, but Not the Whole Problem Classical rijāl criticism gives us the materials needed for the critique, even if it does not always draw the source-critical conclusion. It tells us that Hishām was trustworthy but that his Iraqi father-reports drew criticism. It tells us that al-Aʿmash was trustworthy but a mudallis. It tells us that Yazīd b. Ḥayyān was a real Kūfan transmitter from Zayd and that al-Aʿmash narrated from him. It tells us that Abū Muʿāwiya transmitted from both worlds. What it does not do is ask the modern source-critical question: does the Zayd route independently confirm the Hishām dossier, or does it sit inside the same second-century Iraqi-Medinan circulation network? The answer is that it does not independently confirm it in any strong sense. It is a collateral route, but a compromised one. It may preserve a real Kūfan memory of a known story. It may be a reshaped digest. It may even go back to something Zayd said. But as evidence, it does not do the work apologists often assign to it. What is strong The Hishām dossier is widely collected and has multiple lower transmitters below Hishām. What is weak Above Hishām, the main canonical report still returns to the ʿUrwa family line, and Bukhārī’s own note points to Āl ʿUrwa as an early family-memory source. What is suspicious The Zayd route shares the skeleton but not the diagnostic details, travels through al-Aʿmash’s ʿanʿana, and is narrow below al-Aʿmash. What follows The Zayd route should be treated as a secondary Kūfan collateral, not as a secure independent witness. Conclusion The bewitchment narrative is not supported by two equal pillars. Its main pillar is the ʿĀʾisha → ʿUrwa → Hishām family dossier, with an earlier Medinan legal residue visible through al-Zuhrī and ʿAbd al-Razzāq. The supposed second pillar, Zayd b. Arqam through Yazīd b. Ḥayyān and al-Aʿmash, is too narrow and too contextually exposed to carry the weight of independent corroboration. The most responsible conclusion is not that al-Aʿmash has been caught beyond doubt fabricating an isnād. The evidence does not prove that. The responsible conclusion is more damaging to the apologetic use of the report: the Kūfan route cannot rescue the historicity of the Hishām dossier. It is exactly the kind of route source criticism should hesitate over — a vivid story already circulating in Medinan family and legal contexts, a known Iraqi expansion environment around Hishām, a Kūfan mudallis transmitting with ʿan, and a secondary matn that conveniently replaces ʿĀʾisha’s room with ʿAlī’s action. If the report is defended, it should be defended honestly as a report canonized through Hishām’s family transmission and accepted by later hadith compilers. It should not be presented as if the Zayd b. Arqam route gives independent, multi-regional historical certainty. Source notes The citations below separate the hadith variants, the rijāl evidence, and the source-critical claims. title: Flogging, Torture, and the Transmission of Hadith
description: A source-critical look at how caliphal coercion, court patronage, doctrinal inquisition, and later scholarly boundary-policing shaped the world in which hadith survived.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The standard defense of hadith often imagines transmission as if it took place in a clean scholarly vacuum. A transmitter heard a report, memorized it, passed it to a student, and later critics checked the names. That picture captures one part of the process, but it leaves out the political world in which those transmitters lived. Scholars were not floating above governors, oaths of allegiance, court salaries, prisons, public humiliations, theological inquisitions, and the fear of being marked as a deviant. The question is not whether every hadith was fabricated by rulers. That would be too crude. The stronger argument is more precise: the surviving hadith corpus was filtered through institutions of power. A report could be favored, ignored, sharpened, suppressed, or made dangerous depending on what it did in the political and theological struggles of its age. The hadith tradition should not be treated as a purely scholarly archive that later politics merely quoted. It was produced, transmitted, and canonized inside a coercive environment. Sometimes rulers punished scholars. Sometimes scholars used rulers. Sometimes victorious orthodoxies projected their later dogmas back onto earlier authorities. This does not automatically falsify every report, but it does mean that politically useful reports require source criticism, not pious trust. The evidence is not limited to polemical anecdotes. The same pattern appears in the canonization of Qurʾānic readings, the punishment of Mālik b. Anas, the Abbasid miḥna, later anti-miḥna boundary-policing, and the career of al-Zuhrī at the Umayyad court. These are not identical events, but together they show a historical ecology in which textual authority and political power repeatedly touched each other. Transmission Pressure Map How Power Enters a Religious Archive Political interference does not need to invent every text. It can also decide which texts become safe, repeated, written, taught, and later canonical. 1 Scholarly dispute A jurist, reader, or transmitter holds a position with legal or theological consequences. 2 Political risk The position threatens an oath, a caliphal doctrine, a public canon, or the legitimacy of a ruling faction. 3 Coercive intervention The state or its allies demand recantation, public conformity, written confession, imprisonment, flogging, or exclusion. 4 Archive effect The surviving record begins to look like consensus because losing positions become costly to transmit. ## The Canon Was Not Always Persuasion The case of Ibn Mujāhid is a useful starting point because it shows that the textual disciplines of Islam could become enforceable by state power. Ibn Mujāhid did not merely prefer seven Qurʾānic readings in a private academic sense. In the generation after him, readers who stood outside the emerging canon were tried, pressured, and made to recant. The most vivid case is Ibn Shanabūdh. Al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī reports that he used to read publicly with letters attributed to Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and others, including readings that differed from the ʿUthmānic codex. The matter was raised to the authorities. He was arrested, brought to the house of the vizier Ibn Muqla, and debated in the presence of judges, jurists, and Qurʾān readers. When he refused to abandon the readings, the assembly approved punishment. The report then says that he was stripped, placed between the wooden frames, beaten on the back of the neck about ten times, and only then agreed to repent. A written document of repentance was taken from him.[^1] فَوَجَّهَ السُّلْطَانُ فَقَبَضَ عَلَيْهِ ... وَأَحْضَرَ الْقُضَاةَ وَالْفُقَهَاءَ وَالْقُرَّاءَ ... فَأَمَرَ بِتَجْرِيدِهِ ... وَضَرْبِهِ بِالدِّرَّةِ عَلَى قَفَاهُ ... فَلَمْ يَصْبِرْ وَاسْتَغَاثَ وَأَذْعَنَ بِالرُّجُوعِ وَالتَّوْبَةِ. “The ruler sent and had him seized ... the judges, jurists, and readers were summoned ... he ordered that he be stripped ... and beaten with the whip on the back of his neck ... he could not endure it, cried for help, and submitted to retracting and repenting.” Ibn Miqsam was treated less violently in the surviving report, but the mechanism is the same. He had argued that if a reading had a sound Arabic basis and agreed with the consonantal outline of the muṣḥaf, it could be recited. His critics saw this as opening the door to uncontrolled textual choice. Al-Khaṭīb says the affair reached the authorities, he was brought before readers and jurists, made to repent, and a written record of his repentance was witnessed by those present.[^2] This matters for hadith because the canon of readings and the canon of hadith were built by overlapping kinds of men: readers, transmitters, jurists, judges, viziers, and court-connected scholars. Ibn Mujāhid’s project was scholarly, but its success was not only scholarly. Once a canon becomes enforceable, the surviving “consensus” must be read as the result of both argument and power. The point is not that Qurʾānic readings and hadith are the same discipline. They are not. The point is that both relied on chains, expert communities, public recitation, written transmission, and later canonization. If political enforcement could help close the canon of readings, it is historically naive to assume that hadith transmission was immune from similar pressures. ## Mālik’s Flogging Was About More Than a Legal Detail The punishment of Mālik b. Anas is often softened into a pious anecdote: a great imam was tested, endured, and emerged with higher status. That is true as devotional memory, but the historical content is sharper. The report is not merely about a private legal disagreement. It connects a hadith-based legal opinion to the political legitimacy of the Abbasid oath. The account preserved through al-Wāqidī and transmitted by Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Dhahabī, and others says that Mālik’s rivals reported him to Jaʿfar b. Sulaymān, the Abbasid governor of Medina. They accused him of holding that the people’s oath of allegiance to the Abbasids did not count for anything because he used a report about coerced divorce: **ṭalāq al-mukrah laysa bi-shayʾ**, the divorce of a coerced person is nothing. The governor understood the implication. If legal acts under coercion are invalid, then a coerced bayʿa might also be invalid. Mālik was stripped, stretched out, flogged, and his shoulders were dislocated.[^3] قَالُوا: إِنَّهُ لَا يَرَى أَيْمَانَ بَيْعَتِكُمْ بِشَيْءٍ، وَهُوَ يَأْخُذُ بِحَدِيثٍ رَوَاهُ ... فِي طَلَاقِ الْمُكْرَهِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَجُوزُ ... ثُمَّ جَرَّدَهُ وَمَدَّهُ وَضَرَبَهُ بِالسِّيَاطِ، وَمُدَّتْ يَدُهُ حَتَّى انْخَلَعَ كَتِفَاهُ. “They said: ‘He does not regard the oaths of your allegiance as anything, and he relies on a report ... about the coerced divorce, that it is not valid.’ ... Then he stripped him, stretched him out, and beat him with whips. His arm was pulled until his shoulders were dislocated.” This episode exposes the political stakes of a single legal report. Mālik did not need to preach rebellion. A hadith about coercion was enough to make the governor hear a threat to Abbasid allegiance. The danger came from the report’s legal implication. This is a model for reading politically charged hadith. A report may look abstract when quoted in a later book, but in its original environment it could touch bayʿa, rebellion, taxation, dynastic legitimacy, succession, or the status of defeated rivals. The historical question is not only “is the narrator reliable?” It is also “what did this report do in the world where it circulated?” ## The Miḥna Shows That Hadith Scholars Could Be Broken The Abbasid miḥna is the clearest case of theological coercion in early Sunni memory. Al-Maʾmūn’s officials examined judges and transmitters over the claim that the Qurʾān was created. Those who would not answer correctly could be chained, transported, imprisoned, or threatened with death. Later chronicles describe Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and Muḥammad b. Nūḥ being put in irons after refusing to affirm the doctrine. Under al-Muʿtaṣim, Aḥmad was flogged until he lost consciousness.[^4] The case of Abū Mushir al-Ghassānī is especially important because it shows a hadith transmitter at the point where coercion changes speech. Ibn ʿAsākir and Ibn Ḥajar preserve the report that Abū Mushir was brought from Damascus, asked about the Qurʾān, and refused to say it was created. When the sword and execution mat were called for, he gave the required answer. The authorities did not trust the coerced answer. He was sent to Baghdad, imprisoned, and died soon afterward.[^5] فَسَأَلَهُ عَنِ الْقُرْآنِ فَقَالَ: كَلَامُ اللهِ. وَأَبَى أَنْ يَقُولَ مَخْلُوقٌ. فَدَعَا لَهُ بِالسَّيْفِ وَالنَّطْعِ لِيَضْرِبَ عُنُقَهُ. فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذَلِكَ قَالَ: مَخْلُوقٌ. “He asked him about the Qurʾān, and he said: ‘The speech of God.’ He refused to say ‘created.’ So he called for the sword and the execution mat in order to strike his neck. When he saw that, he said: ‘created.’” This is not a side issue. The miḥna became part of rijāl memory. Later critics discussed who answered under pressure and who refused. Ibn Ḥajar records Aḥmad as saying, “If I were to narrate from anyone who answered in the miḥna, I would have narrated from Abū Maʿmar and Abū Kurayb.”[^6] The statement presumes that the inquisition affected the moral and scholarly standing of transmitters. Coercion was not just a political event. It entered the evaluation of narrators. Before pressure Many possible voices Readers, jurists, transmitters, theologians, court scholars, dissenters, and local teachers all occupy the same public space. → Pressure point Oath, creed, canon, dynasty A report or doctrine becomes dangerous because it touches rule, allegiance, public orthodoxy, or sectarian legitimacy. → After pressure Surviving consensus The archive remembers what remained safe enough, authoritative enough, or useful enough to transmit. ## The Victors Also Policed Boundaries It would be misleading to frame this as “bad rulers versus innocent scholars.” Scholars themselves could ask the state to punish, exclude rivals, and stabilize their own orthodoxy. The Ibn Shanabūdh and Ibn Miqsam cases already show jurists and readers participating in state-backed enforcement. The same phenomenon appears after the miḥna, when anti-created-Qurʾān traditionalism became dominant. Al-Khaṭīb preserves a striking statement from Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā al-Dhuhlī. He declares that whoever says the Qurʾān is created is an unbeliever, separated from his wife, required to repent, and if he does not repent, his neck is to be struck and his property becomes fayʾ for the Muslims. In the same polemical environment, al-Dhuhlī warns against those who attend the sessions of al-Bukhārī during the dispute over “my utterance of the Qurʾān.”[^7] مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ مَخْلُوقٌ فَقَدْ كَفَرَ ... تُسْتَتَابُ فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا ضُرِبَتْ عُنُقُهُ، وَجُعِلَ مَالُهُ فَيْئًا بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ. “Whoever claims that the Qurʾān is created has disbelieved ... He is asked to repent. If he repents, [he is spared]; otherwise his neck is struck and his property is made fayʾ among the Muslims.” This matters because later orthodoxy did not merely preserve earlier doctrine; it also retrojected later doctrine into earlier names. Al-Khaṭīb transmits a report in which Mālik is asked about someone who says the Qurʾān is created and replies, “An unbelieving heretic; take him and kill him.”[^8] But other evidence makes such retrojection suspicious. Ibn Ḥajar preserves Aḥmad’s answer when asked about reports from Mālik and others saying the Qurʾān is uncreated: “I did not hear it.”[^9] The point is not that every anti-miḥna report is forged. The point is that after a doctrinal battle, later transmitters had a strong incentive to recruit earlier authorities. A famous early imam could be made to sound like a later polemicist. That is precisely the kind of retrojection that source criticism must detect. The miḥna is often remembered as the state persecuting the people of hadith. That memory is partly correct. But once the people of hadith won the symbolic battle, their own boundary-policing could become coercive. Power can work through caliphs, judges, crowds, students, schools, and canon-makers. ## Al-Zuhrī: Court Patronage Without Cartoon Villainy No figure illustrates the problem of court-linked transmission better than Muḥammad b. Shihāb al-Zuhrī. He was not a marginal transmitter. He is one of the great hubs of early hadith and sīra transmission. Because of that, his relationship with the Umayyads has to be handled carefully. Calling him a mere “stooge” is too easy, but pretending the court connection does not matter is also dishonest. Classical rijāl material already preserves discomfort. Ibn Ḥajar, quoting al-Ḥākim from Ibn Maʿīn, records a comparison between al-Aʿmash and al-Zuhrī. When someone asked whether al-Aʿmash was like al-Zuhrī, Ibn Maʿīn reportedly answered that al-Aʿmash should be cleared from such a comparison: al-Zuhrī accepted transmission by presentation and license, **worked for Banū Umayya**, while al-Aʿmash was poor, patient, distant from the ruler, pious, and learned in the Qurʾān.[^10] الزُّهْرِيُّ يَرَى الْعَرْضَ وَالْإِجَازَةَ، وَيَعْمَلُ لِبَنِي أُمَيَّةَ، وَالْأَعْمَشُ فَقِيرٌ صَبُورٌ مُجَانِبٌ لِلسُّلْطَانِ، وَرِعٌ عَالِمٌ بِالْقُرْآنِ. “Al-Zuhrī accepted presentation and license, and he worked for Banū Umayya; al-Aʿmash was poor, patient, distant from the ruler, pious, and learned in the Qurʾān.” Other reports complicate the picture. Al-Fasawī records al-Zuhrī traveling with a member of Hishām’s household and mentions that Hishām removed a very large debt from him. Ibn Ḥibbān likewise preserves a report in which Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik pays off thousands of dinars of al-Zuhrī’s debt.[^11] Modern scholarship has therefore treated al-Zuhrī as a court-connected transmitter whose independence cannot simply be assumed, while also warning that court connection does not prove that he fabricated at will. Lecker’s formulation is useful: al-Zuhrī’s long relationship with the Umayyad court makes it implausible to describe him as completely independent, but it does not require reducing him to a puppet; the court may have shaped what he wrote, taught, emphasized, omitted, or softened.[^12] That is the methodological middle ground. Court patronage is not proof of forgery. It is a reason to investigate. When a report through al-Zuhrī flatters Umayyad interests, legitimizes caliphal policy, blunts an embarrassing memory, or supplies sacred geography useful to the court, the proper response is not automatic rejection. It is isnād-cum-matn analysis, variant collection, and comparison with non-court routes. ## What Political Pressure Actually Does to Transmission Political power rarely needs to create an entire archive from nothing. It has subtler tools. It can make one report safer to repeat than another. It can make a legal implication too dangerous to teach publicly. It can sponsor writing, reward useful scholars, punish dissenters, and encourage students to attach later positions to earlier authorities. This produces several archive effects. Effect 1 Selective survival Reports that threaten power may survive only weakly, locally, anonymously, or in hostile quotation. Reports that support power can gain institutional routes. Effect 2 Matn sharpening A vague report can acquire a politically useful clause below the common-link layer: a name, a father-name, a city, a dynasty, a banner, or a legal trigger. Effect 3 Retrojection Later schools place their victorious doctrine in the mouth of earlier imams to make a contested position look ancient. Effect 4 Silencing through risk When transmitting a view carries prison, flogging, public shame, or loss of patronage, silence becomes a rational survival strategy. This is why “but it is in a hadith collection” is not enough. A report can be widely collected and still be late. A report can have a respectable chain and still carry a political addition. A report can be transmitted by a trustworthy person and still reflect the pressures of his patronage network. Classical rijāl criticism noticed some of these problems, but it usually handled them through individual reliability labels. It did not always ask how power shaped the archive itself. ## A Better Test for Politically Charged Hadith The proper response is not blanket rejection. It is a sharper test. First, collect all variants, not just the canonical wording. A politically useful phrase often appears unevenly. If the controversial clause is absent in the simplest route but present in later partial common links, the clause may be secondary. Second, map the common link and partial common links. A report with many collector-level attestations can still collapse into one second-century transmitter. Breadth at the bottom of the diagram is not the same as early independence at the top. Third, ask what the report does. Does it justify a ruler, sanctify a dynasty, criminalize an opposition group, neutralize a rival memory, or give legal cover to a political arrangement? Function does not prove fabrication, but it tells us where motive may lie. Fourth, compare hostile and non-hostile sources. A report that appears only where it serves one faction is weaker than a report preserved across hostile networks without useful alteration. Fifth, check whether later critics noticed discomfort. Sometimes the tradition itself remembers the problem: “he worked for Banū Umayya,” “he answered in the miḥna,” “he was made to repent,” “he transmitted by license,” “he was punished for this opinion.” These remarks are not decoration. They are data. Source-Critical Rule Do not ask only whether the chain is famous. Ask why this wording survived. Variant map: does the political clause appear everywhere or only in selected routes? Common-link map: does the report reach behind the transmitter who benefits from the setting? Function test: what legal, dynastic, sectarian, or theological work does the report perform? Counter-memory: do rival groups preserve, resist, or ignore the report? Archive pressure: who could safely transmit the opposite view? ## The Conclusion The history of hadith transmission contains piety, memory, learning, travel, and real scholarly labor. It also contains coercion. Ibn Shanabūdh was beaten into retracting readings outside the emerging canon. Ibn Miqsam was forced into formal repentance. Mālik’s hadith-based legal position was treated as a threat to Abbasid allegiance. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and others were dragged through the miḥna. Abū Mushir’s answer changed under the shadow of the sword. Later traditionalists could threaten opponents with execution and retroject their theology into earlier imams. Al-Zuhrī’s court career was remembered by critics as a real feature of his transmission profile. None of this proves that every hadith is false. It proves something narrower and more damaging to naive apologetics: hadith did not travel through history untouched by power. The corpus we inherited is not simply “what the Prophet said.” It is what survived through transmitters, patrons, schools, judges, caliphs, students, scribes, punishments, silences, and later acts of canon-making. A serious hadith criticism has to study those pressures directly. Otherwise, the political history of transmission disappears, and the archive is mistaken for the event itself.
