fullText: The standard defense of hadith often imagines transmission as if it took place in a clean scholarly vacuum. A transmitter heard a report, memorized it, passed it to a student, and later critics checked the names. That picture captures one part of the process, but it leaves out the political world in which those transmitters lived. Scholars were not floating above governors, oaths of allegiance, court salaries, prisons, public humiliations, theological inquisitions, and the fear of being marked as a deviant. The question is not whether every hadith was fabricated by rulers. That would be too crude. The stronger argument is more precise: the surviving hadith corpus was filtered through institutions of power. A report could be favored, ignored, sharpened, suppressed, or made dangerous depending on what it did in the political and theological struggles of its age. The hadith tradition should not be treated as a purely scholarly archive that later politics merely quoted. It was produced, transmitted, and canonized inside a coercive environment. Sometimes rulers punished scholars. Sometimes scholars used rulers. Sometimes victorious orthodoxies projected their later dogmas back onto earlier authorities. This does not automatically falsify every report, but it does mean that politically useful reports require source criticism, not pious trust. The evidence is not limited to polemical anecdotes. The same pattern appears in the canonization of Qurʾānic readings, the punishment of Mālik b. Anas, the Abbasid miḥna, later anti-miḥna boundary-policing, and the career of al-Zuhrī at the Umayyad court. These are not identical events, but together they show a historical ecology in which textual authority and political power repeatedly touched each other. Transmission Pressure Map How Power Enters a Religious Archive Political interference does not need to invent every text. It can also decide which texts become safe, repeated, written, taught, and later canonical. 1 Scholarly dispute A jurist, reader, or transmitter holds a position with legal or theological consequences. 2 Political risk The position threatens an oath, a caliphal doctrine, a public canon, or the legitimacy of a ruling faction. 3 Coercive intervention The state or its allies demand recantation, public conformity, written confession, imprisonment, flogging, or exclusion. 4 Archive effect The surviving record begins to look like consensus because losing positions become costly to transmit. The Canon Was Not Always Persuasion The case of Ibn Mujāhid is a useful starting point because it shows that the textual disciplines of Islam could become enforceable by state power. Ibn Mujāhid did not merely prefer seven Qurʾānic readings in a private academic sense. In the generation after him, readers who stood outside the emerging canon were tried, pressured, and made to recant. The most vivid case is Ibn Shanabūdh. Al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī reports that he used to read publicly with letters attributed to Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, and others, including readings that differed from the ʿUthmānic codex. The matter was raised to the authorities. He was arrested, brought to the house of the vizier Ibn Muqla, and debated in the presence of judges, jurists, and Qurʾān readers. When he refused to abandon the readings, the assembly approved punishment. The report then says that he was stripped, placed between the wooden frames, beaten on the back of the neck about ten times, and only then agreed to repent. A written document of repentance was taken from him.[^1] فَوَجَّهَ السُّلْطَانُ فَقَبَضَ عَلَيْهِ ... وَأَحْضَرَ الْقُضَاةَ وَالْفُقَهَاءَ وَالْقُرَّاءَ ... فَأَمَرَ بِتَجْرِيدِهِ ... وَضَرْبِهِ بِالدِّرَّةِ عَلَى قَفَاهُ ... فَلَمْ يَصْبِرْ وَاسْتَغَاثَ وَأَذْعَنَ بِالرُّجُوعِ وَالتَّوْبَةِ. “The ruler sent and had him seized ... the judges, jurists, and readers were summoned ... he ordered that he be stripped ... and beaten with the whip on the back of his neck ... he could not endure it, cried for help, and submitted to retracting and repenting.” Ibn Miqsam was treated less violently in the surviving report, but the mechanism is the same. He had argued that if a reading had a sound Arabic basis and agreed with the consonantal outline of the muṣḥaf, it could be recited. His critics saw this as opening the door to uncontrolled textual choice. Al-Khaṭīb says the affair reached the authorities, he was brought before readers and jurists, made to repent, and a written record of his repentance was witnessed by those present.[^2] This matters for hadith because the canon of readings and the canon of hadith were built by overlapping kinds of men: readers, transmitters, jurists, judges, viziers, and court-connected scholars. Ibn Mujāhid’s project was scholarly, but its success was not only scholarly. Once a canon becomes enforceable, the surviving “consensus” must be read as the result of both argument and power. The point is not that Qurʾānic readings and hadith are the same discipline. They are not. The point is that both relied on chains, expert communities, public recitation, written transmission, and later canonization. If political enforcement could help close the canon of readings, it is historically naive to assume that hadith transmission was immune from similar pressures. Mālik’s Flogging Was About More Than a Legal Detail The punishment of Mālik b. Anas is often softened into a pious anecdote: a great imam was tested, endured, and emerged with higher status. That is true as devotional memory, but the historical content is sharper. The report is not merely about a private legal disagreement. It connects a hadith-based legal opinion to the political legitimacy of the Abbasid oath. The account preserved through al-Wāqidī and transmitted by Ibn Saʿd, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Dhahabī, and others says that Mālik’s rivals reported him to Jaʿfar b. Sulaymān, the Abbasid governor of Medina. They accused him of holding that the people’s oath of allegiance to the Abbasids did not count for anything because he used a report about coerced divorce: **ṭalāq al-mukrah laysa bi-shayʾ**, the divorce of a coerced person is nothing. The governor understood the implication. If legal acts under coercion are invalid, then a coerced bayʿa might also be invalid. Mālik was stripped, stretched out, flogged, and his shoulders were dislocated.[^3] قَالُوا: إِنَّهُ لَا يَرَى أَيْمَانَ بَيْعَتِكُمْ بِشَيْءٍ، وَهُوَ يَأْخُذُ بِحَدِيثٍ رَوَاهُ ... فِي طَلَاقِ الْمُكْرَهِ أَنَّهُ لَا يَجُوزُ ... ثُمَّ جَرَّدَهُ وَمَدَّهُ وَضَرَبَهُ بِالسِّيَاطِ، وَمُدَّتْ يَدُهُ حَتَّى انْخَلَعَ كَتِفَاهُ. “They said: ‘He does not regard the oaths of your allegiance as anything, and he relies on a report ... about the coerced divorce, that it is not valid.’ ... Then he stripped him, stretched him out, and beat him with whips. His arm was pulled until his shoulders were dislocated.” This episode exposes the political stakes of a single legal report. Mālik did not need to preach rebellion. A hadith about coercion was enough to make the governor hear a threat to Abbasid allegiance. The danger came from the report’s legal implication. This is a model for reading politically charged hadith. A report may look abstract when quoted in a later book, but in its original environment it could touch bayʿa, rebellion, taxation, dynastic legitimacy, succession, or the status of defeated rivals. The historical question is not only “is the narrator reliable?” It is also “what did this report do in the world where it circulated?” The Miḥna Shows That Hadith Scholars Could Be Broken The Abbasid miḥna is the clearest case of theological coercion in early Sunni memory. Al-Maʾmūn’s officials examined judges and transmitters over the claim that the Qurʾān was created. Those who would not answer correctly could be chained, transported, imprisoned, or threatened with death. Later chronicles describe Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and Muḥammad b. Nūḥ being put in irons after refusing to affirm the doctrine. Under al-Muʿtaṣim, Aḥmad was flogged until he lost consciousness.[^4] The case of Abū Mushir al-Ghassānī is especially important because it shows a hadith transmitter at the point where coercion changes speech. Ibn ʿAsākir and Ibn Ḥajar preserve the report that Abū Mushir was brought from Damascus, asked about the Qurʾān, and refused to say it was created. When the sword and execution mat were called for, he gave the required answer. The authorities did not trust the coerced answer. He was sent to Baghdad, imprisoned, and died soon afterward.[^5] فَسَأَلَهُ عَنِ الْقُرْآنِ فَقَالَ: كَلَامُ اللهِ. وَأَبَى أَنْ يَقُولَ مَخْلُوقٌ. فَدَعَا لَهُ بِالسَّيْفِ وَالنَّطْعِ لِيَضْرِبَ عُنُقَهُ. فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذَلِكَ قَالَ: مَخْلُوقٌ. “He asked him about the Qurʾān, and he said: ‘The speech of God.’ He refused to say ‘created.’ So he called for the sword and the execution mat in order to strike his neck. When he saw that, he said: ‘created.’” This is not a side issue. The miḥna became part of rijāl memory. Later critics discussed who answered under pressure and who refused. Ibn Ḥajar records Aḥmad as saying, “If I were to narrate from anyone who answered in the miḥna, I would have narrated from Abū Maʿmar and Abū Kurayb.”[^6] The statement presumes that the inquisition affected the moral and scholarly standing of transmitters. Coercion was not just a political event. It entered the evaluation of narrators. Before pressure Many possible voices Readers, jurists, transmitters, theologians, court scholars, dissenters, and local teachers all occupy the same public space. → Pressure point Oath, creed, canon, dynasty A report or doctrine becomes dangerous because it touches rule, allegiance, public orthodoxy, or sectarian legitimacy. → After pressure Surviving consensus The archive remembers what remained safe enough, authoritative enough, or useful enough to transmit. The Victors Also Policed Boundaries It would be misleading to frame this as “bad rulers versus innocent scholars.” Scholars themselves could ask the state to punish, exclude rivals, and stabilize their own orthodoxy. The Ibn Shanabūdh and Ibn Miqsam cases already show jurists and readers participating in state-backed enforcement. The same phenomenon appears after the miḥna, when anti-created-Qurʾān traditionalism became dominant. Al-Khaṭīb preserves a striking statement from Muḥammad b. Yaḥyā al-Dhuhlī. He declares that whoever says the Qurʾān is created is an unbeliever, separated from his wife, required to repent, and if he does not repent, his neck is to be struck and his property becomes fayʾ for the Muslims. In the same polemical environment, al-Dhuhlī warns against those who attend the sessions of al-Bukhārī during the dispute over “my utterance of the Qurʾān.”[^7] مَنْ زَعَمَ أَنَّ الْقُرْآنَ مَخْلُوقٌ فَقَدْ كَفَرَ ... تُسْتَتَابُ فَإِنْ تَابَ وَإِلَّا ضُرِبَتْ عُنُقُهُ، وَجُعِلَ مَالُهُ فَيْئًا بَيْنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ. “Whoever claims that the Qurʾān is created has disbelieved ... He is asked to repent. If he repents, [he is spared]; otherwise his neck is struck and his property is made fayʾ among the Muslims.” This matters because later orthodoxy did not merely preserve earlier doctrine; it also retrojected later doctrine into earlier names. Al-Khaṭīb transmits a report in which Mālik is asked about someone who says the Qurʾān is created and replies, “An unbelieving heretic; take him and kill him.”[^8] But other evidence makes such retrojection suspicious. Ibn Ḥajar preserves Aḥmad’s answer when asked about reports from Mālik and others saying the Qurʾān is uncreated: “I did not hear it.”[^9] The point is not that every anti-miḥna report is forged. The point is that after a doctrinal battle, later transmitters had a strong incentive to recruit earlier authorities. A famous early imam could be made to sound like a later polemicist. That is precisely the kind of retrojection that source criticism must detect. The miḥna is often remembered as the state persecuting the people of hadith. That memory is partly correct. But once the people of hadith won the symbolic battle, their own boundary-policing could become coercive. Power can work through caliphs, judges, crowds, students, schools, and canon-makers. Al-Zuhrī: Court Patronage Without Cartoon Villainy No figure illustrates the problem of court-linked transmission better than Muḥammad b. Shihāb al-Zuhrī. He was not a marginal transmitter. He is one of the great hubs of early hadith and sīra transmission. Because of that, his relationship with the Umayyads has to be handled carefully. Calling him a mere “stooge” is too easy, but pretending the court connection does not matter is also dishonest. Classical rijāl material already preserves discomfort. Ibn Ḥajar, quoting al-Ḥākim from Ibn Maʿīn, records a comparison between al-Aʿmash and al-Zuhrī. When someone asked whether al-Aʿmash was like al-Zuhrī, Ibn Maʿīn reportedly answered that al-Aʿmash should be cleared from such a comparison: al-Zuhrī accepted transmission by presentation and license, **worked for Banū Umayya**, while al-Aʿmash was poor, patient, distant from the ruler, pious, and learned in the Qurʾān.[^10] الزُّهْرِيُّ يَرَى الْعَرْضَ وَالْإِجَازَةَ، وَيَعْمَلُ لِبَنِي أُمَيَّةَ، وَالْأَعْمَشُ فَقِيرٌ صَبُورٌ مُجَانِبٌ لِلسُّلْطَانِ، وَرِعٌ عَالِمٌ بِالْقُرْآنِ. “Al-Zuhrī accepted presentation and license, and he worked for Banū Umayya; al-Aʿmash was poor, patient, distant from the ruler, pious, and learned in the Qurʾān.” Other reports complicate the picture. Al-Fasawī records al-Zuhrī traveling with a member of Hishām’s household and mentions that Hishām removed a very large debt from him. Ibn Ḥibbān likewise preserves a report in which Hishām b. ʿAbd al-Malik pays off thousands of dinars of al-Zuhrī’s debt.[^11] Modern scholarship has therefore treated al-Zuhrī as a court-connected transmitter whose independence cannot simply be assumed, while also warning that court connection does not prove that he fabricated at will. Lecker’s formulation is useful: al-Zuhrī’s long relationship with the Umayyad court makes it implausible to describe him as completely independent, but it does not require reducing him to a puppet; the court may have shaped what he wrote, taught, emphasized, omitted, or softened.[^12] That is the methodological middle ground. Court patronage is not proof of forgery. It is a reason to investigate. When a report through al-Zuhrī flatters Umayyad interests, legitimizes caliphal policy, blunts an embarrassing memory, or supplies sacred geography useful to the court, the proper response is not automatic rejection. It is isnād-cum-matn analysis, variant collection, and comparison with non-court routes. What Political Pressure Actually Does to Transmission Political power rarely needs to create an entire archive from nothing. It has subtler tools. It can make one report safer to repeat than another. It can make a legal implication too dangerous to teach publicly. It can sponsor writing, reward useful scholars, punish dissenters, and encourage students to attach later positions to earlier authorities. This produces several archive effects. Effect 1 Selective survival Reports that threaten power may survive only weakly, locally, anonymously, or in hostile quotation. Reports that support power can gain institutional routes. Effect 2 Matn sharpening A vague report can acquire a politically useful clause below the common-link layer: a name, a father-name, a city, a dynasty, a banner, or a legal trigger. Effect 3 Retrojection Later schools place their victorious doctrine in the mouth of earlier imams to make a contested position look ancient. Effect 4 Silencing through risk When transmitting a view carries prison, flogging, public shame, or loss of patronage, silence becomes a rational survival strategy. This is why “but it is in a hadith collection” is not enough. A report can be widely collected and still be late. A report can have a respectable chain and still carry a political addition. A report can be transmitted by a trustworthy person and still reflect the pressures of his patronage network. Classical rijāl criticism noticed some of these problems, but it usually handled them through individual reliability labels. It did not always ask how power shaped the archive itself. A Better Test for Politically Charged Hadith The proper response is not blanket rejection. It is a sharper test. First, collect all variants, not just the canonical wording. A politically useful phrase often appears unevenly. If the controversial clause is absent in the simplest route but present in later partial common links, the clause may be secondary. Second, map the common link and partial common links. A report with many collector-level attestations can still collapse into one second-century transmitter. Breadth at the bottom of the diagram is not the same as early independence at the top. Third, ask what the report does. Does it justify a ruler, sanctify a dynasty, criminalize an opposition group, neutralize a rival memory, or give legal cover to a political arrangement? Function does not prove fabrication, but it tells us where motive may lie. Fourth, compare hostile and non-hostile sources. A report that appears only where it serves one faction is weaker than a report preserved across hostile networks without useful alteration. Fifth, check whether later critics noticed discomfort. Sometimes the tradition itself remembers the problem: “he worked for Banū Umayya,” “he answered in the miḥna,” “he was made to repent,” “he transmitted by license,” “he was punished for this opinion.” These remarks are not decoration. They are data. Source-Critical Rule Do not ask only whether the chain is famous. Ask why this wording survived. Variant map: does the political clause appear everywhere or only in selected routes? Common-link map: does the report reach behind the transmitter who benefits from the setting? Function test: what legal, dynastic, sectarian, or theological work does the report perform? Counter-memory: do rival groups preserve, resist, or ignore the report? Archive pressure: who could safely transmit the opposite view? The Conclusion The history of hadith transmission contains piety, memory, learning, travel, and real scholarly labor. It also contains coercion. Ibn Shanabūdh was beaten into retracting readings outside the emerging canon. Ibn Miqsam was forced into formal repentance. Mālik’s hadith-based legal position was treated as a threat to Abbasid allegiance. Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and others were dragged through the miḥna. Abū Mushir’s answer changed under the shadow of the sword. Later traditionalists could threaten opponents with execution and retroject their theology into earlier imams. Al-Zuhrī’s court career was remembered by critics as a real feature of his transmission profile. None of this proves that every hadith is false. It proves something narrower and more damaging to naive apologetics: hadith did not travel through history untouched by power. The corpus we inherited is not simply “what the Prophet said.” It is what survived through transmitters, patrons, schools, judges, caliphs, students, scribes, punishments, silences, and later acts of canon-making. A serious hadith criticism has to study those pressures directly. Otherwise, the political history of transmission disappears, and the archive is mistaken for the event itself. title: Hadith Cannot Logically Be Treated as Wahi
description: A source-critical and theological argument for why later hadith reports, even when they preserve genuine prophetic teaching, cannot be identified with divine revelation itself.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: A hadith can be a human report about something the Prophet may have said, done, approved, remembered, inferred, or taught; it cannot logically become *wahi* itself when its wording, context, legal force, and even historical setting reach us through fallible, meaning-based transmission. The argument that hadith are *wahi* usually begins with a sound instinct: the Prophet was not an ordinary religious commentator. He was a messenger. His mission was not merely to recite isolated verses and leave the community with no guidance about worship, judgment, or moral life. The Qurʾān commands obedience to the Messenger, speaks of God teaching the Book and Wisdom, and describes the Prophet as a recipient of revelation. The question is not whether the Prophet was guided by God. The question is whether later hadith reports, collected through human chains, often transmitted by meaning, stabilized centuries after the events they describe, can themselves be classified as divine revelation. Those are not the same question. A prophet can be guided without every later report about him being revelation. A report can preserve a valuable memory without becoming scripture. A narration can carry a true meaning without preserving the revealed form in which that meaning was first known. This distinction matters because the traditional claim often slides between three different things: God’s revelation to the Prophet, the Prophet’s own guidance and judgment, and the later hadith archive. Once those layers are separated, the usual argument becomes much weaker. Source authority Three things are being treated as one thing The Qurʾān is public, recited revelation. The Prophet’s guidance is the historical activity of the Messenger. A hadith is a later report about that activity. The debate over *wahi* often collapses these into a single category. 1 God’s revealed recitation Qurʾān: fixed wording, recited as scripture ↓ 2 Prophetic guidance teaching, judgment, explanation, example ↓ 3 Hadith report human transmission, paraphrase, selection, grading ## The word *wahi* is broader than “scripture” The first problem is semantic. In the Qurʾān, *wahi* does not always mean a scripture revealed to a prophet. God “reveals” to the bee, inspires the mother of Moses, communicates to the angels, and even says that devils “inspire” their allies. The word can denote divine communication, command, inspiration, prompting, or disclosure depending on context.[^1] That broad usage does not make the bee’s instinct scripture. It does not make the mother of Moses a prophetess whose words became a binding book. It does not make every inspired action a second Qurʾān. The Qurʾān’s language therefore cannot be reduced to a simple formula: “wahi equals binding textual revelation.” If someone wants to call the Prophet’s non-Qurʾānic guidance *wahi* in some broad sense, he still has to explain what kind of *wahi* it is, how it was preserved, and whether the later hadith text is identical with it. This is where the argument usually moves too fast. It says: the Prophet received *wahi*; the Prophet taught things outside the Qurʾān; hadith report those teachings; therefore hadith are *wahi*. But the conclusion does not follow. At most, it would show that some prophetic guidance may have had divine support. It does not show that every later report about that guidance is itself divine revelation. The Qurʾānic range of wahi Bees instinctive direction 16:68 Moses’ mother private inspiration 28:7 Angels divine instruction 8:12 Heavens cosmic command 41:12 Devils corrupt prompting 6:121 Messengers prophetic revelation 42:51 The distinction is simple: the Qurʾān can use *wahi* broadly, but the theological status of the Qurʾān is not produced by the word *wahi* alone. It is produced by the Qurʾān’s own claim to be a recited, guarded, detailed, public revelation from God. A hadith report does not inherit that status merely because it is about the Prophet. ## The An-Najm proof does not carry the hadith corpus The most common proof-text is Sūrat al-Najm: The argument is familiar: the Prophet does not speak from desire; it is only revelation revealed; therefore the Prophet’s speech is revelation; therefore hadith are revelation. But that reading imports far more into the passage than the passage says. The immediate context is the Prophet’s revelatory encounter and the message he recites. The passage defends the Messenger against the charge that he is astray or inventing the recitation. It does not say that every later report attributed to him, every paraphrased legal formulation, every remembered judgment, every personal instruction, and every narrator’s reconstruction of an event is *wahi* in the same sense as the Qurʾān.[^2] There is also an internal Qurʾānic problem. The Qurʾān corrects the Prophet in several places. It asks why he permitted something before God made the matter clear, rebukes him in the episode of the blind man, challenges a restriction he imposed on himself, and denies that he has control over certain divine decisions.[^3] These passages do not diminish the Prophet. They clarify his role. He is a messenger guided and corrected by God, not an independent source whose every human judgment is already identical with God’s revealed speech. If every prophetic utterance were automatically *wahi* in the same theological sense as Qurʾān, then the correction passages would lose their force. Correction assumes a difference between the Prophet’s human judgment before correction and God’s revealed judgment after correction. The argument does not deny the Prophet’s authority in his own lifetime. It denies a later category mistake: turning fallible reports about the Prophet into a second body of revelation with divine status. ## “Obey the Messenger” is not “canonize every report” A second proof-text is the Qurʾānic command to obey the Messenger. This is a stronger argument than the careless use of Sūrat al-Najm, because the Qurʾān genuinely commands obedience to the Prophet. But it still does not prove that the hadith corpus is *wahi*. There is a difference between obeying a living messenger and granting scriptural status to a later archive. The first is a direct Qurʾānic duty. The second requires a separate theory of preservation, attribution, wording, scope, contradiction, abrogation, and legal force. The Qurʾān can command obedience to the Messenger without telling later Muslims to treat every report graded *ṣaḥīḥ* by medieval specialists as divine revelation. The logic becomes clearer if we put the categories side by side. Living Messenger Direct authority in the prophetic mission. The community hears, obeys, asks, and is corrected in real time. Later Report A narrated claim about what the Prophet said or did. It must be transmitted, remembered, paraphrased, selected, and authenticated by later people. Qurʾānic Revelation The recited book that defines itself as God’s revealed criterion and is used liturgically as scripture. The traditional theory of *wahi ghayr matlūw*, “unrecited revelation,” emerged to solve this gap. It allows Sunnah or hadith to be treated as revelation while preserving the Qurʾān’s unique status as recited revelation. Modern scholars often describe this as part of the long process by which *sunna* became increasingly identified with hadith literature, especially after al-Shāfiʿī’s legal theory placed prophetic reports at the center of proof.[^4] But that theory does not remove the logical problem. It relocates it. If hadith are unrecited revelation, then where is that revelation now? Is it the exact Arabic wording of each report? The meaning behind the wording? The compiler’s selected version? The jurist’s extracted ruling? The reconstructed common denominator across variants? Once the answer becomes “the meaning,” the claim has shifted from “this text is revelation” to “a fallible human process may have preserved a revealed meaning.” That is a much weaker claim. ## The Qurʾān treats its own wording as revelation, not merely its gist The Qurʾān’s status depends on its revealed wording. Muslims do not recite paraphrases of al-Fātiḥa in prayer. They do not replace *qul huwa God aḥad* with a theologically equivalent sentence and call it Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. Meaning matters, but the Qurʾān’s revealed status is tied to the words themselves. Consider the difference: Revealed wording قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ “Say: He is God, One.” Theological paraphrase قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ “Say: He is God, the Unique One.” The second sentence may be true. It may convey a nearly identical theological idea. But it is not Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. It is not the revealed Qurʾānic wording. It cannot replace the revealed verse in prayer. Its truth does not make it scripture. This is the heart of the hadith problem. If a hadith is admitted to be transmitted by meaning, then the surviving formulation is not the revealed form. If the wording is not the revealed form, then the hadith text before us is not *wahi*. At most it is a report that may convey a meaning thought to derive from prophetic guidance. Calling that “revelation” blurs the distinction between God’s speech and human paraphrase. ## Hadith theory itself allows narration by meaning Classical hadith theory does not require every narrator to preserve the Prophet’s exact wording. The permission of *riwāya bi-l-maʿnā*, narration by meaning, is one of the most important admissions in the tradition’s own theory of transmission. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ explains the rule in the section on transmitting and performing hadith. If a narrator does not understand the words, their meanings, and the differences between expressions, he may not narrate by meaning. But if he is qualified, “the sounder view” allows it. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ explicitly states that the Companions and early predecessors often transmitted one meaning in one matter with different wordings, because their reliance was on the meaning rather than the exact wording.[^5] وَالْأَصَحُّ: جَوَازُ ذَلِكَ فِي الْجَمِيعِ، إِذَا كَانَ عَالِمًا بِمَا وَصَفْنَاهُ قَاطِعًا بِأَنَّهُ أَدَّى مَعْنَى اللَّفْظِ الَّذِي بَلَغَهُ؛ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الَّذِي تَشْهَدُ بِهِ أَحْوَالُ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالسَّلَفِ الْأَوَّلِينَ، وَكَثِيرًا مَا كَانُوا يَنْقُلُونَ مَعْنًى وَاحِدًا فِي أَمْرٍ وَاحِدٍ بِأَلْفَاظٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ، وَمَا ذَلِكَ إِلَّا لِأَنَّ مُعَوَّلَهُمْ كَانَ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى دُونَ اللَّفْظِ. > “The sounder view is that this is permissible in all of it, if he is knowledgeable in the way we have described and certain that he has conveyed the meaning of the wording that reached him. This is what the practice of the Companions and the first predecessors bears witness to. They often transmitted one meaning in one matter with different wordings, and that was only because their reliance was on the meaning rather than the wording.” > > **Source:** Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, *ʿUlūm al-ḥadīth*, type 26, on *riwāya bi-l-maʿnā*. Al-Suyūṭī gives the later summarized rule in *Tadrīb al-rāwī*: the majority of the early and later scholars allowed narration by meaning if the narrator was certain that he conveyed the meaning. He adds that the narrator should say something like “or as he said,” “or the like of it,” when there is uncertainty.[^6] This is a devastating admission for the *wahi* claim. It means that the hadith system itself often authenticates a report without claiming that the exact wording is preserved. But revelation, in the Qurʾānic sense, is not merely a historian’s confidence that a meaning survived. It is God’s disclosed communication. If the surviving text is a narrator’s wording, then the surviving text is not God’s revelation. If the wording is prophetic but not divine, and later transmitters may replace even that prophetic wording with equivalent wording, then the final hadith text is two steps away from revelation: first from divine meaning to prophetic expression, then from prophetic expression to narrator paraphrase. ## Ibn Ḥajar’s practical admission: wide transmission produces variant wording Ibn Ḥajar makes the same point in a different setting. While discussing comprehensive reports and the problem of identifying the Prophet’s exact concise wording, he notes that the way to know such wording is for a hadith’s routes to be few and its wording to agree. If the routes multiply, the wording rarely agrees, because most transmitters restrict themselves to narration by meaning according to what seems to them to preserve the intended sense.[^7] والطريق إلى معرفة ذلك أن تَقِلَّ مخارج الحديث وتتفق ألفاظه، وإلا فإن مخارج الحديث إذا كثرت قلّ أن تتفق ألفاظه؛ لتوارد أكثر الرواة على الاقتصار على الرواية بالمعنى بحسب ما يظهر لأحدهم أنه واف به. > “The way to know that is that the routes of the hadith be few and that its wordings agree. Otherwise, when the routes of a hadith are many, its wordings rarely agree, because most transmitters converge on limiting themselves to narration by meaning according to what appears to each of them to have conveyed it.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, cited from *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 13:250. This is not a hostile modern claim. It is a classical hadith-critical observation. Multiple routes do not necessarily preserve multiple identical copies of the Prophet’s wording. Often, they preserve multiple approximations of a remembered meaning. That may be acceptable for ordinary historical transmission. It is not acceptable for calling the surviving wording *wahi*. ## Even the corpus preserves a boundary around Qurʾān One report in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* is especially important because it preserves a memory of documentary separation between Qurʾān and non-Qurʾānic material. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports that the Prophet said: لاَ تَكْتُبُوا عَنِّي، وَمَنْ كَتَبَ عَنِّي غَيْرَ الْقُرْآنِ فَلْيَمْحُهُ، وَحَدِّثُوا عَنِّي وَلاَ حَرَجَ، وَمَنْ كَذَبَ عَلَيَّ — قَالَ هَمَّامٌ: أَحْسِبُهُ قَالَ — مُتَعَمِّدًا، فَلْيَتَبَوَّأْ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنَ النَّارِ. > “Do not write from me. Whoever wrote from me anything other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it. Narrate from me, and there is no harm. Whoever lies against me — Hammām said: I think he said ‘deliberately’ — let him take his seat in the Fire.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 3004. Traditional scholars usually explain this report by saying that the Prophet temporarily forbade writing hadith to prevent confusion with the Qurʾān, then later allowed writing. That explanation may solve a legal question about writing. It does not erase the theological boundary preserved in the report. The Qurʾān is the thing that must not be confused with the Prophet’s other speech. Even within the hadith corpus, the Qurʾān is treated as a distinct written revelation whose documentary status differs from non-Qurʾānic reports.[^8] Michael Cook’s study of early opposition to writing tradition is useful here. He shows that the anti-writing material was not a fantasy produced in an illiterate world. It belonged to a literate environment in which some transmitters still valued oral transmission and resisted turning traditions into fixed written texts. He describes the standard prophetic anti-writing report as a major tradition with a recognizable early transmission profile.[^9] The point is not that all hadith-writing was permanently forbidden. The point is that early Muslims themselves knew there was a category difference between the Qurʾān and other transmitted material. The later doctrine of hadith as unrecited revelation tries to narrow that difference. The early documentary anxiety widens it. ## The women-leadership report as a test case The strongest way to see the problem is to follow a concrete hadith across variants. The report about a people ruled by a woman is useful because it is famous, legally and politically consequential, and transmitted through recognizable routes from Abū Bakra. Al-Bazzār, after citing one version, makes a revealing source-critical note: وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ قَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي بَكْرَةَ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ، وَلَا نَعْلَمُ رَوَاهُ غَيْرُ أَبِي بَكْرَةَ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ. > “This hadith has been narrated from Abū Bakra through several routes, and we do not know that anyone besides Abū Bakra narrated it from the Prophet.” > > **Source:** al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 3113. That is already important. The report is not a public prophetic maxim preserved by many Companions. It is a bottlenecked Companion memory with several later routes. When we compare the wording, the report begins to behave exactly as hadith theory predicts: the meaning is relatively stable, but the wording and framing shift. Source Historical frame Prophetic wording What changed? al-Ṭayālisī 919; Aḥmad 20402 No Persian scene preserved لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ أَسْنَدُوا أَمْرَهُمْ إِلَى امْرَأَةٍ General maxim; “entrusted their affair.” Aḥmad 20518 No developed Persian scene لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ تَمْلِكُهُمْ امْرَأَةٌ Verb shifts to “a woman rules them.” Bukhārī 4425 / 7099 News reaches the Prophet that Persians placed Kisrā’s daughter over them لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً Persian setting and “appointed over their affair.” al-Ḥākim 4608 Kisrā dies; the Prophet asks, “Who succeeded him?” لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً Dialogue added; ʿĀʾisha/Jamal application explicit. al-Ḥākim 7790 King of Dhū Yazan dies; a woman is appointed لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ تَمْلِكُهُمُ امْرَأَةٌ Historical frame shifts from Persia to Yemen. The report’s legal meaning is recognizable across the variants, but the exact form is not. The negation, verbs, syntax, framing, historical referent, dialogue, and political application shift across the tradition family. That does not automatically prove fabrication. It proves something narrower and more relevant: the hadith is not being transmitted as a fixed revealed text. It is being transmitted as a remembered meaning, adapted into different narrative frames.[^10] That is enough to break the *wahi* claim. The issue is not whether the report is morally acceptable, legally valid, historically plausible, or politically weaponized. The issue here is textual status. A revealed text cannot be “the same revelation” when one version says Persia, another says Dhū Yazan, one says “they entrusted their affair,” another says “a woman rules them,” and another inserts a dialogue about succession. These may be narrations about an alleged prophetic statement. They are not a stable revealed utterance. ## If the meaning is revelation, who decides the meaning? A defender may answer: “The wording is not revelation, but the meaning is revelation.” This is the usual escape route. But it creates a new problem: who determines the revealed meaning when the wordings differ? In practice, the answer is not “God.” The answer is a human discipline: transmitter criticism, matn comparison, juristic preference, compiler selection, reconciliation, abrogation theory, and legal interpretation. The revealed meaning is reconstructed by scholars. That reconstruction may be careful. It may be pious. It may be intellectually impressive. But it is not identical with revelation. How “revealed meaning” is reconstructed Variant reports → Hadith grading → Matn comparison → Juristic extraction → Claimed ruling The final legal or theological meaning is not simply “the revelation.” It is a scholarly conclusion drawn from transmitted materials. This is why the word *wahi* becomes misleading. It gives divine certainty to a human inferential process. A hadith critic can say: “This report probably preserves a prophetic teaching.” A jurist can say: “This report is sufficient for legal action.” A theologian can say: “The Prophet was guided by God in his teaching.” But none of those statements logically entails: “This transmitted hadith text is divine revelation.” ## The āḥād problem: probability cannot become revelation by naming it revelation A further problem is epistemological. Large parts of the hadith corpus are solitary or limited-channel reports, *akhbār al-āḥād*. Many classical legal theorists held that such reports yield probable knowledge, *ẓann*, while still being legally actionable. That is already a concession that the report’s epistemic status is not the same as the Qurʾān’s public recited certainty.[^11] This creates a dilemma: If hadith are revelation Then revelation is being mediated through probabilistic chains, narrator memory, paraphrase, and later grading. If hadith are probable reports Then they may be used as historical or legal evidence by those who accept that method, but they are not revelation itself. Traditionalists sometimes try to solve this by saying that sound reports can produce certainty when supported by external indicators, communal acceptance, or canonical placement. But that again confirms the point: the certainty is produced by a later scholarly apparatus. It is not identical with the original revelatory event. A report does not become *wahi* because a later community decides to treat it as reliable. ## Hadith qudsī does not solve the problem The same logic applies to *ḥadīth qudsī*. These reports are introduced as words from God conveyed by the Prophet, but they remain hadith reports. They have chains, variants, gradings, and transmission histories. They are not recited as Qurʾān, not arranged in the muṣḥaf, not protected by the same liturgical and textual system, and not treated as Qurʾānic wording. A *ḥadīth qudsī* may say “God said,” but the report that God said it is still a report. The historian still asks who transmitted it, through which route, with what wording, in what collection, and with what variants. If the wording differs, the same question returns: is the revelation the wording, the meaning, the compiler’s selection, or the later paraphrase? A report that claims to quote God is not automatically God’s speech. It is a humanly transmitted claim that God said something. That claim requires authentication before it can be believed, and authentication is not revelation. ## The Qurʾān’s own source boundary The Qurʾān repeatedly presents itself as the revealed criterion, the detailed book, and the sufficient basis for judging religious claims. These verses do not merely say that the Qurʾān is important. They establish a boundary around what is being sent down as binding revelation. The Qurʾān also warns against following conjecture in matters where one lacks knowledge. A hadith-centered theologian may respond that authentic hadith are not conjecture because the hadith sciences establish their reliability. That response may work inside the hadith-theoretical system. It does not answer the logical problem. The hadith sciences are still human sciences. They evaluate narrators, compare chains, classify defects, and assign probabilities. They do not convert fallible transmission into divine speech. The Qurʾān even warns the Prophet himself about attributing speech to God: This passage makes sense only if there is a strict boundary between what is recited as God’s revelation and what is not. The Prophet is not free to place his own sayings into God’s mouth. Later transmitters are even less free to do so. ## The strongest version of the traditional view, and why it still fails The strongest traditional view should be stated fairly: > The Qurʾān is *wahi matlūw*, recited revelation. The Sunnah is *wahi ghayr matlūw*, unrecited revelation. The meanings of the Prophet’s binding teachings come from God, while the Qurʾān alone has the special status of inimitable recited wording. This position is more sophisticated than saying every hadith wording is God’s literal speech. But it still faces four problems. 1. Category problem It identifies God’s guidance to the Prophet with later reports about that guidance. 2. Textual problem Hadith wording is often transmitted by meaning, so the surviving text is not a revealed wording. 3. Epistemic problem Many reports rest on limited chains and yield probability, not public scriptural certainty. 4. Interpretive problem The “revealed meaning” must be reconstructed by jurists and hadith critics from conflicting forms. The position can be made coherent only by reducing “revelation” to something like “a divine meaning that may lie behind some historically authenticated reports.” But that is not what people usually mean when they tell ordinary Muslims that hadith are *wahi*. They usually mean that hadith possess divine authority comparable to the Qurʾān. The evidence does not support that leap. ## A report about revelation is not revelation This is the cleanest way to state the argument. A report may be about revelation without being revelation. A historian may write that God revealed a verse; the historian’s sentence is not the verse. A Companion may report that the Prophet said something; the report is not the prophetic event itself. A compiler may preserve a chain; the compiler’s selected wording is not automatically the original wording. A jurist may extract a rule; the rule is not the revealed speech. Revelation God’s disclosed communication Prophetic event the Prophet teaches, judges, acts, or explains Memory a Companion or Successor remembers and frames it Report a chain and matn are transmitted, often by meaning Doctrine later scholars classify, reconcile, and legislate The traditional claim skips the middle of this ladder. It starts with revelation and ends with the hadith book. But the middle is the entire problem. ## What can still be granted A precise argument should not overstate itself. It does not need to claim that every hadith is fabricated. It does not need to claim that the Prophet never gave binding instruction. It does not need to deny that early Muslims preserved valuable memories. It does not even need to deny that some hadith may preserve the Prophet’s teachings in substance. The claim is narrower and stronger: Even if a hadith preserves a genuine prophetic teaching, the hadith text as transmitted is still a human report. If it is transmitted by meaning, stabilized through variants, and authenticated by probabilistic scholarly judgment, it cannot logically be classified as divine revelation itself. That is why the *wahi* label is so dangerous. It transfers the certainty of God’s speech to the uncertainty of human transmission. It turns a report into a source. It turns a source into a scripture. Then it calls resistance to that move resistance to the Prophet. The better distinction is this: the Qurʾān is revelation. The Prophet was a messenger guided by revelation. Hadith are later reports about the Prophet. Those reports may be studied, compared, criticized, and sometimes historically valued. But they are not *wahi*. Hadith cannot logically be treated as *wahi* in the Qurʾānic sense. The Qurʾān is fixed, recited revelation. Hadith are transmitted reports, often narrated by meaning, preserved through variant wordings, and authenticated by human judgment. The most that can be claimed is that some hadith may preserve traces of prophetic guidance. That does not make the hadith corpus a second revelation. A report about guidance is not the same thing as revelation from God. ## Source notes [^1]: For the Qurʾānic semantic range of *wahi*, see Qurʾān 16:68, 28:7, 8:12, 6:121, 41:12, and 42:51. fullText: A hadith can be a human report about something the Prophet may have said, done, approved, remembered, inferred, or taught; it cannot logically become *wahi* itself when its wording, context, legal force, and even historical setting reach us through fallible, meaning-based transmission. The argument that hadith are *wahi* usually begins with a sound instinct: the Prophet was not an ordinary religious commentator. He was a messenger. His mission was not merely to recite isolated verses and leave the community with no guidance about worship, judgment, or moral life. The Qurʾān commands obedience to the Messenger, speaks of God teaching the Book and Wisdom, and describes the Prophet as a recipient of revelation. The question is not whether the Prophet was guided by God. The question is whether later hadith reports, collected through human chains, often transmitted by meaning, stabilized centuries after the events they describe, can themselves be classified as divine revelation. Those are not the same question. A prophet can be guided without every later report about him being revelation. A report can preserve a valuable memory without becoming scripture. A narration can carry a true meaning without preserving the revealed form in which that meaning was first known. This distinction matters because the traditional claim often slides between three different things: God’s revelation to the Prophet, the Prophet’s own guidance and judgment, and the later hadith archive. Once those layers are separated, the usual argument becomes much weaker. Source authority Three things are being treated as one thing The Qurʾān is public, recited revelation. The Prophet’s guidance is the historical activity of the Messenger. A hadith is a later report about that activity. The debate over *wahi* often collapses these into a single category. 1 God’s revealed recitation Qurʾān: fixed wording, recited as scripture ↓ 2 Prophetic guidance teaching, judgment, explanation, example ↓ 3 Hadith report human transmission, paraphrase, selection, grading The word *wahi* is broader than “scripture” The first problem is semantic. In the Qurʾān, *wahi* does not always mean a scripture revealed to a prophet. God “reveals” to the bee, inspires the mother of Moses, communicates to the angels, and even says that devils “inspire” their allies. The word can denote divine communication, command, inspiration, prompting, or disclosure depending on context.[^1] That broad usage does not make the bee’s instinct scripture. It does not make the mother of Moses a prophetess whose words became a binding book. It does not make every inspired action a second Qurʾān. The Qurʾān’s language therefore cannot be reduced to a simple formula: “wahi equals binding textual revelation.” If someone wants to call the Prophet’s non-Qurʾānic guidance *wahi* in some broad sense, he still has to explain what kind of *wahi* it is, how it was preserved, and whether the later hadith text is identical with it. This is where the argument usually moves too fast. It says: the Prophet received *wahi*; the Prophet taught things outside the Qurʾān; hadith report those teachings; therefore hadith are *wahi*. But the conclusion does not follow. At most, it would show that some prophetic guidance may have had divine support. It does not show that every later report about that guidance is itself divine revelation. The Qurʾānic range of wahi Bees instinctive direction 16:68 Moses’ mother private inspiration 28:7 Angels divine instruction 8:12 Heavens cosmic command 41:12 Devils corrupt prompting 6:121 Messengers prophetic revelation 42:51 The distinction is simple: the Qurʾān can use *wahi* broadly, but the theological status of the Qurʾān is not produced by the word *wahi* alone. It is produced by the Qurʾān’s own claim to be a recited, guarded, detailed, public revelation from God. A hadith report does not inherit that status merely because it is about the Prophet. The An-Najm proof does not carry the hadith corpus The most common proof-text is Sūrat al-Najm: The argument is familiar: the Prophet does not speak from desire; it is only revelation revealed; therefore the Prophet’s speech is revelation; therefore hadith are revelation. But that reading imports far more into the passage than the passage says. The immediate context is the Prophet’s revelatory encounter and the message he recites. The passage defends the Messenger against the charge that he is astray or inventing the recitation. It does not say that every later report attributed to him, every paraphrased legal formulation, every remembered judgment, every personal instruction, and every narrator’s reconstruction of an event is *wahi* in the same sense as the Qurʾān.[^2] There is also an internal Qurʾānic problem. The Qurʾān corrects the Prophet in several places. It asks why he permitted something before God made the matter clear, rebukes him in the episode of the blind man, challenges a restriction he imposed on himself, and denies that he has control over certain divine decisions.[^3] These passages do not diminish the Prophet. They clarify his role. He is a messenger guided and corrected by God, not an independent source whose every human judgment is already identical with God’s revealed speech. If every prophetic utterance were automatically *wahi* in the same theological sense as Qurʾān, then the correction passages would lose their force. Correction assumes a difference between the Prophet’s human judgment before correction and God’s revealed judgment after correction. The argument does not deny the Prophet’s authority in his own lifetime. It denies a later category mistake: turning fallible reports about the Prophet into a second body of revelation with divine status. “Obey the Messenger” is not “canonize every report” A second proof-text is the Qurʾānic command to obey the Messenger. This is a stronger argument than the careless use of Sūrat al-Najm, because the Qurʾān genuinely commands obedience to the Prophet. But it still does not prove that the hadith corpus is *wahi*. There is a difference between obeying a living messenger and granting scriptural status to a later archive. The first is a direct Qurʾānic duty. The second requires a separate theory of preservation, attribution, wording, scope, contradiction, abrogation, and legal force. The Qurʾān can command obedience to the Messenger without telling later Muslims to treat every report graded *ṣaḥīḥ* by medieval specialists as divine revelation. The logic becomes clearer if we put the categories side by side. Living Messenger Direct authority in the prophetic mission. The community hears, obeys, asks, and is corrected in real time. Later Report A narrated claim about what the Prophet said or did. It must be transmitted, remembered, paraphrased, selected, and authenticated by later people. Qurʾānic Revelation The recited book that defines itself as God’s revealed criterion and is used liturgically as scripture. The traditional theory of *wahi ghayr matlūw*, “unrecited revelation,” emerged to solve this gap. It allows Sunnah or hadith to be treated as revelation while preserving the Qurʾān’s unique status as recited revelation. Modern scholars often describe this as part of the long process by which *sunna* became increasingly identified with hadith literature, especially after al-Shāfiʿī’s legal theory placed prophetic reports at the center of proof.[^4] But that theory does not remove the logical problem. It relocates it. If hadith are unrecited revelation, then where is that revelation now? Is it the exact Arabic wording of each report? The meaning behind the wording? The compiler’s selected version? The jurist’s extracted ruling? The reconstructed common denominator across variants? Once the answer becomes “the meaning,” the claim has shifted from “this text is revelation” to “a fallible human process may have preserved a revealed meaning.” That is a much weaker claim. The Qurʾān treats its own wording as revelation, not merely its gist The Qurʾān’s status depends on its revealed wording. Muslims do not recite paraphrases of al-Fātiḥa in prayer. They do not replace *qul huwa God aḥad* with a theologically equivalent sentence and call it Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. Meaning matters, but the Qurʾān’s revealed status is tied to the words themselves. Consider the difference: Revealed wording قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ “Say: He is God, One.” Theological paraphrase قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ “Say: He is God, the Unique One.” The second sentence may be true. It may convey a nearly identical theological idea. But it is not Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ. It is not the revealed Qurʾānic wording. It cannot replace the revealed verse in prayer. Its truth does not make it scripture. This is the heart of the hadith problem. If a hadith is admitted to be transmitted by meaning, then the surviving formulation is not the revealed form. If the wording is not the revealed form, then the hadith text before us is not *wahi*. At most it is a report that may convey a meaning thought to derive from prophetic guidance. Calling that “revelation” blurs the distinction between God’s speech and human paraphrase. Hadith theory itself allows narration by meaning Classical hadith theory does not require every narrator to preserve the Prophet’s exact wording. The permission of *riwāya bi-l-maʿnā*, narration by meaning, is one of the most important admissions in the tradition’s own theory of transmission. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ explains the rule in the section on transmitting and performing hadith. If a narrator does not understand the words, their meanings, and the differences between expressions, he may not narrate by meaning. But if he is qualified, “the sounder view” allows it. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ explicitly states that the Companions and early predecessors often transmitted one meaning in one matter with different wordings, because their reliance was on the meaning rather than the exact wording.[^5] وَالْأَصَحُّ: جَوَازُ ذَلِكَ فِي الْجَمِيعِ، إِذَا كَانَ عَالِمًا بِمَا وَصَفْنَاهُ قَاطِعًا بِأَنَّهُ أَدَّى مَعْنَى اللَّفْظِ الَّذِي بَلَغَهُ؛ لِأَنَّ ذَلِكَ هُوَ الَّذِي تَشْهَدُ بِهِ أَحْوَالُ الصَّحَابَةِ وَالسَّلَفِ الْأَوَّلِينَ، وَكَثِيرًا مَا كَانُوا يَنْقُلُونَ مَعْنًى وَاحِدًا فِي أَمْرٍ وَاحِدٍ بِأَلْفَاظٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ، وَمَا ذَلِكَ إِلَّا لِأَنَّ مُعَوَّلَهُمْ كَانَ عَلَى الْمَعْنَى دُونَ اللَّفْظِ. > “The sounder view is that this is permissible in all of it, if he is knowledgeable in the way we have described and certain that he has conveyed the meaning of the wording that reached him. This is what the practice of the Companions and the first predecessors bears witness to. They often transmitted one meaning in one matter with different wordings, and that was only because their reliance was on the meaning rather than the wording.” > > **Source:** Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, *ʿUlūm al-ḥadīth*, type 26, on *riwāya bi-l-maʿnā*. Al-Suyūṭī gives the later summarized rule in *Tadrīb al-rāwī*: the majority of the early and later scholars allowed narration by meaning if the narrator was certain that he conveyed the meaning. He adds that the narrator should say something like “or as he said,” “or the like of it,” when there is uncertainty.[^6] This is a devastating admission for the *wahi* claim. It means that the hadith system itself often authenticates a report without claiming that the exact wording is preserved. But revelation, in the Qurʾānic sense, is not merely a historian’s confidence that a meaning survived. It is God’s disclosed communication. If the surviving text is a narrator’s wording, then the surviving text is not God’s revelation. If the wording is prophetic but not divine, and later transmitters may replace even that prophetic wording with equivalent wording, then the final hadith text is two steps away from revelation: first from divine meaning to prophetic expression, then from prophetic expression to narrator paraphrase. Ibn Ḥajar’s practical admission: wide transmission produces variant wording Ibn Ḥajar makes the same point in a different setting. While discussing comprehensive reports and the problem of identifying the Prophet’s exact concise wording, he notes that the way to know such wording is for a hadith’s routes to be few and its wording to agree. If the routes multiply, the wording rarely agrees, because most transmitters restrict themselves to narration by meaning according to what seems to them to preserve the intended sense.[^7] والطريق إلى معرفة ذلك أن تَقِلَّ مخارج الحديث وتتفق ألفاظه، وإلا فإن مخارج الحديث إذا كثرت قلّ أن تتفق ألفاظه؛ لتوارد أكثر الرواة على الاقتصار على الرواية بالمعنى بحسب ما يظهر لأحدهم أنه واف به. > “The way to know that is that the routes of the hadith be few and that its wordings agree. Otherwise, when the routes of a hadith are many, its wordings rarely agree, because most transmitters converge on limiting themselves to narration by meaning according to what appears to each of them to have conveyed it.” > > **Source:** Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, cited from *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 13:250. This is not a hostile modern claim. It is a classical hadith-critical observation. Multiple routes do not necessarily preserve multiple identical copies of the Prophet’s wording. Often, they preserve multiple approximations of a remembered meaning. That may be acceptable for ordinary historical transmission. It is not acceptable for calling the surviving wording *wahi*. Even the corpus preserves a boundary around Qurʾān One report in *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim* is especially important because it preserves a memory of documentary separation between Qurʾān and non-Qurʾānic material. Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī reports that the Prophet said: لاَ تَكْتُبُوا عَنِّي، وَمَنْ كَتَبَ عَنِّي غَيْرَ الْقُرْآنِ فَلْيَمْحُهُ، وَحَدِّثُوا عَنِّي وَلاَ حَرَجَ، وَمَنْ كَذَبَ عَلَيَّ — قَالَ هَمَّامٌ: أَحْسِبُهُ قَالَ — مُتَعَمِّدًا، فَلْيَتَبَوَّأْ مَقْعَدَهُ مِنَ النَّارِ. > “Do not write from me. Whoever wrote from me anything other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it. Narrate from me, and there is no harm. Whoever lies against me — Hammām said: I think he said ‘deliberately’ — let him take his seat in the Fire.” > > **Source:** Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 3004. Traditional scholars usually explain this report by saying that the Prophet temporarily forbade writing hadith to prevent confusion with the Qurʾān, then later allowed writing. That explanation may solve a legal question about writing. It does not erase the theological boundary preserved in the report. The Qurʾān is the thing that must not be confused with the Prophet’s other speech. Even within the hadith corpus, the Qurʾān is treated as a distinct written revelation whose documentary status differs from non-Qurʾānic reports.[^8] Michael Cook’s study of early opposition to writing tradition is useful here. He shows that the anti-writing material was not a fantasy produced in an illiterate world. It belonged to a literate environment in which some transmitters still valued oral transmission and resisted turning traditions into fixed written texts. He describes the standard prophetic anti-writing report as a major tradition with a recognizable early transmission profile.[^9] The point is not that all hadith-writing was permanently forbidden. The point is that early Muslims themselves knew there was a category difference between the Qurʾān and other transmitted material. The later doctrine of hadith as unrecited revelation tries to narrow that difference. The early documentary anxiety widens it. The women-leadership report as a test case The strongest way to see the problem is to follow a concrete hadith across variants. The report about a people ruled by a woman is useful because it is famous, legally and politically consequential, and transmitted through recognizable routes from Abū Bakra. Al-Bazzār, after citing one version, makes a revealing source-critical note: وَهَذَا الْحَدِيثُ قَدْ رُوِيَ عَنْ أَبِي بَكْرَةَ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ، وَلَا نَعْلَمُ رَوَاهُ غَيْرُ أَبِي بَكْرَةَ عَنِ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ. > “This hadith has been narrated from Abū Bakra through several routes, and we do not know that anyone besides Abū Bakra narrated it from the Prophet.” > > **Source:** al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 3113. That is already important. The report is not a public prophetic maxim preserved by many Companions. It is a bottlenecked Companion memory with several later routes. When we compare the wording, the report begins to behave exactly as hadith theory predicts: the meaning is relatively stable, but the wording and framing shift. Source Historical frame Prophetic wording What changed? al-Ṭayālisī 919; Aḥmad 20402 No Persian scene preserved لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ أَسْنَدُوا أَمْرَهُمْ إِلَى امْرَأَةٍ General maxim; “entrusted their affair.” Aḥmad 20518 No developed Persian scene لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ تَمْلِكُهُمْ امْرَأَةٌ Verb shifts to “a woman rules them.” Bukhārī 4425 / 7099 News reaches the Prophet that Persians placed Kisrā’s daughter over them لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً Persian setting and “appointed over their affair.” al-Ḥākim 4608 Kisrā dies; the Prophet asks, “Who succeeded him?” لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ وَلَّوْا أَمْرَهُمُ امْرَأَةً Dialogue added; ʿĀʾisha/Jamal application explicit. al-Ḥākim 7790 King of Dhū Yazan dies; a woman is appointed لَنْ يُفْلِحَ قَوْمٌ تَمْلِكُهُمُ امْرَأَةٌ Historical frame shifts from Persia to Yemen. The report’s legal meaning is recognizable across the variants, but the exact form is not. The negation, verbs, syntax, framing, historical referent, dialogue, and political application shift across the tradition family. That does not automatically prove fabrication. It proves something narrower and more relevant: the hadith is not being transmitted as a fixed revealed text. It is being transmitted as a remembered meaning, adapted into different narrative frames.[^10] That is enough to break the *wahi* claim. The issue is not whether the report is morally acceptable, legally valid, historically plausible, or politically weaponized. The issue here is textual status. A revealed text cannot be “the same revelation” when one version says Persia, another says Dhū Yazan, one says “they entrusted their affair,” another says “a woman rules them,” and another inserts a dialogue about succession. These may be narrations about an alleged prophetic statement. They are not a stable revealed utterance. If the meaning is revelation, who decides the meaning? A defender may answer: “The wording is not revelation, but the meaning is revelation.” This is the usual escape route. But it creates a new problem: who determines the revealed meaning when the wordings differ? In practice, the answer is not “God.” The answer is a human discipline: transmitter criticism, matn comparison, juristic preference, compiler selection, reconciliation, abrogation theory, and legal interpretation. The revealed meaning is reconstructed by scholars. That reconstruction may be careful. It may be pious. It may be intellectually impressive. But it is not identical with revelation. How “revealed meaning” is reconstructed Variant reports → Hadith grading → Matn comparison → Juristic extraction → Claimed ruling The final legal or theological meaning is not simply “the revelation.” It is a scholarly conclusion drawn from transmitted materials. This is why the word *wahi* becomes misleading. It gives divine certainty to a human inferential process. A hadith critic can say: “This report probably preserves a prophetic teaching.” A jurist can say: “This report is sufficient for legal action.” A theologian can say: “The Prophet was guided by God in his teaching.” But none of those statements logically entails: “This transmitted hadith text is divine revelation.” The āḥād problem: probability cannot become revelation by naming it revelation A further problem is epistemological. Large parts of the hadith corpus are solitary or limited-channel reports, *akhbār al-āḥād*. Many classical legal theorists held that such reports yield probable knowledge, *ẓann*, while still being legally actionable. That is already a concession that the report’s epistemic status is not the same as the Qurʾān’s public recited certainty.[^11] This creates a dilemma: If hadith are revelation Then revelation is being mediated through probabilistic chains, narrator memory, paraphrase, and later grading. If hadith are probable reports Then they may be used as historical or legal evidence by those who accept that method, but they are not revelation itself. Traditionalists sometimes try to solve this by saying that sound reports can produce certainty when supported by external indicators, communal acceptance, or canonical placement. But that again confirms the point: the certainty is produced by a later scholarly apparatus. It is not identical with the original revelatory event. A report does not become *wahi* because a later community decides to treat it as reliable. Hadith qudsī does not solve the problem The same logic applies to *ḥadīth qudsī*. These reports are introduced as words from God conveyed by the Prophet, but they remain hadith reports. They have chains, variants, gradings, and transmission histories. They are not recited as Qurʾān, not arranged in the muṣḥaf, not protected by the same liturgical and textual system, and not treated as Qurʾānic wording. A *ḥadīth qudsī* may say “God said,” but the report that God said it is still a report. The historian still asks who transmitted it, through which route, with what wording, in what collection, and with what variants. If the wording differs, the same question returns: is the revelation the wording, the meaning, the compiler’s selection, or the later paraphrase? A report that claims to quote God is not automatically God’s speech. It is a humanly transmitted claim that God said something. That claim requires authentication before it can be believed, and authentication is not revelation. The Qurʾān’s own source boundary The Qurʾān repeatedly presents itself as the revealed criterion, the detailed book, and the sufficient basis for judging religious claims. These verses do not merely say that the Qurʾān is important. They establish a boundary around what is being sent down as binding revelation. The Qurʾān also warns against following conjecture in matters where one lacks knowledge. A hadith-centered theologian may respond that authentic hadith are not conjecture because the hadith sciences establish their reliability. That response may work inside the hadith-theoretical system. It does not answer the logical problem. The hadith sciences are still human sciences. They evaluate narrators, compare chains, classify defects, and assign probabilities. They do not convert fallible transmission into divine speech. The Qurʾān even warns the Prophet himself about attributing speech to God: This passage makes sense only if there is a strict boundary between what is recited as God’s revelation and what is not. The Prophet is not free to place his own sayings into God’s mouth. Later transmitters are even less free to do so. The strongest version of the traditional view, and why it still fails The strongest traditional view should be stated fairly: > The Qurʾān is *wahi matlūw*, recited revelation. The Sunnah is *wahi ghayr matlūw*, unrecited revelation. The meanings of the Prophet’s binding teachings come from God, while the Qurʾān alone has the special status of inimitable recited wording. This position is more sophisticated than saying every hadith wording is God’s literal speech. But it still faces four problems. 1. Category problem It identifies God’s guidance to the Prophet with later reports about that guidance. 2. Textual problem Hadith wording is often transmitted by meaning, so the surviving text is not a revealed wording. 3. Epistemic problem Many reports rest on limited chains and yield probability, not public scriptural certainty. 4. Interpretive problem The “revealed meaning” must be reconstructed by jurists and hadith critics from conflicting forms. The position can be made coherent only by reducing “revelation” to something like “a divine meaning that may lie behind some historically authenticated reports.” But that is not what people usually mean when they tell ordinary Muslims that hadith are *wahi*. They usually mean that hadith possess divine authority comparable to the Qurʾān. The evidence does not support that leap. A report about revelation is not revelation This is the cleanest way to state the argument. A report may be about revelation without being revelation. A historian may write that God revealed a verse; the historian’s sentence is not the verse. A Companion may report that the Prophet said something; the report is not the prophetic event itself. A compiler may preserve a chain; the compiler’s selected wording is not automatically the original wording. A jurist may extract a rule; the rule is not the revealed speech. Revelation God’s disclosed communication Prophetic event the Prophet teaches, judges, acts, or explains Memory a Companion or Successor remembers and frames it Report a chain and matn are transmitted, often by meaning Doctrine later scholars classify, reconcile, and legislate The traditional claim skips the middle of this ladder. It starts with revelation and ends with the hadith book. But the middle is the entire problem. What can still be granted A precise argument should not overstate itself. It does not need to claim that every hadith is fabricated. It does not need to claim that the Prophet never gave binding instruction. It does not need to deny that early Muslims preserved valuable memories. It does not even need to deny that some hadith may preserve the Prophet’s teachings in substance. The claim is narrower and stronger: Even if a hadith preserves a genuine prophetic teaching, the hadith text as transmitted is still a human report. If it is transmitted by meaning, stabilized through variants, and authenticated by probabilistic scholarly judgment, it cannot logically be classified as divine revelation itself. That is why the *wahi* label is so dangerous. It transfers the certainty of God’s speech to the uncertainty of human transmission. It turns a report into a source. It turns a source into a scripture. Then it calls resistance to that move resistance to the Prophet. The better distinction is this: the Qurʾān is revelation. The Prophet was a messenger guided by revelation. Hadith are later reports about the Prophet. Those reports may be studied, compared, criticized, and sometimes historically valued. But they are not *wahi*. Hadith cannot logically be treated as *wahi* in the Qurʾānic sense. The Qurʾān is fixed, recited revelation. Hadith are transmitted reports, often narrated by meaning, preserved through variant wordings, and authenticated by human judgment. The most that can be claimed is that some hadith may preserve traces of prophetic guidance. That does not make the hadith corpus a second revelation. A report about guidance is not the same thing as revelation from God. Source notes [^1]: For the Qurʾānic semantic range of *wahi*, see Qurʾān 16:68, 28:7, 8:12, 6:121, 41:12, and 42:51. These uses show that the word can denote instruction, inspiration, prompting, and divine communication in different registers, not only prophetic scripture. [^2]: Qurʾān 53:1–5. The passage is commonly used to argue that all prophetic speech is revelation, but its immediate subject is the Prophet’s revelatory message and the angelic teaching of that message. For the later legal-theoretical development that identifies Sunnah/hadith with an additional form of revelation, see John Burton, *The Sources of Islamic Law: Islamic Theories of Abrogation* (Edinburgh: Edinburgh University Press, 1990), 9–11, 34–35; Aisha Y. Musa, “The Sunnification of Ḥadīth and the Hadithification of Sunna,” in Adis Duderija, ed., *The Sunna and Its Status in Islamic Law* (New York: Palgrave Macmillan, 2015), 75–91. [^3]: See Qurʾān 9:43, 80:1–10, 66:1, 3:128, and 8:67–68. These passages distinguish divine correction from the Prophet’s prior judgment or conduct. [^4]: Musa, “The Sunnification of Ḥadīth and the Hadithification of Sunna,” 78–82. Musa describes al-Shāfiʿī’s role in linking *sunna* to prophetic hadith and notes how this process eventually granted hadith the status of a secondary form of unrecited revelation, *wahi ghayr matlūw*. See also Burton, *Sources of Islamic Law*, 10–11, where al-Shāfiʿī’s identification of *ḥikma* with the Sunnah is discussed. [^5]: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, *ʿUlūm al-ḥadīth*, type 26, “al-riwāya bi-l-maʿnā: ḥukmuhā wa-shurūṭuhā.” The quoted section states that the sounder view permits narration by meaning for a qualified narrator and that the Companions and early predecessors often transmitted the same meaning with different wordings because they relied on meaning rather than wording. [^6]: al-Suyūṭī, *Tadrīb al-rāwī*, type 26, section on *riwāya bi-l-maʿnā*. The passage summarizes the majority position: narration by meaning is allowed for a qualified transmitter who is certain he has conveyed the meaning, while uncertainty should be marked by phrases such as “or as he said” or “or the like of it.” [^7]: Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, *Fatḥ al-Bārī*, 13:250, cited and discussed in Muʿtaz al-Khaṭīb, *Ḥadīth and Ethics through the Lens of Interdisciplinarity* (Leiden: Brill, 2023), 56–57. The point is that when routes multiply, wording rarely agrees because most transmitters report by meaning. [^8]: Muslim, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, no. 3004, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: “Do not write from me; whoever wrote from me anything other than the Qurʾān, let him erase it.” See also al-Nasāʾī, *al-Sunan al-kubrā*, no. 8008; Abū Yaʿlā, *Musnad*, no. 1288, for parallel attestations. [^9]: Michael Cook, “The Opponents of the Writing of Tradition in Early Islam,” *Arabica* 44, no. 4 (1997): 437–530, especially §§14, 72–84, 85–103. Cook discusses the standard prophetic anti-writing report and the broader oralist values behind resistance to recording tradition. [^10]: For the women-leadership report and its variants, see al-Ṭayālisī, *Musnad*, nos. 919–920; Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, *Musnad*, nos. 20402, 20475, 20518; al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, nos. 4425 and 7099; al-Tirmidhī, *Jāmiʿ*, no. 2262; al-Bazzār, *Musnad*, no. 3113; al-Ḥākim, *al-Mustadrak*, nos. 4608 and 7790; al-Bayhaqī, *al-Sunan al-kubrā*, no. 20149. The variants move between “asnadū amrahum ilā imraʾa,” “wallaw amrahum imraʾa,” and “tamlikuhum imraʾa,” and between Persian/Kisrā and Dhū Yazan framing. [^11]: For the common uṣūl distinction in which solitary reports yield probability while remaining legally actionable, see Usman Ghani, “The Concept of Sunna in Muʿtazilite Thought,” in Duderija, ed., *The Sunna and Its Status in Islamic Law*, 70–71, summarizing Abū al-Ḥusayn al-Baṣrī’s position and the broader Sunnī legal-theoretical settlement that *akhbār al-āḥād* are *mūjib al-ʿamal* while yielding *ẓann* unless strengthened by consensus or other indicators. { .wahi-hero-panel, .reconstruction-panel, .source-ladder, .wahi-map { margin: 2.5rem 0; title: Bukhārī’s Blind Spot: ʿĀʾisha, al-Zuhrī, and the First-Revelation Isnād
description: A source-critical reconstruction of the iqraʾ report: why the Hira narrative cannot be a direct ʿĀʾisha memory, how al-Zuhrī fixed the canonical isnād, and why the Zubayrid storyteller stream matters.
