title: Before the Madhhabs: Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr’s Case Against Sectarian Ḥadīth
description: A fresh critical study of Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr’s Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh, the earliest surviving stand-alone theological work on the use of ḥadīth as factional proof, and why its argument matters for the formation of Sunnī authority.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr’s *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is not merely an early rationalist complaint that some ḥadīths are weak. It is an early theory of how sectarian communities manufacture religious certainty by selecting reports that already fit their doctrines, then attributing those doctrines to the Prophet. Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr al-Ghaṭafānī was a second/eighth-century theologian and judge who lived before the later legal madhhabs had hardened into the familiar Sunnī map. His *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh*, preserved in a unique Yemeni manuscript and published in 2014, is one of the most important early witnesses to the dispute over ḥadīth authority. Sean Anthony describes it as the earliest surviving stand-alone work by a theologian associated with the Muʿtazila, and more specifically as a treatise on “the use and authority of prophetic traditions” in a period when ḥadīth were rapidly proliferating.[^1] The usual way to tell this story is too simple. It is not enough to say that Ḍirār was “anti-ḥadīth” or that he was a proto-Muʿtazilī rationalist who preferred reason over transmission. His argument is sharper than that. He thinks the crisis begins when each faction discovers that a prophetic report can be made to speak for its own cause. The problem is not only forgery. The problem is the social function of disputed reports. A report becomes a banner. A banner becomes a faction. A faction then claims the Prophet as its spokesman. That is why the title matters. *Taḥrīsh* means incitement or provocation. Ḍirār takes the word from a report in which the Prophet forbids instigating fights between animals, then applies that image to Muslim disputation. The scholars and sectarians are no longer merely arguing; they are setting communities against each other.[^2] Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh Hadith as a sectarian machine Ḍirār’s target is not isolated fabrication. His target is the repeated pattern by which groups cite only the reports that support them, then use those reports to condemn their opponents. Dispute → Faction → Selected ḥadīth → Doctrine → Takfīr / rupture ## The opening question: why did the community split? The treatise begins as a response to a question: how did the community differ, where did its unity break, and why did its paths scatter? The editors preserve the opening in the manuscript: This is already an important framing. Ḍirār is not writing a neutral catalogue of sects. He is diagnosing a wound. His question is not “which sect is true?” but “what mechanism made sectarian truth-claims possible?” The answer he gives is that the factions learned to narrate the Prophet into their own positions. A later witness, Ibn al-Rāwandī as preserved through al-Khayyāṭ’s *al-Intiṣār*, recognized the work this way. He described *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* as containing the reports in which “each sect” narrates from the Prophet what agrees with its own doctrine, رواية كل فرقة لما هي عليه عن النبي .[^4] This is one of the strongest early confirmations that the book was remembered not as a generic theology manual, but as a critique of sectarian ḥadīth attribution. ## Ḍirār’s core evidence: every faction has its reports The line that should anchor the article is this: The wording is precise. Ḍirār is not saying every report is equally forged, nor that every transmitter is lying. He is saying that factions attach themselves to a *jins* of report, a recognizable genre or family of reports that reinforces their position. This is close to what modern hadith criticism often observes at the level of tradition families: once a dispute becomes politically or theologically useful, reports proliferate around the pressure point. Anthony’s review emphasizes how broad the catalogue is. Ḍirār discusses succession, God’s attributes, free will and predestination, the merits of Syria, poverty, traders, singing, sex, and even debates over Ibn Masʿūd’s Qurʾānic reading.[^6] The range matters because it prevents a narrow reading. Ḍirār is not only attacking Shīʿī reports, or only predestinarian reports, or only legal reports. He is describing a general ecology of religious argument. Succession Reports of precedence, caliphal legitimacy, obedience, and communal separation become weapons in arguments over who had the right to rule. Theology Reports about attributes, predestination, seeing God, and intercession are cited to turn speculative doctrines into prophetic speech. Law and conduct Reports on poverty, trade, singing, sexuality, and ritual practice show that even ordinary legal disputes could be converted into factional proof. Virtues and geography Reports on the merits of Syria and other places show how sacred geography could also be narrated into political and sectarian meaning. The point is not that Ḍirār has produced a modern isnād-cum-matn study. He has not. His method is earlier and cruder. But his intuition is historically valuable: when a doctrinal party repeatedly finds the Prophet endorsing exactly what that party needs, the historian should ask whether the report has been shaped by the controversy rather than merely transmitted through it. ## The “Samaritan” and “Paul” analogy One of the most striking features of the work is Ḍirār’s use of biblical and Qurʾānic analogy. He says every prophetic community has its own deceiver, comparing the Muslim crisis to the Samaritan who led Israel into the calf and to Paul, who in Islamic anti-Pauline polemic corrupted the message of Jesus.[^7] This analogy does real work. It means that Ḍirār is not explaining disagreement as a harmless diversity of schools. He is placing the Muslim community inside a larger pattern: after a prophet dies, later religious specialists claim to preserve him while actually producing division in his name. The most dangerous corruption is not an open rejection of revelation. It is the pious attribution of later doctrine to the founding messenger. That also explains why Ḍirār is so threatening to later ḥadīth-centered orthodoxy. He is not merely saying, “some reports are bad.” Everyone eventually says that. He is saying that factional hadith-use itself can be structurally corrupt even when it speaks in the language of piety. ## His standard of proof: not “no ḥadīth,” but no disputed ḥadīth as sectarian proof The strongest version of the argument must avoid exaggeration. Ḍirār is not a modern Qurʾān-only writer, and he is not simply rejecting all prophetic reports. Anthony notes that he still shows deference to Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ’s earlier position that reports enjoying broad consensus, الأخبار المجتمع عليها , carry weight.[^8] What Ḍirār rejects is the use of contested reports as binding proof in disputes where the community is already divided. This is why his appeal to consensus is so important: This should not be flattened into a slogan that Ḍirār “rejected Sunnah.” His view is more subtle and more historically useful. He accepts the idea that the community can preserve binding knowledge, but denies that rival factions can establish truth by producing rival reports. In other words, the proof must be public, communal, and non-sectarian. A report that only becomes convincing inside one faction’s argumentative world does not settle the dispute. It is part of the dispute. Ḍirār’s hierarchy of evidence Qurʾān public revelation Consensus communal, non-sectarian recognition Agreed reports usable when broadly accepted Factional reports not proof in the very dispute that produced them ## Why this belongs before the madhhabs The title of the blog should not imply that Ḍirār predates all legal activity. He does not. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Awzāʿī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and other early authorities are already part of the landscape. The point is that he stands before the later settlement in which Sunnī identity became tightly bound to a canon of ḥadīth, a hierarchy of transmitters, and a literature devoted to harmonizing apparently contradictory reports. This is where Ibn Qutayba becomes crucial. Hansu and Kaskin argue that large sections of Ibn Qutayba’s *Taʾwīl mukhtalif al-ḥadīth* quote or engage Ḍirār’s work, even though Ibn Qutayba does not name him. Anthony thinks the editors convincingly show that Ḍirār and his works on ḥadīth were a key target of Ibn Qutayba’s treatise, while adding the caution that Ibn Qutayba may sometimes be responding to another work of Ḍirār, *Kitāb Tanāquḍ al-ḥadīth*.[^10] That reception history changes the importance of the text. *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is not a curiosity from the losing side. It is part of the pressure that helped generate the Sunnī apologetic genre of reconciling contradictory reports. If Ibn Qutayba is answering Ḍirār or his circle, then later Sunnī hadith-theory is not simply developing in isolation. It is responding to an early critique that had already identified the central problem: contradictory reports had become ammunition for rival doctrines. Ḍirār Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh Ibn al-Rāwandī cites its sectarian-report thesis al-Khayyāṭ preserves the citation in refutation Ibn Qutayba answers the hadith-contradiction problem al-Jubbāʾī manuscript attests the work in later Muʿtazilī memory ## Dating the argument: the Abbasid horizon One of the strongest improvements to the analysis is chronological. A later story attached to al-Jubbāʾī’s *Maqālāt* tries to place *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* before Ḍirār’s full integration into the Muʿtazilī circle. Anthony warns against taking that story too literally. If Ḍirār had written the book before joining Wāṣil’s circle, it would likely have to predate Wāṣil’s death in 131/749 and the Abbasid revolution in 132/750.[^11] The contents of the treatise make that early date difficult. Anthony notes that *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* shows awareness of Abbasid revolutionary propaganda, including controversies over “the Easterners,” the black banners, and the permissibility of entering the dīwān with the *musawwida*, the black-clad Abbasid movement.[^12] This pushes the text into, or at least very near, the Abbasid revolutionary horizon. This matters because it makes the book less abstract. Ḍirār is writing in a world in which hadith and apocalyptic reports are not merely classroom material. They are connected to revolutions, dynastic claims, sectarian boundaries, and the making of orthodoxy. The same century that canonizes “the people of Sunnah and the community” also produces polemical reports about rulers, rebels, predestination, sectarian salvation, and eschatological armies. Ḍirār’s complaint belongs to that world. If *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* knows debates about black banners and the black-clad Abbasid movement, then Ḍirār is not only reacting to private scholarly disagreement. He is reacting to a post-revolutionary public sphere in which reports about the Prophet could legitimate regimes, movements, and sectarian identities. ## The biographical problem: Muʿtazilī, anti-Shīʿī, or something else? The old labels do not fully work. Later writers variously attach Ḍirār to the Muʿtazila, exclude him from them, accuse him of predestinarian views, call him a Kūfan, describe him as anti-Shīʿī, and treat him as a dangerous rationalist. The introduction to the Arabic edition preserves reports from al-Balkhī, al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Jushamī, Ibn al-Nadīm, and al-Jubbāʾī that already show a contested memory of Ḍirār’s school location.[^13] That contested memory should be used rather than hidden. Ḍirār is valuable precisely because he does not sit comfortably inside a later school. He belongs to the transitional world before labels became clean. He is close enough to the Muʿtazilī problem of reason and consensus to be remembered with them, but odd enough to be excluded by later Muʿtazilīs. He is anti-Shīʿī enough for later Shīʿī theologians to contest him, but his critique of factional reports also threatens Sunnī hadith-apologetics. The result is a rare voice from before the victorious categories arranged the archive. Later Sunnī heresiographers could make him a deviant. Later Muʿtazilīs could make him embarrassing. Later traditionalists could make him dangerous. But *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* lets us see the argument in his own terms: sectarian ḥadīth-use fragments the community. ## A better way to state the thesis The strongest version of the thesis is not: > “Ḍirār proves that all ḥadīth are fabricated.” That overstates the case and makes the article easier to dismiss. The stronger thesis is: > “Ḍirār is one of the earliest surviving Muslim authors to treat disputed ḥadīth as a sociological and epistemological problem: reports do not merely transmit doctrine; in sectarian settings, they manufacture doctrine, authorize doctrine, and intensify communal rupture.” That thesis can be defended from the text. He begins with the breakup of the community. He explains it through factional attachment to report-types. He catalogues rival reports across theology, law, politics, and sectarian identity. He limits binding proof after the Prophet to consensus. And his work was important enough to be remembered by Ibn al-Rāwandī, preserved through al-Khayyāṭ, and answered in the orbit of Ibn Qutayba’s hadith-apologetic project. ## Why this matters for hadith criticism today Ḍirār is not doing modern source criticism, and he should not be turned into a modern academic before his time. He is not drawing isnād diagrams, identifying common links, or reconstructing regional transmission layers. Yet his work anticipates the central question behind those methods: when a report serves a factional need too perfectly, how do we distinguish memory from argument? His answer is not the answer of modern historians, but it is historically revealing. He retreats to consensus because consensus is the only form of post-prophetic proof he thinks can escape factional capture. Modern historians need not accept his solution to recognize the problem he saw. Reports can be true, false, reshaped, selectively quoted, or contextually redeployed. In all cases, they do social work. That is the real power of *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh*. It shows that the anxiety over hadith proliferation was not invented by Orientalists, modern reformers, or anti-traditional polemicists. A second/eighth-century Muslim theologian already saw that rival communities could place their own doctrines on the Prophet’s tongue and then use those attributions to tear the community apart. *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is best read as an early Muslim critique of sectarian hadith-production, not as a simple rejection of every prophetic report. Ḍirār’s target is the disputed report that appears inside a factional controversy and then claims to settle that controversy by prophetic authority. His solution is consensus; his diagnosis is more enduring: when each group has its own prophetic archive, transmission becomes a battlefield. ## Source notes [^1]: Sean W. fullText: Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr’s *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is not merely an early rationalist complaint that some ḥadīths are weak. It is an early theory of how sectarian communities manufacture religious certainty by selecting reports that already fit their doctrines, then attributing those doctrines to the Prophet. Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr al-Ghaṭafānī was a second/eighth-century theologian and judge who lived before the later legal madhhabs had hardened into the familiar Sunnī map. His *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh*, preserved in a unique Yemeni manuscript and published in 2014, is one of the most important early witnesses to the dispute over ḥadīth authority. Sean Anthony describes it as the earliest surviving stand-alone work by a theologian associated with the Muʿtazila, and more specifically as a treatise on “the use and authority of prophetic traditions” in a period when ḥadīth were rapidly proliferating.[^1] The usual way to tell this story is too simple. It is not enough to say that Ḍirār was “anti-ḥadīth” or that he was a proto-Muʿtazilī rationalist who preferred reason over transmission. His argument is sharper than that. He thinks the crisis begins when each faction discovers that a prophetic report can be made to speak for its own cause. The problem is not only forgery. The problem is the social function of disputed reports. A report becomes a banner. A banner becomes a faction. A faction then claims the Prophet as its spokesman. That is why the title matters. *Taḥrīsh* means incitement or provocation. Ḍirār takes the word from a report in which the Prophet forbids instigating fights between animals, then applies that image to Muslim disputation. The scholars and sectarians are no longer merely arguing; they are setting communities against each other.[^2] Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh Hadith as a sectarian machine Ḍirār’s target is not isolated fabrication. His target is the repeated pattern by which groups cite only the reports that support them, then use those reports to condemn their opponents. Dispute → Faction → Selected ḥadīth → Doctrine → Takfīr / rupture The opening question: why did the community split? The treatise begins as a response to a question: how did the community differ, where did its unity break, and why did its paths scatter? The editors preserve the opening in the manuscript: This is already an important framing. Ḍirār is not writing a neutral catalogue of sects. He is diagnosing a wound. His question is not “which sect is true?” but “what mechanism made sectarian truth-claims possible?” The answer he gives is that the factions learned to narrate the Prophet into their own positions. A later witness, Ibn al-Rāwandī as preserved through al-Khayyāṭ’s *al-Intiṣār*, recognized the work this way. He described *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* as containing the reports in which “each sect” narrates from the Prophet what agrees with its own doctrine, رواية كل فرقة لما هي عليه عن النبي .[^4] This is one of the strongest early confirmations that the book was remembered not as a generic theology manual, but as a critique of sectarian ḥadīth attribution. Ḍirār’s core evidence: every faction has its reports The line that should anchor the article is this: The wording is precise. Ḍirār is not saying every report is equally forged, nor that every transmitter is lying. He is saying that factions attach themselves to a *jins* of report, a recognizable genre or family of reports that reinforces their position. This is close to what modern hadith criticism often observes at the level of tradition families: once a dispute becomes politically or theologically useful, reports proliferate around the pressure point. Anthony’s review emphasizes how broad the catalogue is. Ḍirār discusses succession, God’s attributes, free will and predestination, the merits of Syria, poverty, traders, singing, sex, and even debates over Ibn Masʿūd’s Qurʾānic reading.[^6] The range matters because it prevents a narrow reading. Ḍirār is not only attacking Shīʿī reports, or only predestinarian reports, or only legal reports. He is describing a general ecology of religious argument. Succession Reports of precedence, caliphal legitimacy, obedience, and communal separation become weapons in arguments over who had the right to rule. Theology Reports about attributes, predestination, seeing God, and intercession are cited to turn speculative doctrines into prophetic speech. Law and conduct Reports on poverty, trade, singing, sexuality, and ritual practice show that even ordinary legal disputes could be converted into factional proof. Virtues and geography Reports on the merits of Syria and other places show how sacred geography could also be narrated into political and sectarian meaning. The point is not that Ḍirār has produced a modern isnād-cum-matn study. He has not. His method is earlier and cruder. But his intuition is historically valuable: when a doctrinal party repeatedly finds the Prophet endorsing exactly what that party needs, the historian should ask whether the report has been shaped by the controversy rather than merely transmitted through it. The “Samaritan” and “Paul” analogy One of the most striking features of the work is Ḍirār’s use of biblical and Qurʾānic analogy. He says every prophetic community has its own deceiver, comparing the Muslim crisis to the Samaritan who led Israel into the calf and to Paul, who in Islamic anti-Pauline polemic corrupted the message of Jesus.[^7] This analogy does real work. It means that Ḍirār is not explaining disagreement as a harmless diversity of schools. He is placing the Muslim community inside a larger pattern: after a prophet dies, later religious specialists claim to preserve him while actually producing division in his name. The most dangerous corruption is not an open rejection of revelation. It is the pious attribution of later doctrine to the founding messenger. That also explains why Ḍirār is so threatening to later ḥadīth-centered orthodoxy. He is not merely saying, “some reports are bad.” Everyone eventually says that. He is saying that factional hadith-use itself can be structurally corrupt even when it speaks in the language of piety. His standard of proof: not “no ḥadīth,” but no disputed ḥadīth as sectarian proof The strongest version of the argument must avoid exaggeration. Ḍirār is not a modern Qurʾān-only writer, and he is not simply rejecting all prophetic reports. Anthony notes that he still shows deference to Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ’s earlier position that reports enjoying broad consensus, الأخبار المجتمع عليها , carry weight.[^8] What Ḍirār rejects is the use of contested reports as binding proof in disputes where the community is already divided. This is why his appeal to consensus is so important: This should not be flattened into a slogan that Ḍirār “rejected Sunnah.” His view is more subtle and more historically useful. He accepts the idea that the community can preserve binding knowledge, but denies that rival factions can establish truth by producing rival reports. In other words, the proof must be public, communal, and non-sectarian. A report that only becomes convincing inside one faction’s argumentative world does not settle the dispute. It is part of the dispute. Ḍirār’s hierarchy of evidence Qurʾān public revelation Consensus communal, non-sectarian recognition Agreed reports usable when broadly accepted Factional reports not proof in the very dispute that produced them Why this belongs before the madhhabs The title of the blog should not imply that Ḍirār predates all legal activity. He does not. Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Awzāʿī, Sufyān al-Thawrī, and other early authorities are already part of the landscape. The point is that he stands before the later settlement in which Sunnī identity became tightly bound to a canon of ḥadīth, a hierarchy of transmitters, and a literature devoted to harmonizing apparently contradictory reports. This is where Ibn Qutayba becomes crucial. Hansu and Kaskin argue that large sections of Ibn Qutayba’s *Taʾwīl mukhtalif al-ḥadīth* quote or engage Ḍirār’s work, even though Ibn Qutayba does not name him. Anthony thinks the editors convincingly show that Ḍirār and his works on ḥadīth were a key target of Ibn Qutayba’s treatise, while adding the caution that Ibn Qutayba may sometimes be responding to another work of Ḍirār, *Kitāb Tanāquḍ al-ḥadīth*.[^10] That reception history changes the importance of the text. *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is not a curiosity from the losing side. It is part of the pressure that helped generate the Sunnī apologetic genre of reconciling contradictory reports. If Ibn Qutayba is answering Ḍirār or his circle, then later Sunnī hadith-theory is not simply developing in isolation. It is responding to an early critique that had already identified the central problem: contradictory reports had become ammunition for rival doctrines. Ḍirār Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh Ibn al-Rāwandī cites its sectarian-report thesis al-Khayyāṭ preserves the citation in refutation Ibn Qutayba answers the hadith-contradiction problem al-Jubbāʾī manuscript attests the work in later Muʿtazilī memory Dating the argument: the Abbasid horizon One of the strongest improvements to the analysis is chronological. A later story attached to al-Jubbāʾī’s *Maqālāt* tries to place *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* before Ḍirār’s full integration into the Muʿtazilī circle. Anthony warns against taking that story too literally. If Ḍirār had written the book before joining Wāṣil’s circle, it would likely have to predate Wāṣil’s death in 131/749 and the Abbasid revolution in 132/750.[^11] The contents of the treatise make that early date difficult. Anthony notes that *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* shows awareness of Abbasid revolutionary propaganda, including controversies over “the Easterners,” the black banners, and the permissibility of entering the dīwān with the *musawwida*, the black-clad Abbasid movement.[^12] This pushes the text into, or at least very near, the Abbasid revolutionary horizon. This matters because it makes the book less abstract. Ḍirār is writing in a world in which hadith and apocalyptic reports are not merely classroom material. They are connected to revolutions, dynastic claims, sectarian boundaries, and the making of orthodoxy. The same century that canonizes “the people of Sunnah and the community” also produces polemical reports about rulers, rebels, predestination, sectarian salvation, and eschatological armies. Ḍirār’s complaint belongs to that world. If *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* knows debates about black banners and the black-clad Abbasid movement, then Ḍirār is not only reacting to private scholarly disagreement. He is reacting to a post-revolutionary public sphere in which reports about the Prophet could legitimate regimes, movements, and sectarian identities. The biographical problem: Muʿtazilī, anti-Shīʿī, or something else? The old labels do not fully work. Later writers variously attach Ḍirār to the Muʿtazila, exclude him from them, accuse him of predestinarian views, call him a Kūfan, describe him as anti-Shīʿī, and treat him as a dangerous rationalist. The introduction to the Arabic edition preserves reports from al-Balkhī, al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Jushamī, Ibn al-Nadīm, and al-Jubbāʾī that already show a contested memory of Ḍirār’s school location.[^13] That contested memory should be used rather than hidden. Ḍirār is valuable precisely because he does not sit comfortably inside a later school. He belongs to the transitional world before labels became clean. He is close enough to the Muʿtazilī problem of reason and consensus to be remembered with them, but odd enough to be excluded by later Muʿtazilīs. He is anti-Shīʿī enough for later Shīʿī theologians to contest him, but his critique of factional reports also threatens Sunnī hadith-apologetics. The result is a rare voice from before the victorious categories arranged the archive. Later Sunnī heresiographers could make him a deviant. Later Muʿtazilīs could make him embarrassing. Later traditionalists could make him dangerous. But *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* lets us see the argument in his own terms: sectarian ḥadīth-use fragments the community. A better way to state the thesis The strongest version of the thesis is not: > “Ḍirār proves that all ḥadīth are fabricated.” That overstates the case and makes the article easier to dismiss. The stronger thesis is: > “Ḍirār is one of the earliest surviving Muslim authors to treat disputed ḥadīth as a sociological and epistemological problem: reports do not merely transmit doctrine; in sectarian settings, they manufacture doctrine, authorize doctrine, and intensify communal rupture.” That thesis can be defended from the text. He begins with the breakup of the community. He explains it through factional attachment to report-types. He catalogues rival reports across theology, law, politics, and sectarian identity. He limits binding proof after the Prophet to consensus. And his work was important enough to be remembered by Ibn al-Rāwandī, preserved through al-Khayyāṭ, and answered in the orbit of Ibn Qutayba’s hadith-apologetic project. Why this matters for hadith criticism today Ḍirār is not doing modern source criticism, and he should not be turned into a modern academic before his time. He is not drawing isnād diagrams, identifying common links, or reconstructing regional transmission layers. Yet his work anticipates the central question behind those methods: when a report serves a factional need too perfectly, how do we distinguish memory from argument? His answer is not the answer of modern historians, but it is historically revealing. He retreats to consensus because consensus is the only form of post-prophetic proof he thinks can escape factional capture. Modern historians need not accept his solution to recognize the problem he saw. Reports can be true, false, reshaped, selectively quoted, or contextually redeployed. In all cases, they do social work. That is the real power of *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh*. It shows that the anxiety over hadith proliferation was not invented by Orientalists, modern reformers, or anti-traditional polemicists. A second/eighth-century Muslim theologian already saw that rival communities could place their own doctrines on the Prophet’s tongue and then use those attributions to tear the community apart. *Kitāb al-Taḥrīsh* is best read as an early Muslim critique of sectarian hadith-production, not as a simple rejection of every prophetic report. Ḍirār’s target is the disputed report that appears inside a factional controversy and then claims to settle that controversy by prophetic authority. His solution is consensus; his diagnosis is more enduring: when each group has its own prophetic archive, transmission becomes a battlefield. Source notes [^1]: Sean W. Anthony describes the work as the first published edition of the treatise, calls it the earliest surviving stand-alone work by a theologian associated with the Muʿtazila, and stresses that it is a treatise on the use and authority of prophetic traditions. title: Dr. Shadee Elmasry’s Hadith Defense: A Methodological Critique
description: A fresh critique of the apologetic response to academic hadith criticism, showing why the issue is not Western disbelief, but whether a late, human transmission archive can prove Prophetic speech with the certainty claimed for it.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The public dispute over hadith and the academy became confused almost immediately because the discussion was pushed into the wrong frame. The question was made to sound like this: should Muslims trust their own tradition, or should they surrender to a secular Western method that hates revelation? Once the issue is stated that way, the answer is already emotionally loaded. No religious audience wants to be told that its memory must be judged by outsiders who do not share its faith commitments. But that is not the real question. The real question is much narrower and much more difficult: **what can a post-Prophetic hadith archive prove about the first/seventh century, and what kind of certainty can it honestly produce?** That question does not disappear because the person asking it is Western, Muslim, atheist, Christian, secular, or traditional. A chain still has to be examined. A narrator still has to be dated. A report still has to be compared with its variants. A matn still has to be tested against what we know of law, politics, sectarian conflict, scripture, and the historical setting in which the report first becomes visible. The strongest critique of the apologetic defense is not that hadith scholars were careless. It is that the defense treats a disciplined human archive as though it can deliver revelation-level certainty, while avoiding the historical burden needed to prove that claim. This article therefore does not treat academic hadith criticism as automatically correct. It also does not treat the classical hadith sciences as worthless. The classical critics developed powerful internal tools. They tracked transmitters, compared wordings, identified anomalies, noticed hidden defects, and preserved a large amount of disagreement. But those tools still operate inside a later archive. They can show that a report became stable by a certain point. They can show that a transmitter was considered dependable by later critics. They can show that one version is better attested than another. What they cannot do, by themselves, is transform every accepted solitary report into demonstrable Prophetic speech. Theological possibility Could God reveal? Yes. A historian does not need to deny God, prophecy, or miracles in order to examine a report. ≠ Historical demonstration Did this report preserve it? This requires evidence: early attestation, variant control, plausible transmission, and freedom from later motive. ## The “Western Epistemology” Move The first problem is the attempt to dismiss historical criticism by branding it “Western epistemology.” That phrase sounds precise, but it often functions as a container into which several different things are thrown: secularism, Enlightenment suspicion, Orientalism, colonial power, Christian trauma, atheism, and academic source criticism. These are not the same thing. A historian can bracket theology without denying theology. A historian can say, “I cannot use divine protection as a public historical premise,” without saying, “divine protection is impossible.” A historian can say, “This report has to be tested like other late reports,” without saying, “God cannot speak.” That distinction is basic, and once it is missed the whole debate becomes a caricature. The Qur’an itself does not teach blind acceptance of transmitted claims. It tells believers to verify reports, not to accept them because a trusted group repeats them. These verses do not create modern historical criticism. But they do destroy the lazy idea that verification is an alien value. The Qur’anic posture is not “trust every religious report because it is religious.” It is to avoid following what one does not know, and to investigate reports that can produce harm or error. A Muslim does not need European skepticism to understand that principle. The issue is not whether the academy has assumptions. It does. The issue is whether the traditional defense can answer the evidence without retreating into identity language. ## The Academy Is Not One Thing The second problem is that “the academy” is treated as a single enemy with a single doctrine. This is not accurate. Academic hadith studies includes very skeptical approaches, more conservative source-critical approaches, and many intermediate positions. Schacht and Juynboll represent a more skeptical line, especially regarding legal traditions and common links. Motzki developed isnād-cum-matn analysis in ways that sometimes pushed dates earlier than Schacht would allow. Schoeler and Görke argued for recoverable early material in some sīra and maghāzī corpora. Jonathan Brown has written sympathetically about the sophistication and social function of Sunni hadith canonization while still distinguishing confessional authority from academic proof. Shahab Ahmed’s work on the Satanic Verses is not the same kind of project as Schacht’s work on legal traditions. Joshua Little’s work on ʿĀʾisha reports is not simply Juynboll repeated under a new name.[^1] More skeptical Goldziher · Schacht · Juynboll Later legal, sectarian, and communal needs explain many Prophetic attributions. Source-critical Motzki · Schoeler · Görke Some early material may be recoverable through careful isnād-cum-matn analysis. Tradition-aware Brown · Ahmed · Little The tradition must be studied as a historical archive, not simply dismissed or canonized. Once the field is described this way, the apologetic move becomes much weaker. If the academy were merely a secular church of anti-Islamic suspicion, we would expect a single conclusion and a single method. Instead we find a field full of disagreement over dating, source recovery, common links, family isnāds, legal projection, oral transmission, written notebooks, and the reliability of individual corpora. That disagreement does not vindicate the Sunni hadith sciences as a religious authority. But it does show that dismissing the whole field as “Western bias” is not a serious answer. ## The Genetic Fallacy Turns Against the Apologist Another common defense says that modern historical criticism grew out of European disillusionment with Church corruption, forged documents, fake relics, and ecclesiastical claims that could not survive scrutiny. Therefore, the method is psychologically contaminated by distrust. Even if that simplified origin story were granted, the argument would still fail. A method is not refuted by describing why people first needed it. Fire inspection developed because buildings burned. Forensic accounting developed because people committed fraud. Isnād criticism developed because people lied about the Prophet. A method created in response to deception can be more necessary, not less. The classical Muslim tradition makes exactly this admission. Muslim preserves the famous statement of Ibn Sīrīn: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَسْأَلُونَ عَنِ الإِسْنَادِ، فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْفِتْنَةُ قَالُوا: سَمُّوا لَنَا رِجَالَكُمْ، فَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ فَيُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ، وَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ فَلَا يُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ. “They did not use to ask about the isnād. But when the fitna occurred, they said: name your men for us. The people of the Sunna would be examined and their reports taken, and the people of innovation would be examined and their reports not taken.” Muslim also transmits the maxim: إِنَّ هَذَا الْعِلْمَ دِينٌ، فَانْظُرُوا عَمَّنْ تَأْخُذُونَ دِينَكُمْ. “This knowledge is religion, so examine from whom you take your religion.” These are not Orientalist slogans. They are internal Sunni memory. The isnād was not always policed with the same intensity. The need for scrutiny became urgent after social rupture, factional conflict, and fabrication. That means the apologetic attack on “methods born from suspicion” cuts against hadith science itself. Forgery or conflict appears → A method of verification develops → The method must be judged by results, not by origin If a method is invalid because it arose in response to deception, then classical hadith criticism is invalid for the same reason. The better question is whether the method can actually detect the kind of errors it claims to detect. ## What Hadith Criticism Can and Cannot See The classical definition of a ṣaḥīḥ report is disciplined. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ defines the sound report as one with a connected isnād, transmitted by upright and precise transmitters, free from anomaly and hidden defect.[^2] That is not a foolish definition. It is a serious attempt to filter reports. The problem is the distance between **filtering a later archive** and **proving an original utterance**. A report can satisfy the later criteria and still remain historically uncertain at the earliest layer. The criteria work best where the evidence is visible: named transmitters, known teachers, competing pupils, variant wording, hidden breaks, regional oddities, and contradictions with stronger routes. They work less well where the evidence disappears: the first decades before formal isnād policing, political motive hidden behind a respected authority, family transmission that cannot be independently checked, or a common link who has already attached a report to an earlier figure. Visible to the critic named transmitters teacher-pupil plausibility variant comparison known weak narrators contradictions among routes Harder to see early anonymous circulation retrojected Companion authority ideological motive before documentation common-link reshaping lost variants and suppressed alternatives This is where modern isnād-cum-matn analysis becomes useful. It does not simply laugh at isnāds. It takes them seriously enough to map them. It asks where the report first becomes historically visible, which wording appears at which layer, and whether the matn develops along the same lines as the isnād. Schacht’s common-link theory, Juynboll’s refinements, and Motzki’s critiques of both are not identical positions, but they all force a question that simple apologetics avoids: **where does the report actually begin in the evidence we possess?**[^3] A hadith may be “authentic” in the technical sense of a later Sunni collection and still be historically late in origin. That is not a contradiction. It only becomes a contradiction if one silently equates Sunni grading with historical demonstration. ## Ṣaḥīḥ Does Not Mean Revelation-Level Certainty A serious traditionalist knows that not every authenticated report occupies the same epistemic rank as the Qur’an. The usūl tradition debated solitary reports precisely because the issue was not simple. Mutawātir reports were treated differently from āḥād reports. Legal obligation was often distinguished from certain knowledge. Al-Shāfiʿī’s argument for accepting qualified solitary reports is one of the most important classical defenses, but even there the distinction remains. In *al-Risāla*, after defending obligation to act on certain reports, he does not make them equal to the Qur’an or public transmission. He says: لا أن ذلك إحاطة كما يكون نص الكتاب وخبر العامة “Not that this is comprehensive certainty as with the text of the Book and public report.” That admission matters. It means a report can be practically binding within a legal theory without becoming epistemically equal to the Qur’an. The apologetic defense often blurs this distinction. It speaks as though doubting a solitary hadith is the same as doubting revelation itself. But that is not how the classical hierarchy of proof actually works. Highest public proof Qur’an / mass-recited text Public, communal, liturgical, manuscript and recitational transmission. Mass report Mutawātir-type knowledge Claimed certainty through wide, independent transmission. Limited report Āḥād / specialist transmission May create legal obligation inside a school, but does not become Qur’an-level certainty. This is where the academy’s challenge bites. The academic historian is not required to accept the legal theory that turns a qualified solitary report into binding religious practice. The historian asks a different question: what is the earliest recoverable point of the report, and what best explains its formation? That is a historical question, not an anti-religious insult. ## “Orientalism” Is Not an Answer Orientalism was real. Colonial knowledge production was real. European scholars did sometimes write about Islam through hostile, Christian, racial, or imperial frames. A serious critic should admit this plainly. But admitting the existence of Orientalism does not answer a single hadith argument. It does not show that a chain is continuous. It does not show that a common link is early. It does not explain why one matn appears only in one regional cluster. It does not solve contradictions between variants. It does not make a weak narrator reliable. It does not turn a late political slogan into Prophetic speech. Valid use Expose bias, power, framing, translation choices, and selective attention. Invalid use Dismiss evidence without answering it, as if motive analysis replaced source analysis. The word “Orientalist” can identify a problem in a scholar’s assumptions. It cannot function as a universal solvent. Once a critic produces a concrete argument from isnād distribution, matn stratification, chronology, political setting, or manuscript evidence, the response must address that argument. Otherwise “Orientalism” becomes a way of protecting inherited claims from examination. ## The Satanic Verses as a Stress Test The Satanic Verses incident is a useful test case because it exposes how selective apologetics can become. The common apologetic line says the story is one weak narration, rejected by the tradition, and impossible because the Qur’an says the Prophet did not speak from desire. That framing is too neat. The point here is not that every detail of the story must be accepted. The point is that the tradition is much harder to dismiss than the apologetic summary admits. Shahab Ahmed’s book-length study collected and analyzed no less than fifty historical reports of the incident transmitted in the first generations of Islam.[^4] The material appears in early tafsīr, sīra, maghāzī, and historical writing. It is connected with figures such as Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zuhrī, and Ibn ʿAbbās-associated exegetical material. It is not simply one isolated isnād in a fringe polemical book.[^5] The Qur’an itself contains a verse that many early exegetes connected to the problem of Satan casting something into a prophet’s recitation or wish, followed by God abolishing what Satan casts and confirming His verses. Ibn Taymiyyah is especially awkward for the later apologetic line because he does not treat the entire early memory as an obvious heresy. In his discussion of Q 22:52, he says that what is transmitted from the early Muslims agrees with the Qur’anic wording, while later scholars objected to the reported addition in Sūrat al-Najm and tried to reinterpret or reject it.[^6] Whether one agrees with Ibn Taymiyyah or not, his discussion shows that the apologetic claim “the real tradition always rejected this as a lie” is historically false. Apologetic reduction “One weak story” The report is treated as a marginal fabrication that can be dismissed without serious source analysis. Archive reality Multiple early reports The episode appears across tafsīr, sīra, maghāzī, and historical materials with several early transmitter attributions. Historical question How did this memory form? The burden is to explain the emergence, spread, discomfort, and later rejection of the narrative. Later scholars did push back. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Bayhaqī, and modern defenders such as al-Albānī rejected the incident in different ways. That later rejection is part of the evidence. It shows a shift in the boundaries of acceptable Prophetic memory. Early transmitters could preserve the story as an explanation of Q 22:52 and the Meccan prostration after Sūrat al-Najm. Later theologians, operating with a hardened doctrine of prophetic protection, increasingly found the story intolerable. That is precisely why the episode matters. It demonstrates the difference between **early archive** and **later orthodoxy**. The apologist often reads the later orthodoxy backward and then calls the early archive impossible. A historian cannot do that. A historian has to explain both layers. ## “The Qur’an Refutes It” Is Not Enough One might say that Sūrat al-Najm itself refutes the Satanic Verses story because it says the Prophet does not speak from desire. But this is not a historical argument by itself. It is a theological harmonization. The early transmitters who preserved the story knew Sūrat al-Najm existed. The exegetes who connected the story to Q 22:52 knew the Qur’an. Ibn Taymiyyah knew the Qur’an. The question is therefore not whether a modern reader can construct a theological objection. The question is why many early Muslim transmitters and exegetes did not see the objection as decisive. That does not prove the incident happened exactly as narrated. But it does prove that the apologetic dismissal is too simple. A serious answer would have to explain the spread of the reports, their early exegetical function, their relation to Q 22:52, their connection to the prostration at Sūrat al-Najm, and the later doctrinal pressure that made the story unacceptable. The Satanic Verses case is not a side issue. It reveals the whole methodological problem: when the inherited archive becomes uncomfortable, apologetics often stops doing hadith criticism and starts doing damage control. ## The Real Weakness in the Defense The defense of hadith often points to the sophistication of narrator criticism. That sophistication is real. The early critics were not naïve. They knew that transmitters could lie, confuse, paraphrase, conceal teachers, merge reports, raise stopped reports, or transmit after memory decline. They built a technical vocabulary around those dangers. But the defense then makes a leap. It moves from “the critics had tools” to “therefore the authenticated archive is historically secure.” That leap is not justified. A tool can be sophisticated and still limited. A metal detector cannot find wood. A microscope cannot detect motive. Rijāl criticism can catch visible transmitter problems, but it cannot automatically recover every earlier stage of a report. It often depends on the very tradition whose reliability is under investigation. A narrator is trustworthy because earlier critics say he is trustworthy; earlier critics are trusted because they belong to the same epistemic tradition; the report is then accepted because the trustworthy narrators transmitted it. That circle may be useful inside a confessional system, but it cannot simply be imposed as public historical proof. Critics define reliability → Narrators receive grades → Reports inherit confidence → The system validates itself The historian does not have to accept that circle. He may still use the data. In fact, he should. Rijāl books, isnād bundles, biographical notices, and early collections are invaluable evidence. But they are evidence to be analyzed, not authorities to be obeyed. ## A Better Traditionalist Response A stronger traditionalist response would not be to mock the academy as traumatized, colonial, or anti-God. It would admit the real difference between confessional and historical reasoning. It would say: yes, the Sunni hadith sciences rely on theological premises that academic historians do not grant, including the collective uprightness of the Companions, the authority of inherited communal practice, the binding force of qualified solitary reports, and confidence in the major critics. It would also say: yes, many hadith judgments are probabilistic, not mathematically certain. It would then defend why a Muslim legal-theological system may act on those probabilities even though the academic historian cannot treat them as public proof. That would at least be honest. It would stop pretending that the dispute is merely between reverent Muslims and biased Westerners. It would recognize that the academy and the madrasa are often asking different questions. Weak defense “The academy rejects hadith because it hates miracles and inherited Western trauma.” Stronger defense “The hadith sciences are a confessional legal-historical method that produces graded probability inside a theological system.” The stronger defense still would not prove the hadith archive historically. But it would at least locate the disagreement correctly. The conflict is not simply “Western disbelief versus Islamic faith.” It is a conflict over what kind of evidence can establish a claim about the past, and whether a confessional system may treat probabilities as religiously binding. ## The Bottom Line Dr. Shadee Elmasry’s defense fails because it does not meet the academic critique at its strongest point. The strongest critique is not that miracles are impossible. It is not that Muslims are uniquely gullible. It is not that every transmitter lied. The strongest critique is that hadith authentication is a later human method working on a later human archive, and its conclusions are limited by the evidence available to it. The classical critics knew that fabrication existed. They knew that isnāds could be manipulated. They knew that transmitters differed. They knew that hidden defects mattered. Their discipline is worth studying for that very reason. But the discipline cannot be transformed into certainty by accusing critics of Western bias. The question is not whether God could reveal through the Prophet. The question is whether a particular hadith can be historically demonstrated as Prophetic speech. That burden is not met by calling criticism “Western,” “Orientalist,” or “secular.” It is met only by evidence. ## Source notes [^1]: For the range of academic approaches, see Joseph Schacht, *The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence*; G. H. A. Juynboll, *Muslim Tradition*; Harald Motzki, “Dating Muslim Traditions: A Survey,” *Arabica* 52 (2005): 204–253; Gregor Schoeler, *The Oral and the Written in Early Islam*; Andreas Görke and Gregor Schoeler, *The Earliest Writings on the Life of Muḥammad*; Jonathan A. C. Brown, *Hadith: Muhammad’s Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World*; Shahab Ahmed, *Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam*; Joshua Little, *The Hadith of ʿĀʾiša’s Marital Age*. [^2]: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, *Muqaddima fī ʿulūm al-ḥadīth*, definition of the ṣaḥīḥ report: a connected isnād through upright and precise transmitters, free from shudhūdh and ʿilla. This classical definition is also summarized throughout later hadith manuals. [^3]: Motzki’s survey is useful because it does not merely repeat Schacht. See Motzki, “Dating Muslim Traditions,” especially the sections on Schacht, Juynboll, common links, and isnād-cum-matn analysis. [^4]: Shahab Ahmed, *Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam* (Harvard University Press, 2017). The question was made to sound like this: should Muslims trust their own tradition, or should they surrender to a secular Western method that hates revelation? Once the issue is stated that way, the answer is already emotionally loaded. No religious audience wants to be told that its memory must be judged by outsiders who do not share its faith commitments. But that is not the real question. The real question is much narrower and much more difficult: **what can a post-Prophetic hadith archive prove about the first/seventh century, and what kind of certainty can it honestly produce?** That question does not disappear because the person asking it is Western, Muslim, atheist, Christian, secular, or traditional. A chain still has to be examined. A narrator still has to be dated. A report still has to be compared with its variants. A matn still has to be tested against what we know of law, politics, sectarian conflict, scripture, and the historical setting in which the report first becomes visible. The strongest critique of the apologetic defense is not that hadith scholars were careless. It is that the defense treats a disciplined human archive as though it can deliver revelation-level certainty, while avoiding the historical burden needed to prove that claim. This article therefore does not treat academic hadith criticism as automatically correct. It also does not treat the classical hadith sciences as worthless. The classical critics developed powerful internal tools. They tracked transmitters, compared wordings, identified anomalies, noticed hidden defects, and preserved a large amount of disagreement. But those tools still operate inside a later archive. They can show that a report became stable by a certain point. They can show that a transmitter was considered dependable by later critics. They can show that one version is better attested than another. What they cannot do, by themselves, is transform every accepted solitary report into demonstrable Prophetic speech. Theological possibility Could God reveal? Yes. A historian does not need to deny God, prophecy, or miracles in order to examine a report. ≠ Historical demonstration Did this report preserve it? This requires evidence: early attestation, variant control, plausible transmission, and freedom from later motive. These are not the same thing. A historian can bracket theology without denying theology. The Qur’an itself does not teach blind acceptance of transmitted claims. It tells believers to verify reports, not to accept them because a trusted group repeats them. These verses do not create modern historical criticism. But they do destroy the lazy idea that verification is an alien value. The Qur’anic posture is not “trust every religious report because it is religious.” It is to avoid following what one does not know, and to investigate reports that can produce harm or error. A Muslim does not need European skepticism to understand that principle. The issue is not whether the academy has assumptions. It does. The issue is whether the traditional defense can answer the evidence without retreating into identity language. The Academy Is Not One Thing The second problem is that “the academy” is treated as a single enemy with a single doctrine. This is not accurate. Academic hadith studies includes very skeptical approaches, more conservative source-critical approaches, and many intermediate positions. Schacht and Juynboll represent a more skeptical line, especially regarding legal traditions and common links. Motzki developed isnād-cum-matn analysis in ways that sometimes pushed dates earlier than Schacht would allow. Schoeler and Görke argued for recoverable early material in some sīra and maghāzī corpora. Jonathan Brown has written sympathetically about the sophistication and social function of Sunni hadith canonization while still distinguishing confessional authority from academic proof. Shahab Ahmed’s work on the Satanic Verses is not the same kind of project as Schacht’s work on legal traditions. Joshua Little’s work on ʿĀʾisha reports is not simply Juynboll repeated under a new name.[^1] More skeptical Goldziher · Schacht · Juynboll Later legal, sectarian, and communal needs explain many Prophetic attributions. Source-critical Motzki · Schoeler · Görke Some early material may be recoverable through careful isnād-cum-matn analysis. Tradition-aware Brown · Ahmed · Little The tradition must be studied as a historical archive, not simply dismissed or canonized. Once the field is described this way, the apologetic move becomes much weaker. If the academy were merely a secular church of anti-Islamic suspicion, we would expect a single conclusion and a single method. Instead we find a field full of disagreement over dating, source recovery, common links, family isnāds, legal projection, oral transmission, written notebooks, and the reliability of individual corpora. That disagreement does not vindicate the Sunni hadith sciences as a religious authority. But it does show that dismissing the whole field as “Western bias” is not a serious answer. The Genetic Fallacy Turns Against the Apologist Another common defense says that modern historical criticism grew out of European disillusionment with Church corruption, forged documents, fake relics, and ecclesiastical claims that could not survive scrutiny. Therefore, the method is psychologically contaminated by distrust. Even if that simplified origin story were granted, the argument would still fail. A method is not refuted by describing why people first needed it. Fire inspection developed because buildings burned. Forensic accounting developed because people committed fraud. Isnād criticism developed because people lied about the Prophet. A method created in response to deception can be more necessary, not less. The classical Muslim tradition makes exactly this admission. Muslim preserves the famous statement of Ibn Sīrīn: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَسْأَلُونَ عَنِ الإِسْنَادِ، فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْفِتْنَةُ قَالُوا: سَمُّوا لَنَا رِجَالَكُمْ، فَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ فَيُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ، وَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ فَلَا يُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ. “They did not use to ask about the isnād. But when the fitna occurred, they said: name your men for us. The people of the Sunna would be examined and their reports taken, and the people of innovation would be examined and their reports not taken.” Muslim also transmits the maxim: إِنَّ هَذَا الْعِلْمَ دِينٌ، فَانْظُرُوا عَمَّنْ تَأْخُذُونَ دِينَكُمْ. “This knowledge is religion, so examine from whom you take your religion.” These are not Orientalist slogans. They are internal Sunni memory. The isnād was not always policed with the same intensity. The need for scrutiny became urgent after social rupture, factional conflict, and fabrication. That means the apologetic attack on “methods born from suspicion” cuts against hadith science itself. Forgery or conflict appears → A method of verification develops → The method must be judged by results, not by origin If a method is invalid because it arose in response to deception, then classical hadith criticism is invalid for the same reason. The better question is whether the method can actually detect the kind of errors it claims to detect. What Hadith Criticism Can and Cannot See The classical definition of a ṣaḥīḥ report is disciplined. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ defines the sound report as one with a connected isnād, transmitted by upright and precise transmitters, free from anomaly and hidden defect.[^2] That is not a foolish definition. It is a serious attempt to filter reports. The problem is the distance between **filtering a later archive** and **proving an original utterance**. A report can satisfy the later criteria and still remain historically uncertain at the earliest layer. The criteria work best where the evidence is visible: named transmitters, known teachers, competing pupils, variant wording, hidden breaks, regional oddities, and contradictions with stronger routes. They work less well where the evidence disappears: the first decades before formal isnād policing, political motive hidden behind a respected authority, family transmission that cannot be independently checked, or a common link who has already attached a report to an earlier figure. Visible to the critic named transmitters teacher-pupil plausibility variant comparison known weak narrators contradictions among routes Harder to see early anonymous circulation retrojected Companion authority ideological motive before documentation common-link reshaping lost variants and suppressed alternatives This is where modern isnād-cum-matn analysis becomes useful. It does not simply laugh at isnāds. It takes them seriously enough to map them. It asks where the report first becomes historically visible, which wording appears at which layer, and whether the matn develops along the same lines as the isnād. Schacht’s common-link theory, Juynboll’s refinements, and Motzki’s critiques of both are not identical positions, but they all force a question that simple apologetics avoids: **where does the report actually begin in the evidence we possess?**[^3] A hadith may be “authentic” in the technical sense of a later Sunni collection and still be historically late in origin. That is not a contradiction. It only becomes a contradiction if one silently equates Sunni grading with historical demonstration. Ṣaḥīḥ Does Not Mean Revelation-Level Certainty A serious traditionalist knows that not every authenticated report occupies the same epistemic rank as the Qur’an. The usūl tradition debated solitary reports precisely because the issue was not simple. Mutawātir reports were treated differently from āḥād reports. Legal obligation was often distinguished from certain knowledge. Al-Shāfiʿī’s argument for accepting qualified solitary reports is one of the most important classical defenses, but even there the distinction remains. In *al-Risāla*, after defending obligation to act on certain reports, he does not make them equal to the Qur’an or public transmission. He says: لا أن ذلك إحاطة كما يكون نص الكتاب وخبر العامة “Not that this is comprehensive certainty as with the text of the Book and public report.” That admission matters. It means a report can be practically binding within a legal theory without becoming epistemically equal to the Qur’an. The apologetic defense often blurs this distinction. It speaks as though doubting a solitary hadith is the same as doubting revelation itself. But that is not how the classical hierarchy of proof actually works. Highest public proof Qur’an / mass-recited text Public, communal, liturgical, manuscript and recitational transmission. Mass report Mutawātir-type knowledge Claimed certainty through wide, independent transmission. Limited report Āḥād / specialist transmission May create legal obligation inside a school, but does not become Qur’an-level certainty. This is where the academy’s challenge bites. The academic historian is not required to accept the legal theory that turns a qualified solitary report into binding religious practice. The historian asks a different question: what is the earliest recoverable point of the report, and what best explains its formation? That is a historical question, not an anti-religious insult. “Orientalism” Is Not an Answer Orientalism was real. Colonial knowledge production was real. European scholars did sometimes write about Islam through hostile, Christian, racial, or imperial frames. A serious critic should admit this plainly. But admitting the existence of Orientalism does not answer a single hadith argument. It does not show that a chain is continuous. It does not show that a common link is early. It does not explain why one matn appears only in one regional cluster. It does not solve contradictions between variants. It does not make a weak narrator reliable. It does not turn a late political slogan into Prophetic speech. Valid use Expose bias, power, framing, translation choices, and selective attention. Invalid use Dismiss evidence without answering it, as if motive analysis replaced source analysis. The word “Orientalist” can identify a problem in a scholar’s assumptions. It cannot function as a universal solvent. Once a critic produces a concrete argument from isnād distribution, matn stratification, chronology, political setting, or manuscript evidence, the response must address that argument. Otherwise “Orientalism” becomes a way of protecting inherited claims from examination. The Satanic Verses as a Stress Test The Satanic Verses incident is a useful test case because it exposes how selective apologetics can become. The common apologetic line says the story is one weak narration, rejected by the tradition, and impossible because the Qur’an says the Prophet did not speak from desire. That framing is too neat. The point here is not that every detail of the story must be accepted. The point is that the tradition is much harder to dismiss than the apologetic summary admits. Shahab Ahmed’s book-length study collected and analyzed no less than fifty historical reports of the incident transmitted in the first generations of Islam.[^4] The material appears in early tafsīr, sīra, maghāzī, and historical writing. It is connected with figures such as Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Zuhrī, and Ibn ʿAbbās-associated exegetical material. It is not simply one isolated isnād in a fringe polemical book.[^5] The Qur’an itself contains a verse that many early exegetes connected to the problem of Satan casting something into a prophet’s recitation or wish, followed by God abolishing what Satan casts and confirming His verses. Ibn Taymiyyah is especially awkward for the later apologetic line because he does not treat the entire early memory as an obvious heresy. In his discussion of Q 22:52, he says that what is transmitted from the early Muslims agrees with the Qur’anic wording, while later scholars objected to the reported addition in Sūrat al-Najm and tried to reinterpret or reject it.[^6] Whether one agrees with Ibn Taymiyyah or not, his discussion shows that the apologetic claim “the real tradition always rejected this as a lie” is historically false. Apologetic reduction “One weak story” The report is treated as a marginal fabrication that can be dismissed without serious source analysis. Archive reality Multiple early reports The episode appears across tafsīr, sīra, maghāzī, and historical materials with several early transmitter attributions. Historical question How did this memory form? The burden is to explain the emergence, spread, discomfort, and later rejection of the narrative. Later scholars did push back. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Bayhaqī, and modern defenders such as al-Albānī rejected the incident in different ways. That later rejection is part of the evidence. It shows a shift in the boundaries of acceptable Prophetic memory. Early transmitters could preserve the story as an explanation of Q 22:52 and the Meccan prostration after Sūrat al-Najm. Later theologians, operating with a hardened doctrine of prophetic protection, increasingly found the story intolerable. That is precisely why the episode matters. It demonstrates the difference between **early archive** and **later orthodoxy**. The apologist often reads the later orthodoxy backward and then calls the early archive impossible. A historian cannot do that. A historian has to explain both layers. “The Qur’an Refutes It” Is Not Enough One might say that Sūrat al-Najm itself refutes the Satanic Verses story because it says the Prophet does not speak from desire. But this is not a historical argument by itself. It is a theological harmonization. The early transmitters who preserved the story knew Sūrat al-Najm existed. The exegetes who connected the story to Q 22:52 knew the Qur’an. Ibn Taymiyyah knew the Qur’an. The question is therefore not whether a modern reader can construct a theological objection. The question is why many early Muslim transmitters and exegetes did not see the objection as decisive. That does not prove the incident happened exactly as narrated. But it does prove that the apologetic dismissal is too simple. A serious answer would have to explain the spread of the reports, their early exegetical function, their relation to Q 22:52, their connection to the prostration at Sūrat al-Najm, and the later doctrinal pressure that made the story unacceptable. The Satanic Verses case is not a side issue. It reveals the whole methodological problem: when the inherited archive becomes uncomfortable, apologetics often stops doing hadith criticism and starts doing damage control. The Real Weakness in the Defense The defense of hadith often points to the sophistication of narrator criticism. That sophistication is real. The early critics were not naïve. They knew that transmitters could lie, confuse, paraphrase, conceal teachers, merge reports, raise stopped reports, or transmit after memory decline. They built a technical vocabulary around those dangers. But the defense then makes a leap. It moves from “the critics had tools” to “therefore the authenticated archive is historically secure.” That leap is not justified. A tool can be sophisticated and still limited. A metal detector cannot find wood. A microscope cannot detect motive. Rijāl criticism can catch visible transmitter problems, but it cannot automatically recover every earlier stage of a report. It often depends on the very tradition whose reliability is under investigation. A narrator is trustworthy because earlier critics say he is trustworthy; earlier critics are trusted because they belong to the same epistemic tradition; the report is then accepted because the trustworthy narrators transmitted it. That circle may be useful inside a confessional system, but it cannot simply be imposed as public historical proof. Critics define reliability → Narrators receive grades → Reports inherit confidence → The system validates itself The historian does not have to accept that circle. He may still use the data. In fact, he should. Rijāl books, isnād bundles, biographical notices, and early collections are invaluable evidence. But they are evidence to be analyzed, not authorities to be obeyed. A Better Traditionalist Response A stronger traditionalist response would not be to mock the academy as traumatized, colonial, or anti-God. It would admit the real difference between confessional and historical reasoning. It would say: yes, the Sunni hadith sciences rely on theological premises that academic historians do not grant, including the collective uprightness of the Companions, the authority of inherited communal practice, the binding force of qualified solitary reports, and confidence in the major critics. It would also say: yes, many hadith judgments are probabilistic, not mathematically certain. It would then defend why a Muslim legal-theological system may act on those probabilities even though the academic historian cannot treat them as public proof. That would at least be honest. It would stop pretending that the dispute is merely between reverent Muslims and biased Westerners. It would recognize that the academy and the madrasa are often asking different questions. Weak defense “The academy rejects hadith because it hates miracles and inherited Western trauma.” Stronger defense “The hadith sciences are a confessional legal-historical method that produces graded probability inside a theological system.” The stronger defense still would not prove the hadith archive historically. But it would at least locate the disagreement correctly. The conflict is not simply “Western disbelief versus Islamic faith.” It is a conflict over what kind of evidence can establish a claim about the past, and whether a confessional system may treat probabilities as religiously binding. The Bottom Line Dr. Shadee Elmasry’s defense fails because it does not meet the academic critique at its strongest point. The strongest critique is not that miracles are impossible. It is not that Muslims are uniquely gullible. It is not that every transmitter lied. The strongest critique is that hadith authentication is a later human method working on a later human archive, and its conclusions are limited by the evidence available to it. The classical critics knew that fabrication existed. They knew that isnāds could be manipulated. They knew that transmitters differed. They knew that hidden defects mattered. Their discipline is worth studying for that very reason. But the discipline cannot be transformed into certainty by accusing critics of Western bias. The question is not whether God could reveal through the Prophet. The question is whether a particular hadith can be historically demonstrated as Prophetic speech. That burden is not met by calling criticism “Western,” “Orientalist,” or “secular.” It is met only by evidence. Source notes [^1]: For the range of academic approaches, see Joseph Schacht, *The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence*; G. H. A. Juynboll, *Muslim Tradition*; Harald Motzki, “Dating Muslim Traditions: A Survey,” *Arabica* 52 (2005): 204–253; Gregor Schoeler, *The Oral and the Written in Early Islam*; Andreas Görke and Gregor Schoeler, *The Earliest Writings on the Life of Muḥammad*; Jonathan A. C. Brown, *Hadith: Muhammad’s Legacy in the Medieval and Modern World*; Shahab Ahmed, *Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam*; Joshua Little, *The Hadith of ʿĀʾiša’s Marital Age*. [^2]: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, *Muqaddima fī ʿulūm al-ḥadīth*, definition of the ṣaḥīḥ report: a connected isnād through upright and precise transmitters, free from shudhūdh and ʿilla. This classical definition is also summarized throughout later hadith manuals. [^3]: Motzki’s survey is useful because it does not merely repeat Schacht. It maps Goldziher, Schacht, Juynboll, Speight, and isnād-cum-matn approaches, while criticizing overconfident arguments from silence and simplistic matn dating. See Motzki, “Dating Muslim Traditions,” especially the sections on Schacht, Juynboll, common links, and isnād-cum-matn analysis. [^4]: Shahab Ahmed, *Before Orthodoxy: The Satanic Verses in Early Islam* (Harvard University Press, 2017). The point is not that every strand is sound by later hadith standards, but that the episode is not reducible to one isolated weak report.
