title: Al-Shāfiʿī’s Probabilistic Hadith Argument Refuted
description: Al-Shāfiʿī tried to defend solitary reports by comparing them to legal judgment, testimony, and practical uncertainty. The comparison only works if one confuses applying a revealed command with creating an additional source of religious law.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The argument for solitary hadith reports is usually presented as if it were just common sense. Human beings often act without absolute certainty. Judges weigh testimony. Travelers estimate the direction of prayer. Two fair people assess a penalty when exact equivalence is impossible. If Islamic law already accepts disciplined probability in those cases, why should a solitary report from a reliable transmitter be rejected simply because it is probabilistic? That is the strongest version of al-Shāfiʿī’s move. It is also where the problem begins. The examples do not prove what they are asked to prove. They show that people use judgment **inside** a command whose authority has already been established. They do not show that fallible reports can become an additional source of divine law. Al-Shāfiʿī’s argument does not fail because probability is useless. It fails because he uses probability for two different jobs. One job is applying an already revealed command. The other is admitting a new body of reports as binding religion. The first is unavoidable. The second requires a separate proof. The difference is not small. A person who estimates the Qiblah is trying to obey a command he already accepts from the Qur’an. A judge who weighs witnesses is applying a legal procedure whose authority is already granted. But when a solitary report is used to create a rule, qualify a Qur’anic rule, or add religious content not found in the Qur’an, probability is no longer helping someone apply revelation. It is being used to decide what counts as revelation-like authority in the first place. That is the category shift. The entire article turns on it. ## Al-Shāfiʿī’s Actual Argument Al-Shāfiʿī did not merely say, “accept hadith because narrators are reliable.” His argument in *al-Risāla* is more structured. He divides knowledge into public knowledge and specialist knowledge. Public knowledge includes the Qur’an and the widely transmitted religious duties. Specialist knowledge includes reports known through limited transmitters. In his section on **khabar al-wāḥid**, he defines the minimum report that can establish proof for scholars as a report carried by one person from one person until it reaches the Prophet or the authority below him.[^1] He then gives conditions. The transmitter must be religiously upright, known for truthfulness, aware of what he is transmitting, capable of preserving wording, free from deceptive transmission, and supported by a connected chain of similarly qualified transmitters.[^2] ولا تقوم الحجة بخبر الخاصة حتى يجمع أموراً “Proof is not established by specialist report until it gathers certain conditions.” That is a serious attempt to control transmission. It should not be caricatured. Al-Shāfiʿī is not defending every rumor. He is defending a restricted class of reports. But even this improved version of the argument still leaves the central question unanswered: who authorized this restricted class of reports to function as a source of binding religion? public proof Qur’an and public transmission Known by the community, denied only by rejecting the manifest foundation. → specialist proof Khabar al-khāṣṣa Accepted by qualified scholars through transmitter evaluation, but not with the certainty of public proof. → legal result Outward obligation The report is treated as binding for practice, like judgment by upright witnesses. The crucial point is that al-Shāfiʿī himself knows this is not the same as the Qur’an or public transmission. In *al-Risāla*, after defending the obligation to act on such reports, he concedes that this is not **iḥāṭa**, not comprehensive certainty like the Book or public report from the Messenger.[^3] لا أن ذلك إحاطة كما يكون نص الكتاب وخبر العامة “Not that this is comprehensive certainty as with the text of the Book and public report.” That admission is not a minor footnote. It is the epistemic ceiling of the whole argument. Al-Shāfiʿī can argue that the scholar must act on a qualified solitary report. He cannot honestly make it equal to the Qur’an or to universally transmitted religious knowledge. His own language places it below certainty. ## The Analogy to Testimony Al-Shāfiʿī repeatedly compares solitary reports to testimony. A judge does not know with absolute certainty what happened between two litigants. He hears witnesses, checks their uprightness, and rules according to the apparent truth. The possibility of error does not paralyze the court. Therefore, al-Shāfiʿī argues, the possibility of error should not paralyze the jurist when a reliable report reaches him. That analogy is persuasive only until we ask what testimony is being used for. court testimony Limited judgment A judge resolves a dispute between parties using evidence that can be challenged, contradicted, or procedurally revised. ≠ same epistemic role? hadith legislation Source authority A report is used to attach law, ritual, doctrine, or sacred history to the Prophet and therefore to religion itself. Court testimony does not create revelation. It does not add a devotional practice. It does not redefine God’s completed book. It gives an outward judgment in a particular case. If the witnesses lied, the divine command did not change. The judge’s ruling was simply wrong at the human level. A solitary hadith used as law does something different. If it adds an obligation, restricts a Qur’anic permission, expands a punishment, inserts an eschatological claim, or defines ritual detail not present in the Qur’an, it is not merely resolving a dispute. It is functioning as a second stream of religious normativity. The analogy to testimony proves only that fallible evidence may be used for practical judgments. It does not prove that fallible evidence may become an independent source of divine law. This is why the testimony argument is weaker than it first appears. A judge may be required to act on apparent truth because society cannot function otherwise. That does not mean a religious community may add sacred law on the basis of the same level of outward probability. The burden is higher when the claim is not “this contract was signed,” but “God bound the community through this report.” ## The Qubāʾ Example The strongest example al-Shāfiʿī uses is the report about the people of Qubāʾ. They were praying toward Jerusalem when someone came and told them that revelation had come down commanding the Prophet to face the Kaʿba. They turned during prayer. Al-Shāfiʿī argues that they left an established obligation because of one report, and the Prophet did not condemn them.[^4] The hadith is well known in Bukhārī. Its logic is simple: one person communicated a new command, and the worshipers acted immediately.[^5] فاستداروا إلى الكعبة “So they turned toward the Kaʿba.” But the example proves less than al-Shāfiʿī needs. The people of Qubāʾ were not evaluating a post-prophetic archive two centuries later. They were in the Prophet’s living community. The reported command was connected to a public Qur’anic event. Verification was possible. The Prophet was alive. The social distance between report and source was almost nothing. Qubāʾ Living Prophet Fresh Qur’anic command Immediate public verification possible Single social step from source cannot be stretched into Later hadith archive Prophet absent Reports competing across regions Chains reconstructed through biographical judgment Generations between source and collector If a messenger walks from the Prophet’s mosque to Qubāʾ while the Prophet is alive, that is one problem. If a collector in the third/ninth century receives a chain through several dead transmitters, contradictory regional corpora, and post-fitna sectarian pressures, that is another. The first may justify obedience to a living prophetic administration. It does not automatically authorize a later report archive to generate binding law. The same problem appears in the wine-prohibition example. Al-Shāfiʿī notes that Abū Ṭalḥa and those with him destroyed their wine after a public caller announced that wine had been forbidden.[^6] Again, this is not the same as later hadith authentication. It is a public command circulating in the Prophet’s community. People can ask, confirm, and observe whether the whole community changes. The example is administrative, not archival. ## What the Qur’anic Examples Actually Prove Al-Shāfiʿī also appeals to Qur’anic cases where the law itself requires estimation or judgment. The hunting penalty during pilgrimage is assessed by two equitable people. Compensation and retaliation require human adjudication. Prayer direction can require practical estimation. These examples prove that law cannot be applied without human judgment. They do not prove that human judgment can create new religious sources. Al-Shāfiʿī’s defense of solitary reports is strongest when treated as a rule of juristic procedure inside Sunni law. They show that people use judgment **inside** a command whose authority has already been established. They do not show that fallible reports can become an additional source of divine law. Al-Shāfiʿī’s argument does not fail because probability is useless. It fails because he uses probability for two different jobs. One job is applying an already revealed command. The other is admitting a new body of reports as binding religion. The first is unavoidable. The second requires a separate proof. The difference is not small. A person who estimates the Qiblah is trying to obey a command he already accepts from the Qur’an. A judge who weighs witnesses is applying a legal procedure whose authority is already granted. But when a solitary report is used to create a rule, qualify a Qur’anic rule, or add religious content not found in the Qur’an, probability is no longer helping someone apply revelation. It is being used to decide what counts as revelation-like authority in the first place. That is the category shift. The entire article turns on it. He divides knowledge into public knowledge and specialist knowledge. Public knowledge includes the Qur’an and the widely transmitted religious duties. Specialist knowledge includes reports known through limited transmitters. In his section on **khabar al-wāḥid**, he defines the minimum report that can establish proof for scholars as a report carried by one person from one person until it reaches the Prophet or the authority below him.[^1] He then gives conditions. The transmitter must be religiously upright, known for truthfulness, aware of what he is transmitting, capable of preserving wording, free from deceptive transmission, and supported by a connected chain of similarly qualified transmitters.[^2] ولا تقوم الحجة بخبر الخاصة حتى يجمع أموراً “Proof is not established by specialist report until it gathers certain conditions.” That is a serious attempt to control transmission. It should not be caricatured. Al-Shāfiʿī is not defending every rumor. He is defending a restricted class of reports. But even this improved version of the argument still leaves the central question unanswered: who authorized this restricted class of reports to function as a source of binding religion? public proof Qur’an and public transmission Known by the community, denied only by rejecting the manifest foundation. → specialist proof Khabar al-khāṣṣa Accepted by qualified scholars through transmitter evaluation, but not with the certainty of public proof. → legal result Outward obligation The report is treated as binding for practice, like judgment by upright witnesses. The wording defines the minimum report as “khabar al-wāḥid ʿan al-wāḥid” until it reaches the Prophet or the authority below him. [^2]: al-Shāfiʿī, *al-Risāla*, §§1000–1001. The conditions include religious uprightness, truthfulness, awareness of meaning, preservation of wording, memory or book control, agreement with other preservers, avoidance of tadlīs, and connected transmission. [^3]: al-Shāfiʿī, *al-Risāla*, final discussion of **khabar al-khāṣṣa** and certainty, where he compares acting on solitary report to accepting upright witnesses while denying that it is **iḥāṭa** like the Book and public report. [^4]: al-Shāfiʿī, *al-Risāla*, “al-Ḥujja fī tathbīt khabar al-wāḥid,” §§1101ff., where he gathers proofs for accepting the solitary report. [^5]: al-Bukhārī, *Ṣaḥīḥ*, report of the people of Qubāʾ turning during prayer after news of the Qiblah change reached them. [^6]: al-Shāfiʿī, *al-Risāla*, in the same proof section, uses the wine-prohibition announcement as a precedent for acting on a transmitted command before direct public confirmation. [^7]: al-Shāfiʿī, *al-Risāla*, discussion after the Qubāʾ and envoy examples. His statement that the matter is an **aṣl** and not a qiyās is important because it raises, rather than lowers, the burden of proof. [^8]: al-Shāfiʿī, *Jamāʿ al-ʿIlm*, debate over **ijmāʿ**, where he restricts certain consensus to public obligations and challenges claims about dispersed scholarly agreement. [^9]: Joseph Schacht, *The Origins of Muhammadan Jurisprudence*, especially his discussion of sunna, living tradition, and al-Shāfiʿī’s elevation of Prophetic reports over Companion and Successor material. Christopher Melchert’s work on al-Shāfiʿī and the Kufan school gives a more cautious historical framing of al-Shāfiʿī’s polemics against regional legal traditions. He states that the solitary report does not yield knowledge in itself, though it may create obligation to act under legal proof. [^11]: Later uṣūl works often distinguish between what produces certainty and what produces probable practical obligation. title: Hume’s Problem of Induction vs. Hadith
description: Hadith authentication is not a deductive machine. It is a historical inference from observed transmitter behavior to unobserved reports, and that inference needs to be treated as probability, not certainty.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The usual defense of hadith authentication sounds simple. A report is reliable when its chain is continuous, its transmitters are upright and accurate, and the report is not anomalous or defective. The method looks disciplined because it has technical terms, biographies, grades, comparisons, and long lists of authorities. But beneath that structure is a philosophical move that is rarely stated plainly. The critic observes a transmitter in some cases and then projects that judgment onto other cases. He observes a narrator’s reputation, a set of teacher-student relations, a sample of reports, or the judgments of earlier critics, and then uses that evidence to classify a new report as sound, weak, anomalous, or defective. That is not deduction. It is induction: an inference from what has been observed to what has not been observed. This does not make the method worthless. Hume’s problem of induction is not that induction is useless. We all use it. The problem is that induction cannot deliver the kind of certainty people often smuggle into the word **ṣaḥīḥ**. A report may be more probable or less probable. A route may be better or worse. A cluster may be earlier or later. But the move from “this narrator was often reliable” to “this specific unobserved report is Prophetic speech” is not a logical proof. It is a historical guess, sometimes a very disciplined one, but still a guess. The strongest version of the argument is not “hadith scholars used induction, therefore all hadith are false.” The stronger argument is that hadith authentication depends on inductive projections that can never yield demonstrative certainty. Once that is admitted, hadith reports must be treated as ranked historical probabilities, not as recovered revelation. ## The Classical Machine A standard definition of the authentic report requires five things: a connected chain, upright transmitters, accurate transmitters, freedom from contradiction, and freedom from hidden defect. Modern summaries of the classical definition usually state it in those terms: continuity of the isnād, trustworthy and precise transmitters, no **shudhūdh**, and no **ʿilla**.[^1] 1 Continuity Each narrator must plausibly receive from the one above him. 2 Uprightness The transmitter must not be judged morally disqualified. 3 Precision Memory, books, and performance must be judged dependable. 4 No anomaly The report must not oppose stronger preserved material. 5 No hidden defect A subtle problem must not be detected by comparison. Those criteria are not random. They represent a real attempt to control transmission. Early critics compared routes, tracked teachers, distinguished similarly named narrators, and noticed when a report moved from one authority to another. Ibn Ḥibbān’s introduction to *al-Majrūḥīn* is full of admiration for critics who could distinguish two near-identical names, detect a dropped letter, identify a weak narrator hidden behind a kunyā, or separate the reports of a transmitter before and after his memory failed.[^2] So the point cannot be that early critics were stupid. They were often extremely careful inside their own archive. The problem is the epistemic status of the archive itself. The five conditions turn a collection of observations into a conclusion about an unobserved past. That is precisely where Hume becomes useful. ## Hume’s Question: Where Is the Bridge? Hume divided knowledge into two broad kinds. Some truths are demonstrative, like mathematics. Their denial creates a contradiction. Other claims are matters of fact. They concern the world, the past, testimony, memory, and cause-and-effect. Their denial may be false, but it is still conceivable. That matters because hadith authentication is a claim about matters of fact. It claims that a particular sentence was uttered, preserved, and transmitted through a series of human beings. Hume’s point was that such claims cannot be proven like geometry. In his words, “there are no demonstrative arguments” when we project from past experience to future or unobserved cases.[^3] Observed Sample Some reports by a transmitter look stable, familiar, or supported. habit → “Where is the medium?” Generalized Rating The transmitter becomes “trustworthy,” “precise,” or “weak.” projection → unobserved case Unobserved Report A specific Prophetic attribution is accepted as historically sound. The question is not whether this move is useful. It often is. The question is whether the move creates certainty. Hume answers no. He argues that “all inferences from experience” are effects of custom rather than demonstrative reasoning.[^4] The mind sees repeated patterns and expects the pattern to continue. That is how human beings function. It is not how one proves that an unseen report from the first/seventh century is the speech of the Prophet. Hume is even more relevant in his discussion of human testimony. He does not reject testimony. He says our confidence in testimony depends on experience: memory, truthfulness, shame before exposure, the character of witnesses, the number of witnesses, the manner of delivery, and whether the claim fits what is otherwise known.[^5] That is close to what a good hadith critic should be doing. But Hume’s standard does not produce a binary “authentic / fabricated” world. It produces degrees of confidence. Hume is not a magic weapon against every report. He is a pressure test. If a hadith argument claims only probability, it can survive Hume. If it claims certainty from narrator reputation, it collapses into an unjustified inductive leap. ## Hadith Criticism Already Admits the Problem The most useful evidence against overconfident hadith authentication comes from the hadith tradition itself. The early discipline did not emerge because everyone calmly transmitted a pristine archive. It emerged because reports could be misremembered, manipulated, regionalized, sectarianized, and back-projected. Muslim preserves the famous statement of Ibn Sīrīn: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَسْأَلُونَ عَنِ الإِسْنَادِ، فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْفِتْنَةُ قَالُوا: سَمُّوا لَنَا رِجَالَكُمْ، فَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ فَيُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ، وَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ فَلَا يُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ. “They did not use to ask about the isnād. But when the fitna occurred, they said: name your men for us. The people of the Sunna would be examined and their reports taken, and the people of innovation would be examined and their reports not taken.” This statement is usually quoted to glorify the isnād. It can also be read more soberly. It admits that isnād policing became necessary after a historical rupture. That means the most important period, the first phase of transmission, is also the least directly controlled. The method was built after the very social conditions that made the method necessary. Ibn Ḥibbān gives the same kind of admission in a different way. He reports that people would ask Zayd b. Arqam for Prophetic reports, and he would answer: إِنَّا قَدْ كَبِرْنَا وَنَسِينَا، وَالْحَدِيثُ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللهِ ﷺ شَدِيدٌ. “We have grown old and forgotten, and narrating from the Messenger of God is a serious matter.” Ibn ʿAbbās is then cited as saying that they used to narrate when lying about the Prophet was not common, but when people began taking every path, they left narration from him.[^6] These are not skeptical Orientalist talking points. They are internal acknowledgments that memory, age, social conditions, and fabrication mattered. That is why the strongest critique of hadith science should not be that it never noticed error. It noticed error constantly. The critique is that it could notice only the errors that left visible traces in the later archive. Hume’s gap remains where the traces disappear. ## Reliability Is Not a Fixed Substance Classical critics did sometimes make conditional judgments. Those conditional judgments are actually more damaging to the certainty claim, because they show that reliability is not a permanent substance inside a person. It changes by teacher, region, book, age, and circumstance. Ibn Ḥibbān states that some trustworthy transmitters became confused at the end of their lives until their sound reports mixed with unsound ones and could no longer be distinguished.[^7] He also says that there are reports of accurate trustworthy transmitters that are not used as proof, because specific classes of their reports contain mistakes such as scribal confusion, raising a stopped report, connecting a disconnected one, or inserting one report into another.[^8] One example is Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh. Yaḥyā b. Maʿīn is quoted as saying: إِذَا حَدَّثَ عَنِ الشَّامِيِّينَ فَحَدِيثُهُ صَحِيحٌ، وَإِذَا حَدَّثَ عَنِ الْعِرَاقِيِّينَ أَوِ الْمَدَنِيِّينَ خَلَطَ مَا شِئْتَ. “When he narrates from Syrians, his hadith is sound; when he narrates from Iraqis or Medinans, he confuses as much as you like.” That single notice breaks the myth of simple narrator essence. A person can be reliable in one domain and unreliable in another. He can be accurate from one teacher and poor from another. He can be stable in one decade and confused in another. He can preserve legal material better than eschatological material. He can recite from a book in one setting and from memory in another. Classical admission What it means philosophically Ikhtilāṭ A transmitter can become confused late in life. Time-specific reliability A global rating hides the question: did this report come before or after the change? Regional weakness Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh is treated differently by regional source. Domain-specific reliability The same narrator does not carry the same probability in every context. Solitary mistakes Ibn Ḥibbān refuses to use some transmitters when they stand alone. Independence matters A report needs corroboration that is not just the same error spreading outward. The philosophical result is simple. If reliability is conditional, then a universal label like **thiqa** cannot authenticate a report by itself. It is a compression of many judgments. Sometimes that compression may be reasonable. Sometimes it may erase exactly the information needed to judge the report. ## The Bootstrap Problem Hadith grading often moves in a circle. A narrator is judged reliable partly because his reports resemble accepted material. Then his reliability is used to authenticate additional material. The additional material becomes part of the accepted record, and the accepted record reinforces the narrator’s reputation. Bootstrap 1 Sample reports 2 Assign reliability 3 Authenticate new reports 4 Expand accepted corpus 5 Reinforce narrator reputation This does not mean every judgment is circular in the same way. Critics did compare, reject, and detect anomalies. But the deeper problem remains: the method lacks an independent calibration set for the first century. We cannot take a known list of Prophetic utterances, test how often each transmitter preserved them correctly, calculate individual error rates, and then apply those rates to unknown reports. The authenticated corpus is the thing being tested and the evidence used to perform the test. This is why “many chains” does not automatically solve the problem. Multiple isnāds increase probability only if they are meaningfully independent. If they converge on one common link, one teaching session, one written notebook, one regional school, or one political milieu, then they may not be many witnesses. They may be one source echoing through many students. Modern isnād-cum-matn analysis is useful precisely because it tries to test this independence. It asks where the variants actually branch, which wording belongs to which sub-route, whether a phrase appears at the common-link layer or later, and whether the content fits a legal, political, exegetical, or sectarian setting. A recent methodological summary in *Modern Hadith Studies* notes the advantage of combining isnād-cum-matn analysis with the legal, political, and exegetical concerns behind a tradition’s wording.[^9] That is a better method than treating a chain as a certificate. ## Ibn Khaldūn Saw the Same Historical Problem This is not only Hume. Ibn Khaldūn also criticized the habit of relying on transmission alone. In the *Muqaddima*, he writes that historical reports require multiple kinds of knowledge, sound judgment, and verification. He warns that when reports are accepted by “mere transmission” without testing them against custom, politics, social organization, and the conditions of human society, historians and transmitters fall into error.[^10] لأنّ الأخبار إذا اعتمد فيها على مجرّد النّقل ... فربّما لم يؤمن فيها من العثور ومزلّة القدم والحيد عن جادّة الصّدق. Ibn Khaldūn, al-Muqaddima Ibn Khaldūn’s point is not identical to Hume’s, but it pushes in the same direction. Transmission is not self-validating. A report must be tested against the world in which it claims to exist. A chain may show who transmitted a claim. It does not prove that the claim fits the social, political, linguistic, or historical conditions of its alleged origin. This is exactly why prophecy reports, sectarian virtue reports, anti-sectarian polemics, apocalyptic schedules, and legal proof-texts require special caution. They are not neutral memories floating through clean channels. They are often the kinds of material that communities had reasons to create, sharpen, sanitize, or back-project. ## The Qurʾānic Standard Is Verification, Not Reputation A Qurʾānic epistemology does not require blind rejection of all reports. It requires proportion and verification. The Qurʾān tells believers not to pursue what they have no knowledge of, warns that conjecture does not replace truth, and commands verification when a report comes from a morally compromised source. 17:36 Do not pursue what you have no knowledge of. 10:36 Conjecture does not avail anything against the truth. 6:116 Most people follow only conjecture. 49:6 When a report arrives, verify before acting on it. The tension is obvious. Hadith authentication often shifts the burden from the report to the reputation of the people in the chain. The Qurʾānic standard pushes in the other direction: do not let social confidence become knowledge. Verification must reach the claim itself. This is why matn criticism cannot be a decorative afterthought. If a report contradicts the Qurʾān, creates a doctrine absent from it, imports a sectarian agenda, fits a later political crisis too neatly, or appears only through a bottleneck with motive and opportunity, then its chain cannot rescue it. The chain becomes part of the historical explanation of how the report traveled, not proof that it originated with the Prophet. ## The Stronger Historical Method A better method does not pretend to escape induction. It uses induction honestly. It treats every report as a hypothesis and asks how strongly the evidence supports it. 1 Collect variants Do not argue from a single collector’s version. 2 Map the isnād Find the real bottlenecks, not the claimed origin. 3 Compare the matn Track which phrases appear at which layers. 4 Ask motive Locate legal, political, exegetical, or sectarian pressure. 5 Test externally Use Qurʾān, chronology, history, language, and material context. 6 State probability Do not call a historical inference revelation-level knowledge. This is where the older hadith categories are too blunt. “Ṣaḥīḥ” can hide a report with a strong-looking lower chain but a late common link. “Ḥasan” can preserve an old memory with weak later packaging. “Ḍaʿīf” can still be useful evidence for what a community in a certain place believed. “Mawḍūʿ” can still teach us who needed the report and why. A source-critical approach asks a different question. Not merely: “Is the chain acceptable by later rules?” But: “What is the earliest recoverable form of this report, where does it become visible, and what historical work was it doing there?” ## What Hadith Authentication Can Still Do The critique should not be overstated. Rijāl can still do useful work. It can expose impossible meetings, late fabricators, hidden transmitters, sectarian transmitters, regional routes, and suspicious solitary reports. It can show that one version is later than another. It can sometimes show that a report existed earlier than a collector. It can help reconstruct intellectual networks. What it cannot do is convert human transmission into certainty. It cannot make a Companion attribution immune to historical questioning. It cannot prove that a respected transmitter never erred in this specific report. It cannot turn a post-fitna security mechanism into direct access to the Prophet’s voice. The responsible conclusion is not “every hadith is false.” The responsible conclusion is that hadith reports are historical evidence, not epistemic foundations. They may be early or late, plausible or implausible, useful or useless, but they do not escape the normal limits of human testimony. Hume’s problem does not destroy all historical reasoning. It destroys inflated certainty. Hadith criticism can produce probabilities only when it is joined to variant collection, matn analysis, source criticism, and historical context. A chain of reputable names is not knowledge. It is an argument. And arguments must be weighed. ## Source notes [^1]: For the standard five-part technical definition, see Mustafa Shah, ed., *The Hadith: Critical Concepts in Islamic Studies*, vol. 1, “Codification, Authenticity,” discussion of ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan, and ḍaʿīf classifications; the same basic definition is also summarized in Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ’s later hadith-theory tradition. See also Darul Iftaa, “Principles of Hadith Verification and Acceptance,” which explicitly treats a ṣaḥīḥ label as a technical judgment rather than an infallible statement of fact. He praises critics who distinguished similar names, corrected scribal confusion, and separated the routes of transmitters such as Saʿīd, Shuʿba, Sufyān, and Shaybān. fullText: The usual defense of hadith authentication sounds simple. A report is reliable when its chain is continuous, its transmitters are upright and accurate, and the report is not anomalous or defective. The method looks disciplined because it has technical terms, biographies, grades, comparisons, and long lists of authorities. But beneath that structure is a philosophical move that is rarely stated plainly. The critic observes a transmitter in some cases and then projects that judgment onto other cases. He observes a narrator’s reputation, a set of teacher-student relations, a sample of reports, or the judgments of earlier critics, and then uses that evidence to classify a new report as sound, weak, anomalous, or defective. That is not deduction. It is induction: an inference from what has been observed to what has not been observed. This does not make the method worthless. Hume’s problem of induction is not that induction is useless. We all use it. The problem is that induction cannot deliver the kind of certainty people often smuggle into the word **ṣaḥīḥ**. A report may be more probable or less probable. A route may be better or worse. A cluster may be earlier or later. But the move from “this narrator was often reliable” to “this specific unobserved report is Prophetic speech” is not a logical proof. It is a historical guess, sometimes a very disciplined one, but still a guess. The strongest version of the argument is not “hadith scholars used induction, therefore all hadith are false.” The stronger argument is that hadith authentication depends on inductive projections that can never yield demonstrative certainty. Once that is admitted, hadith reports must be treated as ranked historical probabilities, not as recovered revelation. The Classical Machine A standard definition of the authentic report requires five things: a connected chain, upright transmitters, accurate transmitters, freedom from contradiction, and freedom from hidden defect. Modern summaries of the classical definition usually state it in those terms: continuity of the isnād, trustworthy and precise transmitters, no **shudhūdh**, and no **ʿilla**.[^1] 1 Continuity Each narrator must plausibly receive from the one above him. 2 Uprightness The transmitter must not be judged morally disqualified. 3 Precision Memory, books, and performance must be judged dependable. 4 No anomaly The report must not oppose stronger preserved material. 5 No hidden defect A subtle problem must not be detected by comparison. Those criteria are not random. They represent a real attempt to control transmission. Early critics compared routes, tracked teachers, distinguished similarly named narrators, and noticed when a report moved from one authority to another. Ibn Ḥibbān’s introduction to *al-Majrūḥīn* is full of admiration for critics who could distinguish two near-identical names, detect a dropped letter, identify a weak narrator hidden behind a kunyā, or separate the reports of a transmitter before and after his memory failed.[^2] So the point cannot be that early critics were stupid. They were often extremely careful inside their own archive. The problem is the epistemic status of the archive itself. The five conditions turn a collection of observations into a conclusion about an unobserved past. That is precisely where Hume becomes useful. Hume’s Question: Where Is the Bridge? Hume divided knowledge into two broad kinds. Some truths are demonstrative, like mathematics. Their denial creates a contradiction. Other claims are matters of fact. They concern the world, the past, testimony, memory, and cause-and-effect. Their denial may be false, but it is still conceivable. That matters because hadith authentication is a claim about matters of fact. It claims that a particular sentence was uttered, preserved, and transmitted through a series of human beings. Hume’s point was that such claims cannot be proven like geometry. In his words, “there are no demonstrative arguments” when we project from past experience to future or unobserved cases.[^3] Observed Sample Some reports by a transmitter look stable, familiar, or supported. habit → “Where is the medium?” Generalized Rating The transmitter becomes “trustworthy,” “precise,” or “weak.” projection → unobserved case Unobserved Report A specific Prophetic attribution is accepted as historically sound. The question is not whether this move is useful. It often is. The question is whether the move creates certainty. Hume answers no. He argues that “all inferences from experience” are effects of custom rather than demonstrative reasoning.[^4] The mind sees repeated patterns and expects the pattern to continue. That is how human beings function. It is not how one proves that an unseen report from the first/seventh century is the speech of the Prophet. Hume is even more relevant in his discussion of human testimony. He does not reject testimony. He says our confidence in testimony depends on experience: memory, truthfulness, shame before exposure, the character of witnesses, the number of witnesses, the manner of delivery, and whether the claim fits what is otherwise known.[^5] That is close to what a good hadith critic should be doing. But Hume’s standard does not produce a binary “authentic / fabricated” world. It produces degrees of confidence. Hume is not a magic weapon against every report. He is a pressure test. If a hadith argument claims only probability, it can survive Hume. If it claims certainty from narrator reputation, it collapses into an unjustified inductive leap. Hadith Criticism Already Admits the Problem The most useful evidence against overconfident hadith authentication comes from the hadith tradition itself. The early discipline did not emerge because everyone calmly transmitted a pristine archive. It emerged because reports could be misremembered, manipulated, regionalized, sectarianized, and back-projected. Muslim preserves the famous statement of Ibn Sīrīn: لَمْ يَكُونُوا يَسْأَلُونَ عَنِ الإِسْنَادِ، فَلَمَّا وَقَعَتِ الْفِتْنَةُ قَالُوا: سَمُّوا لَنَا رِجَالَكُمْ، فَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ السُّنَّةِ فَيُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ، وَيُنْظَرُ إِلَى أَهْلِ الْبِدَعِ فَلَا يُؤْخَذُ حَدِيثُهُمْ. “They did not use to ask about the isnād. But when the fitna occurred, they said: name your men for us. The people of the Sunna would be examined and their reports taken, and the people of innovation would be examined and their reports not taken.” This statement is usually quoted to glorify the isnād. It can also be read more soberly. It admits that isnād policing became necessary after a historical rupture. That means the most important period, the first phase of transmission, is also the least directly controlled. The method was built after the very social conditions that made the method necessary. Ibn Ḥibbān gives the same kind of admission in a different way. He reports that people would ask Zayd b. Arqam for Prophetic reports, and he would answer: إِنَّا قَدْ كَبِرْنَا وَنَسِينَا، وَالْحَدِيثُ عَنْ رَسُولِ اللهِ ﷺ شَدِيدٌ. “We have grown old and forgotten, and narrating from the Messenger of God is a serious matter.” Ibn ʿAbbās is then cited as saying that they used to narrate when lying about the Prophet was not common, but when people began taking every path, they left narration from him.[^6] These are not skeptical Orientalist talking points. They are internal acknowledgments that memory, age, social conditions, and fabrication mattered. That is why the strongest critique of hadith science should not be that it never noticed error. It noticed error constantly. The critique is that it could notice only the errors that left visible traces in the later archive. Hume’s gap remains where the traces disappear. Reliability Is Not a Fixed Substance Classical critics did sometimes make conditional judgments. Those conditional judgments are actually more damaging to the certainty claim, because they show that reliability is not a permanent substance inside a person. It changes by teacher, region, book, age, and circumstance. Ibn Ḥibbān states that some trustworthy transmitters became confused at the end of their lives until their sound reports mixed with unsound ones and could no longer be distinguished.[^7] He also says that there are reports of accurate trustworthy transmitters that are not used as proof, because specific classes of their reports contain mistakes such as scribal confusion, raising a stopped report, connecting a disconnected one, or inserting one report into another.[^8] One example is Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh. Yaḥyā b. Maʿīn is quoted as saying: إِذَا حَدَّثَ عَنِ الشَّامِيِّينَ فَحَدِيثُهُ صَحِيحٌ، وَإِذَا حَدَّثَ عَنِ الْعِرَاقِيِّينَ أَوِ الْمَدَنِيِّينَ خَلَطَ مَا شِئْتَ. “When he narrates from Syrians, his hadith is sound; when he narrates from Iraqis or Medinans, he confuses as much as you like.” That single notice breaks the myth of simple narrator essence. A person can be reliable in one domain and unreliable in another. He can be accurate from one teacher and poor from another. He can be stable in one decade and confused in another. He can preserve legal material better than eschatological material. He can recite from a book in one setting and from memory in another. Classical admission What it means philosophically Ikhtilāṭ A transmitter can become confused late in life. Time-specific reliability A global rating hides the question: did this report come before or after the change? Regional weakness Ismāʿīl b. ʿAyyāsh is treated differently by regional source. Domain-specific reliability The same narrator does not carry the same probability in every context. Solitary mistakes Ibn Ḥibbān refuses to use some transmitters when they stand alone. Independence matters A report needs corroboration that is not just the same error spreading outward. The philosophical result is simple. If reliability is conditional, then a universal label like **thiqa** cannot authenticate a report by itself. It is a compression of many judgments. Sometimes that compression may be reasonable. Sometimes it may erase exactly the information needed to judge the report. The Bootstrap Problem Hadith grading often moves in a circle. A narrator is judged reliable partly because his reports resemble accepted material. Then his reliability is used to authenticate additional material. The additional material becomes part of the accepted record, and the accepted record reinforces the narrator’s reputation. Bootstrap 1 Sample reports 2 Assign reliability 3 Authenticate new reports 4 Expand accepted corpus 5 Reinforce narrator reputation This does not mean every judgment is circular in the same way. Critics did compare, reject, and detect anomalies. But the deeper problem remains: the method lacks an independent calibration set for the first century. We cannot take a known list of Prophetic utterances, test how often each transmitter preserved them correctly, calculate individual error rates, and then apply those rates to unknown reports. The authenticated corpus is the thing being tested and the evidence used to perform the test. This is why “many chains” does not automatically solve the problem. Multiple isnāds increase probability only if they are meaningfully independent. If they converge on one common link, one teaching session, one written notebook, one regional school, or one political milieu, then they may not be many witnesses. They may be one source echoing through many students. Modern isnād-cum-matn analysis is useful precisely because it tries to test this independence. It asks where the variants actually branch, which wording belongs to which sub-route, whether a phrase appears at the common-link layer or later, and whether the content fits a legal, political, exegetical, or sectarian setting. A recent methodological summary in *Modern Hadith Studies* notes the advantage of combining isnād-cum-matn analysis with the legal, political, and exegetical concerns behind a tradition’s wording.[^9] That is a better method than treating a chain as a certificate. Ibn Khaldūn Saw the Same Historical Problem This is not only Hume. Ibn Khaldūn also criticized the habit of relying on transmission alone. In the *Muqaddima*, he writes that historical reports require multiple kinds of knowledge, sound judgment, and verification. He warns that when reports are accepted by “mere transmission” without testing them against custom, politics, social organization, and the conditions of human society, historians and transmitters fall into error.[^10] لأنّ الأخبار إذا اعتمد فيها على مجرّد النّقل ... فربّما لم يؤمن فيها من العثور ومزلّة القدم والحيد عن جادّة الصّدق. Ibn Khaldūn, al-Muqaddima Ibn Khaldūn’s point is not identical to Hume’s, but it pushes in the same direction. Transmission is not self-validating. A report must be tested against the world in which it claims to exist. A chain may show who transmitted a claim. It does not prove that the claim fits the social, political, linguistic, or historical conditions of its alleged origin. This is exactly why prophecy reports, sectarian virtue reports, anti-sectarian polemics, apocalyptic schedules, and legal proof-texts require special caution. They are not neutral memories floating through clean channels. They are often the kinds of material that communities had reasons to create, sharpen, sanitize, or back-project. The Qurʾānic Standard Is Verification, Not Reputation A Qurʾānic epistemology does not require blind rejection of all reports. It requires proportion and verification. The Qurʾān tells believers not to pursue what they have no knowledge of, warns that conjecture does not replace truth, and commands verification when a report comes from a morally compromised source. 17:36 Do not pursue what you have no knowledge of. 10:36 Conjecture does not avail anything against the truth. 6:116 Most people follow only conjecture. 49:6 When a report arrives, verify before acting on it. The tension is obvious. Hadith authentication often shifts the burden from the report to the reputation of the people in the chain. The Qurʾānic standard pushes in the other direction: do not let social confidence become knowledge. Verification must reach the claim itself. This is why matn criticism cannot be a decorative afterthought. If a report contradicts the Qurʾān, creates a doctrine absent from it, imports a sectarian agenda, fits a later political crisis too neatly, or appears only through a bottleneck with motive and opportunity, then its chain cannot rescue it. The chain becomes part of the historical explanation of how the report traveled, not proof that it originated with the Prophet. The Stronger Historical Method A better method does not pretend to escape induction. It uses induction honestly. It treats every report as a hypothesis and asks how strongly the evidence supports it. 1 Collect variants Do not argue from a single collector’s version. 2 Map the isnād Find the real bottlenecks, not the claimed origin. 3 Compare the matn Track which phrases appear at which layers. 4 Ask motive Locate legal, political, exegetical, or sectarian pressure. 5 Test externally Use Qurʾān, chronology, history, language, and material context. 6 State probability Do not call a historical inference revelation-level knowledge. This is where the older hadith categories are too blunt. “Ṣaḥīḥ” can hide a report with a strong-looking lower chain but a late common link. “Ḥasan” can preserve an old memory with weak later packaging. “Ḍaʿīf” can still be useful evidence for what a community in a certain place believed. “Mawḍūʿ” can still teach us who needed the report and why. A source-critical approach asks a different question. Not merely: “Is the chain acceptable by later rules?” But: “What is the earliest recoverable form of this report, where does it become visible, and what historical work was it doing there?” What Hadith Authentication Can Still Do The critique should not be overstated. Rijāl can still do useful work. It can expose impossible meetings, late fabricators, hidden transmitters, sectarian transmitters, regional routes, and suspicious solitary reports. It can show that one version is later than another. It can sometimes show that a report existed earlier than a collector. It can help reconstruct intellectual networks. What it cannot do is convert human transmission into certainty. It cannot make a Companion attribution immune to historical questioning. It cannot prove that a respected transmitter never erred in this specific report. It cannot turn a post-fitna security mechanism into direct access to the Prophet’s voice. The responsible conclusion is not “every hadith is false.” The responsible conclusion is that hadith reports are historical evidence, not epistemic foundations. They may be early or late, plausible or implausible, useful or useless, but they do not escape the normal limits of human testimony. Hume’s problem does not destroy all historical reasoning. It destroys inflated certainty. Hadith criticism can produce probabilities only when it is joined to variant collection, matn analysis, source criticism, and historical context. A chain of reputable names is not knowledge. It is an argument. And arguments must be weighed. title: The Scroll and the Sword: The Polemical Use of Ali
description: A full isnad-cum-matn re-examination of the Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī tradition across five independent clusters — al-Shaʿbī, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and Sharīk — arguing each is a distinct polemical fabrication built on a shared rhetorical frame, not fragments of one authentic Alid document.

al-Jaṣṣāṣ (Ḥanafī fiqh citation)', kind: 'collector', labelPos: 'below' } ]; { from: 'event', to: 'tariq', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'tariq', to: 'mukhariq', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'mukhariq', to: 'sharik', kind: 'trunk' }, { from: 'sharik', to: 'pcls5' }, { from: 'pcls5', to: 'collectors6' } ]; { y: 700, label: 'Live legal dispute' }, { y: 590, label: 'Companion' }, { y: 370, label: 'Common link — sitting judge' }, { y: 110, label: 'Compilers' } ]; { x: 420, y: 300, text: 'An entirely Kufan chain — the CL is the very judge whose court needed this ruling', kind: 'note', anchor: 'start' } ]; Seyfeddin Kara has argued, across thirty-five hadith organized into five clusters, that the tradition in which ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib denies possessing any secret Prophetic knowledge beyond the Qurʾān and a document on his sword-scabbard traces back to ʿAlī himself — that ʿAlī may have compiled the earliest known legal text in Islamic history. On his reading, the five clusters are partial testimonies to a single document: different questioners heard different passages on different occasions, and their divergent contents are simply different fragments of one comprehensive original. This piece takes Kara seriously on his own methodological terms. It does not dispute that isnad-cum-matn analysis (ICMA) is the right tool. It disputes that thirty-five variants are enough material to sustain the conclusion. Applied to the wider surviving corpus, the same method does not refine Kara's picture — it overturns the premise it rests on. The Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī tradition is not one document remembered in five fragments. It is five independent fabrications, each built on a shared rhetorical mold — ʿAlī is asked if he has secret Prophetic knowledge, denies it, and then reveals a scabbard document with enumerable contents — and each filled with different legal content by a different transmitter answering a different, dateable communal crisis. Al-Shaʿbī originated the frame against Mukhtār's revolt; Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and Sharīk each independently reused it for their own city's needs. ## Why Kara's Method Doesn't Get There ICMA can date a tradition to its earliest common link (CL). What it cannot do on its own is verify the single strand running from that CL up to the named Companion above him — that strand has no fan-out to check it against. Kara identifies several independent CLs all reporting on ʿAlī's scroll and treats their multiplicity, plus their shared content, as corroboration that some such scroll existed. That inference only holds if the CL-strands are genuinely independent of each other. Narrator substitution — a transmitter reissuing material he received through one line under a different, more prestigious or strategically useful authority, while keeping the wording essentially stable — is a documented, classically-acknowledged practice, not a modern suspicion.[^1] If even one or two of Kara's supposedly independent CLs acquired their material from a shared, unacknowledged source and re-attributed the isnād above it, his method has no way to detect this. It would register multiple independent lines converging on ʿAlī where there is really only one — or none — laundered through invented authorities. Matn corroboration across chains cannot, by itself, rule this out, and Kara's own treatment of weaker links elsewhere shows the pattern: a transmitter graded "closer to weak" is nonetheless accepted because the content matches other clusters, which quietly makes the conclusion immune to the very possibility of a false attribution.[^2] ## The Shared Architecture Every variant in every cluster, regardless of transmission line, geography, or legal content, follows the same fourfold shape: ʿAlī is asked whether he possesses anything from the Prophet beyond the Qurʾān; he denies it; the questioner presses; ʿAlī reveals a document in his sword-scabbard and lists what is in it. Not one cluster departs from this. That invariance is the single most important fact about the corpus, and it is exactly what a single-document theory cannot explain on its own — because the five clusters diverge in every other respect that matters. Different companions are present (Abū Juḥayfa in one, Abū al-Ṭufayl in another). Different cities produce them (Kufa, Baṣra, Mecca). And the legal registers are not compatible fragments of one code — blood-money and captive-ransom law in one cluster, constitutional protection for combatants in another, anti-tax-farming fiscal law in a third. Read as one document, the Ṣaḥīfa would have to be a complete Prophetic legal corpus. Read as five independent productions, the divergence is exactly what the theory predicts. ## Cluster I — al-Shaʿbī: The Originator Eight partial common links carry Muṭarrif's redaction forward: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna (to al-Shāfiʿī, al-Ḥumaydī, Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, al-Bazzār, al-Nasāʾī), Sufyān al-Thawrī (to ʿAbd al-Razzāq), Zuhayr b. Muʿāwiya (to al-Bukhārī and al-Bayhaqī), Hushaym b. Bashīr (to al-Tirmidhī), Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh (to Ibn Mājah), Yazīd b. ʿAṭāʾ (to al-Ṭayālisī), Jarīr b. ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd (to al-Dārimī), and Asbāṭ b. Muḥammad (to al-Ṭaḥāwī).[^3] Comparing what is invariant across all eight recovers a stable ur-text: the oath formula with its collective "we," the *fahm* exception, and a fixed three-item scroll — blood-money, captive-ransom, and the homicide ruling. Below that layer, the variation is diagnostic rather than random. The dominant wording bars killing a Muslim for a *kāfir* (unbeliever generally); a narrower sub-line — Yazīd b. ʿAṭāʾ, Jarīr, and one branch under Zuhayr — narrows this to *mushrik* (polytheist specifically).[^4] The same Zuhayr split is the clearest evidence for reading *kāfir* as original: his student Aḥmad b. Yūnus, who fed Bukhārī, kept *kāfir*; his student ʿAmr b. Marzūq, who fed al-Bayhaqī, has *mushrik* and also uniquely preserves Muṭarrif's own teaching glosses on the two technical terms — evidence that a single PCL sub-line juridically narrowed the rule while also carrying the most explicit record of Muṭarrif's classroom explanation of it.[^5] Muṭarrif is the checkable common link, but he is not the originator: nothing about his own biography explains why this exact material was needed. Al-Shaʿbī does. Born c. 17–19 AH into a Hamdānī family in Kufa, he fled the city for Medina out of fear of Mukhtār al-Thaqafī's movement, later served as judicial administrator under al-Ḥajjāj, was personally requisitioned by Caliph ʿAbd al-Malik as a court narrator, and died c. 103/721 as Kufa's most respected scholar.[^6] He is independently placed inside Mukhtār's own documentary world — present when Mukhtār produced a letter attributed to Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya to win over Ibrāhīm b. al-Ashtar, and described as the one who physically handed the letter over.[^7] Mukhtār's movement claimed that Prophetic knowledge was physical (transmitted in private documents to ʿAlī), private (passed only to ʿAlī and then the Imāms), and divinely delegated (*ʿahida ilaykum*, "entrusted specifically to you" — a formula that surfaces, tellingly, in the weakest sub-strand of this very cluster).[^8] Al-Shaʿbī's tradition answers all three claims at once. The only physical item ʿAlī possesses is a scroll of three bureaucratic rulings — not cosmology, not esoterica. What he has beyond the Qurʾān is *fahm*, an understanding God may grant any man, not a household monopoly. And if the household possesses nothing beyond ordinary jurisprudential insight, no theological basis for exclusive political authority survives. The three rulings are not a random legal sample. They answer the three zones of disorder Mukhtār's revolt actually produced: *al-ʿaql* converts the *thaʾr* (vengeance) ideology driving Mukhtār's movement into adjudicable, court-administered liability;[^9] *fakāk al-asīr* answers a live captive-execution controversy on both sides of the civil war, including one report of al-Ḥajjāj ordering a captive killed and Ibn ʿUmar refusing by citing the Qurʾān's own "favor or ransom" clause;[^10] and *lā yuqtalu muslimun bi-kāfir* answers a real Iraqi *qawād* dispute over executing a Muslim for killing a protected non-Muslim, amid al-Ḥajjāj's unstable dhimmī and mawālī fiscal policy.[^11] A single Umayyad-aligned scholar asserting outright that ʿAlī had no secret knowledge would have been dismissed as propaganda. Putting the denial in ʿAlī's own mouth, through a minor Kufan companion resident in exactly the milieu al-Shaʿbī administered, is what let it circulate. ## Cluster II — Qatāda: The Baṣran Constitutionalist Every isnād in this cluster converges on Qatāda ibn Diʿāma al-Sadūsī (d. 117/735), a blind Baṣran scholar of the generation after the Companions, independently documented as a *mudallis* and Qadarī in his theology.[^12] Below him the tradition splits into two structurally distinct pathways: one through al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī to Qays b. ʿUbād, carried almost entirely by Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba; the other bypassing al-Ḥasan entirely, reaching ʿAlī directly through Abū Ḥassān al-Aʿraj. The two pathways' cleanest forms — ʿUmar b. ʿĀmir's and Ḥajjāj b. Minhāl's versions of Ḥammām's own transmission — carry only the minimalist constitutional triad, with no Medina material at all.[^13] But a version of Ḥammām's own line, carried by Bahz b. Asad into Aḥmad's *Musnad* and by Hudba b. Khālid into al-Bayhaqī's *Maʿrifat al-Sunan*, adds a full Medinan sanctuary passage — the two lava-plain boundary markers, an Abrahamic invocation, a tree-cutting prohibition, and a "reluctance before disclosure" narrative motif.[^14] Rijāl assessment of Ḥammām ibn Yaḥyā (d. 164/780) explains why: Abū Ḥātim called him "trustworthy, truthful, but there is something in his memory," al-Dhahabī records his own admission "we used to err," and Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān specifically criticized disruptions in his transmissions from Qatāda.[^15] The most economical reading is that Ḥammām merged a separate, genuinely Medinan sanctuary tradition — one that reached Baṣra via al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's own transmission network, most plausibly formulated in the aftermath of the Battle of al-Ḥarra (63 AH) — into his recitation of Qatāda's scroll. A further sub-tradition, reaching al-Dāraquṭnī's *Sunan* through Ḥajjāj (identified by al-Dāraquṭnī himself as Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāt, d. 145/762), carries the same Medina-Haram material but suppresses Ḥammām's name entirely, restructures Abū Ḥassān into "Muslim al-Ajrad," and inserts Mālik al-Ashtar as questioner in his place.[^16] Ibn al-Mubārak independently accuses Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāt of exactly this kind of *tadlīs* elsewhere — falsely attributing a hadith directly to a transmitter's own teachers, skipping the actual intermediate source.[^17] Al-Dāraquṭnī's own verdict, weighing the evidence himself, prefers Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba's uncontaminated version.[^18] Qatāda's childhood and adolescence coincided with the most violent phase of the Azāriqa insurgency in Baṣra, 64–78 AH — a movement that, unlike Khārijism broadly, endorsed *istiʿrāḍ*: indiscriminate killing of anyone judged an unbeliever, including polytheist children, and the reclassification of ordinary Basran Muslims as legitimate targets.[^19] Abū Bilāl Mirdās, by contrast, explicitly rejected *istiʿrāḍ* and fought only those who fought him — Khalīfa ibn Khayyāṭ records that his own uprising "killed no one, and did not molest the road or property."[^20] Qatāda's own tribe, Sadūs, produced the poet ʿImrān b. Ḥiṭṭān, who elegized Abū Bilāl — placing Qatāda's constitutional cluster inside a documented intra-tribal argument over how far Khārijite sympathy should extend.[^21] Each clause of the scroll answers a specific Azraqī claim.[^22] "Believers are equal in blood" blocks the Azraqī move of reclassifying mainstream Basran Muslims as killable. "One hand against outsiders" inverts the Azraqī camp/*dār kufr* model that treated the Muslim community itself as split into believers and enemies. "The lowest of them may extend protection" — later applied by Abū Yūsuf even to a slave's grant of *amān* — directly answers *istiʿrāḍ*'s refusal to honor protection extended by anyone but its own leadership. And the treaty clause answers Najda ibn ʿĀmir's own accusation that Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq refused to honor trusts.[^23] ## Cluster III — al-Aʿmash: The Anti-Ḥajjājī Inversion This cluster's ur-text, recovered by comparing every substantive PCL, contains three elements found nowhere else in the corpus: camel-age and wound-compensation schedules, a Medina sanctuary declaration bounded "between ʿAyr and Thawr," and a prohibition on falsely claiming or reassigning *walāʾ* (clientage) ties.[^24] It conspicuously lacks the *fahm* exception, the blood-equality triad, and the killing-prohibition formula — this is not a variant of al-Shaʿbī's or Qatāda's material, but an independently constructed cluster sharing only the frame. Thawr is a mountain in Mecca. It has no place in Medina's own geography, whose conventional southern and eastern boundaries are marked by two lava plains (al-lābatān) and, separately, ʿAyr — never Thawr.[^25] Al-Aʿmash, a careful and well-connected Kufan scholar, is argued to have known the correct toponymy and substituted the Meccan landmark deliberately.[^26] The effect is to redirect a curse that genuinely belongs to the Umayyad sack of Medina during the Battle of al-Ḥarra (63/683) — three days of killing and plunder under Muslim b. ʿUqba, ordered by Yazīd I — toward al-Ḥajjāj's own siege and bombardment of Mecca in 692 CE, ensuring the Prophetic curse lands on al-Ḥajjāj by name rather than on the Umayyad house that actually sacked Medina. Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, al-Aʿmash's own named source, is independently reported to have been imprisoned by al-Ḥajjāj for refusing to betray Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, and to have died there.[^27] The dhimma and *walāʾ* clauses read as a direct broadside against al-Ḥajjāj's mawālī policy in the wake of the Ibn al-Ashʿath revolt (83/701): converts expelled from garrison cities back to their villages of origin, jizya collected from them despite their conversion, mawālī barred from leading prayer or serving as judges.[^28] The dhimma clause specifically protects a subordinate's grant of *amān* from being overridden — precisely what al-Ḥajjāj is recorded doing at al-Zāwiya, where men who surrendered under a guarantee of safety were killed once they laid down arms.[^29] The *walāʾ* prohibition is unique to this cluster and targets the administrative manipulation of clientage ties among Kufa's large mawālī population for fiscal purposes.[^30] ## Cluster IV — Abū al-Ṭufayl: The Alid Witness This is the one cluster in the entire corpus where two PCLs genuinely diverge in a way that looks like independent memory rather than shared fabrication: different question-wording (*khaṣṣakum*, open, versus *yusirru ilayka*, presupposing a confidence), a physical document in one strand and pure oral recitation in the other, and a consistent lexical split (*saraqa*, "stole," in al-Qāsim's line; *ghayyara*, "altered," in Manṣūr's).[^31] Both nonetheless converge on the same four cursed acts and the same fourfold frame — the divergence is at the PCL level, the frame itself is still shared with every other cluster. Abū al-Ṭufayl (b. 3/625, d. 100–110/718–728) fought at Ṣiffīn on ʿAlī's side and is described by al-Mizzī as "among ʿAlī's shīʿa."[^32] Al-Balādhurī records him confronting Muʿāwiya to his face over ʿUthmān's killing, retorting, "What prevented you from helping him, when you had the people of Syria with you?"[^33] Al-Ḥajjāj later imprisoned him; he was released only through the intercession of al-Ḥajjāj's own son-in-law, and his son Muṭarrif was killed fighting alongside Ibn al-Ashʿath in the anti-Ḥajjāj revolt of 83/701 — Abū al-Ṭufayl composed a lament for him and died not long after.[^34] Each curse targets something concrete in his lifetime. The sacrifice curse — rendered *ahalla* (the ritual utterance) rather than simply *dhabaḥa* (slaughtered) in one strand — targets the Zoroastrian *zamzama*, the mandatory priestly muttering before slaughter, preserved administratively because the Sawād's dīwān remained staffed by Persian-speaking dahāqīn until Arabicization around 80–83 AH.[^35] The parental-cursing clause activates against Muʿāwiya's institutionalized cursing of ʿAlī from the pulpit — a practice Abū al-Ṭufayl's own teacher, Zayd b. Arqam, is independently recorded publicly rebuking an Umayyad commander for continuing even after ʿAlī's death.[^36] The boundary-markers curse tracks al-Ḥajjāj's canal-building and land seizures in the Sawād, which al-Balādhurī records collapsing the province's kharāj revenue from 100 million dirhams under ʿUmar to 40 million under al-Ḥajjāj as land was alienated into Marwānid *iqṭāʿ*.[^37] And the *muḥdith*-shelter curse fits ʿUbaydallāh b. Ziyād's reception by the Marwānid court after fleeing Baṣra — al-Balādhurī records the Umayyads sheltering him and dispatching him safely to Syria, after which he commanded Marwānid forces against Mukhtār's own army at the Battle of Khāzir.[^38] ## Cluster V — Sharīk: The Kufan Tax Ledger Sharīk b. ʿAbdullāh al-Nakhaʿī (d. 177/793), al-Aʿmash's own student and his successor as Kufa's leading juristic authority, later served as Chief Judge of Kufa under the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdī.[^39] Every isnād in this cluster is Kufan end to end — no Medinan, Basran, or Syrian link appears anywhere in it. Below Sharīk, seven partial common links carry the report into Aḥmad's *Musnad*, Ibn Abī Shayba's *Muṣannaf*, and al-Jaṣṣāṣ's Ḥanafī legal literature.[^40] The content nests three descriptions of the same fiscal material — *farāʾiḍ al-ṣadaqa* ("the obligations of charity"), *farāʾiḍ al-ibil* ("the obligations of camels"), and *asnān al-ibil* ("camel age-brackets") — plausibly master code, chapter, and schedule of the same document.[^41] Two live Kufan-versus-Medinan legal disputes turn on exactly this schedule. For herds above 120 camels, Medina's rule alternates tax brackets by exact herd size; Kufa's simpler flat bracket can yield fewer animals owed depending on herd size, a real fiscal variable for Iraq's wealthy tribal herders.[^42] For the standard hundred-camel indemnity in accidental killing, Kufa's schedule of five equal age-groups (including male camels) is cheaper than Medina's schedule, which excludes males and demands proportionally older females.[^43] Al-Jaṣṣāṣ cites Sharīk's report explicitly as Ḥanafī evidence resolving both disputes in Kufa's favor.[^44] Notably, the same camel-tax mathematics recurs in early Kufan Imāmī Shīʿī sources transmitted via Imām al-Ṣādiq[^45] — Kufan Ḥanafīs and Kufan Shīʿīs, theologically opposed, sharing identical local tax arithmetic, which points to a regional administrative convention rather than a sectarian invention. Sharīk was not a passive link in a chain. He was the sitting judge whose own court needed exactly this ruling, constructing an isnād concentrated entirely on *farāʾiḍ al-ṣadaqa* in apparent response to earlier Medinan constructions (Nāfiʿ, Thumāma, and especially al-Zuhrī, whose version elevates the sword-scroll to the Prophet himself and routes it through Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, bypassing ʿAlī altogether) that had already put competing tax law into circulation under the same documentary form.[^46] ## What the Five Clusters Are, Together None of this requires believing that every transmitter below each cluster's originator was dishonest. Muṭarrif, Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba, and the many PCLs feeding the canonical collections were, in the ordinary case, faithfully passing on what they had received. The fabrication — where it occurred — sits at the cluster's point of origin, not throughout its downstream transmission. What the five clusters share is not a document. It is a documentary *form*: early Islamic legal culture repeatedly located public-law rulings inside physical objects — swords, scabbards, sheets, treaties — because a ruling housed inside an ancient, tangible, Prophetic artifact carries authority a bare legal opinion does not. Al-Shaʿbī needed that authority to answer Kaysānī theology. Qatāda needed it to answer Azraqī doctrine. Al-Aʿmash needed it to indict al-Ḥajjāj without naming him directly. Abū al-Ṭufayl needed it to curse the Umayyads by name across two generations of grievance. Sharīk needed it to settle a live tax dispute from the bench. Each reused a mold that was already available and already carried ʿAlī's name — not because a real scroll existed to remember, but because the mold itself had become a portable form of legal authority any community could fill with what it needed. The Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī tradition is not one Alid legal archive partially remembered by five witnesses. It is five separate common-link fabrications — al-Shaʿbī, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and Sharīk — each dateable to a specific city and a specific crisis between the 60s and 170s AH, each filling a shared rhetorical frame with the legal content its own community needed. The frame's invariance across clusters that share no transmitter, no companion, and no legal register is not evidence of one remembered document. It is evidence of one reusable polemical instrument, deployed competitively and repeatedly for a century, in ʿAlī's name but never, on the evidence recoverable here, in his hand. ## Source Notes Hadith and page references follow the print editions cited in each note below.
