On his reading, the five clusters are partial testimonies to a single document: different questioners heard different passages on different occasions, and their divergent contents are simply different fragments of one comprehensive original. This piece takes Kara seriously on his own methodological terms. It does not dispute that isnad-cum-matn analysis (ICMA) is the right tool. It disputes that thirty-five variants are enough material to sustain the conclusion. Applied to the wider surviving corpus, the same method does not refine Kara's picture — it overturns the premise it rests on. The Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī tradition is not one document remembered in five fragments. It is five independent fabrications, each built on a shared rhetorical mold — ʿAlī is asked if he has secret Prophetic knowledge, denies it, and then reveals a scabbard document with enumerable contents — and each filled with different legal content by a different transmitter answering a different, dateable communal crisis. Al-Shaʿbī originated the frame against Mukhtār's revolt; Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and Sharīk each independently reused it for their own city's needs. Why Kara's Method Doesn't Get There ICMA can date a tradition to its earliest common link (CL). What it cannot do on its own is verify the single strand running from that CL up to the named Companion above him — that strand has no fan-out to check it against. Kara identifies several independent CLs all reporting on ʿAlī's scroll and treats their multiplicity, plus their shared content, as corroboration that some such scroll existed. That inference only holds if the CL-strands are genuinely independent of each other. Narrator substitution — a transmitter reissuing material he received through one line under a different, more prestigious or strategically useful authority, while keeping the wording essentially stable — is a documented, classically-acknowledged practice, not a modern suspicion.[^1] If even one or two of Kara's supposedly independent CLs acquired their material from a shared, unacknowledged source and re-attributed the isnād above it, his method has no way to detect this. It would register multiple independent lines converging on ʿAlī where there is really only one — or none — laundered through invented authorities. Matn corroboration across chains cannot, by itself, rule this out, and Kara's own treatment of weaker links elsewhere shows the pattern: a transmitter graded "closer to weak" is nonetheless accepted because the content matches other clusters, which quietly makes the conclusion immune to the very possibility of a false attribution.[^2] The Shared Architecture Every variant in every cluster, regardless of transmission line, geography, or legal content, follows the same fourfold shape: ʿAlī is asked whether he possesses anything from the Prophet beyond the Qurʾān; he denies it; the questioner presses; ʿAlī reveals a document in his sword-scabbard and lists what is in it. Not one cluster departs from this. That invariance is the single most important fact about the corpus, and it is exactly what a single-document theory cannot explain on its own — because the five clusters diverge in every other respect that matters. Different companions are present (Abū Juḥayfa in one, Abū al-Ṭufayl in another). Different cities produce them (Kufa, Baṣra, Mecca). And the legal registers are not compatible fragments of one code — blood-money and captive-ransom law in one cluster, constitutional protection for combatants in another, anti-tax-farming fiscal law in a third. Read as one document, the Ṣaḥīfa would have to be a complete Prophetic legal corpus. Read as five independent productions, the divergence is exactly what the theory predicts. Cluster I — al-Shaʿbī: The Originator Eight partial common links carry Muṭarrif's redaction forward: Sufyān b. ʿUyayna (to al-Shāfiʿī, al-Ḥumaydī, Ibn Abī Shayba, Aḥmad, al-Bazzār, al-Nasāʾī), Sufyān al-Thawrī (to ʿAbd al-Razzāq), Zuhayr b. Muʿāwiya (to al-Bukhārī and al-Bayhaqī), Hushaym b. Bashīr (to al-Tirmidhī), Abū Bakr b. ʿAyyāsh (to Ibn Mājah), Yazīd b. ʿAṭāʾ (to al-Ṭayālisī), Jarīr b. ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd (to al-Dārimī), and Asbāṭ b. Muḥammad (to al-Ṭaḥāwī).[^3] Comparing what is invariant across all eight recovers a stable ur-text: the oath formula with its collective "we," the *fahm* exception, and a fixed three-item scroll — blood-money, captive-ransom, and the homicide ruling. Below that layer, the variation is diagnostic rather than random. The dominant wording bars killing a Muslim for a *kāfir* (unbeliever generally); a narrower sub-line — Yazīd b. ʿAṭāʾ, Jarīr, and one branch under Zuhayr — narrows this to *mushrik* (polytheist specifically).[^4] The same Zuhayr split is the clearest evidence for reading *kāfir* as original: his student Aḥmad b. Yūnus, who fed Bukhārī, kept *kāfir*; his student ʿAmr b. Marzūq, who fed al-Bayhaqī, has *mushrik* and also uniquely preserves Muṭarrif's own teaching glosses on the two technical terms — evidence that a single PCL sub-line juridically narrowed the rule while also carrying the most explicit record of Muṭarrif's classroom explanation of it.[^5] Muṭarrif is the checkable common link, but he is not the originator: nothing about his own biography explains why this exact material was needed. Al-Shaʿbī does. Born c. 17–19 AH into a Hamdānī family in Kufa, he fled the city for Medina out of fear of Mukhtār al-Thaqafī's movement, later served as judicial administrator under al-Ḥajjāj, was personally requisitioned by Caliph ʿAbd al-Malik as a court narrator, and died c. 103/721 as Kufa's most respected scholar.[^6] He is independently placed inside Mukhtār's own documentary world — present when Mukhtār produced a letter attributed to Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyya to win over Ibrāhīm b. al-Ashtar, and described as the one who physically handed the letter over.[^7] Mukhtār's movement claimed that Prophetic knowledge was physical (transmitted in private documents to ʿAlī), private (passed only to ʿAlī and then the Imāms), and divinely delegated (*ʿahida ilaykum*, "entrusted specifically to you" — a formula that surfaces, tellingly, in the weakest sub-strand of this very cluster).[^8] Al-Shaʿbī's tradition answers all three claims at once. The only physical item ʿAlī possesses is a scroll of three bureaucratic rulings — not cosmology, not esoterica. What he has beyond the Qurʾān is *fahm*, an understanding God may grant any man, not a household monopoly. And if the household possesses nothing beyond ordinary jurisprudential insight, no theological basis for exclusive political authority survives. The three rulings are not a random legal sample. They answer the three zones of disorder Mukhtār's revolt actually produced: *al-ʿaql* converts the *thaʾr* (vengeance) ideology driving Mukhtār's movement into adjudicable, court-administered liability;[^9] *fakāk al-asīr* answers a live captive-execution controversy on both sides of the civil war, including one report of al-Ḥajjāj ordering a captive killed and Ibn ʿUmar refusing by citing the Qurʾān's own "favor or ransom" clause;[^10] and *lā yuqtalu muslimun bi-kāfir* answers a real Iraqi *qawād* dispute over executing a Muslim for killing a protected non-Muslim, amid al-Ḥajjāj's unstable dhimmī and mawālī fiscal policy.[^11] A single Umayyad-aligned scholar asserting outright that ʿAlī had no secret knowledge would have been dismissed as propaganda. Putting the denial in ʿAlī's own mouth, through a minor Kufan companion resident in exactly the milieu al-Shaʿbī administered, is what let it circulate. Cluster II — Qatāda: The Baṣran Constitutionalist Every isnād in this cluster converges on Qatāda ibn Diʿāma al-Sadūsī (d. 117/735), a blind Baṣran scholar of the generation after the Companions, independently documented as a *mudallis* and Qadarī in his theology.[^12] Below him the tradition splits into two structurally distinct pathways: one through al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī to Qays b. ʿUbād, carried almost entirely by Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba; the other bypassing al-Ḥasan entirely, reaching ʿAlī directly through Abū Ḥassān al-Aʿraj. The two pathways' cleanest forms — ʿUmar b. ʿĀmir's and Ḥajjāj b. Minhāl's versions of Ḥammām's own transmission — carry only the minimalist constitutional triad, with no Medina material at all.[^13] But a version of Ḥammām's own line, carried by Bahz b. Asad into Aḥmad's *Musnad* and by Hudba b. Khālid into al-Bayhaqī's *Maʿrifat al-Sunan*, adds a full Medinan sanctuary passage — the two lava-plain boundary markers, an Abrahamic invocation, a tree-cutting prohibition, and a "reluctance before disclosure" narrative motif.[^14] Rijāl assessment of Ḥammām ibn Yaḥyā (d. 164/780) explains why: Abū Ḥātim called him "trustworthy, truthful, but there is something in his memory," al-Dhahabī records his own admission "we used to err," and Yaḥyā b. Saʿīd al-Qaṭṭān specifically criticized disruptions in his transmissions from Qatāda.[^15] The most economical reading is that Ḥammām merged a separate, genuinely Medinan sanctuary tradition — one that reached Baṣra via al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī's own transmission network, most plausibly formulated in the aftermath of the Battle of al-Ḥarra (63 AH) — into his recitation of Qatāda's scroll. A further sub-tradition, reaching al-Dāraquṭnī's *Sunan* through Ḥajjāj (identified by al-Dāraquṭnī himself as Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāt, d. 145/762), carries the same Medina-Haram material but suppresses Ḥammām's name entirely, restructures Abū Ḥassān into "Muslim al-Ajrad," and inserts Mālik al-Ashtar as questioner in his place.[^16] Ibn al-Mubārak independently accuses Ḥajjāj b. Arṭāt of exactly this kind of *tadlīs* elsewhere — falsely attributing a hadith directly to a transmitter's own teachers, skipping the actual intermediate source.[^17] Al-Dāraquṭnī's own verdict, weighing the evidence himself, prefers Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba's uncontaminated version.[^18] Qatāda's childhood and adolescence coincided with the most violent phase of the Azāriqa insurgency in Baṣra, 64–78 AH — a movement that, unlike Khārijism broadly, endorsed *istiʿrāḍ*: indiscriminate killing of anyone judged an unbeliever, including polytheist children, and the reclassification of ordinary Basran Muslims as legitimate targets.[^19] Abū Bilāl Mirdās, by contrast, explicitly rejected *istiʿrāḍ* and fought only those who fought him — Khalīfa ibn Khayyāṭ records that his own uprising "killed no one, and did not molest the road or property."[^20] Qatāda's own tribe, Sadūs, produced the poet ʿImrān b. Ḥiṭṭān, who elegized Abū Bilāl — placing Qatāda's constitutional cluster inside a documented intra-tribal argument over how far Khārijite sympathy should extend.[^21] Each clause of the scroll answers a specific Azraqī claim.[^22] "Believers are equal in blood" blocks the Azraqī move of reclassifying mainstream Basran Muslims as killable. "One hand against outsiders" inverts the Azraqī camp/*dār kufr* model that treated the Muslim community itself as split into believers and enemies. "The lowest of them may extend protection" — later applied by Abū Yūsuf even to a slave's grant of *amān* — directly answers *istiʿrāḍ*'s refusal to honor protection extended by anyone but its own leadership. And the treaty clause answers Najda ibn ʿĀmir's own accusation that Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq refused to honor trusts.[^23] Cluster III — al-Aʿmash: The Anti-Ḥajjājī Inversion This cluster's ur-text, recovered by comparing every substantive PCL, contains three elements found nowhere else in the corpus: camel-age and wound-compensation schedules, a Medina sanctuary declaration bounded "between ʿAyr and Thawr," and a prohibition on falsely claiming or reassigning *walāʾ* (clientage) ties.[^24] It conspicuously lacks the *fahm* exception, the blood-equality triad, and the killing-prohibition formula — this is not a variant of al-Shaʿbī's or Qatāda's material, but an independently constructed cluster sharing only the frame. Thawr is a mountain in Mecca. It has no place in Medina's own geography, whose conventional southern and eastern boundaries are marked by two lava plains (al-lābatān) and, separately, ʿAyr — never Thawr.[^25] Al-Aʿmash, a careful and well-connected Kufan scholar, is argued to have known the correct toponymy and substituted the Meccan landmark deliberately.[^26] The effect is to redirect a curse that genuinely belongs to the Umayyad sack of Medina during the Battle of al-Ḥarra (63/683) — three days of killing and plunder under Muslim b. ʿUqba, ordered by Yazīd I — toward al-Ḥajjāj's own siege and bombardment of Mecca in 692 CE, ensuring the Prophetic curse lands on al-Ḥajjāj by name rather than on the Umayyad house that actually sacked Medina. Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, al-Aʿmash's own named source, is independently reported to have been imprisoned by al-Ḥajjāj for refusing to betray Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, and to have died there.[^27] The dhimma and *walāʾ* clauses read as a direct broadside against al-Ḥajjāj's mawālī policy in the wake of the Ibn al-Ashʿath revolt (83/701): converts expelled from garrison cities back to their villages of origin, jizya collected from them despite their conversion, mawālī barred from leading prayer or serving as judges.[^28] The dhimma clause specifically protects a subordinate's grant of *amān* from being overridden — precisely what al-Ḥajjāj is recorded doing at al-Zāwiya, where men who surrendered under a guarantee of safety were killed once they laid down arms.[^29] The *walāʾ* prohibition is unique to this cluster and targets the administrative manipulation of clientage ties among Kufa's large mawālī population for fiscal purposes.[^30] Cluster IV — Abū al-Ṭufayl: The Alid Witness This is the one cluster in the entire corpus where two PCLs genuinely diverge in a way that looks like independent memory rather than shared fabrication: different question-wording (*khaṣṣakum*, open, versus *yusirru ilayka*, presupposing a confidence), a physical document in one strand and pure oral recitation in the other, and a consistent lexical split (*saraqa*, "stole," in al-Qāsim's line; *ghayyara*, "altered," in Manṣūr's).[^31] Both nonetheless converge on the same four cursed acts and the same fourfold frame — the divergence is at the PCL level, the frame itself is still shared with every other cluster. Abū al-Ṭufayl (b. 3/625, d. 100–110/718–728) fought at Ṣiffīn on ʿAlī's side and is described by al-Mizzī as "among ʿAlī's shīʿa."[^32] Al-Balādhurī records him confronting Muʿāwiya to his face over ʿUthmān's killing, retorting, "What prevented you from helping him, when you had the people of Syria with you?"[^33] Al-Ḥajjāj later imprisoned him; he was released only through the intercession of al-Ḥajjāj's own son-in-law, and his son Muṭarrif was killed fighting alongside Ibn al-Ashʿath in the anti-Ḥajjāj revolt of 83/701 — Abū al-Ṭufayl composed a lament for him and died not long after.[^34] Each curse targets something concrete in his lifetime. The sacrifice curse — rendered *ahalla* (the ritual utterance) rather than simply *dhabaḥa* (slaughtered) in one strand — targets the Zoroastrian *zamzama*, the mandatory priestly muttering before slaughter, preserved administratively because the Sawād's dīwān remained staffed by Persian-speaking dahāqīn until Arabicization around 80–83 AH.[^35] The parental-cursing clause activates against Muʿāwiya's institutionalized cursing of ʿAlī from the pulpit — a practice Abū al-Ṭufayl's own teacher, Zayd b. Arqam, is independently recorded publicly rebuking an Umayyad commander for continuing even after ʿAlī's death.[^36] The boundary-markers curse tracks al-Ḥajjāj's canal-building and land seizures in the Sawād, which al-Balādhurī records collapsing the province's kharāj revenue from 100 million dirhams under ʿUmar to 40 million under al-Ḥajjāj as land was alienated into Marwānid *iqṭāʿ*.[^37] And the *muḥdith*-shelter curse fits ʿUbaydallāh b. Ziyād's reception by the Marwānid court after fleeing Baṣra — al-Balādhurī records the Umayyads sheltering him and dispatching him safely to Syria, after which he commanded Marwānid forces against Mukhtār's own army at the Battle of Khāzir.[^38] Cluster V — Sharīk: The Kufan Tax Ledger Sharīk b. ʿAbdullāh al-Nakhaʿī (d. 177/793), al-Aʿmash's own student and his successor as Kufa's leading juristic authority, later served as Chief Judge of Kufa under the Abbasid caliph al-Mahdī.[^39] Every isnād in this cluster is Kufan end to end — no Medinan, Basran, or Syrian link appears anywhere in it. Below Sharīk, seven partial common links carry the report into Aḥmad's *Musnad*, Ibn Abī Shayba's *Muṣannaf*, and al-Jaṣṣāṣ's Ḥanafī legal literature.[^40] The content nests three descriptions of the same fiscal material — *farāʾiḍ al-ṣadaqa* ("the obligations of charity"), *farāʾiḍ al-ibil* ("the obligations of camels"), and *asnān al-ibil* ("camel age-brackets") — plausibly master code, chapter, and schedule of the same document.[^41] Two live Kufan-versus-Medinan legal disputes turn on exactly this schedule. For herds above 120 camels, Medina's rule alternates tax brackets by exact herd size; Kufa's simpler flat bracket can yield fewer animals owed depending on herd size, a real fiscal variable for Iraq's wealthy tribal herders.[^42] For the standard hundred-camel indemnity in accidental killing, Kufa's schedule of five equal age-groups (including male camels) is cheaper than Medina's schedule, which excludes males and demands proportionally older females.[^43] Al-Jaṣṣāṣ cites Sharīk's report explicitly as Ḥanafī evidence resolving both disputes in Kufa's favor.[^44] Notably, the same camel-tax mathematics recurs in early Kufan Imāmī Shīʿī sources transmitted via Imām al-Ṣādiq[^45] — Kufan Ḥanafīs and Kufan Shīʿīs, theologically opposed, sharing identical local tax arithmetic, which points to a regional administrative convention rather than a sectarian invention. Sharīk was not a passive link in a chain. He was the sitting judge whose own court needed exactly this ruling, constructing an isnād concentrated entirely on *farāʾiḍ al-ṣadaqa* in apparent response to earlier Medinan constructions (Nāfiʿ, Thumāma, and especially al-Zuhrī, whose version elevates the sword-scroll to the Prophet himself and routes it through Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, bypassing ʿAlī altogether) that had already put competing tax law into circulation under the same documentary form.[^46] What the Five Clusters Are, Together None of this requires believing that every transmitter below each cluster's originator was dishonest. Muṭarrif, Saʿīd b. Abī ʿArūba, and the many PCLs feeding the canonical collections were, in the ordinary case, faithfully passing on what they had received. The fabrication — where it occurred — sits at the cluster's point of origin, not throughout its downstream transmission. What the five clusters share is not a document. It is a documentary *form*: early Islamic legal culture repeatedly located public-law rulings inside physical objects — swords, scabbards, sheets, treaties — because a ruling housed inside an ancient, tangible, Prophetic artifact carries authority a bare legal opinion does not. Al-Shaʿbī needed that authority to answer Kaysānī theology. Qatāda needed it to answer Azraqī doctrine. Al-Aʿmash needed it to indict al-Ḥajjāj without naming him directly. Abū al-Ṭufayl needed it to curse the Umayyads by name across two generations of grievance. Sharīk needed it to settle a live tax dispute from the bench. Each reused a mold that was already available and already carried ʿAlī's name — not because a real scroll existed to remember, but because the mold itself had become a portable form of legal authority any community could fill with what it needed. The Ṣaḥīfat ʿAlī tradition is not one Alid legal archive partially remembered by five witnesses. It is five separate common-link fabrications — al-Shaʿbī, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, Abū al-Ṭufayl, and Sharīk — each dateable to a specific city and a specific crisis between the 60s and 170s AH, each filling a shared rhetorical frame with the legal content its own community needed. The frame's invariance across clusters that share no transmitter, no companion, and no legal register is not evidence of one remembered document. It is evidence of one reusable polemical instrument, deployed competitively and repeatedly for a century, in ʿAlī's name but never, on the evidence recoverable here, in his hand. title: The Kharijite and the Beast: Tracing a Severe Ruling Back to Ikrima
description: An isnad-cum-matn analysis of the Ibn Abbas beast tradition. Three transmitters below Ikrima each preserve a different version of the ruling, and two of them are independently flagged by classical critics as reliable except when they quote Ikrima.

It says the opposite thing', kind: 'note', anchor: 'end' } ]; There is an old hadith that says a man who has sex with an animal should be killed, and the animal should be killed with him. It sounds like a single simple ruling. It is not. Once you pull together every place this saying shows up, it turns into three different versions that do not agree with each other, plus a fourth report where Ibn Abbas himself says there is no fixed punishment for this at all. This piece walks through where each version came from, who is responsible for the differences, and why the harsh version most likely was not around before three specific men started passing it on. Every raised version of this hadith passes through one man, Ikrima, the freed slave of Ibn Abbas. Below Ikrima the story splits into three branches that each look different, and two of those three branches are separately said by classical critics to be reliable everywhere except when they are quoting Ikrima. A fourth, completely separate report has Ibn Abbas himself denying any fixed punishment exists. The most likely explanation is that a severe ruling started circulating through Ikrima and his students, in a legal argument that was still very much open, rather than the ruling going back cleanly to the Prophet.

sections.heading: Four different things people call the same hadith
sections.text: People often talk about "the beast hadith" as if it is one saying. It is really four separate things that got grouped together because they touch the same topic. Form What it says Where it comes from The plain killing rule Kill the man and kill the animal Amr son of Abi Amr, from Ikrima The combined rule The beast case is grouped with two other serious sex offenses and given the same punishment Dawud son of al-Husayn, from Ikrima The borrowed wording The beast case is described using language that really belongs to a different offense Abbad son of Mansur, from Ikrima The denial There is no fixed punishment for this at all Asim, from Abu Razin, a completely different line back to Ibn Abbas Only the first three come from Ikrima. The fourth is a rival claim about what Ibn Abbas actually believed, and it does not share a single transmitter with the other three. That last point matters a lot, because it means two different people, at two different points, both said "this is what Ibn Abbas told me," and they said the opposite thing.

sections.heading: The plain version, from Amr son of Abi Amr
sections.text: This is the version everyone reaches for when they want a short, clean proof text for the death penalty. Notice the second half of the report though. Someone is already uncomfortable with the idea of killing an animal that did not choose anything, so an explanation gets tacked on. That explanation changes from version to version. In one place it is about the meat not being eaten. In another place, preserved by al-Bayhaqi, the reasoning is different again, that the animal is killed so people stop pointing at it and saying this is the one it happened to. Two different reasons for the same rule is a sign that the rule came first and the justification was added afterward by different people trying to make sense of it. Amr son of Abi Amr was a Medinan, and he was generally seen as a decent transmitter. Malik used him. Bukhari and Muslim both relied on him elsewhere. But when it comes to this specific material, the material he says he got from Ikrima, the judgment is much narrower. Al-Bukhari's own verdict on him was that he was honest, but that what he passed on from Ikrima specifically contained anomalies.[^1] Abu Dawud said the same report was simply not strong.[^2] So the criticism is not aimed at Amr as a person. It is aimed at exactly the one thing this whole piece is about, his material from Ikrima.

sections.heading: The combined version, from Dawud son of al-Husayn
sections.text: Here the beast case is no longer standing alone. It gets folded together with a completely different offense, sex with a close relative, and in some versions a third offense as well, the act of the people of Lot. One expanded form of this same branch even adds two unrelated insults as separate crimes, calling a man effeminate or calling him a Jew, each earning forty lashes.[^3] That is not one ruling growing naturally. That looks like a small legal code being built up over time out of separate pieces, all riding on Ikrima's name. Dawud son of al-Husayn also gives us the clearest single piece of evidence in this entire investigation. Classical sources describe him this way. Dawud son of al-Husayn is described in the biographical literature as trustworthy, except regarding Ikrima, and he is also said to have held Kharijite views.[^4] Separately, Abu Dawud said his hadiths from his other teachers were sound, but his hadiths from Ikrima specifically were anomalies.[^5] A third source records a critic being challenged over why he transmitted from Dawud son of al-Husayn at all, given that Dawud was accused of Qadari views.[^6] Put plainly, this is the exact same shape of criticism found on Amr son of Abi Amr, and it comes from a completely separate source. Two different men, both otherwise treated as reliable, both get the identical warning label attached to them, and the warning label always points at the same name, Ikrima. When a pattern like that shows up twice independently, it stops looking like two unrelated coincidences.

sections.heading: The borrowed version, from Abbad son of Mansur
sections.text: This phrase, active and passive participant, belongs to a different crime altogether, the act of the people of Lot, where two people are involved. Applied to an animal it barely makes sense, since an animal cannot be a legal participant in anything. The most natural explanation is that this wording was borrowed from the Lot tradition and pasted onto the beast case by mistake or by habit, since the two topics already traveled together in Dawud's branch. Abbad son of Mansur was Basran, and he was a weaker transmitter than the other two. He is separately accused of holding Qadari views.[^7] His own material even disagrees with itself about whether this is something the Prophet said or just something Ibn Abbas said on his own authority, with one collection recording it one way and another collection recording it the other way. That kind of instability is exactly what you would expect from the weakest of the three branches.

sections.heading: The denial, a completely different Ibn Abbas
sections.text: This line goes back to Ibn Abbas a completely different way, through two Kufans, Asim and Abu Razin, and it shares no transmitter at all with Ikrima's branch. Abu Dawud says plainly that this report weakens the earlier report from Amr son of Abi Amr.[^8] Al-Tirmidhi goes further and says this report is more reliable than the first one.[^9] This was not some fringe opinion either. It matched what most of the early jurists actually held. Jurist Position Ata No fixed punishment, left to the judge's discretion al-Hakam Flogging, but less than the full punishment al-Hasan Treated the same as regular sex outside marriage al-Zuhri Said he had never heard a specific ruling, but guessed it should match regular sex outside marriage al-Shabi No fixed punishment Ibrahim al-Nakhai No fixed punishment, and reported that Umar held the same view Every major early school eventually landed on discretionary punishment, not execution. That is not what you would expect if a clear command from the Prophet to kill the man and the animal had really been circulating from the very beginning.

sections.heading: Why the harsh version does not look early
sections.text: Two things point the same direction. First, the harsh Ikrima version never shows up in the earliest Medinan legal writing. Malik's Muwatta is the obvious place to look, since two of the three men who carried this tradition, Amr and Dawud, were both Medinan themselves. It is not there. Every mention of the word for animal in the Muwatta is about something else entirely, an unrelated hadith about newborn babies and a Quran verse about livestock. If a Prophetic order to execute someone for this crime had genuinely been circulating among Medinan scholars in that generation, this is exactly the kind of ruling Malik's book was built to collect, and it collected nothing. Second, the harsh version is missing from the oldest Kufan legal material too, the material that later became the base of the Hanafi school. What that material does contain is the opposite ruling, the no punishment position, traced back to Umar through Ibrahim al-Nakhai himself, preserved even inside Abu Hanifa's own collection of reports. So the city that had every reason to use a severe execution ruling if it existed simply used the mild one instead. A saying missing from the exact books that should have recorded it, if it had really been in circulation, is not proof by itself that the saying is false. But when that silence shows up in two separate cities, and lines up with independent criticism of the very transmitters who supposedly carried the saying between those cities, the silence stops being a small detail and starts being real evidence.

sections.heading: Who was probably responsible
sections.text: Nobody needs to accuse Ikrima's students of lying. The far simpler explanation is that a severe ruling was already circulating under Ikrima's name by the time these three men were teaching, and each of them handled that inherited material differently. Amr kept it short and added an explanation for the part that troubled him. Dawud folded it into a bigger legal package alongside other serious sex crimes. Abbad reused language from a nearby offense because the two topics were already sitting next to each other in circulation. What makes Ikrima himself the most likely point of origin, rather than any one of his three students, is the pattern repeating across all of them. Ikrima's own reputation already carried an association with Kharijite sympathies. Now we can add that Dawud son of al-Husayn independently carries both a Kharijite accusation and a Qadari accusation, and that Abbad son of Mansur independently carries a Qadari accusation, and that two of the three students are separately described in the exact same words, reliable in general but specifically unreliable from Ikrima. Three different names, three different cities, and the same warning sign keeps appearing in the same place. That is not the kind of coincidence that happens by accident.

sections.heading: Putting it together
sections.text: The severe version of this ruling cannot be traced further back than Ikrima with any confidence. Below him it splits into three inconsistent forms, two of which are separately flagged by name as reliable everywhere except from Ikrima. A rival, unconnected report has Ibn Abbas denying any fixed punishment exists, and this denial matches what most early jurists actually taught. The harsh version is missing from the earliest legal writing in both Medina and Kufa, exactly the two cities where it should have shown up if it were genuinely old. The most reasonable conclusion is that a severe capital ruling entered circulation through Ikrima and his circle during a period when the actual legal question was still open, and that it competed with, but never replaced, an earlier and milder position.

fullText: There is an old hadith that says a man who has sex with an animal should be killed, and the animal should be killed with him. It sounds like a single simple ruling. It is not. Once you pull together every place this saying shows up, it turns into three different versions that do not agree with each other, plus a fourth report where Ibn Abbas himself says there is no fixed punishment for this at all. This piece walks through where each version came from, who is responsible for the differences, and why the harsh version most likely was not around before three specific men started passing it on. Every raised version of this hadith passes through one man, Ikrima, the freed slave of Ibn Abbas. Below Ikrima the story splits into three branches that each look different, and two of those three branches are separately said by classical critics to be reliable everywhere except when they are quoting Ikrima. A fourth, completely separate report has Ibn Abbas himself denying any fixed punishment exists. The most likely explanation is that a severe ruling started circulating through Ikrima and his students, in a legal argument that was still very much open, rather than the ruling going back cleanly to the Prophet. Four different things people call the same hadith People often talk about "the beast hadith" as if it is one saying. It is really four separate things that got grouped together because they touch the same topic. Form What it says Where it comes from The plain killing rule Kill the man and kill the animal Amr son of Abi Amr, from Ikrima The combined rule The beast case is grouped with two other serious sex offenses and given the same punishment Dawud son of al-Husayn, from Ikrima The borrowed wording The beast case is described using language that really belongs to a different offense Abbad son of Mansur, from Ikrima The denial There is no fixed punishment for this at all Asim, from Abu Razin, a completely different line back to Ibn Abbas Only the first three come from Ikrima. The fourth is a rival claim about what Ibn Abbas actually believed, and it does not share a single transmitter with the other three. That last point matters a lot, because it means two different people, at two different points, both said "this is what Ibn Abbas told me," and they said the opposite thing. The plain version, from Amr son of Abi Amr This is the version everyone reaches for when they want a short, clean proof text for the death penalty. Notice the second half of the report though. Someone is already uncomfortable with the idea of killing an animal that did not choose anything, so an explanation gets tacked on. That explanation changes from version to version. In one place it is about the meat not being eaten. In another place, preserved by al-Bayhaqi, the reasoning is different again, that the animal is killed so people stop pointing at it and saying this is the one it happened to. Two different reasons for the same rule is a sign that the rule came first and the justification was added afterward by different people trying to make sense of it. Amr son of Abi Amr was a Medinan, and he was generally seen as a decent transmitter. Malik used him. Bukhari and Muslim both relied on him elsewhere. But when it comes to this specific material, the material he says he got from Ikrima, the judgment is much narrower. Al-Bukhari's own verdict on him was that he was honest, but that what he passed on from Ikrima specifically contained anomalies.[^1] Abu Dawud said the same report was simply not strong.[^2] So the criticism is not aimed at Amr as a person. It is aimed at exactly the one thing this whole piece is about, his material from Ikrima. The combined version, from Dawud son of al-Husayn Here the beast case is no longer standing alone. It gets folded together with a completely different offense, sex with a close relative, and in some versions a third offense as well, the act of the people of Lot. One expanded form of this same branch even adds two unrelated insults as separate crimes, calling a man effeminate or calling him a Jew, each earning forty lashes.[^3] That is not one ruling growing naturally. That looks like a small legal code being built up over time out of separate pieces, all riding on Ikrima's name. Dawud son of al-Husayn also gives us the clearest single piece of evidence in this entire investigation. Classical sources describe him this way. Dawud son of al-Husayn is described in the biographical literature as trustworthy, except regarding Ikrima, and he is also said to have held Kharijite views.[^4] Separately, Abu Dawud said his hadiths from his other teachers were sound, but his hadiths from Ikrima specifically were anomalies.[^5] A third source records a critic being challenged over why he transmitted from Dawud son of al-Husayn at all, given that Dawud was accused of Qadari views.[^6] Put plainly, this is the exact same shape of criticism found on Amr son of Abi Amr, and it comes from a completely separate source. Two different men, both otherwise treated as reliable, both get the identical warning label attached to them, and the warning label always points at the same name, Ikrima. When a pattern like that shows up twice independently, it stops looking like two unrelated coincidences. The borrowed version, from Abbad son of Mansur This phrase, active and passive participant, belongs to a different crime altogether, the act of the people of Lot, where two people are involved. Applied to an animal it barely makes sense, since an animal cannot be a legal participant in anything. The most natural explanation is that this wording was borrowed from the Lot tradition and pasted onto the beast case by mistake or by habit, since the two topics already traveled together in Dawud's branch. Abbad son of Mansur was Basran, and he was a weaker transmitter than the other two. He is separately accused of holding Qadari views.[^7] His own material even disagrees with itself about whether this is something the Prophet said or just something Ibn Abbas said on his own authority, with one collection recording it one way and another collection recording it the other way. That kind of instability is exactly what you would expect from the weakest of the three branches. The denial, a completely different Ibn Abbas This line goes back to Ibn Abbas a completely different way, through two Kufans, Asim and Abu Razin, and it shares no transmitter at all with Ikrima's branch. Abu Dawud says plainly that this report weakens the earlier report from Amr son of Abi Amr.[^8] Al-Tirmidhi goes further and says this report is more reliable than the first one.[^9] This was not some fringe opinion either. It matched what most of the early jurists actually held. Jurist Position Ata No fixed punishment, left to the judge's discretion al-Hakam Flogging, but less than the full punishment al-Hasan Treated the same as regular sex outside marriage al-Zuhri Said he had never heard a specific ruling, but guessed it should match regular sex outside marriage al-Shabi No fixed punishment Ibrahim al-Nakhai No fixed punishment, and reported that Umar held the same view Every major early school eventually landed on discretionary punishment, not execution. That is not what you would expect if a clear command from the Prophet to kill the man and the animal had really been circulating from the very beginning. Why the harsh version does not look early Two things point the same direction. First, the harsh Ikrima version never shows up in the earliest Medinan legal writing. Malik's Muwatta is the obvious place to look, since two of the three men who carried this tradition, Amr and Dawud, were both Medinan themselves. It is not there. Every mention of the word for animal in the Muwatta is about something else entirely, an unrelated hadith about newborn babies and a Quran verse about livestock. If a Prophetic order to execute someone for this crime had genuinely been circulating among Medinan scholars in that generation, this is exactly the kind of ruling Malik's book was built to collect, and it collected nothing. Second, the harsh version is missing from the oldest Kufan legal material too, the material that later became the base of the Hanafi school. What that material does contain is the opposite ruling, the no punishment position, traced back to Umar through Ibrahim al-Nakhai himself, preserved even inside Abu Hanifa's own collection of reports. So the city that had every reason to use a severe execution ruling if it existed simply used the mild one instead. A saying missing from the exact books that should have recorded it, if it had really been in circulation, is not proof by itself that the saying is false. But when that silence shows up in two separate cities, and lines up with independent criticism of the very transmitters who supposedly carried the saying between those cities, the silence stops being a small detail and starts being real evidence. Who was probably responsible Nobody needs to accuse Ikrima's students of lying. The far simpler explanation is that a severe ruling was already circulating under Ikrima's name by the time these three men were teaching, and each of them handled that inherited material differently. Amr kept it short and added an explanation for the part that troubled him. Dawud folded it into a bigger legal package alongside other serious sex crimes. Abbad reused language from a nearby offense because the two topics were already sitting next to each other in circulation. What makes Ikrima himself the most likely point of origin, rather than any one of his three students, is the pattern repeating across all of them. Ikrima's own reputation already carried an association with Kharijite sympathies. Now we can add that Dawud son of al-Husayn independently carries both a Kharijite accusation and a Qadari accusation, and that Abbad son of Mansur independently carries a Qadari accusation, and that two of the three students are separately described in the exact same words, reliable in general but specifically unreliable from Ikrima. Three different names, three different cities, and the same warning sign keeps appearing in the same place. That is not the kind of coincidence that happens by accident. Putting it together The severe version of this ruling cannot be traced further back than Ikrima with any confidence. Below him it splits into three inconsistent forms, two of which are separately flagged by name as reliable everywhere except from Ikrima. A rival, unconnected report has Ibn Abbas denying any fixed punishment exists, and this denial matches what most early jurists actually taught. The harsh version is missing from the earliest legal writing in both Medina and Kufa, exactly the two cities where it should have shown up if it were genuinely old. The most reasonable conclusion is that a severe capital ruling entered circulation through Ikrima and his circle during a period when the actual legal question was still open, and that it competed with, but never replaced, an earlier and milder position.
